🏠 Master Summary & Implementation RoadmapSTART HERE

🎯 What This Document Is — And How To Use It

This is your complete CKA exam preparation system. It's not just a study guide — it's a training simulator built around a real Django application (easypj/jobpost) running on your 6-cluster lab. Every section is designed to build muscle memory through progressive difficulty: theory → troubleshooting → hands-on practice.

📝 Part 1: 200 Multiple Choice Questions

Purpose: Build foundational knowledge across all 5 CKA domains. Every question has a detailed explanation with real-world context from easypj/jobpost.

Domains covered: Storage (Q1-Q20), Troubleshooting (Q21-Q80), Workloads (Q81-Q110), Cluster Architecture (Q111-Q160), Networking (Q161-Q200).

How to use: Answer 20-30 questions per study session. Read the explanation even for correct answers — they contain deeper insights. Target: 85%+ correct before moving to Part 2.

🔧 Part 2: 100 Troubleshooting Issues

Purpose: Learn systematic diagnostic reasoning. Each issue follows the same pattern: Symptom → Terminal Output → 15 Causes (Most Likely / Less Likely / New Cluster) → Diagnostic Commands → Solution → Personal Advice.

Categories: ST1-ST10 (Storage), TR1-TR30 (Troubleshooting), WS1-WS15 (Workloads), CA1-CA25 (Cluster Architecture), SN1-SN20 (Networking).

How to use: Read the symptom first — try to diagnose BEFORE reading the causes. This builds the diagnostic muscle memory critical for 30% of your CKA score.

🧪 Part 3: 100 Hands-On Lab Scenarios

Purpose: Practice real CKA exam tasks on your 6-cluster lab. Each scenario deploys easypj/jobpost with an intentional bug — you find and fix it.

Structure per scenario: APP STORY → FILE STRUCTURE → Deploy YAML (with bug) → Observe symptoms → Debug commands → Full answer with before/after outputs → Fix commands → Cleanup.

How to use: Run each scenario on the specified cluster (ksw → 1-6). Time yourself — aim for 5-7 minutes per scenario. Target: Complete all 100 scenarios before exam day.

🌳 Decision Trees + Appendices

Decision Trees (DT1-DT15): Quick diagnostic flowcharts for the 15 most common CKA issues. Start at the symptom, answer yes/no questions, arrive at the fix.

Appendices (A-L): Top 50 commands, YAML templates, exam-day survival guide, cheat sheets, architecture diagrams, difficulty index, and the ⚡ Appendix L: 20 Exam Day Command Patterns — your last-30-minutes cram sheet.

How to use: Decision trees for quick reference during practice. Appendix L in the 30 minutes before exam. Cheat sheet (Appendix H) for last-minute review.

✅ Daily Implementation Checklist
  • Morning (30 min): Read 5-10 MCQs from Part 1 + review explanations. Focus on one domain per day.
  • Afternoon (45 min): Study 3-5 Part 2 issues. Read the symptom, try to diagnose, then read the solution. Note patterns you missed.
  • Evening (60 min): Run 3-5 Part 3 lab scenarios on your cluster. Type every command — don't copy-paste. Time each scenario.
  • Weekend (2-3 hours): Full review of the week's topics. Run 10 scenarios back-to-back. Review decision trees for any weak areas.

🏆 Skills You'll Master — Before vs After This Guide

❌ BEFORE — Common Beginner Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Why is my pod stuck in Pending?" — No idea where to look
  • ❌ "The Service works but returns 503" — Don't know about selectors
  • ❌ "I updated the ConfigMap but nothing changed" — Didn't know pods need restart
  • ❌ "kubectl commands take forever" — Never checked etcd or API server health
  • ❌ "The node is down but I can't drain it" — PDB concept unknown
  • ❌ "I ran commands on the wrong cluster" — No context discipline
  • ❌ "etcd backup? What's etcd?" — No disaster recovery plan

✅ AFTER — Skills This Guide Builds

  • ✅ Diagnose any pod failure in <2 min using systematic Tenet Flow
  • ✅ Fix Service/NetworkPolicy/DNS issues using endpoint & selector checks
  • ✅ Trigger rolling restarts, rollbacks, and canary deployments confidently
  • ✅ Monitor etcd health, compact & defrag, restore from snapshots
  • ✅ Cordon → Drain → Work → Uncordon with PDB awareness
  • ✅ Switch contexts safely and verify before every destructive command
  • ✅ Backup/restore etcd, renew TLS certs, upgrade clusters without downtime

🚨 Critical Do's & Don'ts During The Exam
  • ✅ DO: Use kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate YAML in seconds — never type manifests from scratch.
  • ✅ DO: Run kubectl config use-context <given-context> as the FIRST command for every task. Wrong context = 0 points.
  • ✅ DO: Use kubectl explain <resource> --recursive when you forget a field name. It's faster than searching docs.
  • ✅ DO: Create a debug pod: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh to test DNS, connectivity, and curl from inside the cluster.
  • ❌ DON'T: Spend more than 7 minutes on any single task. Flag it, move on, return with fresh eyes.
  • ❌ DON'T: Forget to set the namespace. Many tasks require -n flag. Use kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> to save typing.
  • ❌ DON'T: Leave any task blank. Even partial work (creating the namespace, writing partial YAML) may earn partial credit.
  • ❌ DON'T: Use kubectl delete pod on a static pod — you must delete the manifest file from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

📊 Exam Overview & StrategySTRATEGY

CKA Exam Format & Preparation Strategy

Exam Duration: 2 hours | Format: Performance-based (hands-on CLI) | Passing Score: 66% | Cost: $395 (includes one free retake) | Certification Validity: 3 years

5 Official Domains: Storage (10%), Troubleshooting (30%), Workloads & Scheduling (15%), Cluster Architecture (25%), Services & Networking (20%). Troubleshooting is the heaviest — focus your study time accordingly.

Exam Strategy: Read all questions first (5 min) → Solve easy questions first → Flag and return to hard ones → Use kubectl explain and kubectl --help liberally → Always verify your work with kubectl describe/get. The exam environment provides full access to kubernetes.io documentation.

Your 6-cluster lab (below) mirrors real exam conditions. Use ksw to switch between clusters. Each scenario in Part 3 specifies which cluster to use.

📚 Pre-Learning: Kubernetes FoundationsF.1–F.5

🟢 Novice-Friendly: Building Your Mental Model

F.1 What Problem Does Kubernetes Solve? — From bare metal to VMs to containers to orchestration. The "it works on my machine" problem and how Kubernetes provides a consistent deployment platform.

F.2 Containers 101 — Docker & OCI — What IS a container? Dockerfile anatomy, image layers, registries. Multi-stage builds and distroless images for production.

F.3 Kubernetes Core Concepts — The "Big Picture" mental model: Cluster = Control Plane + Worker Nodes. Pods, declarative vs imperative, desired state reconciliation, kubectl basics.

F.4 The easypj/jobpost Application Stack — Web tier (Django templates), API tier (Django REST Framework), Database tier (PostgreSQL 15), Redis (Celery + caching). Service discovery via DNS.

F.5 Kubernetes vs Docker Compose — Mental bridge: docker-compose.yml → Kubernetes YAML mapping. Why Kubernetes when Docker Compose works? The "Day 2" problem: self-healing, scaling, rolling updates.

If you're new to Kubernetes: Read through F.1–F.5 before diving into Part 1. These foundations will give you the mental models needed to understand the MCQs, troubleshooting issues, and lab scenarios. The entire guide uses the easypj/jobpost Django application as its running example.

💾 Category 1: Storage (10%)Q1-Q20

🟢 Novice-Friendly: Understanding Kubernetes Storage

This category is about where your application's data lives and how to make it survive pod restarts. Think of storage in Kubernetes like deciding where to keep your files — a whiteboard (emptyDir — wiped clean on restart), a filing cabinet (persistent volume — survives restarts), or a cloud drive (CSI — network-attached storage). For easypj/jobpost, the PostgreSQL database needs persistent storage so job listings, user accounts, and applications survive pod crashes.

Q1-Q20 20 Questions 🟢 Beginner

1.1 Storage FundamentalsQ1-Q4

Storage Q1 of 200
What happens to data stored inside a running container when that container is restarted or the pod is deleted?
A) The data is automatically backed up to the node's local disk and restored on restart
B) The data is lost because the container's writable layer is ephemeral — it exists only for the lifetime of the container
C) The data persists inside the container image and is available after restart
D) The data is automatically saved to a cloud storage bucket if one is configured
✅ Correct Answer: B

Containers use an ephemeral writable layer — any files written inside the container (outside of mounted volumes) exist only as long as that specific container instance is running. When the container stops or the pod is deleted, that writable layer is destroyed.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Container Filesystem Layers — Why Data Is Ephemeral
  Container Image (READ-ONLY)          Container Instance (EPHEMERAL)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │ Layer 4: Application    │         │ Writable Layer (Container)  │
  │   (Django + Gunicorn)   │         │   /tmp/my-data.txt ← LOST! │
  ├─────────────────────────┤         │   pip install extra-pkg     │
  │ Layer 3: Dependencies   │    +    │   apt-get install vim       │
  │   (pip requirements)    │         │                              │
  ├─────────────────────────┤         │  ❌ Deleted when container  │
  │ Layer 2: Python Runtime │         │     stops or pod dies      │
  ├─────────────────────────┤         └─────────────────────────────┘
  │ Layer 1: Ubuntu Base    │         
  └─────────────────────────┘         ✅ Survives → Persistent Volume
  
  To keep data: mount a Volume (emptyDir, hostPath, PVC)

This is why Volumes exist in Kubernetes — they solve two distinct problems: storage that outlives individual containers, and a shared filesystem when multiple containers in the same pod need to read/write the same files (e.g., an init container generating static assets for a sidecar to serve). For the easypj/jobpost PostgreSQL database, you MUST mount a PersistentVolumeClaim (bound to a PersistentVolume) as a Volume, otherwise all job listings and user data vanish when the DB pod restarts.

Storage Q2 of 200
What is the key difference between a Volume and a VolumeMount in a Kubernetes Pod specification?
A) Volume defines where storage is attached; VolumeMount defines the size of the storage
B) They are different names for the same thing — no functional difference
C) Volume declares WHAT storage is available to the pod (the "plug"); VolumeMount specifies WHERE inside each container that storage appears (the "socket")
D) Volume is used for persistent storage only; VolumeMount is used for temporary storage only
✅ Correct Answer: C

volumes: is defined at the Pod level — it declares "this pod has access to this storage." volumeMounts: is defined inside each container — it says "mount that pod-level volume at this path inside this container."

📝 Detailed Explanation
Volume vs VolumeMount — The "Plug and Socket" Pattern
  Pod: easypj-db
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  spec.volumes:          ← Declare at POD level            │
  │  - name: db-data                                         │
  │    persistentVolumeClaim:                                 │
  │      claimName: easypj-pvc    ◄── "Plug" (what storage?)  │
  │                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ Container: postgres                              │    │
  │  │  volumeMounts:              ← Define in CONTAINER │    │
  │  │  - name: db-data                                  │    │
  │  │    mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data  ◄ "Socket"│    │
  │  │                                                   │    │
  │  │  Result: PVC data appears at:                     │    │
  │  │    /var/lib/postgresql/data/                      │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This separation means multiple containers in the same pod can mount the SAME volume at DIFFERENT paths. Example: a sidecar container could mount the database volume at /backup to run pg_dump, while the main postgres container uses it at /var/lib/postgresql/data.

Storage Q3 of 200
You deployed the easypj-db PostgreSQL pod. The database writes data to /var/lib/postgresql/data but you forgot to add a Volume. The pod crashes and restarts. What happens to the data?
A) All database data is lost — the container's writable layer was destroyed when the pod restarted
B) The data survives because PostgreSQL writes to a special protected directory
C) Kubernetes automatically creates a PersistentVolume for databases
D) The data is cached in etcd and restored when the pod comes back
✅ Correct Answer: A

Without a Volume, ALL data written by the container lives in the ephemeral writable layer. When the pod restarts (even on the same node), that writable layer is destroyed and a fresh one is created from the container image. Your database is gone.

📝 Detailed Explanation
The REAL Cost of No Volume — easypj-db Disaster
  TIME                     EVENT                              DATA STATE
  ────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ──────────
  T0    kubectl apply -f easypj-db.yaml                      Empty
  T1    Pod Running — PostgreSQL initializes                  Data created
  T2    500 job listings, 200 users, 10K applications saved  💾 50MB
  T3    Pod crashes (node reboot / OOM / eviction)           💥 CRASH
  T4    Pod restarts — NEW writable layer, NO volume         ❌ EMPTY!
  ────  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ──────────
  Result: 500 jobs, 200 users, 10K applications — ALL LOST

  ✅ FIX: Add to pod spec:
  volumes:
  - name: db-data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: easypj-pvc

This is the #1 mistake beginners make with stateful applications. Rule of thumb: If your container writes data that must survive a restart, you MUST mount a Volume. For easypj: PostgreSQL, Redis (if you care about queue data), and uploaded files all need persistent storage.

Storage Q4 of 200
Why should the easypj-db PostgreSQL pod use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?
A) StatefulSets are faster at rolling updates than Deployments
B) Deployments cannot use PersistentVolumeClaims at all
C) StatefulSets automatically create database tables and schemas
D) StatefulSets provide stable pod identities (easypj-db-0, easypj-db-1) and ordered, graceful deployment/scaling — each pod gets its OWN PersistentVolumeClaim (via volumeClaimTemplates) that follows it across reschedules
✅ Correct Answer: D

StatefulSets guarantee stable, unique pod identities (ordinal index: 0, 1, 2...) and sticky storage — each pod's PVC follows it even if it's rescheduled to a different node. Deployments use random pod names and shared storage patterns.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Deployment vs StatefulSet — Why Databases Need StatefulSets
  DEPLOYMENT (Stateless)               STATEFULSET (Stateful)
  ┌─────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ easypj-api-7d8f9-x  │             │ easypj-db-0 ◄── Stable name  │
  │ easypj-api-7d8f9-y  │             │   PVC: db-data-easypj-db-0  │
  │ easypj-api-7d8f9-z  │             │                              │
  │                      │             │ easypj-db-1 ◄── Stable name  │
  │ ❌ Random pod names  │             │   PVC: db-data-easypj-db-1  │
  │ ❌ Shared storage    │             │                              │
  │ ✅ Parallel updates  │             │ ✅ Each pod has OWN PVC       │
  │ ✅ Stateless scale   │             │ ✅ Ordered start (0→1→2)     │
  └─────────────────────┘             │ ✅ Graceful stop (2→1→0)     │
                                       │ ✅ PVC survives reschedule   │
  USE FOR: easypj-web, easypj-api      └──────────────────────────────┘
  (stateless HTTP servers)
                                       USE FOR: easypj-db (PostgreSQL)
                                       (stateful database)

With a Deployment, if pod easypj-db-abc123 dies and is replaced by easypj-db-xyz789, the new pod might not get the same PVC — data inconsistency. With a StatefulSet, easypj-db-0 ALWAYS gets db-data-easypj-db-0, even on a different node.

1.2 StorageClasses & Dynamic ProvisioningQ5-Q10

Storage Q5 of 200
What is a StorageClass in Kubernetes? Think of it with an analogy.
A) A StorageClass is a physical disk attached to a worker node
B) A StorageClass is a Kubernetes object that stores files for pods
C) A StorageClass is like a "menu" of storage options — it defines WHAT type of storage to provision (SSD vs HDD, AWS EBS vs GCE PD) and HOW to provision it (which provisioner to use, parameters like disk type, replication, encryption)
D) A StorageClass is a pod that manages database connections
✅ Correct Answer: C

A StorageClass is the "menu" you hand to Kubernetes saying "when a PVC asks for storage, provision it using THIS provisioner with THESE settings." Without a StorageClass, dynamic provisioning cannot happen — you'd have to manually create every PV.

📝 Detailed Explanation
StorageClass — The "Storage Menu" for Dynamic Provisioning
  STORAGECLASS: "fast-ssd"                    STORAGECLASS: "slow-hdd"
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │ provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com│            │ provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com│
  │ parameters:                 │            │ parameters:                 │
  │   type: gp3                 │            │   type: st1                 │
  │   iops: 3000                │            │   encrypted: true           │
  │   throughput: 125           │            │                              │
  │   encrypted: true           │            │ 💰 Cheap, slower             │
  │                              │            │ ✅ Good for: logs, backups   │
  │ ⚡ Fast, expensive           │            │                              │
  │ ✅ Good for: databases       │            └─────────────────────────────┘
  └─────────────────────────────┘
  
  PVC says: "I want 20Gi of fast-ssd" → StorageClass provisions gp3 EBS volume automatically

For easypj/jobpost, you'd create a "fast-ssd" StorageClass for PostgreSQL (needs low latency) and a "standard" class for file uploads. The key fields: provisioner (which CSI driver), parameters (disk type, encryption), reclaimPolicy (Retain/Delete), volumeBindingMode (Immediate/WaitForFirstConsumer).

Storage Q6 of 200
What does reclaimPolicy: Retain do when a PVC is deleted?
A) The PV is NOT deleted — it enters "Released" state and the underlying storage (EBS volume, disk) is preserved. An admin must manually clean it up
B) The PV and all its data are immediately and permanently deleted
C) The PV is renamed and moved to a backup namespace
D) The PV is automatically re-bound to any pending PVC in the same namespace
✅ Correct Answer: A

Retain means "keep the data even after the PVC is gone." The PV becomes "Released" — not available for new claims until an admin manually cleans it (kubectl delete pv then delete the cloud disk). This is critical for production databases.

📝 Detailed Explanation
reclaimPolicy: Retain vs Delete — Data Safety
  RECLAIM POLICY: DELETE ❌                     RECLAIM POLICY: RETAIN ✅
  ┌─────────────────────────┐                  ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ kubectl delete pvc db   │                  │ kubectl delete pvc db     │
  │         │               │                  │         │                 │
  │         ▼               │                  │         ▼                 │
  │ PVC deleted              │                  │ PVC deleted               │
  │ PV deleted ⚡             │                  │ PV → "Released" state     │
  │ EBS volume DELETED 💥    │                  │ EBS volume PRESERVED 💾   │
  │                          │                  │                            │
  │ 😱 ALL DATA GONE         │                  │ 😌 Data safe — manually    │
  │                          │                  │    delete when ready      │
  └─────────────────────────┘                  └───────────────────────────┘
  
  ⚠️  Never use Delete for production databases!
  ✅ Use Retain + manual cleanup workflow for easypj-db

For easypj/jobpost: ALWAYS use reclaimPolicy: Retain for the PostgreSQL StorageClass. If someone accidentally runs kubectl delete pvc easypj-pvc, your database data survives. You can then create a new PVC that references the same PV (with volumeName) and recover.

Storage Q7 of 200
What is the difference between volumeBindingMode: Immediate and volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer?
A) Immediate means the volume is encrypted; WaitForFirstConsumer means it's unencrypted
B) Immediate provisions the PV as soon as the PVC is created (regardless of which pod will use it). WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until a pod that uses the PVC is scheduled — ensuring the PV is created in the same availability zone as the pod
C) Immediate requires manual approval; WaitForFirstConsumer auto-approves
D) Both behave identically — the names are historical
✅ Correct Answer: B

Immediate provisions the PV right when the PVC is created. WaitForFirstConsumer WAITS until a pod that references the PVC is scheduled, THEN provisions the PV in the same zone as the pod. Immediate is the default when the field is unset — WaitForFirstConsumer must be set explicitly, but it's the recommended mode for cloud environments.

📝 Detailed Explanation
volumeBindingMode — Why WaitForFirstConsumer Matters in AWS
  IMMEDIATE (❌ Problematic in Multi-AZ)   WAITFORFIRSTCONSUMER (✅ Correct)
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. PVC created               │        │ 1. PVC created               │
  │ 2. PV provisioned in us-east-1a (random)│ 2. No PV yet — waiting...  │
  │ 3. Pod scheduled to us-east-1b│        │ 3. Pod scheduled to us-east-1b│
  │ 4. ❌ Pod CAN'T mount volume  │        │ 4. PV provisioned in us-east-1b│
  │    from different AZ!         │        │ 5. ✅ Pod mounts PV — same AZ │
  │                               │        │                               │
  │ ⚠️  EBS volumes are ZONE-LOCKED│       │ ✅ No cross-AZ attachment issue│
  └──────────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────────┘
  
  AWS EBS Rule: An EC2 instance in us-east-1a CANNOT attach an EBS volume in us-east-1b

For easypj on AWS: ALWAYS use WaitForFirstConsumer. EBS volumes are locked to a single availability zone. If the PV is created in us-east-1a but the pod lands in us-east-1b, the pod will be stuck in ContainerCreating forever with a "Multi-Attach error" or "volume is in zone X, node is in zone Y."

Storage Q8 of 200
What does allowVolumeExpansion: true in a StorageClass enable?
A) It allows multiple pods to write to the same volume simultaneously
B) It allows the StorageClass to be modified after creation
C) It automatically increases the volume size when disk usage exceeds 80%
D) It allows you to increase the size of an existing PVC (and its underlying PV) by editing spec.resources.requests.storage in the PVC — the CSI driver handles the actual disk resize
✅ Correct Answer: D

allowVolumeExpansion: true enables online volume resizing. You edit the PVC to request more storage, and the CSI driver expands the underlying disk without downtime. This is NOT automatic — you must still edit the PVC.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Volume Expansion — Growing Your Database Disk Live
  STEP 1: StorageClass setup             STEP 2: Expand PVC
  ┌──────────────────────────┐           kubectl patch pvc easypj-pvc -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'
  │ kind: StorageClass       │           
  │   allowVolumeExpansion:  │           STEP 3: CSI driver resizes
  │     true  ◄── Required!  │           ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │                          │           │ Before: 5Gi EBS gp3     │
  └──────────────────────────┘           │ After:  20Gi EBS gp3    │
                                          │ Pod keeps running!      │
  ⚠️  Without allowVolumeExpansion:       │ NO DOWNTIME ✅          │
  true, the PVC edit will be             └─────────────────────────┘
  REJECTED with: "only dynamically
  provisioned pvc can be resized"        STEP 4: Filesystem resize
                                         │ (handled automatically   │
  easypj: jobpost DB grows from          │  by CSI driver)         │
  500MB → 50GB as listings increase      └─────────────────────────┘

Note: Volume expansion is one-way — you can grow a volume but CANNOT shrink it. For easypj: plan your initial PVC size generously (5Gi-10Gi for dev, 50Gi+ for production) and enable expansion so you can grow it later without recreating the database.

Storage Q9 of 200
You created a StorageClass but PVCs are not provisioning. What is the MOST common cause?
A) The provisioner (CSI driver) specified in the StorageClass is not installed or not running on the cluster
B) The StorageClass name must start with "sc-"
C) StorageClasses only work on GKE, not EKS or AKS
D) You need to reboot all worker nodes after creating a StorageClass
✅ Correct Answer: A

A StorageClass points to a provisioner — a CSI driver that actually creates the storage. If the driver isn't installed (e.g., ebs.csi.aws.com on EKS without the EBS CSI add-on), PVCs referencing that StorageClass will stay Pending forever.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Troubleshooting PVC Pending — The Provisioner Check
  kubectl describe pvc easypj-pvc
  ...
  Events:
    Type     Reason                Age   Message
    ----     ------                ----  -------
    Warning  ProvisioningFailed    2m    failed to provision volume with
                                         StorageClass "fast-ssd": 
                                         ❌ driver "ebs.csi.aws.com" not found
  
  FIX:
  kubectl get csidrivers.storage.k8s.io   ← Check if CSI driver exists
  # If missing on EKS:
  eksctl create addon --name aws-ebs-csi-driver --cluster easypj
  
  The Chain:
  PVC → StorageClass → provisioner → CSI Driver → Cloud API → Actual Disk
  ⬆️                                                    ⬆️
  Missing driver = broken chain                        EBS volume created

Always verify: kubectl get csidrivers to see which CSI drivers are installed, kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi to verify the driver pods are running. On EKS, install the EBS CSI driver add-on. On self-managed clusters, deploy it manually.

Storage Q10 of 200
What happens if you have multiple StorageClasses and a PVC does NOT specify a storageClassName?
A) Kubernetes randomly picks one StorageClass to use
B) The PVC fails immediately with a validation error — storageClassName is required
C) Kubernetes uses the StorageClass marked as "default" (via the storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" annotation). If no default exists, the PVC stays Pending forever
D) Kubernetes provisions storage using the first StorageClass alphabetically
✅ Correct Answer: C

When a PVC omits storageClassName, Kubernetes looks for the default StorageClass — the one annotated with storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true". If no default is set, the PVC waits forever because it doesn't know which provisioner to call.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Default StorageClass — The "Fallback" Provisioner
  PVC WITHOUT storageClassName              PVC WITH storageClassName
  ┌────────────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ kind: PVC              │               │ kind: PVC                    │
  │   name: easypj-pvc     │               │   name: easypj-pvc           │
  │   resources:           │               │   storageClassName: fast-ssd │
  │     requests:          │               │   resources:                 │
  │       storage: 10Gi    │               │     requests:                │
  │   ← NO storageClassName│               │       storage: 10Gi          │
  └────────────────────────┘               └──────────────────────────────┘
           │                                         │
           ▼                                         ▼
  ┌─────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Is there a DEFAULT   │              │ Uses fast-ssd StorageClass     │
  │ StorageClass?        │              │ directly (explicit match)      │
  │                      │              └────────────────────────────────┘
  │ ✅ YES → use default  │
  │ ❌ NO  → PVC Pending │
  └─────────────────────┘
  
  Set default: kubectl annotate sc fast-ssd storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true

For easypj: ALWAYS explicitly set storageClassName in your PVCs. Relying on defaults is fragile — if someone removes the default annotation, all your PVCs stop working. Explicit is better than implicit.

1.3 Persistent Volumes & Persistent Volume ClaimsQ11-Q16

Storage Q11 of 200
What is the relationship between a PersistentVolume (PV) and a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)? Use the analogy.
A) PV is the request and PVC is the actual storage — opposite of what most people think
B) PV is the "parking spot" (the actual storage provisioned in the cluster). PVC is the "parking reservation" (a request for storage by a pod). Kubernetes matches PVCs to PVs based on size, access mode, and StorageClass
C) PV and PVC are the same object with different names — they're interchangeable
D) PV manages the pod; PVC manages the container
✅ Correct Answer: B

The PV is the actual storage resource (like a 100Gi EBS volume). The PVC is a request: "I need 20Gi of fast-ssd storage." Kubernetes acts as a matchmaker — finding a PV that satisfies the PVC's requirements.

📝 PV + PVC YAML — See the Matchmaking in Action
Static Provisioning: Admin Creates PV, Dev Creates PVC, K8s Binds Them
  # ADMIN: Creates the actual storage (or it's auto-created by StorageClass)
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: PersistentVolume
  metadata:
    name: pv-fast-100gi
  spec:
    capacity:
      storage: 100Gi           # ← "Parking lot has 100 spots"
    accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce          # ← "Single car only"
    persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
    storageClassName: fast-ssd
    awsElasticBlockStore:      # ← Actual EBS volume in AWS
      volumeID: vol-0a1b2c3d4e5f
      fsType: ext4
  ---
  # DEVELOPER: Requests storage for the app
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
  metadata:
    name: easypj-db-pvc
    namespace: easypj
  spec:
    accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce          # ← Must match PV!
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 20Gi          # ← "I need 20 spots" (100 ≥ 20 ✅)
    storageClassName: fast-ssd # ← Must match PV!
  ---
  # RESULT: kubectl get pv shows "Bound" to easypj-db-pvc
  # PVC can now be used in a Pod: persistentVolumeClaim.claimName: easypj-db-pvc
🔍 The Matching Algorithm — 3 Criteria, ALL Must Pass
Match Criteria: Size + Access Mode + StorageClass
  PVC Request                          Available PVs               Match?
  ──────────────────────────────────   ─────────────────────────  ──────
  storage: 20Gi, RWO, fast-ssd    →   PV-1: 100Gi, RWO, fast-ssd  ✅ YES
  storage: 20Gi, RWO, fast-ssd    →   PV-2: 10Gi,  RWO, fast-ssd  ❌ SIZE (10 < 20)
  storage: 20Gi, RWX, fast-ssd    →   PV-3: 100Gi, RWO, fast-ssd  ❌ ACCESS (RWO ≠ RWX)
  storage: 20Gi, RWO, fast-ssd    →   PV-4: 100Gi, RWO, slow-hdd  ❌ CLASS (fast ≠ slow)
  storage: 20Gi, RWO, ""          →   PV-5: 100Gi, RWO, ""        ✅ YES (empty matches empty)
  
  Winner: PV-1 → PVC.Status: Bound

This separation is brilliant: Admins provision PVs. Developers request PVCs. Neither needs to know the other's details. Kubernetes does the matchmaking. kubectl get pv shows which PVC claimed each PV in the CLAIM column.

Storage Q12 of 200
What do the access modes RWO, ROX, and RWX mean for PersistentVolumes?
A) RWO = ReadWriteOnce (single node read/write). ROX = ReadOnlyMany (many nodes read-only). RWX = ReadWriteMany (many nodes read/write)
B) RWO = ReadWriteOften. ROX = ReadOnlyExecute. RWX = ReadWriteExecute
C) All three mean the same thing — they are deprecated aliases
D) RWO = 1 pod, ROX = 2-3 pods, RWX = unlimited pods
✅ Correct Answer: A

The key insight: "Once" and "Many" refer to NODES, not pods. RWO = one node (multiple pods on same node OK). RWX = multiple nodes (pods on different nodes all read/write). ROX = multiple nodes read-only.

📝 Access Modes — Real-World Examples with YAML
RWO vs RWX — Which Storage Backend Supports What
  ACCESS MODE    AWS                GCP              ON-PREM         EASYPJ USE CASE
  ────────────   ────────────────   ──────────────  ─────────────   ───────────────────
  RWO            EBS (gp3/io2) ✅   Persistent Disk  Local PV        PostgreSQL (DB)
                 (single AZ only)   ✅              NFS (single      Redis (single node)
  ────────────   ────────────────   ──────────────  ─────────────   ───────────────────
  RWX            EFS ✅             Filestore ✅     NFS ✅          Shared file uploads
                 (multi-AZ, NFS)    (multi-zone)    CephFS ✅       Multiple API pods
                                                                    writing user files
  ────────────   ────────────────   ──────────────  ─────────────   ───────────────────
  ROX            EFS ✅             Filestore ✅     NFS ✅          Read-only config
                 (same as RWX but   (same as RWX)   CephFS ✅       shared across pods
                  mounted readOnly)

  ⚠️  CRITICAL: EBS volumes are ZONE-LOCKED. An EC2 in us-east-1a
      CANNOT attach an EBS volume in us-east-1b. Use WaitForFirstConsumer!
🔬 YAML: How Access Modes Are Declared
PV and PVC — accessModes Must Align
  # PV: must SUPPORT the mode (or modes)
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: PersistentVolume
  spec:
    accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce      # Can also list multiple: [RWO, ROX, RWX]
  
  # PVC: requests a SPECIFIC mode
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
  spec:
    accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce      # Must be a SUBSET of PV's supported modes
  
  # Pod: references PVC by claimName
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: postgres
      volumeMounts:
      - name: db-data
        mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
    volumes:
    - name: db-data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: easypj-db-pvc
        readOnly: false     # ← Set to true for ROX volumes

For easypj: PostgreSQL StatefulSet uses RWO (EBS gp3, single writer). File uploads use RWX (EFS, mounted by multiple API pods in different AZs). If you accidentally use RWO for shared uploads, only ONE API pod will work — the others get "volume is already attached" errors. A fourth mode, ReadWriteOncePod (stable since v1.29, CSI-only), restricts mounting to a single POD rather than a single node — use it when you need a true single-writer guarantee instead of RWO's node-level exclusivity.

Storage Q13 of 200
Your PVC is stuck in Pending state. The StorageClass exists, the CSI driver is running, and there ARE available PVs. What is the MOST likely reason?
A) PVC names must match PV names exactly
B) PVCs only work with StatefulSets, not Deployments
C) No available PV matches ALL the PVC's requirements — the PV might be too small, have the wrong access mode, or have a different StorageClass. Check with kubectl describe pvc
D) You need to run kubectl activate-pvc to trigger binding
✅ Correct Answer: C

PVC binding is an ALL-OR-NOTHING match. If the PVC asks for 100Gi RWO fast-ssd but the available PV is 50Gi RWO fast-ssd, the binding fails because the PV is too small. Use kubectl describe pvc to see the exact mismatch in the Events section.

📝 PVC Debugging — Step-by-Step Diagnostic
Debug: PVC Stuck in Pending — The 4-Point Checklist
  STEP 1: kubectl describe pvc easypj-pvc
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Events:                                                     │
  │   Warning  ProvisioningFailed  2m   storageclass.storage.   │
  │   k8s.io "fast-ssd" not found   ← ❌ StorageClass missing!  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 2: Check StorageClass exists
  $ kubectl get sc
  NAME       PROVISIONER          RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE
  fast-ssd   ebs.csi.aws.com      Delete          Immediate

  STEP 3: Check available PVs
  $ kubectl get pv
  NAME         CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS
  pv-slow-100  100Gi      RWO            Retain           Available  ← SIZE OK
  pv-fast-50   50Gi       RWO            Delete           Available  ← TOO SMALL!

  PVC asks: 100Gi, RWO, fast-ssd    PV offers: 50Gi, RWO, fast-ssd
                                      ❌ SIZE MISMATCH!

  STEP 4: Fix — Create a matching PV or adjust PVC size
  $ kubectl patch pvc easypj-pvc -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'

The match criteria are: (1) Size — PV capacity ≥ PVC request, (2) Access Mode — exact match, (3) StorageClass — exact match (or PV has none and PVC has ""), (4) volumeMode — Filesystem vs Block must also match; a Block-mode PVC will not bind to a Filesystem-mode PV. If ANY criterion fails, the PVC stays Pending.

Storage Q14 of 200
What is claimRef on a PersistentVolume, and why is it important?
A) It's a reference to the StorageClass that created the PV
B) It's a comment field for administrators to document the PV's purpose
C) It's a backup reference used only during disaster recovery
D) It's the binding between a PV and PVC — once set, the PV is "claimed" and cannot be used by any other PVC. It also prevents the PV from being deleted while the PVC exists (via the pv-protection finalizer)
✅ Correct Answer: D

claimRef is the one-to-one binding between a PV and its PVC. It includes the PVC's name, namespace, and UID. Once set, the PV is reserved for that specific PVC. The pv-protection finalizer prevents the PV from being deleted until the PVC is deleted first — protecting your data.

📝 claimRef — The Binding Contract Between PV and PVC
How claimRef Locks a PV to One PVC
  PV: pv-fast-100gi                               PVC: easypj-db-pvc
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ apiVersion: v1                  │            │ apiVersion: v1       │
  │ kind: PersistentVolume          │            │ kind: Persistent...  │
  │ metadata:                       │            │   Claim              │
  │   name: pv-fast-100gi           │   BIND     │ metadata:            │
  │ spec:                           │ ◄────────► │   name: easypj-pvc   │
  │   capacity:                     │            │   namespace: easypj  │
  │     storage: 100Gi              │            │   uid: a1b2c3-d4e5   │
  │   claimRef:          ◄── THE    │            │ spec:                │
  │     name: easypj-pvc   LOCK!    │            │   resources:         │
  │     namespace: easypj            │            │     requests:        │
  │     uid: a1b2c3-d4e5            │            │       storage: 20Gi  │
  │   status: Bound                 │            │   storageClassName:  │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘            │     fast-ssd         │
                                                  └──────────────────────┘
  Without claimRef:                      With claimRef:
  ❌ Any PVC can steal the PV            ✅ Only easypj-pvc can use it
  ❌ PV can be deleted accidentally      ✅ pv-protection finalizer blocks
  ❌ Data can be lost                    ✅ until PVC is deleted first

Key insight: claimRef uses the PVC's UID (not just name). If you delete and recreate a PVC with the same name, it gets a NEW UID — and the old PV won't bind to it automatically. You'd need to manually clear the claimRef or use volumeName in the PVC spec to pre-bind.

Storage Q15 of 200
You edit a PVC to increase spec.resources.requests.storage from 5Gi to 20Gi. The edit is accepted but the PVC still shows 5Gi. Why?
A) PVC sizes can only be changed by deleting and recreating the PVC
B) The underlying StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: false or the CSI driver doesn't support expansion. Check the StorageClass and CSI driver capabilities
C) You need to restart the pod using the PVC for the change to take effect
D) The PVC needs to be in "Available" status to resize — you must unbind it first
✅ Correct Answer: B

Volume expansion requires BOTH: (1) StorageClass.allowVolumeExpansion: true AND (2) a CSI driver that supports the EXPAND_VOLUME capability. If either is missing, the PVC edit is silently ignored or rejected.

📝 Volume Expansion — Requirements Checklist & Flow
Why Your PVC Won't Expand — The 3 Requirements
  REQUIREMENT 1: StorageClass allows expansion
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1            │
  │ kind: StorageClass                       │
  │   name: fast-ssd                         │
  │   provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com           │
  │   allowVolumeExpansion: true  ◄── MUST!  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  REQUIREMENT 2: CSI driver supports EXPAND_VOLUME
  $ kubectl get csidriver ebs.csi.aws.com -o yaml | grep -A5 capabilities
    capabilities:
    - EXPAND_VOLUME         ◄── MUST be listed!

  REQUIREMENT 3: Filesystem resize (automatic in most CSI drivers)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PVC edited: 5Gi → 20Gi                       │
  │     │                                         │
  │     ├─ PVC.Status.Conditions:                 │
  │     │   Resizing = True                       │
  │     │                                         │
  │     ├─ CSI Controller: ExpandVolume()          │
  │     │   → AWS API: ModifyVolume (5→20Gi)      │
  │     │                                         │
  │     ├─ CSI Node: NodeExpandVolume()            │
  │     │   → resize2fs /dev/nvme1n1 (5→20Gi)     │
  │     │                                         │
  │     └─ PVC.Status.Capacity: 20Gi ✅            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ❌ If any step fails: PVC shows old size, pod keeps running
  ✅ All 3 pass: PVC shows new size, pod sees expanded disk

For easypj-db: Before deploying, verify kubectl describe sc fast-ssd | grep AllowVolumeExpansion. If false, you must recreate the StorageClass. Existing PVCs can only expand if their StorageClass allows it — changing the SC later doesn't retroactively enable expansion for already-provisioned PVCs.

Storage Q16 of 200
What happens when you delete a PVC that is bound to a pod?
A) The PVC enters "Terminating" state but stays until the pod stops using it. Once the pod is gone, the PVC is deleted. What happens to the PV depends on reclaimPolicy — Retain preserves it, Delete destroys it
B) The pod is immediately killed and the PVC is deleted instantly
C) The PVC cannot be deleted while a pod is using it — kubectl returns an error
D) The pod continues running but writes to a temporary local disk
✅ Correct Answer: A

Kubernetes protects in-use storage. The PVC gets a kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer when in use by a pod. When you delete the PVC, it enters Terminating but WAITS until no pods are using it.

📝 PVC Deletion Protection — The Finalizer Mechanism
Timeline: What Happens When You Delete an In-Use PVC
  TIME   ACTION                                    PVC STATE
  ─────  ────────────────────────────────────────  ─────────────
  T0     kubectl delete pvc easypj-db-pvc          Bound
  T1     PVC gets deletionTimestamp set            Terminating
         Finalizer: kubernetes.io/pvc-protection
         ← Blocks actual deletion!
  
  T2     Pod easypj-db-0 still running             Terminating
         Volume still mounted at /var/lib/...      (PVC NOT deleted yet)
         Database still writing data ✅
  
  T3     kubectl delete pod easypj-db-0            Terminating
         Pod terminates gracefully
  
  T4     No pods using PVC → finalizer removed     Terminating
         PVC actually deleted from etcd            → GONE
  
  T5     reclaimPolicy determines PV fate:
         ├─ Delete: PV deleted + EBS volume destroyed 💥
         └─ Retain: PV becomes "Released" state 💾
                    (EBS volume preserved — manual cleanup needed)

  ⚠️  CRITICAL: If reclaimPolicy=Delete AND pod is still running,
      the PV and EBS volume are NOT deleted until T4.
      The finalizer protects your running database!
🔬 How to Check & Remove a Stuck Finalizer

If a PVC is stuck Terminating forever (pod already gone but finalizer wasn't removed): kubectl patch pvc easypj-pvc -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}' --type=merge. ⚠️ Only do this if you're SURE no pod is using the volume — removing the finalizer bypasses Kubernetes' safety check.

1.4 Volume Types Deep DiveQ17-Q20

Storage Q17 of 200
What is an emptyDir volume and when should you use it?
A) A pre-populated directory from the container image — read-only
B) A network filesystem shared across all pods in the cluster
C) An ephemeral directory created when a pod starts (initially empty). It lives as long as the pod lives on that node — data is deleted if the pod is removed. Best for temporary scratch space, caches, or sharing data between containers in the same pod
D) A persistent volume that is automatically backed up to cloud storage
✅ Correct Answer: C

emptyDir = "scratch space." Created when the pod starts, destroyed when the pod is deleted. Survives container restarts WITHIN the same pod but NOT pod deletion/reschedule.

📝 emptyDir YAML & Use Cases
emptyDir Volume — Sharing Data Between Containers
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: easypj-worker
  spec:
    volumes:
    - name: temp-data
      emptyDir: {}            # Simple empty directory
    # - name: cache
    #   emptyDir:
    #     medium: Memory       # RAM-backed (faster, but counts against pod memory)
    #     sizeLimit: "256Mi"   # Max size before pod is evicted
    containers:
    - name: worker
      image: easypj/jobpost
      volumeMounts:
      - name: temp-data
        mountPath: /tmp/processing   # Worker writes temp files here
    - name: archiver
      image: busybox
      volumeMounts:
      - name: temp-data
        mountPath: /data             # Archiver reads from same volume!
      command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /data/*.json /archive/"]
  
  Same emptyDir mounted at TWO different paths in different containers!
  Worker writes → Archiver reads → Data shared without network!
🔬 emptyDir Lifecycle
When Data Survives vs When It's Lost
  EVENT                          emptyDir DATA        PV DATA
  ─────                          ─────────────        ───────
  Container restart (same pod)   ✅ SURVIVES          ✅ SURVIVES
  Pod deleted                    ❌ DELETED            ✅ SURVIVES
  Pod evicted to new node        ❌ DELETED            ✅ SURVIVES
  Node reboot                    ❌ DELETED*           ✅ SURVIVES
  
  * Unless medium: Memory was used (always lost on reboot)

  easypj: emptyDir for Celery worker /tmp. PV for PostgreSQL /data.
  NEVER use emptyDir for anything you'd cry about losing!

Setting medium: Memory backs the emptyDir with tmpfs (RAM) instead of the node's disk — much faster, but the files written there count against that container's memory limit, and everything is lost immediately on node reboot rather than persisting on disk.

Storage Q18 of 200
Why is hostPath considered a security risk and generally discouraged for production use?
A) hostPath volumes are slower than other volume types
B) hostPath is deprecated and will be removed in future Kubernetes versions
C) hostPath requires a special license from the Linux Foundation
D) hostPath mounts the NODE's filesystem into the pod — if the pod is compromised, the attacker can access host files (kubelet configs, container runtime socket), and data is lost when the pod moves to a different node
✅ Correct Answer: D

hostPath gives the pod direct access to the worker node's filesystem. A compromised pod can access kubelet configs, the container runtime socket, host secrets, and more. Data is also lost if the pod moves to another node.

📝 hostPath YAML — When It's Acceptable vs Dangerous
hostPath — The Double-Edged Sword
  # LEGITIMATE: Fluentd reading container logs (DaemonSet)
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  spec:
    volumes:
    - name: varlog
      hostPath:
        path: /var/log/containers   # ← Required for log collection
    containers:
    - name: fluentd
      volumeMounts:
      - name: varlog
        mountPath: /var/log
        readOnly: true              # ← ALWAYS use readOnly!
  ---
  # DANGEROUS: Mounting docker socket (container escape!)
  volumes:
  - name: docker-sock
    hostPath:
      path: /var/run/docker.sock   # ← NEVER mount this!
  # Attacker with this mount can:
  # docker run -v /:/host alpine chroot /host
  # → FULL ROOT on the node!
🔬 hostPath vs PV — When to Use Which
Decision Table: hostPath vs PV vs emptyDir
  USE CASE                      BEST CHOICE     WHY
  ────────                      ───────────     ───
  PostgreSQL data               PersistentVolume Survives pod/node restarts
  Log collection (DaemonSet)    hostPath        Must read node's /var/log
  Node monitoring (Prometheus)  hostPath        Must access host /proc, /sys
  Temp processing               emptyDir        Ephemeral, auto-cleaned
  Database config               ConfigMap       Kubernetes-native
  Database password             Secret          Base64-encoded, RBAC-controlled
  User file uploads             PV (RWX)        Shared across API pods
  
  Rule: If data must survive → PV. If node access is required → hostPath.
        If temporary → emptyDir. If config → ConfigMap/Secret.

Official guidance: if hostPath must be used, scope it to only the specific file or directory actually needed (never the host root) and mount it readOnly: true whenever the workload doesn't need to write — this limits the blast radius if the pod is ever compromised.

Storage Q19 of 200
What is a projected volume in Kubernetes?
A) A volume that automatically scales based on pod count
B) A volume that combines MULTIPLE sources (ConfigMap, Secret, downwardAPI, serviceAccountToken) into a SINGLE directory — like merging several folders into one
C) A volume that is projected onto a cloud provider's storage array
D) A volume type that only exists in Kubernetes documentation but is not implemented
✅ Correct Answer: B

A projected volume merges multiple volume sources into one directory — ConfigMap + Secret + downwardAPI + serviceAccountToken, all in a single mount point instead of four separate ones.

📝 Projected Volume YAML — Combining 4 Sources Into 1 Directory
Projected Volume — The "Merge Folder" Pattern
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  spec:
    volumes:
    - name: app-config
      projected:
        sources:
        - configMap:                    # Source 1: App settings
            name: easypj-config
            items:
            - key: database-host
              path: db/host
        - secret:                       # Source 2: Credentials
            name: easypj-creds
            items:
            - key: password
              path: db/password        # Mounted at: /etc/app/db/password
        - downwardAPI:                  # Source 3: Pod metadata
            items:
            - path: labels
              fieldRef:
                fieldPath: metadata.labels
        - serviceAccountToken:          # Source 4: K8s API token
            path: token
            expirationSeconds: 3600     # Auto-rotates after 1 hour!
    containers:
    - name: api
      volumeMounts:
      - name: app-config
        mountPath: /etc/app            # ALL 4 sources merged here!
  
  Result directory: /etc/app/
    db/host        ← from ConfigMap
    db/password    ← from Secret
    labels         ← from downwardAPI
    token          ← from serviceAccountToken (auto-rotated!)
Storage Q20 of 200
What is CSI (Container Storage Interface) and why was it introduced?
A) CSI is a standardized interface between Kubernetes and storage systems — like a "universal remote" for storage. It allows ANY storage vendor (AWS, GCP, NetApp, Ceph) to write ONE driver that works with ANY container orchestrator (not just Kubernetes). It replaced the old "in-tree" volume plugins that required modifying Kubernetes core code
B) CSI is a Kubernetes-specific file system format for containers
C) CSI is a command-line tool for managing container images
D) CSI stands for "Container Security Initiative" and handles encryption
✅ Correct Answer: A

Before CSI, every storage plugin was "in-tree" — baked into Kubernetes core. Adding support for a new storage system required modifying and recompiling Kubernetes. CSI decouples storage from Kubernetes — vendors write a CSI driver once, and it works with any CSI-compatible orchestrator.

📝 CSI Architecture — In-Tree vs CSI Comparison
The CSI Driver Architecture & Components
  PRE-CSI (In-Tree)                        CSI (Out-of-Tree)
  ┌──────────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Kubernetes Core           │            │ Kubernetes Core               │
  │ ├── AWS EBS plugin        │            │ ├── CSI Interface (generic)   │
  │ ├── GCE PD plugin         │            │ └── External Components:      │
  │ ├── Azure Disk plugin     │            │     ├── CSI Controller        │
  │ └── NFS plugin            │            │     │   (creates/deletes vols) │
  │                           │            │     └── CSI Node DaemonSet    │
  │ ❌ Vendor code in K8s     │            │         (mounts/unmounts)     │
  │ ❌ Need K8s release for   │            │                              │
  │    driver update          │            │       ↓ Talks gRPC ↓          │
  │ ❌ Only works with K8s    │            │ ┌────────────────────────────┐│
  └──────────────────────────┘            │ │ CSI Driver (vendor)        ││
                                           │ │ ebs.csi.aws.com            ││
  ✅ CSI: Vendor ships driver              │ │ (CreateVolume, DeleteVol,  ││
     independently. Updates                │ │  ControllerPublish,        ││
     without touching K8s.                  │ │  NodeStage, NodePublish)   ││
                                           │ └────────────────────────────┘│
                                           └──────────────────────────────┘
🔬 CSI Driver Verification & Migration
Checking CSI Drivers on Your Cluster
  # List installed CSI drivers:
  kubectl get csidrivers
  
  NAME                ATTACH REQUIRED   POD INFO ON MOUNT   MODES
  ebs.csi.aws.com     true              false               Persistent
  efs.csi.aws.com     true              false               Persistent
  
  # Check CSI driver pods:
  kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi
  ebs-csi-controller-xxx     Running   ← Controller (create/delete)
  ebs-csi-node-yyy           Running   ← DaemonSet (mount/unmount)
  
  # In-tree → CSI migration (EKS example):
  # Old: storageClassName: gp2 (in-tree)
  # New: storageClassName: ebs-sc (CSI, ebs.csi.aws.com)
  # EKS auto-migrates in-tree PVCs to CSI!

🔧 Category 2: Troubleshooting (30%)Q21-Q80

🟡 Most Important Category — 30% of the Exam

This is the BIGGEST and most practical category. Troubleshooting is 30% of the CKA because in real life, you spend 30% of your time fixing things. Learn the systematic approach: Observe → Hypothesize → Test → Fix. Every question here mirrors a real scenario you'll face running easypj/jobpost in production.

Q21-Q8060 Questions🟡 Intermediate

2.1 Cluster & Node TroubleshootingQ21-Q32

Troubleshooting Q21 of 200
You run kubectl get nodes and one node shows NotReady. What is the FIRST command to investigate?
A) kubectl delete node and recreate it
B) kubectl describe node <node-name> — check the Conditions section for MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, NetworkUnavailable
C) kubectl restart-node <node-name>
D) Immediately reboot the node via SSH
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl describe node shows the Conditions section — the single most important diagnostic tool. Look for: Ready=False (node not accepting pods), MemoryPressure=True (node running out of RAM), DiskPressure=True (disk nearly full), PIDPressure=True (too many processes), NetworkUnavailable=True (CNI not ready). Each condition tells you exactly what's wrong.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Node Conditions — Your Diagnostic Dashboard
  kubectl describe node worker-1
  Conditions:
    Type                 Status    Reason                   Message
    ────                 ──────    ──────                   ───────
    NetworkUnavailable   False     CalicoIsUp               Calico is running
    MemoryPressure       False     KubeletHasSufficientMem  kubelet has sufficient memory
    DiskPressure         True      KubeletHasDiskPressure   ❌ 85% disk used!
    PIDPressure          False     KubeletHasSufficientPID  kubelet has sufficient PID
    Ready                False     KubeletNotReady          ❌ node not ready
  
  Fix for DiskPressure: ssh worker-1 → df -h → clean /var/log/containers
Troubleshooting Q22 of 200
What does kubectl cordon do to a node?
A) Deletes all pods on the node and removes it from the cluster
B) Reboots the node safely
C) Marks the node as "unschedulable" — no NEW pods will be scheduled there, but existing pods continue running. This is the first step in safe node maintenance
D) Upgrades the kubelet on the node
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl cordon = "put a fence around the node." Existing pods keep running undisturbed. New pods won't be scheduled here. The typical safe maintenance flow: cordon → drain → maintain → uncordon.

Node Maintenance Flow — cordon → drain → uncordon
  kubectl cordon worker-1    ← 🚧 "No new pods here"
  kubectl drain worker-1     ← 📦 Move existing pods to other nodes
    --ignore-daemonsets      ← Skip DaemonSet pods
    --delete-emptydir-data   ← Allow emptyDir data loss
  [Maintenance: upgrade kubelet, patch kernel, replace hardware]
  kubectl uncordon worker-1  ← ✅ "Welcome back!"
Troubleshooting Q23 of 200
During kubectl drain, pods protected by a PodDisruptionBudget are NOT being evicted. Why?
A) The PDB ensures a minimum number of pods stay running. If evicting this pod would violate the PDB (e.g., minAvailable: 2 and only 2 pods exist), the drain command refuses. You must either scale up first or override with --disable-eviction
B) PDB-protected pods can never be evicted under any circumstances
C) You must delete the PDB first before draining
D) PDBs only work with StatefulSets, not Deployments
✅ Correct Answer: A

PDBs are safety valves. If easypj-api has minAvailable: 2 and exactly 2 replicas, kubectl drain's eviction requests get rejected — the tool doesn't give up, it automatically retries until the PDB allows the eviction or a timeout is reached. Solution: temporarily scale up to 3 replicas, drain, then scale back down (or use --disable-eviction to bypass the PDB entirely as a last resort).

📝 PDB Eviction Protection — How It Works
PodDisruptionBudget Prevents Over-Eviction
  easypj-api: 3 replicas, PDB minAvailable: 2
  
  kubectl drain worker-1:
    Pod-1 on worker-1 → EVICT ✅ (2 remaining ≥ minAvailable 2)
    Pod-2 on worker-2 → EVICT ❌ BLOCKED! (1 remaining < minAvailable 2)
  
  Fix: kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=4
       Now drain can evict up to 2 while keeping 2 running
Troubleshooting Q24 of 200
How do you check the kubelet logs on a worker node?
A) kubectl logs kubelet -n kube-system
B) kubectl logs -n kube-system daemonset/kubelet
C) docker logs kubelet
D) SSH to the node and run journalctl -u kubelet (kubelet runs as a systemd service, not a pod — so kubectl logs won't work)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Key insight: kubelet is a systemd service, not a pod. kubectl logs only works on pods. For kubelet: journalctl -u kubelet -f (follow), journalctl -u kubelet --since "10 min ago" (recent). Same applies to containerd/docker.

📝 Kubelet Log Access — Why kubectl logs Won't Work
kubelet Runs as systemd Service, NOT a Pod
  # kubelet is a systemd service → journalctl, not kubectl logs
  ssh worker-1
  
  journalctl -u kubelet -f              # Follow kubelet logs live
  journalctl -u kubelet --since "10m"   # Last 10 minutes
  journalctl -u kubelet -n 100          # Last 100 lines
  journalctl -u containerd -f           # Container runtime logs
  
  # Also check kubelet config:
  cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep -E "maxPods|clusterDNS"
Troubleshooting Q25 of 200
A pod is stuck in Terminating state for 10 minutes. What is the MOST likely cause?
A) The pod is waiting for a new node to be provisioned
B) The pod has a finalizer that hasn't been removed, or a preStop hook that's hanging. Check kubectl describe pod for finalizers — if one is stuck, patch it out directly; if a preStop hook is hanging, kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 skips waiting for it
C) Kubernetes is waiting for user confirmation before deleting
D) All pods take exactly 10 minutes to terminate — that's the default
✅ Correct Answer: B

Finalizers are pre-deletion cleanup hooks. If a controller that set the finalizer crashes, the pod is stuck — force-delete does NOT remove finalizers, you must patch them out directly (kubectl patch pod stuck-pod -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' --type=merge). PreStop hooks can hang if the command never exits; kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 helps there by skipping the wait for kubelet confirmation, though it risks a duplicate running process if the old pod is actually still alive.

📝 Pod Stuck Terminating — The Finalizer Problem
Why Pods Get Stuck in Terminating State
  kubectl describe pod stuck-pod | grep -A5 Finalizers
  Finalizers:
    example.com/custom-cleanup   ← Controller must remove this
  
  The controller that set this finalizer must:
  1. Execute cleanup logic (deregister from LB, flush queues)
  2. Remove its finalizer from the pod
  3. ONLY THEN can Kubernetes actually delete the pod
  
  Nuclear option (last resort):
  kubectl delete pod stuck-pod --force --grace-period=0
Troubleshooting Q26 of 200
What does a Taint on a node do?
A) It permanently deletes the node from the cluster
B) It marks the node as a control plane node only
C) It REPELS pods from being scheduled on that node UNLESS the pod has a matching Toleration. Think of it as a "No Entry" sign that pods need a "VIP pass" (toleration) to bypass
D) It encrypts all data on the node
✅ Correct Answer: C

Taints and Tolerations work together: Taint says "stay away" (node-level), Toleration says "I'm allowed" (pod-level). Example: Taint worker-1 with dedicated=database:NoSchedule, then give easypj-db pod the matching toleration. Now only the DB pod can run on that node. The effect matters: NoSchedule only blocks new pods (pods already running there stay put), while NoExecute additionally evicts already-running pods that lack a matching toleration.

📝 Taints & Tolerations YAML — Dedicated Database Node
Node Taint + Pod Toleration = Reserved Node
  # 1. Taint the node (admin):
  kubectl taint nodes db-node-1 dedicated=database:NoSchedule
  
  # 2. Pod tolerates the taint:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  spec:
    tolerations:
    - key: "dedicated"
      operator: "Equal"
      value: "database"
      effect: "NoSchedule"
  
  # Result: Only pods with this toleration can run on db-node-1
  # All other pods (web, api) are repelled!
Troubleshooting Q27 of 200
What does kubectl top node show, and what must be installed for it to work?
A) It shows CPU and memory usage per node. Requires metrics-server to be installed — without it, you get "error: Metrics API not available"
B) It shows the top 10 busiest pods on each node
C) It shows network bandwidth usage
D) It shows disk I/O statistics
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl top requires metrics-server. Check: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics-server. If missing, install: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml. Current metrics-server releases (v0.6.0+) collect from the kubelet's /metrics/resource endpoint every 15s; only older metrics-server versions used the legacy /stats/summary Summary API.

📝 metrics-server — Architecture & Troubleshooting
How kubectl top Gets Its Data
  kubectl top node/pod
       │
       ▼
  API Server (metrics.k8s.io API)
       │
       ▼
  metrics-server pod (kube-system)
       │  (every 15s)
       ▼
  Kubelet metrics endpoint (:10250/metrics/resource; legacy versions use /stats/summary)
       │
       ▼
  cAdvisor (container metrics)
  
  Check: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics-server
  Fix: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
Troubleshooting Q28 of 200
What causes the OOMKilled (exit code 137) status on a pod?
A) The pod requested more CPU than available
B) The pod image is corrupted
C) Someone ran kubectl delete pod --force
D) The container exceeded its memory limit. The Linux kernel's OOM (Out-Of-Memory) killer terminated the process with SIGKILL (128+9=137). Check kubectl describe pod for "OOMKilled" in the State section
✅ Correct Answer: D

Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). The pod used more memory than its resources.limits.memory. Fix: increase the memory limit, or optimize the application (e.g., reduce Django worker memory, add swap awareness). This per-container cgroup OOM kill is independent of QoS class — QoS only governs a separate mechanism, kubelet's node-pressure eviction, which picks BestEffort pods first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed, when the whole node (not just one container) is short on memory.

📝 QoS Classes — Eviction Priority Under Memory Pressure
OOM Killer Eviction Order
  QoS CLASS          REQUEST vs LIMIT       EVICTION PRIORITY
  ─────────         ─────────────────       ─────────────────
  BestEffort        No requests/limits      1st to die 💀
                    (any excess usage)
  
  Burstable         requests < limits       2nd to die ⚠️
                    (pod using more than
                     its request)
  
  Guaranteed        requests = limits       LAST to die ✅
                    (for both CPU+Mem)
  
  For easypj-db: Set requests.memory = limits.memory
  → Guaranteed QoS → Protected from OOM eviction!
Troubleshooting Q29 of 200
Where are container logs stored on a Kubernetes worker node?
A) Inside the container at /var/log/app.log — that's the only location
B) On the node at /var/log/containers/ and /var/log/pods/. The kubelet symlinks container stdout/stderr to these directories using the container runtime's log driver
C) In etcd as part of the pod's state
D) In a cloud logging service — Kubernetes doesn't store logs locally
✅ Correct Answer: B

The full path: /var/log/containers/<pod>_<namespace>_<container>.log → symlink → /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>/<container>/*.log. These are managed by the container runtime (containerd/Docker) and symlinked by kubelet for easy access.

📝 Container Log Path — Where Logs Live on the Node
Log File Path Structure
  /var/log/containers/
    easypj-api-xxx_easypj_web-<hash>.log  → symlink → 
  /var/log/pods/
    easypj_easypj-api-xxx/web/
      0.log    ← Container stdout (rotated: 0.log, 1.log, ...)
  
  # Direct access (on the node):
  tail -f /var/log/containers/easypj-api-*.log
  
  # Cleanup old logs:
  find /var/log/containers -mtime +7 -delete

Rotation is kubelet-managed: containerLogMaxSize (default 10Mi) and containerLogMaxFiles (default 5) control when a log file rotates and how many old ones are kept. kubectl logs only ever shows the current (latest) file — if a container has logged more than fits in one rotation, older lines are gone from kubectl logs even before containerLogMaxFiles is reached.

Troubleshooting Q30 of 200
You need to drain worker-1 for maintenance but DaemonSet pods (like the CNI plugin) are blocking the drain. What flag solves this?
A) --force
B) --delete-all-pods
C) --ignore-daemonsets — DaemonSet pods are managed separately and will be recreated on the node after uncordon
D) --skip-daemonsets-verification
✅ Correct Answer: C

DaemonSets place one pod per node. Draining a node means evicting pods — but DaemonSet pods would just be recreated immediately by the DaemonSet controller. --ignore-daemonsets skips them. Typical drain command: kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

📝 DaemonSet Drain — Why --ignore-daemonsets Is Needed
DaemonSet Pods Are Managed Differently
  kubectl drain worker-1
  ❌ Error: cannot delete DaemonSet pods (use --ignore-daemonsets)
  
  Why? DaemonSet controller recreates evicted pods immediately:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Drain evicts calico-node-xxx  → DaemonSet recreates  │
  │   calico-node-yyy on worker-1 (infinite loop!)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  # Correct drain command:
  kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
Troubleshooting Q31 of 200
What happens when containerd (the container runtime) on a worker node stops running?
A) The node eventually becomes NotReady. Existing pods continue running (processes stay alive) but no new pods can be created. The node controller (in kube-controller-manager) marks the node NotReady once kubelet's heartbeats stop for longer than node-monitor-grace-period (default ~40s)
B) All pods immediately crash and the node is deleted from the cluster
C) Nothing — containers don't need a runtime once they're started
D) Kubernetes automatically installs Docker as a replacement
✅ Correct Answer: A

Running containers keep running (their processes are already forked). But kubelet can't create new pods or report container status, so its heartbeats to the API server stop — after node-monitor-grace-period (~40s) the node controller marks the node NotReady. Check: systemctl status containerd on the node, restart with systemctl restart containerd.

📝 Container Runtime Failure — Impact Assessment
What Stops When containerd Goes Down
  containerd stops:
  
  ✅ Existing containers KEEP RUNNING (processes already started)
  ❌ kubelet can't create NEW pods (ImagePullBackOff, CreateContainerError)
  ❌ kubelet can't report container status (node → NotReady after ~40s grace period)
  ❌ kubectl exec/logs fail (need runtime to access containers)
  
  Fix: ssh worker-1 → systemctl restart containerd
  Check: systemctl status containerd | grep Active
Troubleshooting Q32 of 200
How do you find out WHY a pod was restarted?
A) kubectl logs <pod> --previous is the only way
B) Check the node's /var/log/messages file
C) Restart reasons are not tracked by Kubernetes
D) Use kubectl describe pod and look at the "Last State" section — it shows the reason (OOMKilled, Error, Completed) and exit code. Also check kubectl logs --previous to see the crashed container's logs
✅ Correct Answer: D

The "Last State" in kubectl describe pod is your restart forensics. It shows: Reason (OOMKilled/Error/Completed), Exit Code (137=SIGKILL, 1=app error, 0=normal), and timestamps. Combine with kubectl logs --previous to see what the container was doing right before it died.

📝 Pod Restart Forensics — Reading the Crime Scene
Decoding kubectl describe pod Output
  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-xxx
  ...
  Last State:     Terminated
    Reason:       OOMKilled        ← Out of Memory!
    Exit Code:    137              ← 128 + 9 (SIGKILL)
    Started:      Wed, 04 Jun 10:00
    Finished:     Wed, 04 Jun 10:15  (ran 15 min)
  
  Exit Code Cheat Sheet:
  0   = Normal exit
  1   = Application error
  137 = SIGKILL (OOM or force delete)
  143 = SIGTERM (graceful shutdown)
  
  # See what the pod was doing before it died:
  kubectl logs easypj-api-xxx --previous --tail=50

2.2 Control Plane Component TroubleshootingQ33-Q44

Troubleshooting Q33 of 200
The kube-apiserver is not responding. Where do you find its logs?
A) kubectl logs -n kube-system pod/kube-apiserver
B) If running as a static pod: crictl logs <container-id> or check /var/log/pods/kube-system_kube-apiserver-*/. If running as a systemd service: journalctl -u kube-apiserver
C) The API server doesn't produce logs — only etcd does
D) Check the browser console when accessing the Kubernetes dashboard
✅ Correct Answer: B

In kubeadm clusters, the API server runs as a static pod (manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml). Since it's a pod, crictl logs works (kubeadm clusters use CRI, not Docker). You can also check /var/log/pods/ on the control plane node.

📝 Control Plane Log Locations — Quick Reference
Where to Find Logs for Each Component
  COMPONENT           LOG ACCESS METHOD
  ─────────           ─────────────────────────────────
  kube-apiserver      crictl logs $(crictl ps --name kube-apiserver -q)
                      OR /var/log/pods/kube-system_kube-apiserver-*/
  etcd                crictl logs $(crictl ps --name etcd -q)
  kube-controller-mgr crictl logs $(crictl ps --name kube-controller -q)
  kube-scheduler      crictl logs $(crictl ps --name kube-scheduler -q)
  
  # Alternative: check /var/log/pods/ on control plane node
  ls /var/log/pods/kube-system_kube-apiserver-*/
Troubleshooting Q34 of 200
What is etcd's role in Kubernetes, and what happens if etcd loses quorum?
A) etcd stores container images — if lost, pods can't start
B) etcd is a backup system — losing it has no impact on running pods
C) etcd is the distributed key-value store holding ALL cluster state (pods, services, configs, secrets). If quorum is lost (majority of etcd nodes unreachable), the cluster becomes READ-ONLY — no new resources can be created, modified, or deleted until quorum is restored
D) etcd only stores RBAC rules — everything else is in the kubelet
✅ Correct Answer: C

etcd uses RAFT consensus. Quorum = (N/2)+1 nodes. With 3 etcd nodes, you need 2 for quorum. If 2 fail, the remaining 1 can't elect a leader — cluster is read-only. All kubectl apply/create/delete fail. Running pods continue but no changes are possible.

📝 etcd RAFT Quorum — Why Odd Numbers Matter
Quorum = (N/2)+1 — Minimum Nodes for Consensus
  CLUSTER SIZE    QUORUM NEEDED    CAN TOLERATE FAILURE
  ────────────    ─────────────    ────────────────────
  1 node          1                0 (any failure = down)
  3 nodes         2                1 node failure
  5 nodes         3                2 node failures
  7 nodes         4                3 node failures
  
  With 3 etcd nodes, losing 2 = quorum lost = READ-ONLY cluster
  kubectl apply/create/delete all FAIL until quorum restored
Troubleshooting Q35 of 200
What is a static pod, and how does kubeadm use them?
A) A static pod is defined by a YAML file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. The kubelet watches this directory and manages these pods directly — they are NOT controlled by the API server, scheduler, or any controller. kubeadm uses static pods for all control plane components (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager)
B) Static pods are pods that never restart
C) Static pods are created via kubectl but never deleted
D) Static pods are pods with fixed IP addresses
✅ Correct Answer: A

This is why control plane components appear as pods in kubectl get pods -n kube-system — the kubelet creates a mirror pod in the API server to represent each static pod. The name always ends with the node hostname (e.g., kube-apiserver-controlplane).

📝 Static Pods — How kubelet Manages Control Plane
Static Pod Lifecycle
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
    kube-apiserver.yaml      ← kubelet watches this directory
    etcd.yaml                ← Any YAML added here → pod created
    kube-controller-manager.yaml  ← YAML removed → pod deleted
    kube-scheduler.yaml
  
  kubelet creates "mirror pods" in API server:
  kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controlplane
  kube-apiserver-controlplane     (mirror of static pod)
  
  To restart a control plane component:
  mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /tmp/
  sleep 5
  mv /tmp/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
Troubleshooting Q36 of 200
How does the kube-scheduler decide which node to place a new pod on?
A) It picks the node with the lowest CPU usage
B) It randomly assigns pods to nodes in round-robin order
C) It asks etcd which node has the most free disk space
D) It uses a two-phase process: (1) FILTERING — eliminate nodes that can't run the pod (insufficient resources, taint mismatch, node selector mismatch), then (2) SCORING — rank remaining nodes by priority (least requested resources, pod affinity, topology spread)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Filtering (predicates): NodeHasSufficientCPU, NodeHasSufficientMemory, MatchNodeSelector, NoVolumeZoneConflict, ToleratesTaint. Scoring (priorities): LeastRequestedPriority, BalancedResourceAllocation, NodeAffinityPriority, InterPodAffinityPriority. Highest score wins. Note: these predicate/priority names are the legacy Scheduling Policy API — the modern scheduler implements the same two phases as named plugins (e.g. NodeResourcesFit at Filter, NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation at Score) under the Scheduling Framework.

📝 Scheduler — Filtering + Scoring Algorithm
How the Scheduler Picks a Node
  PHASE 1: FILTERING (Predicates) — Eliminate unfit nodes
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ NodeHasSufficientCPU    → Remove nodes without CPU     │
  │ NodeHasSufficientMemory → Remove nodes without RAM     │
  │ MatchNodeSelector       → Remove nodes without label   │
  │ NoVolumeZoneConflict    → Remove wrong AZ              │
  │ ToleratesTaint          → Remove tainted nodes         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  PHASE 2: SCORING (Priorities) — Rank remaining nodes
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ LeastRequestedPriority  → Favor less-busy nodes        │
  │ BalancedAllocation      → Favor balanced CPU/Mem       │
  │ NodeAffinityPriority    → Favor matching affinities    │
  │ InterPodAffinityPriority → Favor pod affinity matches  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Highest score wins → Pod scheduled to that node!
Troubleshooting Q37 of 200
How do you check if Kubernetes certificates are about to expire?
A) openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt -text
B) kubeadm certs check-expiration — shows all certificates and their expiry dates. Certificates typically expire after 1 year. Renew with kubeadm certs renew all
C) kubectl get certificates
D) Certificates never expire in Kubernetes — they auto-renew
✅ Correct Answer: B

Expired certificates = cluster down. The API server, kubelet, and etcd all use TLS certificates. After 1 year, they expire and components can't communicate. kubeadm certs check-expiration is your warning system. Any kubeadm upgrade apply/kubeadm upgrade node run also auto-renews all kubeadm-managed certs on that node by default (this isn't gated to a specific version) — routine version upgrades double as certificate renewal, unless you opt out with --certificate-renewal=false.

📝 Certificate Management — Check & Renew
Certificate Expiration Commands
  # Check all certificate expirations:
  kubeadm certs check-expiration
  
  OUTPUT:
  CERTIFICATE                    EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL
  admin.conf                     Jun 04, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
  apiserver                      Jun 04, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
  apiserver-etcd-client          Jun 04, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
  
  # Renew ALL certificates:
  kubeadm certs renew all
  
  # After renewal, restart control plane:
  # (kubelet auto-restarts static pods when it detects changes)
Troubleshooting Q38 of 200
What is the difference between kubectl get componentstatuses (or kubectl get cs) and checking control plane health directly?
A) There is no difference — they are the same command
