Cluster Arch Q118 of 200
What is kube-proxy's actual job? (Hint: it's NOT a proxy!)
A) kube-proxy is a RULE PROGRAMMER — it watches Services and EndpointSlices, then writes iptables/IPVS rules on each node. Traffic goes directly from pod to pod via kernel rules — kube-proxy does NOT sit in the data path
B) kube-proxy is a forward proxy that all pod traffic passes through
C) kube-proxy is a reverse proxy that terminates TLS for Services
D) kube-proxy is a DNS proxy that resolves Service names
✅ Correct Answer: A

kube-proxy writes rules, not routes traffic. In iptables mode: pod sends packet to Service ClusterIP → kernel iptables DNAT rewrites destination to random backend pod IP → packet goes directly to backend pod. kube-proxy never touches the packet!

kube-proxy — Rule Programmer, NOT a Proxy
  kube-proxy DOES NOT sit in the data path!

  ┌─────────┐                    ┌─────────┐
  │ Pod A   │──packet──────────▶│ Pod B   │
  │10.244.1.5│  dst: 10.96.0.10  │10.244.2.7│
  └─────────┘                    └─────────┘
       │                              ▲
       │                              │
       ▼                              │
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ LINUX KERNEL (iptables/IPVS rules)  │
  │                                     │
  │ Rule (written by kube-proxy):       │
  │   DNAT 10.96.0.10:80               │
  │   → 10.244.2.7:8080 (random pod)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
                   ▲
                   │ watches Services + EndpointSlices
              ┌────┴─────┐
              │kube-proxy│ (writes rules, then STAYS OUT)
              └──────────┘

  iptables mode: O(n) chain traversal (slow with many Services)
  IPVS mode:    Hash-table lookup (O(1)) — now deprecated in favor
                of the newer nftables mode
Cluster Arch Q119 of 200
What does the kube-scheduler do when a new pod needs placement?
A) Randomly assigns the pod to any available node
B) Places the pod on the node with the lowest CPU usage
C) Asks etcd which node has the most free memory
D) FILTERING (eliminate nodes that can't run the pod) → SCORING (rank remaining nodes by fitness) → BINDING (assign pod to highest-scoring node via API server)
✅ Correct Answer: D

This three-phase pipeline runs for every unscheduled pod. Filtering removes nodes that flat-out can't work (insufficient resources, taints without tolerations); scoring ranks what's left; binding writes the pod-to-node assignment back to the API server as an atomic Binding object rather than instructing the node directly.

📝 Scheduler Algorithm
Filter → Score → Bind
  Phase 1: FILTERING (Predicates)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PodFitsResources (CPU/RAM sufficient?) │
  │ MatchNodeSelector (label match?)       │
  │ NoVolumeZoneConflict (same AZ?)        │
  │ ToleratesTaint (toleration match?)     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘
  → Unsuitable nodes eliminated
  
  Phase 2: SCORING (Priorities)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ LeastRequestedPriority (less busy = higher)│
  │ BalancedResourceAllocation              │
  │ NodeAffinityPriority                    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘
  → Remaining nodes ranked 0-10
  
  Phase 3: BINDING
  → Highest-scoring node gets the pod!

A) It only manages Deployments and nothing else
B) It's a backup for the API server — takes over if API server fails
C) It runs multiple controllers as a single process: Node controller (monitors node health), Replication controller (ensures correct pod count), EndpointSlice controller (populates EndpointSlice objects linking Services to Pods), ServiceAccount controller (creates default SAs), and many more
D) It controls the container runtime on each node
✅ Correct Answer: C

Despite the singular name, kube-controller-manager is really a bundle of independent control loops compiled into one binary and process for efficiency. Each controller watches the API server for changes to its resource type and reconciles actual state toward desired state — this reconcile loop is the core pattern behind almost everything in Kubernetes.

Key Controllers in kube-controller-manager
  CONTROLLER              WHAT IT DOES
  ─────────              ────────────
  Node Controller         Monitors node health (--node-monitor-period)
                          Marks node NotReady after --node-monitor-grace-period
  Replication Controller  Ensures correct # of pods per ReplicaSet
  EndpointSlice Ctrl      Populates EndpointSlices for Services (pod IP:port)
  ServiceAccount Ctrl     Creates default SA per namespace, manages tokens
  Deployment Controller   Manages rollout/rollback of Deployments
  Job Controller          Manages Job/CronJob execution
  Garbage Collector       Removes objects whose owner no longer exists

Cluster Arch Q121 of 200
What happens when you run kubeadm init? (Step by step)
A) It only installs Docker and kubectl
B) Preflight checks → Generate CA + certs → Create kubeconfig files → Generate static pod manifests → Start etcd + API server + controller + scheduler as static pods → Upload kubeadm/kubelet ConfigMaps → Bootstrap tokens for worker joins
C) It downloads container images and starts all pods as Deployments
D) It connects to an existing etcd cluster and joins as a worker node
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubeadm init is really a scripted sequence, not a single action — it's worth memorizing the order since kubeadm upgrade and kubeadm join follow similar patterns. Note that etcd and the control plane components are bootstrapped as static pods (managed directly by kubelet from manifests on disk), which is exactly why they can start before the API server itself exists.

kubeadm init — Step by Step
  kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
  
  [preflight]     Check root, CPU, memory, disk, container runtime
  [certs]         Generate CA + apiserver/etcd/kubelet certs
  [kubeconfig]    admin.conf, kubelet.conf, controller-manager.conf
  [control-plane] Static pod manifests → /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  [etcd]          Start etcd as static pod
  [apiserver]     Start kube-apiserver as static pod
  [mark-control]  Taint: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
  [bootstrap]     Generate token for kubeadm join
  [addons]        Install CoreDNS + kube-proxy

What is --pod-network-cidr and why must you specify it during kubeadm init?
A) It sets the IP address of the API server
B) It configures the node's hostname
C) It defines the IP range for pods. CNI plugins need this to allocate pod IPs — Calico uses 192.168.0.0/16, Flannel uses 10.244.0.0/16. Without it, CNI plugins can't properly configure pod networking
D) It sets the Service ClusterIP range
✅ Correct Answer: C

Every CNI plugin needs a pool of IP addresses to hand out to pods, and --pod-network-cidr is how you tell kubeadm which range to use. Get this wrong — or forget to match it in the CNI YAML you apply afterward — and CoreDNS and every other pod will sit in Pending/ContainerCreating forever waiting for an IP.

CNI CIDR Compatibility

  ──────────    ────────────        ───────
  Calico        192.168.0.0/16      kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16
  Flannel       10.244.0.0/16       kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
  Cilium        10.0.0.0/8          kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.0.0.0/8
  Weave         10.32.0.0/12        kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.32.0.0/12
  
  After init: kubectl apply -f <cni-manifest-url>

How does kubeadm join work? What information does the worker need?
A) Two pieces: (1) API server address + port, (2) Bootstrap token + CA cert hash (for TLS verification). kubeadm join --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash> <api-server-ip>:6443
B) Only the cluster name — everything else is auto-discovered
C) SSH credentials for the control plane node
D) The kubeconfig file from the control plane copied directly
✅ Correct Answer: A

The bootstrap token authenticates the new node just long enough to fetch the cluster CA certificate; the CA cert hash lets the joining node verify it's actually talking to the real API server, protecting against a man-in-the-middle during join. Once joined, the kubelet automatically requests and receives a real client certificate, and the temporary token is no longer needed.

kubeadm join — Worker Node Bootstrap
  # ON CONTROL PLANE (generate token):
  kubeadm token create --print-join-command
  
  # ON WORKER (run the output):
  kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 \
    --token abc123.def456 \
    --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash \
    sha256:1a2b3c...
  
  # Tokens expire in 24 hours!
  # List tokens: kubeadm token list
  # Create new:   kubeadm token create

How do you check when Kubernetes certificates expire?
A) openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt -text -noout | grep "Not After"

✅ Correct Answer: D

kubeadm-managed clusters default to 1-year certificate validity, and an expired API server cert can lock you out of your own cluster with almost no warning — this is a genuinely common real-world outage, not just exam trivia. Run kubeadm certs check-expiration proactively, and know that kubeadm upgrade apply also silently renews all certs as a side effect.

  admin.conf                     Jun 04, 2027

  apiserver-etcd-client          Jun 04, 2027

Cluster Arch Q125 of 200
How do you upgrade a kubeadm cluster from v1.28 to v1.29?
A) kubectl apply -f upgrade.yaml
B) (1) Upgrade kubeadm package: apt-get install kubeadm=1.29.x. (2) kubeadm upgrade plan → kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.x on control plane. (3) Drain control plane node. (4) Upgrade kubelet + kubectl. (5) Uncordon. (6) Repeat for each worker node
C) Delete and recreate the cluster with new version
D) kubeadm init --upgrade v1.29
✅ Correct Answer: B

Kubernetes only supports upgrading one minor version at a time (e.g. 1.28→1.29, never 1.27→1.29 directly), and the control plane must be upgraded before any worker nodes. The version skew policy is exactly why the drain-upgrade-uncordon cycle happens node-by-node rather than all at once.

kubeadm Upgrade — Full Workflow
  CONTROL PLANE:
  apt-mark unhold kubeadm && apt-get install kubeadm=1.29.x
  kubeadm upgrade plan
  kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.x
  kubectl drain cp-node --ignore-daemonsets
  apt-get install kubelet=1.29.x kubectl=1.29.x
  systemctl restart kubelet
  kubectl uncordon cp-node
  
  WORKER NODES (one at a time):
  kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  apt-get install kubeadm=1.29.x && kubeadm upgrade node
  apt-get install kubelet=1.29.x && systemctl restart kubelet
  kubectl uncordon worker-1
  
  Version skew: kube-apiserver can be +/- 1 minor version from kubelet

        - "lb.example.com"

Cluster Arch Q131 of 200
What are the two HA control plane topologies?
A) Stacked etcd (etcd runs on same nodes as control plane — simpler, fewer nodes) vs External etcd (etcd runs on separate dedicated nodes — more complex, better failure isolation)
B) Active-Passive and Active-Active only
C) Single-node and dual-node — three nodes is not supported
D) Cloud and on-premises — the topology is determined by the provider
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubeadm defaults to the stacked topology because it needs fewer machines and is simpler to reason about for exam-sized (and most real) clusters. External etcd trades that simplicity for blast-radius isolation — a control plane node crashing doesn't also take down an etcd member — which matters more as cluster size and etcd's I/O load grow.

Stacked vs External etcd
  STACKED etcd (default)              EXTERNAL etcd
  ┌──────────────────┐              ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │ CP-1              │              │ CP-1     │ │ CP-2     │ │ CP-3     │
  │ ┌──────────────┐  │              │ apiserver│ │ apiserver│ │ apiserver│
  │ │apiserver     │  │              └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘
  │ │controller-mgr│  │                   │           │           │
  │ │scheduler     │  │              ┌────▼─────┐ ┌───▼─────┐ ┌───▼─────┐
  │ │etcd ⬅──local  │              │ etcd-1   │ │ etcd-2  │ │ etcd-3  │
  │ └──────────────┘  │              └──────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘
  └──────────────────┘
  
  kubeadm default: Stacked (3 control planes = 3 etcd members)
  Production recommendation: External etcd for large clusters (>100 nodes)

How do you back up etcd?
A) kubectl backup etcd
B) Copy /var/lib/etcd/member/snap/ to another directory
C) ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
D) etcd automatically backs up to S3
✅ Correct Answer: C

etcd backup is a point-in-time snapshot of the entire cluster state. Verify: etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot.db. Restore: etcdctl snapshot restore. Schedule regular backups (daily minimum) and store off-node.

etcd Backup & Restore — CKA Exam Essential
  BACKUP:
  ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
    --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
    --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
    --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

  VERIFY:
  etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot.db
  → Hash: aa3b..., Revision: 54321, TotalKeys: 15234

  RESTORE:
  etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
    --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored

  THEN update /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
    volumes:
    - hostPath:
        path: /var/lib/etcd-restored  # ← point to restored data

  Schedule: Daily cron job, store off-node (S3/GCS)
Cluster Arch Q134 of 200
How do you restore etcd from a snapshot?
A) etcdutl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored (etcdutl, not etcdctl, is the documented tool for restoring — etcdctl remains the tool for snapshot save). Then update the etcd static pod manifest to use the new data-dir. All API server data (pods, services, etc.) is restored
B) kubectl apply -f etcd-snapshot.yaml
C) Reboot the control plane node — etcd auto-recovers
D) Delete and recreate the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: A

Restore procedure: (1) Stop API server (move manifest out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests/). (2) etcdutl snapshot restore. (3) Update etcd.yaml to point to restored data-dir. (4) kubelet restarts etcd with restored data. (5) Restore API server manifest.

Full etcd Restore Procedure — Step by Step
  STEP 1: Stop kube-apiserver (it writes to etcd!)
  mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
  → kubelet detects removal → stops apiserver pod

  STEP 2: Restore the snapshot (etcdutl, NOT etcdctl, does restores)
  etcdutl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db \
    --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored \
    --name=cp-1 \
    --initial-cluster=cp-1=https://cp-1:2380 \
    --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://cp-1:2380

  STEP 3: Update etcd manifest
  sed -i 's|/var/lib/etcd|/var/lib/etcd-restored|' \
    /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
  → kubelet restarts etcd with restored data

  STEP 4: Restore API server
  mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  → kubelet restarts apiserver → cluster is BACK!
Cluster Arch Q135 of 200
What is the Kubernetes version skew policy?
A) All components must be exactly the same version
B) Only the API server version matters — other components can be any version
C) Any combination of versions is supported
D) kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver, but may be up to 3 minor versions older (e.g. apiserver v1.28 → kubelet v1.25 through v1.28, never v1.29). kubectl can be +/- 1 minor version from apiserver. This allows rolling upgrades without downtime
✅ Correct Answer: D

Example: API server v1.28 → kubelet can be v1.25, v1.26, v1.27, or v1.28 (never v1.29 — kubelet must never be newer than the apiserver). This allows upgrading control plane first, then workers one at a time while the cluster remains operational throughout.

Kubernetes Version Skew Policy
  VERSION SKEW MATRIX (v1.28 example)
  ┌─────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
  │ COMPONENT       │ ALLOWED VERSION RANGE     │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ kube-apiserver  │ v1.28 (reference)         │
  │ kube-controller │ v1.25 – v1.28             │
  │ kube-scheduler  │ v1.25 – v1.28             │
  │ kubelet         │ v1.25 – v1.28             │
  │                 │ (up to 3 minor older;     │
  │                 │  never newer than apiserver)│
  │ kube-proxy      │ v1.25 – v1.28             │
  │ kubectl         │ v1.27, v1.28, v1.29       │
  └─────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

  RULE: kube-apiserver version = X
        kubelet/controller-manager/scheduler/kube-proxy: X down to X-3, never newer than X
        kubectl: X-1 to X+1 (the one component allowed to run AHEAD)

  This allows: Upgrade CP → then workers one-by-one
Cluster Arch Q136 of 200
Why must you drain a node before upgrading it?
A) To save electricity
B) Draining safely evicts pods to other nodes. This prevents application downtime — pods keep running on other nodes while you upgrade the kubelet on this one. Uncordon only marks the node schedulable again for NEW pods — it doesn't move the original evicted pods back
C) Draining is optional — kubectl does it automatically
D) To clean up disk space before upgrade
✅ Correct Answer: B

Without draining: pods crash when kubelet restarts, causing service disruption. With draining: pods move to other nodes first, kubelet restarts on the now-empty node. Uncordon doesn't bring the original pods back — it just re-enables scheduling, so future replicas (or a future rollout) can land there again. PDBs ensure minimum replicas survive during the drain.

Node Upgrade Flow — Drain → Upgrade → Uncordon
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          SAFE NODE UPGRADE PROCEDURE                 │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │                                                      │
  │  1. CORDON:                                          │
  │     kubectl cordon worker-1                          │
  │     → Node marked Unschedulable (🚧 no new pods)     │
  │                                                      │
  │  2. DRAIN:                                           │
  │     kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets \     │
  │       --delete-emptydir-data                         │
  │     → Pods gracefully evicted to other nodes         │
  │                                                      │
  │  3. UPGRADE:                                         │
  │     apt-get install kubeadm=1.29.x                   │
  │     kubeadm upgrade node                             │
  │     apt-get install kubelet=1.29.x                   │
  │     systemctl restart kubelet                        │
  │                                                      │
  │  4. UNCORDON:                                        │
  │     kubectl uncordon worker-1                        │
  │     → ✅ Node schedulable again for NEW pods only    │
  │        (original evicted pods do NOT come back)      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Cluster Arch Q137 of 200
What happens if 2 out of 3 etcd nodes fail?
A) The remaining node takes over as leader — continues normally
B) Kubernetes automatically provisions 2 new etcd nodes
C) QUORUM LOST — the remaining node cannot elect itself as leader (needs 2/3 votes). Cluster becomes READ-ONLY — no kubectl create/apply/delete works. Running pods continue but no new changes possible
D) The cluster crashes entirely — all pods stop running
✅ Correct Answer: C

This is why etcd needs special care: fast disks (SSD, 500+ IOPS), regular backups, monitoring (disk latency, leader changes). Running etcd on overloaded nodes or slow disks causes frequent leader elections — performance killer.

etcd Quorum — What Happens When Nodes Fail
  3-NODE etcd CLUSTER (Quorum = 2)

  ALL 3 HEALTHY (✓ quorum):
  ┌────┐  ┌────┐  ┌────┐
  │ L  │  │ F  │  │ F  │   Reads/Writes: ✅ OK
  └────┘  └────┘  └────┘

  1 NODE DOWN (✓ quorum, 2/3):
  ┌────┐  ┌────┐  ┌────┐
  │ L  │  │ F  │  │ ❌  │   Reads/Writes: ✅ OK
  └────┘  └────┘  └────┘   Can tolerate 1 failure!

  2 NODES DOWN (✗ quorum, 1/3):
  ┌────┐  ┌────┐  ┌────┐
  │ L  │  │ ❌  │  │ ❌  │   Reads/Writes: ❌ FAILED
  └────┘  └────┘  └────┘   CLUSTER READ-ONLY!
                           1 node can't elect itself leader
                           (needs 2 votes for quorum)

  FORMULA: N nodes → tolerates (N-1)/2 failures
  3→1, 5→2, 7→3 (always use ODD numbers!)

B) Pods that never move between nodes

Cluster Arch Q140 of 200
How do multiple API servers in an HA setup stay synchronized?
A) They sync state between each other via a gossip protocol
B) All API servers READ and WRITE to the SAME etcd cluster. API servers are stateless — they just proxy requests to etcd. Multiple API servers don't need to sync with each other because the truth is in etcd
C) Only one API server is active at a time — others are standby
D) They use a shared cache that replicates across nodes
✅ Correct Answer: B

API servers are stateless. They all connect to etcd. A kubectl apply to API server 1 writes to etcd → API server 2 reading from etcd sees the new data immediately (via etcd watch). The load balancer distributes requests across all API servers.

Stateless API Servers — Single Source of Truth
  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐
  │ API-1    │   │ API-2    │   │ API-3    │
  │(stateless)│   │(stateless)│   │(stateless)│
  └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘
       │              │              │
       └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                      │ all read/write
                      ▼
              ┌───────────────┐
              │     etcd      │ ← SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH
              │  (all state)  │
              └───────────────┘

  kubectl apply → LB → API-1 → write to etcd
  kubectl get   → LB → API-2 → read from etcd (sees the update!)

  API servers are:
  ✓ Stateless (no local cache that matters)
  ✓ Identical (any can serve any request)
  ✓ Horizontally scalable (add more for read throughput)

4.4 RBAC & SecurityQ141-Q150

Cluster Arch Q141 of 200
What are the four actions in the API request pipeline? (AuthN → AuthZ → Admission → etcd)
A) Encrypt → Compress → Store → Respond
B) Authentication (WHO are you? — certs, tokens, OIDC) → Authorization (WHAT can you do? — RBAC, Node, Webhook) → Admission Control (IS this valid? — mutating/validating webhooks) → Persist to etcd
C) Validate → Route → Execute → Log
D) Login → Verify → Allow → Deny
✅ Correct Answer: B

Every kubectl command passes through Authentication and Authorization in order — Authentication only proves identity; it grants nothing. Authorization (RBAC in almost all real clusters) decides if that identity may perform the verb. Admission Control only applies to write requests (create/update/patch/delete/connect) — read-only get/list/watch requests bypass it entirely, since there's nothing to mutate or validate before persisting. This is why a write can pass RBAC and still fail against, say, a ResourceQuota or a validating webhook, while an equivalent read never even reaches that stage.

API Request Pipeline
  kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
  │
  ▼
  API SERVER
  │
  ├─ 1. AUTHENTICATION (Who?)
  │   ├─ X.509 client certificate
  │   ├─ Bearer token (ServiceAccount token)
  │   ├─ OpenID Connect (OIDC)
  │   └─ Webhook token authentication
  │
  ├─ 2. AUTHORIZATION (Can?)
  │   ├─ RBAC (Role + RoleBinding / ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding)
  │   ├─ Node authorizer (kubelet permissions)
  │   ├─ ABAC (Attribute-Based — legacy)
  │   └─ Webhook authorization
  │
  ├─ 3. ADMISSION CONTROL (Valid?)
  │   ├─ MutatingAdmissionWebhook (inject sidecar)
  │   ├─ ValidatingAdmissionWebhook (policy check)
  │   ├─ LimitRanger (enforce resource limits)
  │   └─ ResourceQuota (enforce namespace quotas)
  │
  └─ 4. PERSIST to etcd

  │ apiVersion: rbac/v1 │       │ apiVersion: rbac/v1      │
  │ kind: Role           │       │ kind: ClusterRole        │
  │ metadata:            │       │ metadata:                 │
  │   namespace: dev     │       │   name: pod-reader       │
  │   name: pod-reader   │       │   (NO namespace!)        │
  │ rules:               │       │ rules:                    │
  │ - apiGroups: [""]    │       │ - apiGroups: [""]        │
  │   resources: [pods]  │       │   resources: [nodes]     │
  │   verbs: [get,list]  │       │   verbs: [get,list]      │

Cluster Arch Q143 of 200
You need to grant user 'alice' permission to create and list pods in namespace 'frontend'. What resources do you create?
A) (1) Create a Role in namespace 'frontend' with rules: apiGroups:[""], resources:["pods"], verbs:["create","get","list","watch"]. (2) Create a RoleBinding that binds this Role to user 'alice' in the same namespace
B) Create only a ClusterRole — Roles don't support pods
C) Add alice to the 'admin' group — RBAC is not needed
D) Create a ServiceAccount for alice — users can't be bound directly
✅ Correct Answer: A

A Role only defines permissions; nothing happens until a RoleBinding attaches it to a subject (user, group, or ServiceAccount). Both the Role and RoleBinding must live in the same namespace as the resources you're granting access to — a Role in 'frontend' has zero effect on pods in any other namespace.

RBAC: Role + RoleBinding for Alice
# role-pod-editor.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: frontend
  name: pod-editor
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["create", "get", "list", "watch", "update", "delete"]
---
# rolebinding-alice.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  namespace: frontend
  name: alice-pod-editor
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-editor
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

D) Read the RoleBinding YAML — kubectl can't check permissions
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl auth can-i is the permission checker. Use --as to impersonate any user/SA. Use --list to see all permissions. Remember: a user might have permission via multiple RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings.

kubectl auth can-i — Permission Checker
  # Check if user bob can delete deployments in prod
  kubectl auth can-i delete deployments --as=bob -n prod
  → yes / no
  
  # Check specific resource
  kubectl auth can-i get pod/nginx --as=bob -n prod
  
  # Check all permissions for current user
  kubectl auth can-i --list
  
  # Check as a ServiceAccount
  kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:ci-bot
  
  # Useful for debugging RBAC: impersonate and test!
  kubectl get pods --as=bob -n prod
Cluster Arch Q145 of 200
What is a ServiceAccount and how is it different from a regular user?
A) ServiceAccounts are for human users, regular users are for pods
B) ServiceAccounts are Kubernetes-managed identities for PODS (not humans). Each pod runs with a SA. The SA token is mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. SA is a namespaced resource; User is external (managed by cluster admin via certs/OIDC)
C) They are different names for the same thing
D) ServiceAccounts are deprecated — use Users instead
✅ Correct Answer: B

Every namespace has a 'default' SA. Creating a pod without specifying SA → uses default SA. Each SA gets a token Secret (auto-mounted). Use RBAC to grant SA permissions: Role or ClusterRole bound to the ServiceAccount.

ServiceAccount vs User
  SERVICEACCOUNT (for PODS)          USER (for HUMANS)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Created by: YAML/kubectl│       │ Managed externally:  │
  │ Namespaced: YES          │       │   X.509 certs        │
  │ Token: auto-mounted at   │       │   OIDC (Google/GitHub)│
  │   /var/run/secrets/...   │       │   Webhook            │
  │                          │       │ Namespaced: NO       │
  │ kubectl create sa ci-bot│       │                      │
  │                          │       │ kubectl config set-  │
  │ Every ns has 'default' SA│       │   credentials bob ...│
  └─────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────┘
Cluster Arch Q146 of 200
What does kubectl create clusterrolebinding do?
A) Creates a new namespace
B) Binds a Role to a ServiceAccount in a specific namespace
C) Creates a new cluster
D) Binds a ClusterRole to a user, group, or ServiceAccount CLUSTER-WIDE. kubectl create clusterrolebinding read-nodes --clusterrole=view --user=bob gives bob read-only access to ALL nodes in the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: D

ClusterRoleBinding grants the ClusterRole permissions across ALL namespaces (and for cluster-scoped resources). RoleBinding grants a Role (namespace-scoped) or ClusterRole (cluster-scoped but restricted to one namespace) in a SINGLE namespace.

RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding
  RoleBinding                         ClusterRoleBinding
  ┌────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ Binds: Role or         │         │ Binds: ClusterRole ONLY    │
  │   ClusterRole          │         │                             │
  │ Scope: SINGLE namespace│         │ Scope: ALL namespaces +    │
  │                        │         │   cluster-scoped resources │
  │ kubectl create         │         │                             │
  │   rolebinding ...      │         │ kubectl create             │
  │   -n dev               │         │   clusterrolebinding ...   │
  └────────────────────────┘         └────────────────────────────┘
  
  KEY: Binding a ClusterRole via RoleBinding → ClusterRole
       permissions restricted to that ONE namespace!
Cluster Arch Q147 of 200
What are the built-in ClusterRoles? (Hint: view, edit, admin, cluster-admin)
A) view = read-only on most resources, but NOT Secrets (prevents reading ServiceAccount tokens). edit = view + modify (includes Secrets — but still can't modify RBAC). admin = edit + manage RBAC in a namespace. cluster-admin = superuser — can do anything including delete nodes
B) There are no built-in ClusterRoles — all must be created manually
C) view/edit/admin are namespaced Roles, not ClusterRoles
D) Only cluster-admin exists — it's the only built-in role
✅ Correct Answer: A

Quick setup: kubectl create rolebinding alice-view --clusterrole=view --user=alice -n dev. This gives alice read-only in dev namespace. Never give cluster-admin to non-admin users — it's the Kubernetes equivalent of root. Note why edit's Secrets access matters: since Secrets hold ServiceAccount tokens, edit effectively lets you impersonate any ServiceAccount in the namespace — that's why view specifically carves Secrets out.

Built-in ClusterRoles
  ROLE           PERMISSIONS              USE CASE
  ────           ───────────              ────────
  view           Read-only on most        Auditors, read-only users
                 resources (NOT secrets)
  edit           view + modify resources  Developers (can't touch RBAC)
                 (NOT RBAC, NOT secrets)
  admin          edit + manage RBAC       Namespace admins
                 within ONE namespace
  cluster-admin  EVERYTHING               Cluster administrators
                 (including delete nodes)  ⚠️ Equivalent to ROOT!
  
  Quick bind: kubectl create rolebinding bob-view \
                --clusterrole=view --user=bob -n dev

What is the difference between Mutating and Validating Admission Webhooks?
A) Both do the same thing — the names are just different
B) Validating webhooks modify resources, Mutating webhooks check them

D) Mutating webhooks are deprecated in favor of Validating webhooks
✅ Correct Answer: C

Order: MutatingAdmissionWebhook → Object is modified → ValidatingAdmissionWebhook → final object is checked. If any validating webhook denies → request is rejected. If any mutating webhook fails → request is rejected.

Mutating vs Validating Webhooks
  API REQUEST
  │
  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. MUTATING WEBHOOKS (runs 1st) │
  │    Can MODIFY the object        │
  │    ├─ Inject sidecar container  │
  │    ├─ Add default tolerations   │
  │    └─ Add labels/annotations    │
  └────────────┬────────────────────┘
               │ modified object
               ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 2. VALIDATING WEBHOOKS (2nd)   │
  │    Can ACCEPT or DENY           │
  │    ├─ Enforce image registry    │
  │    ├─ Check security policies   │
  │    └─ Validate resource limits  │
  └────────────┬────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
          etcd (if all pass)
Cluster Arch Q149 of 200
How do you create a ClusterRole that allows reading Secrets, ConfigMaps, and Pods across all namespaces?
A) This can only be done with the 'cluster-admin' ClusterRole
B) Create a ClusterRole with rules for each resource (secrets, configmaps, pods) with verbs: ["get","list","watch"], then bind it with a ClusterRoleBinding. kubectl create clusterrole read-core --verb=get,list,watch --resource=secrets,configmaps,pods
C) Create a Role in each namespace — ClusterRoles can't be used
D) Add the user to the 'system:masters' group
✅ Correct Answer: B

One-liner: kubectl create clusterrole read-core --verb=get,list,watch --resource=secrets,configmaps,pods. Then: kubectl create clusterrolebinding bob-read-core --clusterrole=read-core --user=bob. Bob can now read those resources in all namespaces. Caution: this grants cluster-wide read access to every Secret in every namespace — since Secrets hold ServiceAccount tokens, that's effectively the ability to impersonate any ServiceAccount cluster-wide, broader than even the built-in "view" role allows.

One-Liner: Create Cross-Namespace Read ClusterRole
  kubectl create clusterrole read-core \
    --verb=get,list,watch \
    --resource=secrets,configmaps,pods
  
  kubectl create clusterrolebinding bob-read-core \
    --clusterrole=read-core \
    --user=bob
  
  # Verify:
  kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=bob --all-namespaces
  → yes
  
  kubectl auth can-i delete secrets --as=bob --all-namespaces  
  → no (only get,list,watch granted)
Cluster Arch Q150 of 200
What is the 'system:masters' group and why is it dangerous?
A) system:masters is a group that gets automatically bound to cluster-admin by a built-in ClusterRoleBinding. Anyone in this group has COMPLETE cluster control. The admin certificate generated by kubeadm puts you in this group
B) It's just a display name — no special permissions
C) It's the group for all worker nodes
D) It's a deprecated group replaced by 'cluster-admin'
✅ Correct Answer: A

Built-in ClusterRoleBinding: 'cluster-admin' ClusterRole → 'system:masters' group. kubeadm admin cert: Organization (O) = system:masters. Removing 'system:masters' from the cert would revoke admin access.

system:masters — The Root Group
  Built-in CRB (created by kubeadm):
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ClusterRoleBinding: cluster-admin          │
  │   roleRef:                                 │
  │     kind: ClusterRole                      │
  │     name: cluster-admin                    │
  │   subjects:                                │
  │   - kind: Group                            │
  │     name: system:masters                   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  kubeadm admin cert: O = system:masters
  
  Anyone in system:masters = CLUSTER ROOT!
  Never share admin cert or add users to this group!

4.5 Helm, Kustomize & CRDsQ151-Q160

Cluster Arch Q151 of 200
What is Helm? What are charts, releases, and repositories?
A) Helm is a container runtime alternative to containerd
B) Helm is a monitoring tool similar to Prometheus
C) Helm is the "Kubernetes package manager." Chart = templated Kubernetes YAML files (package). Release = an installed instance of a chart. Repository = where charts are stored (like Docker Hub for Helm). helm install my-nginx bitnami/nginx creates a release named 'my-nginx' from the bitnami repo's nginx chart
D) Helm is a CI/CD tool for Kubernetes
✅ Correct Answer: C

Think of Helm the way you'd think of apt or yum, but for Kubernetes manifests: charts are the installable packages, releases are what you get when you actually install one (and you can have multiple releases of the same chart running side by side), and repositories are just HTTP servers that index available charts.

Helm Architecture
  HELM CLI → Kubernetes API Server
  
  Chart structure:
  nginx/
  ├── Chart.yaml          (metadata: name, version, appVersion)
  ├── values.yaml         (default configuration values)
  ├── templates/          (Go-templated Kubernetes YAML)
  │   ├── deployment.yaml
  │   ├── service.yaml
  │   └── _helpers.tpl    (template helpers)
  └── charts/             (sub-charts / dependencies)
  
  Release lifecycle:
  helm install → helm upgrade → helm rollback → helm uninstall
Cluster Arch Q152 of 200
What is the difference between helm install and helm upgrade?
A) They are the same command — just aliases
B) helm install creates a NEW release. helm upgrade updates an EXISTING release. Use helm upgrade --install (or helm upgrade -i) to create if not exists or upgrade if exists — idempotent for CI/CD
C) helm install is for production, helm upgrade for development
D) helm install only works with Helm 2, helm upgrade with Helm 3
✅ Correct Answer: B

Releases are stored as Secrets (Helm 3). Each upgrade creates a new Secret with the release revision. helm history my-release shows all revisions. helm rollback my-release 2 reverts to revision 2.

Helm Release Lifecycle
  helm install my-app bitnami/nginx
  → Release "my-app" created (Revision 1)
  
  helm upgrade my-app bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount=3
  → Release "my-app" upgraded (Revision 2)
  
  helm upgrade --install my-app bitnami/nginx
  → Creates if not exists, upgrades if exists (idempotent!)
  
  helm rollback my-app 1
  → Rolled back to Revision 1 (creates Revision 3 = copy of 1)
  
  helm history my-app
  REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS      DESCRIPTION
  1         Thu Jun  4 10:00:00 2026  superseded  Install complete
  2         Thu Jun  4 10:05:00 2026  superseded  Upgrade complete
  3         Thu Jun  4 10:10:00 2026  deployed    Rolled back to 1
Cluster Arch Q153 of 200
What is Kustomize and how is it different from Helm?
A) Kustomize replaces kubectl — it's an alternative CLI
B) Kustomize is a templating engine that works exactly like Helm
C) Kustomize is only for managing Secrets
D) Kustomize is DECLARATIVE overlay-based configuration management (built into kubectl: kubectl apply -k). Unlike Helm (templates), Kustomize takes BASE YAML + OVERLAYS (patches) to produce environment-specific configs. No templates — just YAML patching
✅ Correct Answer: D

Helm's templating (Go templates + values.yaml) is powerful but adds a layer of indirection that can be hard to debug. Kustomize deliberately avoids templates entirely — every file is valid, plain YAML, and overlays just patch fields on top of a shared base — which is why it was folded directly into kubectl (kubectl apply -k) instead of needing a separate CLI.

Kustomize: Base + Overlays
  myapp/
  ├── base/
  │   ├── deployment.yaml    (replicas: 2, image: nginx:1.25)
  │   ├── service.yaml
  │   └── kustomization.yaml (resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml])
  │
  └── overlays/
      ├── dev/
      │   ├── kustomization.yaml  (bases: [../../base], replicas: 1)
      │   └── env.yaml            (DEBUG=true)
      └── prod/
          ├── kustomization.yaml  (bases: [../../base], replicas: 10)
          └── env.yaml            (DEBUG=false)
  
  kubectl apply -k overlays/dev/
  kubectl apply -k overlays/prod/
Cluster Arch Q154 of 200
What is a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)?
A) CRD EXTENDS the Kubernetes API. It lets you define your own resource types (e.g., kind: MySQLCluster). Once created, you can kubectl get mysqlclusters, kubectl apply -f mysql.yaml. The CRD defines the schema; a custom controller (operator) implements the logic
B) CRD is a way to define custom container images
C) CRD replaces YAML for Kubernetes configuration
D) CRD is a debugging tool for API server requests
✅ Correct Answer: A

CRD = Custom Resource Definition (the schema). CR = Custom Resource (the instance, e.g., one MySQLCluster named 'prod-db'). Operator = Controller that watches CRs and creates Deployments/PVCs/Services to implement them. Together: CRD + CR + Operator = the Operator Pattern.

CRD + CR + Controller = Operator Pattern
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. CRD (CustomResourceDefinition) — defines schema  │
  │    kubectl apply -f mysql-crd.yaml                  │
  │    → New API: apiVersion: db.example.com/v1         │
  │              kind: MySQLCluster                      │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 2. CR (Custom Resource) — the instance              │
  │    kubectl apply -f my-prod-db.yaml                 │
  │    kind: MySQLCluster, replicas: 3, storage: 100Gi  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 3. Controller (Operator) — watches CR, creates real │
  │    resources: StatefulSet + Service + PVC + Secrets │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  kubectl get mysqlclusters  ← Your custom resource!
  NAME         REPLICAS   STORAGE   AGE
  my-prod-db   3          100Gi     5m
Cluster Arch Q155 of 200
How does Helm 3 differ from Helm 2?
A) Helm 3 uses YAML instead of Go templates
B) Helm 3 is a completely separate project — charts are incompatible
C) Helm 3 REMOVED TILLER (the server-side component). Helm 2 required Tiller (installed in cluster, had cluster-admin, security risk). Helm 3 is client-only — uses your kubeconfig RBAC permissions directly. Releases are stored as Secrets instead of ConfigMaps
D) Helm 3 only works on Kubernetes 1.28+
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm 2 → 3 migration: Tiller was a major security concern (cluster-admin, namespace-wide). Helm 3 uses the user's kubeconfig directly — permissions are whatever your RBAC allows. Also added: OCI support for chart storage in container registries.

Helm 2 vs Helm 3
  HELM 2 (deprecated)                HELM 3 (current)
  ┌────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Client (helm CLI)  │            │ Client (helm CLI)  │
  │        │           │            │        │           │
  │        ▼           │            │        ▼           │
  │ TILLER (server)    │            │ Kubernetes API     │
  │  ⚠️ cluster-admin  │            │ (uses user RBAC)   │
  │  ⚠️ no RBAC        │            │ ✅ your permissions│
  │        │           │            │                    │
  │        ▼           │            │ Releases stored as │
  │ Releases as CM     │            │ Secrets (not CM)   │
  └────────────────────┘            └────────────────────┘
  
  Helm 3: NO TILLER! Uses your kubeconfig RBAC directly.

When should you use Helm vs Kustomize?
A) Always use Helm — Kustomize is deprecated
B) Helm: when distributing software to OTHERS (parameterized charts with values.yaml). Kustomize: when managing YOUR OWN deployments across environments (dev/staging/prod overlays). Helm = packaging/distribution. Kustomize = configuration management. They complement each other — you can Kustomize Helm charts!
C) Always use Kustomize — Helm is too complex
D) They are mutually exclusive — you must choose one
✅ Correct Answer: B

Real-world: Use Helm to install third-party software (Prometheus, NGINX Ingress). Use Kustomize to manage your own app configs across environments. ArgoCD supports both natively. Helm Kustomize hybrid: helm template | kustomize build.

Helm vs Kustomize — When to Use Which
  HELM                                KUSTOMIZE
  ┌──────────────────────┐           ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ Template-based        │           │ Overlay-based           │
  │ {{ .Values.replicas }}│           │ patchesStrategicMerge   │
  │ Parameterized charts  │           │ Base + overlays         │
  ├──────────────────────┤           ├────────────────────────┤
  │ BEST FOR:             │           │ BEST FOR:               │
  │ Installing 3rd-party  │           │ Managing YOUR apps      │
  │ software (Prometheus, │           │ across environments     │
  │ nginx-ingress, cert-  │           │ (dev/staging/prod)      │
  │ manager)              │           │                         │
  ├──────────────────────┤           ├────────────────────────┤
  │ Distribution/packaging│           │ Configuration mgmt     │
  └──────────────────────┘           └────────────────────────┘
  
  ArgoCD supports BOTH natively!

Common Helm repos: bitnami (comprehensive catalog), ingress-nginx (Ingress controller), jetstack (cert-manager), grafana (Grafana/Loki/Tempo). helm repo update refreshes all repo indexes.

Helm Repository Workflow

Cluster Arch Q158 of 200
What is the Operator Pattern? (CRD + Controller = Operator)
A) An Operator is a custom controller that manages an application's full lifecycle using domain knowledge. CRD defines the desired state → Controller reconciles → creates/manages Deployments, Services, PVCs, etc. Example: Prometheus Operator creates and manages Prometheus instances and ServiceMonitors automatically
B) An Operator is a human who manages Kubernetes clusters
C) An Operator is a special type of Deployment with higher privileges
D) An Operator replaces the kube-controller-manager
✅ Correct Answer: A

Operators encode human operational knowledge into software. A MySQL Operator knows how to set up replication, handle backups, recover from failures — things a generic controller doesn't know. OperatorHub.io is the catalog of Operators.

Operator Pattern — Encoding Human Knowledge
  WITHOUT Operator:
  Admin manually: create StatefulSet, config replication, 
  set up backup, monitor, handle failover, scale...
  
  WITH Operator:
  Admin writes: kind: MySQLCluster, replicas: 3
  Operator automatically:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ✅ Creates StatefulSet (3 replicas)         │
  │ ✅ Configures primary/replica replication  │
  │ ✅ Sets up backup CronJob                   │
  │ ✅ Creates monitoring ServiceMonitors       │
  │ ✅ Handles automated failover               │
  │ ✅ Scales when needed                       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  OperatorHub.io → Catalog of Operators
Cluster Arch Q159 of 200
How do you check the history and rollback a Helm release?
A) helm release list and helm undo
B) kubectl rollout history deployment/my-release
C) helm history my-release (shows all revisions). helm rollback my-release <revision-number> (reverts to that revision). Each revision is stored as a Secret — kubectl get secret -l owner=helm
D) Helm doesn't support rollbacks — reinstalling is the only option
✅ Correct Answer: C

helm rollback creates a NEW revision (revision 3 = copy of revision 1) — it doesn't delete revisions. helm uninstall --keep-history keeps release history for potential re-install. Revision limit: configurable, default 10.

Helm Rollback Mechanics
  helm history my-release
  REVISION  STATUS      DESCRIPTION
  1         superseded  Initial install
  2         superseded  Upgraded image to v2
  3         deployed    Current version
  
  helm rollback my-release 1
  → Creates Revision 4 (copy of Revision 1's config)
  
  REVISION  STATUS      DESCRIPTION
  1         superseded  Initial install
  2         superseded  Upgraded image to v2
  3         superseded  Current version
  4         deployed    Rolled back to revision 1
  
  Each revision = a Secret: kubectl get secret -l owner=helm
