kubectl explain — Your CKA Documentation
  kubectl explain pod.spec.containers
  KIND:       Pod
  VERSION:    v1
  FIELD:      containers <[]Container>
  DESCRIPTION:
    List of containers belonging to the pod.
  
  kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive
  → Shows ALL nested fields (CKA exam life-saver!)
  
  kubectl explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers.resources
  → Shows resource limits/requests field structure
  
  CKA tip: No internet in exam → kubectl explain is your ONLY doc!

🌐 Category 5: Services & Networking (20%)Q161-Q200

🔴 Advanced — Connect Everything Together

This category covers how pods communicate — Services, DNS, Ingress controllers, NetworkPolicies, CNI plugins, and CoreDNS. For easypj in production, this means exposing Django via Ingress, securing pod-to-pod traffic with NetworkPolicies, and ensuring reliable DNS resolution.

Q161-Q20040 Questions🔴 Advanced

5.1 Service Types & DNSQ161-Q170

Networking Q161 of 200
What are the four Service types and their use cases?
A) HTTP, TCP, UDP, ICMP
B) Ingress, Egress, North-South, East-West
C) ClusterIP (internal-only, default), NodePort (exposes on each node's IP at a static port 30000-32767), LoadBalancer (provisions cloud LB — AWS NLB, GCP LB), ExternalName (maps Service to external DNS name via CNAME)
D) Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet
✅ Correct Answer: C

Each type builds on the one before it: NodePort automatically creates a ClusterIP, and LoadBalancer automatically creates both a NodePort and a ClusterIP underneath. In practice you'll default to ClusterIP for internal traffic and put a real Ingress in front of it rather than exposing every Service directly via NodePort or LoadBalancer.

Four Service Types
  TYPE         ACCESS              USE CASE
  ────         ──────              ────────
  ClusterIP    Internal only       Microservice-to-microservice
  NodePort     External via node   Dev/test, quick access
  LoadBalancer External via cloud  Production ingress
  ExternalName CNAME alias         Proxy to external DB/SaaS
  
  ClusterIP is the DEFAULT.
  NodePort creates a ClusterIP automatically.
  LoadBalancer creates NodePort + ClusterIP automatically.
Networking Q162 of 200
How does a ClusterIP Service route traffic to pods?
A) ClusterIP is a real IP assigned to a load balancer pod
B) ClusterIP is a VIRTUAL IP. kube-proxy writes iptables/IPVS rules on each node: traffic to ClusterIP:Port → DNAT (rewrite) to random backend pod IP:TargetPort. The ClusterIP doesn't actually exist on any interface
C) ClusterIP uses DNS round-robin — no iptables involved
D) ClusterIP forwards traffic through the API server
✅ Correct Answer: B

There's no process anywhere in the cluster actually listening on the ClusterIP address — it's a purely virtual IP that only exists as iptables (or IPVS) DNAT rules that kube-proxy programs on every node. This is why a ClusterIP Service still works even if the pod behind it moves to a different node: kube-proxy just rewrites the rule to point at the new pod IP.

ClusterIP Traffic Flow
  Client Pod → my-svc.default.svc.cluster.local:80
  │
  ▼
  CoreDNS resolves → ClusterIP 10.96.0.10
  │
  ▼
  Kernel iptables (written by kube-proxy):
  DNAT 10.96.0.10:80 → 10.244.1.5:8080 (backend pod)
  │
  ▼
  Packet arrives at backend pod!
  
  ClusterIP is NOT on any interface — it's pure iptables magic!
Networking Q163 of 200
What is the DNS name format for a Service in Kubernetes?
A) <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Example: nginx-svc.default.svc.cluster.local. Pods in the same namespace can use just <service-name>. Across namespaces: <service-name>.<namespace>
B) <namespace>/<service-name>
C) cluster.local/<service-name>/<namespace>
D) DNS is not available by default — it requires a custom plugin
✅ Correct Answer: A

CoreDNS provides this resolution. Pod DNS config: search <namespace>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local. So a pod in 'dev' namespace can resolve 'nginx-svc' (same namespace) or 'nginx-svc.prod' (different namespace).

Kubernetes DNS Name Format
  FULL DNS: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
  
  EXAMPLES:
  nginx-svc.default.svc.cluster.local      (service in default ns)
  api-svc.production.svc.cluster.local     (service in production ns)
  
  SHORT FORMS (same namespace):
  Pod in 'default' → nginx-svc            (just service name)
  Pod in 'default' → nginx-svc:8080       (with port)
  
  CROSS-NAMESPACE:
  Pod in 'dev' → api-svc.production       (namespace.service)
  Pod in 'dev' → api-svc.production.svc   (with svc suffix)
  
  Pod DNS: <pod-ip-dashes>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local
  Example: 10-244-1-5.default.pod.cluster.local
Networking Q164 of 200
What is the difference between port, targetPort, and nodePort in a Service spec?
A) They are all the same — just different names for the same field
B) port = pod port, targetPort = node port, nodePort = service port
C) port = 80 (required), targetPort = 8080 (required), nodePort = 443 (required)
D) port = the Service port (what other pods connect to). targetPort = the port on the backend pod containers. nodePort = the port on each Node's IP (30000-32767, only for NodePort/LoadBalancer Services)
✅ Correct Answer: D

These three fields answer three different questions: what port do other things in the cluster use to reach this Service (port), what port is the container actually listening on (targetPort), and what port is exposed on every node's own IP for external access (nodePort, only relevant for NodePort/LoadBalancer types). Mixing these up is one of the most common Service YAML mistakes on the exam.

Service Port Mapping
  Service spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80           # Service port (what clients use)
    targetPort: 8080   # Container port on backend pods
    nodePort: 30080    # Port on each Node (for NodePort/LB)
  
  Traffic flow (NodePort):
  INTERNET → Node-IP:30080 → Service ClusterIP:80 → Pod:8080
  
  If targetPort is not specified, it defaults to port.
Networking Q165 of 200
What is a headless Service and when would you use it?
A) A Service without any backend pods — used for maintenance mode
B) A Service that doesn't have a YAML definition
C) A Service with clusterIP: None — NO virtual IP. DNS returns the individual pod IPs (A records) instead of the ClusterIP. Used with StatefulSets when each pod needs a stable network identity and for client-side load balancing
D) A Service that has been deleted but is still running
✅ Correct Answer: C

Headless Service: DNS query returns pod IPs directly. Used with StatefulSet (each pod gets stable DNS: <pod-name>.<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, e.g. web-0.nginx.default.svc.cluster.local), Kafka, Cassandra, and applications that need peer discovery. Non-headless Service returns the ClusterIP instead.

Headless Service — clusterIP: None
  Headless Service:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  spec:
    clusterIP: None         # ← KEY: No virtual IP!
    selector:
      app: cassandra
  
  DNS query → returns POD IPs directly (A records):
  nslookup cassandra-svc.default.svc.cluster.local
  → 10.244.1.5
  → 10.244.2.8
  → 10.244.3.2
  
  Used with StatefulSet: web-0.nginx.default.svc.cluster.local
                          (pod).(service).(namespace).svc.cluster.local
Networking Q166 of 200
How does a LoadBalancer Service work on a cloud provider?
A) Kubernetes runs a software load balancer as a pod
B) The cloud-controller-manager detects the LoadBalancer Service and provisions an EXTERNAL cloud LB (AWS NLB, GCP LB). It creates a NodePort Service underneath, then configures the cloud LB to forward traffic to all nodes' NodePort
C) LoadBalancer only works on bare-metal — not on clouds
D) The API server acts as the load balancer for external traffic
✅ Correct Answer: B

On AWS: creates an NLB → targets all worker nodes' NodePort. On GCP: creates a Network LB. On bare-metal (no cloud LB): LoadBalancer Service stays Pending forever unless you install MetalLB.

LoadBalancer Service — Cloud Integration
  kind: Service
  spec:
    type: LoadBalancer
  
  Cloud Controller creates:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ AWS:  NLB → targets NodePort on all nodes  │
  │ GCP:  TCP LB → targets NodePort             │
  │ Azure: Azure LB → targets NodePort          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  kubectl get svc my-svc
  NAME     TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
  my-svc   LoadBalancer   10.96.0.50    54.123.45.67  80:30080/TCP
  
  On bare-metal: EXTERNAL-IP stays <pending> forever
  → Solution: Install MetalLB!
Networking Q167 of 200
How do Services select which pods to route traffic to?
A) Via LABEL SELECTORS. The Service spec.selector matches pod metadata.labels. Only pods with matching labels receive traffic. Endpoints (or EndpointSlices) track the actual IP:Port of matching pods
B) Via pod name — the Service spec lists pod names
C) Via namespace — all pods in the namespace receive traffic
D) Via annotations — pods with matching annotations are selected
✅ Correct Answer: A

Service selector: app: nginx matches pods with label app: nginx. The EndpointSlice controller (the modern successor to the legacy Endpoint controller/Endpoints object) watches for pods matching the selector → populates EndpointSlice objects with pod IPs → kube-proxy uses those to program iptables rules.

Service Label Selector Matching
  Service:                          Pods:
  selector:                         metadata:
    app: nginx          ──────────▶   labels:
    tier: frontend                    app: nginx
                                      tier: frontend
                                    → MATCH! ✅ Receives traffic
  
  selector:                         metadata:
    app: nginx          ──────────▶   labels:
                                      app: nginx
                                    → MATCH! ✅
  
  selector:                         metadata:
    app: nginx          ──────────▶   labels:
    tier: backend                      app: api
                                    → NO MATCH ❌ No traffic
Networking Q168 of 200
What is an ExternalName Service used for?
A) Exposing a Service to the internet via a domain name
B) Creating an alias for another Kubernetes Service
C) Configuring TLS certificates for external access
D) Creating a CNAME alias inside the cluster to an EXTERNAL DNS name (e.g., database.example.com). Pods use the cluster-internal Service name, and CoreDNS resolves it to the external address. Useful for abstracting external dependencies
✅ Correct Answer: D

Example: A pod connects to 'my-db-svc'. If it's ExternalName → 'rds.aws.example.com', traffic goes to the RDS instance. If you migrate to Cloud SQL, just change the ExternalName — no app changes needed!

ExternalName Service — CNAME Alias
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: my-db-svc
  spec:
    type: ExternalName
    externalName: rds-prod.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
  
  Pod resolves: my-db-svc → CNAME → rds-prod.abc123...
  
  BENEFIT: Migrate DB without changing app code!
  Just update externalName in the Service.
  
  ExternalName = Kubernetes-native DNS CNAME record
Networking Q169 of 200
What is sessionAffinity in a Service?
A) It controls how long a pod can live before being replaced
B) It defines pod affinity rules for scheduling
C) sessionAffinity: ClientIP makes kube-proxy route traffic from the SAME client IP to the SAME pod (sticky sessions). Default is None (random load balancing). Uses iptables recent match module or IPVS persistence
D) It ensures pods from the same ReplicaSet run on different nodes
✅ Correct Answer: C

Use case: WebSocket applications, stateful in-memory sessions, shopping carts. Not ideal for stateless apps — breaks even load distribution. sessionAffinityConfig can set a timeout (default 10800 seconds).

sessionAffinity — Sticky Sessions
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 10800  # 3 hours default
  
  Client 10.1.1.5 → Pod A (first request)
  Client 10.1.1.5 → Pod A (same pod, sticky!)
  Client 10.1.1.5 → Pod A (for 3 hours)
  Client 10.1.1.8 → Pod B (different client)
  
  Uses iptables recent module or IPVS persistence
  NOT for stateless apps! Breaks even load distribution
Networking Q170 of 200
How does kube-proxy in IPVS mode differ from iptables mode?
A) IPVS mode doesn't actually work — it's experimental
B) IPVS uses Linux kernel's L4 load balancer (hash table-based) — much faster than iptables (rule chain traversal). IPVS supports more load balancing algorithms (rr, lc, sh, dh). iptables uses sequential rule evaluation — slow with many Services
C) They are identical in performance — just different names
D) IPVS only works on Windows nodes
✅ Correct Answer: B

iptables mode creates O(n²) chains — at 5000+ Services, rule processing is noticeable, which is why IPVS was long recommended for very large clusters. To enable: kube-proxy --proxy-mode=ipvs. Requires ip_vs kernel module. Note: IPVS mode is now deprecated in favor of a newer nftables proxy mode, which replaces both iptables and IPVS with better performance than either — check which mode your target Kubernetes version recommends.

iptables vs IPVS — kube-proxy Modes
  IPTABLES MODE                       IPVS MODE
  ┌────────────────────┐             ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Sequential rules    │             │ Hash table lookup  │
  │ O(n) complexity     │             │ O(1) complexity    │
  │ 5000 Services =     │             │ 5000 Services =    │
  │   ~25K rules        │             │   1 hash lookup    │
  │ Slow at scale       │             │ Fast at any scale  │
  ├────────────────────┤             ├────────────────────┤
  │ 1 algorithm: random │             │ Multiple: rr, lc,  │
  │                     │             │ sh, dh, sed, nq    │
  └────────────────────┘             └────────────────────┘
  
  Enable: kube-proxy --proxy-mode=ipvs (requires ip_vs kmod)
  Now deprecated — nftables mode is the modern replacement

5.2 Ingress & Ingress ControllersQ171-Q180

Networking Q171 of 200
What is an Ingress and why do you need an Ingress Controller?
A) Ingress is the RULES object (YAML) defining HTTP routing. Ingress Controller is the IMPLEMENTATION (nginx, traefik, HAProxy) that reads Ingress rules and configures itself. Ingress without a controller does NOTHING — it's just a stored rule
B) Ingress is a built-in Kubernetes component — no controller needed
C) Ingress replaces Services entirely — Services are not needed
D) Ingress is only for TCP traffic — not HTTP/HTTPS
✅ Correct Answer: A

Ingress = routing rules (host-based, path-based). Ingress Controller = the actual proxy that enforces those rules. Install one: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml.

Ingress vs Ingress Controller
  INGRESS (rules YAML)                INGRESS CONTROLLER (running pod)
  ┌──────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ apiVersion: net/v1   │           │ nginx-ingress-controller pod │
  │ kind: Ingress        │  reads    │ (or traefik, haproxy, etc.)  │
  │ spec:                │◀──────────│                              │
  │   rules:             │           │ Listens on :80/:443          │
  │   - host: app.com    │           │ Watches Ingress resources    │
  │     paths:           │           │ Configures itself (nginx)    │
  │     - path: /api     │           │ Routes traffic accordingly   │
  │       backend: api   │           └──────────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────┘
  
  Without controller: Ingress is just stored YAML — does NOTHING!
Networking Q172 of 200
What are the components of an Ingress resource?
A) Only a list of pod IPs and ports
B) A deployment of the web server and a Service
C) Rules (host + path → backend Service:Port), TLS section (Secret with cert + key), default backend (catches unmatched traffic), annotations (controller-specific config like rewrite-target, ssl-redirect)
D) A ConfigMap and a Secret only
✅ Correct Answer: C

An Ingress resource on its own is just a set of routing rules — host/path combinations mapped to backend Services — it does nothing without an Ingress Controller actually watching and enforcing them. The TLS block references a Secret containing the cert/key pair, and annotations are how you reach controller-specific features (like URL rewriting) that aren't part of the core Ingress spec.

Ingress YAML Structure
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx       # which controller to use
  tls:
  - hosts: [example.com]
    secretName: example-tls     # TLS cert stored in Secret
  rules:
  - host: example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-svc
            port:
              number: 8080
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-svc
            port:
              number: 80
Networking Q173 of 200
What is the difference between pathType: Prefix and pathType: Exact?
A) Prefix matches the beginning of the URL path, Exact matches the entire URL including query parameters
B) They are identical in behavior
C) Prefix only works with nginx, Exact only with traefik
D) Prefix: /api matches /api, /api/v1, /api/v1/users (prefix match). Exact: /foo only matches /foo exactly — not /foo/ or /foobar. ImplementationSpecific delegates matching logic to the controller
✅ Correct Answer: D

Prefix matching is the most common. Always order Ingress rules from most specific to least specific. A wildcard path (/*) should be last. The Ingress controller picks the longest matching path (not the first match). Prefix matching is element-wise on / boundaries, not a raw string prefix: /api matches /api/v1 but does NOT match /apiv2 — the diagram's "❌ /apiv2" result is exactly this rule in action.

pathType: Prefix vs Exact vs ImplementationSpecific
  Path: /api, pathType: Prefix
  ✅ /api          ✅ /api/v1      ✅ /api/v1/users
  ✅ /api/         ❌ /apiv2       ❌ /application
  
  Path: /foo, pathType: Exact
  ✅ /foo          ❌ /foo/        ❌ /foobar
  ❌ /foo?q=1     (only /foo exactly!)
  
  Path: /*, pathType: Prefix (catch-all)
  ✅ /anything    ✅ /             ✅ /deep/nested/path
  
  ORDER: Most specific paths first, wildcard last!
Networking Q174 of 200
How does an Ingress Controller get traffic from the internet?
A) Ingress Controller creates its own external IP automatically
B) The Ingress Controller runs as pods exposed via a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service. External traffic hits the LB → forwards to controller pod → controller reads Ingress rules → routes to backend Service → backend pod
C) Ingress Controller binds directly to port 80/443 on every node
D) The API server routes external traffic to the Ingress Controller
✅ Correct Answer: B

The Ingress Controller is not magic — it's just an ordinary pod (usually running nginx or similar) exposed like any other Service, most commonly via a cloud LoadBalancer or NodePort. What makes it special is that it watches the API server for Ingress objects and reconfigures its own proxy rules to match, so the internet-facing entry point never changes even as your Ingress rules do.

Ingress Traffic Flow
  INTERNET
  │
  ▼
  Cloud Load Balancer (AWS NLB)
  │
  ▼
  Ingress Controller Pod (nginx)  ← reads Ingress rules
  │
  ├─ host: api.example.com/path → ClusterIP api-svc:8080 → Pod
  │
  ├─ host: web.example.com/     → ClusterIP web-svc:80   → Pod
  │
  └─ no match                   → Default backend (404)
Networking Q175 of 200
What is ingressClassName and why is it important?
A) It specifies WHICH Ingress Controller should handle this Ingress. Multiple Ingress Controllers can run in the same cluster — ingressClassName ensures the right controller picks up the right Ingress. Replaces the deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation
B) It defines the Java class name for a custom Ingress plugin
C) It's the DNS class of the Ingress — A, CNAME, MX
D) It's a Kubernetes resource class for billing purposes
✅ Correct Answer: A

Cluster with nginx AND traefik Ingress Controllers: Ingress with ingressClassName: nginx → picked up by nginx controller. Different Ingress with ingressClassName: traefik → picked up by traefik controller. Without this, both controllers might fight over the same Ingress.

ingressClassName — Multi-Controller Cluster
  Cluster runs TWO Ingress Controllers:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ NGINX Ingress (internal apps)                     │
  │   IngressClassName: nginx                         │
  │   Picks up: Ingress with ingressClassName: nginx  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Traefik Ingress (external APIs)                   │
  │   IngressClassName: traefik                       │
  │   Picks up: Ingress with ingressClassName: traefik│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Without ingressClassName: BOTH controllers might fight!
  Replaces: kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation (deprecated)
Networking Q176 of 200
How do you configure TLS for an Ingress?
A) TLS is automatic — Ingress handles it without configuration
B) Add the certificate directly in the Ingress YAML as a base64 string
C) (1) Create a TLS Secret: kubectl create secret tls my-tls --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem. (2) In the Ingress spec, add tls: hosts: [domain.com], secretName: my-tls. (3) For auto-TLS, use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt
D) TLS is only supported on LoadBalancer Services, not Ingress
✅ Correct Answer: C

TLS Secret must be in the SAME namespace as the Ingress. For production: cert-manager + Let's Encrypt automates TLS certificate issuance and renewal. cert-manager creates a Certificate resource → obtains cert → stores in Secret → Ingress uses it.

Ingress TLS Setup
  # 1. Create TLS Secret
  kubectl create secret tls my-tls \
    --cert=fullchain.pem \
    --key=privkey.pem
  
  # 2. Ingress spec
  spec:
    tls:
    - hosts:
      - app.example.com
      secretName: my-tls
    rules:
    - host: app.example.com
  
  # 3. Auto-TLS (production)
  # Install cert-manager + Let's Encrypt
  # Creates Certificate CR → gets cert → stores in Secret → Ingress uses it
Networking Q177 of 200
What is the Ingress Gateway API and how is it different from Ingress?
A) It's the same thing — just a renamed CRD
B) Gateway API replaces kubectl — it's a new CLI
C) Gateway API is only for service mesh — not for regular Kubernetes
D) Gateway API is the NEXT-GEN Ingress — more expressive, role-oriented (infra admin creates Gateway, app dev creates HTTPRoute), supports TCP/UDP/TLS routing, traffic splitting, header-based routing. It separates concerns better than classic Ingress
✅ Correct Answer: D

Classic Ingress: one resource, combined config. Gateway API: GatewayClass (infra), Gateway (infra), HTTPRoute (app dev). Supports canary deployments, A/B testing, header matching. GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, and GRPCRoute are already stable/GA (apiVersion v1) — the established current standard for new ingress-style routing, not just an upcoming feature.

Ingress vs Gateway API
  CLASSIC INGRESS                GATEWAY API (next-gen)
  ┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ One resource      │          │ Three resources:          │
  │ (Ingress)         │          │ GatewayClass (infra)      │
  │                   │          │ Gateway (cluster admin)   │
  │ Annotations for   │          │ HTTPRoute (app developer) │
  │ controller config │          │                           │
  │                   │          │ ✅ Role separation        │
  │ ❌ One-size-fits  │          │ ✅ TCP/UDP/TLS routing    │
  │ ❌ No role split  │          │ ✅ Traffic splitting      │
  └──────────────────┘          │ ✅ Header-based routing   │
                                 └──────────────────────────┘
Networking Q178 of 200
What are common Ingress annotations for the NGINX Ingress Controller?
A) Annotations are not used — everything is in the Ingress spec
B) nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target (rewrite URLs to backend), ssl-redirect (force HTTPS), proxy-body-size (max upload size), cors (enable CORS), whitelist-source-range (IP allowlisting), affinity (sticky sessions)
C) Annotations are only for documentation purposes
D) Only kubernetes.io annotations are valid
✅ Correct Answer: B

Each Ingress Controller has its own annotations. nginx-ingress has 100+ annotations for fine-tuning. Traefik uses different annotations. Annotations are controller-specific — not portable between controllers.

Common NGINX Ingress Annotations
  ANNOTATION                                  WHAT IT DOES
  ──────────                                  ────────────
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target  Rewrite /app → /
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect    Force HTTP → HTTPS
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size Max upload (e.g., 50m)
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/cors-enable     Enable CORS
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range  IP allowlist
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity        Sticky sessions ("cookie")
  
  Each controller has its OWN annotations — not portable!
Networking Q179 of 200
What happens if your Ingress has no matching backend for a request?
A) The Ingress Controller routes to the "default backend" — typically a 404 page. You can customize it with a custom default backend Service. Without a default backend, the controller returns its built-in 404 response
B) The request hangs until timeout
C) The API server automatically creates a new backend
D) The Ingress Controller forwards the request to a random Service
✅ Correct Answer: A

Default backend can be customized: kubectl create deploy custom-404 --image=nginx. Then configure: --default-backend-service=<namespace>/<service> on the Ingress Controller. This is useful for custom error pages or logging unmatched requests.

Default Backend — Catch-All Routing
  Ingress rules:
  ├─ host: api.app.com/*  → api-svc
  └─ host: web.app.com/*  → web-svc
  
  Request: random.app.com/ → NO MATCH!
  → Routed to DEFAULT BACKEND → 404 page
  
  Custom default backend:
  kubectl create deploy custom-404 --image=nginx
  Ingress Controller flag:
    --default-backend-service=default/custom-404
  
  Default backend = catch-all for unmatched requests
Networking Q180 of 200
How do you troubleshoot "Ingress not working"? (Systematic approach)
A) Delete and recreate the Ingress — that fixes everything
B) Restart the entire cluster
C) (1) kubectl describe ingress → check for events/errors. (2) Check Ingress Controller pods are running. (3) Check Ingress Controller logs. (4) Verify backend Service exists and has Endpoints (kubectl get endpoints). (5) Test directly: curl -H "Host: domain" http://ingress-controller-ip. (6) Check DNS resolves to load balancer IP
D) Only check the Ingress YAML — runtime debugging is not possible
✅ Correct Answer: C

Common causes: Ingress Controller not installed, wrong ingressClassName, no TLS Secret, backend Service has no Endpoints (label mismatch), firewall blocking port 80/443, DNS not pointing to LB IP.

Ingress Troubleshooting Flowchart
  Ingress not working? Check in order:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. kubectl describe ingress <name>       │
  │    → Any events? Errors?                  │
  │                                          │
  │ 2. Is Ingress Controller running?        │
  │    kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress    │
  │                                          │
  │ 3. Check backend Service Endpoints       │
  │    kubectl get endpoints <svc-name>     │
  │    → Must have pod IPs, not empty!       │
  │                                          │
  │ 4. Test directly from temp pod            │
  │    curl -H "Host: app.com" <ingress-ip> │
  │                                          │
  │ 5. Check firewall/security group         │
  │    Port 80/443 open to LB?               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

5.3 Network PoliciesQ181-Q190

Networking Q181 of 200
What is a NetworkPolicy and what does it control?
A) NetworkPolicy controls pod scheduling based on network bandwidth
B) NetworkPolicy is a firewall for the API server — controlling kubectl access
C) NetworkPolicy controls which nodes can join the cluster
D) NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes FIREWALL for pods. It controls INGRESS (who can connect TO selected pods) and EGRESS (where selected pods can connect TO). Default: ALL traffic allowed. Once a NetworkPolicy selects a pod, only allowed traffic gets through — ALL other traffic is denied
✅ Correct Answer: D

CRITICAL: NetworkPolicy only works if your CNI plugin SUPPORTS it. Calico, Cilium, Weave support it. Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy. Without a supporting CNI, NetworkPolicy YAML can be created but has NO EFFECT.

NetworkPolicy — Pod Firewall
  WITHOUT NetworkPolicy:
  ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐  ┌─────┐
  │Pod A│──│Pod B│──│Pod C│  ALL traffic allowed!
  └─────┘  └─────┘  └─────┘
  
  WITH NetworkPolicy (selects app: api):
  ┌─────┐       ┌─────┐       ┌─────┐
  │Pod A│──✅──▶│Pod B│◀──❌──│Pod C│
  │web  │       │api  │       │other│
  └─────┘       └─────┘       └─────┘
  (allowed)     (selected)    (blocked!)
  
  Default: ALL traffic allowed
  One NP selects a pod → DEFAULT DENY for that pod
Networking Q182 of 200
What is the default behavior WITHOUT any NetworkPolicy?
A) All pod traffic is blocked by default
B) ALL traffic is ALLOWED — any pod can talk to any other pod across all namespaces. NetworkPolicies are opt-in restrictions. Once a pod is selected by ANY NetworkPolicy, it becomes DENY-ALL by default — only explicitly allowed traffic passes
C) Only same-namespace traffic is allowed
D) Only traffic to Services is allowed — direct pod IP traffic is blocked
✅ Correct Answer: B

Default: wide open. After a NetworkPolicy selects a pod, it's "default deny" — only what's explicitly allowed passes. This is opposite to typical firewall behavior. Always test NetworkPolicies in a dev environment first.

NetworkPolicy Default Behavior
  NO NETWORKPOLICIES:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ All pods ↔ All pods (cross-namespace too!) │
  │ COMPLETELY OPEN by default                 │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  NP SELECTS app: db:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ app: db pod → ALL ingress DENIED           │
  │ app: db pod → ALL egress DENIED            │
  │ (unless explicitly allowed in NP rules)    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Key insight: NP is OPT-IN restriction.
  Once selected, DEFAULT IS DENY.
Networking Q183 of 200
Which CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy? (CKA exam critical)
A) All CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy — it's mandatory
B) Only the default CNI (kubenet) supports it
C) Calico, Cilium, Weave Net, and Kube-router SUPPORT NetworkPolicy. Flannel does NOT (by itself). Canal (Flannel + Calico policy) and Antrea also support it
D) NetworkPolicy support depends on the Kubernetes version, not CNI
✅ Correct Answer: C

This is a common CKA trap. You create a NetworkPolicy, but if Flannel is the CNI, it silently does nothing. Always verify the CNI before troubleshooting NetworkPolicy. Calico is the CKA default — it supports NetworkPolicy.

CNI Plugin NetworkPolicy Support
  CNI PLUGIN    NETWORKPOLICY?    NOTES
  ──────────    ──────────────    ─────
  Calico        ✅ YES            Full support, BGP routing
  Cilium        ✅ YES            eBPF-based, L7 policies
  Weave Net     ✅ YES            Full support
  Antrea        ✅ YES            OVS-based
  Canal         ✅ YES            Flannel + Calico policy
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  Flannel       ❌ NO             Pod network only
  kubenet       ❌ NO             Basic bridge mode
  
  CKA TRAP: NP YAML applies successfully,
  but with Flannel it silently does NOTHING!
Networking Q184 of 200
How do you write a NetworkPolicy that denies ALL ingress to pods with label app: db?
A) Create a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: app: db, policyTypes: [Ingress], and NO ingress rules (empty ingress: []). This means "no ingress is allowed" — default deny all incoming traffic
B) Delete all Services pointing to app: db pods
C) Add an annotation to the pods: "network-policy: deny-all"
D) Create a NetworkPolicy with ingress: - from: [] — this is the deny syntax
✅ Correct Answer: A

An empty ingress: [] list combined with policyTypes: [Ingress] is the canonical "default deny" pattern — it doesn't mean "no restrictions," it means "no rule matches, so nothing is allowed in." This is usually applied cluster-wide first (podSelector: {} to match all pods), then narrower allow policies are layered on top for the traffic that should get through.

Default Deny All Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress: []         # EMPTY = nothing allowed!
  
  # Result: No incoming traffic to app:db pods from ANYWHERE
Networking Q185 of 200
How do you allow ingress from pods with label app: frontend to pods with label app: api on port 8080?
A) kubectl allow-traffic --from=app=frontend --to=app=api --port=8080
B) Create a NetworkPolicy selecting app: api pods. In ingress.from, specify podSelector: app: frontend. In ingress.ports, specify port: 8080, protocol: TCP. This allows ONLY frontend → api on port 8080
C) Add a Service with selector app: frontend — traffic is auto-allowed
D) Label both pods with network.allow: "true"
✅ Correct Answer: B

NetworkPolicies are additive and namespace-scoped: once any policy selects a pod, only explicitly allowed traffic gets through — everything else is denied by default. Here the podSelector on the policy itself picks the destination pods (api), while the podSelector inside ingress.from picks the allowed source pods (frontend) — mixing these two up is the most common NetworkPolicy mistake.

Allow Specific Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-api
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api                    # applies TO these pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend           # FROM these pods
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080                  # ON this port
Networking Q186 of 200
How do you restrict pod egress to ONLY pods in the same namespace and a specific external IP?
A) Egress cannot be restricted — only Ingress
B) Use a firewall on the node — NetworkPolicy doesn't support egress
C) Create a NetworkPolicy with policyTypes: [Egress], egress rules allowing: (1) to: podSelector: {} (all pods in same namespace), (2) to: ipBlock: cidr: 10.0.0.0/8 except: [10.0.0.0/24]
D) Set the pod's DNS policy to "None" — this blocks egress
✅ Correct Answer: C

Egress rules control outbound traffic. Common use: block pods from calling external APIs (allow only internal communication). DNS egress: Allow UDP port 53 to CoreDNS for name resolution. Note: regardless of any ipBlock CIDR/except ranges you write, traffic to and from the pod's own node is always allowed — NetworkPolicy can never block node-local traffic.

NetworkPolicy Egress Rules
  Egress: restrict OUTBOUND traffic from pods
  
  spec:
    policyTypes:
    - Egress
    egress:
    - to:
      - podSelector:           # Allow to pods with label
          matchLabels:
            app: api
      ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 8080
    - to:
      - ipBlock:               # Allow to external IP range
          cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
          except:
          - 10.0.0.0/24        # Except this subnet
    - to:
      - namespaceSelector: {}  # Allow to all namespaces
  
  Tip: Always allow UDP 53 to CoreDNS for name resolution!
Networking Q187 of 200
How do NetworkPolicy selectors work with namespaces?
A) NetworkPolicy can only select pods in its own namespace
B) Namespaces are not used in NetworkPolicy
C) You must create a NetworkPolicy in each namespace you want to control
D) You can use namespaceSelector to allow/deny traffic from ALL pods in matching namespaces. Combine with podSelector for fine-grained control. namespaceSelector: matchLabels: team: dev allows all pods from namespaces with label team=dev
✅ Correct Answer: D

from can include: podSelector (pods by label), namespaceSelector (all pods in matching namespaces), ipBlock (IP CIDR ranges). Multiple selectors in the same from entry are ANDed. Multiple from entries are ORed.

NetworkPolicy Selectors — Combining podSelector + namespaceSelector
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:             # AND condition
        matchLabels:
          role: frontend
      namespaceSelector:        # BOTH must match
        matchLabels:
          team: dev
  → Allow from pods with role=frontend
    that are in namespaces with team=dev
  
  Multiple from entries = OR:
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: web
    - namespaceSelector:        # OR
        matchLabels:
          env: monitoring
  → Allow from app=web pods OR any pod in env=monitoring ns
Networking Q188 of 200
What happens when multiple NetworkPolicies select the same pod?
A) Only the first one applied takes effect — others are ignored
B) They are COMBINED (UNION). If NP1 allows traffic from A and NP2 allows traffic from B, the pod accepts traffic from BOTH A and B. NetworkPolicies are additive — they never deny more, they only allow more when combined
C) The most restrictive policy wins
D) An error is thrown — you can't have multiple policies for the same pod
✅ Correct Answer: B

NetworkPolicies are UNION-based: allowed = NP1_allow ∪ NP2_allow. This is why you can have "global" policies (allow monitoring namespace from all namespaces) plus "app-specific" policies (allow frontend to backend on port 8080).

Multiple NetworkPolicies — UNION Behavior
  Pod selected by TWO NetworkPolicies:
  
  NP-1: Allow ingress from app: frontend on port 8080
  NP-2: Allow ingress from app: monitoring on port 9090
  
  RESULT (union):
  ✅ app: frontend → port 8080 (from NP-1)
  ✅ app: monitoring → port 9090 (from NP-2)
  ❌ app: other → BLOCKED
  
  UNION, not intersection! Policies are ADDITIVE.
  They never deny more — they only allow more.
Networking Q189 of 200
How do you create a "default deny all" NetworkPolicy for a namespace?
A) Create a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} (matches ALL pods), policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress], and NO ingress or egress rules. This blocks all ingress and egress traffic to/from other pods and IPs for every pod in the namespace — except traffic to/from each pod's own node, which no NetworkPolicy can block
B) Delete the namespace — that's the only way to deny all
C) Set the namespace annotation: "networking/deny-all: true"
D) Create a ResourceQuota with network deny
✅ Correct Answer: A

Naming convention: 'deny-all' or 'default-deny'. After this, create additional NetworkPolicies to open specific traffic. This is the recommended security posture: default deny, then explicit allow — just like cloud security groups.

Default Deny All — Namespace Lockdown
  # Default deny ALL ingress:
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: deny-all-ingress
    namespace: prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}        # SELECTS ALL PODS
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    # NO ingress rules = nothing allowed!
  
  # Default deny ALL egress:
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes:
    - Egress
    # NO egress rules = nothing allowed!
  
  THEN create specific allow policies to open needed traffic
Networking Q190 of 200
How do you test and verify NetworkPolicy is working?
A) kubectl test network-policy <name>
B) Check the NetworkPolicy status — it shows if it's active
C) Run a test pod (busybox/ netshoot) and use curl/nc/wget to test connectivity. Before policy → connection succeeds. After policy → connection times out (or succeeds if allowed). kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh, then wget -O- http://target-svc:port --timeout=5
D) NetworkPolicy automatically generates a YAML report — check that
✅ Correct Answer: C

Testing approach: (1) Deploy two pods with appropriate labels. (2) Test connectivity without NetworkPolicy → should work. (3) Apply NetworkPolicy. (4) Test again → verify denied/allowed as expected. Use netshoot image (nicolaka/netshoot) for advanced networking tools.

Testing NetworkPolicy — Verification Script
  # 1. Deploy test pods
  kubectl run web --image=nginx --labels=app=web
  kubectl run api --image=nginx --labels=app=api
  kubectl expose pod api --port=80
  
  # 2. Test BEFORE policy (should work)
  kubectl exec web -- wget -O- --timeout=3 api-svc
  → <html>...nginx welcome...</html>  ✅
  
  # 3. Apply deny-all policy for app=api
  # 4. Test AFTER policy (should fail)
  kubectl exec web -- wget -O- --timeout=3 api-svc
  → wget: download timed out  ❌ (blocked!)
  
  Use netshoot image for advanced network testing tools

5.4 CNI, CoreDNS & Pod NetworkingQ191-Q200

Networking Q191 of 200
What is CNI and what does it do in Kubernetes?
A) CNI is the Container Network Interface — it replaces kube-proxy
B) CNI (Container Network Interface) is a PLUGIN specification. CNI plugins: assign IP addresses to pods, set up network routes between pods, configure network interfaces. The container runtime (not kubelet directly, since v1.24) loads and calls CNI plugins when creating/deleting pods. Examples: Calico, Flannel, Cilium, Weave
C) CNI is the Kubernetes-native DNS service
D) CNI is an alternative to etcd for storing network config
✅ Correct Answer: B

Without CNI: pods get no IP, stay in ContainerCreating state forever. CNI config is in /etc/cni/net.d/. CNI binaries are in /opt/cni/bin/. kubelet requests pod sandbox creation via CRI, and the container runtime itself loads and invokes the CNI plugin to set up networking — kubelet stopped managing CNI directly as of Kubernetes v1.24.

CNI — Container Network Interface
  Pod Creation → kubelet → CRI → Container Runtime → CNI Plugin
  (runtime loads/invokes CNI; kubelet stopped managing CNI as of v1.24)
  
  CNI Plugin responsibilities:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Allocate IP address for pod             │
  │ 2. Create veth pair (pod ↔ host)           │
  │ 3. Configure routes (pod ↔ pod across nodes)│
  │ 4. Set up IPAM (IP management)             │
  │ 5. Enforce NetworkPolicy (if supported)    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  CNI config: /etc/cni/net.d/*.conf
  CNI binaries: /opt/cni/bin/
  
  Without CNI: pods stuck in ContainerCreating!
Networking Q192 of 200
What are the key differences between Calico and Flannel?
A) Calico: uses BGP routing (no overlay, better performance), supports NetworkPolicy, IP-in-IP or VXLAN for cross-subnet. Flannel: uses VXLAN or host-gw overlay (simpler), does NOT support NetworkPolicy natively, easier to set up but less features
B) Calico is for small clusters, Flannel for enterprise
C) They are identical — just different vendors
D) Flannel replaces Calico — Calico is deprecated
✅ Correct Answer: A

Calico: choice for enterprise (NetworkPolicy, BGP peering, wireguard encryption). Flannel: choice for simplicity (just pod networking, no policy). Cilium: choice for eBPF-based (next-gen, service mesh replacement, observability). CKA default: Calico.

Calico vs Flannel vs Cilium
  FEATURE          CALICO        FLANNEL       CILIUM
  ───────          ──────        ───────       ──────
  Routing          BGP           VXLAN/host-gw eBPF
  Overlay          Optional      VXLAN         No (direct routing)
  NetworkPolicy    ✅ YES        ❌ NO          ✅ YES (L3/L4/L7)
  Encryption       WireGuard     ❌             WireGuard/IPsec
  Performance      High          Medium        Highest (eBPF)
  Complexity       Medium        Low           High
  Service Mesh     ❌            ❌             ✅ (replaces sidecar)
  
  CKA Default: Calico (supports NetworkPolicy)
  Enterprise: Cilium (eBPF, observability, L7 policies)
  Simple: Flannel (but no NetworkPolicy!)
Networking Q193 of 200
How does pod-to-pod networking work across different nodes?
A) All pods share the same IP — they don't need cross-node routing
B) Traffic goes through the API server — it routes between nodes
C) CNI plugin creates an overlay network (VXLAN/IP-in-IP) or uses BGP routing. Pod A on Node-1 sends packet to Pod B on Node-2 → CNI encapsulates (overlay) or routes (BGP) the packet to Node-2 → Node-2 decapsulates → delivers to Pod B. Pods see each other's IPs directly
D) Pods can't communicate across nodes — only within the same node
✅ Correct Answer: C

Kubernetes networking model: all pods can communicate with all other pods without NAT, regardless of which node they're on. The CNI plugin makes this happen via tunnels, routing, or eBPF.

Cross-Node Pod Communication
  NODE-1                           NODE-2
  ┌──────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Pod A             │            │ Pod B             │
  │ IP: 10.244.1.5    │            │ IP: 10.244.2.7    │
  └────────┬─────────┘            └────────▲─────────┘
           │                               │
           ▼                               │
  ┌──────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────┐
  │ CNI (Calico)     │            │ CNI (Calico)     │
  │ Encapsulate in   │────────────│ Decapsulate      │
  │ IP-in-IP tunnel  │  NETWORK   │ deliver to pod   │
  └──────────────────┘            └──────────────────┘
  
  Packet: [Outer: Node-1→Node-2][Inner: 10.244.1.5→10.244.2.7]
  
  Pods see each other's REAL IPs — CNI handles the tunneling!
Networking Q194 of 200
What is CoreDNS and how does it provide service discovery?
A) CoreDNS is an alternative to etcd for storing service data
B) CoreDNS is the cluster DNS server (runs as Deployment, exposed via Service kube-dns). It watches the API server for Services and Pods, creates DNS records: A/AAAA for Services (ClusterIP) and pods (with hostname), SRV for named ports. Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf points to CoreDNS
C) CoreDNS is a Kubernetes-native load balancer
D) CoreDNS replaces the API server for service discovery
✅ Correct Answer: B

CoreDNS replaced kube-dns as the default cluster DNS server and works by continuously watching the API server, translating Services and Pods into standard DNS records. Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf is automatically configured to query CoreDNS first, with a search path that lets short names like my-svc resolve within the pod's own namespace.

CoreDNS Resolution Flow
  Pod: nslookup my-svc.default.svc.cluster.local
  │
  ▼
  /etc/resolv.conf → nameserver 10.96.0.10 (kube-dns Service IP)
  │
  ▼
  CoreDNS pod (kube-system)
  │
  ├─ my-svc.default → A record → 10.96.0.50 (ClusterIP)
  ├─ pod-ip.default → A record → 10.244.1.5 (pod IP)
  └─ Unknown → upstream DNS (from Corefile config)
  
  CoreDNS = DNS server + service discovery = essential!
Networking Q195 of 200
What is the CoreDNS Corefile and where is it configured?
A) Corefile is a Go file compiled into CoreDNS — can't be changed
B) Corefile is stored in etcd under /dns/config
C) Corefile is defined in the CoreDNS deployment YAML as an annotation
D) The Corefile is stored in a ConfigMap (coredns) in kube-system namespace. It defines DNS zones, plugins (kubernetes, forward, cache, errors, log). Edit the ConfigMap and CoreDNS auto-reloads (or kubectl rollout restart deployment/coredns -n kube-system)
✅ Correct Answer: D

kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system. Common Corefile plugins: kubernetes (cluster domain), forward (upstream DNS), cache (performance), errors (logging), health (readiness), prometheus (metrics).

CoreDNS Corefile Configuration
  kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml
  
  Corefile: |
    .:53 {
        errors          # Log errors
        health          # Health check endpoint
        ready           # Readiness check
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
            pods insecure
            fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
        }
        prometheus :9153 # Metrics for monitoring
        forward . /etc/resolv.conf  # Upstream DNS
        cache 30         # Cache responses for 30s
        loop             # Detect loops
        reload           # Auto-reload on ConfigMap change
        loadbalance      # Round-robin DNS
    }
Networking Q196 of 200
How do you troubleshoot DNS issues in Kubernetes? (Pod can't resolve Service names)
A) (1) kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup svc-name → check if resolution works. (2) Check CoreDNS pods are running → kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns. (3) Check CoreDNS logs → kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns. (4) Check pod's /etc/resolv.conf has correct nameserver. (5) Test with a busybox pod
B) Reboot all nodes — DNS will auto-fix
C) Delete and recreate the Service — DNS is cached in pods
D) kubectl fix-dns — a built-in repair command
✅ Correct Answer: A

Common DNS failures: CoreDNS pods not running, kube-dns Service missing, NetworkPolicy blocking DNS (UDP 53), pod's dnsPolicy set incorrectly, CoreDNS ConfigMap misconfigured, node DNS not working.

DNS Troubleshooting Checklist
  Pod can't resolve Service names? Check:
  
  1. CoreDNS pods running?
     kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
  
  2. CoreDNS logs:
     kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
  
  3. Test from busybox:
     kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes.default
  
  4. Check pod's /etc/resolv.conf:
     kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
     → nameserver should be kube-dns Service IP (10.96.0.10)
  
  5. Is NetworkPolicy blocking DNS (UDP 53)?
     kubectl get networkpolicy -A
  
  6. kube-dns Service exists?
     kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system
Networking Q197 of 200
What does dnsPolicy control on a pod?
A) Whether DNS is enabled or disabled — boolean setting
B) The DNS server version to use
C) dnsPolicy controls how the pod's /etc/resolv.conf is generated. ClusterFirst (the actual default when unset): CoreDNS first, then node DNS. Default (despite the name, NOT what's used by default): inherits ONLY the node's own DNS config, no cluster DNS at all. ClusterFirstWithHostNet: same as ClusterFirst but for hostNetwork pods. None: custom DNS via dnsConfig
D) The TTL for DNS cache entries
✅ Correct Answer: C

ClusterFirst is the default and correct for most pods. Use 'Default' only for pods that need node DNS. Use 'None' + dnsConfig for custom DNS (e.g., pods using an external DNS service). hostNetwork pods keep dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst but fall back to Default-like behavior unless you explicitly set 'ClusterFirstWithHostNet'.

dnsPolicy Options
  dnsPolicy              BEHAVIOR
  ─────────              ───────
  ClusterFirst (default) CoreDNS first, then node DNS
                         search: <ns>.svc.cluster.local
  
  Default                Inherit node's /etc/resolv.conf
                         (no cluster DNS!)
  
  ClusterFirstWithHostNet Same as ClusterFirst, for
                         hostNetwork: true pods
  
  None                   Custom DNS via dnsConfig
                         spec:
                           dnsPolicy: None
                           dnsConfig:
                             nameservers:
                             - 8.8.8.8
  
  Most pods → ClusterFirst (default)
  hostNetwork pods → ClusterFirstWithHostNet
Networking Q198 of 200
What is the Kubernetes networking model's fundamental requirement?
A) All pods must use the same IP range as the nodes
B) ALL pods can communicate with ALL other pods WITHOUT NAT (regardless of node). ALL nodes can communicate with ALL pods without NAT. The IP a pod sees itself as is the same IP others see it as. This is enforced by the CNI plugin
C) Pods can only communicate through Services — direct IP communication is blocked
D) Only pods in the same namespace can communicate
✅ Correct Answer: B

This is the fundamental Kubernetes networking assumption. It means: (1) Pods have cluster-wide unique IPs. (2) No port conflicts (each pod has its own IP). (3) Services provide load balancing, not connectivity. The CNI plugin makes this work.

Kubernetes Networking Model — 3 Requirements
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. All pods CAN communicate with ALL other pods         │
  │    WITHOUT NAT (regardless of which node they're on)    │
  │                                                         │
  │ 2. All nodes CAN communicate with ALL pods              │
  │    WITHOUT NAT                                           │
  │                                                         │
  │ 3. The IP a pod sees itself as is the SAME IP           │
  │    that other pods see it as                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Consequences:
  ✓ Each pod gets its own unique, routable IP
  ✓ No port conflicts (pods have unique IPs)
  ✓ Services provide load balancing, NOT connectivity
  ✓ CNI plugin implements this model
Networking Q199 of 200
What happens when CoreDNS is down? Can pods still communicate?
A) All pod traffic stops — nothing works without DNS
B) Pods can only communicate via IP addresses — Services stop working
C) Kubernetes API server takes over DNS resolution
D) Pod-to-pod communication via IP still works (CNI handles that). Service resolution by NAME fails (CoreDNS is the DNS server). Pods using environment variables for Service discovery still work. New Service name lookups fail. DNS unavailability causes application-level failures but pod networking is unaffected
✅ Correct Answer: D

CoreDNS is critical for service discovery by name. If CoreDNS is down: existing connections keep working (IP-based), but new name-based lookups fail. Running CoreDNS as a Deployment with multiple replicas (anti-affinity across nodes) ensures high availability.

CoreDNS is Down — What Still Works?
  COREDNS DOWN SCENARIO:
  
  ✅ STILL WORKS:
    - Existing TCP connections (already resolved)
    - Pod ↔ Pod via IP (10.244.x.x)
    - Service env vars (pre-injected at pod start)
    - Pods using IP addresses directly
  
  ❌ BROKEN:
    - Service name resolution (nslookup, curl svc-name)
    - New pod-to-service connections by name
    - External DNS resolution (if CoreDNS is sole resolver)
    - New pod startup (needs DNS for config)
  
  SOLUTION: Deploy CoreDNS as multi-replica Deployment
            with pod anti-affinity across nodes
Networking Q200 of 200
🎉 FINAL QUESTION: What is the complete path of a packet from an external user to a pod through Ingress?
A) User → DNS → Cloud Load Balancer → NodePort → Ingress Controller Pod → (reads Ingress rules) → ClusterIP Service → (iptables DNAT) → Backend Pod. Each step: DNS resolves domain to LB IP, LB forwards to node, node forwards to controller, controller routes by Host header and path, Service load balances to pod
B) User → API server → Pod (two hops)
C) User → kube-proxy → Pod (bypasses Ingress)
D) User → etcd → Pod (etcd routes traffic)
✅ Correct Answer: A

This question ties together nearly every networking concept in this guide: DNS resolution, cloud load balancing, NodePort, Ingress routing, and Service-to-pod DNAT via kube-proxy. If you can trace this path from memory, you understand Kubernetes networking end-to-end — which is exactly what the exam is testing when it asks you to debug connectivity issues. Note this is one common path (e.g., NGINX Ingress via a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service) — Kubernetes deliberately leaves controller mechanics open, and some controllers (e.g., certain cloud-native LB integrations) route the load balancer directly to pod IPs, skipping the NodePort/kube-proxy DNAT hop entirely.

🎉 Complete Request Journey — External to Pod
  INTERNET USER: https://api.example.com/v1/users
  │
  ▼
  [1] DNS: api.example.com → LB Public IP (53.12.34.56)
  │
  ▼
  [2] Cloud LB (AWS NLB/GCP LB) → forwards to Node-IP:30080
  │
  ▼
  [3] Node iptables (NodePort rule) → DNAT to Ingress Controller Pod IP
  │
  ▼
  [4] NGINX Ingress Controller Pod:
      Reads Ingress rules:
      ┌─ Host: api.example.com + Path: /v1/* → api-svc:8080
      └─ Host: web.example.com + Path: /*    → web-svc:80
      Forwards to api-svc ClusterIP 10.96.0.50:8080
  │
  ▼
  [5] kube-proxy iptables: DNAT 10.96.0.50:8080 → 10.244.2.7:8080
  │
  ▼
  [6] Backend Pod (10.244.2.7:8080) processes request!
  
  Response follows reverse path.
  Every hop matters on the CKA exam!

Real-world Kubernetes failure scenarios — each with symptom, 15 categorized causes (5 most likely + 5 less likely + 5 new cluster), diagnostic commands, solutions, and personal advice. Patterned after the 5+5+5 cause-card format.

100Issues
5Categories
15Causes per Issue

💾 Category 1: Storage Troubleshooting (10 Issues)ST1-ST10

🟢 Storage Issues — PVC, PV, StorageClass, and Mount Failures

Storage is often the FIRST thing to break because it involves multiple components: PVC → StorageClass → Provisioner → PV → Mount. When any link in this chain fails, your pod can't start or your data is at risk.

📌 ST1–ST3: PVC Binding Failures

ST1
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST1
PVC Stuck in Pending State — No PV Bound

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pvc shows STATUS: Pending indefinitely. kubectl describe pvc shows "no persistent volumes available for this claim." The easypj-db PostgreSQL pod can't start because its PVC won't bind.

  kubectl get pvc
  NAME         STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS   AGE
  easypj-pvc   Pending                      fast-ssd       5m

  kubectl describe pvc easypj-pvc
  Events:
    Warning  VolumeBinding  no persistent volumes available for this claim
    Warning  VolumeBinding  storageclass.storage.k8s.io "fast-ssd" not found
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. StorageClass does not exist: The PVC references a StorageClass that hasn't been created. kubectl get sc — if "fast-ssd" is missing, create it or fix the PVC's storageClassName.
  2. No matching PV available: In static provisioning, no PV matches the PVC's storage size, access mode, or selector. kubectl get pv — check capacity and accessModes.
  3. StorageClass provisioner not installed: The CSI driver (e.g., ebs.csi.aws.com) is not deployed. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi — provisioner pods must be Running.
  4. Access mode mismatch: PVC requests ReadWriteMany but only ReadWriteOnce PVs exist. Check kubectl get pv -o yaml | grep -A2 accessModes.
  5. StorageClass has volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer and no pod uses the PVC yet. The PV is only created when a pod actually references the PVC.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CSI driver pod CrashLoopBackOff — provisioner can't create volumes
  2. Cloud provider API rate limiting — too many PVCs created simultaneously
  3. PVC selector labels don't match any PV labels
  4. Node where CSI driver runs has taint without toleration
  5. storageClassName: "" (empty string, not null!) — requests a PV with NO StorageClass, but all PVs have one
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No default StorageClass set: kubectl get sc — look for "(default)". Without it, PVCs without storageClassName won't bind. Set: kubectl patch sc <name> -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'
  2. CSI driver not yet installed — common in fresh kubeadm clusters
  3. Cloud credentials not configured for CSI driver to provision volumes
  4. RBAC for CSI driver service account missing
  5. Legacy-cluster concern only: in-tree cloud provider volume plugins are removed from current Kubernetes (kubelet's --cloud-provider flag now only accepts "" or "external") — on current clusters, look for a missing external cloud-controller-manager instead of a missing in-tree flag
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get sc,pv,pvc --all-namespaces — the full storage stack in one view. kubectl describe pvc <name> — the Events section tells you exactly why binding failed.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get sc — verify the StorageClass exists
2. kubectl describe sc <name> — check provisioner and parameters
3. For static: kubectl get pv — create a PV matching the PVC's size/accessMode
4. For dynamic: install CSI driver: kubectl apply -f <csi-driver-url>
5. Set default SC: kubectl patch sc <name> -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass...is-default-class":"true"}}}'

💡 Personal Advice: The #1 PVC issue on the CKA exam is a missing or misnamed StorageClass. The exam environment may have a StorageClass named "standard" but your PVC says "fast-ssd". Always run kubectl get sc FIRST before writing any PVC YAML. Also: storageClassName: "" (empty string) is NOT the same as omitting storageClassName — empty string requests a PV with NO StorageClass. One rarer gotcha: the "use the default StorageClass when storageClassName is omitted" behavior is implemented by the DefaultStorageClass admission controller — if that controller is disabled on the API server, an omitted storageClassName will NOT fall back to the default even if one is correctly annotated, and the PVC stays Pending exactly like this issue.
ST2
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST2
PVC Bound But Pod Shows "FailedMount" — Volume Not Attached

🔍 Symptom: PVC shows STATUS: Bound, but pod stays Pending with event: "Unable to attach or mount volumes: timed out waiting for the condition." The easypj-db pod is stuck waiting for its volume to mount.

  kubectl describe pod easypj-db-0
  Events:
    Warning  FailedMount   Unable to attach or mount volumes:
      unmounted volumes=[db-data], unattached volumes=[db-data]:
      timed out waiting for the condition

  kubectl get pvc
  NAME         STATUS   VOLUME              CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS
  easypj-pvc   Bound    pvc-abc123def456    10Gi       fast-ssd
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CSI driver attacher/driver pods not running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi — both controller and node plugins must be Running.
  2. Volume is already attached to another node: Most block storage (EBS, GCE PD) can only be attached to ONE node at a time. kubectl get volumeattachment — check attachment status.
  3. Node doesn't support the volume type: AWS EBS CSI node plugin not running on this specific node. Check DaemonSet status: kubectl get ds -n kube-system | grep csi.
  4. Cloud API call failing: CSI driver can't call AWS/GCP API to attach volume. Check CSI driver logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=ebs-csi-node.
  5. Volume is in wrong availability zone: EBS volume in us-east-1a, pod scheduled on us-east-1b node. Check: kubectl get pv <name> -o yaml | grep topology.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. volumeAttachment resource stuck — needs manual deletion
  2. Node has reached max volume attachments limit (AWS: 25-40 EBS volumes per instance type)
  3. fsGroup or fsGroupChangePolicy causing SELinux relabeling timeout on large volumes
  4. kubelet PLEG (Pod Lifecycle Event Generator) not healthy — delayed volume operations
  5. Device path conflict: /dev/xvdb already in use by another volume
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CSI driver CRDs not installed: Run kubectl get csidriver — should show the driver. If missing, re-apply the full CSI driver manifest.
  2. Node missing necessary packages: EBS CSI needs ebs-utils, GCE PD CSI needs gce-compute. dpkg -l | grep ebs on the node.
  3. IAM/Service Account permissions missing for CSI driver to call cloud API
  4. Security group or firewall blocking CSI driver communication to cloud metadata API
  5. Wrong kubelet root-dir: CSI driver expects /var/lib/kubelet but kubelet uses different path
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get volumeattachment — the bridge between PV and node. kubectl describe volumeattachment for the specific PV. CSI driver logs on the node: kubectl logs -n kube-system csi-<node>-<pod>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check CSI node plugin: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=ebs-csi-node -o wide
2. Verify VolumeAttachment: kubectl get volumeattachment | grep <pv-name>
3. Force detach stuck attachment: kubectl delete volumeattachment <name>
4. If AZ mismatch: create StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer and allowedTopologies
5. Check cloud API from node: aws ec2 attach-volume or equivalent

💡 Personal Advice: The AZ mismatch between volume and pod is a classic gotcha. Always use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer in your StorageClass — this delays volume creation until the pod is scheduled, ensuring the volume is created in the same AZ as the pod. This single setting eliminates 50% of CSI attachment issues.
ST3
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST3
PVC Bound to Wrong PV — Wrong Size or StorageClass

🔍 Symptom: PVC shows Bound, but it's attached to a 1Gi PV when you requested 10Gi, or it's using HDD when you wanted SSD. The easypj-db pod starts but runs out of disk space quickly.

  kubectl get pvc
  NAME         STATUS   VOLUME              CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS
  easypj-pvc   Bound    pvc-small-hdd       1Gi        slow-hdd

  kubectl get pv pvc-small-hdd -o yaml | grep -A3 "capacity\|storageClassName"
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi               # ❌ Requested 10Gi!
  storageClassName: slow-hdd   # ❌ Requested fast-ssd!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. PVC storageClassName was wrong: Requested "fast-ssd" but "slow-hdd" is the default. Check: kubectl get pvc -o yaml | grep storageClassName.
  2. PVC size request didn't match any larger PV: Only a 1Gi PV was available. PV binding selects the SMALLEST PV that fits — not an exact match.
  3. PVC selector labels matched wrong PV: kubectl get pv --show-labels — selector may have matched an unintended PV.
  4. Multiple default StorageClasses exist: Kubernetes uses the MOST RECENTLY CREATED default SC, not an alphabetical or predictable choice. kubectl get sc — check if multiple have "(default)".
  5. PVC was pre-created with wrong spec before the correct StorageClass existed
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. PV was manually created with wrong labels matching PVC selector
  2. Dynamic provisioning created wrong size because StorageClass defaults were wrong
  3. PVC modified after binding: storageClassName/accessModes/volumeName are immutable once bound — only the storage size request can be edited post-binding (to trigger expansion), not the class or access mode
  4. GKE default StorageClass creates standard-rwo (HDD) instead of premium-rwo (SSD)
  5. CSI driver provisioner ignores StorageClass parameters due to version mismatch
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Cloud provider's default volume type is HDD: AWS gp2 (SSD) is default, but custom launch templates may default to st1 (HDD).
  2. StorageClass parameters incorrectly formatted for the CSI driver version
  3. Default StorageClass annotation set on wrong SC during cluster setup
  4. Provisioner doesn't support requested size (e.g., min 10Gi but requested 1Gi)
  5. Cloud quota: requested size exceeds project/account quota — provisioner created smaller volume
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pv -o wide shows all PVs with their StorageClass and capacity. kubectl describe pvc <name> shows which PV was bound and why.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Delete PVC and recreate with correct storageClassName and size
2. Ensure correct StorageClass is default: kubectl patch sc fast-ssd -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass...is-default-class":"true"}}}'
3. Remove default from wrong SC: kubectl patch sc slow-hdd -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass...is-default-class":null}}}'
4. For existing data: create new correct PVC, use kubectl cp or volume cloning to migrate data
5. Use PVC label selectors to prevent binding to unintended PVs

💡 Personal Advice: Always explicitly set storageClassName in your PVCs — never rely on the default. In the CKA exam, the default StorageClass may be intentionally misconfigured. Run kubectl get sc and note which one has "(default)". Also, PV binding selects the smallest PV that SATISFIES the PVC — not exact match. A 10Gi PVC will bind to a 100Gi PV if that's the only available one.

📌 ST4–ST6: Storage Provisioner Failures

ST4
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST4
Dynamic Provisioning Fails — "failed to provision volume"

🔍 Symptom: PVC uses dynamic provisioning but shows "failed to provision volume with StorageClass" in Events. The CSI provisioner logs show cloud API errors or timeout.

  kubectl describe pvc easypj-pvc
  Events:
    Warning  ProvisioningFailed  failed to provision volume with 
      StorageClass "fast-ssd": rpc error: code = Internal desc =
      Could not create volume: UnauthorizedOperation
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CSI provisioner pod not running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi.*controller — the controller plugin (provisioner) must be Running.
  2. Cloud credentials invalid or expired: CSI driver uses IAM roles or Service Account keys. Check provisioner logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/ebs-csi-controller.
  3. StorageClass parameters invalid: Wrong volume type string (e.g., "gp3" vs "gp3"), invalid IOPS value, or unsupported combination.
  4. Rate limiting from cloud provider: Too many volumes created in short time. Wait and retry.
  5. Cloud quota exceeded: Reached maximum number of volumes in the region/account. Check cloud console quotas.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Provisioner image pull failed — controller pod in ImagePullBackOff
  2. StorageClass reclaimPolicy: Delete combined with PV protection finalizer blocking cleanup
  3. Provisioner leader election issue — multiple controller replicas fighting
  4. CSI socket not available: /var/lib/csi/sockets/... missing or permissions wrong
  5. Kubernetes API server version mismatch with CSI driver CRD versions
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CSI driver not installed at all: kubectl get csidriver — should list the driver. Install via: kubectl apply -k "github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-ebs-csi-driver/deploy/kubernetes/overlays/stable/"
  2. IAM role for worker nodes missing EC2 volume permissions (for AWS EBS CSI)
  3. Cloud provider credentials Secret not created or in wrong namespace
  4. StorageClass provisioner field doesn't match any installed CSI driver name
  5. CSI driver requires specific Kubernetes version — check compatibility matrix
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get csidriver,csnode — verifies CSI driver registration. Provisioner logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/<csi-controller> --tail=50 — the actual API error from the cloud provider.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify CSI driver: kubectl get csidriver and kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=<csi-driver>
2. Check provisioner logs for the exact cloud API error
3. Verify StorageClass parameters match the CSI driver's expectations
4. Test with minimal StorageClass (no parameters) to isolate parameter issues
5. For cloud auth: verify IAM roles / service account keys are valid

💡 Personal Advice: Dynamic provisioning failures are almost always cloud credentials or StorageClass parameter typos. On the CKA exam, you won't have a cloud provider — dynamic provisioning is tested via NFS or hostPath provisioners. Know how to create a StorageClass with provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner for static provisioning, and how to use NFS CSI drivers for dynamic. One gotcha that isn't a provisioner bug at all: a PVC with storageClassName: "" (empty string) explicitly disables dynamic provisioning by design — it will only bind to a pre-existing classless PV and never calls the provisioner, which is easily misdiagnosed as a provisioner failure.
ST5
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST5
PVC Deleted But PV Stuck in "Released" or "Failed" State

🔍 Symptom: You deleted a PVC, but the PV shows STATUS: Released (not Available) or STATUS: Failed. New PVCs can't reuse this PV. Storage space is wasted on orphaned PVs.

  kubectl get pv
  NAME              CAPACITY   STATUS     CLAIM                  RECLAIM POLICY
  pvc-abc123        10Gi       Released   default/easypj-pvc     Retain
  pvc-def456        20Gi       Failed     default/old-pvc        Delete
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. reclaimPolicy is Retain: PV kept after PVC deletion. Manually delete and recreate PV to reuse. kubectl get sc -o yaml | grep reclaimPolicy.
  2. PV has kubernetes.io/pv-protection finalizer: Prevents deletion while referenced. kubectl get pv <name> -o yaml | grep finalizers.
  3. Underlying storage deleted externally (cloud console) — PV in Failed state
  4. Released PV's claimRef still points to the deleted PVC: Kubernetes doesn't auto-clear it — manually remove claimRef from the PV spec before it can be rebound.
  5. CSI driver failed DeleteVolume call — PV stuck in Terminating
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kubernetes garbage collector not processing orphaned PVs
  2. PV annotation pv.kubernetes.io/bound-by-controller: "no" prevents cleanup
  3. Reclaim operation timed out — PV stuck between states
  4. Multiple controllers managing same PV
  5. Underlying storage has dependent snapshots preventing deletion
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default StorageClass with reclaimPolicy: Retain — unexpected manual cleanup needed
  2. No CSI driver installed — Delete reclaim can't call cloud API
  3. Cloud credentials expired — DeleteVolume fails silently
  4. StorageClass missing explicit reclaimPolicy — defaults differ between static/dynamic
  5. RBAC missing delete permissions for CSI driver on PV resources
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pv -o wide — STATUS and RECLAIM POLICY columns. kubectl describe pv <name> — Message field explains stuck state.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. For Retain: kubectl delete pv <name>, then recreate for new PVC
2. Remove finalizers: kubectl patch pv <name> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}'
3. Change reclaimPolicy: kubectl patch sc <name> -p '{"reclaimPolicy":"Delete"}'
4. For Failed PVs: delete and let provisioner create new ones
5. Clean underlying storage manually via cloud console if CSI can't

💡 Personal Advice: reclaimPolicy: Retain is safe for production DBs — prevents accidental data loss. For dev/test use Delete. CKA exam: you'll likely encounter a PV stuck Released and need to manually delete/recreate. Key: kubectl patch pv <name> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}'.
ST6
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST6
StorageClass Not Working — "provisioner not found"

🔍 Symptom: StorageClass exists but PVC events show "provisioner not found." The provisioner name doesn't match any installed CSI driver, or the CSI controller pod isn't running.

  kubectl describe pvc easypj-pvc
  Events:
    Warning  ProvisioningFailed  provisioner "ebs.csi.aws.com"
      not found — StorageClass references unregistered driver

  kubectl get csidriver
  No resources found         # ❌ CSI driver not installed!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CSI controller pod not running: kubectl get deploy -n kube-system | grep csi. The provisioner runs in controller Deployment.
  2. Provisioner name typo in StorageClass: Must exactly match CSIDriver name. Check: kubectl get csidriver.
  3. CSIDriver registered but controller plugin not deployed — CRDs exist, no pod running
  4. In-tree provisioner deprecated: kubernetes.io/aws-ebs replaced by ebs.csi.aws.com.
  5. csi-provisioner sidecar CrashLoopBackOff within CSI controller pod
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CSI controller RBAC issues — can't watch PVCs or create PVs
  2. Provisioner leader election failure — multiple replicas competing
  3. Sidecar version incompatible with Kubernetes version
  4. StorageClass parameters the provisioner doesn't understand
  5. Node taint repelling CSI controller pod
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CSI manifests applied without controller plugin — only node plugin
  2. Wrong driver name: ebs.csi.aws.com vs ebs.aws.csi.com
  3. CSI controller in wrong namespace — SC expects it elsewhere
  4. StorageClass created before CSI driver initialized
  5. Kubernetes 1.27+ removed in-tree provisioner — must use CSI
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get csidriver -o yaml — registered drivers. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep csi — controller/node plugin status.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify: kubectl get csidriver — note exact driver name
2. Verify controller: kubectl get deploy,statefulset -A | grep csi
3. Fix SC provisioner name to match CSIDriver exactly
4. Install CSI driver per cloud provider's guide
5. For CKA: use kubernetes.io/no-provisioner for static provisioning

💡 Personal Advice: Provisioner name is an exact string match. ebs.csi.aws.com ≠ ebs.csi.amazonaws.com. On CKA: primarily work with kubernetes.io/no-provisioner (static). Know that the provisioner field connects SC to the actual CSI driver.

📌 ST7–ST8: Volume Mount Failures

ST7
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST7
Pod Fails — "MountVolume.SetUp failed" for ConfigMap/Secret/PVC

🔍 Symptom: Pod stays Pending: "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume 'config': configmap 'app-config' not found." The pod references a volume source that doesn't exist or is in the wrong namespace.

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-7d8f9-x
  Events:
    Warning  FailedMount  MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume
      "config" : configmap "app-config" not found
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Referenced ConfigMap/Secret doesn't exist: kubectl get cm,secret -n <ns>. Create before pod.
  2. ConfigMap/Secret in different namespace: Volumes can only reference same-namespace resources.
  3. PVC referenced but doesn't exist or is Pending: kubectl get pvc -n <ns> — must be Bound.
  4. Volume name typo: Pod references "config-data" but volume defined as "app-config".
  5. Non-optional volume missing — add optional: true if the volume truly is optional.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. kubelet can't access volume plugin directory — permission issue
  2. SELinux context prevents kubelet reading ConfigMap/Secret files
  3. subPath references non-existent key in ConfigMap
  4. Node disk full — kubelet can't create tmpfs for Secret/ConfigMap
  5. kubelet PLEG unhealthy — volume operations delayed
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Pod created BEFORE ConfigMap/Secret — apply resources first
  2. Namespace not yet created — pod and volume sources must be same ns
  3. RBAC: ServiceAccount lacks permission to GET referenced Secret
  4. PodSecurityAdmission blocking hostPath or certain volume types
  5. CSI driver not registered for volume type on this node
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod <name> — Events show exactly which volume mount failed. kubectl get cm,secret,pvc -n <namespace> — verify all exist.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Create missing resource: kubectl create cm app-config --from-literal=key=value -n <ns>
2. Fix namespace: pod and volume sources in same namespace
3. Fix YAML typo in volume name reference
4. Delete and recreate pod for spec re-evaluation
5. For optional volumes: add optional: true

💡 Personal Advice: Most common CKA lab scenario: pod won't start because ConfigMap/Secret missing. Run kubectl describe pod FIRST, identify missing resource, create it. The pod auto-retries and succeeds.
ST8
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST8
Volume Mounted But Application Can't Write — Permission Denied

🔍 Symptom: Volume mounts successfully, pod Running, but app throws "Permission denied" writing to mount path. PostgreSQL: "could not create directory /var/lib/postgresql/data: Permission denied."

  kubectl exec easypj-db-0 -- ls -la /var/lib/postgresql
  drwxr-xr-x  root  root  /var/lib/postgresql/data
   # Container runs as postgres (UID 999), dir owned by root!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. fsGroup not set: Volume mounted root:root, container runs as non-root. Fix: securityContext: fsGroup: 999.
  2. Container UID/GID mismatch with volume ownership: kubectl exec <pod> -- id.
  3. InitContainer needed: Run initContainer as root to chown -R 999:999 /data.
