  4. SELinux context mismatch on SELinux-enabled nodes
  5. ReadOnlyMany volume mounted read-only — app needs write access
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. NFS root_squash enabled — maps root to nobody
  2. CSI driver applies restrictive default permissions
  3. PodSecurityAdmission blocking chown privilege escalation
  4. Volume previously used by different pod with different UID/GID
  5. Filesystem corruption — fsck needed
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No PodSecurityAdmission config — restricted profile blocks fsGroup
  2. StorageClass provisioned ext4 but app needs xfs
  3. Container image uses undocumented non-default UID
  4. SELinux enforcing on node — MCS labels needed per pod
  5. Cloud volume provisioned without filesystem — mkfs needed
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- id and kubectl exec <pod> -- ls -la /mount/path. kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 securityContext.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Add fsGroup: securityContext: fsGroup: 999 — kubelet chgrps volume recursively
2. InitContainer: command: ['chown','-R','999:999','/data']; securityContext: runAsUser: 0
3. Pre-create volume with Job running correct permissions
4. NFS: configure exports with no_root_squash or match UID/GID
5. Use runAsUser + runAsGroup matching volume owner

💡 Personal Advice: Permission denied on volumes is top-3 real-world issue. Simplest fix: add securityContext: fsGroup: <GID> to pod spec. For PostgreSQL: fsGroup: 999. For StatefulSets: spec.template.spec.securityContext. One line saves hours.

📌 ST9–ST10: Storage Performance & Capacity

ST9
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST9
Application Slow — High Storage Latency / Low IOPS

🔍 Symptom: PostgreSQL queries slow, iostat shows await >50ms, app logs show "slow query." Database on gp2 (burst) instead of gp3 (baseline) — burst credits exhausted.

  Node iostat -x 1:
  Device     await  %util
  nvme1n1    85.3   98.5       # ❌ >10ms is concerning for SSD!

  kubectl get pv pvc-db-data -o yaml | grep type
  type: gp2                     # ❌ Burst credits exhaust under load
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong volume type: gp2 (burst, 3 IOPS/GB) instead of gp3 (baseline 3000 IOPS). gp2 33GB = only 100 baseline IOPS.
  2. Volume too small: gp2 IOPS tied to size. Database needs 1000+ IOPS but 33GB gp2 = 100 IOPS.
  3. Throughput bottleneck: gp3 default 125MB/s. May need provisioning up to 1000MB/s.
  4. Noisy neighbor pods consuming all node disk I/O: Kubernetes has no native disk-I/O request/limit (only cpu, memory, ephemeral-storage, hugepages) — mitigate via node isolation (dedicated pool + taints), not resource limits.
  5. Network-attached storage (NFS/EFS) latency over network
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Filesystem fragmentation on long-lived volumes
  2. Node hardware storage controller issues — dmesg SCSI errors
  3. Cloud storage tiering — data moved to slower tiers
  4. Wrong I/O scheduler (cfq for SSD instead of none)
  5. Volume snapshot in progress degrades source performance
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default SC uses gp2/low-cost HDD — change to gp3/io2
  2. SC has no IOPS/throughput params — lowest cloud defaults
  3. Volume in wrong AZ — cross-AZ traffic latency
  4. Cloud quota limiting high-IOPS volume creation
  5. KMS encryption key limits throttling encrypted volumes
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe sc — type, iops, throughput params. iostat -x 1 and iotop on node. CloudWatch: BurstBalance, VolumeQueueLength.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Switch to gp3: update SC with type: gp3, iops: 3000, throughput: 125
2. Create new PVC with better SC, migrate data via pg_dump/pg_restore
3. Isolate noisy neighbors onto a dedicated node pool (taints/tolerations) — Kubernetes has no native disk-I/O limit to set
4. Use volume snapshots for migration
5. Production DBs: io2 Block Express (up to 256K IOPS)

💡 Personal Advice: gp2 vs gp3 is slow vs fast database difference. gp2 burst credits exhaust under sustained load — gp3 gives baseline 3000 IOPS regardless of size. For easypj production: gp3, 3000 IOPS, 125MB/s minimum. Check CloudWatch BurstBalance — near 0% = throttled volume.
ST10
💾 CATEGORY 1: STORAGE — Issue ST10
Disk Full — Node Under DiskPressure, Pods Evicted

🔍 Symptom: Node DiskPressure=True, pods evicted. df -h shows /var/lib/containerd at 95%+. Application writes fail "No space left on device." Container logs and images consuming all disk.

  kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep DiskPressure
  DiskPressure    True    KubeletHasDiskPressure

  ssh worker-1 → df -h
  /dev/xvda1    50G   48G   2G  96%  /var/lib/containerd

  ssh worker-1 → du -sh /var/lib/containerd /var/log/containers
  35G  /var/lib/containerd        # Images + container layers
  8G   /var/log/containers        # Unrotated logs!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Container logs filling disk: du -sh /var/log/containers/. Unrotated logs consume GBs.
  2. emptyDir/hostPath not cleaned: du -sh /var/lib/kubelet/pods/*/volumes/.
  3. Container images accumulation: crictl images | wc -l. Prune: crictl rmi --prune.
  4. GC threshold too high: Default triggers at 85%. Lower to 70% for safety.
  5. Application writing excessive data — runaway logging, unbounded data
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Core dumps filling /var/lib/systemd/coredump/
  2. OverlayFS layers not cleaned after container deletion
  3. Snapshotter leaking snapshots — containerd bug
  4. CSI driver local temp files during volume operations
  5. Inode exhaustion — df -i shows 0% free
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Root disk too small: 50GB minimum for K8s nodes. CKA nodes often 20-40GB.
  2. No log rotation: --container-log-max-size and --container-log-max-files not set.
  3. Image GC not tuned: --image-gc-high-threshold defaults at 85%.
  4. emptyDir no sizeLimit — pod can fill entire disk
  5. No monitoring — no alert on disk >80%
🔍 What to Look At: df -h; du -sh /var/lib/containerd /var/log /var/lib/kubelet. kubectl describe node for DiskPressure. crictl images for image count.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. crictl rmi --prune — remove unused images
2. journalctl --vacuum-size=500M — clean systemd logs
3. Set kubelet: --container-log-max-size=10Mi --container-log-max-files=5
4. Set emptyDir: sizeLimit: 1Gi in pod spec
5. Expand node disk or add dedicated data disk

💡 Personal Advice: DiskPressure is most preventable node issue. Always set container-log-max-size on kubelet and sizeLimit on emptyDir. CKA exam: SSH into node, du -sh /* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head to find culprit, clean, verify DiskPressure resolves. Tests ability to diagnose and fix — not just identify.

🔧 Category 2: Core Troubleshooting (30 Issues)TR1-TR30

🔴 Node Failures, Control Plane, Pod Lifecycle — The Core of CKA Troubleshooting

This is where real SRE work happens. Node failures, control plane crashes, pod startup issues — these are the scenarios that determine if your cluster stays up. 30% of the CKA is troubleshooting, and these 30 issues cover the most common failure patterns.

📌 TR1–TR5: Node-Level Failures

TR1
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR1
Node Shows NotReady — kubelet Stopped

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get nodes shows one node as NotReady. kubectl describe node shows KubeletNotReady. The kubelet service has crashed or stopped on that worker node.

  kubectl get nodes
  NAME       STATUS     ROLES    AGE   VERSION
  worker-2   NotReady   <none>   30d   v1.28.0
  worker-1   Ready      <none>   30d   v1.28.0

  ssh worker-2
  systemctl status kubelet
  Active: inactive (dead)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. kubelet service crashed: systemctl status kubelet — check if active. Restart: systemctl restart kubelet.
  2. Node out of disk/memory: Check df -h and free -m. Under pressure, kubelet evicts pods (not itself) to try to reclaim node resources.
  3. kubelet config corrupted: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml has invalid YAML. Check journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i error.
  4. Container runtime (containerd) stopped: kubelet depends on CRI. systemctl status containerd.
  5. API server unreachable from node: curl -k https://<api-server>:6443/healthz from the node.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Node certificate expired — kubelet can't authenticate to API server
  2. Kubelet binary updated but service not restarted — version mismatch
  3. Swap re-enabled after reboot — kubelet refuses to run with swap on
  4. SELinux policy update blocking kubelet operations
  5. CNI plugin not ready — kubelet can't set up pod networking
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Swap not disabled: swapoff -a and remove from /etc/fstab.
  2. kubelet not enabled: systemctl enable --now kubelet.
  3. Wrong node IP: kubelet --node-ip flag pointing to wrong interface.
  4. Firewall blocking kubelet port 10250 — node can't report status
  5. kubeconfig missing: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf not generated by kubeadm join.
🔍 What to Look At: systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet -n 50. kubectl describe node <name> — Conditions section shows the exact failure reason.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. systemctl restart kubelet — restart if crashed
2. journalctl -u kubelet -f — watch logs for startup errors
3. systemctl status containerd — container runtime must be running
4. swapoff -a if swap is enabled
5. For cert issues: kubeadm certs renew all && systemctl restart kubelet

💡 Personal Advice: NotReady is the most common node issue on the CKA. The fix is almost always: SSH to node → systemctl restart kubelet. If that doesn't work, check journalctl -u kubelet for the specific error. 90% of the time it's swap, disk full, or containerd stopped. Remember: kubelet is a systemd service, not a pod — kubectl logs won't work.
TR2
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR2
Node Shows MemoryPressure or DiskPressure — Resource Exhaustion

🔍 Symptom: kubectl describe node shows MemoryPressure=True or DiskPressure=True. Pods are being evicted from the node. New pods won't schedule there. The node is running out of resources.

  kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 Conditions
  Conditions:
    MemoryPressure   True    KubeletHasInsufficientMemory
    DiskPressure     True    KubeletHasDiskPressure
    PIDPressure      False   KubeletHasSufficientPID
    Ready            False   KubeletNotReady

  ssh worker-1
  free -m
                total   used   free
  Mem:          3827    3712    115    ← 97% used!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pod memory/disk usage too high: kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory. Find the culprit pod.
  2. No resource limits set: Pods without limits can consume all node memory. kubectl get pods -o yaml | grep -A2 resources.
  3. Container logs filling disk: du -sh /var/log/containers/. Rotate or clean logs.
  4. Node overcommitted: Too many pods scheduled. kubectl describe node | grep -A5 "Allocated resources".
  5. System services (not K8s) consuming resources: top -o %MEM to find non-container processes.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Memory leak in kubelet or containerd — restart the services
  2. Systemd-journald consuming excessive memory for log storage
  3. Node hardware failure — bad RAM causing kernel memory corruption
  4. Tmpfs (emptyDir) not bounded — pod filling node memory via tmpfs
  5. KSM (Kernel Same-page Merging) disabled — VMs with identical pages not deduplicated
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Node under-provisioned: Minimum 2GB RAM for kubelet + OS. Add more pods = needs more.
  2. System-reserved not configured: kubelet --system-reserved should reserve CPU/memory for OS.
  3. Eviction thresholds too low: the default --eviction-hard (memory.available<100Mi) leaves a small buffer before OOM — consider raising it for memory-heavy nodes.
  4. kube-reserved not set: kubelet and container runtime need dedicated resources.
  5. No node autoscaler — cluster can't add nodes when resources run low.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl top nodes and kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory. kubectl describe node <name> | grep -A10 "Allocated".
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Identify culprit: kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head
2. Add limits: kubectl set resources deploy <name> --limits=memory=256Mi
3. Evict pods: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets to move workloads
4. Clean logs: journalctl --vacuum-size=200M
5. Add node: scale cluster or add worker node

💡 Personal Advice: MemoryPressure is the #1 preventable issue. Always set resource limits on every container. A single pod without limits can OOM the entire node. On CKA: the exam gives you a node under pressure — you need to identify which pod is the culprit, evict or limit it, and verify the node recovers. kubectl top is your best friend (requires metrics-server).
TR3
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR3
kubelet Certificate Expired — Node Can't Join/Rejoin Cluster

🔍 Symptom: Node shows NotReady, kubelet logs show "certificate has expired" or "x509: certificate has expired." The kubelet client certificate (valid 1 year by default) has expired and the node can't authenticate to the API server.

  journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i cert
  x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid
  Failed to register node with API server

  openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem -noout -dates
  notBefore=Jun  4 2025 10:00:00 GMT
  notAfter=Jun  4 2026 10:00:00 GMT  ← EXPIRED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. kubelet client cert expired: Default validity 1 year. openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem -noout -dates.
  2. API server cert expired: kubeadm certs check-expiration — check ALL certs.
  3. Node was offline for extended period: Cert expired while node was powered off. Auto-renewal didn't run.
  4. Clock skew: date on node vs API server. NTP must be synced. >5min skew breaks TLS.
  5. kubelet.conf still points to old cert after manual rotation attempt
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CA certificate expired — entire cluster PKI needs rotation
  2. Node hostname changed — cert SAN doesn't match new hostname
  3. kubelet bootstrap cert expired before joining — recreate bootstrap token
  4. Manual cert rotation deleted old cert before new one was ready
  5. Intermediate CA rotation broke the cert chain on this node
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Cluster age >1 year: kubeadm's client/leaf certs expire after 1 year by default (the CA cert itself lasts 10 years). Run kubeadm certs check-expiration.
  2. kubeadm upgrade not done: Upgrades renew certs. Stale clusters accumulate expired certs.
  3. NTP not configured: timedatectl status — clock must be synced.
  4. kubelet auto-renewal disabled: kubelet --rotate-certificates flag missing.
  5. /var/lib/kubelet/pki/ directory permissions wrong — kubelet can't write new cert
🔍 What to Look At: kubeadm certs check-expiration on control plane. openssl x509 -in <cert> -noout -dates on the node.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubeadm certs renew all on control plane
2. On worker: rm /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-*.pem && systemctl restart kubelet
3. If cert auto-renewal fails: kubeadm certs renew kubelet-client and copy to worker
4. Fix clock: timedatectl set-ntp true
5. For expired CA: kubeadm certs renew all and redistribute new kubeconfig to all nodes

💡 Personal Advice: Certificate expiry is a ticking time bomb. Set a calendar reminder 1 month before your cluster's 1-year anniversary. Run kubeadm certs check-expiration monthly. kubeadm has automatically renewed all certs during kubeadm upgrade since v1.15 (stable, on by default) — keep your cluster on a regular upgrade cadence rather than waiting for a version-gated auto-renewal feature that doesn't exist. On CKA: you may need to manually renew certs and restart kubelet — know the kubeadm certs renew commands cold.
TR4
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR4
Node NetworkUnavailable — CNI Plugin Failed

🔍 Symptom: Node shows NetworkUnavailable=True. Pods on this node are stuck in ContainerCreating with "network plugin not ready." The CNI plugin (Calico/Flannel/Cilium) is not running or misconfigured on this node.

  kubectl describe node worker-2 | grep NetworkUnavailable
  NetworkUnavailable   True    CalicoIsNotReady

  kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep calico
  calico-node-abc123   1/2  Running    worker-1  ...
  calico-node-def456   0/2  CrashLoop  worker-2  ...  ← Not healthy!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CNI DaemonSet pod not running on this node: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep calico.
  2. CNI config file missing: ls /etc/cni/net.d/ — must have the CNI plugin config.
  3. CNI binary not installed: ls /opt/cni/bin/ — missing the binary for the CNI plugin.
  4. IPPool exhausted (Calico): calicoctl get ippool — no free IPs for new pods.
  5. Network plugin CrashLoopBackOff: kubectl describe pod -n kube-system <cni-pod>.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Node has taint that the CNI DaemonSet doesn't tolerate
  2. MTU mismatch between overlay network and underlying NIC — causes fragmented/dropped packets across nodes
  3. Firewall/iptables interfering with CNI traffic between nodes
  4. BGP peering down (Calico) — pod routes not advertised to other nodes
  5. Kernel module missing: lsmod | grep vxlan (for VXLAN-based CNI)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CNI not installed: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|flannel|cilium|weave" — must have a CNI.
  2. Wrong pod CIDR: kubeadm --pod-network-cidr must match CNI expected CIDR.
  3. kube-proxy mode mismatch: iptables vs ipvs conflict with CNI.
  4. CNI DaemonSet tolerations don't match control-plane taint
  5. Dual-stack misconfiguration — IPv6 not enabled but CNI expects it
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E "calico|flannel|cni". ls /etc/cni/net.d/ on the node.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify CNI pod: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node
2. Check CNI config: ls /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist
3. Restart CNI pod: kubectl delete pod -n kube-system <cni-pod>
4. Check BGP: calicoctl node status (Calico specific)
5. Reinstall CNI: kubectl apply -f <cni-manifest>

💡 Personal Advice: CNI issues often masquerade as pod startup issues. If pods are stuck in ContainerCreating, check the CNI BEFORE checking anything else. kubectl describe pod will show "network plugin not ready" in Events. On CKA: you'll likely work with Calico or Flannel. Know that Calico uses BGP (no overlay) while Flannel uses VXLAN. The fix is usually restarting the CNI pod on the affected node.
TR5
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR5
kubectl exec/logs Times Out — Node Port 10250 Blocked

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec, kubectl logs, and kubectl port-forward all timeout or fail for pods on a specific node. kubectl get/describe work fine. The kubelet API port (10250) is blocked by a firewall or network policy.

  kubectl exec -it nginx-pod -- sh
  Error from server: error dialing backend: dial tcp 10.0.1.5:10250: i/o timeout

  ssh worker-2
  curl -k https://localhost:10250/healthz
  ok  ← kubelet is healthy locally!

  # From control plane node:
  curl -k https://worker-2:10250/healthz
  curl: (7) Failed to connect  ← Firewall blocking!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Firewall/security group blocking TCP 10250: The API server connects to kubelet on port 10250 for exec/logs/port-forward. Firewall must allow this.
  2. kubelet --node-ip set to wrong IP: API server tries to connect to an IP that doesn't exist or is firewalled.
  3. Node network interface issue: kubelet bound to wrong interface. Check netstat -tlnp | grep 10250.
  4. Cloud provider security group rules: Node-to-node traffic on 10250 blocked. Check AWS SG / GCP firewall rules.
  5. NetworkPlugin cni failing on this node — kubelet health check responding but API unreachable
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. iptables rules on node blocking port 10250 from API server subnet
  2. kubelet TLS cert not trusted by API server — cert verification fails silently
  3. kubelet rate limiting — too many concurrent exec/logs requests
  4. Reverse DNS lookup failure — API server resolves node name to wrong IP
  5. Container runtime socket permissions — kubelet can reach containerd but API can't reach kubelet
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default cloud firewall blocks all inter-node traffic — must explicitly allow 10250.
  2. kubeadm join used wrong --apiserver-advertise-address: API server resolves worker IP incorrectly.
  3. Multi-subnet cluster: API server in one subnet, workers in another — firewall between subnets.
  4. kubelet --anonymous-auth=false without proper authorization configuration
  5. Node hostname doesn't resolve to the correct IP in DNS
🔍 What to Look At: curl -k https://<worker-ip>:10250/healthz from control plane. netstat -tlnp | grep 10250 on worker. Check cloud firewall/SG rules for port 10250.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify kubelet is listening: netstat -tlnp | grep 10250 on the worker
2. Test connectivity: curl -k https://worker-ip:10250/healthz from cp
3. Cloud: add security group rule allowing TCP 10250 from control plane
4. On-prem: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 10250 -j ACCEPT
5. Fix kubelet node-ip: --node-ip=<correct-ip>

💡 Personal Advice: When exec/logs fail but get/describe work, it's always port 10250. The API server proxies exec/logs requests to the kubelet on the node. If 10250 is blocked, you get timeout errors. This is a classic CKA scenario — the fix is almost always a firewall rule. Test with curl -k from the control plane to the worker's kubelet port.

📌 TR6–TR10: Control Plane Failures

TR6
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR6
kube-apiserver Not Responding — kubectl Times Out

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get nodes times out with "The connection to the server <ip>:6443 was refused." or "i/o timeout." The API server is down or unreachable. No kubectl commands work.

  kubectl get nodes
  The connection to the server 192.168.1.10:6443 was refused

  ssh cp-node
  docker ps | grep kube-apiserver
  (empty — apiserver container is not running!)

  crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver
  (empty — static pod is not running)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. API server static pod stopped: ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml — manifest moved/deleted. kubelet stops the pod.
  2. etcd unreachable: API server can't reach etcd. Check etcdctl endpoint health.
  3. API server cert expired: kubeadm certs check-expiration. Expired certs prevent startup.
  4. Port 6443 already in use: Another process bound to the API server port.
  5. API server manifest has invalid YAML: crictl logs <apiserver-container> shows parse errors.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Load balancer (for HA) misconfigured — pointing to wrong or dead backends
  2. --etcd-servers flag pointing to wrong etcd endpoint after etcd migration
  3. Admission webhook (mutating/validating) timing out — API server hangs
  4. API server OOMKilled due to too many requests or large objects
  5. Audit log directory full — API server can't write audit logs, refuses to start
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm init failed partway: Manifests exist but certs are missing or wrong.
  2. Wrong --advertise-address: API server can't bind to non-existent IP.
  3. Firewall blocking 6443: New cloud security group rules blocking the port.
  4. kubelet not running: Static pods depend on kubelet. systemctl status kubelet.
  5. Docker/containerd socket missing: kubelet can't start any containers.
🔍 What to Look At: crictl ps | grep apiserver. journalctl -u kubelet | grep apiserver. ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. kubeadm certs check-expiration.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check kubelet: systemctl status kubelet — must be running for static pods
2. Check manifests: ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. Check certs: kubeadm certs check-expiration && kubeadm certs renew all
4. Check etcd: crictl ps | grep etcd — must be running first
5. Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet — forces static pod recreation

💡 Personal Advice: When kubectl fails completely, SSH to the control plane FIRST. Check if kubelet is running (systemctl status kubelet), then check if static pods are running (crictl ps). The API server is a static pod — it depends on kubelet, not the other way around. On CKA: you may need to fix a broken API server manifest (typo, wrong flag, missing cert) and then restart kubelet to apply the fix.
TR7
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR7
etcd Leader Elections Frequent — Cluster Unstable

🔍 Symptom: etcdctl endpoint status shows frequent leader changes. kubectl commands are intermittently slow or timeout. etcd logs show "leader changed" or "failed to send heartbeat." High disk latency or network issues between etcd members.

  etcdctl endpoint status --endpoints=cp-1:2379,cp-2:2379,cp-3:2379
  cp-1:2379, 8f3a..., 3.5.0, 25 MB, leader
  cp-2:2379, 2d9b..., 3.5.0, 25 MB, follower
  cp-3:2379, 7c1f..., 3.5.0, 25 MB, follower

  journalctl -u etcd | grep -i leader
  etcd: leader changed 5 times in last 10 minutes
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. High disk latency: etcd is VERY sensitive to disk I/O. fio test: write latency >10ms causes issues. Use SSD only.
  2. Network latency between etcd members: Check ping -c 100 between nodes. Latency >50ms or packet loss triggers elections.
  3. etcd database too large: etcdctl endpoint status — DB size exceeding the 2GB default quota (--quota-backend-bytes) triggers a NOSPACE alarm, putting etcd into a read-only state that rejects writes until compacted + defragged.
  4. Other process competing for disk/CPU: etcd needs dedicated resources. Co-located workloads cause starvation.
  5. Too many writes (events, lease renewals): Check kubectl get events -A | wc -l. Event storm overloads etcd.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. etcd member hardware different specs — one slow node drags down quorum
  2. Firewall between etcd members blocking or rate-limiting peer traffic (2379-2380)
  3. NTP clock drift >1 second between etcd members — lease timing issues
  4. etcd compaction not running — database fragmentation causes I/O spikes
  5. Too many watchers — applications creating excessive watch connections
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. etcd on HDD: etcd REQUIRES SSD. HDD latency causes constant leader elections.
  2. Only 1 etcd member: No quorum possible. Must have odd number ≥3.
  3. etcd not configured for production: Default limits too low. Need --quota-backend-bytes tuning.
  4. etcd running in Docker with poor I/O isolation — fsync latency spikes
  5. No etcd monitoring set up — can't see disk latency, leader changes, DB size trends
🔍 What to Look At: etcdctl endpoint status -w table. etcdctl endpoint health. Disk: iostat -x 1 on etcd nodes.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check disk: iostat -x 1 — await must be <10ms
2. Check network: ping -c 100 <peer-node> — latency <10ms, 0% loss
3. Compact DB: etcdctl compact <revision> && etcdctl defrag
4. Reduce events: check for excessive event creation from misconfigured controllers
5. Dedicated nodes: run etcd on separate nodes (external etcd topology)

💡 Personal Advice: etcd is the heartbeat of Kubernetes. If etcd is unhappy, the entire cluster is unhappy. The #1 cause of etcd issues on CKA is network latency or disk I/O. Always check etcdctl endpoint health first. If you see frequent leader changes, it's almost certainly slow disk or network. etcd MUST run on SSD with consistent low latency. This is non-negotiable for production.
TR8
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR8
kube-scheduler Not Scheduling Pods — Pods Stuck Pending

🔍 Symptom: New pods stay in Pending state with no "Scheduled" event. kubectl describe pod shows no Events from scheduler. The kube-scheduler static pod is not running or has crashed.

  kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling
  No resources found.  ← Scheduler isn't even trying!

  crictl ps | grep kube-scheduler
  (empty — scheduler pod not running)

  kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler
  (empty — no scheduler pods visible)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Scheduler static pod not running: crictl ps | grep scheduler — manifest may be missing from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
  2. Scheduler port already in use: Default port 10259. netstat -tlnp | grep 10259.
  3. Scheduler has leader election issue: In HA, one scheduler must win leader election. kubectl get lease -n kube-system kube-scheduler.
  4. Scheduler configuration (--config) file invalid YAML: Check /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf.
  5. API server unreachable from scheduler: Check scheduler logs for connection refused errors.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Scheduler profile with wrong plugin configuration — no pods match scoring criteria
  2. All nodes have taints with NoSchedule that scheduler can't satisfy
  3. Scheduler extender webhook failing — custom scheduling extension broken
  4. Scheduler OOMKilled — memory limit too low for large cluster
  5. NodeAffinity/PodAffinity rules impossible to satisfy — no matching nodes exist
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm init --skip-phases didn't create scheduler manifest
  2. Scheduler manifest accidentally deleted from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  3. Scheduler --leader-elect=false with multiple schedulers — conflicts
  4. Wrong kubeconfig path in scheduler manifest — can't connect to API server
  5. Scheduling framework plugins misconfigured in scheduler config
🔍 What to Look At: crictl ps | grep scheduler. kubectl get events -A -w to see if ANY scheduling happens. kubectl describe pod <stuck-pod> — Events section.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify manifest: ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
2. Check scheduler logs: crictl logs <scheduler-container-id>
3. Verify connection: scheduler should connect to localhost:6443
4. Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet to recreate static pods
5. For HA: check kubectl get lease -n kube-system kube-scheduler

💡 Personal Advice: When pods stay Pending with NO events, the scheduler is the culprit. A healthy scheduler creates a "Scheduled" event within seconds. If there's no event, the scheduler isn't running or can't communicate with the API server. On CKA: the fix is usually restoring the scheduler manifest to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and restarting kubelet. Remember: scheduler, controller-manager, and API server are ALL static pods managed by kubelet.
TR9
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR9
kube-controller-manager Not Running — No Reconciliation

🔍 Symptom: Deployments don't create pods, ReplicaSets don't scale, Endpoints not populated. kubectl get deploy shows desired=3, ready=0 but no pods created. The controller-manager static pod is down.

  kubectl get deploy
  NAME       READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
  nginx      0/3     3            0   ← No pods created by ReplicaSet!

  crictl ps | grep controller-manager
  (empty)

  kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controller
  (empty — no controller-manager mirror pod)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Controller-manager static pod not running: Manifest missing or kubelet not starting it. ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
  2. Controller-manager port conflict: Default 10257. netstat -tlnp | grep 10257.
  3. --service-account-private-key-file missing: Controller needs this to sign tokens. Invalid or missing path.
  4. Leader election stuck: kubectl get lease -n kube-system — check controller-manager lease.
  5. RBAC changes removed controller-manager permissions: Can't watch/create resources anymore.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. --controllers flag set to exclude critical controllers accidentally
  2. Cloud-controller-manager taking over but misconfigured — both controllers confused
  3. Controller-manager OOMKilled — too many objects to reconcile
  4. etcd watch timeout — controller loses connection to API server
  5. Node life-cycle controller stuck — blocks other controllers in same process
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm init --skip-phases didn't create controller-manager manifest
  2. --cluster-signing-cert-file and --cluster-signing-key-file paths wrong
  3. Controller-manager --use-service-account-credentials not enabled
  4. Cloud provider config missing but cloud-controller-manager flags present
  5. --root-ca-file not accessible — controller can't verify API server cert
🔍 What to Look At: crictl ps | grep controller. kubectl get events -A -w for any controller activity. kubectl get deploy,rs,ds — all should show reconciliation activity.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify manifest: ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
2. Check logs: crictl logs <controller-container-id>
3. Check certs: kubeadm certs check-expiration
4. Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet
5. Recreate manifest if missing: copy from /etc/kubernetes/ backup or kubeadm config

💡 Personal Advice: The controller-manager is the "brain" of Kubernetes — without it, no reconciliation happens. Pods won't be created, endpoints won't be populated, nodes won't be monitored. The symptom is subtle: everything LOOKS configured but nothing HAPPENS. On CKA: check crictl ps on the control plane if deployments aren't creating pods. The controller-manager and scheduler are the two most commonly broken static pods.
TR10
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR10
All Control Plane Static Pods Stopped — kubelet Issue

🔍 Symptom: kubectl fails completely, and ALL control plane static pods (API server, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd) are not running. crictl ps shows no control plane containers. The root cause is usually the kubelet itself.

  ssh cp-node
  systemctl status kubelet
  Active: failed (Result: exit-code)

  journalctl -u kubelet -n 20
  Fatal: failed to run Kubelet: misconfiguration: kubelet cgroup driver
  "systemd" is different from containerd cgroup driver "cgroupfs"
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. kubelet service failed: systemctl status kubelet. Crashed, misconfigured, or dependency failed.
  2. Cgroup driver mismatch: kubelet uses systemd, containerd uses cgroupfs. Must match. Check kubelet config and containerd config.
  3. Container runtime (containerd) not running: systemctl status containerd. kubelet can't start any pods.
  4. /etc/kubernetes/manifests directory missing or wrong permissions: kubelet can't read static pod manifests.
  5. Disk full — kubelet can't write pod logs or update status to disk
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. SELinux enforcing blocking kubelet from reading manifest files
  2. kubelet binary corrupted — reinstall kubelet package
  3. /var/lib/kubelet corrupted — delete and restart kubelet to regenerate
  4. Kernel upgrade broke cgroup v1/v2 compatibility with kubelet
  5. kubelet config.yaml has invalid YAML after manual edit
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. swap enabled: kubelet refuses to start with swap. swapoff -a mandatory.
  2. containerd not configured for Kubernetes: containerd config default > /etc/containerd/config.toml.
  3. kubelet not enabled to start on boot: systemctl enable kubelet.
  4. NetworkManager overriding CNI config — disable NM on the interface.
  5. Missing --pod-manifest-path in kubelet config — doesn't know where static pods are.
🔍 What to Look At: systemctl status kubelet containerd. journalctl -u kubelet -n 50. ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. crictl info | grep cgroupDriver.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. systemctl status kubelet — check if running
2. Fix cgroup driver: set both kubelet and containerd to "systemd"
3. swapoff -a and remove swap from /etc/fstab
4. systemctl restart containerd && systemctl restart kubelet
5. If all else fails: kubeadm reset && kubeadm init (last resort)

💡 Personal Advice: When ALL control plane components are down, don't debug each one individually — debug kubelet. kubelet is the parent of all static pods. If kubelet is broken, nothing runs. The #1 kubelet issue is cgroup driver mismatch between kubelet (systemd) and containerd (cgroupfs). Both MUST use the same driver. On CKA: this is a high-value troubleshooting scenario — know how to check and fix cgroup driver configuration.

📌 TR11–TR15: Pod Startup Failures

TR11
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR11
ImagePullBackOff — Can't Pull Container Image

🔍 Symptom: Pod shows STATUS: ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull. kubectl describe pod shows "Failed to pull image." Registry unreachable, image doesn't exist, or credentials wrong.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME          READY   STATUS            RESTARTS
  nginx-7d8f9   0/1     ImagePullBackOff  0

  kubectl describe pod nginx-7d8f9 | grep -A5 Events
  Failed to pull image "nginx:1.99": tag 1.99 not found
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Image tag doesn't exist: Typo or deleted tag. crictl pull <image> to test.
  2. Private registry — no imagePullSecret: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=<url> --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<pass>.
  3. Registry unreachable from node: curl https://registry.example.com/v2/ from node.
  4. imagePullSecret wrong or expired: Credentials changed. Regenerate and update.
  5. Docker Hub rate limit: Anonymous pulls limited. Authenticate or use mirror.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Node disk full — containerd can't unpack image layers
  2. Proxy not configured on containerd for registry access
  3. Registry TLS certificate expired/self-signed
  4. Image architecture mismatch (amd64 vs arm64)
  5. containerd image store corruption
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No internet from nodes — need private registry mirror
  2. imagePullPolicy: Always with no registry
  3. containerd registry mirror config wrong
  4. SA doesn't have imagePullSecrets attached
  5. CRI socket permissions — containerd can't read auth file
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod | grep -A10 Events. crictl pull <image> on the node.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify image exists: crictl pull <image> on node
2. Create secret: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=...
3. Add to pod: imagePullSecrets: - name: regcred
4. Fix tag: update deployment with correct image version
5. Add secret to SA for all pods in namespace

💡 Personal Advice: ImagePullBackOff is top-3 pod errors. Fix is almost always: wrong tag, missing pull secret, or registry unreachable. On CKA: know kubectl create secret docker-registry cold. Common task: create pull secret, attach to SA, verify pod pulls successfully.
TR12
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR12
CrashLoopBackOff — Container Crashes on Startup

🔍 Symptom: Pod STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff, restart count increasing. Container starts and immediately exits. Application error, wrong command, or missing config.

  kubectl logs crash-pod --previous
  Error: Cannot find module '/app/server.js'

  kubectl describe pod crash-pod | grep -E "Exit Code|Reason"
    Exit Code:    1
    Reason:       Error
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Application error: kubectl logs <pod> --previous shows what the crashed container printed.
  2. Wrong command/args: ENTRYPOINT overridden incorrectly in pod spec.
  3. Missing ConfigMap/Secret: App needs env vars from missing resource.
  4. Database/backend unreachable: App connects on startup, fails, exits.
  5. Missing file/volume: App expects config file at mounted path that's empty.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. OOMKilled — memory limit hit, exit code 137
  2. Liveness probe misconfigured — kills healthy container
  3. InitContainer failed — main never starts
  4. Permission denied — app runs as non-root, needs root
  5. Shared volume mount permission issue
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Wrong architecture — amd64 image on arm64 node
  2. Missing system deps in image
  3. SecurityContext blocks needed syscall
  4. PSA mutating pod and breaking command
  5. DNS failure — app resolves hostname on startup
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl logs <pod> --previous (CRASHED container). kubectl describe pod — exit code, Reason. Exit 1=app error, 137=OOM, 139=segfault.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl logs <pod> --previous — most important diagnostic
2. Check Events in kubectl describe pod
3. Fix application error (missing file, wrong config)
4. Add missing ConfigMap/Secret
5. Fix command: override with correct command: and args:

💡 Personal Advice: CrashLoopBackOff = container starts then dies. Key is kubectl logs --previous — shows the crashed container's output. Without --previous, you see the new container's empty logs. Exit code 1 = app error, 137 = OOMKilled. On CKA: find the error, fix the config/volume/secret, verify pod recovers.
TR13
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR13
Pod Stuck Pending — No Suitable Node (Taints/Selector/Resources)

🔍 Symptom: Pod stays Pending with: "0/3 nodes are available: node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity, had untolerated taint, or insufficient resources."

  kubectl describe pod stuck-pod | grep -A10 Events
  0/3 nodes: 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {control-plane: }
  3 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Node taint without pod toleration: Control plane taint repels regular pods.
  2. nodeSelector label missing: kubectl get nodes --show-labels — verify.
  3. Resource requests exceed node capacity: Pod wants 8GB, max node has 4GB free.
  4. NodeAffinity zone mismatch: Required us-east-1c but nodes in us-east-1a.
  5. All nodes cordoned: kubectl get nodes — SchedulingDisabled.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. topologySpreadConstraints can't be met with available nodes
  2. Inter-pod anti-affinity blocks placement near existing pods
  3. PVC WaitForFirstConsumer — volume in wrong zone
  4. RuntimeClass not available on any node
  5. GPU/extended resource not available
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Only control plane node — no workers for regular pods
  2. All workers tainted with NoSchedule
  3. nodeSelector label never added to nodes
  4. PodSecurityAdmission blocking all namespaces
  5. Scheduler not running — no events at all
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod — Events explain why. kubectl get nodes --show-labels. kubectl describe nodes | grep Taint.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Remove taint: kubectl taint node <name> <key>-
2. Add toleration to pod spec
3. Add label: kubectl label node <name> <key>=<value>
4. Reduce resource requests
5. Uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>

💡 Personal Advice: Pending with detailed Events is helpful — the scheduler tells you exactly why. Most common CKA: pod can't schedule because all nodes are control-plane with taints. Fix: add toleration or remove taint. Or nodeSelector label missing — add it. Events are your roadmap.
TR14
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR14
CreateContainerConfigError — ConfigMap/Secret Reference Broken

🔍 Symptom: Pod shows CreateContainerConfigError. Events: "configmap 'X' not found" or "couldn't find key 'Y' in Secret." Referenced resource doesn't exist or key is wrong.

  kubectl describe pod web-7d8f9-s9 | grep -A5 Events
  Error: configmap "app-config" not found

  kubectl get cm,secret -n prod
  No resources found in prod namespace.  ← Missing!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMap/Secret doesn't exist: kubectl get cm,secret -n <ns>.
  2. Key doesn't exist in resource: password vs PASSWORD — case matters!
  3. Wrong namespace: Pod and ConfigMap must be same namespace.
  4. Created AFTER pod: Delete and recreate pod.
  5. Typo in reference name
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. RBAC blocks SA from reading Secret
  2. Secret deleted while pod still references it
  3. ConfigMap exceeds 1MB etcd limit
  4. Immutable CM/Secret — can't update, pod refs old version
  5. FieldRef pointing to non-existent field
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Namespace not created yet
  2. Pod from Deployment — fix template, not just pod
  3. Helm chart generates wrong name at render time
  4. Kustomize overlay overwrites reference
  5. GitOps synced pod before ConfigMap
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod — Events name the missing resource. kubectl get cm,secret -n <ns>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Identify missing resource from Events
2. Create it: kubectl create cm app-config --from-literal=key=value -n <ns>
3. Delete pod: kubectl delete pod <name> (Deployment recreates)
4. For Deployments: kubectl edit deploy to fix template
5. Verify: kubectl get pods — should show Running

💡 Personal Advice: CreateContainerConfigError = container config can't be built. Container never starts. On CKA: pod is broken, describe shows missing CM/Secret, create it, delete pod, it recovers. Always check namespace — CM/Secret are namespace-scoped.
TR15
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR15
InitContainer Failed — Pod Stuck in Init:Error

🔍 Symptom: Pod STATUS: Init:Error or Init:CrashLoopBackOff. Main container never starts. kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container> shows the init failure.

  kubectl logs db-0 -c init-db
  Error: could not connect to postgres: connection refused

  kubectl describe pod db-0 | grep "Init Containers" -A20
  Init Containers:
    init-db:
      State:  Terminated, Exit Code: 1
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Init command failed: kubectl logs <pod> -c <init> shows error.
  2. Dependency not ready: Init waits for DB/service before proceeding.
  3. Volume permission setup failed: chown in init fails due to security.
  4. ConfigMap/Secret for init container missing
  5. Init container image pull failed
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Init runs as non-root but needs root for setup
  2. NetworkPolicy blocks init from reaching dependency
  3. Init resource limits too low — OOMKilled
  4. DNS not resolving dependency hostname
  5. Race condition with other pods' init containers
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Init containers run in ORDER — container 1 fails blocks all
  2. Init retries follow the POD's restartPolicy: Always/OnFailure — kubelet retries the failed init container until it succeeds; Never — the Pod is immediately marked Failed with no retry at all
  3. Init shares pod network namespace — port conflicts
  4. Init has no SA token access by default
  5. restartPolicy: Never can cause permanent block
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-name>. kubectl describe pod — which init failed, exit code.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl logs <pod> -c <init> — see what failed
2. Fix init command or dependency
3. Add retry: until nc -z svc 5432; do sleep 2; done
4. Add missing ConfigMap/Secret/volume
5. Fix permissions: add securityContext if chown needed

💡 Personal Advice: Init containers run BEFORE main and MUST complete. If init fails, pod stuck forever. On CKA: pod in Init:Error — check logs with -c <init-name>. Inits usually: wait for dependency, set up volumes, run migrations, or download files. Fix is often creating a missing service or adding retry logic. Check whether the init container has restartPolicy: Always set — that turns it into a sidecar that runs for the Pod's whole lifetime instead of exiting before the main container starts, which changes what "stuck in Init" actually means.

📌 TR16–TR20: Pod Runtime Failures

TR16
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR16
OOMKilled (Exit Code 137) — Container Hit Memory Limit

🔍 Symptom: Pod restarts with exit code 137. kubectl describe pod shows "OOMKilled." The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel OOM killer terminated it. Application memory leak or limit too low.

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7d8f9 | grep -A5 State
  State:          Running
    Started:      Thu, 04 Jun 2026 10:00:00
  Last State:     Terminated
    Reason:       OOMKilled
    Exit Code:    137

  kubectl top pod easypj-api-7d8f9
  NAME               CPU    MEMORY
  easypj-api-7d8f9   50m    512Mi  ← Limit was 256Mi!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Memory limit too low: App needs more than the configured limit. Check kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep -A2 limits.
  2. Memory leak in application: Memory usage grows over time until limit hit. Check Grafana/Prometheus trends.
  3. Traffic spike: Sudden increase in requests causes memory surge. Check HPA/autoscaling.
  4. Large request payload: Application loads large files into memory (uploads, data processing).
  5. No memory limit set: without a limit, the container's cgroup boundary is the node's allocatable memory — the kernel OOM killer (not kubelet eviction) kills it once that's exhausted.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Child process memory not accounted: Forked processes consume memory outside main process tracking.
  2. JVM/Node.js heap configured larger than container limit
  3. Memory fragmentation: Application can't free unused memory fast enough.
  4. Cgroup v1 memory accounting bug — inaccurate memory reporting
  5. Kernel page cache counted against container limit
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default limit too low: LimitRange sets 128Mi default for all containers.
  2. No resource monitoring set up — can't see memory trends.
  3. Java -Xmx not set relative to container limit — JVM uses 1/4 of node RAM.
  4. Node has less memory than expected — cloud instance type wrong.
  5. Swap enabled — kernel may swap instead of OOM, causing extreme slowness.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod | grep OOMKilled. kubectl top pod for current usage. kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep -A5 resources for limits.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Increase limit: kubectl set resources deploy <name> --limits=memory=512Mi
2. Fix memory leak in application code
3. Add HPA: kubectl autoscale deploy <name> --min=2 --max=10 --cpu=80
4. Set JVM/Node flags: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 or --max-old-space-size
5. Add monitoring: Prometheus + Grafana dashboards

💡 Personal Advice: Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). Almost always OOM — but confirm via the explicit "Reason: OOMKilled" field in describe pod, not the exit code alone (a force-deleted pod also exits 137). Don't confuse with 143 (SIGTERM, graceful shutdown). On CKA: pod keeps restarting — check describe for OOMKilled, increase memory limit, verify pod stabilizes. For Java apps: set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 so the JVM respects container limits. Without it, JVM uses node RAM and gets OOMKilled prematurely.
TR17
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR17
Pod Evicted — Node Under Pressure, Pods Moved

🔍 Symptom: Pod shows STATUS: Evicted. kubectl describe pod shows "The node was low on resource: memory." The node ran out of resources and kubelet evicted pods to reclaim them.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  web-7d8f9-s9   0/1     Evicted   0
  api-5g3h2-k7   0/1     Evicted   0

  kubectl describe pod web-7d8f9-s9 | grep Message
  Message: The node was low on resource: memory. Threshold quantity: 100Mi
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Node memory exhausted: kubectl top node. Memory usage > eviction threshold (default 100Mi available).
  2. No resource limits on pods: Unbounded pods consume all node memory. Add limits.
  3. QoS class BestEffort pod evicted first: Pods without requests/limits are first eviction targets.
  4. Memory spike from one pod: Check kubectl top pod --sort-by=memory for the culprit.
  5. Node has less RAM than expected: Cloud instance type too small or memory reservation wrong.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. system-reserved not set — OS processes consume memory kubelet doesn't track
  2. Eviction thresholds too aggressive — set too high, evicts unnecessarily
  3. Tmpfs (emptyDir) consuming memory — unbounded, counted against node memory
  4. Kernel memory leak after long uptime — node needs reboot
  5. Cadvisor memory reporting delay — actual usage higher than reported
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kube-reserved and system-reserved not configured — kubelet overcommits node.
  2. All pods BestEffort QoS — no requests/limits anywhere, first to be evicted.
  3. --eviction-hard not tuned for node specs — defaults may be too high/low.
  4. Node too small for workload — need more nodes or larger instances.
  5. No priority classes — critical pods evicted alongside non-critical ones.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe node | grep -A5 Conditions. kubectl top node and kubectl top pod -A --sort-by=memory.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check node: kubectl describe node <name> — MemoryPressure/DiskPressure?
2. Add limits to all pods
3. Use Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits) for critical pods
4. Set eviction thresholds: --eviction-hard=memory.available<200Mi
5. Add nodes or increase instance sizes

💡 Personal Advice: Eviction is kubelet's safety valve — it kills pods to save the node. Eviction order isn't a hardcoded QoS rule — kubelet sorts candidates by (1) whether usage exceeds requests, (2) Pod Priority, (3) magnitude of the overage. BestEffort-first/Guaranteed-last is the typical emergent result since BestEffort pods have no request to stay under, but it's not absolute: if untracked system daemons consume node resources, kubelet can still evict a Guaranteed pod, picking the lowest-Priority one first. On CKA: you'll see Evicted pods and need to identify why — usually resource exhaustion. Fix: add limits, reduce workload, or add nodes. Evicted pods' logs are lost — check the Deployment for the reason.
TR18
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR18
Pod Stuck Terminating — Finalizers Blocking Deletion

🔍 Symptom: kubectl delete pod hangs forever. Pod shows Terminating for 10+ minutes. Finalizer or preStop hook is preventing deletion from completing.

  kubectl delete pod stuck-pod
  (hangs — never completes)

  kubectl get pod stuck-pod -o yaml | grep -A5 finalizers
  finalizers:
  - example.com/custom-cleanup  ← Controller must remove this!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Finalizer set by controller: Controller must execute cleanup and remove its finalizer. If controller is down, pod stuck forever.
  2. preStop hook hanging: Hook command never returns. Pod waits for graceful termination period (default 30s).
  3. Container not responding to SIGTERM: App ignores TERM signal. kubelet waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds then SIGKILL.
  4. Volume unmount stuck: NFS/CIFS volume can't unmount because server is unreachable.
  5. CSI driver can't detach volume: Cloud API failure prevents volume detachment from node.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Node where pod runs is NotReady — kubelet can't process deletion
  2. etcd write failure during finalizer removal — API server can't update object
  3. Network policy blocking kubelet from API server during graceful shutdown
  4. Pod has too many finalizers from multiple controllers — race condition
  5. Kubelet PLEG stuck — not processing pod lifecycle events
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Operator installed a finalizer but operator pod was deleted without cleanup.
  2. CRD with finalizer deleted before CR instances — orphans left.
  3. preStop hook misconfigured with infinite loop or missing binary.
  4. terminationGracePeriodSeconds too long — set to 3600+ seconds unnecessarily.
  5. Node drain in progress but PDB blocks eviction and finalizer blocks deletion.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | grep -A10 finalizers. kubectl describe pod — check for preStop hook definition.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Remove finalizers: kubectl patch pod <name> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}'
2. Force delete: kubectl delete pod <name> --force --grace-period=0
3. Fix preStop hook: update deployment with corrected hook
4. Restart stuck controller that should remove finalizer
5. For CSI detach: kubectl delete volumeattachment <name>

💡 Personal Advice: Terminating pods are a common pain. The nuclear option: kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 — this removes the pod from API server without waiting for kubelet to confirm deletion. But if the pod still runs on the node, you'll have a zombie. Removing a finalizer with kubectl patch is a last resort, not a routine fix — finalizers usually exist for a reason (e.g. deprovisioning a cloud LB or volume), so only remove one once you understand what cleanup it was protecting, or you'll orphan external resources. On CKA: you'll likely need to force-delete a stuck pod and verify it's gone.
TR19
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR19
Pod Can't Connect to Service — DNS Not Resolving

🔍 Symptom: App logs show "connection refused" or "no such host" when connecting to a Service. nslookup <svc> from within the pod fails. CoreDNS is down or misconfigured.

  kubectl exec web-pod -- nslookup api-svc
  ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached

  kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
  No resources found in kube-system.  ← CoreDNS not running!

  kubectl exec web-pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
  nameserver 10.96.0.10  ← CoreDNS Service IP
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CoreDNS pods not running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns.
  2. NetworkPolicy blocking DNS (UDP 53): Pods can't reach CoreDNS on port 53.
  3. kube-dns Service missing or wrong ClusterIP: kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns.
  4. Pod's /etc/resolv.conf wrong: Nameserver IP incorrect or search domain mismatched.
  5. CoreDNS ConfigMap misconfigured: Wrong upstream DNS, broken Corefile syntax.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CoreDNS OOMKilled — memory limit too low for large cluster with many Services
  2. DNS cache poisoning or stale entries — restart CoreDNS pods
  3. Node-local DNS cache (nodelocaldns) intercepting and failing requests
  4. Custom dnsPolicy on pod pointing to wrong server
  5. Upstream DNS forward failing — CoreDNS can't resolve external names
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CoreDNS deployment scaled to 0 or accidentally deleted.
  2. kube-dns Service ClusterIP changed — pods have old IP in resolv.conf.
  3. Network plugin doesn't support UDP — VXLAN drops UDP DNS packets.
  4. Firewall between nodes blocks inter-node DNS resolution.
  5. Pod created before CoreDNS — resolv.conf has stale bootstrap DNS.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup kubernetes.default. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns. kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Scale CoreDNS: kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=2
2. Check NetworkPolicy allows UDP 53 from all pods
3. Verify kube-dns Service: kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns
4. Restart CoreDNS: kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
5. Test: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes

💡 Personal Advice: DNS issues are "everything is broken" issues because pods can't find each other. CoreDNS runs as a Deployment in kube-system. Check its pods FIRST. On CKA: common fix is restarting CoreDNS or creating a NetworkPolicy that allows DNS. Test with busybox: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes.default. If that fails, DNS is broken cluster-wide.
TR20
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR20
Pod Running But Not Accessible — Service Endpoints Empty

🔍 Symptom: Pod is Running, but Service doesn't route traffic to it. kubectl get endpoints <svc> shows empty endpoints. Service selector doesn't match pod labels, or readiness probe failing.

  kubectl get endpoints api-svc
  NAME       ENDPOINTS
  api-svc    <none>   ← No endpoints!

  kubectl get pods -l app=api --show-labels
  NAME              READY   LABELS
  api-7d8f9-s9      1/1     app=api-server  ← Label mismatch!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Service selector doesn't match pod labels: kubectl get svc -o yaml | grep selector -A5 vs kubectl get pod --show-labels.
  2. Pod readiness probe failing: Pod is Running but not Ready. kubectl get pods shows 0/1 in READY column.
  3. Wrong namespace: Service and pods in different namespaces. Endpoint controller only watches same namespace.
  4. Service port name doesn't match pod port name: When using named ports, names must match.
  5. Pod is in terminating state or has deletion timestamp: Endpoint controller removes terminating pods.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Endpoint controller not running — part of kube-controller-manager (see TR9)
  2. Service type ExternalName — no endpoints by design
  3. Headless Service (clusterIP: None) with no matching pods
  4. NetworkPolicy silently dropping health checks from kubelet
  5. Service has publishNotReadyAddresses: false (the default) and backing pod is not Ready — endpoint excluded until the pod passes its readiness probe
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Service was created with wrong selector — fix and recreate.
  2. Pods were deployed with labels that don't match the Service spec.
  3. Readiness probe path wrong — pods never become Ready.
  4. Service account RBAC blocking endpoint controller from listing pods.
  5. Namespace label filtering — endpoint controller filters by namespace selectors.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get endpoints <svc>. kubectl get pods -l <selector> using the Service's selector. kubectl describe svc.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Compare: kubectl get svc <name> -o yaml | grep -A3 selector vs pod labels
2. Fix label mismatch: kubectl label pod <name> app=api --overwrite
3. Fix readiness probe: update deployment with correct probe path/port
4. Fix Deployment template labels to match Service selector
5. Verify with: kubectl get endpoints <svc> — should show pod IP:port

💡 Personal Advice: Empty Endpoints is THE most common Service issue. The Service selector MUST match pod labels exactly (case-sensitive!). Even one character off = no traffic. On CKA: you'll debug a Service that doesn't work. Check kubectl get endpoints first — empty = label mismatch or readiness issue. Fix the labels or the readiness probe, and endpoints populate within seconds.

📌 TR21–TR25: Health Probes Misconfiguration

TR21
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR21
Liveness Probe Killing Healthy Pod — Probe Misconfigured

🔍 Symptom: Pod is Running but keeps restarting every few minutes. kubectl describe pod shows "Liveness probe failed." The probe configuration is too aggressive — wrong path, low timeout, or insufficient initialDelaySeconds.

  kubectl describe pod api-7d8f9 | grep -A10 Liveness
  Liveness:  http-get http://:8080/health delay=0s timeout=1s
  Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.5:8080/health": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. initialDelaySeconds too short: App needs 30s to start but probe fires at 0s. App not ready yet.
  2. Wrong probe path/port: Probe hits /healthz but app exposes /health. Returns 404 = probe fails.
  3. timeoutSeconds too low: App takes 3s to respond but timeout is 1s. Probe fails on slow responses.
  4. Probe hitting wrong endpoint: Health endpoint does CPU-heavy work under load and times out.
  5. failureThreshold set to 1: Single probe failure kills pod. Should be 3-5 for resilience.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Probe uses exec with a command that doesn't exist in the container
  2. TCP probe to a port the app doesn't listen on
  3. Probe hitting a path that requires authentication — returns 401/403
  4. Container is CPU-throttled — health check times out from CPU starvation
  5. periodSeconds too frequent — probe fires every second, overwhelming app
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No liveness probe configured — app can hang indefinitely without restart.
  2. Liveness and readiness probes share same endpoint — kills pod when it's just overloaded.
  3. Probe httpGet scheme: HTTPS but app serves HTTP on that port.
  4. Probe httpHeaders missing required Host header for virtual hosting.
  5. Probe port specified by name that doesn't match any containerPort name.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod | grep -A15 Liveness. kubectl logs <pod> --previous — was app working before killed?
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Fix probe: initialDelaySeconds: 30, periodSeconds: 10, timeoutSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3
2. Verify path: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl localhost:8080/health
3. Separate liveness (is app alive?) from readiness (is app ready for traffic?)
4. Use exec probe if httpGet path is complex: exec: command: ['curl','-f','http://localhost:8080/health']
5. Never make liveness probe dependent on external services (databases, APIs)

💡 Personal Advice: Liveness probes KILL your pod — use them carefully. Golden rule: liveness should ONLY check if the app is hung/deadlocked, NOT if it's slow or overloaded. Slow ≠ dead. If your liveness probe checks a database connection, a DB blip will kill ALL your pods. Use readiness probes for dependency checks instead. On CKA: you'll see pods restarting from probe failures — increase initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold.
TR22
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR22
Readiness Probe Failing — Pod Running But Not Receiving Traffic

🔍 Symptom: Pod shows Running but READY 0/1. Service Endpoints don't include this pod. Readiness probe is failing, so the pod is removed from Service load balancing.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  api-7d8f9-s9   0/1     Running   0   ← Running but not Ready!

  kubectl describe pod api-7d8f9-s9 | grep -A10 Readiness
  Readiness:  http-get http://:8080/ready delay=5s timeout=2s
  Warning  Unhealthy  Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. App returns non-2xx/3xx from readiness endpoint: Probe expects 200-399. App returns 503 (not ready yet).
  2. App startup not complete: Database connection, cache warming, or config loading still in progress.
  3. Wrong readiness path/port: Probe hitting wrong endpoint that doesn't reflect app readiness.
  4. initialDelaySeconds too short for app startup: App needs 60s but probe fires at 5s.
  5. Dependency (DB, cache) not available: App can't become ready without its dependencies.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Readiness probe failureThreshold defaults to 3, not 1 — a single failed check does NOT immediately pull the pod from Endpoints, it takes 3 consecutive failures
  2. Service with publishNotReadyAddresses: false — needs pod to be Ready
  3. Load balancer health check different from K8s readiness — LB sees pod as unhealthy
  4. Container restarting readiness probe endpoint process without kubelet knowing
  5. Probe exec command has no timeout — runs forever if hung
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No readiness probe configured — pod considered Ready immediately on start.
  2. Readiness endpoint returns 200 for liveness but doesn't check dependencies.
  3. Pod startup dependencies (init containers) completed but app itself not initialized.
  4. Probe periodSeconds too frequent — app can't keep up with readiness checks.
  5. Multiple containers in pod — one is Ready but others aren't (pod is Ready when ALL are).
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod | grep -A10 Readiness. kubectl get endpoints <svc> — is pod in the list? kubectl exec <pod> -- curl localhost:<port>/ready.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check probe config: kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep -A20 readinessProbe
2. Test manually: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -v localhost:8080/ready
3. Increase initialDelaySeconds to give app time to start
4. Increase failureThreshold: 3-5 before marking NotReady
5. Fix app readiness endpoint to return 200 only when truly ready

💡 Personal Advice: 0/1 Ready but Running = readiness probe failing. The app is alive but not ready for traffic. This is usually correct behavior during startup — the probe ensures traffic only hits pods that can serve requests. If it stays 0/1 indefinitely, the app has a dependency issue (DB unreachable, cache down, config missing). Fix the dependency, and the readiness probe will pass. Never remove the readiness probe — fix what it's checking.
TR23
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR23
Startup Probe Missing — Slow-Starting App Killed by Liveness

🔍 Symptom: Application needs 2+ minutes to start (database migrations, cache warming), but liveness probe kills it after 30s. Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff even though the app would eventually work if given enough time.

  kubectl describe pod slow-app-7d8f9 | grep -A10 Liveness
  Liveness:  http-get /health delay=30s timeout=5s
  Killing container: failed liveness probe after 30s
  (App needs 120s to start — was still loading when killed!)

  kubectl get pod slow-app-7d8f9 -o yaml | grep startupProbe
  (empty — no startup probe configured!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No startup probe configured: Liveness fires immediately. Startup probe disables liveness/readiness until it succeeds.
  2. initialDelaySeconds too short: Set to 30s but app needs 120s. Increase or add startup probe.
  3. App startup is slow due to migrations/data loading: Optimize startup or account for it with probe timing.
  4. failureThreshold exhausted during startup: Liveness fails 3 times in a row = pod killed.
  5. Container CPU limit too low during startup: App starts slow because it's CPU-throttled.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Image pull takes too long — container start overlaps with probe timer
  2. Init container takes long but liveness probe timer starts after init completes
  3. PostStart hook takes too long — blocks container readiness
  4. Persistent volume mount slow — NFS/CIFS mount delays container start
  5. Node disk I/O contention slows image unpacking — startup delayed
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Kubernetes 1.16+ (GA 1.20): Startup probe available. Use it for slow-starting apps.
  2. No startup probe on Java/Spring Boot apps — notorious for slow startup.
  3. Default initialDelaySeconds=0 — liveness fires immediately on container start.
  4. Database migration in initContainer vs startup probe — choose one pattern.
  5. PostStart hook runs concurrently with probes — race condition.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep -A10 startupProbe — does it exist? kubectl logs <pod> --previous — was app still starting when killed?
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Add startup probe: startupProbe: httpGet: path: /health, port: 8080, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 10
2. This gives 30*10=300s for startup — liveness/readiness disabled until startup succeeds
3. Or increase liveness initialDelaySeconds to match app startup time
4. Optimize app startup: parallelize migrations, lazy-load caches
5. Increase container CPU limit during startup phase

💡 Personal Advice: Startup probe was introduced in K8s 1.16 and is a GAME CHANGER for slow-starting apps. Without it, you have to choose between: (a) long initialDelaySeconds (pod stays "ready" during startup even if broken), or (b) short delay with risk of killing slow starters. Startup probe gives the best of both: liveness/readiness are DISABLED until startup succeeds. Every production deployment should use startup probes for Java, Python, and Node.js apps.
TR24
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR24
Exec Probe Failing — Command Not Found in Container

🔍 Symptom: Liveness probe uses exec with a command that doesn't exist in the container. Probe fails with "command not found" or "exec format error."

  kubectl describe pod api-7d8f9 | grep -A5 Liveness
  Liveness:  exec [curl -f http://localhost:8080/health]
  Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: rpc error

  kubectl exec api-7d8f9 -- which curl
  curl: not found  ← curl not installed in this image!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Binary not in image: curl/wget not installed. Distroless/scratch images have no shell.
  2. Command array format wrong: ["curl -f http://..."] → should be ["curl","-f","http://..."].
  3. Shell syntax without shell: ["cat /tmp/healthy"] needs sh -c.
  4. Wrong architecture binary (amd64 vs arm64)
  5. Command depends on missing env vars
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. NetworkPolicy blocks egress for probe command
  2. Required file doesn't exist yet (startup order)
  3. /proc or /sys blocked by securityContext
  4. Child process never terminates — exec times out
  5. Read-only filesystem — can't create temp files
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Distroless images have NO shell — use httpGet probe instead.
  2. Scratch images have nothing — no /bin/sh, curl, or cat.
  3. Bash-ism in probe but container only has sh/dash.
  4. Relative command path — should be absolute.
  5. Probe exec runs from wrong workingDir context.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod | grep -A10 Liveness. kubectl exec <pod> -- which <cmd>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Use httpGet instead of exec when possible
2. Ensure binary exists: kubectl exec <pod> -- which curl
3. Use proper array: ["/usr/bin/curl","-f","http://localhost:8080/health"]
4. For shell: ["/bin/sh","-c","curl -f http://localhost:8080/health"]
5. For distroless: switch to httpGet or tcpSocket
6. For gRPC services in distroless images: use a grpc probe instead — the target must implement the gRPC health-checking protocol, no exec/shell needed

💡 Personal Advice: Exec probes are powerful but tricky. The command runs INSIDE the container — if the binary doesn't exist, probe fails. For distroless images, MUST use httpGet or tcpSocket. On CKA: kubectl exec into pod and try the probe command manually to see what's missing. Most common fix: switch to httpGet.
TR25
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR25
All Probes Failing — NetworkPolicy Blocking Kubelet

🔍 Symptom: All readiness/liveness probes failing with timeout. NetworkPolicy default-deny blocks kubelet-to-pod traffic. Kubelet probes come from node IP, not within pod network.

  kubectl describe pod api-7d8f9 | grep -A5 Events
  Liveness probe failed: dial tcp 10.244.1.5:8080: i/o timeout
  Readiness probe failed: dial tcp 10.244.1.5:8080: i/o timeout

  kubectl get networkpolicy -A
  NAMESPACE  NAME        POD-SELECTOR
  default    deny-all    <none>  ← Blocks kubelet probes too!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. NetworkPolicy default-deny blocks kubelet: Kubelet probes from node IP. NP must allow node CIDR.
  2. Wrong probe port vs app listening port
  3. App binds 127.0.0.1 only — kubelet from node can't reach
  4. CNI plugin not fully functional
  5. Container CPU-throttled — probe times out
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Pod securityContext blocks incoming connections
  2. App connection limit reached — probe rejected
  3. IPv6/IPv4 mismatch between probe and app
  4. Kubelet source IP changed after node IP change
  5. Service mesh sidecar intercepting probe traffic
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Deny-all NP created without allowing kubelet probes.
  2. hostNetwork pod — probes target wrong IP.
  3. Named port mismatch between probe and containerPort.
  4. IPv6-only cluster with IPv4 probe config.
  5. Istio/Linkerd sidecar intercepting health checks.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod | grep -A20 Liveness. kubectl get networkpolicy -A. kubectl exec <pod> -- netstat -tlnp.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Allow kubelet in NP: ingress: - from: - ipBlock: cidr: <node-cidr>
2. Fix probe port to match app
3. Ensure app listens on 0.0.0.0
4. Remove over-restrictive NP during debug
5. Check CNI pods are running

💡 Personal Advice: All probes failing = systemic, not app-specific. #1 cause: NetworkPolicy default-deny without allowing kubelet. Kubelet probes come from NODE's IP. NP must allow node CIDR. On CKA: apply deny-all NP → probes fail → add ingress rule for node IPs. Classic troubleshooting chain.

📌 TR26–TR30: Logging & Observability

TR26
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR26
kubectl logs Returns Nothing — App Writes to Files Not stdout

🔍 Symptom: kubectl logs empty or "failed to get log file." App writes to files instead of stdout/stderr. kubectl logs only captures console output.

  kubectl logs api-7d8f9
  failed to get log file: no such file

  kubectl exec api-7d8f9 -- ls /var/log/app/
  app.log  error.log  ← App logs to files, not stdout!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. App logs to files not stdout: kubectl logs = stdout/stderr only. Configure console logging.
  2. Log rotation broke symlink: /var/log/containers/ symlink stale.
  3. Multi-container pod — wrong container: kubectl logs <pod> -c <name>.
  4. Pod restarted — use --previous
  5. Node disk full — can't write new logs
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Symlink broken after reboot — pod recreate fixes
  2. Log rotation too aggressive
  3. Containerd log driver misconfigured
  4. Application buffers stdout instead of using line-buffered/unbuffered I/O — logs only flush on buffer-full or exit, appearing delayed or missing
  5. Logging sidecar intercepts stdout
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Wrong CRI socket — kubelet can't find container logs.
  2. Log aggregator consuming/deleting log files.
  3. --container-log-max-size too low.
  4. Non-default container log path misconfigured.
  5. json-file vs journald driver mismatch.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl logs --previous. kubectl logs -c <container> --tail=50. kubectl exec -- ls /var/log/.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Fix app: log to stdout/stderr
2. Sidecar: tail log files and print to stdout
3. kubectl logs --previous for previous instance
4. kubectl logs -c <container> for multi-container
5. Recreate pod for fresh log symlink

💡 Personal Advice: K8s logs = stdout/stderr ONLY. File-based logging = invisible to kubectl logs. Options: make app log to console, or use sidecar that tails and prints. Even for console-logging apps: kubelet's default rotation is containerLogMaxSize=10Mi, containerLogMaxFiles=5, and kubectl logs only ever shows the CURRENT rotated file — a chatty app can silently lose early output even without a restart. On CKA: if kubectl logs empty, try --previous and -c for other containers.
TR27
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR27
kubectl top Fails — "Metrics API Not Available"

🔍 Symptom: kubectl top nodes/pods returns "Metrics API not available." metrics-server not installed or not running.

  kubectl top nodes
  error: Metrics API not available

  kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
  v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io   kube-system/metrics-server   False
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. metrics-server not installed: Not default in kubeadm. Manually install.
  2. metrics-server pod not running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=metrics-server.
  3. TLS cert verification failing: metrics-server can't scrape kubelets.
  4. APIService not registered correctly
  5. Network issue between metrics-server and kubelet (10250)
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. --kubelet-insecure-tls missing for self-signed certs
  2. metrics-server OOMKilled
  3. Kubelet metrics endpoint disabled
  4. Custom metrics without Prometheus adapter
  5. Cluster-autoscaler interference
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Not part of kubeadm — must add separately.
  2. kubeadm init without metrics-server addon.
  3. Custom CA — metrics-server rejects kubelet certs.
  4. Firewall blocks 10250 between pods and nodes.
  5. Cloud managed K8s may or may not include it.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=metrics-server.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Install: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
2. Add --kubelet-insecure-tls for self-signed certs
3. Wait 30s for first scrape
4. Verify: kubectl top nodes

💡 Personal Advice: metrics-server is NOT default in kubeadm. Must install manually. 90% of failures: missing --kubelet-insecure-tls — kubeadm certs are self-signed. On CKA: install metrics-server as one-liner, add the flag, verify with top.
TR28
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR28
HPA Shows <unknown> — No Resource Requests on Pods

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get hpa shows <unknown>/50%. HPA needs container resource requests to calculate utilization percentage.

  kubectl describe hpa api-hpa
  Warning  FailedGetResourceMetric  missing request for cpu
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pods have no resource requests: HPA needs requests for % calculation.
  2. metrics-server not running (see TR27)
  3. HPA target reference wrong Deployment name
  4. New pod — metrics take 30-60s after creation
  5. Resource type in HPA doesn't exist (memory without metrics)
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Custom metrics without Prometheus adapter
  2. minReplicas > current — scaling calculation stuck
  3. Case-sensitive name mismatch (cpu vs CPU)
  4. Multiple HPAs targeting same resource
  5. v2beta2 API deprecated — use autoscaling/v2
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. HPA created before metrics-server installed.
  2. New Deployment without requests — HPA can't calculate.
  3. HPA v2 requires specific target format.
  4. No node autoscaler — HPA scales pods but nodes can't grow.
  5. CPU limit without request: Kubernetes deterministically defaults the request to equal the limit (unless a LimitRange overrides it) — HPA math still works, but the baseline request ends up higher than you may have intended.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe hpa — Events. kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep -A5 resources.
🔧 How to Solve:
