1. Add requests: kubectl set resources deploy <name> --requests=cpu=100m,memory=256Mi
2. Install metrics-server (TR27)
3. Wait 60s
4. Verify: kubectl get hpa — numeric values

💡 Personal Advice: HPA needs THREE things: metrics-server, resource requests, valid HPA. Missing any = unknown. On CKA: create HPA, see unknown, add resource requests to Deployment. HPA uses REQUESTS not limits for % calculation.
TR29
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR29
Node-Level Logging — Finding kubelet/containerd Logs

🔍 Symptom: Need kubelet/containerd logs but kubectl logs doesn't work — they're systemd services. Must SSH and use journalctl.

  ssh worker-1
  journalctl -u kubelet -f
  journalctl -u containerd -n 50 --no-pager
  journalctl -u kubelet --since "10 min ago"
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Trying kubectl logs for systemd services — must use journalctl.
  2. Journal rotation too aggressive — logs gone quickly.
  3. Logs in /var/log/syslog not journald
  4. SSH not available for cloud-managed nodes
  5. Log level too low (-v=0 shows almost nothing)
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Persistent journal not enabled — logs lost on reboot
  2. Disk full — journald stops silently
  3. systemd-journald service stopped
  4. Logs forwarded to remote syslog — not local
  5. containerd writes to files not journald
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubelet without systemd service — custom init system.
  2. containerd configured for file-based logging.
  3. Cloud provider blocks SSH by default.
  4. Log agent (Fluentd) consuming local logs.
  5. /var/log as tmpfs — logs gone on reboot.
🔍 What to Look At: journalctl -u kubelet -n 50. journalctl -u containerd -n 50. /var/log/containers/ and /var/log/pods/ for pod logs on disk.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubelet: journalctl -u kubelet -f
2. containerd: journalctl -u containerd -f
3. Pod logs on node: ls /var/log/containers/
4. Increase verbosity: -v=4 in kubelet config
5. Enable persistent journal: mkdir -p /var/log/journal

💡 Personal Advice: CKA exam requires SSH to nodes for kubelet/containerd logs. Know: journalctl -u kubelet (NOT kubectl logs!). Common: -f (follow), -n 50 (last 50), --since "10 min ago", --no-pager. Fallback: /var/log/syslog.
TR30
🔧 CATEGORY 2: TROUBLESHOOTING — Issue TR30
Targeted Diagnostics — Better Than cluster-info dump

🔍 Symptom: kubectl cluster-info dump times out or fails. Large cluster, too much data. Need targeted commands for efficient troubleshooting.

  # DON'T: kubectl cluster-info dump (slow, massive output)
  # DO: Targeted diagnostics
  kubectl describe nodes > nodes.txt
  kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp > events.txt
  kubectl get pods -A -o wide > pods.txt
  kubectl top nodes,pods -A
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Cluster too large for dump — thousands of resources timeout.
  2. API server 60s timeout exceeded by dump
  3. etcd overload from reading all resources at once
  4. Network bandwidth — massive JSON over kubectl
  5. API server rate limiting blocks dump requests
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. --all-namespaces collecting unnecessary data
  2. kubectl version mismatch with API server
  3. RBAC limits prevent listing certain resources
  4. Proxy dropping large HTTP responses
  5. kubectl client-side OOM with massive dump
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. dump is rarely needed — learn targeted alternatives.
  2. Use --output-directory for offline instead of stdout.
  3. Small cluster — dump works now but won't scale.
  4. No logging stack — kubectl is only observability.
  5. No monitoring — need manual diag for everything.
🔍 What to Look At: Use: kubectl describe node, kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp, kubectl top node,pod -A.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Don't use dump — use targeted diagnostics
2. kubectl describe node <name>
3. kubectl get events -A -o wide
4. kubectl get pods -A -o wide
5. For offline: kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=/tmp/diag

💡 Personal Advice: cluster-info dump is a sledgehammer — use a scalpel. On CKA: targeted commands: describe, logs, get events, top. Faster and give exactly what you need. Dump for offline analysis only (--output-directory), never first step.

⚙️ Category 3: Workloads & Scheduling (15 Issues)WS1-WS15

🟡 Deployments, Scheduling, Config/Secrets, Autoscaling & Resilience

Workloads and Scheduling issues cover everything from Deployment rollouts to pod placement, configuration management, autoscaling, and resilience patterns. When your app isn't running correctly, these are the issues you'll face.

📌 WS1–WS3: Deployment Failures

WS1
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS1
RollingUpdate Stuck — Deployment Not Progressing

🔍 Symptom: kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api hangs. New pods are created but old pods aren't terminated. The Deployment shows "Available: 1/3" but 3 replicas are desired. The easypj-api is partially degraded — some users get old version, some get new.

  kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
  Waiting for deployment "easypj-api" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas updated...
  (hangs indefinitely)

  kubectl get rs -n easypj
  NAME                    DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
  easypj-api-7d8f9abcde   2         2         2       10m  ← old RS still has pods!
  easypj-api-9g2h3xyz12   1         1         1       2m   ← new RS only 1 pod
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. New pods CrashLoopBackOff: The new version crashes on startup. kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api — check the new pod's logs. Rollout waits for the new pod to be Ready.
  2. Insufficient cluster resources: New pods can't schedule because nodes are full. kubectl describe rs <new-rs> — check for "insufficient cpu/memory" events.
  3. Readiness probe failing: New pod is Running but not Ready. kubectl describe pod <new-pod> — check readiness probe status. Deployment waits for Ready pods.
  4. ImagePullBackOff on new image: The new image tag doesn't exist or registry is unreachable. kubectl describe pod <new-pod> | grep Failed.
  5. maxUnavailable: 0 with no surplus nodes: Can't evict old pods because maxUnavailable=0 and no extra nodes exist. Increase maxUnavailable or add nodes.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. NOT a PDB issue — Deployments delete old pods directly during rollout, not via the Eviction API, so PDBs never gate a rolling update (PDB only blocks drain/descheduler/cluster-autoscaler evictions, see WS13). Look elsewhere: a NetworkPolicy or admission webhook rejecting new-pod creation is a more likely culprit
  2. progressDeadlineSeconds exceeded — Deployment times out waiting for progress
  3. minReadySeconds not satisfied — new pods are Ready but haven't been Ready for minReadySeconds yet
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking new pods from registering with Services
  5. RevisionHistoryLimit too low — old ReplicaSets pruned, can't rollback
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No nodes available: Single-node cluster with the old pod occupying the only node. Add worker nodes.
  2. Default resource requests too high for small cluster — lower requests or add nodes
  3. Container runtime not pulling images — containerd/docker not configured with registry mirrors
  4. RBAC preventing the Deployment controller from creating new ReplicaSets
  5. kubelet version mismatch between nodes — pods schedule but can't start
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> — shows progress. kubectl describe deploy <name> — check Conditions section. kubectl get rs -l app=<label> — see old vs new ReplicaSet status.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n easypj — immediate rollback to previous version
2. Check new pod logs: kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api --tail=50
3. Check resource availability: kubectl top nodes and kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 Allocated
4. Fix the issue and re-deploy: kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api api=easypj/api:v2.1-fixed

💡 Personal Advice: When a rollout is stuck, kubectl rollout undo is your best friend — it's instant and gives you a working system while you debug. On CKA: if asked to fix a stuck deployment, check the new pods FIRST (logs, describe, events). 80% of stuck rollouts are caused by the new pods not becoming Ready.
WS2
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS2
Deployment Scaled to 0 — All Pods Gone

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pods shows no pods for the easypj-api Deployment. kubectl get deploy shows DESIRED: 0, CURRENT: 0. The API is completely DOWN. Someone (or an autoscaler) scaled the Deployment to zero.

  kubectl get deploy -n easypj
  NAME         READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
  easypj-api   0/0     0            0           2d

  kubectl get pods -n easypj
  No resources found in easypj namespace.   ← ALL GONE!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Someone ran kubectl scale --replicas=0: Check kubectl get events -n easypj | grep Scaling to see who/what scaled down.
  2. HPA scaled to 0: Check kubectl get hpa -n easypj — if minReplicas=0 and no traffic, HPA scaled down. Increase minReplicas to 1+.
  3. ResourceQuota exceeded: kubectl describe resourcequota -n easypj — if quota is full, new pods can't be created.
  4. All nodes cordoned/drained: kubectl get nodes — if all nodes are SchedulingDisabled, no pods can be placed.
  5. Deployment spec changed to replicas: 0: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -o yaml | grep replicas — check the spec.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Namespace was deleted and recreated — all resources wiped
  2. CronJob or script periodically scaling down during maintenance window
  3. GitOps tool (ArgoCD/Flux) synced a config with replicas: 0
  4. Deployment overwritten by a Helm upgrade with wrong values
  5. Kustomize overlay applied with replicas set to 0 for dev environment
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Cluster autoscaler removed all nodes: If running on cloud and cluster autoscaler scales to 0 nodes, all pods are gone. Check cloud console.
  2. PodSecurityPolicy/Admission webhook rejecting pod creation — pods can't be created
  3. All nodes tainted — no pods can schedule without tolerations
  4. Default ResourceQuota created cluster-wide with count/pods limit at 0
  5. kubelet not running on any node — pods can't be created anywhere
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe deploy <name> — check the Conditions and Events. kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp — recent scaling events.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Scale back: kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api -n easypj --replicas=3
2. If HPA caused it: kubectl patch hpa easypj-api -n easypj --patch '{"spec":{"minReplicas":1}}'
3. If ResourceQuota: increase quota or delete unused resources
4. If nodes cordoned: kubectl uncordon <node>

💡 Personal Advice: Never set minReplicas to 0 in production unless you have a VERY good reason. On CKA: if you see a Deployment with 0 replicas, scale it back up — it's usually a 10-second fix worth full points.
WS3
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS3
Rollback Fails — No Revision History Available

🔍 Symptom: kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api returns "no rollout history found" or "revision not found." A bad deployment is live and you can't rollback. The easypj API is serving errors and there's no quick way back.

  kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
  REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
  1         <none>
  (only 1 revision — no history to rollback to!)

  kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n easypj --to-revision=2
  error: unable to find revision 2
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. revisionHistoryLimit too low: Default is 10, but someone set it to 0 or 1. kubectl get deploy easypj-api -o yaml | grep revisionHistoryLimit. Old ReplicaSets were pruned.
  2. Old ReplicaSets manually deleted: Someone ran kubectl delete rs --all or cleaned up old ReplicaSets. Without the old RS, there's nothing to rollback to.
  3. Deployment was recreated (not updated): The Deployment was deleted and created anew, losing all history.
  4. Only one version ever deployed: The Deployment has always used the same image — there's nothing to rollback to.
  5. CHANGE-CAUSE not recorded: kubectl annotate deploy/easypj-api kubernetes.io/change-cause="v2.0" not set, so history has <none> for all revisions.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Deployment controller not running — no controllers in kube-system to manage Deployments
  2. etcd data loss — cluster restored from old snapshot without recent revision history
  3. GitOps sync overwrote the Deployment spec including revision history
  4. RBAC preventing the Deployment controller from listing ReplicaSets
  5. Namespace was recreated — all history is per-Deployment, per-namespace
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Only one deployment: New cluster with first deployment — no history exists yet. Set revisionHistoryLimit: 10 before deploying.
  2. Controller manager not watching Deployment resources — upgrade cluster version
  3. API server version mismatch between what created the RS and current — RS not recognized
  4. Custom controller replacing the built-in Deployment controller
  5. Cluster restored from backup but revision history was in a different etcd key space
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl rollout history deploy/<name> — see available revisions. kubectl get rs -l app=<label> — check if old ReplicaSets exist. kubectl describe deploy <name> | grep RevisionHistoryLimit.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. If you have the old YAML: kubectl apply -f old-deploy.yaml — redeploy the known-good version
2. If you have the old image tag: kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api api=easypj/api:v1.0
3. PREVENTION: Set revisionHistoryLimit: 10 (default) — never set to 0
4. PREVENTION: Always record change-cause: kubectl annotate deploy <name> kubernetes.io/change-cause="v2.0 deploy"

💡 Personal Advice: Always set revisionHistoryLimit to at least 3. On CKA: if you're asked to rollback and there's no history, redeploy the previous version manually by changing the image tag. Keep a copy of your last working Deployment YAML — it's your insurance policy.

📌 WS4–WS6: Scheduling Failures

WS4
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS4
Pod Stuck Pending — nodeSelector Matches No Nodes

🔍 Symptom: Pod stays Pending with event: "0/N nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector." The easypj-db pod requires disktype=ssd but no node has this label.

  kubectl describe pod easypj-db-0 -n easypj | tail -10
  Events:
    Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available:
    3 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector

  kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep disktype
  (no output — no nodes have the disktype label!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Required label doesn't exist on any node: The pod's nodeSelector/affinity references a label that was never applied. kubectl get nodes --show-labels — check if any node has the required label.
  2. Label was removed accidentally: Someone ran kubectl label node <name> disktype- (removing the label). Check audit logs.
  3. Pod spec copied from another cluster: The Deployment YAML was copied from a cluster where nodes had different labels.
  4. nodeSelector key typo: disktype: ssd vs disk-type: ssd — hyphen vs no hyphen. Check the exact key.
  5. Affinity with matchExpressions too restrictive: Multiple In/NotIn operators that can't all be satisfied simultaneously.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. All matching nodes are cordoned — labels match but nodes are unschedulable
  2. PodAntiAffinity blocking — requiredDuringScheduling conflicts with existing pod placement
  3. Topology spread constraints with maxSkew that can't be satisfied with the current topology
  4. CPU/Memory requests too high for the matching nodes — labels match but resources insufficient
  5. Taint on matching nodes without pod toleration — labels match but taint blocks scheduling
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Control plane taints not tolerated: New cluster where all nodes have the control-plane taint. Add toleration to pod spec.
  2. Node labels not yet set up for the cluster's topology — no zone/region labels
  3. Cloud provider hasn't added node labels yet (takes ~1 min after node joins)
  4. Worker nodes haven't joined the cluster yet — only control plane exists
  5. Custom scheduler not running — if schedulerName is specified but the scheduler doesn't exist
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe pod <name> — the Events say exactly why scheduling failed. kubectl get nodes --show-labels — compare against pod's nodeSelector.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Add the missing label: kubectl label node <node> disktype=ssd
2. Remove the impossible nodeSelector from the Deployment: kubectl edit deploy <name>
3. Add toleration if tainted: kubectl patch deploy <name> --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/tolerations","value":[{"key":"key","operator":"Exists"}]}]'

💡 Personal Advice: nodeSelector is the #1 cause of Pending pods in the CKA exam. The exam scenario will have a pod with disktype=ssd but no nodes have that label. The fix is either to label a node OR remove the selector — look at the question to determine which is correct.
WS5
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS5
Pod Evicted — Node Under Memory Pressure

🔍 Symptom: Pods show STATUS: Evicted. The easypj-api pods keep getting evicted and recreated. Node shows MemoryPressure=True. The kubelet is evicting pods to prevent the node from running out of memory completely.

  kubectl get pods -n easypj
  NAME                        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-api-7d8f9abcde-xyz   1/1     Evicted   0          2m
  easypj-api-7d8f9abcde-abc   1/1     Running   0          30s

  kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 Conditions
  MemoryPressure   True    ...  ← Node is under memory pressure!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pod memory usage exceeds requests: Pods are using more memory than their requests. Kubelet evicts pods using more than requested when node memory is low.
  2. Too many pods on one node: Combined memory requests exceed node capacity. kubectl describe node | grep -A5 "Allocated resources".
  3. Node has less memory than expected: System processes consuming significant memory. ssh node "free -h".
  4. Memory leak in application: Pod memory usage growing over time. kubectl top pod <name> shows increasing memory.
  5. No memory limits set: Pods without limits can consume all node memory. Always set limits.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kubelet eviction thresholds too aggressive — --eviction-hard set too low
  2. System Reserved memory not configured — kubelet doesn't reserve memory for system daemons
  3. HPA scaling up too aggressively, creating more pods than the node can handle
  4. DaemonSet pods consuming memory on every node without resource limits
  5. Node allocatable memory misconfigured — kubelet --system-reserved flag missing
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Small nodes: New cluster with nodes that have only 2GB RAM. Deploy smaller pods or add larger nodes.
  2. No resource requests defined — all pods are BestEffort QoS, evicted first under pressure
  3. kubelet not configured with --kube-reserved — system pods compete with user pods
  4. Control plane and workloads on same node in single-node cluster — memory shared
  5. Container runtime (containerd) memory leak — runtime consuming increasing memory over time
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe node <name> | grep -A10 Conditions — check MemoryPressure. kubectl top node and kubectl top pods -A — actual usage.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Add memory limits: kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-api --limits=memory=512Mi --requests=memory=256Mi
2. Scale down non-critical pods to free memory
3. Add nodes: kubeadm join new workers
4. Reduce memory requests: kubectl patch deploy <name> --patch '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"api","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"128Mi"}}}]}}}}'

💡 Personal Advice: Always set memory requests AND limits on every container. Without requests, pods are BestEffort QoS and get evicted first. Without limits, a single pod can OOM the entire node. Note: node-pressure eviction ignores PodDisruptionBudgets and terminationGracePeriodSeconds entirely — hard eviction thresholds use a 0s grace period, so you can't PDB your way out of a MemoryPressure eviction the way you can protect against a drain. On CKA: if you see Evicted pods, check node conditions FIRST then check resource requests.
WS6
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS6
Taint Repels All Pods — Nothing Can Schedule on Node

🔍 Symptom: Node has pods stuck Pending (a NoSchedule taint blocks only NEW pods — already-running pods are unaffected; only a NoExecute taint would evict them immediately). kubectl describe node shows taint db-only=true:NoSchedule. No pods have the matching toleration. The easypj-web pods can't run on the database node — but they need to because it's the only node left.

  kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep Taints
  Taints:  db-only=true:NoSchedule

  kubectl get pods -n easypj
  NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-web-0   0/1     Pending   0          5m    ← Taint blocks scheduling!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Taint added without adding tolerations to pods: Someone tainted the node to reserve it but forgot to add tolerations to the pods that SHOULD run there.
  2. Wrong taint effect: NoSchedule vs NoExecute vs PreferNoSchedule. NoExecute evicts EXISTING pods immediately.
  3. All nodes tainted: Every node has a taint that the pods don't tolerate. No pods can schedule anywhere.
  4. Toleration key/value mismatch: Pod toleration says key: db-only, operator: Equal, value: true but taint is db-only=yes:NoSchedule.
  5. Pod spec doesn't include tolerations: The Deployment was updated but tolerations weren't added to the pod template.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Taint was added by a controller or operator automatically (e.g., node problem detector)
  2. Kubelet automatically tainted node due to resource pressure — MemoryPressure/DiskPressure taint
  3. Cloud provider added taint during node maintenance — spot instance termination notice
  4. Taint added via infrastructure-as-code (Terraform/Pulumi) without updating pod specs
  5. Multiple taints on node — pods must tolerate ALL of them (AND condition)
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Control plane taint: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule blocks all pods by default on control plane nodes.
  2. All nodes are control-plane nodes in single-node cluster — no worker nodes exist
  3. Cloud provider taints not documented — new node group has unexpected taints
  4. Kubeadm init added taints that weren't removed after adding workers
  5. Custom admission webhook adding taints to all new nodes automatically
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe node <name> | grep Taints. kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | grep -A10 tolerations — check if pod has matching toleration.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Remove taint: kubectl taint node <node> db-only=true:NoSchedule- (note the trailing -)
2. Add toleration to pod: kubectl patch deploy <name> --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/tolerations","value":[{"key":"db-only","operator":"Equal","value":"true","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}]'

💡 Personal Advice: To remove a taint, add a minus sign at the end: kubectl taint node <n> key=value:Effect-. This is easy to forget under exam pressure. On CKA: taint/toleration questions are common — know the syntax for both adding taints and adding tolerations to pod specs.

📌 WS7–WS9: ConfigMap & Secret Issues

WS7
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS7
ConfigMap Updated — Pods Still Using Old Values

🔍 Symptom: You updated a ConfigMap (changed DEBUG from false to true), but the easypj-api pods still show the OLD value. kubectl exec into the pod shows the old config. Kubernetes does NOT automatically restart pods when a ConfigMap changes.

  kubectl get cm easypj-config -n easypj -o yaml | grep DEBUG
  DEBUG: "true"    ← ConfigMap IS updated

  kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- env | grep DEBUG
  DEBUG=false      ← Pod still has OLD value!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pods don't auto-restart on ConfigMap change: This is expected behavior. ConfigMap updates don't trigger pod restarts. You must manually restart.
  2. ConfigMap mounted as environment variable: env vars are set at pod startup. They never update while the pod is running.
  3. ConfigMap mounted as volume with subPath: subPath mounts prevent automatic file updates. Remove subPath for auto-refresh.
  4. ConfigMap key name mismatch: Pod references DEBUG_LEVEL but ConfigMap key is DEBUG.
  5. ConfigMap in different namespace: Pod and ConfigMap must be in the same namespace.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kubelet sync period hasn't elapsed yet — ConfigMap volume updates take ~1 minute
  2. Update exceeds the 1 MiB ConfigMap data cap — the API server rejects the update outright at apply time; the pod keeps serving the last successfully-applied version, this isn't a kubelet mount failure
  3. Immutable ConfigMap — created with immutable: true, can't be updated at all
  4. Pod uses cached values in application — app reads config once at startup into a static variable
  5. Stale file handle — kubelet uses symlinks, sometimes the old symlink persists
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Kubelet not running on the node where the pod is — volume can't be synced
  2. Disk full on node — kubelet can't write updated ConfigMap files
  3. API server latency high — ConfigMap changes not propagating to kubelet
  4. RBAC preventing kubelet from watching ConfigMaps in that namespace
  5. ConfigMap created with generateName — name doesn't match what pod references
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get cm <name> -o yaml — verify the ConfigMap content. kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/config/<key> — check mounted file content.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Trigger restart: kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
2. For auto-restart on ConfigMap change: Use kubectl apply -k with Kustomize configMapGenerator (adds hash to pod template)
3. For auto-refresh (volumes): Mount WITHOUT subPath — the entire directory is a symlink that kubelet refreshes
4. Use Reloader tool: stakater/Reloader watches ConfigMaps and restarts pods automatically

💡 Personal Advice: ConfigMap updates not reflecting is the #1 "gotcha" for beginners. Remember: env vars NEVER update while pod is running. Volume mounts update after ~1 minute BUT NOT with subPath. On CKA: if you update a ConfigMap and the pod doesn't see it, run kubectl rollout restart deploy/<name>.
WS8
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS8
Secret Not Found — Pod Fails to Start

🔍 Symptom: Pod stays Pending with event: "secret <name> not found." The easypj-api Deployment references secretKeyRef for DATABASE_URL but the Secret was never created. The pod can't start without its database credentials.

  kubectl get pods -n easypj
  NAME                        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-api-7d8f9abcde-xyz   0/1     CreateContainerConfigError   0  2m

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7d8f9abcde-xyz -n easypj
  Events:
    Warning  Failed  secret "db-credentials" not found
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Secret was never created: kubectl get secrets -n <ns> — the Secret doesn't exist. Create it with kubectl create secret generic.
  2. Secret in different namespace: Secrets are namespace-scoped. The pod and Secret must be in the same namespace.
  3. Secret name typo in pod spec: Pod references db-credentials but Secret is named db-creds.
  4. Secret key name mismatch: Pod references secretKeyRef.key: password but Secret has DB_PASSWORD as the key.
  5. Secret deleted accidentally: Someone ran kubectl delete secret --all. Check audit logs.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Secret is optional but value is required by app — optional: true hides the error but app crashes
  2. RBAC preventing the service account from reading Secrets
  3. Secret was created but immediately deleted by a cleanup script
  4. Immutable Secret — created with immutable: true; the update is REJECTED by the API server with an explicit "Forbidden: field is immutable" error, not silently — delete+recreate or version the Secret name instead
  5. Secret data is base64 encoded incorrectly — the value decodes to garbage
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No Secrets created yet: Brand new namespace with no Secrets. The Deployment was applied before the Secret YAML.
  2. etcd encryption not configured — Secrets stored in plaintext, compliance flag raised
  3. Secret referenced from a different cluster's kubeconfig
  4. Namespace was deleted and recreated — all Secrets wiped with it
  5. ArgoCD/Flux sync hasn't applied the Secret yet — ordering issue in GitOps pipeline
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get secrets -n <ns> — list all Secrets. kubectl describe pod <name> — Events show which Secret is missing.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Create the missing Secret: kubectl create secret generic db-credentials -n easypj --from-literal=password=secret123
2. Fix the name in pod spec if Secret exists but name is wrong: kubectl edit deploy <name>
3. Verify keys: kubectl get secret <name> -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq

💡 Personal Advice: Create Secrets BEFORE Deployments that reference them. On CKA: the exam often gives you a Deployment that references a non-existent Secret. Create the Secret with the EXACT name and key that the pod expects. Use kubectl create secret generic — it's faster than writing YAML.
WS9
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS9
Immutable ConfigMap — Can't Update Without Recreate

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml returns "ConfigMap 'easypj-config' is invalid: spec: Forbidden: immutable field." The ConfigMap was created with immutable: true and now the easypj-api needs updated database URL configuration for a migration. You can't update it — you must delete and recreate.

  kubectl apply -f updated-configmap.yaml
  The ConfigMap "easypj-config" is invalid: spec: Forbidden: immutable
  field. ConfigMap is marked as immutable and cannot be updated.

  kubectl get configmap easypj-config -n easypj -o yaml | grep immutable
  immutable: true   ← Locked!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMap created with immutable: true: This is a safety feature to prevent accidental changes. Once set, the data/binaryData content (and the immutable flag itself) can never change again — labels and annotations remain editable, only the config values are frozen.
  2. Helm chart template sets immutable: true by default: Helm charts often use immutable ConfigMaps to ensure deterministic rollouts.
  3. Kustomize patch sets immutable: true: A kustomization.yaml overlay added immutability for production but now you can't update dev.
  4. Someone added immutable: true for security compliance: Immutable ConfigMaps prevent configuration drift — but also prevent ANY changes.
  5. Copy-paste from Helm chart example that had immutable: true: The example was for a specific use case where immutability was intentional.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Immutable ConfigMap was auto-generated by a controller (e.g., cert-manager, Prometheus)
  2. GitOps operator (Flux/ArgoCD) sets immutable: true and enforces it
  3. ConfigMap was part of a Helm release — helm upgrade should replace it but immutable blocks it
  4. Pod using the ConfigMap as a subPath volume — subPath mounts don't auto-update anyway
  5. OPA/Gatekeeper policy requires immutable ConfigMaps for all production namespaces
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New users unaware of immutable field: immutable is a relatively new feature (K8s 1.21+). Many don't know it exists.
  2. Accidentally set immutable: true while experimenting with ConfigMap options
  3. Confusion about immutable vs update behavior — ConfigMaps usually auto-update but subPath mounts don't
  4. First time using Helm — helm upgrade wants to replace immutable ConfigMap but can't
  5. New cluster policy enforces immutability on all ConfigMaps and Secrets
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get configmap <name> -o yaml | grep immutable — is it true? kubectl describe configmap <name> — Events may show update rejections.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Delete and recreate: kubectl delete configmap easypj-config -n easypj && kubectl create configmap easypj-config -n easypj --from-literal=DB_HOST=new-db.easypj.svc
2. Create with new name: easypj-config-v2 — update Deployment to reference new ConfigMap
3. Restart pods after new ConfigMap is applied: kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
4. For Helm: helm upgrade easypj ./chart --set config.immutable=false

💡 Personal Advice: Immutable ConfigMaps/Secrets are GREAT for production stability — they prevent configuration drift. But they require a specific workflow: when config changes, create a NEW named ConfigMap and update the Deployment to reference it. This triggers a proper rolling update. On CKA: if you get "immutable field" error, the ONLY fix is delete + recreate or use a new name.

📌 WS10–WS12: Autoscaling Failures

WS10
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS10
HPA Shows Unknown/<unknown> — Metrics Not Available

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get hpa shows TARGETS: <unknown>/70%. The HPA can't read CPU metrics. The easypj-api is under heavy load but HPA isn't scaling up. Users are experiencing 503 errors.

  kubectl get hpa -n easypj
  NAME         REFERENCE               TARGETS           MINPODS   MAXPODS
  easypj-api   Deployment/easypj-api   <unknown>/70%     2         10

  kubectl top pods -n easypj
  error: Metrics API not available
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. metrics-server not installed: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics-server — if no pod, install it. Without metrics-server, HPA can't read CPU/memory metrics.
  2. Pod missing resource requests: HPA requires CPU or memory requests on the target pods. kubectl get deploy easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A5 resources.
  3. metrics-server pod not Ready: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=metrics-server — CrashLoopBackOff?
  4. Wrong metric name in HPA spec: HPA references cpu but the metric is cpu utilization or vice versa.
  5. API service for metrics.k8s.io not registered: kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io — must be Available: True.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. metrics-server kubelet-insecure-tls not configured on kind/kubeadm clusters
  2. NetworkPolicy blocking metrics-server from scraping kubelet metrics endpoints
  3. RBAC preventing metrics-server from accessing /metrics/resource endpoint
  4. metrics-server --metric-resolution too high — metrics not granular enough
  5. HPA references a Deployment that doesn't exist or has different API version
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. metrics-server not part of default kubeadm install: Must be installed separately. kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
  2. kubelet serving certificates not trusted by metrics-server — need --kubelet-insecure-tls
  3. API server aggregation layer not configured — can't register metrics API service
  4. Control plane node taints prevent metrics-server from scheduling
  5. Firewall blocking kubelet port 10250 — metrics-server can't scrape
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io — must be AVAILABLE. kubectl top pods -A — if this fails, metrics-server is broken.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Install metrics-server: kubectl apply -f <metrics-server-manifest>
2. On kind/kubeadm: patch for insecure TLS: kubectl patch deploy metrics-server -n kube-system --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'
3. Add resource requests to pods if missing
4. Wait ~60s for metrics to populate: kubectl top pods -n easypj

💡 Personal Advice: HPA requires BOTH metrics-server AND resource requests on pods. These are the top 2 causes of <unknown>. On CKA: if HPA shows <unknown>, check metrics-server first, then check if pods have CPU requests defined. You can't have HPA without both.
WS11
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS11
HPA Oscillating — Constant Scale Up/Down

🔍 Symptom: HPA keeps scaling up then down every few minutes. Pod count fluctuates between 2 and 10. The easypj-api pods are in a constant churn — new pods start, serve a few requests, then get terminated. Users see intermittent errors during scale-down events.

  kubectl describe hpa easypj-api -n easypj
  Events:
    Normal   SuccessfulRescale  New size: 8; reason: cpu resource utilization above target
    Normal   SuccessfulRescale  New size: 3; reason: cpu resource utilization below target
    Normal   SuccessfulRescale  New size: 9; reason: cpu resource utilization above target
    (repeats every 2-3 minutes — oscillation!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Target utilization too close to normal load: Target is 50% but normal load fluctuates between 45-55%. HPA oscillates around the threshold.
  2. Asymmetric stabilization: scale-up defaults to 0s (reacts instantly, no smoothing) while scale-down defaults to 300s/5min. A brief CPU spike triggers an immediate scale-up with nothing to dampen it — add scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds in the HPA's behavior block to smooth spikes.
  3. Pod startup time vs scale-down delay mismatch: New pods take 60s to become ready but scale-down happens in 30s.
  4. Multiple metrics with conflicting signals: HPA uses CPU AND memory — CPU says scale up, memory says scale down.
  5. HPA behavior period too short: Default --horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period is 15s — checking too frequently.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. External metrics from Prometheus have high latency — stale data causes wrong decisions
  2. Custom metrics adapter returning incorrect values sporadically
  3. HPA minReplicas set to 1 with bursty traffic — single pod gets overwhelmed
  4. Container resource requests don't match actual usage — metrics are skewed
  5. Multiple HPAs targeting the same Deployment with different metrics
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. metrics-server just installed: Metrics take time to stabilize. Wait 5-10 minutes before relying on HPA decisions.
  2. Small cluster with few nodes — scaling up pods creates resource contention, triggering scale-down
  3. Default kube-controller-manager HPA flags not tuned for workload — use production defaults
  4. Node autoscaler interacting with HPA — both scaling simultaneously creates feedback loop
  5. Fresh cluster with no historical metrics — HPA has no baseline, makes aggressive decisions
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe hpa <name> — watch the Events over 10 minutes. kubectl top pods -n <ns> — actual resource usage.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Increase target: kubectl patch hpa easypj-api -n easypj --patch '{"spec":{"targetCPUUtilizationPercentage":80}}'
2. Add scale-up damping via the HPA v2 behavior block: scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60 — the cause is scale-up's default 0s, not scale-down (already 300s by default), so a controller-manager flag alone won't fix this
3. Set minReplicas to handle base load: kubectl patch hpa easypj-api --patch '{"spec":{"minReplicas":3}}'
4. Use behavior section (v2 API): configure BOTH scaleUp and scaleDown stabilizationWindowSeconds and policies

💡 Personal Advice: HPA oscillation is called "flapping" and it's a sign your target threshold is too close to normal load. Set minReplicas to handle ~70% of peak traffic so HPA only handles the remaining 30%. On CKA: if you see HPA constantly scaling, raise the target percentage or increase minReplicas.
WS12
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS12
VPA + HPA Conflict — Both Trying to Control Replicas

🔍 Symptom: The easypj-api Deployment has both VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler) and HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) configured. VPA is in "Auto" mode — it updates resource requests, which triggers a rolling restart. But HPA is also scaling replicas based on CPU. The two autoscalers fight: VPA increases CPU requests, HPA sees lower utilization and scales down. Then VPA lowers requests, CPU spikes, HPA scales up. The pod count and resource settings oscillate continuously.

  kubectl get vpa -n easypj
  NAME          MODE   RECOMMENDER              AGE
  easypj-vpa    Auto   default                  2h

  kubectl get hpa -n easypj
  NAME         REFERENCE               TARGETS    MINPODS   MAXPODS
  easypj-api   Deployment/easypj-api   45%/70%    2         10

  kubectl get events -n easypj --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -5
  10:05  VPA updated CPU request: 200m → 800m (pod restart triggered)
  10:06  HPA scaled down: 8 → 3 (CPU utilization dropped after request increase)
  10:08  CPU spike (requests too high for 3 pods) → HPA scaled up: 3 → 8
  10:10  VPA updated CPU request: 800m → 200m (usage dropped after scale up)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. VPA in Auto mode with HPA active: VPA changes resource requests → pods restart → HPA sees CPU fluctuation → HPA scales → VPA sees new baseline → VPA changes requests → loop continues.
  2. VPA updateMode: "Auto" instead of "Off": Auto mode actively updates pod specs. Use Off mode for recommendations only when HPA is managing replicas.
  3. VPA and HPA both configured on same Deployment: This is the fundamental conflict — two controllers managing the same workload with different goals.
  4. VPA using CPU/memory as target metric: Same metric as HPA. VPA adjusts requests, HPA adjusts replicas — both reacting to the same signal.
  5. No communication between VPA and HPA: They are independent controllers with no awareness of each other's actions.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. VPA minAllowed/maxAllowed set too wide — VPA makes large resource adjustments that destabilize HPA
  2. VPA updatePolicy with minReplicas set — VPA tries to control replicas too
  3. HPA uses custom metrics (Prometheus) and VPA recommendations are based on different metrics source
  4. Cluster Autoscaler also in the mix — three autoscalers (VPA + HPA + CA) interacting chaotically
  5. VPA recommender interval too short — VPA recalculates before HPA stabilizes from previous change
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New users unaware of VPA+HPA incompatibility: VPA in Auto mode should NOT be used on workloads managed by HPA. This is documented but often missed.
  2. Installed both VPA and HPA as "best practice" without understanding the conflict
  3. VPA was set up for initial resource tuning and left in Auto mode when HPA was added later
  4. Helm chart installs both VPA and HPA by default for "full autoscaling"
  5. Testing autoscaling on fresh cluster — both controllers react to synthetic load simultaneously
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get vpa,hpa -n <ns> — are both targeting same Deployment? kubectl describe vpa <name> — check updateMode. kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' — oscillation pattern.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Set VPA to Off mode: kubectl patch vpa easypj-vpa -n easypj --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"updatePolicy":{"updateMode":"Off"}}}' — VPA still provides recommendations but doesn't change pods
2. Or remove VPA entirely: kubectl delete vpa easypj-vpa -n easypj — keep HPA for horizontal scaling
3. Or remove HPA: use VPA in Auto mode for vertical scaling only — singles replica with VPA-adjusted resources
4. Best practice: VPA for stateless workloads (Off mode for recommendations), HPA for horizontal scaling

💡 Personal Advice: VPA and HPA are NOT meant to work together on the same CPU/memory metrics. VPA adjusts pod SIZE (vertical), HPA adjusts pod COUNT (horizontal). If you need both: use VPA in "Off" mode to get recommendations that you manually apply, and let HPA manage replicas. On CKA: if you see pods constantly restarting and replicas oscillating, check if VPA and HPA are both targeting the same Deployment.

📌 WS13–WS15: Resilience & Disruption

WS13
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS13
PodDisruptionBudget Blocks Node Drain

🔍 Symptom: kubectl drain worker-1 hangs. The drain process can't evict pods because a PDB requires at least 2 pods to be Available, but evicting one would drop below that. Node maintenance is blocked. The easypj-api has PDB minAvailable: 2 with only 2 replicas.

  kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets
  (hangs for several minutes)
  error: cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget

  kubectl get pdb -n easypj
  NAME         MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
  easypj-api   2               N/A               0                     30d
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. PDB minAvailable too high: PDB requires 2 pods but only 2 exist. Evicting ANY pod violates the PDB. Increase replicas or lower PDB.
  2. PDB doesn't match actual pod count: PDB was set when there were 5 replicas, but someone scaled to 2. PDB still requires 2.
  3. PDB targets wrong pods: PDB selector matches pods it shouldn't (or doesn't match the ones it should).
  4. Multiple nodes need draining simultaneously: All nodes need maintenance but PDB prevents any pod from being evicted.
  5. PDB set to maxUnavailable: 0: Even ONE pod down is forbidden. Change to maxUnavailable: 1 or use minAvailable with headroom.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. PDB references a Deployment that no longer exists — stale PDB blocking everything
  2. Voluntary disruption (drain) vs involuntary (node crash) — PDB only applies to voluntary
  3. PDB created with percentages — 80% of 3 pods = 2.4, rounded up to 3 = all pods required
  4. Cluster autoscaler trying to scale down a node but PDB blocks pod eviction
  5. PDB status shows 0 disruptions allowed with 3 healthy pods — selector mismatch
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No PDBs created: New cluster with no PDBs — drain could evict ALL pods. Create PDBs before going to production.
  2. Default PDB template too restrictive for small cluster — adjust for cluster size
  3. PDB prevents kubeadm upgrade — drain step in upgrade can't proceed
  4. All pods on one node — PDB see's all pods at risk if that node drains
  5. Pod topology spread constraints work against PDB — pods can't be moved to satisfy both
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pdb -A — all PDBs. kubectl describe pdb <name> — status shows allowed disruptions. kubectl get pods -l <selector> — count matching pods.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Temporarily increase replicas: kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=3 — then drain works
2. Lower PDB: kubectl patch pdb easypj-api -n easypj --patch '{"spec":{"minAvailable":1}}'
3. Delete PDB temporarily (not recommended for prod): kubectl delete pdb easypj-api -n easypj
4. Add --disable-eviction to drain (force, not recommended): kubectl drain <node> --disable-eviction

💡 Personal Advice: PDB formula: minAvailable = totalReplicas - 1 for stateless apps. This ensures at least one pod can be evicted during maintenance. Stateful apps may need stricter PDBs. Also set unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow on your PDBs — otherwise an already-unhealthy (crashlooping) pod counts against the budget and can block drain indefinitely even when the replica math looks fine. On CKA: if drain hangs, check PDBs. The question may ask you to adjust the PDB so drain can proceed.
WS14
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS14
QoS Class Unexpected — Request ≠ Limit Changes Behavior

🔍 Symptom: The easypj-api pod was OOMKilled during a traffic spike even though memory usage was well below the limit. Investigation reveals QoS class is "Burstable" instead of "Guaranteed" because CPU request (200m) ≠ CPU limit (500m). The node was under memory pressure and the OOM killer targeted Burstable pods before Guaranteed pods.

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7d8f9abcde-xyz -n easypj | grep -A5 "QoS\|State\|Reason"
  QoS Class:       Burstable
  State:           Terminated
  Reason:          OOMKilled
  Exit Code:       137

  kubectl get pod easypj-api-7d8f9abcde-xyz -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A4 resources
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 256Mi
    limits:
      cpu: 500m        ← CPU request ≠ CPU limit → Burstable, not Guaranteed!
      memory: 512Mi
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CPU request ≠ CPU limit: For Guaranteed QoS, EVERY container must have request == limit for BOTH CPU and memory. Even one mismatch drops to Burstable.
  2. Memory request ≠ Memory limit: Same rule — both must match. requests.memory: 256Mi but limits.memory: 512Mi = Burstable.
  3. One container in pod has mismatched values: QoS is per-pod. If init container or sidecar has request≠limit, the whole pod is Burstable.
  4. Limits set but requests omitted: Kubernetes sets request=limit for that resource, but only if limit is specified without request. If you explicitly set different values, QoS drops.
  5. Eviction risk from falling to Burstable QoS: unlike a true Guaranteed pod (parked at its request), a Burstable pod can exceed its request and becomes an eviction candidate under memory pressure — kubelet sorts primarily by usage-over-request and Priority, not a hardcoded QoS order, but your pod's Burstable status made it exceed-eligible where Guaranteed wouldn't have been.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. LimitRange in namespace sets default requests different from limits — every pod becomes Burstable
  2. Helm chart template sets requests from values.yaml but limits from a different value path
  3. VPA modified resource requests, breaking previously Guaranteed QoS
  4. ResourceQuota forces low requests but high limits — misconfiguration causes QoS drift
  5. PodPreset or mutating admission webhook injects resources that mismatch existing values
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New users unaware of QoS classes: Guaranteed = every container has request==limit for both CPU AND memory. Burstable = at least one container has a request or limit. BestEffort = no requests or limits at all.
  2. Testing with BestEffort pods that get killed first under any memory pressure
  3. Default namespace has no LimitRange — pods created without requests/limits become BestEffort
  4. Node memory pressure on small dev clusters (kind, minikube) triggers OOM more aggressively
  5. Confusion about QoS impact — QoS affects eviction priority, not scheduling priority (that's PriorityClass)
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | grep -A10 resources — check every container. QoS class is shown in kubectl describe pod.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Set request == limit for BOTH CPU and memory: kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-api -n easypj --requests=cpu=500m,memory=512Mi --limits=cpu=500m,memory=512Mi
2. Verify QoS: kubectl describe pod <new-pod> | grep "QoS Class" — should show Guaranteed
3. Check all containers: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
4. For multi-container pods, ensure ALL containers have request==limit

💡 Personal Advice: Guaranteed QoS is the "VIP treatment" — your pods are LAST to be evicted under resource pressure. For production databases and critical APIs, always use Guaranteed QoS (request==limit for CPU AND memory in every container). On CKA: QoS is one of those "trick" topics — remember it's per-pod, all containers must match, and BOTH CPU and memory must have request==limit.
WS15
⚙️ CATEGORY 3: WORKLOADS — Issue WS15
Preemption — Lower Priority Pod Evicted Unexpectedly

🔍 Symptom: A high-priority pod (easypj-api-critical) was scheduled successfully, but the easypj-worker pod disappeared without warning. kubectl get pods shows the worker pod was "Preempted." The cluster is at capacity and the PriorityClass system evicted the lower-priority Worker pod to make room for the higher-priority API critical pod.

  kubectl get pods -n easypj
  NAME                  READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-api-critical   1/1     Running     0          2m   ← New high-priority pod
  easypj-worker         0/1     Terminated  0          1h   ← Preempted!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-worker -n easypj | tail -10
  Status:       Terminated
  Reason:       Preempted
  Message:      Preempted by easypj-api-critical-6a3f8bc9-xz2q
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Cluster at capacity: All nodes are full. When a high-priority pod is pending, scheduler preempts lower-priority pods to make room.
  2. Worker pod has low or no PriorityClass: Default priority is 0. A pod with priority 1000+ can preempt priority-0 pods.
  3. Multiple pods with different priorities competing for same node: Scheduler picks the lowest-priority victim(s) to evict.
  4. Node autoscaler not adding nodes fast enough: Cluster is full, autoscaler is slow, preemption happens before new node is ready.
  5. PDB preventing eviction of some pods: Scheduler tries to evict lowest-priority pods first, but PDB blocks some. It moves to next-lowest, which might be your worker. Note this protection is best-effort only — if NO PDB-safe victim exists at all, the scheduler preempts anyway and the PDB gets violated.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. PriorityClass globalDefault set to a high value — all new pods get high priority, making preemption common
  2. Non-preempting PriorityClass used — pod stays Pending instead of preempting others
  3. Anti-affinity rules force pod onto a node that's already full of lower-priority pods
  4. Custom scheduler plugin changes preemption scoring — unexpected victim selection
  5. Resource requests overestimated — pod requests 4 CPUs but only uses 200m, causing unnecessary preemption
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. All pods use default priority (0): No PriorityClasses defined means preemption never happens — pods just stay Pending. This is the default state.
  2. Critical system pods have high priority: kube-system pods like CoreDNS often have priority 2000000000 (system-cluster-critical). They can preempt anything.
  3. Small dev cluster with limited resources — preemption happens frequently during testing
  4. PriorityClass not created before being referenced — pod creation fails with "PriorityClass not found"
  5. Misunderstanding preemptionPreemptionPolicy: Never — pod will NEVER preempt others, will stay Pending
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get priorityclass — all defined priority classes. kubectl describe pod <victim> — see Reason: Preempted and which pod preempted it. kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Preempted.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Give worker pods a higher PriorityClass: kubectl create priorityclass worker-priority --value=500 --description="Worker pods"
2. Update worker Deployment: add priorityClassName: worker-priority to pod spec
3. Scale cluster or reduce resource requests if preemption is frequent
4. Use preemptionPolicy: Never on a HIGH-value PriorityClass when you want it to queue-jump ahead of lower-priority pending pods but never actually evict running ones (e.g. Kubernetes' own "high-priority-nonpreempting" example) — low-priority pods already can't preempt anyone regardless of this flag
5. Set realistic resource requests — over-requesting triggers unnecessary preemption

💡 Personal Advice: Preemption is Kubernetes' way of saying "something more important needs this spot." It's not a bug — it's a feature. The fix is assigning proper PriorityClasses to ALL your workloads. Production databases: priority 1000+. Batch workers: priority 100. Dev/test: priority 0. On CKA: know that preemption happens when a high-priority pod is Pending and there's no free capacity. Lower-priority pods are evicted (gracefully if possible) to make room.

🏗️ Category 4: Cluster Architecture (25 Issues)CA1-CA25

🔴 kubeadm, etcd, HA, RBAC & Extensibility

Cluster architecture issues focus on the control plane and cluster management — kubeadm bootstrapping, etcd health, high availability, RBAC security, and extensibility with Helm/CRDs/Operators.

📌 CA1–CA5: kubeadm Bootstrapping Failures

CA1
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA1
kubeadm init Fails — Preflight Checks Error

🔍 Symptom: kubeadm init fails with preflight errors: swap enabled, port in use, or container runtime not found. Cluster can't be bootstrapped.

$ kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
❌ [preflight] Some fatal errors occurred:
❌   [ERROR Swap]: running with swap on is not supported
❌   [ERROR Port-6443]: Port 6443 is in use
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Swap enabled: kubeadm preflight fails by default with swap on. Either swapoff -a (and remove from /etc/fstab), or set failSwapOn: false in the kubelet config to tolerate swap instead.
  2. Port 6443 already in use: Another API server or process bound to the port. netstat -tlnp | grep 6443.
  3. Container runtime not detected: containerd/CRI-O not installed or not running. systemctl status containerd.
  4. Existing /etc/kubernetes/manifests directory: Previous init left manifests. Run kubeadm reset first.
  5. Insufficient CPU/memory: kubeadm requires minimum 2 CPUs and 2GB RAM per machine.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Wrong Kubernetes version: installed kubeadm version incompatible with desired control plane version.
  2. Firewall blocking required ports: 6443 (API), 10250 (kubelet), 2379-2380 (etcd).
  3. kubelet not running: kubeadm init depends on kubelet being active. systemctl start kubelet.
  4. Cgroup driver mismatch: kubelet uses systemd but containerd uses cgroupfs.
  5. DNS resolution failure: Node can't resolve itself. Check /etc/hosts.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Swap not disabled: swapoff -a and comment out swap in /etc/fstab.
  2. Port conflicts: stop the conflicting process or use --apiserver-bind-port for non-standard port.
  3. Container runtime: install containerd: apt-get install containerd and configure for K8s.
  4. Existing config: kubeadm reset then retry init.
  5. Minimum specs: ensure node meets 2 CPU + 2GB RAM requirements.
🔍 What to Look At: systemctl status kubelet containerd. swapoff -a && free -m. netstat -tlnp | grep -E "6443|10250|2379".
🔧 How to Solve:

1. swapoff -a and remove from /etc/fstab
2. kubeadm reset -f to clean previous attempts
3. systemctl restart containerd && systemctl restart kubelet
4. Retry: kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
5. For preflight bypass: --ignore-preflight-errors=Swap,NumCPU (not recommended for production)

💡 Personal Advice: Preflight errors are 90% of init failures. The #1 cause is swap — must be disabled. #2 is port conflicts — another kubeadm init or process using 6443. Always run kubeadm reset before retrying init. On CKA: you'll need to fix preflight issues and successfully run kubeadm init. Know the preflight checks and their fixes cold.
CA2
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA2
kubeadm join Fails — Worker Can't Join Cluster

🔍 Symptom: kubeadm join fails with "connection refused," "token not found," or "certificate signed by unknown authority." Worker node can't join the cluster.

$ kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 --token abc.123 --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:xxx
❌ Failed to request cluster info: dial tcp 192.168.1.10:6443: connect: connection refused
❌ error execution phase preflight: token not found
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. API server unreachable: Wrong IP/port or firewall blocking 6443. curl -k https://cp-ip:6443/healthz.
  2. Token expired or invalid: Bootstrap tokens expire in 24h. kubeadm token create --print-join-command on CP.
  3. CA cert hash mismatch: Wrong --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash. Get correct: openssl x509 -pubkey -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt | openssl rsa -pubin -outform der 2>/dev/null | openssl dgst -sha256 -hex | sed 's/^.* //'.
  4. Node already joined: Worker thinks it's already part of a cluster. kubeadm reset on worker first.
  5. Clock skew: Worker clock differs from CP by >5min. TLS certificates invalid. timedatectl set-ntp true.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Wrong API server address: --apiserver-advertise-address on CP differs from what worker targets.
  2. Firewall between worker subnet and control plane subnet blocking 6443.
  3. kubelet on worker not running: systemctl status kubelet.
  4. Worker hostname not resolvable by DNS or /etc/hosts on CP node.
  5. Different Kubernetes minor version: kubelet must never be newer than the API server, and may be up to 3 minor versions older (2 for versions <1.25) — not a symmetric +1/-1 skew.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Token not created: Run kubeadm token create on control plane.
  2. CA hash not provided: Always include --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash for security.
  3. kubeadm reset not run on worker: Worker must be clean before joining.
  4. Network not configured: Worker can't reach CP. Check routing and firewall.
  5. kubelet config not present: kubeadm join generates /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.
🔍 What to Look At: kubeadm token list on CP. curl -k https://cp-ip:6443/healthz from worker. systemctl status kubelet.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. On CP: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
2. Copy the full join command to worker
3. On worker: kubeadm reset -f then run join command
4. Verify: kubectl get nodes on CP
5. Fix networking: ensure port 6443 is open between worker and CP

💡 Personal Advice: Join failures are almost always: token expired, wrong CA hash, or network/firewall issue. The safest approach: always generate a fresh join command with kubeadm token create --print-join-command and copy it EXACTLY. On CKA: you'll need to add a worker node — know the join command and how to troubleshoot token/cert issues.
CA3
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA3
kubeadm upgrade Fails — Version Skew or Dependency Issue

🔍 Symptom: kubeadm upgrade plan or kubeadm upgrade apply fails. Cluster stuck on old version. Component version mismatch or etcd upgrade issue.

$ kubeadm upgrade plan
❌ couldn't upgrade: the desired version is not compatible
❌ kubelet version is too new compared to kubeadm version
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Version skew violation: kubelet > apiserver. kubelet can't be NEWER than apiserver. Must upgrade CP first.
  2. kubeadm not upgraded first: apt-get install kubeadm=1.29.x must precede kubeadm upgrade apply.
  3. etcd upgrade blocked: etcd version gap too large. Must upgrade one minor version at a time.
  4. Unschedulable pods: drain node before upgrading kubelet. kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets.
  5. CRD version incompatibility: Custom resources not compatible with target K8s version.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. kubeadm config outdated: kubeadm-config ConfigMap doesn't match current cluster state.
  2. CoreDNS/kube-proxy version mismatch with target K8s version.
  3. Cluster was set up with non-standard feature gates that changed in target version.
  4. Deprecated API versions in use: resources using APIs removed in target version.
  5. Third-party controllers or webhooks incompatible with target K8s version.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. First upgrade: Always check kubeadm upgrade plan before applying.
  2. Major version jump: Can only upgrade one MINOR version at a time (1.28→1.29, not 1.27→1.29).
  3. No backup: Always backup etcd before upgrade: etcdctl snapshot save.
  4. kubeadm not held: Use apt-mark hold kubeadm after upgrade to prevent unintended changes.
  5. No dry-run: kubeadm upgrade supports --dry-run to simulate without applying.
🔍 What to Look At: kubeadm version and kubectl version. kubeadm upgrade plan. kubectl get nodes for versions.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. apt-mark unhold kubeadm && apt-get install kubeadm=<target>
2. kubeadm upgrade plan to verify compatibility
3. kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.x on CP
4. Drain each worker: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets
5. Upgrade kubelet on each: apt-get install kubelet=<target> && systemctl restart kubelet

💡 Personal Advice: Version skew is the #1 upgrade killer. Golden rule: kube-apiserver is the ceiling — no component may be newer. kube-controller-manager/kube-scheduler: X or X-1. kubelet and kube-proxy: X down to X-3 (same skew for both). Never X+1 for anything. Always upgrade CP first, then workers. On CKA: you'll perform a cluster upgrade — know the exact sequence: kubeadm → plan → apply → drain workers → upgrade kubelet → uncordon.
CA4
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA4
kubeadm certs expired — Cluster PKI Broken

🔍 Symptom: kubectl fails with "x509: certificate has expired." Cluster certificates (1-year validity) have expired. API server, kubelet, or etcd certs are invalid.

$ kubeadm certs check-expiration
CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES
❌ admin.conf               Jan 01, 2026 10:00 UTC (EXPIRED!)
❌ apiserver                Jan 01, 2026 10:00 UTC (EXPIRED!)
❌ apiserver-etcd-client    Jan 01, 2026 10:00 UTC (EXPIRED!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Certificates expired: Default validity 1 year. kubeadm certs check-expiration shows all expired.
  2. kubelet client cert expired: Worker nodes can't authenticate. kubelet shows NotReady.
  3. etcd peer cert expired: etcd members can't communicate. Cluster unstable.
  4. CA certificate expired: All issued certs become invalid. Requires CA rotation — complex.
  5. Clock skew making certs appear expired: timedatectl status — ensure NTP synced.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Manual cert rotation failed: Old cert still referenced in kubeconfig files.
  2. front-proxy-client cert expired: Aggregated API services (metrics-server) failing.
  3. Certificate files deleted but not regenerated: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ files missing.
  4. kubeadm upgrade not done for >1 year: Upgrades auto-renew certs. Stale clusters accumulate expired certs.
  5. Custom CA renewal done incorrectly: Intermediate CA chain broken.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New cluster unaware: kubeadm certs expire 1 year after init. No monitoring set up.
  2. No auto-renewal for control-plane certs outside upgrades: kubeadm only renews them during kubeadm upgrade (or manual kubeadm certs renew) — there is no separate always-on auto-renewal feature. Only kubelet's own client/serving certs auto-rotate.
  3. Calendar reminder missed: Set reminder 1 month before cluster anniversary.
  4. kubeadm upgrade renews certs: If you never upgrade, certs never renew.
  5. External etcd: certs managed separately from kubeadm — different renewal process.
🔍 What to Look At: kubeadm certs check-expiration. openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubeadm certs check-expiration — identify all expired certs
2. kubeadm certs renew all — renew ALL certificates
3. Restart control plane: move static pod manifests out and back
4. Copy new admin.conf: cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config
5. For workers: kubeadm certs renew kubelet-client and restart kubelet

💡 Personal Advice: Certificate expiry is the silent cluster killer. Every kubeadm cluster WILL face this after 1 year. Run kubeadm certs check-expiration MONTHLY. Set a recurring calendar reminder. On CKA: you may need to renew certs and restart control plane. Know: kubeadm certs renew all and then restart kubelet (which restarts all static pods).
CA5
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA5
kubeadm reset Leaves Orphaned Resources

🔍 Symptom: kubeadm reset seems successful but leaves behind iptables rules, CNI config, or mounted directories. New kubeadm init fails with "port in use" or "directory exists."

$ kubeadm reset
✅ [reset] Stopping the kubelet service
✅ [reset] Deleting /etc/kubernetes/
❌ [reset] Failed to remove CNI config: /etc/cni/net.d/ still exists
❌ [reset] iptables rules may still be present
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CNI config not cleaned: /etc/cni/net.d/ directory has leftover config files. Manually remove.
  2. iptables rules persisted: Reset doesn't always flush all chains. iptables -F && iptables -t nat -F.
  3. Mounted volumes not unmounted: /var/lib/kubelet has active mounts. umount /var/lib/kubelet/* manually.
  4. containerd containers still running: Reset stops kubelet but not existing containers. crictl rm -a.
  5. kubelet service not stopped/disabled: After reset, kubelet may restart and recreate static pods.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Network interfaces not cleaned: CNI-created interfaces (tunl0, vxlan.calico) remain.
  2. containerd images not cleaned: Old images consume disk space. crictl rmi --prune.
  3. etcd data directory not removed: /var/lib/etcd/member still has data. Manual deletion needed.
  4. kubeconfig file not removed from user home: ~/.kube/config still references old cluster.
  5. systemd service overrides not removed: /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/ leftover config.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Partial reset: kubeadm reset run with errors but ignored.
  2. Additional CNI components: Calico/BGP configs outside /etc/cni/net.d/.
  3. Custom kubelet flags: --node-ip or --hostname-override persisted in service file.
  4. Docker (legacy) containers not cleaned: dockershim-era images/containers remain.
  5. Cloud provider resources: Load balancers, volumes not cleaned by reset.
🔍 What to Look At: ls /etc/cni/net.d/ and ls /var/lib/kubelet/. iptables -L -n | grep KUBE. crictl ps.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubeadm reset -f
2. rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d/*
3. iptables -F && iptables -t nat -F && iptables -t mangle -F
4. umount /var/lib/kubelet/* 2>/dev/null; rm -rf /var/lib/kubelet
5. ip link delete <cni-interface> 2>/dev/null

💡 Personal Advice: kubeadm reset is NOT a complete nuclear option. It cleans up the obvious stuff but leaves CNI config, iptables rules, and sometimes mounted volumes. It also does NOT touch $HOME/.kube — the old admin.conf credentials in ~/.kube/config remain valid and usable until you delete that file yourself, which matters if the cluster is being decommissioned for security reasons. On CKA: after reset, always manually verify: empty /etc/cni/net.d/, flushed iptables, unmounted /var/lib/kubelet. If init fails after reset, check these three things first.

📌 CA6–CA10: etcd Health, HA Load Balancing & RBAC

CA6
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA6
etcd Cluster Lost Quorum — Read-Only Mode

🔍 Symptom: etcd cluster lost quorum (2 of 3 members down). Cluster is read-only — no kubectl create/apply/delete works. etcdctl endpoint health shows unhealthy members.

$ etcdctl endpoint health --endpoints=cp1:2379,cp2:2379,cp3:2379
❌ cp1:2379 is healthy: committed proposal took 5ms
❌ cp2:2379 is unhealthy: failed to connect: dial tcp: connect: connection refused
❌ cp3:2379 is unhealthy: failed to connect: dial tcp: connect: connection refused
✅ 1 of 3 endpoints healthy (QUORUM LOST — need 2)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Too many etcd members failed: 2 of 3 down = no quorum. Cluster becomes read-only.
  2. Network partition: Members can't reach each other on peer port 2380.
  3. Two members crashed simultaneously: OOM, disk full, or node failure.
  4. Member data corrupted: WAL or snapshot corruption prevents etcd from starting.
  5. etcd process killed by OOM killer: Node memory exhausted, etcd terminated.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Slow disk causing heartbeat timeouts: Members think peers are dead, trigger election.
  2. Firewall between members blocking peer port 2380 after security update.
  3. One node in different availability zone with high latency (>200ms).
  4. etcd compaction interrupted: Database in inconsistent state after partial compaction.
  5. Incorrect etcd member removal: trying to remove leader while cluster is unstable.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Only 1 etcd member: No redundancy. Any failure = total cluster loss.
  2. 3+ etcd members but no monitoring: Can't detect quorum loss until kubectl fails.
  3. etcd on HDD not SSD: Slow disk causes frequent timeouts and false leader elections.
  4. No etcd backups: Quorum loss without backup = unrecoverable cluster state loss.
  5. Unencrypted peer communication: Man-in-the-middle can disrupt etcd consensus.
🔍 What to Look At: etcdctl endpoint health and etcdctl endpoint status. kubectl get events -A (if API is up).
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Identify which members are down: SSH to each CP node
2. Restart failed members: systemctl restart kubelet (restarts etcd static pod)
3. If quorum can't be restored: restore from backup on a healthy member
4. etcdutl snapshot restore to create a fresh single-member cluster (etcdutl, not etcdctl, is the documented restore tool)
5. Add new members to restored cluster

💡 Personal Advice: etcd quorum loss is the WORST failure — cluster becomes read-only but running pods continue. Act fast: restore failed members if possible. If unrecoverable, restore from etcd snapshot. ALWAYS run 3+ etcd members and TAKE REGULAR BACKUPS. On CKA: you may need to restore etcd from a snapshot — know the exact etcdutl snapshot restore command with all cert flags (etcdctl saves the snapshot; etcdutl is what restores it).
CA7
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA7
etcd Database Too Large — Performance Degradation

🔍 Symptom: etcd database >2GB. kubectl get commands slow, API server requests timeout. etcd compaction hasn't run or is failing. Events and leases accumulating without cleanup.

$ etcdctl endpoint status --endpoints=cp1:2379 -w table
+---------+------+---------+-------+--------+
| ENDPOINT| ID   | VERSION | DB SIZE| LEADER |
❌ cp1:2379 | abc  | 3.5.0   | 6.2 GB | true   |  ← 6GB is dangerous!

$ kubectl get events -A --no-headers | wc -l
152345  ← 150K+ events!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Events not cleaned: kubectl get events -A | wc -l. Events TTL (default 1h) not working.
  2. etcd compaction not running: etcdctl compact never called. DB fragmentation grows.
  3. Too many ConfigMaps/Secrets: Thousands of small objects bloating etcd.
  4. Leases not expiring: Leader election leases accumulating. Check kubectl get lease -A | wc -l.
  5. Large objects stored in etcd: ConfigMaps >1MB or CRs with huge data blobs.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Defragmentation not done after compaction: etcdctl defrag reclaims free space.
  2. --quota-backend-bytes too high: Default 2GB, raised to 8GB — hides the problem.
  3. --auto-compaction-retention not set: etcd relies on manual compaction calls.
  4. History compaction not configured: --auto-compaction-mode=periodic --auto-compaction-retention=1h.
  5. Too many watchers: Applications creating thousands of watch connections on etcd.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default 2GB quota: New cluster with no compaction configured — will fill up within months.
  2. Events generated by every pod action: 100 pods × 10 restarts/day = 1000 events/day.
  3. No event TTL set: kube-apiserver --event-ttl=1h defaults may not be enough.
  4. K8s 1.19+ has auto-compaction enabled by default but may need tuning.
  5. Monitoring not set up: No alert when etcd DB exceeds 75% of quota.
🔍 What to Look At: etcdctl endpoint status -w table — check DB SIZE. etcdctl compact <revision>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. etcdctl compact $(etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=json | jq .[0].Status.header.revision)
2. etcdctl defrag --endpoints=cp1:2379,cp2:2379,cp3:2379
3. Enable auto-compaction: --auto-compaction-mode=periodic --auto-compaction-retention=1h
4. Clean old events: kubectl delete events --all -A
5. Set event TTL: --event-ttl=30m in API server config

💡 Personal Advice: etcd is a database — it needs maintenance. Compact + defrag monthly. The #1 cause of oversized etcd is accumulated Events. A busy cluster can generate 10K+ events per day. On CKA: you may see a slow cluster and need to check etcd DB size. Know: etcdctl endpoint status shows DB size, etcdctl compact + etcdctl defrag shrinks it.
CA8
🔧 CA CATEGORY — Issue CA8
etcd Member Corrupted — WAL or Snapshot Damage

🔍 Symptom: Single etcd member fails to start with "wal: corrupted" or "snapshot: out of date." Member needs to be removed and re-added to the cluster.

$ journalctl -u kubelet | grep etcd
❌ etcd: wal: corrupted wal file /var/lib/etcd/member/wal/0000000000000002-0000000000000002.wal
❌ etcd: failed to open WAL: wal: corrupted
✅ Other 2 members healthy and operational
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. WAL corruption: Write-ahead log corrupted on disk. Usually from hard shutdown or disk failure.
  2. Snapshot corruption: etcd snapshot file damaged. Member can't recover from snapshot.
  3. Disk full during write: etcd couldn't write to WAL — partial writes corrupt the file.
  4. Unclean shutdown: Node crashed or power loss without graceful etcd stop.
  5. Disk I/O error: Bad sectors on the physical disk corrupted etcd data files.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Filesystem corruption: ext4/xfs journal corruption affecting etcd data directory.
  2. Incorrect member re-add: Adding member with same name but different peer URL.
  3. Data directory manually modified: Someone edited etcd files directly instead of using etcdctl.
  4. Backup restore on wrong member: Restored snapshot onto a member that still has peers.
  5. Running multiple etcd processes on same data directory by accident.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No persistent storage: etcd data on ephemeral disk — lost on node restart.
  2. etcd data not on SSD: HDD latency causes WAL sync delays and potential corruption.
  3. No disk monitoring: Bad sectors or SMART errors undetected until corruption.
  4. Node running on spot/preemptible instance: Frequent terminations corrupt etcd.
  5. etcd data directory not backed by reliable storage (local SSD or high-IOPS EBS).
🔍 What to Look At: ls -la /var/lib/etcd/member/wal/ and ls -la /var/lib/etcd/member/snap/. dmesg | grep -i error for disk errors.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Remove corrupted member: etcdctl member remove <member-id>
2. Clean data: rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/member
3. Re-add member: etcdctl member add <name> --peer-urls=https://<ip>:2380
4. Start etcd on member with fresh data directory
5. Verify: etcdctl endpoint health — all members healthy

💡 Personal Advice: Single member corruption is survivable — just remove and re-add. Don't try to fix the WAL files manually. The healthy members will stream a snapshot to the new member. On CKA: you may need to remove a broken etcd member and add a fresh one. Know: etcdctl member remove <id> and etcdctl member add <name> --peer-urls=....
CA9
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA9
HA API Server Load Balancer Misconfigured

🔍 Symptom: API server behind LB times out intermittently. kubectl works sometimes, fails others. LB health check failing or routing to a dead API server backend.

$ curl -k https://lb-ip:6443/healthz
❌ curl: (7) Failed to connect (intermittent)

$ kubectl get nodes
❌ The connection to the server was refused (sometimes works)
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. LB health check path wrong: /healthz is deprecated (since v1.16) and /livez only signals "should this be restarted" — the documented-correct endpoint for a load balancer's routing decision is /readyz ("route traffic away from me").
  2. LB routing to dead API server: One CP node down, LB still sends traffic there.
  3. TCP health check not configured: LB uses HTTP check but API server only has TCP 6443.
  4. Sticky sessions not needed for API server: LB using source IP affinity wrongly.
  5. LB timeout too short: API server requests take >30s, LB disconnects.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. LB using round-robin with different API server versions causing inconsistent responses.
  2. TLS termination at LB: client certs not forwarded to API server — auth fails.
  3. LB in different subnet with firewall between LB and CP nodes.
  4. LB health check interval too frequent — overloads API server.
  5. LB DNS name not resolvable from worker nodes (kubelet.conf points to LB).
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. No HA: Single API server = single point of failure. Need 3+ CP nodes + LB.
  2. LB not deployed: kubeadm init without --control-plane-endpoint for HA.
  3. Wrong LB type: Using HTTP LB instead of TCP/NLB for API server (TCP 6443).
  4. LB in front of all 3 CP nodes but 1 node not yet joined — LB doesn't exclude it.
  5. Internal LB not accessible from kubectl client outside VPC.
🔍 What to Look At: curl -k https://lb-ip:6443/healthz from multiple nodes. kubectl get --raw /healthz. LB target group health check status.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Set LB health check to TCP:6443 (not HTTP)
2. Remove unhealthy backends from LB target group
3. Set LB timeout to 60s+ for long API requests
4. Use kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint=lb:6443
5. Test from worker: curl -k https://lb:6443/healthz

💡 Personal Advice: HA without a working LB = worse than single CP. The LB is the single point of entry. On CKA: you may need to configure --control-plane-endpoint during kubeadm init. Use a TCP load balancer, not HTTP. kubeadm-managed clients like kubelets and admin.conf authenticate via client certificates — an HTTP-terminating LB strips those certs and breaks that auth path.
CA10
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA10
RBAC Denied — User/SA Can't Access Resources

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pods returns "forbidden" for a user or ServiceAccount. RBAC RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding is missing or misconfigured.

$ kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice
❌ no

$ kubectl get rolebinding -A | grep alice
