(empty — no bindings for alice!)
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. No RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding for the user: kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A | grep <user>.
  2. Wrong namespace: RoleBinding in "dev" but user trying "prod" namespace.
  3. Wrong verbs: Role grants "get,list" but user needs "create" too.
  4. ClusterRole bound via RoleBinding: Permissions restricted to single namespace despite ClusterRole.
  5. subjects.kind wrong: "User" vs "ServiceAccount" vs "Group" mismatch.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. ServiceAccount used without binding: SA created but no RoleBinding attached.
  2. Default ServiceAccount has no permissions: Every ns has "default" SA with zero permissions.
  3. RBAC aggregated ClusterRoles not updated: Custom roles extending built-in roles not refreshed.
  4. RBAC API version mismatch: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 vs v1beta1.
  5. Impersonation headers stripped by proxy: --as flag doesn't work behind corporate proxy.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. No RBAC configured: Cluster runs with --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow (insecure).
  2. system:masters group overused: Everyone added to admin group instead of granular RBAC.
  3. No ClusterRole aggregator labels: Custom ClusterRoles not picking up new APIs automatically.
  4. Default RBAC from kubeadm: Only cluster-admin exists, no namespace-level roles.
  5. New namespace: No default RBAC setup — users have zero access to new namespaces.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<user> -n <ns>. kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A -o wide.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n <ns>
2. kubectl create rolebinding alice-pod --role=pod-reader --user=alice -n <ns>
3. Verify: kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice -n <ns>
4. For cluster-wide: use ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
5. For SAs: kubectl create rolebinding sa-pod --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=<ns>:<sa>

💡 Personal Advice: RBAC troubleshooting = kubectl auth can-i is your best friend. It impersonates any user/SA and tests permissions. On CKA: you'll create Roles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoles, and ClusterRoleBindings. Know the difference: Role=namespaced, ClusterRole=cluster-wide. RoleBinding can bind EITHER; ClusterRoleBinding binds ONLY ClusterRoles. Also know: roleRef is immutable — you can't edit a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding's role reference after creation (you'll get a validation error); delete and recreate the binding instead.

📌 CA11–CA15: Control Plane Performance, Registration & Security

CA11
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA11
API Server High Latency — etcd Slow or Too Many Requests

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pods takes 10+ seconds to return. API server request latency spikes. kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_request_duration shows p99 > 5s. The control plane is sluggish — new pods take long to schedule, deployments are slow to roll out.

$ kubectl get pods -n easypj --v=6
I0606 14:32:01.123456 round_trippers.go:553 GET https://api:6443/api/v1/namespaces/easypj/pods 200 OK
❌ Request took: 8.2s   ← Normal is <100ms!

$ etcdctl endpoint status -w table
+---------+------+---------+-------+--------+-----------+
| ENDPOINT| ID   | VERSION | DB SIZE| LEADER | RAFT INDEX|
❌ cp1:2379 | abc  | 3.5.0   | 4.8 GB | true   | 12,456,789|  ← 12M+ raft index!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. etcd disk latency high: etcd is I/O bound. Slow disk = slow API server. iotop or fio to test. Must use SSD, preferably NVMe.
  2. Too many LIST requests: Controllers doing unfiltered LIST on all pods/secrets. Use --v=6 to see request volume. Add resourceVersion="0" for caching.
  3. etcd DB too large: >2GB causes slow reads. Need compaction + defragmentation.
  4. Network latency between API server and etcd: They should be co-located (same node or same AZ). ping etcd-node should be <1ms.
  5. Too many concurrent requests: --max-requests-inflight exceeded. API server throttling.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. etcd running on HDD instead of SSD — 100x slower random I/O
  2. Large response bodies: LIST all pods in cluster with full object metadata
  3. Admission webhooks slow: Mutating/validating webhooks adding 5s+ delay per request
  4. Too many watch connections: Thousands of watches flood etcd with notifications
  5. Garbage collection backlog: Many deleted resources pending GC, eating etcd cycles
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. New cluster on low-end hardware: etcd needs SSD, not magnetic disk
  2. All components on one node: etcd competes with other processes for disk I/O
  3. No resource limits on etcd: etcd memory grows unbounded, triggering swap/OOM
  4. No API priority & fairness configured: Non-critical requests starve critical ones
  5. Metrics not collected: No Prometheus monitoring of API server latency
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_request_duration_seconds. etcdctl endpoint status -w table. kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep etcd_db_total_size_in_bytes.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Upgrade etcd disk to SSD (NVMe preferred) — this is the #1 fix
2. etcdctl compact <rev> && etcdctl defrag — reduce DB size
3. Set --max-requests-inflight=400 and --max-mutating-requests-inflight=200
4. Enable API Priority & Fairness (default in K8s 1.29+)
5. Co-locate etcd with API server — no network hop for reads

💡 Personal Advice: API server latency = etcd latency 90% of the time. Every kubectl GET becomes an etcd read. If etcd is slow (HDD, large DB, network hop), the entire cluster feels slow. On CKA: if the cluster is sluggish, check etcd first — DB size >2GB and disk type are the top culprits. Know: etcdctl endpoint status shows DB size and raft index.
CA12
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA12
Stacked etcd vs External etcd — Wrong Architecture Choice

🔍 Symptom: Control plane node crash takes down both API server AND etcd member simultaneously (stacked topology). Or external etcd cluster has network latency to API servers causing timeouts. The architecture choice is causing availability issues — stacked etcd on 2 nodes lacks quorum when one node fails.

$ kubectl get nodes
NAME    STATUS     ROLES           AGE   VERSION
❌ cp-1   NotReady   control-plane   30d   v1.29.0  ← CP + etcd both down!
cp-2   Ready      control-plane   30d   v1.29.0
cp-3   Ready      control-plane   30d   v1.29.0

$ etcdctl endpoint health
❌ cp-1:2379 is unhealthy  ← etcd on same node as failed CP
cp-2:2379 is healthy
cp-3:2379 is healthy  (quorum maintained — 2 of 3)
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Stacked etcd with only 2 CP nodes: 2 nodes with stacked etcd = 2 etcd members. If one fails, quorum is LOST (need 2 of 2, but only 1 is up).
  2. External etcd latency: etcd cluster in different AZ/region adds 50ms+ latency to every API request.
  3. Stacked etcd resource contention: API server and etcd compete for CPU/memory/disk on same node.
  4. External etcd certificate management: Separate PKI for external etcd — certs expire independently, breaking the connection.
  5. Single external etcd member: External etcd with only 1 member = no HA. Single point of failure.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Stacked: kubeadm upgrade restarts etcd and API server together — longer downtime
  2. External: etcd cluster managed by different team — version skew with K8s
  3. Stacked: etcd backups on CP node — lost if node storage fails
  4. External: firewall rules between API servers and etcd cluster blocking peer port 2380
  5. Stacked: 5 CP nodes with 5 etcd members — too many members, slow consensus
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Default kubeadm: Stacked etcd is the default — OK for most clusters
  2. When to use external etcd: >50 nodes, strict security requirements, dedicated etcd team
  3. When stacked is fine: <50 nodes, standard HA (3 CP nodes), same team manages everything
  4. External etcd complexity: Separate backup/restore, separate upgrade cycle, more certs to manage
  5. Stacked is simpler: kubeadm manages etcd as static pod alongside API server — less operational overhead
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep etcd — stacked shows etcd pods on CP nodes. kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml | grep etcd.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Stacked with 3 CP nodes is fine for CKA and most production clusters
2. If using stacked: ensure 3+ CP nodes for etcd quorum (N/2+1 = 2 minimum)
3. If using external etcd: run 3-5 dedicated etcd nodes, co-locate with API servers (same AZ)
4. For CKA: stacked etcd is the default and what you'll work with
5. Know the tradeoffs: stacked=simpler/less nodes, external=better isolation/more operational complexity

💡 Personal Advice: Stacked etcd (default kubeadm) is the right choice for 95% of clusters. External etcd adds complexity without proportional benefit for clusters under 50 nodes. On CKA: know the difference and when to choose each. Stacked = etcd runs as static pod on CP nodes. External = dedicated etcd cluster outside K8s. The exam uses stacked etcd.
CA13
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA13
kubelet Fails to Register Node — Hostname Mismatch

🔍 Symptom: Worker node's kubelet is running but kubectl get nodes doesn't show it. The kubelet log shows "Node 'worker-1' not found" or "node 'ip-10-0-1-5' has inconsistent hostname." The kubelet can't register itself with the API server because the hostname it advertises doesn't match what's expected.

$ journalctl -u kubelet -n 20
❌ E0606 10:00:01 kubelet.go:2345] "Failed to register node" err="nodes \"worker-1\" not found"
❌ E0606 10:00:01 kubelet.go:2420] "Unable to register node with API server" err="node \"worker-1\" is forbidden"

$ hostname
ip-10-0-1-5.ec2.internal    ← Kubelet advertises THIS

$ kubectl get nodes
NAME       STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION
cp-1       Ready    master   30d   v1.29.0
(worker-1 not listed!)
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Hostname mismatch: kubelet uses OS hostname (e.g., ip-10-0-1-5) but kubeadm join expected "worker-1". Use --hostname-override=worker-1.
  2. Cloud provider hostname: AWS/GCP nodes get long FQDN hostnames that differ from what kubeadm configured.
  3. kubelet not authorized: Node authorizer rejects kubelet because it's using wrong credentials or cert CN doesn't match.
  4. kubelet.conf missing or wrong: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf not generated or points to wrong API server.
  5. Node already exists with different name: Worker was registered before with a different hostname. Delete old node object.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. --register-node=false set: kubelet configured NOT to auto-register — manual registration needed
  2. kubelet bootstrap token wrong: Token for TLS bootstrapping expired or invalid
  3. NodeRestriction admission plugin blocks: kubelet trying to modify labels on different node
  4. Duplicate node name: Two workers with same hostname — one overwrites the other
  5. kubelet client cert issued to wrong node name: Cert CN = "system:node:worker-2" but hostname is worker-1
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. kubeadm join with wrong --node-name: Specifying a name that doesn't match the node's actual hostname
  2. New worker clones from VM template: All cloned workers have same hostname — registration conflict
  3. Cloud-init sets hostname differently than kubelet expects
  4. kubelet --hostname-override not set in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — uses default OS hostname
  5. DNS not resolving node names: kubelet can't resolve its own hostname for the node object
🔍 What to Look At: hostname on the worker. journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i "register\|hostname\|not found". cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | grep hostname.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Set explicit hostname: echo 'hostnameOverride: "worker-1"' >> /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
2. Or use CLI flag: --hostname-override=worker-1 in kubelet systemd
3. Delete stale node: kubectl delete node worker-1 then restart kubelet
4. Verify: kubectl get nodes should show the node
5. For new nodes: kubeadm join --node-name=worker-1 ...

💡 Personal Advice: Hostname mismatch is common in cloud environments where the OS hostname is an auto-generated FQDN. Always set --hostname-override or --node-name to a consistent, human-readable name. On CKA: if a node doesn't appear in kubectl get nodes, check the kubelet's hostname vs what the cluster expects.
CA14
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA14
Multiple API Servers — Stale Data from Watch Cache

🔍 Symptom: In an HA setup with multiple API servers behind a load balancer, kubectl get pods sometimes returns stale data. A pod was deleted but still shows up. A ConfigMap was updated but kubectl shows old values. The watch cache on one API server is stale because the request hit a different API server than the one that processed the write.

$ kubectl delete pod easypj-api-abc -n easypj
pod "easypj-api-abc" deleted

$ kubectl get pods -n easypj
❌ NAME              READY   STATUS    AGE
❌ easypj-api-abc    1/1     Running   5m    ← STILL showing! (Stale cache)

$ kubectl get pods -n easypj   (retry — hits different API server)
NAME              READY   STATUS        AGE
easypj-api-abc    0/1     Terminating   5m    ← Now correct
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Watch cache staleness: Each API server maintains an in-memory watch cache. After a write, caches on OTHER API servers may be stale for 1-5s.
  2. etcd watch not yet propagated: Write goes to etcd leader, but watches on other API servers haven't received the update event yet.
  3. LB session affinity: kubectl requests hit different API servers. Read-after-write consistency not guaranteed across API servers.
  4. Watch cache not invalidated: API server --watch-cache-sizes=0 disables watch cache but increases etcd load.
  5. ResourceVersion from stale cache: Client caches ResourceVersion and uses it for subsequent LIST requests, getting stale data.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. etcd read from follower: Etcd allows reads from followers — may return slightly stale data
  2. Large watch cache TTL: --watch-cache-sizes sets cache size, not TTL — large cache = more staleness
  3. Network latency between API server and etcd delaying watch event delivery
  4. API server restart: New API server starts with empty watch cache — must rebuild from etcd
  5. Rate limiting on watch connections: Too many watchers — events dropped/throttled
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Single API server: No staleness issue — but no HA either. Use 3 API servers minimum for HA.
  2. Kubernetes is eventually consistent: Read-after-write not guaranteed across API servers
  3. Watch cache enabled by default: --watch-cache (default true) improves performance at cost of slight staleness
  4. For strict consistency: Use resourceVersion="" to bypass cache and read directly from etcd
  5. Staleness is <5s in practice: For most use cases, this is acceptable — controllers handle eventual consistency
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/<ns>/pods?resourceVersion=0 (cache) vs resourceVersion="" (etcd direct).
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Accept eventual consistency: Staleness is <5s in normal conditions — controllers handle this
2. For critical reads: kubectl get pods --watch — watches are consistent within a single API server
3. Use resourceVersion="" to bypass watch cache: reads directly from etcd (expensive!)
4. Enable sticky sessions on LB: route same client to same API server for cache locality
5. Monitor: kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_watch_cache_stale

💡 Personal Advice: Watch cache staleness is normal and expected in HA setups. Kubernetes is designed for eventual consistency — controllers retry on conflict. Don't fight it. On CKA: you won't deal with this directly, but understand that multiple API servers means reads may be slightly stale. This is a tradeoff for HA.
CA15
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA15
CSR Pending Forever — Manual Approval Required

🔍 Symptom: A new worker node's kubelet sent a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to join the cluster, but the CSR stays in "Pending" state indefinitely. The node can't fully register because its client certificate hasn't been issued. kubectl get csr shows the CSR with CONDITION: Pending and no APPROVED status.

$ kubectl get csr
NAME        AGE   SIGNERNAME                      REQUESTOR        CONDITION
❌ csr-abc12  30m   kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving   system:node:worker-2   Pending   ← 30 minutes!

$ kubectl describe csr csr-abc12
Name:         csr-abc12
Conditions:
❌   Type:    Approved  (not set — needs manual approval)
Requestor:    system:node:worker-2
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Manual CSR approval needed: kubelet TLS bootstrap CSRs require manual approval: kubectl certificate approve <csr-name>.
  2. No auto-approver configured: kube-controller-manager has CSR approving controllers disabled or not configured.
  3. CSR signer not recognized: The CSR's signerName doesn't match any configured signer in kube-controller-manager.
  4. RBAC for CSR approval missing: The user/SA trying to auto-approve doesn't have permission to approve CSRs.
  5. CSR requestor identity invalid: The node is using a bootstrap token that doesn't match the expected organization (system:nodes).
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CSR auto-approver only approves client CSRs (kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet) — serving CSRs like this one (kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving) are never auto-approved by kube-controller-manager and always need manual approval or a separate signer
  2. kube-controller-manager --controllers flag excludes CSR approver controllers
  3. CSR was denied previously — resubmitted but same CSR name causes conflict
  4. CA cert rotated: CSR signed with old CA key — validation fails
  5. Cluster was upgraded: New CSR API version (v1) requires different RBAC rules for auto-approval
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. New cluster unaware of CSR workflow: kubelet TLS bootstrap generates CSRs that need approval
  2. kubeadm join auto-approves by default: kubeadm sets up CSR auto-approver — but custom clusters may not
  3. CSR auto-approval requires specific RBAC: ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding for system:bootstrappers group
  4. Node authorizer doesn't handle CSR approval: Separate from node auth — needs dedicated RBAC
  5. First node addition after cluster setup: CSR workflow not tested during initial deployment
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get csr — check for Pending CSRs. kubectl describe csr <name> — see Conditions. kubectl certificate approve <name> or kubectl certificate deny <name>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Approve manually: kubectl certificate approve csr-abc12
2. Verify: kubectl get csr — should show APPROVED,ISSUED
3. For auto-approval: configure CSR auto-approver in kube-controller-manager
4. Check RBAC: kubectl describe clusterrole system:certificates.k8s.io:certificatesigningrequests:nodeclient
5. For bulk approval: kubectl get csr | grep Pending | awk '{print $1}' | xargs kubectl certificate approve

💡 Personal Advice: Pending CSRs are the "silent blocker" for new nodes. The kubelet on the new node appears running but the node never fully joins. On CKA: you may need to approve a CSR for a new node. Know: kubectl certificate approve <csr> and kubectl certificate deny <csr>. The CSR is the node's identity — without approval, the node can't authenticate to the API server.

📌 CA16–CA20: Helm, CRDs, RBAC & Operators

CA16
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA16
Helm Release Failed — Install/Upgrade Error

🔍 Symptom: helm install or helm upgrade fails with "rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists" or template error.

$ helm install my-app ./chart
❌ Error: rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists
❌ Error: cannot re-use a name that is still in use
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Resource already exists from previous failed install: helm list -A — release may be in failed state.
  2. Template rendering error: Invalid Go template syntax in chart templates. helm template ./chart --debug.
  3. values.yaml has wrong structure: Missing required values or wrong YAML indentation.
  4. Previous release not fully deleted: Secrets (Helm 3) or ConfigMaps (Helm 2) still present.
  5. Namespace doesn't exist: helm install --create-namespace or pre-create namespace.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Helm version incompatibility: Chart requires Helm 3.7+ but cluster has 3.2.
  2. CRDs not installed before chart: Chart requires CRDs that must be applied first.
  3. Helm hook failed: pre-install/pre-upgrade hook pod crashed, blocking release.
  4. RBAC: ServiceAccount used by Helm doesn't have permission to create resources.
  5. Helm repository index stale: helm repo update not run.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First Helm install: helm repo add and helm repo update must be done first.
  2. Helm 3 stores releases as Secrets: Need permission to create/get Secrets in the namespace.
  3. --atomic flag not used: Failed install leaves partial resources. Use --atomic for auto-rollback.
  4. No default StorageClass: PVC in chart can't provision — blocks install.
  5. Helm diff not run: helm diff upgrade would catch issues before applying.
🔍 What to Look At: helm list -A and helm history <release>. helm template ./chart --debug. kubectl get events -n <ns>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. helm uninstall <release> -n <ns> to clean failed release
2. helm template ./chart --debug to validate templates
3. helm install --create-namespace --atomic <name> ./chart
4. Check RBAC: ServiceAccount needs appropriate permissions
5. helm rollback <release> <rev> if upgrade failed

💡 Personal Advice: Helm failures are usually: (1) existing resource conflict — uninstall first, (2) template error — use helm template --debug, or (3) RBAC — your kubeconfig user needs cluster-admin or specific permissions. On CKA: Helm is tested — know install, upgrade, rollback, and troubleshooting with helm list/history/status.
CA17
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA17
CRD Not Working — Custom Resource Not Recognized

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f my-cr.yaml fails with "no matches for kind." CRD is not installed or the API group/version is wrong.

$ kubectl apply -f my-cr.yaml
❌ error: unable to recognize "my-cr.yaml": no matches for kind "MySQL" in version "db.example.com/v1"

$ kubectl get crd
No resources found  ← CRD not installed!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. CRD not installed: kubectl get crd — must see the CRD definition. Apply CRD YAML first.
  2. API group/version mismatch: CR uses db.example.com/v1 but CRD defines v1alpha1.
  3. Kind name mismatch: CR uses kind: MySQLCluster but CRD defines kind: MySQL.
  4. CRD installed but not yet ready: New CRD takes a few seconds to register. Wait and retry.
  5. Schema validation fails: CR doesn't match CRD's openAPIV3Schema — required fields missing.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CRD in wrong scope: Namespaced CRD but CR doesn't specify namespace.
  2. CR references CRD from different API service: Aggregated API not registered.
  3. CRD conversion webhook failing: v1alpha1→v1 conversion not working — CR stuck.
  4. Multiple CRDs with overlapping group/version/kind — API server picks wrong one.
  5. CRD finalizer blocking CR creation: cleanup finalizer from previous CR stuck.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First CRD deployment: Apply CRD BEFORE any CRs. Order matters.
  2. CRD without controller: CR created but no operator watching — no pods/deployments created.
  3. CRD validation schema too strict: Prevents valid configurations.
  4. CRD versioning: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1beta1 was removed (no longer served) in K8s 1.22 — must use apiextensions.k8s.io/v1.
  5. No CRD documentation: kubectl explain <resource> doesn't work without CRD.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get crd and kubectl describe crd <name>. kubectl api-resources | grep <kind>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get crd — verify CRD exists
2. kubectl describe crd <name> | grep -A5 Versions — check version names
3. Fix CR YAML: match kind, apiVersion exactly to CRD
4. kubectl apply -f crd.yaml then wait 5s, then apply CR
5. kubectl explain <resource> --recursive to see schema

💡 Personal Advice: CRDs extend Kubernetes — you're literally creating new API types. The CR must match the CRD exactly. On CKA: you may need to create a CRD and then a CR. Know: CRD defines the schema, CR is the instance, and a Controller (Operator) implements the logic. CRD alone does nothing — you need a controller for actual functionality.
CA18
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA18
ClusterRoleBinding to Wrong Subject — User Still Forbidden

🔍 Symptom: You've created a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding for user "alice," but kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice still returns "no." The ClusterRoleBinding's subjects section points to the wrong user, group, or ServiceAccount. Alice can't access cluster-level resources despite having a binding.

$ kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice
❌ no

$ kubectl get clusterrolebinding pod-reader-binding -o yaml | grep -A5 subjects
subjects:
❌ - kind: User
❌   name: alice@example.com   ← Wrong! User is just "alice"
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Subject name mismatch: CN in certificate is "alice" but binding says "alice@example.com". Kubernetes matches EXACTLY.
  2. Wrong subject kind: Used kind: User but the identity is a ServiceAccount (kind: ServiceAccount). Or vice versa.
  3. Wrong namespace for ServiceAccount: RoleBinding references SA "default" but SA is "default" in wrong namespace.
  4. Group binding vs User binding: Bound to group "developers" but user isn't in that group. Check cert's Organization field.
  5. ClusterRoleBinding binds ClusterRole as namespaced: ClusterRoleBinding gives cluster-wide access. Use RoleBinding for namespace-scoped access.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Multiple bindings conflict: One binding grants access, another denies (no deny in RBAC — additive only)
  2. Aggregated ClusterRole labels wrong: Custom ClusterRole extending system:view not matching aggregation rule
  3. Subject kind: Group uses wrong prefix — OIDC groups have "oidc:" prefix
  4. API version difference: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1beta1 vs v1 — v1beta1 removed in K8s 1.22+
  5. Case sensitivity: "Alice" vs "alice" — subject names are case-sensitive
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Default ServiceAccount "default" has no permissions: Must explicitly bind roles to it
  2. New users confused by subject types: User, Group, ServiceAccount — three different identity types
  3. kubeconfig user name ≠ RBAC user name: The user in kubeconfig (context) may differ from CN in client cert
  4. RBAC is additive only: You can GRANT, never DENY. If one binding grants, access is allowed
  5. system:masters group: Members of this group bypass all RBAC — use sparingly
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe clusterrolebinding <name> — check Subjects section. kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<user>. Check cert CN: openssl x509 -in <cert> -noout -subject.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Fix subject name: kubectl patch clusterrolebinding pod-reader --type=merge -p '{"subjects":[{"kind":"User","name":"alice","apiGroup":"rbac.authorization.k8s.io"}]}'
2. For ServiceAccount: subjects.kind=ServiceAccount, name=<ns>:<sa>
3. For Groups: subjects.kind=Group, name=<group-name>
4. Verify: kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice
5. Delete and recreate: kubectl delete clusterrolebinding <name> && kubectl create clusterrolebinding <name> --clusterrole=<role> --user=<user>

💡 Personal Advice: RBAC subject mismatch is the #1 "I set up permissions but they don't work" issue. The subject name must match EXACTLY what's in the certificate's CN field (for users) or Organization field (for groups). On CKA: use kubectl auth can-i --as=<user> to test. Create bindings imperatively: kubectl create rolebinding <name> --role=<role> --user=<user> -n <ns> — it's harder to get wrong than YAML.
CA19
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA19
kubeconfig Context Wrong — kubectl Talking to Wrong Cluster

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pods shows pods from the wrong cluster or returns "not found" for resources you know exist. kubectl config current-context shows a different cluster than expected. You've been managing the wrong cluster for the last hour without realizing it.

$ kubectl config current-context
❌ kind-cl1    ← You wanted cka-lab!

$ kubectl get pods -n easypj
No resources found in easypj namespace.   ← Wrong cluster!

$ kubectl config get-contexts
CURRENT   NAME          CLUSTER       AUTHINFO      NAMESPACE
          cka-lab       cka-lab       cka-lab-admin
❌ *       kind-cl1      kind-cl1      kind-cl1-admin   ← Current (wrong!)
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Wrong current-context: kubectl config use-context was run earlier pointing to wrong cluster.
  2. KUBECONFIG env var pointing to different kubeconfig file: echo $KUBECONFIG — may override default ~/.kube/config.
  3. Merged kubeconfig files: Multiple kubeconfig files merged — context names collide. Wrong one takes precedence.
  4. Context has wrong namespace set: kubectl is on right cluster but wrong namespace. kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>.
  5. KUBECONFIG points to non-existent file: Set to a file that doesn't exist — kubectl falls back to default behavior unpredictably.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. kubectl plugin that changes context: A kubectl plugin or alias auto-switches context
  2. Shell auto-context script: .bashrc/.zshrc has logic to auto-switch kubeconfig based on directory
  3. Multiple terminal sessions with different KUBECONFIG values
  4. kubeconfig file corruption: YAML parse error causes partial loading — some contexts available, others not
  5. kubectl cache stale: ~/.kube/cache has old discovery data from previous cluster
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. New user with multiple clusters: Easy to lose track of which cluster kubectl is talking to
  2. No prompt indicator: Shell prompt doesn't show current context — always check first
  3. kubectl config view shows merged config: Can be confusing with multiple clusters/users/contexts
  4. Default context after kubeadm init: kubernetes-admin@kubernetes — generic name, easy to confuse
  5. No kubectx/kubens installed: These tools make context/namespace switching visual and explicit
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl config current-context — always check first. kubectl config view — full merged config. kubectl cluster-info — which cluster?
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl config use-context cka-lab — switch to correct context
2. kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj — set default namespace
3. Add shell prompt indicator: export PS1='[\u@\h \W $(kubectl config current-context 2>/dev/null)]\$ '
4. Use kubectx/kubens for visual context switching
5. Validate: kubectl cluster-info and kubectl get nodes — confirm right cluster

💡 Personal Advice: The #1 operational mistake in Kubernetes is running commands against the wrong cluster. ALWAYS check kubectl config current-context before destructive commands. Install kubectx/kubens. On CKA: you'll be given a specific kubeconfig file for each question — set KUBECONFIG env var or use --kubeconfig flag explicitly. Don't mix contexts.
CA20
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA20
Operator Not Reconciling — Controller Loop Broken

🔍 Symptom: You've applied a Custom Resource (CR) for a database operator, but nothing happens. No pods created, no PVCs provisioned. The operator's controller isn't processing the CR — it's either not running, has crashed, or isn't watching the right resources. The CR just sits there with no status updates.

$ kubectl get mysqls.db.example.com -n easypj
NAME        AGE
easypj-db   30m    ← Created 30 min ago, nothing happened!

$ kubectl describe mysql easypj-db -n easypj
Status:  (empty — controller never reconciled)

$ kubectl get pods -n database-operator
❌ NAME                              READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
❌ mysql-operator-7d8f9abcde-xyz    0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   15      ← Operator CRASHED!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Operator pod crashed/not running: Check operator namespace. kubectl get pods -l app=mysql-operator. CrashLoopBackOff = check logs.
  2. RBAC for operator insufficient: Operator's ServiceAccount doesn't have permissions to create pods/PVCs/services.
  3. Operator not watching the correct API group: CRD group/version changed but operator still watches old version.
  4. Leader election stuck: Multiple operator replicas — leader election not resolving. Check kubectl get lease -n <ns>.
  5. Finalizer blocking reconciliation: CR has a finalizer from a previous operator that no longer exists.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Webhook dependency: Operator's webhook service not reachable — admission/mutation fails
  2. Wrong namespace: Operator watching "default" namespace but CR is in "easypj"
  3. Metrics/health endpoint failure: Operator not reporting ready — liveness probe kills it
  4. API deprecation: Operator compiled against old API version that was removed
  5. Image pull error: Operator image not available — ImagePullBackOff
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Operator installed via Helm but CRDs not applied: Helm install --set installCRDs=true
  2. CRD installed, operator installed, but in different namespaces — operator can't see CRs
  3. Operator requires specific CR fields: Missing required spec fields — operator silently ignores
  4. Operator version incompatible with K8s version: Controller-runtime library version mismatch
  5. No operator status conditions: CR doesn't have status subresource — no feedback on reconciliation
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pods -l app=<operator> -A. kubectl logs deploy/<operator> -n <ns>. kubectl describe <cr> <name> — check Status and Events.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check operator pod: kubectl get pods -A | grep operator — must be Running
2. Check operator logs: kubectl logs deploy/<operator> -n <ns> --tail=50
3. Verify RBAC: operator SA needs * on its managed resources
4. Check CR spec matches CRD schema: kubectl explain <resource> --recursive
5. Restart operator: kubectl rollout restart deploy/<operator> -n <ns>

💡 Personal Advice: "Operator not reconciling" = operator pod is dead, wrong permissions, or watching wrong namespace. Check the operator pod FIRST — if it's CrashLoopBackOff, the CR will never be reconciled. On CKA: you may need to debug why an operator isn't working. The answer is usually RBAC (operator SA missing permissions) or the operator pod is crashed.

📌 CA21–CA25: Extensibility — Webhooks, Kustomize & API Lifecycle

CA21
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA21
Admission Webhook Timeout — Pod Creation Stuck

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f pod.yaml hangs for 30+ seconds, then fails with "Internal error: failed calling webhook." A validating or mutating admission webhook is timing out. New pods, Deployments, or ConfigMaps can't be created because the webhook is unreachable or slow.

$ kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
(hangs for 30 seconds)
❌ Error from server (InternalError): error when creating "pod.yaml":
❌ Internal error occurred: failed calling webhook "validate.example.com":
❌ Post "https://webhook-svc.ns.svc:443/validate?timeout=30s":
❌ context deadline exceeded
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Webhook service unreachable: The Service backing the webhook doesn't have healthy endpoints. kubectl get endpoints -n <ns> <webhook-svc>.
  2. Webhook pod not running: The admission webhook's pod crashed. kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l app=<webhook>.
  3. NetworkPolicy blocking API server → webhook traffic: API server can't reach the webhook's Service on port 443.
  4. Certificate expired or invalid: Webhook uses TLS — cert expired or CA bundle not trusted by API server.
  5. Webhook timeout too short: Webhook processing takes 5s but timeoutSeconds is 2s. Increase in ValidatingWebhookConfiguration.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Webhook has failurePolicy: Fail — if webhook is down, ALL matching requests fail (vs Ignore which allows)
  2. Webhook namespace selector wrong: Webhook configured to intercept all namespaces including kube-system
  3. Webhook object selector matches too many objects — overwhelming the webhook
  4. Webhook uses external URL instead of Service reference — external endpoint unreachable
  5. Mutating webhook chain: Multiple mutating webhooks in sequence — cumulative timeout exceeds limit
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Webhook installed via Helm but Service/pod not yet ready: Apply order matters
  2. New cluster unaware of webhook impact: A broken webhook can block ALL pod creations
  3. failurePolicy: Fail is default: If not explicitly set to Ignore, broken webhook = broken cluster
  4. Self-hosted webhook creates chicken-and-egg: Webhook pod can't start because webhook blocks pod creation
  5. Webhook CA bundle must be base64: New users paste raw PEM instead of base64-encoded cert
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations. kubectl describe validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check webhook pod: kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l app=<webhook> — must be Running
2. Check endpoints: kubectl get endpoints -n <ns> <svc>
3. Temporarily set failurePolicy: Ignore: kubectl patch validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> --patch '{"webhooks":[{"name":"<hook>","failurePolicy":"Ignore"}]}'
4. Delete webhook if unrecoverable: kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>
5. Fix the webhook deployment, then re-enable: set failurePolicy back to Fail

💡 Personal Advice: A broken admission webhook can take down your ENTIRE cluster — no pods can be created, deleted, or updated. Always set failurePolicy: Ignore for non-critical webhooks. On CKA: if pod creation hangs with "webhook" error, the fix is either: (1) fix the webhook pod, (2) delete the webhook configuration, or (3) patch failurePolicy to Ignore.
CA22
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA22
Kustomize Build Error — Patch Target Not Found

🔍 Symptom: kustomize build ./overlays/prod fails with "failed to find target for patch" or "no matches for OriginalId." A patch in the kustomization.yaml references a resource that doesn't exist or has a different name/group/version. The CI/CD pipeline fails to render the production manifests.

$ kustomize build ./overlays/prod
❌ Error: accumulating resources: failed to find target for patch:
❌   could not find target for patch: Deployment.v1.apps/easypj-api
❌   in ../base/deployment.yaml

$ grep -r "easypj-api" ./base/
./base/deployment.yaml:  name: easypj-web   ← Deployment is named easypj-web, not easypj-api!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Patch target name mismatch: Patch specifies name: easypj-api but base resource is named easypj-web. Names must match exactly.
  2. Wrong API version in patch target: Patch targets apps/v1 but base has apps/v1beta1. Version mismatch.
  3. Resource not in base: Patch references a resource that was deleted or renamed in the base directory.
  4. Base directory path wrong: kustomization.yaml resources: references ../base but base is at ../../base.
  5. YAML indentation error in patch: Patch file has invalid YAML — kustomize can't parse it to find the target.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Patch type mismatch: strategic merge patch isn't supported on CRDs — use JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch instead
  2. Name prefix/suffix in kustomization.yaml changes resource name — patch target no longer matches
  3. Multiple resources with same name in different groups/versions — kustomize picks wrong one
  4. Patch references resource added by a generator (ConfigMapGenerator) — name includes hash suffix
  5. Kustomize version differences: v4 vs v5 — patch syntax changed slightly
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First time using Kustomize: Overlay/patch system is different from Helm templates — declarative, not templated
  2. Kustomize is built into kubectl: kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod — but standalone kustomize may differ
  3. PatchesStrategicMerge deprecated in favor of patches: New patches field with target selector
  4. Base must be a valid kustomization: Has its own kustomization.yaml with resources listed
  5. Generated resource names: ConfigMapGenerator adds hash — patch target needs exact name or use namePrefix
🔍 What to Look At: kustomize build ./overlays/prod --stack-trace. grep "name:" ./base/*.yaml — verify resource names. kustomize cfg grep "kind:Deployment" ./base/.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Verify base resource name: grep -A2 "kind:" ./base/deployment.yaml
2. Fix patch target: match apiVersion, kind, name, namespace exactly to base resource
3. Use new patches format: patches: - target: {kind: Deployment, name: easypj-web} path: patch.yaml
4. Test: kustomize build ./overlays/prod | kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f -
5. Simplify: kubectl kustomize ./overlays/prod (built-in, always matches kubectl version)

💡 Personal Advice: Kustomize patch target errors are almost always a name mismatch between the overlay patch and the base resource. On CKA: Kustomize is tested — you may need to fix a broken kustomization.yaml. Know: kubectl apply -k <dir> and the difference between patchesStrategicMerge (old) and patches (new). The base resource name is the "source of truth" — your patch must reference it exactly.
CA23
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA23
Deprecated API Removed After Upgrade — Manifests Fail to Apply

🔍 Symptom: After upgrading the cluster, kubectl apply of existing manifests fails with "no matches for kind CronJob in version batch/v1beta1." Running workloads are fine, but every CI/CD or GitOps re-apply now errors. The YAML pins an API version the server no longer serves.

$ kubectl apply -f cronjob-backup.yaml
❌ error: resource mapping not found for name: "easypj-db-backup"
❌ no matches for kind "CronJob" in version "batch/v1beta1"
❌ ensure CRDs are installed first

$ kubectl api-versions | grep batch
batch/v1    ← batch/v1beta1 was REMOVED in v1.25

$ kubectl explain cronjob | head -2
KIND:     CronJob
VERSION:  batch/v1    ← the only served version now
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Manifest pins a removed beta apiVersion: batch/v1beta1 (CronJob, removed 1.25), policy/v1beta1 (PDB, removed 1.25), autoscaling/v2beta2 (HPA, removed 1.26).
  2. Cluster upgraded past the removal version: The API server no longer serves that group/version at all.
  3. Helm chart renders old apiVersions: Chart written for an older cluster — upgrade the chart version.
  4. GitOps repo never migrated: Argo/Flux keeps re-applying stale YAML and now errors on every sync.
  5. Manifests generated by old tooling: Regenerate with a current kubectl (--dry-run=client -o yaml).
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Ingress using extensions/v1beta1 or networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 — removed in 1.22, use networking.k8s.io/v1
  2. RBAC rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1beta1 removed in 1.22 — use v1
  3. CRD apiextensions.k8s.io/v1beta1 removed in 1.22 — v1 requires a structural schema
  4. Webhook admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1beta1 removed in 1.22 — configs fail to re-apply
  5. Client/server version skew makes the error message confusing — check kubectl version vs server version
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Running objects DON'T break: the API server converts stored objects — only your YAML files fail to re-apply
  2. Deprecation warnings appear on kubectl apply BEFORE removal — heed "Warning: ... is deprecated"
  3. kubectl explain <kind> shows the currently served version — fastest way to find the right apiVersion
  4. kubectl convert plugin migrates old manifests: kubectl convert -f old.yaml --output-version batch/v1
  5. Tools like pluto or kubent scan repos for deprecated APIs BEFORE you upgrade
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl api-versions. kubectl api-resources | grep -i <kind>. kubectl explain <kind> — shows the served VERSION. kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f .
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Find the served version: kubectl explain cronjob → VERSION: batch/v1
2. Update apiVersion in the manifest: batch/v1beta1 → batch/v1
3. Fix schema drift that came with the promotion (PDB v1, HPA v2 metrics syntax)
4. Validate the whole directory: kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f manifests/
5. Migrate the Helm chart / GitOps repo so CI stops re-introducing the old version

💡 Personal Advice: "no matches for kind X in version Y" right after an upgrade = the beta API was removed. Your RUNNING pods are fine — only the YAML is stale. Fix = bump apiVersion to what kubectl explain shows, then re-test with --dry-run=server. On CKA: cluster-upgrade tasks love handing you a manifest with a dead apiVersion — know the 1.22/1.25/1.26 removals (Ingress, CronJob/PDB, HPA v2beta2).
CA24
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA24
Aggregated API Unavailable — kubectl top Fails, APIService False

🔍 Symptom: kubectl top nodes fails with "Metrics API not available." kubectl get apiservices shows v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io as False (FailedDiscoveryCheck). HPA targets show <unknown>. The aggregation layer can't reach the metrics-server backing the API.

$ kubectl top nodes
❌ error: Metrics API not available

$ kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics
❌ v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io   kube-system/metrics-server   False (FailedDiscoveryCheck)

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=metrics-server
metrics-server-6d94bc8694-x7k2p   0/1   Running   ← NOT READY
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. metrics-server pod not Ready: Readiness probe failing — kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/metrics-server.
  2. Kubelet TLS verification failure: metrics-server can't verify kubelet certs — on kubeadm/kind labs it needs --kubelet-insecure-tls or proper SAN certs.
  3. APIService has no endpoints: The metrics-server Service selector doesn't match the pod labels — kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system metrics-server.
  4. Network path blocked API server → metrics-server: NetworkPolicy or firewall on port 4443/10250.
  5. Wrong --kubelet-preferred-address-types: metrics-server can't resolve node hostnames — use InternalIP.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. A broken aggregated API degrades discovery — kubectl api-resources prints errors for ALL groups
  2. HPA shows <unknown> because it reads metrics.k8s.io — fix metrics-server and HPA recovers
  3. Custom metrics adapter (prometheus-adapter) fails the same way for external.metrics.k8s.io
  4. Stale caBundle in the APIService spec after certificate rotation — re-apply the manifest
  5. kube-apiserver aggregation flags missing (--proxy-client-cert-file/key-file) on self-built clusters
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. metrics-server is NOT installed by default — kubeadm and kind clusters need it applied manually
  2. kind/minikube need --kubelet-insecure-tls because kubelets use self-signed certs
  3. APIService is the registration object: kubectl get apiservices — any False row = aggregation broken
  4. kubectl top AND HPA both depend on metrics.k8s.io — one fix solves both
  5. Wait 30-60s after metrics-server starts — the first scrape cycle must complete before top works
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get apiservices | grep -v True. kubectl describe apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io — the Message names the exact failure. kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/metrics-server.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get apiservices — find the False one, read its Message
2. kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/metrics-server — TLS error? address-type error?
3. Lab-cluster fix: add args --kubelet-insecure-tls --kubelet-preferred-address-types=InternalIP to the Deployment
4. Verify endpoints exist: kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system metrics-server
5. Test: kubectl top nodes, then confirm HPA targets show real numbers

💡 Personal Advice: APIService False = the aggregation layer can't reach the backing Service. Read kubectl describe apiservice FIRST — its Message tells you exactly what failed. On CKA: if kubectl top fails, check the metrics-server pod and the APIService status; on lab clusters the fix is almost always the two kubelet flags.
CA25
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA25
CRD or Namespace Stuck Terminating — Finalizers Block Deletion

🔍 Symptom: kubectl delete crd or kubectl delete ns hangs forever — the object sits in Terminating. A CRD can't go until every CR is gone, and a CR with a finalizer owned by a dead operator will NEVER be cleaned up on its own.

$ kubectl delete crd mysqls.db.example.com
(hangs...)

$ kubectl get crd mysqls.db.example.com
❌ mysqls.db.example.com   Terminating   ← stuck for 25 min

$ kubectl get mysql easypj-db -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'
❌ ["mysql.operator.example.com/cleanup"]   ← the operator that clears this is GONE
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. CR finalizer owned by a deleted operator: Nothing will ever remove it — you must patch metadata.finalizers to [].
  2. CRD deletion waits for all CRs: kubectl get <kind> -A — every instance must be deleted first.
  3. Namespace blocked by leftover resources with finalizers: kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | xargs -n1 kubectl get -n <ns> finds them (kubectl get all misses CRs).
  4. Aggregated API down blocks namespace finalization: A False APIService breaks discovery — the namespace controller can't verify emptiness. Fix the APIService (see CA24).
  5. Validating webhook intercepting DELETE: failurePolicy Fail + dead webhook = deletions blocked (see CA21).
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Owner-reference cascade stuck — a child with a finalizer blocks foreground deletion of the parent
  2. PV held by kubernetes.io/pv-protection while still Bound to a PVC
  3. PVC held by pvc-protection while a pod still mounts it — delete the pod first
  4. Operator is alive but its cleanup logic errors — check the operator logs before force-clearing
  5. Controller lacks RBAC to update/remove its own finalizer after a permissions change
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Finalizers are just strings in metadata.finalizers — deletion completes only when the list is empty
  2. Force-clear a CR: kubectl patch <kind> <name> --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}' — LAST RESORT, skips the operator's cleanup
  3. Namespace force-finalize: kubectl replace --raw /api/v1/namespaces/<ns>/finalize -f ns.json
  4. kubectl delete --force --grace-period=0 does NOT touch finalizers — it won't fix this
  5. kubectl describe ns <ns> lists Conditions naming exactly which resources/APIs block deletion
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get <obj> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'. kubectl describe ns <ns> — Conditions name the blockers. kubectl get apiservices | grep False.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Identify blockers: kubectl describe ns <ns> → Conditions; for a CRD, list its remaining CRs
2. If the owning controller is dead: patch finalizers empty on each stuck CR
3. Delete the remaining CRs — the CRD then completes automatically
4. For namespaces: fix any False APIService first (often the REAL cause), then /finalize if still stuck
5. Verify the object is gone; recreate cleanly if needed

💡 Personal Advice: Terminating-forever = a finalizer waiting for a controller that will never come. Find the finalizer, decide who owns it, then either restore that controller or patch the finalizer away — accepting you skip its cleanup. On CKA: a namespace or CRD stuck Terminating is a classic; kubectl describe ns names the exact blockers, and a False APIService is the sneaky root cause to remember.

🌐 Category 5: Services & Networking (20 Issues)SN1-SN20

🔴 Service Failures, DNS, Network Policies, Ingress

Networking is 20% of the CKA. Service-to-pod communication, CoreDNS, NetworkPolicies, and Ingress controllers are the most common failure points in production clusters.

📌 SN1–SN5: Service Communication Failures

SN1
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN1
Service Not Accessible — ClusterIP Returns Connection Refused

🔍 Symptom: Pod can't reach a Service by its DNS name. curl <svc>:<port> returns "connection refused" or times out. Service exists but isn't routing traffic.

$ kubectl exec web-pod -- curl api-svc:8080
❌ curl: (7) Failed to connect: Connection refused

$ kubectl get endpoints api-svc
❌ api-svc       ← No endpoints!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Service has no Endpoints: kubectl get endpoints <svc> — empty means no pods match selector.
  2. Pod selector mismatch: Service selector != pod labels. One character off = no match.
  3. Pod not Ready: Pod is Running but Readiness probe failing — not added to Endpoints.
  4. Wrong namespace: Service in "default", pod calling from "dev" — different namespaces.
  5. Service port name doesn't match pod containerPort name: When using named ports.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. kube-proxy not running on node: iptables/IPVS rules not programmed — no DNAT happens.
  2. NetworkPolicy blocks ingress to backend pods from the source pod.
  3. Service type LoadBalancer with externalTrafficPolicy: Local — only routes to local pods.
  4. iptables rules corrupted: kube-proxy rules not updated after Service/pod changes.
  5. Service ClusterIP range conflict: Overlaps with pod CIDR — routing loops.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Service created before pods: No matching pods exist yet.
  2. kube-proxy mode mismatch: iptables vs IPVS — different behavior on different nodes.
  3. Service without selector: Manual Endpoints not created — Service has no targets.
  4. CoreDNS not resolving Service name: Service exists but DNS returns no IP.
  5. Headless Service (clusterIP: None) — DNS returns pod IPs directly, no ClusterIP.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get endpoints <svc>. kubectl get pods -l <selector> --show-labels. kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup <svc>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get endpoints <svc> — must show pod IPs
2. Compare: Service selector vs pod labels (--show-labels)
3. Check pod readiness: kubectl get pods — must show READY 1/1
4. Fix label mismatch: kubectl label pod <name> app=api --overwrite
5. Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl <svc-ip>:<port>

💡 Personal Advice: Empty Endpoints = THE #1 Service issue. The Service selector and pod labels must match EXACTLY. Case matters. On CKA: you'll debug a Service that doesn't work. Run kubectl get endpoints first — empty = label mismatch or pod not Ready. Fix labels and endpoints populate in seconds.
SN2
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN2
NodePort Service Not Accessible Externally

🔍 Symptom: Service type NodePort created but curl <node-ip>:<nodeport> times out from outside the cluster. Port not reachable from external network.

$ kubectl get svc web-svc
NAME      TYPE       CLUSTER-IP    PORT(S)
web-svc   NodePort   10.96.0.50    80:30080/TCP

$ curl http://worker-ip:30080
❌ curl: (7) Failed to connect: Connection refused
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Firewall blocking NodePort range (30000-32767): Cloud security group or host firewall.
  2. kube-proxy not running: iptables rule for NodePort not created. iptables -t nat -L KUBE-NODEPORTS.
  3. Node IP not reachable: Using internal IP instead of external/public IP.
  4. externalTrafficPolicy: Local — traffic dropped if no local pod on that node.
  5. Container not listening on 0.0.0.0: App bound to localhost only, can't receive external traffic.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CNI plugin doesn't support NodePort: Some overlay networks filter NodePort traffic.
  2. NodePort conflict with another service: Two Services using same NodePort.
  3. iptables rules not updated: kube-proxy hasn't synced after Service creation.
  4. Kubelet port range exhausted: All NodePorts in 30000-32767 already allocated.
  5. Cloud provider NAT translating NodePort traffic incorrectly.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First NodePort Service: Need to open firewall for 30000-32767 on ALL worker nodes.
  2. Node has no external IP: Private cluster — nodes only have internal IPs.
  3. kube-proxy mode: IPVS handles NodePort differently than iptables.
  4. Service created without proper selector: No backend pods = NodePort still opens but returns 503.
  5. Cloud LoadBalancer also created: External traffic going to LB, not directly to NodePort.
🔍 What to Look At: netstat -tlnp | grep <nodeport> on the node. iptables -t nat -L KUBE-NODEPORTS. curl localhost:<nodeport> on the node.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Test locally on node: curl localhost:30080 — confirms Service works
2. Check firewall: iptables -L INPUT | grep 30080 — must allow
3. Cloud: open security group for port 30080 from 0.0.0.0/0
4. Use correct IP: Node's EXTERNAL/PUBLIC IP, not internal
5. kubectl get svc -o wide — verify NodePort assigned

💡 Personal Advice: NodePort works INSIDE the cluster but fails externally 90% of the time due to firewall/security groups. On CKA: you'll create a NodePort Service and need to access it. Test locally first (curl localhost:nodeport), then from external. If local works but external doesn't — it's ALWAYS the firewall.
SN3
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN3
LoadBalancer Service Stuck Pending — No External IP

🔍 Symptom: Service type LoadBalancer shows EXTERNAL-IP <pending> indefinitely. Cloud controller can't provision a load balancer. On bare metal without MetalLB.

$ kubectl get svc web-svc
NAME      TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
web-svc   LoadBalancer   10.96.0.50    <pending>     80:30080/TCP

$ kubectl describe svc web-svc
⚠️  Warning  CreatingLoadBalancerFailed  Error creating load balancer
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Bare metal/on-prem: No cloud-controller-manager — LoadBalancer requires MetalLB or similar.
  2. Cloud credentials missing: AWS/GCP/Azure credentials not configured for cloud-controller-manager.
  3. Insufficient cloud permissions: IAM role for CP nodes lacks ELB/NLB creation permissions.
  4. Cloud quota exceeded: Maximum number of LBs per region/account reached.
  5. Subnet configuration wrong: Cloud LB requires public subnets for internet-facing, private for internal.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Cloud controller pod not running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep cloud-controller.
  2. Service annotations misconfigured: Wrong annotation format for cloud-specific LB settings.
  3. Multiple LBs with same name: Naming conflict in cloud provider.
  4. Network tags on nodes missing: Cloud LB targets nodes by tag — tag not applied.
  5. Stale LoadBalancer: Previous LB not cleaned up — name conflict on new creation.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First LoadBalancer: No cloud provider integration — need MetalLB for on-prem.
  2. kubeadm without --cloud-provider flag: Cloud provider not configured.
  3. Private cluster: Nodes in private subnets — can't create internet-facing LB.
  4. Wrong service.beta.kubernetes.io annotations for cloud provider version.
  5. No external IP pool: MetalLB not configured with IP address range.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe svc <name> | grep -A10 Events. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep cloud-controller.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. For cloud: verify cloud-controller-manager is running
2. For bare metal: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/main/config/manifests/metallb-native.yaml
3. Configure MetalLB IP pool or verify cloud IAM permissions
4. Check Events in kubectl describe svc for exact error
5. Alternative: use NodePort + external LB (nginx/haproxy)

💡 Personal Advice: LoadBalancer <pending> on bare metal = you need MetalLB. On cloud = cloud-controller-manager issue or IAM permissions. On CKA: the exam environment is self-contained — you likely won't have cloud LBs. Know how to use NodePort as an alternative and understand that MetalLB provides LoadBalancer services on bare metal.
SN4
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN4
kube-proxy Not Running — No Service Routing

🔍 Symptom: All Services return connection refused. iptables -t nat -L shows no KUBE-SERVICES chain. kube-proxy DaemonSet pods not running on nodes.

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
NAME          READY   STATUS
❌ (empty or CrashLoopBackOff)

$ iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES
❌ iptables: No chain/target/match by that name
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. kube-proxy DaemonSet not running: kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy.
  2. kube-proxy CrashLoopBackOff: ConfigMap changed, invalid config, or missing conntrack module.
  3. Node taint blocks kube-proxy pod: DaemonSet doesn't tolerate control-plane taint.
  4. kube-proxy config file corrupted: /var/lib/kube-proxy/config.conf invalid.
  5. Container runtime not available: Node where kube-proxy scheduled has broken CRI.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CNI plugin not ready on node: kube-proxy waits for CNI before starting.
  2. kube-proxy --proxy-mode mismatch: Configured for IPVS but ip_vs module not loaded. Note: IPVS mode is now deprecated in favor of the newer nftables mode — worth migrating rather than chasing ip_vs kernel-module issues.
  3. kube-proxy hostNetwork: true pod can't start due to port conflict with host process.
  4. Kubernetes API server unreachable from node: kube-proxy can't watch its actual targets, Service and EndpointSlice objects (not the legacy Endpoints API).
  5. Disk full on node: kube-proxy can't write config files or iptables rules.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First cluster: kube-proxy deployed by kubeadm as DaemonSet — must be running on all nodes.
  2. kube-proxy uses hostNetwork: port 10249 (metrics) and 10256 (health) must be free.
  3. New node added: kube-proxy DaemonSet automatically schedules but may fail on tainted node.
  4. Wrong kubeconfig: kube-proxy can't authenticate to API server.
  5. kube-proxy running but iptables rules not updated: Check kube-proxy --write-config-to.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy. kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy. iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES on node.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
2. Check logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
3. Restart: kubectl rollout restart ds kube-proxy -n kube-system
4. On node: lsmod | grep ip_vs if using IPVS
5. Recreate: kubectl delete pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy

💡 Personal Advice: kube-proxy is essential — without it, Services don't work. It runs as a DaemonSet on EVERY node, writing iptables/IPVS rules. If ALL Services fail, check kube-proxy first. On CKA: you may see a node where Services don't work — check if kube-proxy pod is running on that specific node.
SN5
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN5
Session Affinity Broken — Sticky Sessions Not Working

🔍 Symptom: Service configured with sessionAffinity: ClientIP but requests from same client go to different pods. Session state lost. Application session management broken.

$ kubectl get svc web-svc -o yaml | grep -A3 sessionAffinity
sessionAffinity: ClientIP
sessionAffinityConfig:
  clientIP:
    timeoutSeconds: 10800
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Client behind NAT/proxy: Source IP changes — different IP = different session affinity.
  2. kube-proxy in IPVS mode with wrong scheduler: IPVS persistence needs specific configuration.
  3. sessionAffinity timeout too short: Default 10800s (3h) may be too long or too short for your app.
  4. Multiple clients sharing same source IP (corporate NAT): All traffic goes to SAME pod — overload.
  5. Ingress in front of Service: Ingress strips original client IP — Service sees Ingress IP.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. LoadBalancer with externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster — source NAT hides real client IP.
  2. NodePort accessed via different nodes: Each node has independent session affinity tables.
  3. kube-proxy restart: Session affinity table lost on kube-proxy restart.
  4. Multiple Services targeting same pods: Different session tracking tables per Service.
  5. IPv6 to IPv4 NAT: Source IP translation breaks session affinity.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. New Service without sessionAffinity: Default is None (random load balancing).
  2. Sticky sessions at wrong layer: Using L4 (ClientIP) when L7 (cookie-based) needed.
  3. Ingress Controller session affinity not configured: Ingress-level sticky sessions needed for HTTP.
  4. Service mesh sidecar: Istio/Linkerd proxy breaks ClientIP-based affinity.
  5. Cloud LB has its own session affinity: Conflicts with Kubernetes sessionAffinity.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- env | grep HOSTNAME — which pod served request. kubectl logs <pod> | grep <client-ip>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Use Ingress-level cookie-based affinity for HTTP workloads
2. Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve client IP
3. Check if client is behind NAT: kubectl exec <pod> -- echo $REMOTE_ADDR
4. For IPVS: configure persistence timeout in kube-proxy config
5. Consider application-level session management (Redis/JWT) instead of transport-level

💡 Personal Advice: sessionAffinity: ClientIP is a blunt instrument — it only works when the client IP is stable. For modern apps behind load balancers, proxies, and NAT, ClientIP is unreliable. Use application-level sessions (Redis, JWT tokens) or Ingress-level cookie-based affinity. On CKA: understand sessionAffinity exists but know its limitations — never rely on it for production stateful apps.

📌 SN6–SN8: DNS & CoreDNS Failures

SN6
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN6
CoreDNS Pods CrashLoopBackOff — DNS Down Cluster-Wide

🔍 Symptom: All CoreDNS pods crashing, kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns shows CrashLoopBackOff. No DNS resolution anywhere.

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
NAME                      READY   STATUS
❌ coredns-7d8f9-abc        0/1     CrashLoopBackOff

$ kubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-7d8f9-abc
❌ plugin/loop: Loop (127.0.0.1:xxxxx -> 127.0.0.1:53) detected, shutting down
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Loop detection triggered: CoreDNS detects forwarding loop (upstream DNS = CoreDNS itself). Check Corefile config.
  2. CoreDNS ConfigMap corrupted: Invalid Corefile syntax. kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml.
  3. Upstream DNS unreachable: forward . /etc/resolv.conf — node's DNS not working.
  4. CoreDNS OOMKilled: Memory limit too low for cluster size. 10K+ services = more memory needed.
  5. Port 53 conflict: Node-local DNS cache or systemd-resolved using port 53.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Node DNS override: systemd-resolved stub listener on 127.0.0.53 confusing CoreDNS.
  2. CoreDNS using wrong cluster domain: kubernetes cluster.local vs custom domain.
  3. CoreDNS plugin conflict: Both kubernetes and forward plugins for same zone.
  4. Prometheus metrics endpoint causing high memory: Large cluster with scrape enabled.
  5. CoreDNS cache poisoning from upstream DNS returning bad responses.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First deployment: CoreDNS deployed by kubeadm with default ConfigMap — may need tuning.
  2. Node DNS misconfigured: /etc/resolv.conf on nodes has unreachable nameservers.
  3. CoreDNS replicas scaled down from the default: kubeadm deploys CoreDNS with 2 replicas out of the box — if someone scaled it to 1 (or a drain left only one schedulable), a single pod failure takes down DNS.
  4. CoreDNS anti-affinity not configured: All replicas on same node — single point of failure.
  5. Cluster domain mismatch: kubelet --cluster-domain differs from CoreDNS kubernetes plugin config.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50. kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
2. Fix loop: in Corefile, change forward . /etc/resolv.conf to specific upstream (8.8.8.8)
3. kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system and fix syntax errors
4. Restore default redundancy: kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=2 (this restores kubeadm's own default of 2 — it isn't an increase)
5. kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system

💡 Personal Advice: CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff is usually a loop detection or ConfigMap error. The loop detection safety net kills CoreDNS to prevent infinite DNS loops. Fix: edit the ConfigMap and remove the loop by using proper upstream DNS. On CKA: you may need to fix a broken CoreDNS — check logs first, then ConfigMap.
SN7
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN7
Pod DNS Resolution Slow or Intermittent

🔍 Symptom: DNS resolution from pods takes 5+ seconds or sometimes fails. nslookup in pod works sometimes, fails others. CoreDNS overloaded or misconfigured.

$ kubectl exec test-pod -- time nslookup kubernetes.default
real    0m5.234s  ← 5 seconds! (should be <100ms)

$ kubectl top pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
NAME                      CPU    MEMORY
❌ coredns-7d8f9-abc        500m   200Mi  ← High CPU!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. CoreDNS overloaded: Too many DNS queries. Add replicas and enable caching.
  2. Network latency between pod and CoreDNS: Pod in different AZ/region from CoreDNS pod.
  3. DNS search domains too long: /etc/resolv.conf has many search domains — each tried sequentially.
  4. CoreDNS cache disabled: cache 30 missing from Corefile. Every query hits upstream.
  5. Upstream DNS slow: forward . /etc/resolv.conf pointing to slow corporate DNS.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. ndots:5 causing excessive DNS queries: Default ndots=5 makes every name tried with search domains.
  2. CoreDNS autopath misconfigured: autopath normally REDUCES search-path queries via server-side completion (not the cause of extra ones) — but a misconfigured pod-source path can return wrong answers.
  3. Node-local DNS cache missing: Every DNS query goes to CoreDNS pod (network hop).
  4. IPv6 DNS queries timing out: Pod has IPv6 enabled but cluster has no IPv6 DNS.
  5. DNS over TCP retry after UDP failure: UDP packet loss causes 5s TCP fallback delay.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. CoreDNS scaled down from its default 2 replicas: kubeadm deploys 2 out of the box — fewer means any load spike hits harder.
  2. No node-local-dns: Queries traverse overlay network to CoreDNS pod.
  3. Cluster with 100+ services: CoreDNS needs more resources at scale.
  4. ndots:5 (default) too high: Pod tries 3 search-domain variations (one per default search-list entry: namespace.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local) before an absolute lookup — ndots:5 is the dot-count threshold that triggers this, not the number of suffixes tried.
  5. No DNS monitoring: Can't see query rate, latency, error rate trends.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf. kubectl exec <pod> -- time nslookup kubernetes.default.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Scale CoreDNS: kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=3
2. Enable cache: add cache 30 to Corefile
3. Reduce ndots: set dnsConfig: options: - name: ndots value: "2" in pod spec
4. Add node-local-dns: DaemonSet caching DNS on each node
5. Use specific upstream: forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4

💡 Personal Advice: DNS slowness is often ndots=5 + search domains + caching issues. The pod resolver tries 3 suffix combinations (the default search list) before using the absolute name — ndots:5 is just the threshold that triggers the search list. Fix: reduce ndots to 2, enable CoreDNS cache, scale replicas. On CKA: you may see slow DNS — check /etc/resolv.conf for excessive search domains and adjust ndots.
SN8
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN8
External DNS Resolution Fails — Can't Reach Internet

🔍 Symptom: Pods can resolve internal Services but external names (google.com, github.com) fail. forward plugin in CoreDNS misconfigured or node DNS broken.

$ kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup google.com
❌ ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached

$ kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default
✅ Server: 10.96.0.10  Address: 10.96.0.10#53  Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Upstream DNS unreachable: CoreDNS forward block points to bad DNS. Check Corefile.
  2. Node /etc/resolv.conf has wrong DNS: CoreDNS inherits node's upstream DNS by default.
  3. Firewall blocking outbound DNS (UDP 53): CoreDNS can't reach external DNS servers.
  4. Corporate DNS requires specific search domains: Pod search domains don't include corporate domain.
  5. DNS policy on pod: dnsPolicy: None with custom DNS ignoring CoreDNS.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. NetworkPolicy blocks CoreDNS egress to external DNS: Allow UDP 53 to upstream DNS IPs.
  2. Proxy requiring authentication: DNS queries blocked by transparent proxy.
  3. Upstream DNS rate limiting: Too many queries from cluster — external DNS throttling.
  4. DNS64/NAT64 misconfigured: IPv6-only cluster can't reach IPv4 DNS servers.
  5. Stub domain in Corefile: example.com:53 { forward . 10.0.0.1 } not working.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First cluster with no internet: Air-gapped — need internal DNS forwarding for external names.
  2. CoreDNS forward to node DNS by default: forward . /etc/resolv.conf — if node DNS broken, all external fails.
  3. No upstream DNS configured in Corefile: forward . /etc/resolv.conf inherited from kubeadm defaults.
  4. Custom cluster domain: <domain> not resolving because CoreDNS doesn't forward unknown domains.
  5. Cloud DNS (Route 53) VPC resolver not accessible from pod network.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup google.com. kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A5 forward.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Fix Corefile: forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4 instead of /etc/resolv.conf
2. Verify node DNS: nslookup google.com from node — if fails, fix node DNS
3. Allow UDP 53 egress in NetworkPolicy
4. kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
5. For air-gapped: configure internal DNS forwarder for allowed external domains

💡 Personal Advice: Kubernetes DNS (internal) works but external fails = CoreDNS forward plugin issue. CoreDNS uses node's /etc/resolv.conf as upstream by default — if the node's DNS is broken, external resolution fails cluster-wide. On CKA: you may need to configure CoreDNS upstream DNS servers. Know: kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system and the forward . block.

📌 SN9–SN10: Advanced DNS Configuration

SN9
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN9
Custom DNS (Stub Domain) Not Working — External Services Unreachable

🔍 Symptom: The easypj-api pod needs to reach an external database at db.corp.internal, but DNS resolution fails. CoreDNS is configured with a stub domain for corp.internal pointing to a corporate DNS server, but the corporate DNS server is unreachable or the Corefile configuration has a syntax error.

$ kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- nslookup db.corp.internal
❌ ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
Server: 10.96.0.10  Address: 10.96.0.10#53

$ kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A10 "corp.internal"
corp.internal:53 {
    errors
    cache 30
❌   forward . 10.100.0.50   ← Corporate DNS server unreachable!
}
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Corporate DNS unreachable: nslookup db.corp.internal 10.100.0.50 from node — if it fails, CoreDNS can't reach it either. Check firewall/routing.
  2. Corefile syntax error: The stub domain block has wrong indentation or missing closing brace. kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A20 Corefile.
  3. NetworkPolicy blocking CoreDNS egress: CoreDNS needs UDP 53 to the corporate DNS IP. Add egress rule.
  4. Corporate DNS requires specific search path: CoreDNS forwards db.corp.internal. but corporate DNS expects db.corp.internal.company.local.
  5. CoreDNS not reloaded after ConfigMap update: kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system or wait for auto-reload.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Stub domain server only accepts TCP: CoreDNS's forward plugin actually supports both UDP and TCP by default, mirroring the incoming query's protocol — add force_tcp only if the upstream specifically requires TCP regardless of how the query arrived
  2. Corporate DNS requires authentication (TSIG) — CoreDNS doesn't support this by default
  3. Stub domain overlap: corp.internal matches both stub domain and forward . rule — priority wrong
  4. DNS server expecting requests from specific source IP — CoreDNS source IP not authorized
  5. Corporate DNS returns NXDOMAIN for specific record — cached by CoreDNS for cache TTL (30s default)
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First stub domain config: Corefile YAML indentation is tricky — use kubectl edit for validation
  2. Stub domains for multi-cluster: Service discovery across clusters via stub domains
  3. CoreDNS auto-reloads ConfigMap changes via the Corefile's reload plugin — allow ~2 minutes, no restart needed (this has been part of the default kubeadm Corefile for a long time, not a 1.23+-specific feature)
  4. Stub domain in air-gapped environment: Corporate DNS only available via VPN/proxy
  5. Testing: kubectl run -it --rm debug --image=busybox -- nslookup db.corp.internal
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml — check Corefile for stub domains. kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns — CoreDNS logs.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Test corporate DNS from node: nslookup db.corp.internal 10.100.0.50
2. Fix Corefile: kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system — correct stub domain IP
3. Add firewall rule: allow UDP 53 from cluster nodes to corporate DNS
4. Restart CoreDNS: kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
5. Test from pod: kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup db.corp.internal

💡 Personal Advice: Stub domains in CoreDNS are powerful for hybrid cloud setups — route internal DNS queries to corporate servers while keeping Kubernetes DNS for cluster-local names. On CKA: you may need to configure a stub domain in CoreDNS. Know the Corefile syntax: domain:53 { forward . IP }. Always test from both the node and a pod.
SN10
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN10
Service Discovery via SRV Records Not Working

🔍 Symptom: The easypj-api tries to discover the easypj-db StatefulSet pod using SRV DNS records (_http._tcp.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local), but the SRV query returns no records or incorrect port numbers. The app relies on SRV discovery for dynamic port allocation but the records don't match expectations.

$ kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- nslookup -type=SRV _http._tcp.easypj-db.easypj.svc
❌ ** server can't find _http._tcp.easypj-db.easypj.svc: NXDOMAIN

$ kubectl get svc easypj-db -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A5 ports
ports:
❌ - name: postgres    ← Port name is "postgres", not "http"!
    port: 5432
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 5432
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Port name mismatch: SRV record format is _port-name._protocol.service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Port name "postgres" ≠ "http". Use _postgres._tcp.easypj-db.easypj.svc.
  2. Service port not named: SRV records require NAMED ports. If port is unnamed, no SRV record is created. Add name: <name> to port spec.
  3. Wrong protocol in query: Using _tcp for UDP service or vice versa. Protocol must match the port's protocol field.
  4. Headless Service required for per-pod SRV: Regular Service returns one SRV record. Headless Service returns per-pod SRV records.
  5. StatefulSet pods not Ready: SRV records only include Ready pods. If pods are NotReady, SRV records are empty.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. kubernetes plugin misconfigured: SRV generation is built into CoreDNS's kubernetes plugin — there's no separate "SRV plugin" to disable — verify the kubernetes plugin is present and correctly configured in the Corefile
  2. DNS caching: Old SRV record cached — wait for TTL or flush CoreDNS cache
  3. Multiple ports on Service: SRV records created for ALL named ports — check which one you need
  4. StatefulSet with serviceName not set: StatefulSet must have serviceName matching the headless Service to get stable DNS
  5. Custom CoreDNS configuration overriding the kubernetes plugin's default SRV-generation behavior
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First use of SRV records: Kubernetes creates A/AAAA (host) and SRV (service) records automatically for Services with named ports
  2. SRV format: _port-name._protocol.service.namespace.svc.cluster.local — must be exact
  3. SRV for StatefulSet: headless Service + serviceName = per-pod DNS + SRV
  4. Service without named ports: DNS only provides A records, no SRV
  5. SRV records useful for: Database connection strings, gRPC service discovery, custom load balancing
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get svc <name> -o yaml | grep -A10 ports — ports must be NAMED. kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup -type=SRV _port._proto.svc.ns.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Name the port: kubectl patch svc easypj-db -n easypj --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"ports":[{"name":"postgres","port":5432,"targetPort":5432,"protocol":"TCP"}]}}'
2. Query correct SRV: nslookup -type=SRV _postgres._tcp.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local
3. For headless: clusterIP: None + StatefulSet serviceName: easypj-db
4. Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup -type=SRV _postgres._tcp.easypj-db.easypj.svc
5. Check all pods Ready: SRV only returns Ready pod endpoints

💡 Personal Advice: SRV records in Kubernetes are great for service discovery without hardcoding ports, BUT the port MUST be named. This is the #1 gotcha — unnamed ports = no SRV records. On CKA: you may need to debug why SRV records aren't working. The fix is almost always: (1) name the port, or (2) use the correct port name in the SRV query.

📌 SN11–SN15: Network Policy Troubleshooting

SN11
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN11
NetworkPolicy Applied — Pods Can't Communicate
