🔍 Symptom: After applying NetworkPolicy, pods can't reach each other. Policy is too restrictive or default-deny blocks legitimate traffic. Applications broken.

$ kubectl get networkpolicy -A
NAMESPACE  NAME        POD-SELECTOR
default    deny-all    {}  ← Blocks everything!

$ kubectl exec web-pod -- curl api-svc:8080
❌ curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3000ms
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Default-deny applied without allow rules: podSelector: {} and empty ingress/egress = blocks ALL traffic.
  2. podSelector too broad: Selects ALL pods when you meant only specific pods.
  3. Missing allow rule for DNS: UDP 53 not allowed — pods can't resolve Service names.
  4. namespaceSelector mismatch: Rule allows "team: dev" but namespace has label "team: development".
  5. Egress rule blocks the request itself, not the response: NetworkPolicy is stateful — once the initial request is allowed, reply traffic is auto-allowed. If traffic still fails, the outbound request is being blocked, not the return leg.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CNI plugin doesn't support NetworkPolicy: Flannel by itself silently ignores all NetworkPolicies.
  2. ipBlock CIDR too narrow: Allowed range doesn't include the actual source IP of the traffic.
  3. NetworkPolicy ordering: Multiple policies on same pod — UNION of allows. One deny-all blocks nothing if any allow exists.
  4. Pod needs to talk to itself (localhost): Not covered by NetworkPolicy — always allowed.
  5. NOT actually possible: traffic to/from a pod's own node is ALWAYS allowed regardless of any NetworkPolicy — kubelet health checks can never be blocked this way, so don't waste time adding a node-CIDR ipBlock for them
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First NetworkPolicy: Default behavior is ALLOW ALL. NP is opt-in restriction.
  2. Created default-deny first without any allow rules — everything breaks immediately.
  3. CNI not tested with NP: New cluster with Flannel — NetworkPolicy YAML applies but silently ignored.
  4. Namespace label dance: NP selects by namespace labels — labels must exist on namespace objects.
  5. NetworkPolicy is namespaced: Rules apply only within the NP's namespace.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get networkpolicy -A. kubectl describe networkpolicy <name> -n <ns>. kubectl exec <pod> -- curl <svc>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Start with allow rule, then add restrictions: don't start with deny-all
2. Always allow DNS: UDP 53 from all pods
3. Kubelet probes need no rule at all — node-to-pod traffic is always allowed regardless of policy
4. Test: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -O- <svc>
5. Verify CNI supports NP: Calico/Cilium/Weave = yes, Flannel alone = no

💡 Personal Advice: NetworkPolicy is a scalpel — default-deny first = broken cluster. Always start with allow rules, then add a default-deny LAST (after verifying allows work). The #1 mistake: applying deny-all and wondering why everything broke. Also: Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy. On CKA: you'll create policies — always allow DNS first (UDP 53).
SN12
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN12
NetworkPolicy Not Applied — CNI Doesn't Support NetworkPolicy

🔍 Symptom: You've created NetworkPolicies to restrict traffic between the easypj-api and easypj-db pods, but the policies are silently ignored. kubectl describe networkpolicy shows the policy exists, but pods can still communicate freely. The CNI plugin (Flannel) doesn't implement NetworkPolicy — the policies are just YAML in etcd with no enforcement.

$ kubectl get networkpolicy -n easypj
NAME           POD-SELECTOR       AGE
api-to-db      app=easypj-db      10m   ← Policy exists!

$ kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- curl easypj-db:5432
Connected to easypj-db:5432   ← Traffic NOT blocked! Policy ignored!

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave"
❌ (empty — no CNI with NetworkPolicy support!)
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy: Flannel, simple bridge, and some basic CNIs don't implement NetworkPolicy. Policies are ignored.
  2. Wrong CNI installed: Cluster was deployed with default Flannel (no NP support) instead of Calico, Cilium, or Weave Net.
  3. CNI with NP support but NP feature disabled: Calico installed but NetworkPolicy disabled in configuration.
  4. NetworkPolicy isn't a CRD at all: it's a native, always-registered core API type (implemented by the network plugin) — there's no "registration" step that can fail. The real gap is simply that the CNI isn't watching/enforcing it.
  5. CNI plugin crashed/not running: The CNI agent pod is down — all networking works but NP enforcement is gone.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CNI in policy-only mode: Calico in policy-only mode without network enforcement
  2. iptables/nftables rules not created by CNI: CNI agent can't write iptables rules — permission denied
  3. Host-network pods: CNI-dependent, not universal — some plugins apply NetworkPolicy to hostNetwork pods exactly like normal pods, others can't distinguish the traffic and ignore it. Check your specific CNI's docs rather than assuming either way
  4. NetworkPolicy in different IP family: Policy for IPv4 but cluster uses IPv6
  5. CNI version too old: Older Calico versions didn't support Kubernetes NetworkPolicy API
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. New kubeadm cluster with Flannel: Default pod network doesn't support NP — switch to Calico/Cilium
  2. CNI that support NP: Calico, Cilium, Weave Net, Kube-router, Antrea
  3. CNI that DON'T support NP: Flannel (alone), simple bridge, macvlan, ipvlan
  4. kubeadm --pod-network-cidr influences CNI choice: Match CNI's expected CIDR
  5. Always verify: Create a test NP and verify it blocks traffic before relying on NP for security
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave|flannel". kubectl get networkpolicy -A.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check current CNI: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave|flannel|kube-router"
2. If Flannel: replace with Calico: kubectl delete -f flannel.yaml && kubectl apply -f calico.yaml
3. Or add a CNI with NP support alongside existing CNI (multus)
4. Test NP enforcement: create deny-all and verify pods can't communicate
5. For CKA exam: Calico or Cilium are typical — both support NetworkPolicy

💡 Personal Advice: NetworkPolicy is just YAML — it doesn't DO anything by itself. It needs a CNI that IMPLEMENTS it. This is the most frustrating "bug" because everything looks right but doesn't work. On CKA: know which CNIs support NP (Calico, Cilium, Weave) and which don't (Flannel alone). If NP isn't working, check the CNI first.
SN13
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN13
Default-Deny Locks You Out — Can't Reach API Server / Critical Services

🔍 Symptom: You applied a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy to the easypj namespace, and now NOTHING works — pods can't reach the API server, CoreDNS, or each other. Even kubectl exec and health checks fail. The namespace is completely locked down because no allow rules were created before the deny-all.

$ kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- curl -k https://kubernetes.default:443
❌ curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3000ms   ← Can't reach API server!

$ kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- nslookup easypj-db.easypj.svc
❌ ;; connection timed out   ← DNS blocked too!

$ kubectl get networkpolicy -n easypj
❌ NAME        POD-SELECTOR   AGE
❌ deny-all    {}             5m   ← Blocks EVERYTHING to ALL pods!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Default-deny applied FIRST without any allow rules: podSelector: {} + empty ingress/egress = blocks ALL traffic. Create allow rules BEFORE deny-all.
  2. Missing allow rule for API server: Pods need egress to API server IP:6443. Add ipBlock rule for control plane CIDR.
  3. Missing allow rule for DNS: UDP 53 to CoreDNS (kube-system namespace). Critical for service discovery.
  4. NOT actually a gap: kubelet health checks are never affected by NetworkPolicy — traffic to/from a pod's own node is always allowed, so no node-CIDR rule is needed for probes to keep working.
  5. Missing allow rule for metrics-server/Prometheus: Monitoring tools can't scrape metrics from pods.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Default-deny on kube-system namespace: Blocks control plane components — cluster unstable
  2. Deny-all applied by GitOps/ArgoCD automatically: Policy pushed without proper review
  3. Pod relies on init container that needs network: Init container can't pull from registry — pod stuck Init:0/1
  4. Operator/controller can't reach API server: Operator in same namespace — reconciliation loop broken
  5. Egress deny-all blocks image pulls: kubelet pulls images, not pod — but registry access from init containers blocked
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First default-deny: White-list approach — deny all, then explicitly allow. But order matters!
  2. Always allow: DNS (UDP 53), API server (TCP 6443), ingress controller (if any) — node-to-pod traffic (health checks) never needs an explicit rule, it's always allowed
  3. NetworkPolicy is namespace-scoped: Default-deny in one ns doesn't affect other ns — but can block cross-ns traffic
  4. Quick recovery: kubectl delete networkpolicy deny-all -n <ns> — traffic resumes immediately
  5. Test policies in dev namespace first: Never apply deny-all to prod without testing in dev
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get networkpolicy -A — look for empty podSelector. kubectl exec <pod> -- wget -O- --timeout=5 <svc>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Emergency: kubectl delete networkpolicy deny-all -n easypj — traffic resumes immediately
2. Create allow rules FIRST: DNS, API server, required services (skip node CIDR — health checks are never blocked by NetworkPolicy)
3. Reapply deny-all LAST: kubectl apply -f deny-all.yaml after allow rules exist
4. Template: Allow ingress from same namespace, allow egress DNS + API server + world
5. Test: kubectl exec <pod> -- wget -O- --timeout=5 <svc> before and after deny-all

💡 Personal Advice: Default-deny is great for security but TERRIFYING when applied accidentally. The cluster doesn't warn you — it just goes silent. On CKA: if everything suddenly stops working after creating a NetworkPolicy, check for default-deny first. The fix is deleting it and rebuilding with allow rules first. Always: ALLOW first, DENY last.
SN14
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN14
Ingress vs Egress Direction Confusion — Policy Reversed

🔍 Symptom: You created a NetworkPolicy to allow the easypj-api to talk to easypj-db (the database), but the connection still times out. The policy has the direction WRONG — you put the allow rule under egress on the DB pod instead of ingress on the DB pod (or egress on the API pod). Direction confusion: ingress = INTO the pod, egress = OUT OF the pod.

$ kubectl describe networkpolicy api-to-db -n easypj
Spec:
  PodSelector: app=easypj-db
❌ Egress:       ← Egress FROM DB pod? That's DB → API, not API → DB!
    To: namespaceSelector: app=easypj-api
    Ports: 5432

$ kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- curl easypj-db:5432
❌ curl: (28) Connection timed out   ← API can't reach DB!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Ingress/Egress reversed: Ingress = traffic ENTERING the selected pod. Egress = traffic LEAVING the selected pod. If you want API→DB, the rule should be Ingress on DB (allowing API as source) OR Egress on API (allowing DB as destination).
  2. Policy on wrong pod: Applied policy to DB pod but the rule should be on API pod. Or vice versa. Match podSelector to the RECEIVING pod for Ingress, SENDING pod for Egress.
  3. namespaceSelector vs podSelector confusion: namespaceSelector selects entire namespaces, podSelector selects specific pods within a namespace.
  4. Port specified on wrong side: DB listens on 5432, but ingress rule on DB allows port 8080. Must match the LISTENING port.
  5. Only an Ingress rule on DB is needed: (allow API→DB). NetworkPolicy is stateful, so DB's reply traffic back to API is auto-allowed without any matching Egress rule — adding one is redundant, not required.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. From vs To confusion: Ingress uses "from" (sources), Egress uses "to" (destinations)
  2. Combined ingress+egress policy: Both blocks in one policy — complex to debug
  3. Policy on both pods: Redundant policies on both API and DB — one misconfigured blocks traffic
  4. Using namespaceSelector when pods are in same namespace: Use podSelector within same namespace
  5. Multiple NetworkPolicies: UNION of all policies applies — one misconfigured policy doesn't override others
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Mental model: Ingress = "who can knock on MY door", Egress = "which doors can I knock on"
  2. Simplest approach: Put Ingress on destination pod, Egress on source pod
  3. Kubernetes is stateful for NP: Allowing ingress auto-allows response egress — don't need both
  4. Visualize: Draw arrows from source to destination — Ingress rule is at the arrow HEAD, Egress rule is at the arrow TAIL
  5. Common pattern: db pod = Ingress from API pods, api pod = no egress restriction (or egress to db)
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe networkpolicy <name> — check PodSelector, Ingress (From), Egress (To). Trace the traffic flow from source to destination.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Identify traffic direction: API (source) → DB (destination) on port 5432
2. Correct rule: Ingress on DB pod from API pods on port 5432
3. OR: Egress on API pod to DB pods on port 5432
4. Fix: kubectl edit networkpolicy api-to-db -n easypj — move rule from Egress to Ingress
5. Verify: kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -- curl --connect-timeout 5 easypj-db:5432

💡 Personal Advice: The #1 NetworkPolicy logic error is swapping Ingress and Egress. Remember: Ingress = "who can come IN to these pods", Egress = "where can these pods go OUT to." On CKA: if you need API→DB: either Ingress on DB (allowing API) or Egress on API (allowing DB). Both work, pick one. Never put Egress on the destination — that controls where DB can call OUT, not who can call DB.
SN15
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN15
Ingress Controller Not Picking Up Ingress Resources

🔍 Symptom: Ingress YAML applied successfully but kubectl describe ingress shows no events. Ingress controller not running or ingressClassName mismatch.

$ kubectl get ingress
NAME        CLASS    HOSTS   ADDRESS   PORTS
my-ingress  nginx    app.com           80

$ kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress
❌ (empty — no Ingress controller running!)

$ curl http://<node-ip>
❌ curl: (7) Failed to connect
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. No Ingress controller installed: Ingress is just rules — need controller (nginx, traefik) to implement them.
  2. ingressClassName mismatch: Ingress specifies "nginx" but controller uses class "nginx-internal".
  3. Ingress controller pod not running: kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx.
  4. Wrong namespace: Ingress controller in namespace X but Ingress resource expects it in namespace Y.
  5. Ingress controller Service type wrong: NodePort used but firewall blocks the port.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Multiple Ingress controllers: Both trying to handle the same Ingress — conflict.
  2. Ingress controller using different API group: extensions/v1beta1 vs networking.k8s.io/v1.
  3. TLS Secret missing: Ingress references a Secret that doesn't exist — controller rejects the Ingress.
  4. Ingress controller health check failing: Pod not ready — not processing Ingress resources.
  5. RBAC: Ingress controller ServiceAccount doesn't have permission to watch Ingress resources.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First Ingress: Must install controller first, then create Ingress resources.
  2. kubeadm doesn't install Ingress controller: Must add manually (unlike cloud managed K8s).
  3. ingressClassName is optional, not version-gated: if omitted, behavior is controller-dependent — some fall back to a default IngressClass, others ignore classless Ingress entirely. K8s 1.22 only removed the deprecated extensions/v1beta1 Ingress API, unrelated to this field.
  4. Default IngressClass not set: kubectl get ingressclass — must designate one as default.
  5. Controller installed in wrong namespace: Ingress controller expects Ingress resources in specific namespaces.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress. kubectl get ingressclass. kubectl describe ingress <name>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Install controller: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml
2. Verify: kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx
3. Set ingressClassName to match controller
4. Create TLS Secret if referenced in Ingress
5. Test: curl -H "Host: app.com" http://<controller-ip>

💡 Personal Advice: Ingress without controller = just YAML in etcd. Nothing happens until you install an Ingress controller. On CKA: you'll need to create an Ingress resource. Know that the controller must be installed FIRST. Also: ingressClassName isn't API-required at any version — but many controllers silently ignore an Ingress without it, so setting it explicitly avoids controller-dependent surprises.

📌 SN16–SN20: Ingress Routing & TLS Troubleshooting

SN16
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN16
Ingress Returns 502 Bad Gateway — Backend Service/Pod Down

🔍 Symptom: Users accessing https://easypj.com see "502 Bad Gateway" from the nginx Ingress controller. The Ingress resource is configured correctly, but the backend Service or pods are down. The Ingress controller can't forward traffic to the easypj-api backend.

$ curl -I https://easypj.com/api
❌ HTTP/2 502 Bad Gateway

$ kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress -n easypj | grep -A5 "Endpoints\|backend"
Rules:
  Host: easypj.com
  Path: /api → easypj-api-svc:8080
❌ Backends: (none)   ← No healthy backends!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Backend pods not Ready: kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj — if NotReady, Ingress won't route. Check readiness probe.
  2. Service selector mismatch: Service selects app=api but pods have label app=easypj-api. Endpoints empty.
  3. Wrong Service port: Ingress references port 8080 but Service exposes 80. Port numbers must match.
  4. Backend pod crashed: Pod is CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled. kubectl describe pod <name>.
  5. Ingress controller can't reach Service network: NetworkPolicy or firewall between ingress-nginx namespace and easypj namespace.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Service type ClusterIP (default): Ingress controller CAN reach ClusterIP within cluster — this is normal
  2. Ingress controller ServiceAccount missing RBAC: Can't watch Endpoints for backend health
  3. Backend protocol mismatch: Ingress expects HTTP but backend expects HTTPS
  4. Backend timeout too short: nginx proxy_read_timeout (default 60s) exceeded by slow backend
  5. Ingress path rewrite: Path stripped incorrectly — backend receives wrong URL path
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First Ingress: 502 means Ingress controller is WORKING but backend is broken — good news!
  2. Ingress controller logs: kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller — shows exactly which backend failed
  3. Default backend: If no rules match, Ingress routes to default-backend (shows 404 or custom page)
  4. Endpoints = healthy backends: kubectl get endpoints -n <ns> must show pod IPs, not empty
  5. Ingress controller health check: The controller's own health endpoint shows backend health
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller. kubectl get endpoints -n <ns>. kubectl describe ingress <name>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check backend pods: kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj — must be Running + Ready
2. Check endpoints: kubectl get endpoints easypj-api-svc -n easypj — must have IPs
3. Fix Service selector: match labels exactly (app: easypj-api on both pod and Service)
4. Check port mapping: Ingress backend port = Service port = containerPort
5. Restart backend: kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

💡 Personal Advice: 502 is the "backend is broken" error. The Ingress controller is healthy and trying to route — the problem is the backend Service or pods. On CKA: always check kubectl get endpoints for the backend Service — if it's empty, fix the Service selector. Then check pod readiness. The Ingress controller logs will tell you exactly which backend failed.
SN17
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN17
Ingress TLS Certificate Error — Secret Not Found or Wrong Format

🔍 Symptom: HTTPS access to https://easypj.com fails with "NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID" or the Ingress controller uses a fake/default certificate. The TLS Secret referenced in the Ingress doesn't exist, has wrong keys, or the certificate is expired. The Ingress controller falls back to a self-signed default cert.

$ curl -vk https://easypj.com 2>&1 | grep "subject:"
❌ subject: CN=Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate   ← Wrong cert!

$ kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress -n easypj | grep TLS
TLS:
❌   easypj-tls terminates easypj.com   ← Secret "easypj-tls" may not exist!

$ kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj
❌ Error: secrets "easypj-tls" not found
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. TLS Secret doesn't exist: Ingress references a Secret that was never created. kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n easypj --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem.
  2. Secret has wrong keys: TLS Secrets MUST have tls.crt and tls.key as data keys. Wrong names = invalid cert.
  3. Certificate expired: openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -dates — check expiry. Renew if expired.
  4. Certificate CN/SAN mismatch: Cert is for *.easypj.com but host is easypj.com. Wildcard covers subdomains only, not the apex domain.
  5. Secret in wrong namespace: Ingress and Secret must be in the SAME namespace.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Secret created as Opaque instead of kubernetes.io/tls: Type mismatch — Ingress expects type: kubernetes.io/tls
  2. Certificate chain incomplete: tls.crt must include intermediate CA certs — chain of trust broken
  3. Private key doesn't match certificate: openssl x509 -noout -modulus vs openssl rsa -noout -modulus
  4. Multiple TLS sections in Ingress: One host listed twice with different Secrets — conflict
  5. Ingress controller doesn't have permission to read the Secret: RBAC prevents access
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Self-signed cert for testing: openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt
  2. Create TLS Secret: kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n <ns>
  3. Secret must be type kubernetes.io/tls: Not Opaque or generic — type matters for TLS
  4. Ingress controller uses default cert if TLS Secret is invalid: Fake Certificate warning is expected
  5. cert-manager automates TLS: Creates and renews certificates automatically — recommended for production
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe secret <name> — check Type (must be kubernetes.io/tls) and keys. openssl s_client -connect easypj.com:443 -servername easypj.com | openssl x509 -noout -text.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Create TLS Secret: kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n easypj --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem
2. Verify: kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj — Type should be kubernetes.io/tls
3. Verify cert: kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates
4. If cert expired: regenerate, recreate Secret, Ingress controller auto-reloads
5. Test: curl -v --resolve easypj.com:443:<ingress-ip> https://easypj.com

💡 Personal Advice: TLS in Ingress requires TWO things: the Secret must exist AND it must be type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt and tls.key keys. On CKA: you'll create a TLS Secret and reference it in an Ingress. Know: kubectl create secret tls (not generic). The Ingress controller auto-detects new/updated Secrets — no restart needed. Remember where TLS actually terminates: AT the Ingress controller — traffic from the controller to the backend Service/Pods is plain HTTP by default, so "is TLS configured" and "is the backend reachable" are two separate problems to debug.
SN18
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN18
IngressClass Not Set — Multiple Controllers, No Default

🔍 Symptom: The cluster has two Ingress controllers (nginx and traefik), but Ingress resources aren't being picked up by either one. Neither controller is marked as default, and Ingress resources don't specify an ingressClassName. The Ingress just sits there with no ADDRESS assigned.

$ kubectl get ingressclass
NAME     CONTROLLER                     PARAMETERS   AGE
nginx    k8s.io/ingress-nginx           <none>        30d
traefik  traefik.io/ingress-controller  <none>        30d   ← Two controllers, no default!

$ kubectl get ingress -A
NAMESPACE  NAME              CLASS   HOSTS       ADDRESS   AGE
❌ easypj     easypj-ingress   <none>  easypj.com            1h   ← ADDRESS empty!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. No default IngressClass: with multiple controllers and none marked default, most controllers ignore a classless Ingress — but this is controller-specific, not universal; some controllers (especially single-controller setups) still pick it up.
  2. ingressClassName not set on Ingress: You must specify which controller should handle this Ingress: spec.ingressClassName: nginx.
  3. Wrong ingressClassName value: Specified "nginx-ingress" but the class is named "nginx". Names must match exactly.
  4. IngressClass doesn't match any controller: The class references a controller that isn't installed.
  5. Both controllers watch same IngressClass: Both set as default or both watching the same class — conflict.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. IngressClass Parameters reference invalid resource: Controller can't configure itself with the given parameters
  2. IngressClass deleted but Ingress still references it: Orphaned reference — no controller picks it up
  3. Ingress controller scoped to specific namespace: Watches only ns-a, but Ingress is in ns-b
  4. Annotation-based class (deprecated): Using kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation instead of spec.ingressClassName
  5. Controller version mismatch: K8s 1.18- uses annotation, 1.19+ prefers IngressClass — but neither version ever made ingressClassName API-required, so "requires it" is a myth
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. ingressClassName is never API-required, even with multiple IngressClasses — but leaving it unset when there's no default class means most controllers will silently ignore the Ingress
  2. Set default: kubectl annotate ingressclass nginx ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true
  3. Only ONE IngressClass can be default: The annotation ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class="true"
  4. IngressClass is cluster-scoped: Same class available in all namespaces
  5. Annotation still works for backward compat: kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "nginx" — but prefer spec.ingressClassName
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get ingressclass — check for default annotation. kubectl describe ingressclass <name>. kubectl get ingress -A -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.ingressClassName}'.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Set default IngressClass: kubectl annotate ingressclass nginx ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true
2. Or add ingressClassName to Ingress: kubectl patch ingress easypj-ingress -n easypj --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"ingressClassName":"nginx"}}'
3. Verify: kubectl get ingress -n easypj — ADDRESS should populate within seconds
4. Remove annotation-based class if using new style
5. Test: curl -H "Host: easypj.com" http://<ingress-ip>

💡 Personal Advice: IngressClass is like a "which controller handles this" label. Without it (and without a default class), most controllers leave your Ingress orphaned — though this is controller-specific behavior, not a universal Kubernetes rule. On CKA: always set spec.ingressClassName on your Ingress resources. Know that kubectl get ingressclass shows available classes and which is default.
SN19
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN19
Path-Based Routing — /api Goes to Wrong Backend (PathType Mismatch)

🔍 Symptom: The Ingress is supposed to route /api to the easypj-api backend and / to the easypj-web frontend. But requests to /api return HTML (the web frontend), not JSON. Or requests to /api/v2 return 404. The pathType (Prefix vs Exact) is wrong, or the path order causes the wrong rule to match first.

$ curl -s https://easypj.com/api | head -5
❌ <!DOCTYPE html>   ← Got HTML, expected JSON! Routing to web, not API!

$ kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress -n easypj | grep -A3 Path
Rules:
  Host: easypj.com
  Path: /    → easypj-web-svc:80     ← Matches EVERYTHING first!
❌ Path: /api → easypj-api-svc:8080   ← This rule never reached!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Path specificity, not order: Kubernetes resolves overlapping matches by the LONGEST matching path (Exact beats Prefix on a tie) — YAML declaration order is irrelevant. If /api is shadowed by /, the fix is path/pathType specificity, not reordering the rules.
  2. PathType Prefix matches element-wise, not by raw string: Prefix /api matches /api and /api/v1, but never /apiv2 — matching is done on "/"-delimited path elements. If /apiv2 is wrongly matching, suspect ImplementationSpecific or a controller bug, not standard Prefix behavior.
  3. PathType Exact too strict: Exact /api only matches /api (no trailing slash). /api/ returns 404. Use Prefix for subtree matching.
  4. Missing trailing slash: Ingress path /api doesn't match /api/ with Exact pathType. Add both paths.
  5. Rewrite target not configured: Ingress forwards /api/users to backend as /api/users, but backend expects /users. Use nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. PathType ImplementationSpecific: Different Ingress controllers handle this differently — non-standard
  2. Case sensitivity: /API vs /api — Path matching is case-sensitive by default
  3. Regular expression paths: Using ~ or regex in path when controller doesn't support it
  4. Rewrite conflicts: Multiple rewrite annotations on same Ingress — last one wins
  5. Backend path appended incorrectly: nginx appends the matched path to backend URL by default
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. PathType Prefix: Matches path prefix with / delimiter — /api matches /api/ but not /apiv2
  2. PathType Exact: Matches exact URL path — case-sensitive, no partial matches
  3. PathType ImplementationSpecific: Controller-specific matching — avoid on CKA, use Prefix or Exact
  4. Longest match wins: If two Prefix paths overlap, the longer (more specific) path wins
  5. Rewrite target: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2 with path: /api(/|$)(.*)
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe ingress <name> -n <ns> — check Path order and PathType. kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Fix path/pathType specificity (declaration order doesn't matter — the longest matching path always wins)
2. Use PathType Prefix for API: path: /api, pathType: Prefix
3. Use PathType Prefix for root as a catch-all fallback: path: /, pathType: Prefix (Exact would break every non-root route like /about — Prefix on / naturally loses to /api anyway since /api is the longer match, regardless of declaration order)
4. Add rewrite if needed: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$1
5. Test: curl -s https://easypj.com/api | head -1 — should return JSON, not HTML

💡 Personal Advice: Path specificity in Ingress is critical, but declaration ORDER is not — Kubernetes always resolves overlapping matches by the longest matching path (Exact beats Prefix on a tie), regardless of where each rule sits in the YAML. On CKA: if /api returns the wrong backend content, check: (1) PathType (Prefix vs Exact) and path specificity, (2) whether a shorter path is unexpectedly winning due to pathType, (3) rewrite-target annotation if the backend expects stripped paths. These cover the large majority of path routing issues.
SN20
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN20
cert-manager Not Issuing Certificate — Challenge Fails

🔍 Symptom: You've created a Certificate resource for easypj.com using cert-manager, but the certificate stays in "Pending" or "Issuing" state indefinitely. kubectl describe certificate shows "Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation." The DNS record or HTTP endpoint for the ACME challenge isn't accessible from Let's Encrypt's servers.

$ kubectl get certificate -n easypj
NAME          READY   SECRET        AGE
❌ easypj-tls   False   easypj-tls    30m   ← Stuck in False!

$ kubectl describe certificate easypj-tls -n easypj | tail -15
Status:
  Conditions:
❌   Type: Ready, Status: False, Reason: WaitingForHTTP01Challenge
❌   Message: Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation: did not get expected response
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Ingress not accessible from internet: Let's Encrypt servers must reach http://easypj.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>. DNS must point to the Ingress controller's IP.
  2. DNS not propagated: A record for easypj.com not pointing to Ingress controller IP. nslookup easypj.com from outside the cluster.
  3. Firewall blocking port 80: ACME HTTP-01 challenge requires port 80 (HTTP). If only 443 (HTTPS) is open, challenge fails.
  4. cert-manager not running: kubectl get pods -n cert-manager — controller, webhook, and cainjector must be Running.
  5. Issuer/ClusterIssuer misconfigured: Wrong ACME server URL, wrong email, or wrong private key secret reference.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Rate limiting by Let's Encrypt: Too many certificate requests for the same domain — 5 per week limit
  2. DNS-01 challenge used but no DNS provider credentials configured
  3. CNAME vs A record: cert-manager follows CNAME during challenge — intermediary DNS not responding
  4. Cluster behind corporate proxy: Outbound connections from cert-manager pod blocked
  5. Multiple Ingress controllers: Challenge solver pod created by wrong Ingress controller
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First cert-manager setup: Install via kubectl apply -f cert-manager.yaml then create Issuer + Certificate
  2. Let's Encrypt staging vs production: Test with staging first (no rate limits), then switch to production
  3. HTTP-01 challenge requires: Publicly accessible port 80 + correct DNS pointing to Ingress IP
  4. Self-signed for internal: Use self-signed Issuer for cluster-internal TLS (no ACME needed)
  5. Certificate is namespaced (Issuer) or cluster-wide (ClusterIssuer): Use ClusterIssuer for wildcard certs
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get certificaterequests,orders,challenges -n <ns>. kubectl describe challenge <name> -n <ns>. kubectl logs -n cert-manager deploy/cert-manager.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check DNS: nslookup easypj.com — must resolve to Ingress controller IP
2. Check port 80 open: curl http://easypj.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/test from external machine
3. Fix Issuer: verify ACME server URL (production: letsencrypt-v2, staging: letsencrypt-staging)
4. Check cert-manager logs: kubectl logs -n cert-manager deploy/cert-manager --tail=50
5. Delete and recreate Certificate: kubectl delete certificate easypj-tls -n easypj && kubectl apply -f cert.yaml

💡 Personal Advice: cert-manager's #1 failure mode is HTTP-01 challenge failure because the domain isn't pointing to your cluster or port 80 is blocked. On CKA: cert-manager may appear. Know that: (1) DNS must point to Ingress IP, (2) port 80 MUST be open, (3) use Let's Encrypt staging for testing. The error message "Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation" almost always means your cluster isn't reachable from the internet on port 80.

💾 Category 1: Storage Lab ScenariosS1-S10

🟢 easypj/jobpost — Full-Stack Django + PostgreSQL Application

What is easypj/jobpost? A Django-based job board application where employers post jobs and applicants apply. It consists of a Django web server, PostgreSQL database, and Redis cache. Each scenario deploys a part of this app with intentional bugs — your job is to find and fix them. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario before applying!

📌 S1–S3: PVC Binding & Expansion

S1
🧪 SCENARIO S1 — Category 1: Storage PVC Debug

Deploy easypj PostgreSQL — Fix PVC Stuck in Pending

The Problem: You deploy the easypj/jobpost PostgreSQL database using a StatefulSet with a PersistentVolumeClaim. The pod stays Pending because the PVC won't bind — the StorageClass name is misspelled as "fast-ssd" but the actual StorageClass is named "fast-ssd-sc". Your job: find the mismatch and fix it so the database starts correctly.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production-like cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy easypj PostgreSQL (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: easypj/jobpost is a Django job board app. Employers post jobs, applicants apply. PostgreSQL stores: users, jobs, applications. Redis caches: job listings, session data. Django serves: REST API at /api, admin at /admin. The database pod won't start because of a StorageClass typo — the entire job board is DOWN.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S1): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-storageclass.yaml           ← fast-ssd-sc (default, no-provisioner)
├── 02-persistentvolume.yaml       ← easypj-db-pv (hostPath, 10Gi)
├── 03-postgres-statefulset.yaml   ← StatefulSet with BUG in volumeClaimTemplates
└── 04-postgres-service.yaml       ← ClusterIP Service (port 5432)
BASH — Create the StorageClass + Deploy PostgreSQL with bug 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S1: PVC Stuck in Pending — StorageClass Mismatch
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE THE STORAGECLASS (correct name: fast-ssd-sc)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd-sc
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
EOF

# 3. CREATE THE PV (static provisioning)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: easypj-db-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: fast-ssd-sc
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/easypj-db
EOF

# 4. DEPLOY STATEFULSET (BUG: storageClassName: "fast-ssd" in volumeClaimTemplates)
# Note: no standalone PVC needed — volumeClaimTemplates auto-generates one per pod
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
# StatefulSet — PostgreSQL Database for easypj/jobpost
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: easypj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: db-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
      storageClassName: fast-ssd  # ❌ BUG! Same typo here
---
# Service — ClusterIP for PostgreSQL (port 5432)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n easypj
✗2. Check PVC: kubectl get pvc -n easypj → STATUS: Pending
✗3. Check pod events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj easypj-db-0 → "persistentvolumeclaim not found" or "pod has unbound PVC"
✗4. The database pod cannot start — job board is DOWN!
3

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Describe the PVC: kubectl describe pvc -n easypj db-data-easypj-db-0 (auto-generated by volumeClaimTemplates — StatefulSets never need a separately authored PVC)
→ Events: "storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'fast-ssd' not found"
2Check available StorageClasses: kubectl get sc
→ Only "fast-ssd-sc" exists (with (default) annotation)
3Check PVC storageClassName: kubectl get pvc -n easypj -o yaml | grep storageClassName
→ storageClassName: fast-ssd (WRONG!)
4Compare: PVC says fast-ssd — StorageClass is fast-ssd-sc
5Root cause: Typo in storageClassName — "fast-ssd" instead of "fast-ssd-sc"
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod Pending → Check Events
②
PVC not binding → Check SC name
③
kubectl get sc → "fast-ssd-sc" exists
④
PVC says "fast-ssd" → MISMATCH!
⑤
Delete StatefulSet → Recreate → Pod starts → DB ready

Tenet: When a PVC stays Pending, the #1 cause is a StorageClass name mismatch. The StorageClass must exist with the EXACT name specified. On a StatefulSet, volumeClaimTemplates are IMMUTABLE — you must DELETE the StatefulSet and recreate it with the corrected StorageClass. Never try to patch or edit a running StatefulSet's PVC template. On the CKA exam, "PVC stuck Pending due to StorageClass typo" is one of the most common tasks.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-db-0 0/1 Pending 0 2m
$ kubectl describe pod easypj-db-0 -n easypj | tail -5 Events: Warning FailedScheduling pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims Warning ProvisioningFailed storageclass.storage.k8s.io "fast-ssd" not found
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY STORAGECLASS db-data-easypj-db-0 Pending fast-ssd ← Wrong SC!
$ kubectl get sc NAME PROVISIONER RECLAIMPOLICY VOLUMEBINDINGMODE fast-ssd-sc (default) kubernetes.io/no-provisioner Retain WaitForFirstConsumer
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY STORAGECLASS db-data-easypj-db-0 Bound easypj-db-pv 10Gi fast-ssd-sc ✅
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-db-0 1/1 Running 0 30s
$ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-db-0 -- psql -U easypj -d jobpost -c "SELECT 1;" ?column? ---------- 1 (1 row) ✅ Database is operational!
5

🔧 Fix — Delete StatefulSet & Recreate with Correct StorageClass

BASH — Delete and recreate (volumeClaimTemplates are immutable) 
# Step 1: Delete the broken StatefulSet (volumeClaimTemplates are IMMUTABLE — can't edit)
# Also delete the PVCs it created so the new StatefulSet starts fresh
kubectl delete statefulset easypj-db -n easypj
kubectl delete pvc db-data-easypj-db-0 -n easypj 2>/dev/null

# Step 2: Recreate StatefulSet with CORRECT storageClassName in volumeClaimTemplates
# ⚠️ The volumeClaimTemplates auto-generates PVC named db-data-easypj-db-0
# You do NOT need a separate PVC — the StatefulSet creates it automatically
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: easypj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: db-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
      storageClassName: fast-ssd-sc  # ✅ FIXED!
---
# Service — ClusterIP for easypj-db
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
EOF

# Step 3: Wait for pod to be Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/easypj-db-0 -n easypj --timeout=120s
6

✅ Verify — Database Is Running

After deleting and recreating the StatefulSet with the corrected storageClassName: fast-ssd-sc, the volumeClaimTemplate auto-generates PVC db-data-easypj-db-0. It binds to the PV, PostgreSQL initializes, and the job board database is ready. kubectl get pods -n easypj shows easypj-db-0 Running 1/1 and kubectl get pvc -n easypj shows db-data-easypj-db-0 STATUS: Bound.

💡 Key takeaway: StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates are immutable — you cannot patch or edit them on a running StatefulSet. The only fix is to delete and recreate; deleting/scaling down a StatefulSet does NOT delete its PVCs by default (a deliberate data-safety guarantee), which is why the fix explicitly deletes the PVC too. The template auto-generates PVCs named <template-name>-<statefulset-name>-<ordinal>. You never need to create PVCs manually for a StatefulSet. One more portability note: this scenario's PV uses hostPath, which is pinned to whatever single node it was created on — fine here on a 1-node cluster, but on a real multi-node cluster a hostPath-backed PV only works if the pod actually gets scheduled onto that exact node (Kubernetes provides no built-in affinity for this), which is why production clusters use local volumes (with node affinity) or a networked CSI driver instead.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv easypj-db-pv

# Delete the StorageClass
kubectl delete sc fast-ssd-sc

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv,sc -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null
S2
🧪 SCENARIO S2 — Category 1: Storage AccessMode Debug

RWO vs RWX — Two easypj API Pods Fighting Over One Volume

The Problem: You deploy two replicas of the easypj-api pod for high availability. Both need to share a single PersistentVolume that stores user session data. One pod starts fine on node-1. The second pod stays Pending forever on node-2 because the PV uses ReadWriteOnce (RWO) — which means only ONE node can mount the volume at a time. Your job: understand Kubernetes accessModes, diagnose why the second pod can't start, and implement the correct fix.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy easypj API with Shared Session Volume (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: easypj/jobpost is a Django job board application. The API tier (easypj-api) serves REST endpoints for job listings. It needs HIGH AVAILABILITY — 2 replicas across 2 nodes. User session data (login tokens, cart state) is stored in a shared volume at /var/lib/sessions. With RWO, the 2nd pod on node-2 can't mount the volume. Result: API is a single-point-of-failure! If node-1 crashes, sessions are lost AND the API is down.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S2): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml               ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-persistentvolume.yaml        ← PV with RWO access (BUG!)
├── 02-persistentvolumeclaim.yaml   ← PVC requesting 1Gi
├── 03-api-deployment.yaml          ← Deployment with 2 replicas
└── 04-api-service.yaml             ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
BASH — Create PV + PVC + Deployment with RWO bug 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S2: RWO vs RWX — Two Pods, One Volume
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE THE PV WITH RWO (the intentional bug)
# RWO = ReadWriteOnce = a SINGLE node can mount this volume
# With 2 pods on 2 different nodes, the 2nd pod WILL fail
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: easypj-session-pv
  labels:
    app: easypj
    purpose: session-storage
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce    # ❌ BUG! Only ONE node can mount at a time
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/easypj-sessions
    type: DirectoryOrCreate
EOF

# 3. CREATE THE PVC (matches the PV)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: easypj-session-pvc
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
  storageClassName: manual
EOF

# 4. DEPLOY EASYPJ API WITH 2 REPLICAS (triggers the bug)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj
    tier: api
spec:
  replicas: 2    # ❌ With RWO, only 1 pod can mount the volume!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: session-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/sessions
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:          # ← Forces pods to DIFFERENT nodes
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj-api
            topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname"
      volumes:
      - name: session-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: easypj-session-pvc
---
# Service — ClusterIP for easypj-api
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide → BOTH pods show Running (one on node-1, one on node-2) — looks healthy!
✗2. Write a session file via pod-1, then try to read it via pod-2: kubectl exec ... pod-2 -- cat /var/lib/sessions/test.txt → No such file!
✗3. No error events anywhere — kubectl describe pod on either pod shows nothing wrong
✗4. Session data is silently NOT shared — users get logged out randomly depending on which pod handles their request!
3

🔍 Debug — Find Why the Second Pod Can't Start

1Check PV accessModes: kubectl get pv easypj-session-pv -o yaml | grep -A3 accessModes
→ accessModes: ReadWriteOnce — but both pods mounted it anyway!
2Check pod distribution: kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide
→ Pod-1 on node-1, Pod-2 on node-2 — BOTH Running, no scheduling block at all
3Check volume type: kubectl get pv easypj-session-pv -o yaml | grep -A2 hostPath
→ hostPath: path /mnt/data/easypj-sessions — a LOCAL directory on whatever node the pod lands on
4Key insight: RWO's "single node" guarantee is enforced by the scheduler's attach/detach machinery — which only applies to attachable volume types (cloud disks, CSI). hostPath is NOT attachable, so kube-scheduler never blocks a second node from scheduling a pod that references it. Each node just silently resolves the same path to its OWN local filesystem.
5Root cause: hostPath's accessMode is effectively decorative for cross-node enforcement — it doesn't stop 2 nodes from independently using the SAME path with completely isolated data. For genuinely shared storage across multiple nodes, you need ReadWriteMany (RWX) backed by real networked storage (NFS, EFS, GlusterFS, CephFS) — OR pod affinity to co-locate both pods on the same node so they share the same local disk.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Deploy 2 replicas → both Running (no error!)
②
Write via pod-1, read via pod-2 → file missing
③
Check PV → hostPath, ReadWriteOnce
④
hostPath isn't attachable → RWO never enforced
⑤
Fix: podAffinity or real RWX storage

Tenet: Understanding accessModes is critical for the CKA exam — but so is knowing WHERE they're enforced. RWO (ReadWriteOnce) allows mounting by a SINGLE node — it does NOT mean "one pod" — multiple pods on the SAME node can share an RWO volume. That single-node guarantee is enforced by the scheduler's attach/detach logic, which only applies to attachable volume types (cloud disks, CSI). hostPath isn't attachable, so nothing stops a second node from silently using its own local copy of the same path — no error, no Pending pod, just silently unshared data. For production shared storage across real nodes, you MUST use RWX-capable networked storage (NFS, EFS, GlusterFS) or use pod affinity to co-locate pods on one node. Always check the volume TYPE, not just the accessMode, before trusting "shared storage" claims.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS NODE easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-abcde 1/1 Running 0 node-1 easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-xyz12 1/1 Running 0 node-2 ← Both Running, looks fine!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-abcde -- sh -c "echo session_abc > /var/lib/sessions/test.txt" $ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-xyz12 -- cat /var/lib/sessions/test.txt cat: /var/lib/sessions/test.txt: No such file or directory ← ❌ Not shared!
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-xyz12 | tail -5 Events: Type Reason Age From Message ---- ------ ---- ---- ------- Normal Scheduled 2m default-scheduler Successfully assigned to node-2 Normal Started 2m kubelet Started container api ← No warnings at all!
$ kubectl get pv easypj-session-pv -o yaml | grep -A2 "accessModes\|hostPath" accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce hostPath: path: /mnt/data/easypj-sessions ← ❌ Local path, resolved independently per node!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (podAffinity — both pods on same node)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS NODE easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-new1 1/1 Running 0 node-1 easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-new2 1/1 Running 0 node-1
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- wget -qO- http://localhost:80 <!DOCTYPE html> <html> <head><title>Welcome to nginx!</title></head> <body><h1>Welcome to nginx on easypj API!</h1></body> </html> ✅ Both API pods serving traffic — job board is HIGHLY AVAILABLE!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- sh -c "echo 'session_data_here' > /var/lib/sessions/test.txt && cat /var/lib/sessions/test.txt" session_data_here ✅ Both pods share the same session volume (same node)
5

🔧 Fix — Three Solutions (Choose Based on Your Environment)

BASH — Fix options for the RWO multi-pod problem 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
# SOLUTION A: Pod Affinity (Quick Fix — CKA Exam)
# Force both pods to schedule on the SAME node
# RWO works when both pods are on the same node
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 1: Delete the old Deployment
kubectl delete deploy easypj-api -n easypj

# Step 2: Recreate with podAffinity — both pods on same node
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj-api
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname    # ✅ Both pods on SAME node
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: session-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/sessions
      volumes:
      - name: session-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: easypj-session-pvc
EOF

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
# SOLUTION B: Scale to 1 (Simplest — Dev/Test)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
kubectl scale deploy easypj-api -n easypj --replicas=1

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
# SOLUTION C: Use RWX Storage (Production)
# Create an NFS server and change PV to RWX:
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
# 1. Install NFS server on a node:
#    sudo apt-get install nfs-kernel-server
#    sudo mkdir -p /srv/nfs/easypj-sessions
#    echo "/srv/nfs/easypj-sessions *(rw,sync,no_root_squash)" | sudo tee -a /etc/exports
#    sudo exportfs -a
#
# 2. Create PV with RWX:
#    apiVersion: v1
#    kind: PersistentVolume
#    metadata:
#      name: easypj-session-pv-rwx
#    spec:
#      capacity:
#        storage: 1Gi
#      accessModes:
#      - ReadWriteMany    # ✅ RWX = many nodes!
#      nfs:
#        server: <NFS-SERVER-IP>
#        path: /srv/nfs/easypj-sessions
6

✅ Verify — Both Pods Running & Sharing Data

With podAffinity applied: kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide now shows both pods Running on the same node. The API is highly available. Both pods can read/write to the shared session volume at /var/lib/sessions. For production: migrate to RWX storage (NFS/EFS/GlusterFS) so pods can run on different nodes with full data sharing.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv easypj-session-pv

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null
S3
🧪 SCENARIO S3 — Category 1: Storage PVC Expansion

Expand PVC for Growing jobpost Database

The Problem: The easypj/jobpost PostgreSQL database is running low on disk (5Gi PVC almost full). You patch the PVC from 5Gi to 20Gi. The patch succeeds but the PVC stays at 5Gi. The StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: false. Your job: enable expansion and grow the database volume.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production-like cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy PostgreSQL with Small PVC (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: easypj/jobpost launched 6 months ago with a 5Gi database. Now there are 50,000 job listings, 10,000 users, 200,000 applications. The DB is at 92% capacity — INSERTs are failing! DevOps patches PVC to 20Gi — but nothing happens. The StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: false. Lesson: Always set allowVolumeExpansion: true on production SCs!
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S3): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml               ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-storageclass.yaml            ← SC with allowVolumeExpansion: false (BUG!)
├── 02-persistentvolume.yaml        ← 5Gi PV (hostPath)
├── 03-postgres-statefulset.yaml    ← StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates (5Gi, too small)
└── 04-postgres-service.yaml        ← ClusterIP Service (port 5432)
BASH — SC + PV + PVC + StatefulSet 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S3: PVC Binding Failure — StorageClass allowVolumeExpansion
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE STORAGECLASS + PV + PVC + STATEFULSET (BUG: allowVolumeExpansion: false)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: expandable-sc
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
allowVolumeExpansion: false    # ❌ BUG! Blocks PVC resize
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
---
# PersistentVolume — 20Gi hostPath PV
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: easypj-db-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi   # Matches the PVC request — a statically-bound PVC always reports the PV's actual capacity, not the requested amount
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: expandable-sc
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/easypj-db-s3
---
# StatefulSet — PostgreSQL with volumeClaimTemplates (auto-generates its own PVC, no standalone PVC needed)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: easypj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: db-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 5Gi
      storageClassName: expandable-sc
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Try to Expand, It Fails

✗1. Try resize: kubectl patch pvc db-data-easypj-db-0 -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'
✗2. Check PVC: kubectl get pvc -n easypj → CAPACITY still 5Gi
✗3. Describe PVC: "FileSystemResizePending" — not progressing
✗4. Database filling up — jobpost may crash!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Won't the PVC Expand?

1Check SC: kubectl get sc expandable-sc -o yaml | grep allowVolumeExpansion
→ allowVolumeExpansion: false — BLOCKED!
2Check PVC conditions: kubectl get pvc -n easypj -o yaml
→ FileSystemResizePending but SC blocks it
3Root cause: StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: false. PVC resize request is recorded but never executed. Must enable expansion on SC first.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
PVC patch → Size unchanged
②
Check SC → allowVolumeExpansion: false
③
Enable expansion → Restart pod
④
PVC resized → DB has room

Tenet: PVC expansion needs: (1) SC allowVolumeExpansion:true, (2) PVC spec updated, (3) Pod restarted. On CKA: always check kubectl get sc -o yaml | grep allowVolumeExpansion when resize fails.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl patch pvc db-data-easypj-db-0 -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}' persistentvolumeclaim/db-data-easypj-db-0 patched
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS CAPACITY db-data-easypj-db-0 Bound 5Gi ← STILL 5Gi!
$ kubectl get sc expandable-sc -o yaml | grep allow allowVolumeExpansion: false ← BLOCKED!
$ kubectl describe pvc -n easypj db-data-easypj-db-0 | grep -A3 Conditions Conditions: Type: FileSystemResizePending Status: True
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS CAPACITY db-data-easypj-db-0 Bound 20Gi ← EXPANDED!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sdb 20G 1.2G 19G 6% /var/lib/postgresql/data ✅
5

🔧 Fix — Enable Volume Expansion

BASH — Enable expansion + patch PVC + restart pod 
# Step 1: Enable volume expansion
kubectl patch sc expandable-sc -p '{"allowVolumeExpansion": true}'

# Step 2: hostPath/no-provisioner storage has NO CSI resizer — the built-in expand-volume
# controller can't grow it for you. For statically-provisioned storage like this, the admin
# must confirm the underlying disk actually has the room, then patch the PV's declared
# capacity directly (PV.spec.capacity, unlike a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates, IS editable):
kubectl patch pv easypj-db-pv -p '{"spec":{"capacity":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}'

# Step 3: Patch PVC to 20Gi (now that the bound PV is declared big enough to satisfy it)
kubectl patch pvc db-data-easypj-db-0 -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'

# Step 4: Restart StatefulSet to trigger filesystem resize
kubectl rollout restart statefulset easypj-db -n easypj

# Step 5: Wait and verify
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=easypj-db -n easypj --timeout=120s
kubectl get pvc -n easypj
kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data
6

✅ Verify — PVC Expanded to 20Gi

kubectl get pvc -n easypj shows CAPACITY: 20Gi. The filesystem inside the pod has 20Gi usable. jobpost can grow for months.

💡 Key takeaway: a statically-bound PVC always reports the bound PV's actual capacity, not the amount it originally requested — that's why the PV here starts at exactly 5Gi (matching the PVC), not pre-sized to 20Gi. hostPath/no-provisioner storage has no CSI resizer behind it, so the SC-level allowVolumeExpansion flag alone can't grow it — for statically-provisioned storage, the admin must also patch the PV object's own spec.capacity directly (confirming the underlying disk really has the room) before the PVC's requested size can be honored. True online expansion (where a real CSI driver resizes the backing block device automatically) requires a dynamically-provisioned CSI/cloud-disk StorageClass — this drill shows the manual, static-storage equivalent of that same workflow.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv easypj-db-pv

# Delete the StorageClass
kubectl delete sc expandable-sc

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv,sc -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null

📌 S4–S6: ConfigMap, emptyDir & Secret Volumes

S4
🧪 SCENARIO S4 — Category 1: Storage ConfigMap Volume

ConfigMap as Volume — Mount nginx Config into easypj-web

The Problem: You mount a custom nginx config into the easypj-web pod via ConfigMap as a volume, using subPath. Later you update the ConfigMap — but the pod still serves the OLD config. subPath prevents automatic ConfigMap updates from reaching the mounted file. Your job: understand subPath behavior and fix the config delivery.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy ConfigMap + Pod with subPath (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-web pod serves the job board frontend via nginx. DevOps mounts a custom nginx config via ConfigMap + subPath. They update the ConfigMap to change from VERSION-1 to VERSION-2. But the pod still says "VERSION-1" — subPath BLOCKS live updates! Lesson: subPath mounts are STATIC snapshots. For live ConfigMap updates, mount the ENTIRE directory (not a subPath file).
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S4): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml        ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-configmap.yaml        ← nginx config (VERSION-1)
└── 02-web-deployment.yaml   ← Deployment with subPath mount (BUG!)
BASH — ConfigMap + Pod with subPath bug 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S4: ConfigMap subPath — Updates Not Reflected in Pod
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE CONFIGMAP + DEPLOYMENT (BUG: subPath blocks ConfigMap auto-updates)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-config
  namespace: easypj
data:
  default.conf: |
    server {
      listen 80;
      location / { return 200 "VERSION-1"; }
    }
---
# Deployment — easypj-web Nginx with subPath mount (BUG)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-web
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-vol
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
          subPath: default.conf    # ❌ BUG! subPath blocks updates
      volumes:
      - name: config-vol
        configMap:
          name: nginx-config
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — ConfigMap Updated, Pod Serves Old Config

✗1. Update ConfigMap: kubectl patch cm nginx-config -n easypj --type merge -p '{"data":{"default.conf":"server { listen 80; location / { return 200 \"VERSION-2\"; } }"}}'
✗2. Wait 2 min (kubelet sync period) — check pod: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost → Still "VERSION-1"!
✗3. ConfigMap updated — pod NOT reflecting changes!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Isn't the Config Refreshing?

1Check mount: kubectl describe pod -n easypj easypj-web | grep -A5 Mounts
→ subPath: default.conf — prevents symlink updates!
2Check ConfigMap hash: kubectl get cm nginx-config -n easypj -o yaml | head
→ ConfigMap IS updated — but pod can't see it
3Root cause: subPath mounts use bind-mount of a specific file. The kubelet does NOT update subPath mounts when the ConfigMap changes. Without subPath, the entire directory is a symlink that gets refreshed.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Update CM → Pod unchanged
②
Check mount → subPath used
③
subPath = no auto-update
④
Remove subPath or restart pod

Tenet: subPath mounts are static file bind-mounts. They do NOT receive ConfigMap updates. For auto-updating configs, mount the entire ConfigMap as a directory (no subPath). On CKA: if config updates aren't reflected in pods, check for subPath usage.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost VERSION-1
$ kubectl get cm nginx-config -n easypj -o yaml | grep VERSION location / { return 200 "VERSION-2"; } ← ConfigMap IS updated!
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -l app=easypj-web -o yaml | grep subPath subPath: default.conf ← Blocks auto-refresh!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost VERSION-2 ✅ Config refreshed!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-web -- cat /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf server { listen 80; location / { return 200 "VERSION-2"; } }
5

🔧 Fix — Remove subPath or Restart Pod

BASH — Fix options 
# Option A: Remove subPath — recreate Deployment without subPath
kubectl delete deploy easypj-web -n easypj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-web
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config-vol
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d    # ✅ No subPath — auto-updates work
      volumes:
      - name: config-vol
        configMap:
          name: nginx-config
EOF

# Option B: Trigger restart to pick up new ConfigMap
kubectl rollout restart deploy easypj-web -n easypj

# Option C: Use checksum annotation to force restart on CM change
kubectl patch deploy easypj-web -n easypj --patch "
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: $(kubectl get cm nginx-config -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data}' | sha256sum)"
6

✅ Verify — Config Refreshes Automatically

After removing subPath, kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost shows VERSION-2. Future ConfigMap changes will propagate within ~1 min (kubelet sync period).

kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get cm,pods -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null
S5
🧪 SCENARIO S5 — Category 1: Storage emptyDir vs Persistent

emptyDir vs Persistent — Data After Pod Restart

The Problem: You deploy Redis for the jobpost cache using an emptyDir volume. Redis stores session data and cached job listings. The pod gets evicted or restarted — and all the cached data is GONE. emptyDir is ephemeral — data lives only as long as the pod. Your job: understand when to use emptyDir vs PersistentVolume and migrate Redis to durable storage.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Quick dev/test cluster for volume demos
1

📋 Deploy Redis with emptyDir (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj/jobpost platform uses Redis for session cache and job listing caching. After a routine pod eviction, users report losing their session state. All cached job listings need re-fetching from the PostgreSQL DB — causing a 500ms latency spike. DevOps discovers Redis was deployed with emptyDir — all data vanished on pod restart! Lesson: NEVER use emptyDir for stateful workloads. Use PVC for databases, caches, and any data that must survive pod restarts.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S5): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml        ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-redis-deployment.yaml  ← emptyDir volume (BUG! data lost on restart)
BASH — Redis Pod with emptyDir volume 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S5: emptyDir — Data Lost on Pod Restart
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE REDIS DEPLOYMENT + SERVICE (BUG: emptyDir loses data on restart)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-redis
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-redis
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-redis
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: redis
        image: redis:7-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
        volumeMounts:
        - name: redis-data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: redis-data
        emptyDir: {}    # ❌ BUG! Ephemeral — data lost on restart
---
# Service — ClusterIP for Redis (port 6379)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-redis
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-redis}
  ports:
  - port: 6379
EOF

# Load test data into Redis
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli SET job-count 500
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli SET last-crawl "2025-06-04"
2

⚠️ Observe — Kill the Pod, Data Disappears

✗1. Verify data exists: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count → "500"
✗2. Kill the pod: kubectl delete pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis
✗3. Pod restarts — check data: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count → (nil) — DATA GONE!
✗4. Cached job listings, session data — ALL LOST!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the Data Gone?

1Check volume type: kubectl get pod -n easypj easypj-redis -o yaml | grep -A2 emptyDir
→ emptyDir: {} — no backing storage!
2Understand emptyDir: emptyDir is tied to the pod's lifecycle. It's created when the pod starts on a node and destroyed when the pod is removed.
3Root cause: emptyDir is ephemeral storage. When the pod restarts (even on same node), a new emptyDir is created — all previous data is lost. For databases/caches, use PersistentVolume instead.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Data written to /data
②
Pod deleted → emptyDir destroyed
③
New pod → new emptyDir
④
Data gone → Use PVC instead

Tenet: emptyDir = scratch space, caching, temp files. PersistentVolume = databases, stateful apps. On CKA: if asked to preserve data across pod restarts, NEVER use emptyDir. Always use PVC+PV.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli SET job-count 500 OK
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count "500"
$ kubectl delete pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis pod "easypj-redis-xxxxx" deleted
$ sleep 3 && kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count (nil) ← DATA GONE! emptyDir wiped with pod
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (with PVC)
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count "500"
$ kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-redis -n easypj && sleep 5 && kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count "500" ✅ Data survived pod restart with PVC!
5

🔧 Fix — Migrate to PersistentVolume

BASH — PVC + PV for Redis 
# Step 1: Create PV + PVC
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: easypj-redis-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 2Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ""   # minikube ships a default StorageClass — must explicitly opt OUT to force static binding to this PV
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/easypj-redis
---
# PersistentVolumeClaim — 2Gi for Redis (replaces emptyDir)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: easypj-redis-pvc
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ""   # omitting this would let the DefaultStorageClass admission controller dynamically provision instead of binding to easypj-redis-pv
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 2Gi
EOF

# Step 2: Recreate Redis Deployment with PVC
kubectl delete deploy easypj-redis -n easypj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-redis
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-redis
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-redis
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: redis
        image: redis:7-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
        volumeMounts:
        - name: redis-data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: redis-data
        persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: easypj-redis-pvc}    # ✅ Durable!
EOF

# Step 3: Test persistence
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli SET job-count 500
kubectl delete pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis
sleep 5
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count    # Should return "500"!
6

✅ Verify — Data Survives Pod Restart

After migrating to PVC: delete the Redis pod, wait for recreation, run redis-cli GET job-count → returns "500". Data persists because the PVC outlives the pod. jobpost cache is now durable.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv easypj-redis-pv

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null
S6
🧪 SCENARIO S6 — Category 1: Storage Secret Injection

Secret as Environment Variable — Database Password for easypj-api

The Problem: The easypj-api Deployment references a Secret named easypj-db-credentials for the PostgreSQL password via secretKeyRef. But the Secret was never created. The API pod starts but can't connect to the database — it crashes with password authentication failed because the env var is empty. Your job: create the Secret correctly and verify the API connects.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy API referencing non-existent Secret (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj/jobpost API needs a PostgreSQL password to connect. The DevOps team used secretKeyRef in the Deployment manifest but forgot to create the Secret first. The pod starts but can't authenticate — users see "500 Internal Server Error" on the job board. Lesson: Always create Secrets BEFORE Deployments that reference them. Use kubectl create secret generic for quick Secret creation.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S6): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← References missing Secret (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy API pod referencing missing Secret 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S6: Missing Secret — secretKeyRef Points to Non-Existent Secret
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: secretKeyRef references non-existent Secret)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c","echo DB_PASS=$DB_PASSWORD; sleep 3600"]
        env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: easypj-db-credentials    # ❌ BUG! Secret doesn't exist
              key: password
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Can't Access Database

✗1. Check pod status: kubectl get pods -n easypj → CreateContainerConfigError (container never starts!)
✗2. Try logs anyway: kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api → error, container has never been created — no logs exist
✗3. Check events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj → "Error: secret \"easypj-db-credentials\" not found"
✗4. API pod can't even start — jobpost is completely DOWN, not just degraded!
3
