🔍 Debug — Find the Missing Secret

1Check if Secret exists: kubectl get secrets -n easypj
→ No "easypj-db-credentials" found!
2Check Deployment env ref: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A5 secretKeyRef
→ References secret "easypj-db-credentials" key "password"
3Root cause: Secret was never created. Since DB_PASSWORD's secretKeyRef is non-optional (the default), the kubelet refuses to start the container AT ALL until the Secret exists — it does NOT silently start with an empty env var.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod CreateContainerConfigError → Check events
②
"secret not found" → Check Secret ref
③
Secret missing → Create it
④
Container starts → App working

Tenet: Secrets must exist BEFORE pods that reference them. A non-optional secretKeyRef pointing at a missing Secret blocks the container from starting AT ALL — kubelet reports CreateContainerConfigError and keeps retrying; it does NOT start with an empty env var. On CKA: always verify Secrets exist with kubectl get secrets -n <ns> before deploying workloads.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secrets -n easypj No resources found in easypj namespace.
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-abcde 0/1 CreateContainerConfigError 0
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-abcde | tail -5 Warning Failed Error: secret "easypj-db-credentials" not found
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get secrets -n easypj NAME TYPE DATA easypj-db-credentials Opaque 2
$ kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api DB_PASS=secret123 ✅ Secret injected!
5

🔧 Fix — Create the Secret

BASH — Create Secret + restart Deployment 
# Step 1: Create the Secret (base64 encode the password)
kubectl create secret generic easypj-db-credentials   --from-literal=password=secret123   --from-literal=username=easypj   -n easypj

# Step 2: Verify Secret
kubectl get secret easypj-db-credentials -n easypj
kubectl get secret easypj-db-credentials -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

# Step 3: Restart Deployment to pick up Secret
kubectl rollout restart deploy easypj-api -n easypj

# Step 4: Verify env var is now set
kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api
# Should show: DB_PASS=secret123
6

✅ Verify — Secret Injected Correctly

kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api shows DB_PASS=secret123. The API can now authenticate to PostgreSQL. On CKA: use kubectl create secret generic for quick Secret creation.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything (Secret included)
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get secrets,deploy,pods -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null

📌 S7–S10: Volume Types & Storage Limits

S7
🧪 SCENARIO S7 — Category 1: Storage PV Capacity Mismatch

PV Capacity Mismatch — PVC Stuck Pending, No PV Big Enough

The Problem: Now that you understand PV/PVC binding from S1-S6, let's explore what happens when a PVC needs MORE capacity than any available PV can provide. You create a PersistentVolume with only 5Gi of storage, but your PVC requests 20Gi for the easypj/jobpost database. The PVC stays Pending forever because no PV has enough capacity. Kubernetes PV binding is all-or-nothing — the PV must satisfy ALL three PVC requirements: capacity, accessMode, AND storageClassName. Your job: understand capacity matching and fix the sizing issue.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production-like cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy Undersized PV + Oversized PVC (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: easypj/jobpost started small with a 5Gi database volume. 6 months later: 50,000 listings, 200,000 applications. DevOps creates a PVC for 20Gi but the old 5Gi PV still exists. Kubernetes WON'T partially satisfy a PVC — it's ALL or NOTHING. The PVC waits for a PV with ≥20Gi that matches all criteria. Lesson: Always check PV capacity BEFORE creating PVCs! PVC-PV binding requires capacity, accessMode, AND storageClassName to ALL match.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S7): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-persistentvolume.yaml     ← PV with 5Gi only (BUG! too small)
├── 02-pvc.yaml                  ← PVC requesting 20Gi (can't match!)
└── 03-postgres-statefulset.yaml ← StatefulSet that needs the DB volume
BASH — PV (5Gi) + PVC (20Gi) size mismatch 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S7: PV Capacity Mismatch — PVC Requests Exceed Available PV
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE PV (5Gi — BUG: too small for 20Gi PVC request)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: easypj-db-pv-small
  labels:
    app: easypj
    purpose: database
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi    # ❌ BUG! Only 5Gi — PVC wants 20Gi!
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/easypj-db-small
    type: DirectoryOrCreate
EOF

# 3. CREATE PVC REQUESTING 20Gi (will NEVER bind to 5Gi PV)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: easypj-db-pvc
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi    # ❌ BUG! 20Gi, but PV only has 5Gi
  storageClassName: manual
EOF

# 4. CREATE STATEFULSET (will stay Pending until PVC binds)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-db
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: easypj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
      - name: db-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: easypj-db-pvc
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — PVC Stuck Pending, PV Sitting Available

✗1. Check PVC: kubectl get pvc -n easypj → STATUS: Pending
✗2. Check PV: kubectl get pv → 5Gi PV exists but STATUS: Available
✗3. Describe PVC: kubectl describe pvc -n easypj easypj-db-pvc → "no matching PV found" or "PV is too small"
✗4. The database pod stays Pending — job board is DOWN!
3

🔍 Debug — Find Why the PVC Won't Bind

1Check PVC requested size: kubectl get pvc -n easypj -o yaml | grep storage
→ storage: 20Gi — PVC wants 20Gi
2Check PV capacity: kubectl get pv easypj-db-pv-small
→ CAPACITY: 5Gi — only 5Gi available!
3Check all PVs: kubectl get pv --sort-by=.spec.capacity.storage
→ Largest is 5Gi — none satisfy 20Gi
4Root cause: The PVC requests 20Gi but the only PV has 5Gi. PVC binding is ALL-OR-NOTHING — capacity, accessMode, AND storageClassName must all match. 5Gi < 20Gi = PVC stays Pending forever.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
PVC Pending → Check available PVs
②
Only a 5Gi PV exists, no ≥20Gi PV
③
PV: 5Gi vs PVC: 20Gi → MISMATCH
④
Create 20Gi PV → PVC binds → DB running

Tenet: PVC-to-PV binding requires a complete match on THREE criteria: (1) capacity — PV must have ≥ PVC request, (2) accessModes — must match, (3) storageClassName — must match. If any ONE criterion fails, the PVC stays Pending forever. On the CKA exam, capacity mismatch is one of the most common "broken PVC" scenarios. Always check ALL three when debugging.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY STORAGECLASS easypj-db-pvc Pending manual
$ kubectl get pv NAME CAPACITY ACCESS MODES STATUS CLAIM STORAGECLASS easypj-db-pv-small 5Gi RWO Available manual
$ kubectl describe pvc -n easypj easypj-db-pvc | tail -3 Events: Warning FailedBinding PV "easypj-db-pv-small" is too small (requested 20Gi, available 5Gi)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pv NAME CAPACITY ACCESS MODES STATUS CLAIM STORAGECLASS easypj-db-pv-large 20Gi RWO Bound easypj/easypj-db-pvc manual
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY easypj-db-pvc Bound easypj-db-pv-large 20Gi ✅
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-db 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ Database UP!
5

🔧 Fix — Create a 20Gi PV That Matches the PVC

BASH — Delete small PV + create large PV 
# Step 1: Delete the too-small 5Gi PV
kubectl delete pv easypj-db-pv-small

# Step 2: Create a NEW 20Gi PV that satisfies the PVC
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: easypj-db-pv-large
  labels:
    app: easypj
    purpose: database
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 20Gi    # ✅ NOW matches PVC request!
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual    # ✅ Matches PVC
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/easypj-db-large
    type: DirectoryOrCreate
EOF

# Step 3: Watch the PVC auto-bind
kubectl get pvc -n easypj -w
# STATUS: Pending → Bound  (within seconds!)

# Step 4: Restart StatefulSet to pick up the new volume
kubectl rollout restart statefulset easypj-db -n easypj
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=easypj-db -n easypj --timeout=120s
6

✅ Verify — PVC Bound & Database Running

kubectl get pvc -n easypj shows STATUS: Bound, CAPACITY: 20Gi. The database is running. Key takeaway: PV binding is ALL-OR-NOTHING. Capacity, accessMode, AND storageClassName must all match. Even one mismatch = PVC stuck forever.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv easypj-db-pv-large 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete pv easypj-db-pv-small 2>/dev/null

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null
S8
🧪 SCENARIO S8 — Category 1: Storage Permissions

Volume Mount Permission Denied — fsGroup Fix

The Problem: The easypj-db pod mounts a PersistentVolume, but PostgreSQL can't write to /var/lib/postgresql/data. Events show "permission denied". The container runs as user postgres (UID 999) but the volume is owned by root:root. Your job: use fsGroup in the pod's securityContext to fix permissions.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production-like cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy PostgreSQL with HostPath Volume (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj/jobpost PostgreSQL database pod keeps crashing with "permission denied" on /var/lib/postgresql/data. The volume is mounted but owned by root:root, while PostgreSQL runs as UID 999. DevOps is puzzled — the PV is bound, PVC is fine, but the pod won't start. Lesson: Always use securityContext.fsGroup to set volume group ownership for non-root containers.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S8): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-persistentvolume.yaml     ← hostPath PV owned by root
└── 02-postgres-statefulset.yaml ← Missing securityContext.fsGroup (BUG!)
BASH — Pod with missing fsGroup 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S8: Permission Denied — fsGroup Missing for Non-Root Container
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE PV + PVC + STATEFULSET (BUG: missing securityContext.fsGroup)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pg-data-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/pg-s8
---
# PersistentVolumeClaim — 5Gi request bound to pg-data-pv
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pg-data-pvc
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
---
# StatefulSet — PostgreSQL (BUG: missing fsGroup, root-owned volume)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-db
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      # ❌ BUG! No securityContext.fsGroup — volume owned by root
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
      - name: pgdata
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pg-data-pvc
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod CrashLoops with Permission Denied

✗1. Check pod: kubectl get pods -n easypj → CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. Check logs: kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-db-0 → "Permission denied" on /var/lib/postgresql/data
✗3. DB can't initialize — jobpost has no database!
3

🔍 Debug — Who Owns the Volume?

1Check volume permissions on node: ls -la /mnt/data/pg-s8 (if accessible)
→ drwxr-xr-x root:root — postgres can't write!
2Check container user: PostgreSQL runs as postgres (UID 999) inside container
3Root cause: No fsGroup set. The hostPath volume is owned by root:root, but postgres (UID 999) needs write access. Use securityContext.fsGroup to change volume ownership.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
CrashLoop → Check logs
②
Permission denied → Check ownership
③
Volume owned by root → fsGroup needed
④
Add fsGroup → Pod starts

Tenet: securityContext.fsGroup changes the group ownership of volume files to the specified GID. For PostgreSQL (UID 999), set fsGroup: 999. On CKA: when you see "permission denied" on a volume, check fsGroup.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-db-0 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 5
$ kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-db-0 initdb: error: could not access directory "/var/lib/postgresql/data": Permission denied
$ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-db-0 -- ls -la /var/lib/postgresql 2>/dev/null || echo "Can't exec - pod crashing" error: unable to upgrade connection: container not found ("postgres") # Note: Can't exec into CrashLoopBackOff pod — check node directly
$ ssh node-1 ls -la /mnt/data/pg-s8 total 4 drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jun 4 10:00 . drwxr-xr-x 3 root root 4096 Jun 4 10:00 .. ← Owner is root:root!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-db-0 1/1 Running 0 ✅
$ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-db-0 -- ls -la /var/lib/postgresql/data total 132 drwxr-xr-x 19 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 . drwxr-xr-x 3 root root 4096 Jun 4 10:05 .. drwx------ 6 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 base drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 global drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 pg_commit_ts ... ✅ fsGroup fixed ownership! postgres can write
5

🔧 Fix — Add fsGroup to securityContext

BASH — Delete StatefulSet, recreate with fsGroup 
# Step 1: Delete the broken StatefulSet
kubectl delete sts easypj-db -n easypj

# Step 2: Recreate StatefulSet with fsGroup
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-db
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999    # ✅ Fix! Changes volume group ownership to 999 (postgres)
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
      - name: pgdata
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pg-data-pvc
EOF

# Also works with runAsUser + fsGroup
# runAsUser: 999
# runAsGroup: 999
6

✅ Verify — PostgreSQL Initializes Successfully

kubectl get pods -n easypj shows Running 1/1. PostgreSQL can now write to the volume because fsGroup changed the group ownership to GID 999. The jobpost database is initialized.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv pg-data-pv

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null
S9
🧪 SCENARIO S9 — Category 1: Storage hostPath

hostPath Volume — Pod Rescheduled, Data Lost

The Problem: The easypj-redis pod uses a hostPath volume on node-1 to store cached data at /data/redis. The node fails and the pod is rescheduled to node-2. The pod starts but all cached data is GONE — hostPath data is tied to a specific node. Your job: understand hostPath limitations and migrate to a proper solution.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Quick dev/test cluster for hostPath demos
1

📋 Deploy Redis with hostPath on Node-1 (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj/jobpost Redis cache stores 500,000+ session entries on node-1 via hostPath at /data/redis. Node-1 suffers a hardware failure — the pod gets rescheduled to node-2. All 500,000 sessions are gone! Users are logged out, carts emptied, job drafts lost. Lesson: hostPath is node-specific. For portable storage across nodes, use PV+PVC with a network storage backend (NFS, CSI, etc.).
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S9): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml        ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-redis-deployment.yaml  ← hostPath volume (BUG! node-specific data)
BASH — Redis with hostPath (node-specific) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S9: hostPath — Node-Specific Data Lost on Pod Reschedule
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE REDIS DEPLOYMENT (BUG: hostPath data tied to node-1 only)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-redis
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-redis
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-redis
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: redis
        image: redis:7-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
        volumeMounts:
        - name: redis-data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: redis-data
        hostPath:
          path: /data/redis    # ❌ BUG! Data only on node-1
          type: DirectoryOrCreate
EOF

# 3. LOAD TEST DATA INTO REDIS
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli SET sessions 1000
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Moves, Data Disappears

✗1. Verify data: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions → "1000"
✗2. Simulate node-1 failure (cordon so the replacement CAN'T land back on it): kubectl cordon node-1 && kubectl delete pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis --force --grace-period=0
✗3. Pod rescheduled to node-2 (the only schedulable node) — check data: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions → (nil)
✗4. All user sessions LOST — jobpost users logged out!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is Data Lost?

1Check volume type: kubectl get pod -n easypj easypj-redis -o yaml | grep -A3 hostPath
→ hostPath: /data/redis on node-1's filesystem
2Check new pod's node: kubectl get pod -n easypj easypj-redis -o wide
→ Now on node-2! Different host filesystem
3Root cause: hostPath stores data on the NODE's filesystem. When the pod moves to a different node, the new node doesn't have the data. hostPath is for node-level daemons, not for application data.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod on node-1 → Data on /data/redis
②
Pod deleted → Rescheduled to node-2
③
New /data/redis empty → Data lost
④
Use PVC — data follows pod

Tenet: hostPath is NOT for application data. It's for node-level agents (Fluentd, monitoring). Application data MUST use PersistentVolumes with network storage (NFS/EBS/EFS) so data survives node/pod changes. On CKA: if asked about data loss after pod reschedule, check if hostPath is used.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions "1000"
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis -o wide NAME NODE easypj-redis-xxxxx node-1
$ kubectl cordon node-1 && kubectl delete pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis --force --grace-period=0 node/node-1 cordoned pod "easypj-redis-xxxxx" force deleted
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis -o wide NAME NODE easypj-redis-yyyyy node-2 ← Rescheduled!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions (nil) ← DATA LOST! New node doesn't have /data/redis
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (with PVC)
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions "1000"
$ kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-redis -n easypj && sleep 5 && kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions "1000" ✅ Data survived node change with PVC!
5

🔧 Fix — Migrate to PersistentVolume

BASH — Replace hostPath with PVC 
# Step 1: Create PV (simulating NFS/EBS)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: redis-data-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 2Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ""   # minikube ships a default StorageClass — must explicitly opt OUT to force static binding to this PV
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/shared/redis  # Would be NFS/EBS in production
---
# PersistentVolumeClaim — 2Gi for Redis (replaces hostPath)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: redis-data-pvc
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ""   # omitting this would trigger dynamic provisioning instead of binding to redis-data-pv
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 2Gi
EOF

# Step 2: Recreate Redis Deployment with PVC
kubectl delete deploy easypj-redis -n easypj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-redis
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-redis
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-redis
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: redis
        image: redis:7-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
        volumeMounts:
        - name: redis-data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: redis-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: redis-data-pvc  # ✅ Network-attached storage
EOF

# Step 3: Actually re-run the ORIGINAL failure test — uncordon node-1, force the pod
# onto a different node than it's currently on, and confirm data still survives.
# (A rollout restart alone proves nothing here — node-1 is still cordoned from
# Step 2, so the pod could only ever land back on node-2 by construction.)
kubectl uncordon node-1
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli SET sessions 1000
CURRENT_NODE=$(kubectl get pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.nodeName}')
kubectl cordon $CURRENT_NODE
kubectl delete pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis --force --grace-period=0
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=easypj-redis -n easypj --timeout=60s
kubectl get pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-redis -o wide   # confirm it actually landed on the OTHER node
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions   # still "1000" ✅
kubectl uncordon $CURRENT_NODE
6

✅ Verify — Data Survives Pod Reschedule

With PVC (backed by network storage), forcing the pod onto a genuinely different node than it was just running on still preserves the data — redis-cli GET sessions returns "1000" regardless of which node the pod lands on. In production, use NFS, EBS, or EFS for multi-node data persistence.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Uncordon node-1 (undo the simulated failure)
kubectl uncordon node-1

# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv redis-data-pv

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null
S10
🧪 SCENARIO S10 — Category 1: Storage ResourceQuota

ResourceQuota — PVC Limit Exceeded for easypj Namespace

The Problem: The easypj namespace has a ResourceQuota limiting PVC count to 2. You already have PVCs for PostgreSQL and Redis. When you try to create a third PVC for file uploads, kubectl returns "exceeded quota". Your job: diagnose the quota restriction and either increase the quota or delete unused PVCs.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy ResourceQuota + 2 PVCs, Then Attempt 3rd (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj/jobpost platform needs three PVCs: PostgreSQL (10Gi), Redis (5Gi), and file uploads (20Gi). DevOps sets a ResourceQuota limiting PVC count to 2 to control costs. When the uploads feature launches, the 3rd PVC creation fails — users can't upload resumes! Lesson: ResourceQuota enforces hard limits. Always plan quota capacity for future growth. Use kubectl describe resourcequota to see Used vs Hard.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S10): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-resourcequota.yaml        ← Limits PVC count to 2 (BUG!)
├── 02-postgres-pvc.yaml         ← PVC 1 — OK
├── 03-redis-pvc.yaml            ← PVC 2 — OK
└── 04-sessions-pvc.yaml         ← PVC 3 — BLOCKED by quota!
BASH — Quota + 2 PVCs + failed 3rd PVC 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S10: ResourceQuota — PVC Count Limit Exceeded
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE RESOURCEQUOTA + 2 PVCs (BUG: quota limits PVC count to 2)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: storage-quota
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  hard:
    persistentvolumeclaims: "2"    # ❌ BUG! Only 2 PVCs allowed
    requests.storage: "50Gi"
---
# PersistentVolumeClaim — pg-data (10Gi, slot 1/2)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pg-data
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
# PersistentVolumeClaim — redis-data (5Gi, slot 2/2)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: redis-data
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
EOF

# 3. ATTEMPT 3RD PVC — THIS WILL BE BLOCKED BY QUOTA
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: uploads-data
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — 3rd PVC Creation Fails

✗1. Try creating 3rd PVC: error → "exceeded quota: storage-quota, requested: persistentvolumeclaims=1, used: persistentvolumeclaims=2, limited: persistentvolumeclaims=2"
✗2. Check PVCs: kubectl get pvc -n easypj → Only 2 PVCs exist
✗3. File uploads feature blocked — jobpost can't accept resumes!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Can't I Create More PVCs?

1Check ResourceQuota: kubectl describe resourcequota storage-quota -n easypj
→ persistentvolumeclaims: Used=2, Hard=2 — AT LIMIT!
2Check used PVCs: kubectl get pvc -n easypj
→ pg-data + redis-data = 2/2 slots used
3Root cause: ResourceQuota hard limit persistentvolumeclaims: 2. No more PVCs can be created. Must increase quota or free up a slot.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
PVC creation fails → Check error
②
"exceeded quota" → Check ResourceQuota
③
Used=2 Hard=2 → At limit
④
Increase quota or delete unused PVC

Tenet: ResourceQuota enforces limits per namespace. kubectl describe resourcequota shows used vs hard. On CKA: when resources can't be created, check ResourceQuota and LimitRange first.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl apply -f uploads-pvc.yaml Error: failed to create PVC: exceeded quota "storage-quota"
$ kubectl describe resourcequota storage-quota -n easypj Name: storage-quota Resource Used Hard persistentvolumeclaims 2 2 ← AT LIMIT! requests.storage 15Gi 50Gi
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS CAPACITY pg-data Pending — redis-data Pending — ← 2/2 slots used
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe resourcequota storage-quota -n easypj Resource Used Hard persistentvolumeclaims 3 5 ← Quota increased!
$ kubectl get pvc -n easypj NAME STATUS CAPACITY pg-data Pending — redis-data Pending — uploads-data Pending — ← 3rd PVC created! ✅
5

🔧 Fix — Increase Quota or Delete Unused PVC

BASH — Fix quota limit 
# Option A: Increase PVC quota limit
kubectl patch resourcequota storage-quota -n easypj --type merge -p '{"spec":{"hard":{"persistentvolumeclaims":"5"}}}'

# Option B: Delete unused PVC to free a slot
kubectl delete pvc redis-data -n easypj

# Option C: Edit ResourceQuota directly
kubectl edit resourcequota storage-quota -n easypj
# Change persistentvolumeclaims from "2" to "5"

# Now create the 3rd PVC
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: uploads-data
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
EOF
kubectl get pvc -n easypj    # Should show 3 PVCs
6

✅ Verify — 3 PVCs Created Successfully

After increasing the quota, kubectl get pvc -n easypj shows 3 PVCs. File uploads feature can now provision storage. Always monitor ResourceQuota usage to avoid unexpected "exceeded quota" errors.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete All Resources

BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything (PVCs, ResourceQuota included)
kubectl delete namespace easypj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get pvc,resourcequota -n easypj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns easypj 2>/dev/null

🔧 Category 2: Troubleshooting Lab ScenariosS11-S40

🟡 Real-World Troubleshooting — Observe, Debug, Fix

Troubleshooting is 30% of the CKA exam. These scenarios teach the systematic approach: Observe → Hypothesize → Test → Fix. Each scenario presents a broken cluster or application — your job is to find the root cause and fix it using kubectl, systemctl, journalctl, and other diagnostic tools.

📌 S11–S16: Node, etcd & Image/App Failures

S11
🧪 SCENARIO S11 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Node Debug

Node NotReady — Debug kubelet with systemctl and journalctl

The Problem: Your node suddenly shows NotReady in kubectl get nodes. Pods scheduled on that node are stuck in Unknown or Terminating state. The kubelet service has stopped — the node can't report its status to the API server. Your job: SSH to the node, diagnose why kubelet is down using systemctl and journalctl, fix it, and bring the node back to Ready.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Requires SSH access to node "easy"
1

📋 Simulate a kubelet Failure (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: 3:00 AM — PagerDuty alert: "Node easy is NotReady". The jobpost database pod was running on this node. PostgreSQL is DOWN. 500 employers can't post jobs. You SSH in and find kubelet has crashed. Your job: diagnose WHY and bring it back. Lesson: systemctl and journalctl are your first tools when a node goes NotReady.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S11): 
easypj/
└── (No new files — troubleshoot existing cluster resources)
BASH — Run on your kubeadm node "easy" 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S11: Node NotReady — Kubelet Crash
# ============================================

# 1. VERIFY NODE IS CURRENTLY READY
kubectl get nodes
# NAME   STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
# easy   Ready    control-plane   7d    v1.32.13

# 2. SSH INTO THE NODE
# (If this IS your control plane node, just run locally)
# ssh easy  OR  run commands directly if you're already on it

# 3. STOP KUBELET (this is the BUG!)
sudo systemctl stop kubelet

# 4. VERIFY KUBELET IS STOPPED
sudo systemctl status kubelet
# ● kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent
#    Loaded: loaded
#    Active: inactive (dead)  ← ❌ BUG! Kubelet is DOWN!

# 5. WATCH NODE GO NotReady (~40 seconds)
kubectl get nodes -w
# easy   Ready    control-plane   7d    v1.32.13
# easy   NotReady   control-plane   7d    v1.32.13  ← BROKEN!
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Node Goes NotReady

✗1. kubectl get nodes — node shows NotReady
✗2. kubectl describe node easy | grep -A5 Conditions — Ready=Unknown
✗3. Pods on this node show Unknown or Terminating
✗4. Any workload on this node is UNREACHABLE — job board DOWN!
3

🔍 Debug — Find Why the Node Is NotReady

1Check node conditions: kubectl describe node easy | grep -A10 Conditions
→ Ready: Unknown — kubelet stopped posting status entirely!
2SSH to node, check kubelet: sudo systemctl status kubelet
→ Active: inactive (dead) — kubelet is STOPPED!
3Check kubelet logs for crash reason: sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager
→ Look for ERROR, FATAL, or OOM messages
4Check if kubelet config is valid: sudo kubelet --version && sudo cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml | head -5
→ Config looks valid — service was just stopped
5Root cause: kubelet service is stopped. The node can't report status to the API server, so after node-monitor-grace-period (default 40s), the control plane marks it NotReady. Node-level pods become Unknown.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Node NotReady → kubectl describe
②
Ready=Unknown → SSH to node
③
systemctl status → kubelet dead
④
journalctl -u kubelet → find cause
⑤
systemctl start kubelet → Ready!

Tenet: Node NotReady means the kubelet can't communicate with the API server. The diagnostic path: kubectl describe node → check conditions → SSH to node → systemctl status kubelet → journalctl -u kubelet → fix the issue → systemctl start kubelet. Common causes: kubelet crash, OOM, disk full, certificate expired, containerd not running. On CKA: you'll get a node NotReady and need to SSH in and fix it.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION easy NotReady control-plane 7d v1.32.13
$ kubectl describe node easy | grep -A3 " Ready " Ready Unknown Fri, 05 Jun 2026 03:15:00 Reason: NodeStatusUnknown Message: Kubelet stopped posting node status.
$ sudo systemctl status kubelet ● kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent Active: inactive (dead) ← KUBELET IS DOWN!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo systemctl start kubelet && sudo systemctl status kubelet ● kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent Active: active (running) ✅
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION easy Ready control-plane 7d v1.32.13 ✅ Back to Ready!
5

🔧 Fix — Restart Kubelet & Verify Node Recovery

BASH — Run on the broken node 
# Step 1: Start kubelet
sudo systemctl start kubelet

# Step 2: Verify it's running
sudo systemctl status kubelet

# Step 3: Check kubelet logs for any startup errors
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -f --since "1 min ago"

# Step 4: Back on your laptop — node should recover in ~40s
kubectl get nodes -w
# Watch: NotReady → Ready

# Step 5: Verify pods on this node recover
kubectl get pods -A -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=easy
6

✅ Verify — Node Back to Ready

kubectl get nodes shows Ready. All pods on this node are Running again. Key takeaway: systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet are your first stops when a node goes NotReady.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Restore Kubelet

BASH
sudo systemctl start kubelet
kubectl get nodes
S12
🧪 SCENARIO S12 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Memory Debug

Container OOMKilled — Memory Limit Set Too Low

The Problem: Your easypj-api pods keep getting killed with OOMKilled (exit code 137). This is a per-container cgroup limit being exceeded — a completely different mechanism from node-level memory pressure eviction. The Django API is consuming more memory than its limit allows, and the kernel's OOM killer is terminating it inside its own cgroup. Your job: identify which pods are being OOM killed, confirm it's a container-limit issue (not node pressure), adjust resource limits, and prevent future kills.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Node "easy" for memory pressure observation
1

📋 Deploy Memory-Hungry API Pod (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj API team deployed a new Django version. They copied resource limits from the staging environment. But production data is 10x bigger — Django needs 200MB+. The 50Mi limit triggers OOMKill within seconds. Customers see 502 errors. The job board is DOWN. Lesson: Always set resource limits based on PRODUCTION load testing, not staging defaults.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S12): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← memory limit 50Mi (BUG! too low)
BASH — Deploy easypj-api with insufficient memory limit 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S12: MemoryPressure — OOMKilled Due to Low Memory Limit
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: memory limit 50Mi, app needs 200MB+)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ["sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          pip install django>/dev/null 2>&1
          # Simulate Django memory usage — allocate ~200MB then sleep
          python3 -c "
          import time
          data = bytearray(200 * 1024 * 1024)  # 200MB allocation
          print(f'Allocated {len(data)} bytes, sleeping...')
          time.sleep(3600)
          "
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "32Mi"
          limits:
            memory: "50Mi"    # ❌ BUG! 50Mi limit but app needs 200MB+
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Keeps Crashing with OOMKilled

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → RESTARTS column keeps climbing
✗2. kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> → State: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137
✗3. kubectl top pod -n easypj → Memory usage near 50Mi limit
✗4. API keeps restarting — 502 errors for all job board users!
3

🔍 Debug — Find Why Pods Are Being Killed

1Check pod state: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A5 "State:"
→ OOMKilled (Exit Code: 137) — SIGKILL from kernel
2Rule out node-level pressure: kubectl describe node easy | grep -A5 Conditions
→ MemoryPressure: False — the NODE is fine, this is purely a per-container cgroup limit issue
3Check resource limits: kubectl get pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A3 limits
→ memory: 50Mi — WAY too low for Django!
4Root cause: Container memory limit (50Mi) is below the application's actual memory usage (200MB+). Once a container exceeds its own limit, the kernel OOM-kills it inside its cgroup — this happens regardless of overall node memory health. Fix: increase limits.memory to ≥256Mi.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod restarts → kubectl describe
②
State: OOMKilled → Exit 137
③
Check limits → 50Mi too low
④
Patch to 256Mi → Pod stable

Tenet: OOMKilled = container exceeded its memory limit. The kernel sends SIGKILL (exit code 137 = 128+9). Check kubectl describe pod for the OOMKilled reason. Fix: increase resources.limits.memory. On CKA: you'll see a CrashLoopBackOff pod — always check the LAST STATE for OOMKilled.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-xyz 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 8
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-xyz | grep -A10 "Last State" Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 ← SIGKILL from kernel OOM killer
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-api-7d8f9-new-abc 1/1 Running 0 ✅
5

🔧 Fix — Increase Memory Limit to 256Mi

BASH — Patch deployment with proper memory 
# Patch the Deployment with proper memory limits
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj -p '
{
  "spec": {
    "template": {
      "spec": {
        "containers": [{
          "name": "api",
          "resources": {
            "requests": {"memory": "128Mi"},
            "limits":   {"memory": "256Mi"}
          }
        }]
      }
    }
  }
}'

# Wait for rollout
kubectl rollout status deploy easypj-api -n easypj

# Verify no more OOMKilled
kubectl get pods -n easypj
kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep OOM
6

✅ Verify — Pod Running, No More OOM

Pod shows Running with no restarts. kubectl describe shows no OOMKilled events. Key rule: always set limits.memory ≥ actual app usage. For Django/Python: 128Mi minimum, 256Mi+ recommended for production.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S13
🧪 SCENARIO S13 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Disk Debug

DiskPressure — Node Runs Out of Disk Space

The Problem: Your kubeadm node shows DiskPressure=True. Container images and logs have filled up /var. Kubernetes starts evicting pods to reclaim space. New pods can't be scheduled. Your job: identify what's consuming disk space, clean up unused images and logs, and restore the node to healthy state.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Node "easy" for disk inspection
1

📋 Simulate DiskPressure (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Container logs have been accumulating for weeks. Old Docker images from 5 different app versions are cached. /var/lib/containerd is 30GB. /var/log/pods is 15GB. The kubelet eviction threshold is hit — pods get evicted. jobpost API pod was killed mid-request. Users see 500 errors. Lesson: Regularly prune unused images and rotate container logs to prevent DiskPressure.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S13): 
easypj/
└── (No new files — diagnose and clean node disk space)
BASH — Run on node "easy" to simulate disk pressure 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S13: DiskPressure — Node Disk Full
# ============================================

# 1. CHECK CURRENT DISK USAGE
df -h /
# Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
# /dev/sda1        50G   20G   30G  40% /

# 2. FILL UP DISK (SIMULATE THE BUG!)
# Create a 25GB dummy file to push usage above 85%
sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/bigfile bs=1M count=25000 2>/dev/null
# ❌ BUG! Disk is now nearly full!

# 3. CHECK DISK AGAIN — nearly full!
df -h /
# Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
# /dev/sda1        50G   45G    5G  90% /  ← DISK PRESSURE!

# 4. WATCH NODE CONDITIONS
kubectl describe node easy | grep -A5 Conditions
2

⚠️ Observe — Node Shows DiskPressure

✗1. kubectl describe node easy → DiskPressure: True
✗2. kubectl get pods -A → pods being evicted with "Evicted" status
✗3. df -h on node → /var at 90%+
✗4. New pods stuck in Pending — "node has disk pressure"
3

🔍 Debug — Find What's Consuming Disk

1Check disk usage by directory: sudo du -sh /var/lib/containerd/* /var/log/* /tmp/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -10
→ /tmp/bigfile: 25GB, /var/lib/containerd: 12GB, /var/log: 8GB
2Check container images: sudo crictl images | head -20 or sudo ctr -n k8s.io images ls
→ 15+ old unused images cached!
3Check pod logs size: sudo du -sh /var/log/pods/
→ Several GB of old pod logs
4Root cause: Large temp files + accumulated container images + old pod logs filled the disk. Kubelet's default eviction thresholds — nodefs.available<10% (90% used) and imagefs.available<15% (85% used) — triggered DiskPressure and pods were evicted.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Node conditions → DiskPressure
②
SSH → df -h → disk full
③
du -sh → find large dirs
④
Clean up → node recovers

Tenet: DiskPressure = node disk above kubelet's eviction thresholds (nodefs 90% used, imagefs 85% used, by default). Check df -h, du -sh /var/*, clean images with crictl rmi --prune, remove old logs. On CKA: you'll see pods being evicted — check node conditions first.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe node easy | grep DiskPressure DiskPressure True ... KubeletHasDiskPressure
$ sudo du -sh /tmp/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -3 25G /tmp/bigfile ← THE CULPRIT! 1.2G /tmp/another-file 500M /tmp/some-logs
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe node easy | grep DiskPressure DiskPressure False ... KubeletHasNoDiskPressure ✅
$ df -h / Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sda1 50G 20G 30G 40% / ← Back to healthy!
5

🔧 Fix — Clean Up Disk Space

BASH — Run on node to reclaim disk space 
# Step 1: Remove the large dummy file
sudo rm -f /tmp/bigfile

# Step 2: Prune unused container images
sudo crictl rmi --prune 2>/dev/null || sudo ctr -n k8s.io images prune --all

# Step 3: Remove old pod logs (older than 2 days)
sudo find /var/log/pods -type f -mtime +2 -delete 2>/dev/null

# Step 4: Clean systemd journal logs older than 3 days
sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=3d

# Step 5: Verify disk space recovered
df -h /
kubectl describe node easy | grep DiskPressure
6

✅ Verify — DiskPressure Cleared

kubectl describe node easy shows DiskPressure: False. Pods can schedule again. Regular cleanup: prune images weekly, rotate logs, monitor df -h.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Remove Dummy File

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Remove the dummy file that caused DiskPressure
sudo rm -f /tmp/bigfile

# Verify disk space is back to normal
df -h /
kubectl describe node easy | grep DiskPressure
S14
🧪 SCENARIO S14 — Category 2: Troubleshooting etcd Recovery

etcd Backup & Restore — Full Cluster Recovery Drill

The Problem: You accidentally deleted a critical namespace containing all easypj resources. There's no way to undo this — unless you have an etcd snapshot. Your job: take an etcd snapshot BEFORE the disaster, simulate data loss, then restore the entire cluster state from the snapshot. This is the ultimate Kubernetes disaster recovery skill.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Must be kubeadm cluster with etcd access
1

📋 Create Data, Backup etcd, Then Simulate Disaster

📖 APP STORY: A junior admin ran: kubectl delete ns easypj --force. The entire job board application is GONE. 50,000 job listings, 10,000 users — all deleted. But you took an etcd snapshot 10 minutes ago! Time to restore the entire cluster from backup. Lesson: Always schedule regular etcd snapshots — they're your last line of defense against catastrophic data loss.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S14): 
easypj/
└── (No new files — etcd snapshot/restore is a cluster-level operation)
BASH — Full etcd backup & restore workflow on kubeadm 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S14: etcd Backup & Restore Drill
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE IMPORTANT DATA (simulate production workloads)
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-web -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=1
kubectl get all -n easypj
# Two Deployments, 3 pods, 1 namespace — all production data

# 2. TAKE ETCD SNAPSHOT (before disaster!)
# SSH to control plane node (or run locally on kubeadm node)
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db
# Snapshot saved at /tmp/etcd-backup.db ✅

# 3. SIMULATE DISASTER — delete everything!
kubectl delete namespace easypj
# ❌ DISASTER! easypj namespace is GONE!
kubectl get all -n easypj
# No resources found — everything is LOST!
2

⚠️ Observe — Namespace Is Completely Gone

✗1. kubectl get ns easypj → "not found"
✗2. kubectl get all -A | grep easypj → nothing — ALL GONE!
✗3. All Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets — DELETED from etcd!
3

🔍 Debug — Verify Snapshot Exists & Is Valid

1Check snapshot file: sudo ls -lh /tmp/etcd-backup.db
→ File exists, ~5MB — contains full cluster state
2Verify snapshot integrity: sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --write-out=table snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db
→ Hash, revision, total keys — snapshot is VALID!
3Root cause: Namespace was force-deleted from etcd. Recovery requires restoring the entire etcd database from the snapshot. ALL cluster state will be rolled back to snapshot time.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Disaster → Check snapshot
②
Verify integrity → Valid
③
Stop API server → Restore etcd
④
Restart → Cluster recovered!

Tenet: etcd snapshot is your LAST LINE OF DEFENSE. Take regular snapshots (daily minimum). Store them OFF-NODE (S3, external disk). Restore requires stopping kube-apiserver, restoring etcd data, then restarting. This is the CKA's most critical hands-on task. Practice this until you can do it blindfolded.

📟 Command Outputs — Confirming the Snapshot Is Valid (BEFORE disaster)
$ sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db --write-out=table +----------+----------+------------+------------+ | HASH | REVISION | TOTAL KEYS | TOTAL SIZE | +----------+----------+------------+------------+ | 5e7d2a1b | 12345 | 567 | 5.2 MB | +----------+----------+------------+------------+
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get ns easypj NAME STATUS AGE easypj Active 30s ✅ Namespace restored!
$ kubectl get all -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE pod/easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-xyz 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ All resources back!
5

🔧 Fix — Restore etcd from Snapshot

BASH — etcd restore procedure (CRITICAL — run carefully!) 
# ⚠️  WARNING: This restores ALL cluster state to snapshot time!
# ⚠️  Anything created AFTER the snapshot will be LOST!

# Step 1: Move static pod manifests to stop API server
sudo mkdir -p /tmp/manifest-backup
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/manifest-backup/
# API server stops — kubectl will not work now

# Step 2: Stop etcd (also a static pod)
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml /tmp/manifest-backup/
sleep 10  # Wait for etcd to stop

# Step 3: Restore from snapshot (etcdutl, not etcdctl — offline restore uses the utility tool)
sudo etcdutl snapshot restore /tmp/etcd-backup.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore \
  --name=easy \
  --initial-cluster=easy=https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380

# Step 4: Point etcd to restored data
# Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
# Change --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd to --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore (stock kubeadm manifests use this UNQUOTED, so match without the trailing quote)
sudo sed -i 's|/var/lib/etcd|/var/lib/etcd-restore|' /tmp/manifest-backup/etcd.yaml

# Step 5: Restart etcd + API server
sudo mv /tmp/manifest-backup/etcd.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
sleep 30
sudo mv /tmp/manifest-backup/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
sleep 30

# Step 6: Verify recovery
kubectl get ns easypj
kubectl get all -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Cluster Restored from Snapshot

kubectl get ns easypj shows Active. All Deployments and pods are back. The cluster is exactly as it was at snapshot time. ⚠️ Note: This restores ALL cluster state. For production, consider velero.io for selective namespace backup/restore instead of full etcd restore.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Reset Cluster State

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete the restored namespace (undoes the recovery drill)
kubectl delete namespace easypj --ignore-not-found

# Clean up the snapshot file and the orphaned restore artifacts
sudo rm -f /tmp/etcd-backup.db
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/etcd-restore
sudo rm -rf /tmp/manifest-backup

# Verify cluster is healthy
kubectl get nodes
S15
🧪 SCENARIO S15 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Image Debug

ImagePullBackOff — Private Registry Authentication Failure

The Problem: You deploy easypj-api referencing a private container image. The pod shows ImagePullBackOff — Kubernetes can't pull the image because it doesn't have credentials for the private registry. Your job: create an imagePullSecrets (Docker registry credentials), attach it directly to the Deployment's pod template, and get the pod running.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Fake Private Image (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The DevOps team pushed easypj-api:v2.0 to a private registry. They updated the Deployment YAML but forgot to add imagePullSecrets. Kubernetes tries to pull the image — gets "401 Unauthorized". The pod stays in ImagePullBackOff. API is DOWN. Lesson: Always create a docker-registry Secret and reference it via imagePullSecrets for private registries.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S15): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Uses private image, no imagePullSecrets (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy pod referencing private registry image 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S15: ImagePullBackOff — Private Registry Without Credentials
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: private image, no imagePullSecrets)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: registry.easypj.internal/easypj/api:v2.0  # ❌ BUG! Private image, no credentials!
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Stuck in ImagePullBackOff

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → STATUS: ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull
✗2. kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> → "Failed to pull image ... unauthorized"
✗3. Pod never starts — container image can't be downloaded!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Can't Kubernetes Pull the Image?

1Check pod events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A5 Events
→ "Failed to pull image ... authentication required"
2Check if imagePullSecrets exists: kubectl get pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api -o yaml | grep imagePullSecrets
→ No imagePullSecrets configured!
3Root cause: Private registry requires authentication. The Deployment has no imagePullSecrets to authenticate. Kubernetes can't pull the image — pod stays in ImagePullBackOff forever.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Pending → ImagePullBackOff
②
Events → "authentication required"
③
No imagePullSecrets → Create one
④
Fix image to public → Pod runs!

Tenet: ImagePullBackOff = Kubernetes can't pull the container image. Causes: (1) wrong image name/tag, (2) private registry without credentials, (3) network/DNS issue to registry, (4) registry down. On CKA: check events for the exact error message. For private registries: create a Docker registry Secret and add imagePullSecrets to the pod spec.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | tail -8 Events: Normal Pulling Pod pulling image "registry.easypj.internal/easypj/api:v2.0" Warning Failed Failed to pull image ... authentication required Normal BackOff Back-off pulling image "registry.easypj.internal/easypj/api:v2.0"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d8f9-new-xyz 1/1 Running 0 10s ✅ Image pulled!
5

🔧 Fix — Use Public Image + Learn imagePullSecrets

BASH — Fix image to public + learn secret creation 
# Fix 1: Change to a public image for immediate recovery
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api -n easypj api=nginx:alpine

# Fix 2 (production PATTERN — reference only, needs a real reachable registry to actually succeed in your lab): Create Docker registry secret
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.easypj.internal \
  --docker-username=easypj-deploy \
  --docker-password='your-registry-token' \
  --docker-email=devops@easypj.com \
  -n easypj

# Attach secret to Deployment
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj -p '
{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}}}}'

# NOTE (do NOT run in this lab): in a real environment with a reachable private registry,
# you'd now switch back to the real image and it would pull successfully using regcred:
#   kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api -n easypj api=registry.easypj.internal/easypj/api:v2.0
# Leave the Deployment on nginx:alpine here — registry.easypj.internal doesn't actually
# resolve in this lab, so running that command would just put the pod right back into
# ImagePullBackOff.
6

✅ Verify — Pod Running

Pod shows Running. Key takeaway: kubectl create secret docker-registry creates credentials for private registries. Always check Events for the EXACT pull failure reason before debugging.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S16
🧪 SCENARIO S16 — Category 2: Troubleshooting App Debug

CrashLoopBackOff — easypj-api Missing Database Connection String

The Problem: The easypj-api Deployment keeps crashing immediately after startup. The pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. The application exits with code 1 because the database connection string environment variable DATABASE_URL is missing from the Deployment spec. Your job: check the logs, identify the missing env var, and fix the Deployment.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy API Without Database URL (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The API needs DATABASE_URL to connect to PostgreSQL. The YAML was copied from staging but DATABASE_URL was removed. The app starts, checks for DATABASE_URL, finds nothing, and exits. Kubernetes restarts it — same result. CrashLoopBackOff. Lesson: Always verify environment variables are defined when porting Deployment specs between environments.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S16): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Missing DATABASE_URL env var (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy broken easypj-api 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S16: CrashLoopBackOff — Missing DATABASE_URL Env Var
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: missing DATABASE_URL env var)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Starting easypj-api..."
          if [ -z "$DATABASE_URL" ]; then
            echo "FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set!" >&2
            exit 1    # ❌ BUG! App crashes without DATABASE_URL
          fi
          echo "Connected to $DATABASE_URL"
          sleep 3600
        # ❌ BUG! No DATABASE_URL env var defined!
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Keeps Crashing

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS climbing
✗2. kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api → "FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set!"
✗3. kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> → Exit Code: 1
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the App Crashing?

1Check pod logs (current): kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api
→ "FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set!" — app requires this env var
2Check previous crash logs: kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api --previous
→ Same error — confirms app exits immediately every time
3Check Deployment env vars: kubectl get deploy -n easypj easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A10 env
→ No DATABASE_URL defined in Deployment spec!
4Root cause: The DATABASE_URL environment variable is required by the application but is NOT defined in the Deployment. The app exits with code 1, Kubernetes restarts it, infinite loop = CrashLoopBackOff.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod CrashLoop → kubectl logs
②
FATAL: missing DATABASE_URL
③
Check env vars → Not defined
④
Add env → Pod Running

Tenet: CrashLoopBackOff = container exits immediately after starting. Always check kubectl logs FIRST — the app's stderr/stdout tells you exactly why it crashed. Also check --previous for the last crash. Common causes: missing env vars, wrong command, missing files, permission denied. On CKA: 90% of CrashLoopBackOff is solved by reading the logs.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api Starting easypj-api... FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set! ← App dies here
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-api-7d8f9-abcde 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 6
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-8e9f0-new-xyz 1/1 Running 0 15s ✅ No more crashes!
$ kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api Starting easypj-api... Connected to postgresql://easypj:secret123@easypj-db:5432/jobpost ✅ DATABASE_URL is set!
5

🔧 Fix — Add DATABASE_URL Environment Variable

BASH — Set the missing env var 
# Add DATABASE_URL to the Deployment
kubectl set env deploy/easypj-api -n easypj \
  DATABASE_URL=postgresql://easypj:secret123@easypj-db:5432/jobpost

# Wait for rollout
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Verify the app no longer crashes
kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api
6

✅ Verify — App Running, Env Var Set

Pod shows Running 1/1. Logs show "Connected to postgresql://...". Key: kubectl logs is your #1 troubleshooting tool. Always check logs FIRST.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj

📌 S17–S22: Init Containers, Finalizers & Probes

S17
🧪 SCENARIO S17 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Init Debug

Init Container Failure — Database Not Ready Before App Starts

The Problem: The easypj-api pod uses an init container that checks if the PostgreSQL database is ready before starting the main app. The init container's pg_isready command is pointing to the wrong hostname. The init container keeps failing, preventing the main container from ever starting. Your job: debug the init container, find the wrong hostname, and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy API with Broken Init Container (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The init container pattern ensures DB is ready before app starts. But someone copied the YAML and forgot to change the hostname. The init container waits for "wrong-db-host" — which NEVER resolves. The main container never starts. Pod is stuck in Init:0/1. Lesson: Init containers are powerful but brittle — always verify hostnames and endpoints in init container commands.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S17): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Init container with wrong hostname (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy API with broken init container 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S17: Init Container Failure — Wrong Hostname Blocks Pod Start
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE DB SERVICE (so the REAL hostname exists for comparison)
kubectl create service clusterip easypj-db -n easypj --tcp=5432:5432

# 3. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: init container checks wrong-db-host)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: wait-for-db
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Checking database..."
          until nslookup wrong-db-host 2>/dev/null; do  # ❌ BUG! Should be easypj-db!
            echo "Waiting for wrong-db-host..."
            sleep 2
          done
          echo "Database is ready!"
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Stuck at Init:0/1

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → STATUS: Init:0/1
✗2. kubectl logs -n easypj <pod> -c wait-for-db → "Waiting for wrong-db-host..." looping forever
✗3. Main container NEVER starts — API is completely DOWN!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Won't the Init Container Complete?

1Check init container logs: kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -c wait-for-db
→ nslookup wrong-db-host fails — hostname doesn't exist!
2Check available services: kubectl get svc -n easypj
→ Service "easypj-db" exists — init container is looking for WRONG name!
3Root cause: Init container DNS check uses wrong hostname "wrong-db-host" instead of "easypj-db". The init container will NEVER complete, blocking the main container permanently.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Init:0/1 → Check init logs
②
nslookup fails → Wrong hostname
③
Fix hostname → Init completes
④
Main container starts → Pod Running

Tenet: Init containers run BEFORE main containers. If an init container fails, the pod stays in Init:0/1 or Init:Error. Check init container logs with kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container-name>. Common causes: wrong hostnames, missing dependencies, bad commands. On CKA: you'll see a pod stuck in Init state — check init container logs with -c flag.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -c wait-for-db Checking database... Waiting for wrong-db-host... Waiting for wrong-db-host... ← Loops FOREVER!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d8f9-new-xyz 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ Init completed!
5

🔧 Fix — Correct the Hostname in Init Container

BASH — Patch the Deployment with correct DB hostname 
# Fix: Patch init container to use correct hostname (JSON strings can't contain raw newlines — keep it one line)
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/initContainers/0/args/0","value":"until nslookup easypj-db 2>/dev/null; do echo Waiting for easypj-db...; sleep 2; done; echo Database is ready!"}
]'

# Or easier: edit the deployment directly
kubectl edit deploy easypj-api -n easypj
# Change "wrong-db-host" → "easypj-db"
6

✅ Verify — Init Container Completes, App Starts

Pod shows Running 1/1. Init container completed successfully. The main container started. Always use -c <name> to check init container logs.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S18
🧪 SCENARIO S18 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Finalizer

Pod Stuck Terminating — Finalizer Blocking Deletion

The Problem: You try to delete a pod but it stays in Terminating state for 10+ minutes. kubectl delete pod hangs. The pod has a finalizer that hasn't been processed — a controller set a finalizer but the controller is no longer running. Your job: identify the blocking finalizer, remove it, and force-delete the stuck pod.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA practice cluster
1

📋 Create Pod with Blocking Finalizer (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A custom operator used to handle pod cleanup. The operator was uninstalled but left finalizers on pods. Now those pods can't be deleted — they're STUCK. Rolling updates fail because old pods never terminate. Lesson: Finalizers are pre-delete hooks. If no controller processes them, pods stay Terminating forever. Manually patch to remove orphaned finalizers.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S18): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-stuck-pod.yaml            ← Pod with orphaned finalizer (BUG!)
BASH — Create pod with orphaned finalizer 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S18: Pod Stuck Terminating — Orphaned Finalizer Blocks Deletion
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE POD WITH ORPHANED FINALIZER (BUG)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: stuck-pod
  namespace: easypj
  finalizers:
  - custom-protection.example.com/finalizer  # ❌ BUG! No controller handles this!
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
EOF

# 3. ATTEMPT TO DELETE POD — will hang FOREVER due to finalizer
kubectl delete pod stuck-pod -n easypj &
# The command hangs... pod shows "Terminating" forever
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Won't Delete

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → STATUS: Terminating (for 5+ minutes)
✗2. kubectl delete pod command never returns — HANGS!
✗3. kubectl describe pod stuck-pod -n easypj → finalizers block deletion
3

🔍 Debug — Find What's Blocking Deletion

1Check pod metadata: kubectl get pod stuck-pod -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A5 finalizers
→ custom-protection.example.com/finalizer — NO CONTROLLER!
2Check pod status: kubectl describe pod stuck-pod -n easypj
→ deletionTimestamp is set, but finalizer blocks removal
3Root cause: A finalizer is a pre-delete hook. Kubernetes won't remove the pod from etcd until ALL finalizers are processed. Since no controller handles this finalizer, the pod is stuck forever. Fix: manually remove the finalizer or force-delete.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Terminating → Check finalizers
②
Finalizer found → No controller
③
Patch remove finalizer → Deleted!

Tenet: Finalizers = pre-deletion hooks. If a pod is stuck Terminating, check kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep finalizers. The ONLY real fix here is patching the finalizer away: kubectl patch pod -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}'. kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 is often assumed to be an alternative — it isn't: force-delete only skips waiting for kubelet's termination confirmation, it does NOT remove finalizers, so a finalizer-blocked pod stays stuck even after a force-delete. Only patch out a finalizer once you've confirmed no controller will ever process it (as is the case here) — finalizers usually exist to prevent real resource leaks. On CKA: you'll need to remove a finalizer to unstick a pod.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pod stuck-pod -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A3 finalizers finalizers: - custom-protection.example.com/finalizer ← BLOCKING! deletionTimestamp: "2026-06-05T03:15:00Z" ← Marked for deletion!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pod stuck-pod -n easypj Error from server (NotFound): pods "stuck-pod" not found ✅ Pod is GONE!
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj No resources found in easypj namespace. ✅ Clean slate!
5

🔧 Fix — Remove Finalizer or Force Delete

BASH — Remove the blocking finalizer 
# The finalizer patch is the fix — only do this once you've confirmed no controller will ever process it
kubectl patch pod stuck-pod -n easypj -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}' --type=merge

# NOTE: --force --grace-period=0 is NOT a substitute — it only skips waiting for kubelet
# confirmation, it does NOT remove finalizers. A finalizer-blocked pod stays stuck even after this.

# Verify pod is gone
kubectl get pods -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Pod Deleted

Pod is gone. Key: when a resource is stuck Terminating, check finalizers in the YAML output. Patch to empty array to force deletion.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S19
🧪 SCENARIO S19 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Probe Debug

Liveness Probe Too Aggressive — Healthy Pod Restarted Unnecessarily

The Problem: Your easypj-api pod keeps getting restarted even though the app is running fine. The liveness probe is configured with initialDelaySeconds: 3 and periodSeconds: 2 — far too aggressive. Django takes 30-45 seconds to boot. The probe starts checking before the app is ready, fails, and Kubernetes kills the pod. Your job: diagnose the aggressive probe settings and adjust them.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy API with Too-Aggressive Liveness Probe (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The liveness probe checks if nginx is listening on port 80. But the startup script sleeps 30s before starting nginx. Probe fires at 3s, 5s, 7s, 9s, 11s — all FAIL. After failureThreshold=2 failures, kubelet RESTARTS the container (same Pod, RESTARTS count increments — it does NOT delete/recreate the Pod). The new container attempt hits the same 30s sleep — same thing happens. INFINITE RESTART LOOP. Lesson: For slow-starting apps, increase initialDelaySeconds or use a startupProbe.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S19): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Liveness probe too aggressive (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy with aggressive liveness probe 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S19: Liveness Probe Too Aggressive — Healthy Pod Restarted
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: liveness probe fires before app starts)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        command: ["sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Starting Django... (this takes 30 seconds)"
          sleep 30    # Simulate slow Django startup
          echo "Django is ready!"
          nginx -g "daemon off;"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 3    # ❌ BUG! Too soon! App still starting at 3s
          periodSeconds: 2          # ❌ BUG! Checking every 2s — too aggressive
          failureThreshold: 2       # ❌ BUG! Only 2 failures = kill pod
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Keeps Restarting Despite Being "Healthy"

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → RESTARTS climbing, STATUS flapping
✗2. kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> → "Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed"
✗3. App is actually WORKING — but probe says it's DEAD!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is Kubernetes Killing a Working App?

1Check pod events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep Liveness
→ "Liveness probe failed: Get http://... dial tcp ... connection refused" — app not listening yet!
2Check probe config: kubectl get deploy -n easypj easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A8 livenessProbe
→ initialDelaySeconds: 3 — probe fires before app is ready!
3Root cause: Liveness probe starts checking at 3s but the app takes 30s to start. Probe fails repeatedly, kubelet kills the pod thinking it's unhealthy. Fix: increase initialDelaySeconds to ≥35s OR use a startupProbe for slow-starting apps.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod restarts → Liveness failing
②
Check probe timing → Too early
③
Increase initialDelay → App starts
④
Or use startupProbe → Better

Tenet: Liveness probe = "Is my app alive?" If it fails, kubelet RESTARTS the container. For slow-starting apps (Java, Django, Rails), use a startupProbe with a generous failureThreshold instead of tweaking liveness initialDelay. startupProbe runs FIRST — once it succeeds, liveness takes over. This is the recommended pattern for slow apps.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A2 Liveness Warning Unhealthy Liveness probe failed: dial tcp 10.0.1.5:80: connect: connection refused Warning Unhealthy Liveness probe failed: dial tcp 10.0.1.5:80: connect: connection refused Normal Killing Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d8f9c4b5-abcde 1/1 Running 0 45s ✅ Same Pod, no more restarts!
5

🔧 Fix — Add startupProbe + Adjust Liveness Timing

BASH — Patch with proper probe configuration 
# Patch: Add startupProbe for slow-starting apps — this REPLACES tweaking liveness initialDelay, not in addition to it
# Once a startupProbe is present, keep liveness initialDelaySeconds small — the startupProbe is what gates checks until the app is ready
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/periodSeconds","value":10},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/failureThreshold","value":3},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/startupProbe","value":{"httpGet":{"path":"/","port":80},"failureThreshold":30,"periodSeconds":5}}
]'

# Wait for rollout
kubectl rollout status deploy easypj-api -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Pod Stable, No More Unnecessary Restarts

Pod shows Running with 0 restarts. startupProbe gives the app enough time to boot before liveness kicks in. Rule: use startupProbe for apps that take >10s to start.
