Readiness Probe Failing — easypj-api Not Receiving Traffic

The Problem: Your easypj-api pod is Running but the Service shows no endpoints. The readiness probe is checking /healthz but the Django app exposes health at /health (no 'z'). The probe gets 404 every time, so the pod is never added to the Service endpoints. Your job: find the wrong probe path and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy API with Wrong Readiness Probe Path (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The API pod shows STATUS: Running, but READY is 0/1! The Service has NO endpoints — no traffic reaches the pod. Kubernetes health checks pass, but readiness fails because the probe hits /healthz which returns 404. The app is alive but Kubernetes won't send it traffic. Lesson: Readiness probe path must match what the app actually serves. A 404 on readiness = pod removed from Service endpoints.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S20): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment-svc.yaml   ← Readiness probe path /healthz (BUG! should be /)
BASH — Deploy API + Service, wrong readiness path 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S20: Readiness Probe Failing — Pod Running but No Traffic
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE DEPLOYMENT + SERVICE (BUG: readiness probe path /healthz returns 404)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        # nginx only serves / (root) — NOT /healthz!
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz    # ❌ BUG! nginx returns 404 for /healthz!
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 5
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
# Service — ClusterIP for easypj-api (endpoints empty: readiness returns 404)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Pod Running but READY 0/1, Service Has No Endpoints

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → READY: 0/1 (pod is Running but NOT ready)
✗2. kubectl get endpoints -n easypj easypj-api → ENDPOINTS: <none>
✗3. Any curl to the Service IP returns "connection refused"
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the Pod Not Ready?

1Check pod conditions: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A5 Conditions
→ Ready: False — Readiness probe failing
2Check readiness probe response: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- wget -qO- http://localhost:80/healthz
→ 404 Not Found — path doesn't exist!
3Root cause: Readiness probe path /healthz returns 404. Kubernetes thinks the pod is not ready to serve traffic. The Service removes it from endpoints. Fix: change probe path to "/" (which nginx DOES serve).
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Running but 0/1 → Readiness
②
Endpoints empty → Probe failing
③
Check probe path → 404
④
Fix path → Pod Ready → Traffic!

Tenet: Readiness probe ≠ Liveness probe. Readiness = "can this pod receive traffic?" If it fails, the pod is removed from Service endpoints but NOT restarted. Liveness = "is this pod alive?" If it fails, the pod IS restarted. Most common readiness issues: wrong port, wrong path, wrong scheme. On CKA: if a pod is Running but 0/1 Ready, check the readiness probe FIRST.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get endpoints -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api <none> 5m ← NO ENDPOINTS!
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep Readiness Warning Unhealthy Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get endpoints -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api 10.0.1.5:80 5m ✅ Endpoints populated!
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d8f9-abcde 1/1 Running 0 1m ✅ READY 1/1!
5

🔧 Fix — Correct the Readiness Probe Path

BASH — Fix readiness probe path 
# Change readiness probe from /healthz to /
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/"}
]'

# Wait for new pod
kubectl rollout status deploy easypj-api -n easypj

# Verify endpoints now have the pod IP
kubectl get endpoints -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Endpoints Populated, Traffic Flows

Pod shows 1/1 Ready. kubectl get endpoints shows the pod IP. The Service now routes traffic correctly. Rule: always verify your readiness probe path exists in the app!

Slow-Starting App Killed Before Boot — Need startupProbe

The Problem: easypj-api takes 45 seconds to start (Django migrations + cache warmup). The liveness probe fires at 15s, fails, and Kubernetes kills the pod. This repeats infinitely. The fix: add a startupProbe that runs FIRST with generous failure tolerance, then liveness takes over once the app is ready.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy Slow-Starting API Without startupProbe (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Django needs to run migrations and warm the cache on startup. This takes 45 seconds. The liveness probe checks at 10s — FAIL. Kubernetes thinks the app is dead and kills it. New pod starts, same thing. INFINITE RESTART LOOP. Lesson: For slow-starting apps, use a startupProbe with generous failureThreshold. startupProbe runs first — liveness only takes over after startupProbe succeeds.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S21): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Liveness probe but NO startupProbe (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy slow-starting app with only liveness probe 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S21: Slow App Killed Before Boot — Missing startupProbe
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: no startupProbe, liveness fires too early)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        command: ["sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Running Django migrations... (30s)"
          sleep 30
          echo "Warming cache... (15s)"
          sleep 15
          echo "Django is ready!"
          nginx -g "daemon off;"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 10   # ❌ BUG! App needs 45s, probe fires at 10s!
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 3        # ❌ After 3 failures (~25s), pod killed!
        # ❌ BUG! No startupProbe — liveness kills pod before startup completes

        - containerPort: 80

# The APP STORY:
# Django needs to run migrations and warm the cache on startup.
# This takes 45 seconds. The liveness probe checks at 10s — FAIL.
# Kubernetes thinks the app is dead and kills it.
# New pod starts, same thing. INFINITE RESTART LOOP.
# The fix: startupProbe gives app time to boot before liveness kicks in.

⚠️ Observe — Pod Killed Before App Is Ready

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → RESTARTS climbing, STATUS flapping
✗2. kubectl describe pod → "Liveness probe failed ... will be restarted"
✗3. App IS healthy — just slow to start! Probe is too impatient!

🔍 Debug — Why Is Kubernetes Killing a Working App?

1Check pod events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep Liveness
→ Liveness probe failed 3 times — pod being killed and restarted
2Check startup time: kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api --previous
→ "Django is ready!" — app was STILL BOOTING when killed!
3Check probe timing: kubectl get deploy -n easypj easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A8 livenessProbe
→ initialDelay: 10s, failureThreshold: 3 — kills pod at ~25s, app needs 45s!

4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod restarts → Liveness killing it
②
Logs show app still booting
③
No startupProbe → Add one
④
startupProbe completes → Liveness takes over

Tenet: startupProbe runs BEFORE livenessProbe. Once startupProbe succeeds, it NEVER runs again — liveness takes over. For slow-starting apps (Java, Django, Rails), ALWAYS use startupProbe with generous failureThreshold. Never increase liveness initialDelay as a workaround — that delays detection of real crashes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-api-7d8f9-abcde 0/1 Running 5 ← 5 restarts!
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A2 Liveness Warning Unhealthy Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed Normal Killing Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d8f9-new-xyz 1/1 Running 0 50s ✅ startupProbe passed, app is alive!

🔧 Fix — Add startupProbe to Give App Time to Boot

BASH — Patch Deployment with startupProbe

kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/startupProbe","value":{
    "httpGet": {"path":"/","port":80},
    "failureThreshold": 30,
    "periodSeconds": 5
  }},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/initialDelaySeconds","value":0}
]'
# Set liveness initialDelay to 0 — startupProbe handles the delay
kubectl rollout status deploy easypj-api -n easypj

🧪 SCENARIO S22 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Probe Debug

Exec Probe Fails — Wrong Shell in Container (bash vs sh)

The Problem: A liveness probe uses exec.command: ["/bin/bash","-c","health-check.sh"] but the container image is Alpine-based — it only has /bin/sh, not bash. The exec probe ALWAYS fails. Kubernetes thinks the app is dead and restarts it continuously.

1

📋 Deploy API with Bash Exec Probe on Alpine (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: DevOps added a liveness exec probe to check API health with a bash script. The Deployment uses an Alpine-based image (no bash, only sh). The probe runs /bin/bash — which doesn't exist. Probe always fails. Pod gets killed and restarted forever. Lesson: Always match your probe command to the container's shell. Alpine uses /bin/sh, not /bin/bash. Use which <shell> to verify.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S22): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Exec probe uses /bin/bash on Alpine (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy with wrong shell in exec probe 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S22: Exec Probe — Wrong Shell (/bin/bash on Alpine)
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: exec probe uses /bin/bash, Alpine only has /bin/sh)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine    # Alpine — has /bin/sh, NOT /bin/bash!
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - /bin/bash          # ❌ BUG! Alpine has NO bash!
            - -c
            - "echo healthy"
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

⚠️ Observe — Pod Restarts Despite Being Healthy

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → RESTARTS climbing
✗2. kubectl describe pod → "Exec probe failed: exec /bin/bash: no such file or directory"

🔍 Debug — Find Why Exec Probe Always Fails

1Check probe events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A3 Liveness
→ "exec /bin/bash: no such file or directory" — BASH NOT FOUND!
2Check container shell: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- ls /bin/bash 2>&1; ls /bin/sh
→ /bin/bash: NOT FOUND, /bin/sh: EXISTS — Alpine only has sh!
3Root cause: Exec probe uses /bin/bash but the Alpine container only has /bin/sh. Every probe attempt fails. Kubernetes restarts the pod thinking it's unhealthy. Fix: change to /bin/sh or use httpGet instead.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Exec probe fails → Check error
②
"/bin/bash: no such file"
③
Container is Alpine → Use sh
④
Fix command → Probe passes!

Tenet: Exec probes run INSIDE the container. The command must exist in the container's filesystem. Alpine-based images (nginx:alpine, postgres:alpine, python:alpine) have /bin/sh but NOT /bin/bash. Always check the container's available shells before writing exec probes. Better: use httpGet or tcpSocket probes — they don't depend on container contents.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A2 "exec" Warning Unhealthy Liveness probe failed: exec /bin/bash: no such file or directory
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d8f9-new-xyz 1/1 Running 0 20s ✅ Probe passes with /bin/sh!
5

🔧 Fix — Change Exec Probe to Use /bin/sh

BASH — Fix probe command to use /bin/sh 
# Fix: Change /bin/bash to /bin/sh (or better: use httpGet)
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/exec/command/0","value":"/bin/sh"}
]'
kubectl rollout status deploy easypj-api -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Probe Passes, Pod Stable

Pod shows Running with 0 restarts. Rule: check which bash or ls /bin/bash before writing exec probes. Better yet: use httpGet probes whenever possible.

└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Readiness probe on port 8080, nginx on 80 (BUG!)

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S23: HTTP Probe Wrong Port — Readiness Fails on Port Mismatch
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: readiness probe targets port 8080, app on 80)

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api

      containers:

        - containerPort: 80
---
# Service — ClusterIP for easypj-api (endpoints empty: readiness hits wrong port)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF

✗2. kubectl get endpoints -n easypj → ENDPOINTS: <none>

🔍 Debug — Why Is the Pod Not Ready?

1Check readiness events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep Readiness
→ "connection refused" on port 8080 — port mismatch!

→ Works on port 80 — app IS listening!
3Root cause: Probe port 8080 ≠ container port 80. Fix: change readinessProbe port to 80.

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Running 0/1 → Readiness failing
②
"connection refused" → Wrong port
③
Verify app port → Fix probe port
④
Pod Ready → Endpoints populated!

Tenet: Probe port must match the containerPort where the app actually listens. Common mismatch: Java apps default to 8080, nginx to 80, PostgreSQL to 5432. Always verify with kubectl exec before writing probes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)

S24
🧪 SCENARIO S24 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Logging

Missing Container Logs — App Writing to File, Not stdout/stderr

The Problem: kubectl logs returns NOTHING from easypj-api. The app is running and writing logs to /var/log/app.log, but Kubernetes can only capture stdout/stderr. Debugging is impossible without seeing the logs. Your job: understand the 12-Factor App logging principle and redirect logs to stdout.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy App That Logs to File Instead of stdout (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-api writes application logs to /var/log/app.log for audit compliance. But Kubernetes only captures stdout/stderr. kubectl logs returns empty — DevOps can't debug production issues. A 500 error spike has no visible logs. Lesson: Follow 12-Factor App principles — always write logs to stdout. Use tee or a sidecar (Fluentd/Fluent Bit) if you need both file and stdout.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S24): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← App logs to file, not stdout (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy app writing to file 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S24: Missing Container Logs — App Writes to File, Not stdout
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE API DEPLOYMENT (BUG: logs redirected to file, not stdout)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          # ❌ BUG! Writing logs to FILE instead of stdout!
          while true; do
            echo "[$(date)] INFO: Request processed - 200 OK" >> /var/log/app.log
            sleep 2
          done
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — kubectl logs Returns Nothing

✗1. kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api → (empty!)
✗2. Pod IS running — but no visible logs!
3

🔍 Debug — Where Are the Logs?

1Check pod filesystem: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- cat /var/log/app.log
→ Logs ARE there — but in a FILE, not stdout!
2Check process output: kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- ls -la /proc/1/fd/
→ stdout (fd 1) points to /dev/null or pipe — logs redirected to file
3Root cause: The app writes logs to /var/log/app.log using >> (append to file). Kubernetes only captures stdout (fd 1) and stderr (fd 2). Fix: remove the file redirect or use tee to write to both.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
kubectl logs empty → Check files
②
Logs in /var/log/app.log
③
Redirect to stdout → kubectl logs works!

Tenet: 12-Factor App principle: logs should be streamed to stdout. Kubernetes captures stdout/stderr automatically. If your app logs to files, use a sidecar container to tail and forward, or use tee to duplicate output. On CKA: kubectl logs empty + pod running = logs going to file, not stdout.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api (empty — no output)
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- tail -5 /var/log/app.log [Jun 05 10:15] INFO: Request processed - 200 OK [Jun 05 10:17] INFO: Request processed - 200 OK ← Logs ARE here!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api [Fri Jun 05 10:20:01 UTC 2026] INFO: Request processed - 200 OK ✅ Logs now visible! [Fri Jun 05 10:20:03 UTC 2026] INFO: Request processed - 200 OK [Fri Jun 05 10:20:05 UTC 2026] INFO: Request processed - 200 OK
5

🔧 Fix — Redirect Logs to stdout

BASH — Patch to log to stdout (or use tee for both) 
# Patch to remove the file redirect (log to stdout only)
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/0","value":"while true; do echo \"[$(date)] INFO: Request processed - 200 OK\"; sleep 2; done"}
]'
kubectl rollout status deploy easypj-api -n easypj
kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api
6

✅ Verify — kubectl logs Shows Output

kubectl logs now shows the INFO messages. Rule: always log to stdout/stderr. Use sidecar pattern (Fluentd/Fluent Bit) for advanced log forwarding.

S25
🧪 SCENARIO S25 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Multi-Container

kubectl logs Without -c Flag — Multi-Container Pod

The Problem: A pod has 3 containers (api, sidecar-logger, sidecar-metrics). kubectl logs without -c genuinely errors on multi-container pods — it can't guess which container's logs you want. kubectl exec is more dangerous in a different way: it does NOT error without -c — it runs in the FIRST container (or a kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container annotation if set) and only prints a Defaulted container "X" out of: ... warning to stderr, which is easy to miss — especially in scripts/CI that discard stderr — so you can end up executing commands in the wrong container without really noticing.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy Multi-Container Pod (3 containers)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-api pod now runs with a logger sidecar and a metrics sidecar. A developer tries kubectl logs to check for errors — it fails outright, refusing to guess which container. Relieved, they try kubectl exec instead — it doesn't hard-error, it just prints a one-line "Defaulted container" warning to stderr and carries on... but the developer's terminal scrollback buries it, so they don't notice they ran in the wrong container (the sidecar, not the api container they meant to debug). Lesson: For multi-container pods, always use the -c flag — kubectl logs will force you to by erroring, but kubectl exec only nudges you with an easy-to-miss stderr warning.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S25): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-pod.yaml              ← Pod with api + sidecar-logger + sidecar-metrics
BASH — Deploy easypj-api with sidecars 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S25: Multi-Container Pod — kubectl exec Requires -c Flag
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE MULTI-CONTAINER POD (api + sidecar-logger + sidecar-metrics)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
  - name: sidecar-logger
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do echo 'Logging...'; sleep 30; done"]
  - name: sidecar-metrics
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do echo 'Metrics...'; sleep 30; done"]
EOF

# Try kubectl logs WITHOUT -c → this genuinely ERRORS (can't guess which container)
kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-api
# error: a container name must be specified for pod easypj-api, choose one of: [api sidecar-logger sidecar-metrics]

# Try kubectl exec WITHOUT -c → this does NOT error — just a stderr warning, then runs in the FIRST container!
kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-api -- hostname
# Defaulted container "api" out of: api, sidecar-logger, sidecar-metrics   ← easy to miss!
# easypj-api   ← "Worked" — but you're in "api", which may not be the container you meant
2

⚠️ Observe — kubectl exec Fails Without -c

✗1. kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-api → "error: a container name must be specified"
✗2. kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-api -- hostname → runs fine, no hard error — just an easy-to-miss stderr "Defaulted container" warning — and lands in the wrong container!
3

🔍 Debug — List Containers & Use -c Flag

1List containers in pod: kubectl get pod -n easypj easypj-api -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
→ api sidecar-logger sidecar-metrics — 3 containers!
2Root cause: kubectl logs REQUIRES -c on multi-container pods and errors without it. kubectl exec does NOT require -c — it defaults to the first container (or the kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container annotation) and only prints a "Defaulted container" warning to stderr, so an omitted -c on exec is easy to miss rather than a hard failure you can't ignore. Always specify -c explicitly for both commands. For all containers' logs: kubectl logs --all-containers.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
logs errors loudly → Check containers
②
exec fails SILENTLY (wrong container)
③
Always pass -c explicitly → Correct container

Tenet: For multi-container pods, always specify -c on BOTH commands — even though only logs forces you to. Use kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' to list containers. For logs from all containers: kubectl logs --all-containers.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-api error: a container name must be specified for pod easypj-api, choose one of: [api sidecar-logger sidecar-metrics]
$ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-api -c sidecar-logger -- cat /var/log/app.log error: no such file or directory ← Meant to check the API's config, but this is the LOGGER sidecar!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-api -c api -- date Thu Jun 5 10:30:00 UTC 2026 ✅ -c api → correct container this time!
$ kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-api --all-containers [api] Starting API server... [logger] Logging initialized [metrics] Metrics server on :9090 ✅ All containers!
5

🔧 Fix — Always Use -c Flag for Multi-Container Pods

BASH — Correct way to exec/logs multi-container pods 
# Exec into specific container
kubectl exec -it -n easypj easypj-api -c api -- /bin/sh
kubectl exec -n easypj easypj-api -c sidecar-logger -- cat /var/log/app.log

# Logs from specific container
kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-api -c sidecar-metrics
kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-api -c sidecar-logger --tail=20

# Logs from ALL containers
kubectl logs -n easypj easypj-api --all-containers
6

✅ Verify — Exec and Logs Work with -c Flag

Using -c <container-name> works. Key: for multi-container pods, ALWAYS specify the container. Use --all-containers for logs from all containers.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj

metrics-server Not Reporting — kubectl top Returns Error

The Problem: kubectl top pods returns "error: Metrics API not available". The metrics-server is not installed or not running. HPA can't scale, and you have no visibility into resource usage. Your job: check if metrics-server is deployed, install it if missing, and verify kubectl top works.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Check metrics-server on node "easy"

📋 Deploy a Test Pod and Try kubectl top (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The DevOps team wants to set up HPA for the easypj-api based on CPU usage. But kubectl top pods returns "Metrics API not available". The metrics-server was never installed on this cluster. HPA can't scale, resource dashboards are blank. Lesson: kubectl top requires metrics-server. Without it, HPA and VPA are non-functional. Install metrics-server as a standard cluster component.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S26): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Test deployment to verify metrics-server
BASH — Deploy pod + verify metrics-server missing 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S26: metrics-server Not Installed — kubectl top Fails
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE + DEPLOY TEST POD
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2

# 2. TRY kubectl top — FAILS! (metrics-server not installed)
kubectl top pods -n easypj
# error: Metrics API not available

kubectl top nodes
# error: Metrics API not available

# (no results) ← ❌ BUG! metrics-server not installed!

⚠️ Observe — kubectl top Returns Error

✗1. kubectl top pods -n easypj → "Metrics API not available"
✗2. kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics → (no results at all — the APIService object doesn't even exist yet)
✗3. HPA can't function without metrics-server!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Aren't Metrics Available?

1Check API service status: kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics
→ (no results) — the v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io APIService is registered BY metrics-server's own manifest, so it doesn't exist at all until metrics-server is installed
2Check kube-system for metrics pods: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=metrics-server
→ No resources found — metrics-server NOT deployed!
3Root cause: metrics-server is not installed. kubectl top relies on the metrics-server to collect resource data from kubelets. Without it, the metrics API is unavailable and HPA cannot function. Fix: deploy metrics-server.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
kubectl top fails → Check API
②
apiservices shows False → Not deployed
③
Install metrics-server → kubectl top works!

Tenet: metrics-server collects resource metrics from kubelet Summary API. Without it: no kubectl top, no HPA CPU/memory scaling. Install with kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml. For kind clusters, add --kubelet-insecure-tls flag.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl top pods -n kube-system error: Metrics API not available
$ kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics (no results — the APIService is created by metrics-server's own manifest, which was never applied)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl top pods -n kube-system NAME CPU(cores) MEMORY(bytes) coredns-7d8f9-abcde 5m 25Mi ✅ Metrics working!
5

🔧 Fix — Install metrics-server

BASH — Install metrics-server 
# Install metrics-server (latest release)
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

# On kind/kubeadm: patch to allow insecure TLS to kubelet
kubectl patch deploy metrics-server -n kube-system --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}
]'

# Wait for metrics-server to be ready (~30s)
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deploy/metrics-server -n kube-system --timeout=60s

# Verify
kubectl top pods -n kube-system
6

✅ Verify — kubectl top Works

kubectl top pods now shows CPU and memory usage. HPA can now scale based on metrics. metrics-server is essential infrastructure.

🧪 SCENARIO S27 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Connectivity

kubectl exec Timeout — API Server Can't Reach Kubelet (Port 10250)

The Problem: kubectl exec and kubectl logs hang and timeout. The API server proxies these requests to the kubelet on port 10250, but the connection is blocked. Your job: understand the API server → kubelet communication path and diagnose the connectivity issue.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Check port 10250 connectivity
1

📋 Deploy Pod + Block Kubelet Port 10250 (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A developer needs to exec into the easypj-api pod to debug a production issue. But kubectl exec hangs for 30 seconds then times out. kubectl logs also fails. The pod is Running but completely unreachable for interactive debugging. Lesson: kubectl exec/logs/port-forward all proxy through API Server → kubelet:10250. If port 10250 is blocked by firewall/iptables, all exec/logs commands fail with timeout.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S27): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Test pod (needs port 10250 open for exec/logs)
BASH — Deploy pod + block kubelet port (makes exec/logs timeout) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S27: kubectl exec/logs Timeout — Port 10250 Blocked
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE + DEPLOY TEST POD
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=30s

# 2. VERIFY EXEC WORKS BEFORE THE BLOCK
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- date

# 3. BLOCK KUBELET PORT 10250 (simulate firewall — THIS IS THE BUG!)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 10250 -j DROP
# ❌ BUG! kubectl exec/logs go through API server → kubelet:10250
# Blocking 10250 = all exec/logs/port-forward will timeout!

# 4. TRY EXEC — IT WILL HANG AND TIMEOUT!
timeout 5 kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- date || echo "TIMEOUT! Port 10250 is blocked."
2

⚠️ Observe — kubectl exec/logs Hang

✗1. kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- date → hangs, then times out
✗2. kubectl logs -n easypj deploy/easypj-api → same timeout

🔍 Debug — Trace the Exec/Logs Connection Path

1Check if kubelet port is open: sudo ss -tlnp | grep 10250
→ Port should be LISTENING on *:10250 by kubelet
2Check API server connectivity to kubelet: Check firewall/iptables rules
→ Port 10250 must be open between control plane and ALL nodes
3Root cause: kubectl exec/logs require API server → kubelet:10250 connectivity. If blocked by firewall, network policy, or kubelet not running, all exec/logs commands fail with timeout.

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
exec hangs → Check kubelet
②
Port 10250 → Verify listening
③
Check firewall → Fix → Working!

Tenet: kubectl exec/logs/port-forward ALL go through the API server proxy to kubelet:10250. If these commands hang, check: (1) kubelet is running, (2) port 10250 is open on the node, (3) no firewall/iptables blocking the path. On CKA: exec timeout = check kubelet status on that node.

🔧 Fix — Remove iptables Block on Port 10250

🧪 SCENARIO S28 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Events

Event Rate Limiting — kubectl get events Shows Gaps

The Problem: A pod is crashing repeatedly, but a plain kubectl get events -n easypj | tail -5 only shows a handful of RECENT events mixed together from every object in the namespace — the pod's own earlier crash events have scrolled past. Your job: understand why get events looks incomplete by default (it's namespace-wide, not per-object) and how to see the full picture with kubectl describe or a filtered get events.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy a Rapidly Crashing Pod to Trigger Event Rate Limiting

📖 APP STORY: A pod keeps crashing in a loop. kubectl get events -n easypj | tail -5 only shows the last few events across the WHOLE namespace — interleaved with routine events from every other pod, Service, and ConfigMap. The pod's own earlier BackOff events are still there in etcd (same default 1-hour TTL as everything else), just scrolled off-screen by unrelated noise. DevOps assumes the events were "lost". Lesson: kubectl get events is namespace-wide and unfiltered by default — busy namespaces crowd it out fast. kubectl describe pod (or get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod>) filters to one object, so nothing gets lost in the shuffle — it's the same data, just scoped.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S28): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-crash-pod.yaml            ← Pod that crashes rapidly to flood events
BASH — Create crashing pod that generates many events 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S28: Event Rate Limiting — kubectl get events Truncates History
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE CRASH-LOOP POD (generates many events)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c","echo 'Starting...'; exit 1"]  # Crashes instantly!
EOF
# The pod will crash ~10 times, generating repeated Pulling/Started/BackOff events.
# Also create a few unrelated objects so the namespace's event feed has other noise in it —
# this is what actually crowds out the crashing pod's events in an unfiltered/tailed view.
kubectl create deploy easypj-web -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl create configmap easypj-config -n easypj --from-literal=key=value
sleep 30

# Compare: unfiltered/tailed get events vs kubectl describe pod
kubectl get events -n easypj --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -5
kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | tail -15
2

⚠️ Observe — Events Are Incomplete

✗1. kubectl get events -n easypj | tail -5 — namespace-wide feed crowded with events from OTHER objects too; the pod's own earlier BackOff events have scrolled past
✗2. kubectl describe pod — filtered to just this pod, so its full event history is all still there
3

🔍 Debug — Why Are Events Missing?

1Compare scope, not retention: kubectl get events -n easypj --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod> (filtered to just this pod) vs the unfiltered kubectl get events -n easypj | tail -3
→ the FILTERED get events shows the exact same complete per-pod history as describe — the data was never actually missing, just buried under other objects' events in the unfiltered/tailed view!
2Root cause: kubectl get events is namespace-scoped by default and interleaves every object's events — in a busy namespace, one pod's older events get pushed past whatever you're tailing. kubectl describe pod (and a filtered get events) both scope to a single object, so nothing gets crowded out. Both commands read the exact same underlying Event objects with the exact same TTL (--event-ttl on the API server, default 1h) — describe has no special access or extra retention, it's just pre-filtered.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Events seem incomplete → Check describe
②
kubectl describe pod → FULL history
③
Use describe for debugging, events for overview

Tenet: kubectl get events -n <ns> shows every object's events interleaved, namespace-wide — a busy namespace crowds out any one object's history unless you filter it (--field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod>). kubectl describe pod shows events SPECIFIC to that pod only — same underlying data, same retention, just pre-filtered. For debugging one pod, ALWAYS use describe (or a filtered get events). On CKA: if get events looks incomplete, don't assume data was lost — filter by object name or use describe first.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (unfiltered, tailed — LOOKS incomplete)
$ kubectl get events -n easypj --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -3 5m Normal Pulled pod/easypj-web-xxx Successfully pulled image "nginx:alpine" ← a DIFFERENT pod's event! 4m Normal Created configmap/easypj-config ConfigMap easypj-config updated ← unrelated object! 3m Warning BackOff pod/easypj-api-xxx Back-off restarting failed container
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep BackOff Warning BackOff 10s (x12 over 5m) kubelet Back-off restarting failed container ← same 12 repeats, just AGGREGATED into one line with a counter — not 12 separate lines
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (filtered get events — same data as describe)
$ kubectl get events -n easypj --field-selector involvedObject.name=easypj-api-9c8f7-x7z2q --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' 5m Normal Scheduled pod/easypj-api-9c8f7-x7z2q Successfully assigned to node 5m Normal Pulling pod/easypj-api-9c8f7-x7z2q Pulling image "busybox:1.36" 5m Normal Started pod/easypj-api-9c8f7-x7z2q Started container api 10s Warning BackOff pod/easypj-api-9c8f7-x7z2q Back-off restarting failed container (x12 over 5m) ✅ Full per-pod history — nothing was ever missing!
5

🔧 Fix — Scope Events to One Object Instead of Assuming Data Is Lost

BASH — Best practice for event debugging 
# For specific pod debugging — use describe (events filtered to just this object)
kubectl describe pod -n <ns> <pod-name>

# Equivalent — get events filtered to the same single object
kubectl get events -n <ns> --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod-name> --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'

# For cluster-wide overview — use unfiltered get events (namespace/cluster-wide, easy to get crowded)
kubectl get events -A --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'

# For real-time event watching
kubectl get events -n <ns> -w

# Fix the actual crash (exit 1 pod)
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api -n easypj api=nginx:alpine
6

✅ Verify — Full Event Visibility

kubectl describe pod (or a field-selector-filtered get events) shows this pod's complete event history — same data, same 1-hour TTL as unfiltered get events, just scoped to one object instead of the whole namespace. Rule: use describe (or a filtered query) for per-pod debugging, unfiltered get events for cluster overview. Never assume events were "lost" just because an unfiltered, tailed view looks thin.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj

📌 S29–S34: DNS, Services & Network Policy

S29
🧪 SCENARIO S29 — Category 2: Troubleshooting DNS

CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff — Fix Corrupted Corefile ConfigMap

The Problem: Internal DNS is completely broken. Pods can't resolve Service names. easypj-web can't reach easypj-api. CoreDNS pods show CrashLoopBackOff. The Corefile ConfigMap has a syntax error introduced during an edit. Your job: find the syntax error in the CoreDNS ConfigMap and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — CoreDNS is critical infrastructure
1

📋 Break CoreDNS by Corrupting the Corefile (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A well-meaning admin edits the CoreDNS ConfigMap to add a new plugin. They typo the plugin name as "INVALID_PLUGIN". CoreDNS pods restart — and crash immediately. DNS is broken cluster-wide. easypj-web can't resolve easypj-api. Services unreachable. Entire platform DOWN. Lesson: ALWAYS backup the Corefile before editing. A bad CoreDNS ConfigMap = cluster-wide DNS outage. Use kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml > backup.yaml first.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S29): 
easypj/
└── (No new files — CoreDNS is a cluster-level component in kube-system)
BASH — Corrupt CoreDNS ConfigMap then diagnose 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S29: CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff — Bad Corefile ConfigMap
# ⚠️  WARNING: This WILL break DNS for your cluster!
# Only run in a practice/lab environment!
# ============================================

# Step 1: Backup the current Corefile
kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml > /tmp/coredns-backup.yaml

# Step 2: Corrupt the Corefile (add invalid syntax). Write it to a file first —
# kubectl patch --type=json requires a strictly valid JSON document, and a raw
# multi-line Corefile with literal (unescaped) newlines is NOT valid JSON, so
# patch would just fail to parse. Regenerating the ConfigMap from a file sidesteps that.
cat << 'EOF' > /tmp/corefile-bad
.:53 {
    errors
    health
    INVALID_PLUGIN
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
      pods insecure
      ttl 30
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
    loadbalance
}
EOF
kubectl create configmap coredns -n kube-system \
  --from-file=Corefile=/tmp/corefile-bad \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Step 3: Restart CoreDNS to pick up bad config
kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system

# Now pods can't resolve DNS — everything breaks!
2

⚠️ Observe — DNS Is Broken Cluster-Wide

✗1. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns → CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. Pods can't resolve any Service names — nslookup fails
✗3. Health checks fail — pods marked Unhealthy across the cluster!
3

🔍 Debug — Find Why CoreDNS Is Crashing

1Check CoreDNS logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/coredns
→ "plugin/INVALID_PLUGIN: plugin not found" — bad plugin name!
2Check ConfigMap: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A3 Corefile
→ INVALID_PLUGIN in Corefile — not a real CoreDNS plugin!
3Root cause: Corefile ConfigMap has invalid syntax. CoreDNS can't parse the configuration and exits immediately. All DNS resolution across the cluster fails. Fix: restore the Corefile from backup or remove the invalid line.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
DNS broken → Check CoreDNS pods
②
CrashLoopBackOff → Check logs
③
ConfigMap error → Fix Corefile
④
Restart → DNS working!

Tenet: CoreDNS is the DNS server for Kubernetes. Its configuration is stored in the coredns ConfigMap in kube-system. If CoreDNS crashes, ALL service discovery breaks. Always backup the Corefile before editing. On CKA: DNS broken + CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff = check Corefile ConfigMap syntax.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/coredns plugin/INVALID_PLUGIN: plugin not found ← Crash cause!
$ kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep INVALID INVALID_PLUGIN ← Not a real CoreDNS plugin!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE coredns-7d8f9-abcde 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ DNS restored!
5

🔧 Fix — Restore Corefile from Backup

BASH — Restore working CoreDNS config 
# Restore from backup
kubectl apply -f /tmp/coredns-backup.yaml

# OR: Edit directly to remove the bad line
kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system
# Remove the "INVALID_PLUGIN" line

# Restart CoreDNS
kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deploy/coredns -n kube-system --timeout=60s

# Test DNS
kubectl run test-dns --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default
6

✅ Verify — DNS Resolution Restored

CoreDNS pods Running. nslookup resolves Service names. Rule: ALWAYS backup the Corefile before editing. A bad Corefile = cluster-wide DNS outage.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Restore CoreDNS ConfigMap

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Restore CoreDNS from backup or rollout restart
kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system

# If ConfigMap was edited, restore from backup:
# kubectl apply -f coredns-cm-backup.yaml

# Verify
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
S30
🧪 SCENARIO S30 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Service

Service Has No Endpoints — Selector Labels Don't Match Pods

The Problem: kubectl get svc shows the Service exists, but kubectl get endpoints shows <none>. The Service selector says app: easypj-api but the pod labels are app: easypj-api-v2. A simple label mismatch blocks ALL traffic. Your job: find the mismatch and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy Pods + Service with Mismatched Labels (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A version upgrade changed pod labels from app=easypj-api to app=easypj-api-v2. The Service still selects app=easypj-api. Endpoints drop to zero. The API is running healthy but receiving ZERO traffic. Users see "503 Service Unavailable". Lesson: Service selectors must match pod labels EXACTLY. A single character mismatch = no endpoints. Use kubectl get endpoints to verify, and kubectl describe svc to see the selector.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S30): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← Pods labeled app=easypj-api-v2
└── 02-api-service.yaml          ← Service selects app=easypj-api (MISMATCH!)
BASH — Deploy mismatched Service and Pods 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S30: Service Selector Mismatch — No Endpoints
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. DEPLOY PODS — a renamed "v2" Deployment naturally gets app=easypj-api-v2
# (kubectl label deploy only touches the Deployment object's OWN labels, not the pod
#  template — it would NOT actually relabel the running pods, so we create with the
#  v2 name directly so kubectl create deploy's default label is correct from the start)
kubectl create deploy easypj-api-v2 -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2

# 3. CREATE SERVICE WITH MISMATCHED SELECTOR (BUG: selects app=easypj-api, not easypj-api-v2)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api     # ❌ BUG! Pods have app: easypj-api-v2!
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
2

⚠️ Observe — Service Exists but No Endpoints

✗1. kubectl get svc -n easypj → Service exists with ClusterIP
✗2. kubectl get endpoints -n easypj → ENDPOINTS: <none>
✗3. kubectl get pods -n easypj --show-labels → Pods have app=easypj-api-v2
3

🔍 Debug — Why Are Endpoints Empty?

1Check Service selector: kubectl get svc -n easypj easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A2 selector
→ app: easypj-api
2Check pod labels: kubectl get pods -n easypj --show-labels
→ app=easypj-api-v2 — DOESN'T MATCH!
3Root cause: Service selector {app: easypj-api} does not match pod labels {app: easypj-api-v2}. The Service can't find any pods to route traffic to. Fix the Service selector to match — the Deployment's pod-template label can't be changed live since spec.selector is immutable.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Service has no endpoints
②
Check selector vs pod labels
③
app:api ≠ app:api-v2 → MISMATCH!
④
Fix label → Endpoints populated!

Tenet: Service → Endpoints → Pods chain depends on LABEL MATCHING. The Service selector must match EXACTLY the labels on the pods. Mismatch = empty endpoints = no traffic. On CKA: #1 cause of "Service not working" is selector mismatch. Always check kubectl get pods --show-labels and kubectl get svc -o yaml.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get endpoints -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api <none> 5m
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj --show-labels NAME READY LABELS easypj-api-v2-7d8f9-abcde 1/1 app=easypj-api-v2,pod-template-hash=7d8f9 easypj-api-v2-7d8f9-xyz12 1/1 app=easypj-api-v2,pod-template-hash=7d8f9
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get endpoints -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api 10.0.1.5:80,10.0.1.6:80 5m ✅ Endpoints populated!
5

🔧 Fix — Match Service Selector to Pod Labels

BASH — Fix the label mismatch 
# Option A: Fix Service selector to match pods
kubectl patch svc easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/selector/app","value":"easypj-api-v2"}
]'

# Option B (why it's harder than it sounds): you can't just relabel the running pods —
# a Deployment's spec.selector is IMMUTABLE, and the pod template label is what the
# selector matches on. Relabeling running pods directly would make the ReplicaSet stop
# recognizing them (selector mismatch), spin up NEW replacement pods, and orphan the old
# ones. The only real way to change the label is to delete and recreate the Deployment —
# which is why fixing the Service selector (Option A) is almost always the right call.

# Verify endpoints now show pod IPs
kubectl get endpoints -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Endpoints Populated, Traffic Flows

Endpoints now show pod IPs. Service routes traffic correctly. Rule: the Service selector is a LABEL QUERY — it must match EXACTLY. Always verify with kubectl get pods --show-labels.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S31
🧪 SCENARIO S31 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Network

NodePort Not Accessible Externally — Port 30000-32767 Blocked

The Problem: You expose easypj-web via NodePort 30080. But curl to the node IP on port 30080 times out. The NodePort range (30000-32767) is not reachable — either a firewall is blocking it or the kube-proxy isn't forwarding. Your job: diagnose why the NodePort is unreachable.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1)
1

📋 Deploy Web App + NodePort + Block Port (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-web app is exposed via NodePort 30080. A firewall admin accidentally blocks port 30080 with iptables. External users can't reach the job board — curl hangs and times out. The pod is healthy, Service exists, but the NodePort is blocked at the network level. Lesson: NodePort connectivity depends on the node's firewall. Use telnet/nc to verify port accessibility from outside the cluster.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S31): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml       ← Web deployment exposed via NodePort
└── 02-web-service.yaml          ← NodePort Service on port 30080
BASH — Deploy easypj-web with NodePort, then block the port 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S31: NodePort Blocked by iptables
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-web -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deploy easypj-web -n easypj --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=80 --name=easypj-web-np

# Get the assigned NodePort
NODE_PORT=$(kubectl get svc easypj-web-np -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}')
echo "NodePort assigned: $NODE_PORT"

# BLOCK the NodePort with iptables (simulate firewall)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport $NODE_PORT -j DROP
# ❌ BUG! NodePort is now blocked by iptables!

# Try to access — WILL timeout!
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[0].address}')
timeout 3 curl -s http://$NODE_IP:$NODE_PORT || echo "TIMEOUT! NodePort is BLOCKED."
2

⚠️ Observe — curl to NodePort Times Out

✗1. kubectl get svc -n easypj easypj-web-np → NodePort assigned (e.g., 30080)
✗2. curl http://node-ip:30080 → timeout or connection refused
3

🔍 Debug — Why Can't External Traffic Reach NodePort?

1Check NodePort is listening: sudo ss -tlnp | grep 30080
→ kube-proxy should be listening on this port
2Check kube-proxy: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
→ kube-proxy must be Running on the node
3Root cause: NodePort traffic flows: external → NodeIP:30080 → kube-proxy → Service → Pod. If any link is broken (kube-proxy down, firewall, wrong externalTrafficPolicy), NodePort is unreachable.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
NodePort timeout → Check listener
②
ss -tlnp → kube-proxy listening?
③
Check firewall → Port blocked?
④
Fix → curl works!

Tenet: NodePort opens a port on EVERY node. External traffic hits NodeIP:NodePort → kube-proxy routes to Service → Pod. Default range: 30000-32767. Check: (1) kube-proxy running, (2) port listening via ss/netstat, (3) firewall allows the port, (4) externalTrafficPolicy setting.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo ss -tlnp | grep 30080 LISTEN 0 4096 *:30080 *:* users:(("kube-proxy",pid=1234)) ✅
$ timeout 3 curl -s http://192.168.1.10:30080 curl: (28) Failed to connect to 192.168.1.10 port 30080: Connection timed out ❌ Blocked by iptables!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s http://192.168.1.10:30080 | head -c 80 <!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><title>Job Board</title>... ✅ NodePort accessible externally!
5

🔧 Fix — Remove iptables Block on NodePort

BASH
NODE_PORT=$(kubectl get svc easypj-web-np -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}')
# Remove the iptables block
sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport $NODE_PORT -j DROP

# Test access
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get node -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[0].address}')
curl -s --connect-timeout 3 http://$NODE_IP:$NODE_PORT | head -c 50
6

✅ Verify — External Access Works

curl to NodeIP:NodePort returns the web page. Key: NodePort opens a port on EVERY node. If it's unreachable, check iptables/firewall rules on the node.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete NS + Remove iptables

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Capture the NodePort and remove the iptables rule BEFORE deleting the namespace
# (once the Service is gone, its NodePort can't be looked up anymore)
NODE_PORT=$(kubectl get svc easypj-web-np -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}' 2>/dev/null)
[ -n "$NODE_PORT" ] && sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport $NODE_PORT -j DROP 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S32
🧪 SCENARIO S32 — Category 2: Troubleshooting NetworkPolicy

Default-Deny Egress Blocks DNS — Pods Can't Resolve Names

The Problem: You apply a default-deny-all egress NetworkPolicy to secure the easypj namespace. Now pods can't resolve DNS — they can't reach CoreDNS on UDP 53. Your job: add an egress rule to allow DNS traffic while keeping other egress blocked.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Must have Calico/Cilium for NetworkPolicy
1

📋 Apply Default-Deny Egress (CONTAINS THE BUG — Blocks DNS)

📖 APP STORY: A security-minded admin applies a default-deny egress NetworkPolicy to lock down outbound traffic. But they forgot to allow DNS (UDP port 53 to CoreDNS). Pods can't resolve Service names. easypj-web can't reach easypj-api because DNS is blocked. Lesson: Default-deny policies must explicitly allow DNS. Always add an egress rule for UDP port 53 to kube-system/CoreDNS.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S32): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml       ← Web pod that needs DNS
└── 02-deny-egress-policy.yaml   ← Default-deny egress (BUG: blocks DNS!)
BASH — Deploy + apply overly restrictive NetworkPolicy 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S32: Default-Deny Egress Blocks DNS Resolution
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine

# Test DNS works BEFORE policy
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- nslookup kubernetes.default

# Apply default-deny ALL egress (BLOCKS DNS TOO!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-egress
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress: []    # ❌ BUG! Empty egress = DENY ALL — including DNS!
EOF

# Now DNS is broken!
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- nslookup kubernetes.default
# ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
2

⚠️ Observe — DNS Completely Broken

✗1. kubectl exec ... -- nslookup kubernetes.default → timeout
✗2. Pods can't resolve ANY Service names!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is DNS Failing?

1Test DNS from pod: kubectl exec ... -- nslookup kubernetes.default
→ timeout — egress blocked!
2Check NetworkPolicy: kubectl get netpol -n easypj deny-all-egress -o yaml
→ egress: [] — denies ALL outbound traffic!
3Root cause: Empty egress rules = deny all egress. DNS (UDP 53 to CoreDNS) is blocked. Fix: add egress rule allowing UDP 53 to kube-system namespace.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
nslookup fails → Check NetworkPolicy
②
egress: [] → All blocked
③
Add DNS rule → nslookup works!

Tenet: Always allow DNS egress (UDP 53 to CoreDNS) when using default-deny policies. Without DNS, pods can't resolve Service names, external APIs, or anything. CoreDNS runs in kube-system namespace on port 53.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- nslookup kubernetes.default ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- nslookup kubernetes.default Server: 10.96.0.10 Address: 10.96.0.10#53 Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local ✅ DNS restored!
5

🔧 Fix — Allow DNS Egress

BASH
# Add DNS egress to the policy
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-egress
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    # ⚠️ namespaceSelector + podSelector must be fields of the SAME list item (no separate "-")
    # to AND together and scope to "CoreDNS pods specifically" — two separate "-" entries would
    # OR them instead, allowing ALL of kube-system OR any k8s-app=kube-dns pod in any namespace
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53       # ✅ Allow DNS!
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53       # DNS falls back to TCP for large/truncated responses (RFC 7766) — allow both
EOF
6

✅ Verify — DNS Working

nslookup now resolves. Rule: default-deny egress MUST include DNS allow rule. Always test DNS after applying NetworkPolicies.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete NetPol + Namespace

kubectl delete networkpolicy deny-all-egress -n easypj --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S33
🧪 SCENARIO S33 — Category 2: Troubleshooting NetworkPolicy

NetworkPolicy Selector Typo — Policy Silently Applies to Zero Pods

The Problem: A NetworkPolicy is meant to restrict easypj-api so ONLY easypj-web can reach it. But its podSelector has a typo and matches zero pods — a NetworkPolicy whose podSelector matches nothing is a total no-op (Kubernetes' default is "non-isolated"), so the API stays wide open to ANY pod, not just web. This is more dangerous than a policy that blocks too much, because nothing looks broken. Your job: notice the policy isn't actually restricting anything, and fix the selector.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Requires CNI with NetworkPolicy support
1

📋 Deploy Web + API + Broken NetworkPolicy (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A NetworkPolicy is supposed to restrict the API so ONLY web can reach it. But the podSelector targets app=easypj-api-wrong instead of app=easypj-api — no pods have that label, so the policy silently applies to ZERO pods and is a total no-op. Nothing looks broken (web can still reach the API fine), but the API is actually wide open to any pod in the namespace, not locked down as intended. Lesson: NetworkPolicy podSelector must match pod labels EXACTLY — a selector matching zero pods is a silent no-op, not a "deny." Use kubectl get pods --show-labels to verify labels before writing policies, and always test with traffic that SHOULD be blocked, not just traffic that should be allowed.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S33): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml       ← Web frontend
├── 02-api-deployment.yaml       ← API backend
└── 03-network-policy.yaml       ← NetworkPolicy with wrong podSelector (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy pods + NetworkPolicy with wrong selector 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S33: NetworkPolicy Wrong podSelector — Traffic Blocked
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-web -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deploy easypj-api -n easypj --port=80

# Also deploy an unrelated "attacker" pod — used to prove whether the policy is actually restricting anything
kubectl run attacker -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --labels=app=attacker

# Apply NetworkPolicy — MEANT to allow web→api but has WRONG selector
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-web-to-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api-wrong  # ❌ BUG! No pods have this label!
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: easypj-web
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
EOF

# Test connectivity from BOTH web (should be allowed) AND the attacker (should be denied) — if the policy actually worked
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api
kubectl exec -n easypj attacker -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api
2

⚠️ Observe — Traffic Not Flowing as Expected

✗1. kubectl exec deploy/easypj-web -- wget http://easypj-api → works (expected)
✗2. kubectl exec attacker -- wget http://easypj-api → ALSO works! (should be denied — the policy isn't restricting anything!)
✗3. kubectl describe netpol allow-web-to-api -n easypj → podSelector doesn't match any pods!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Isn't the Policy Working?

1Check policy podSelector: kubectl get netpol -n easypj allow-web-to-api -o yaml | grep -A3 podSelector
→ app: easypj-api-wrong — no pods have this label!
2Check API pod labels: kubectl get pods -n easypj -l app=easypj-api --show-labels
→ app=easypj-api — NOT easypj-api-wrong
3Root cause: The NetworkPolicy's podSelector doesn't match any pods. The policy is effectively NO-OP — it applies to zero pods. Fix: change podSelector to matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Policy not blocking → Check selector
②
podSelector wrong → No pods match
③
Fix label → Policy active

Tenet: NetworkPolicy podSelector determines WHICH pods the policy applies to. If it doesn't match any pods, the policy is a NO-OP. Always verify with kubectl get pods -l <selector> that pods exist with those labels.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe netpol allow-web-to-api -n easypj PodSelector: app=easypj-api-wrong No pods match this selector! Policy is inactive.
$ kubectl exec -n easypj attacker -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api API is running ← ❌ Should be DENIED, but the no-op policy lets it through!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-web -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api API is running ✅ Policy active — web is still allowed!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj attacker -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api wget: download timed out ✅ Now correctly DENIED — policy is actually restricting traffic!
5

🔧 Fix — Correct the podSelector

BASH
kubectl patch netpol allow-web-to-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/podSelector/matchLabels/app","value":"easypj-api"}
]'
kubectl describe netpol allow-web-to-api -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Policy Now Actually Restricting Traffic

Policy now applies to API pods: web can still reach the API, but the unrelated attacker pod is now correctly denied. Rule: a podSelector matching zero pods is a silent no-op, not a "deny" — always verify with a negative test (traffic that SHOULD be blocked), not just a positive one.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete NetPol + Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up

kubectl delete networkpolicy allow-web-to-api -n easypj --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete namespace easypj

🧪 SCENARIO S34 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Ingress

Ingress Returns 502 Bad Gateway — Backend Service Has No Endpoints

The Problem: You create an Ingress for easypj-web. curl returns 502 Bad Gateway. The Ingress → Service → Endpoints → Pod chain is broken. The backend pod exists but its readiness probe is failing, so the Service has no healthy endpoints. Your job: trace the full chain and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 4 (kind-cl2)
1

📋 Deploy Web + Ingress with Broken Backend (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: An Ingress is configured to route traffic to easypj-web. But the web pod's readiness probe fails (wrong path). The Service has no endpoints. Nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway. Users see errors instead of the job board. Lesson: Ingress → Service → Endpoints → Pod. If any link in the chain breaks (readiness fails = no endpoints), users get 502. Always verify endpoints before debugging Ingress.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S34): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← API with failing readiness probe (BUG!)
├── 02-api-service.yaml          ← ClusterIP Service
└── 03-ingress.yaml              ← Ingress routing to broken backend
BASH — Deploy web + failing readiness probe + Ingress 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S34: Ingress 502 Bad Gateway
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj

# Deploy web with BROKEN readiness probe (checks /healthz — wrong path!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz   # ❌ BUG! nginx returns 404 for /healthz!
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 5
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
# Service — ClusterIP for easypj-web (Ingress backend)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
---
# Ingress — routes easypj.local to the easypj-web Service
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: easypj.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: easypj-web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# Check endpoints — EMPTY because readiness fails!
kubectl get endpoints -n easypj
# easypj-web   <none>   ← NO ENDPOINTS!

⚠️ Observe — Service Has No Endpoints

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → READY 0/1
✗2. kubectl get endpoints -n easypj → <none>
✗3. curl -H "Host: easypj.local" http://<ingress-ip> → 502 Bad Gateway
3

🔍 Debug — Trace the 502 Chain

1Check readiness: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-web | grep Readiness
→ "Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404"
2Fix probe path: Change from /healthz to / (root) which nginx DOES serve
Readiness probe path /healthz returns 404 — pod never marked Ready → Service has no endpoints → Ingress returns 502.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
502 → Check endpoints
②
Endpoints empty → Readiness probe
③
Probe 404 → Fix path
④
Pod Ready → Endpoints → 200 OK!

Tenet: 502 Bad Gateway = Ingress can't reach backend. Debug chain: kubectl get ingress → check backend service → kubectl get endpoints → kubectl describe pod. 502 = Service has no healthy endpoints. Fix the readiness probe.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get endpoints -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-web <none> 5m ← Empty = 502!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get endpoints -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-web 10.0.1.8:80 5m ✅ Endpoints populated! 200 OK!

🔧 Fix — Correct Readiness Probe Path

BASH
kubectl patch deploy easypj-web -n easypj --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/"}
]'
kubectl rollout status deploy easypj-web -n easypj
kubectl get endpoints -n easypj

✅ Verify — Endpoints Populated

Endpoints now show pod IP. Rule: 502 = check endpoints. No endpoints = check readiness probe. Fix probe → 200 OK.
