📌 S35–S40: Ingress TLS, CNI & Control Plane

S35
🧪 SCENARIO S35 — Category 2: Troubleshooting TLS

Ingress TLS Fails — Secret Has Wrong Type/Keys

The Problem: You configure TLS for easypj-web Ingress. curl https:// returns SSL error. The TLS Secret was created as type Opaque instead of kubernetes.io/tls, or the key names are wrong (cert instead of tls.crt). Your job: fix the Secret format and enable HTTPS.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 4 (kind-cl2)
1

📋 Create Wrong-Format TLS Secret (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: DevOps creates a TLS certificate for the job board's HTTPS endpoint. They use kubectl create secret generic --from-file and the Secret gets type Opaque. The Ingress expects type kubernetes.io/tls — it rejects the Secret. HTTPS is broken. Lesson: TLS Secrets MUST have type: kubernetes.io/tls and keys named tls.crt and tls.key. Use kubectl create secret tls for proper formatting.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S35): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-tls-secret.yaml           ← Secret with wrong type Opaque (BUG!)
└── 02-ingress-tls.yaml          ← Ingress expecting kubernetes.io/tls
BASH — Create TLS secret with wrong type 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S35: TLS Secret Wrong Type — Ingress Rejects Opaque Secret
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-web -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deploy easypj-web -n easypj --port=80

# Generate self-signed cert (for testing)
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout /tmp/tls.key -out /tmp/tls.crt \
  -subj "/CN=easypj.local"

# ❌ BUG! Created as Opaque with wrong key names!
kubectl create secret generic easypj-tls -n easypj \
  --from-file=cert=/tmp/tls.crt \
  --from-file=key=/tmp/tls.key
# This creates type: Opaque with keys "cert" and "key"
# Ingress requires type: kubernetes.io/tls with keys "tls.crt" and "tls.key"

# Check the secret type — WRONG!
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj -o yaml | grep type
# type: Opaque  ← BUG! Should be kubernetes.io/tls
2

⚠️ Observe — Secret Type Is Wrong

✗1. kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj → TYPE: Opaque
✗2. Ingress references this secret — TLS won't work!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is TLS Not Working?

1Check Secret type: kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj -o yaml | grep ^type:
→ type: Opaque — Ingress requires kubernetes.io/tls!
2Root cause: TLS Secrets must be type: kubernetes.io/tls with keys tls.crt and tls.key. kubectl create secret generic creates Opaque type which Ingress can't use. Fix: recreate with kubectl create secret tls.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
TLS broken → Check Secret type
②
Opaque, not kubernetes.io/tls
③
Recreate with kubectl create secret tls
④
HTTPS works!

Tenet: TLS Secrets MUST be type kubernetes.io/tls with specific key names: tls.crt (certificate) and tls.key (private key). Use kubectl create secret tls — it automatically sets the correct type and key names.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj NAME TYPE DATA AGE easypj-tls Opaque 2 5m ← WRONG TYPE!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj NAME TYPE DATA AGE easypj-tls kubernetes.io/tls 2 10s ✅ Correct TLS type!
5

🔧 Fix — Recreate as Proper TLS Secret

BASH
# Delete wrong secret
kubectl delete secret easypj-tls -n easypj

# Recreate with CORRECT type using kubectl create secret tls
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n easypj \
  --cert=/tmp/tls.crt \
  --key=/tmp/tls.key

# Verify type is now kubernetes.io/tls
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — Secret Type Correct

Secret shows TYPE: kubernetes.io/tls. Ingress can now use it. Rule: always use kubectl create secret tls for TLS certs.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
kubectl delete secret easypj-tls --ignore-not-found
S36
🧪 SCENARIO S36 — Category 2: Troubleshooting kube-proxy

kube-proxy Not Routing — Service ClusterIP Unreachable

The Problem: Pods can reach each other directly, but Service ClusterIPs are unreachable. kube-proxy is not creating iptables rules. The kube-proxy ConfigMap may have a wrong mode set or kube-proxy pods are crashing. Your job: diagnose why kube-proxy isn't routing service traffic.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy Service + Test Connectivity (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-web Deployment is running, the Service exists, but curl to the ClusterIP hangs. kube-proxy is responsible for writing iptables rules that route Service IPs to pod IPs. If kube-proxy is down, Service IPs go nowhere. Lesson: kube-proxy is a DaemonSet in kube-system. If Services are unreachable but pods are healthy, check kube-proxy first.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S36): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-web-deployment.yaml       ← Web deployment
└── 02-web-service.yaml          ← ClusterIP Service (unreachable if kube-proxy down)
BASH — Deploy + diagnose kube-proxy 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S36: kube-proxy Not Routing
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deploy easypj-api -n easypj --port=80 --name=easypj-api

# ❌ BUG! Force kube-proxy's DaemonSet off every real node — patch its pod template
# with an impossible nodeSelector. The rolling update then removes the running
# kube-proxy pods and schedules no replacements, so Service routing stops cold.
kubectl -n kube-system patch ds kube-proxy -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"nonexistent":"true"}}}}}'
sleep 10

# Get the Service ClusterIP
CLUSTER_IP=$(kubectl get svc easypj-api -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')
echo "Service IP: $CLUSTER_IP"

# Test from a debug pod
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n easypj -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://$CLUSTER_IP || echo "UNREACHABLE!"

# Check kube-proxy pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy --tail=10

# Check iptables rules (on node)
sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep easypj-api
2

⚠️ Observe — Service ClusterIP Unreachable

✗1. wget http://<ClusterIP> from pod → timeout
✗2. Pod-to-pod direct IP works — but Service IP doesn't
✗3. kubectl get endpoints shows pod IPs — routing is broken!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Isn't the Service IP Working?

1Check kube-proxy pods: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
→ No pods or CrashLoopBackOff — kube-proxy not running!
2Check iptables: sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES
→ No rules for the Service!
3Root cause: kube-proxy is responsible for programming iptables/IPVS rules that route Service ClusterIPs to pod IPs. If kube-proxy is not running, Services don't work even though pods can communicate directly.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Service unreachable → Check kube-proxy
②
No iptables rules → kube-proxy down
③
Restart kube-proxy → Rules created
④
Service IP works!

Tenet: kube-proxy runs on every node as a DaemonSet. It watches the API server for Services and Endpoints, then programs iptables/IPVS rules. Without kube-proxy: pods work (direct IP), Services don't (no iptables rules). Check: kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep easypj-api (no output — no iptables rule for this Service!)
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy No resources found in kube-system namespace. ← kube-proxy missing!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api API is running ✅ Service ClusterIP reachable!
5

🔧 Fix — Restart/Restore kube-proxy

BASH
# Check kube-proxy DaemonSet — DESIRED/CURRENT/READY will all be 0
kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy

# The real cause is the impossible nodeSelector injected on the DaemonSet's pod
# template — a rollout restart alone won't fix this, the selector itself must go
kubectl -n kube-system patch ds kube-proxy --type=json -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector/nonexistent"}]'

# Now kube-proxy pods get (re)scheduled onto every real node
kubectl rollout status ds kube-proxy -n kube-system --timeout=60s

# Verify iptables rules are created
sudo iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep easypj
6

✅ Verify — Service IP Reachable

wget http://ClusterIP now works. kube-proxy has created iptables rules. Service discovery is restored.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Restart kube-proxy + Delete NS

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete test namespace
kubectl delete namespace easypj --ignore-not-found

# Safety net: make sure the injected nodeSelector is gone even if the Fix step was skipped
kubectl -n kube-system patch ds kube-proxy --type=json -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector/nonexistent"}]' 2>/dev/null
kubectl rollout restart ds kube-proxy -n kube-system
S37
🧪 SCENARIO S37 — Category 2: Troubleshooting CNI

CNI Plugin Crash — Cross-Node Pod Communication Broken

The Problem: New pods get stuck in ContainerCreating — kubelet can't find any CNI config file on the node to set up pod networking. The CNI DaemonSet pods themselves (calico-node) are still Running; the config FILE on disk is what's missing. Your job: diagnose the CNI failure, check the CNI config files, and restore networking.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — CNI is critical cluster infrastructure
1

📋 Deploy Pods Across Nodes + Diagnose CNI Failure

📖 APP STORY: New pods are stuck in ContainerCreating. Events show "network plugin not ready". The node's CNI config file (10-calico.conflist) got moved out of /etc/cni/net.d/ — kubelet has nowhere to read CNI config from, even though the calico-node DaemonSet pod itself is still Running. No new pods can get IPs. The easypj-web deployment can't start. Lesson: CNI is the networking foundation, and it has TWO parts — the DaemonSet pod (the running process) and the config file on the node's disk (what kubelet actually reads). A healthy CNI pod doesn't guarantee a healthy CNI config file. Without it, pods can't get IPs — the cluster is effectively dead for scheduling.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S37): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml            ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml       ← API deployment (pods stuck if CNI broken)
BASH — Deploy + diagnose CNI plugin 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S37: CNI Plugin Crash
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj

# ❌ BUG! Move the CNI config file out of /etc/cni/net.d/ on this node — kubelet
# can no longer find any CNI config, so it can't set up networking for new pods.
sudo mv /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist /tmp/10-calico.conflist.bak 2>/dev/null || \
sudo mv /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist /tmp/ 2>/dev/null

kubectl create deploy easypj-web -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3

# Check if pods are stuck in ContainerCreating
kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide

# Check CNI plugin pods (Calico, Flannel, Cilium, etc.)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|flannel|cilium|weave"

# Check CNI config on node
ls /etc/cni/net.d/
cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist 2>/dev/null || cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null

# Check kubelet logs for CNI errors
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "5 min ago" | grep -i cni
2

⚠️ Observe — Cross-Node Networking Broken

✗1. New pods stuck in ContainerCreating — CNI can't set up network
✗2. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep calico → calico-node is still Running (the CNI pod is fine!)
✗3. kubectl describe pod on the stuck pod → "network plugin is not ready: cni config uninitialized"
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the CNI Failing?

1Check CNI pods: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|flannel|cilium"
→ calico-node is Running — the DaemonSet itself is healthy!
2Check kubelet logs: sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "5 min ago" | grep -i cni
→ "no networks found in /etc/cni/net.d" — kubelet has no config to read!
3Check CNI config: ls /etc/cni/net.d/ on node
→ Empty — the conflist file is gone from disk!
4Root cause: The CNI DaemonSet pod running is not the same thing as the CNI config file existing on the node's disk — kubelet reads the config file directly, not the pod's process. With the conflist gone, kubelet can't set up networking for new pods even though calico-node looks perfectly healthy. Fix: restart the CNI DaemonSet pod — its own install-cni init container will rewrite the config file to disk.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pods stuck ContainerCreating → Check CNI pod
②
CNI pod is Running → Check the config FILE instead
③
/etc/cni/net.d/ empty → Restart CNI DaemonSet
④
install-cni init container rewrites file → Network restored!

Tenet: CNI (Container Network Interface) has two independently-failing parts: the DaemonSet pod (a running process) and the config file on the node's disk (what kubelet actually reads). A healthy pod doesn't mean a healthy config file. Check: kubectl get pods -n kube-system for the CNI pod's status, /etc/cni/net.d/ for the config file's presence, kubelet logs for CNI errors. Common CNI plugins: Calico, Flannel, Cilium, Weave.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep calico calico-node-xxxxx 1/1 Running 0 30m ← the POD is fine!
$ ls /etc/cni/net.d/ (empty — the conflist file is gone from this node's disk)
$ sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "5 min ago" | grep -i cni cni.go:237] Unable to update cni config: no networks found in /etc/cni/net.d
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ ls /etc/cni/net.d/ 10-calico.conflist ✅ install-cni init container rewrote it on pod restart!
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide NAME READY STATUS IP NODE easypj-web-1 1/1 Running 10.0.1.5 node1 easypj-web-2 1/1 Running 10.0.1.6 node1 easypj-web-3 1/1 Running 10.0.1.7 node1 ✅ Scheduled and networked!
5

🔧 Fix — Restart CNI + Verify Config

BASH
# Restart the CNI DaemonSet pod — its install-cni init container re-writes
# the config file to /etc/cni/net.d/ on every start, regardless of whether
# the file was already there
kubectl rollout restart ds -n kube-system calico-node

# Verify CNI config file is back on the node
ls /etc/cni/net.d/
cat /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist
6

✅ Verify — Network Restored

The conflist file is back on disk, and new pods now get IPs and start Running. Key takeaway: a CNI DaemonSet pod showing Running tells you the process is alive — it does NOT tell you the node's on-disk CNI config is intact, since kubelet reads that file directly rather than talking to the pod. Always check both.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Restart CNI + Delete NS

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete test namespace
kubectl delete namespace easypj --ignore-not-found

# Ensure CNI is healthy (adjust DaemonSet name to your CNI)
kubectl rollout restart ds -n kube-system calico-node 2>/dev/null || true
kubectl rollout restart ds -n kube-system cilium 2>/dev/null || true

# Verify pods are running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|flannel|weave"
S38
🧪 SCENARIO S38 — Category 2: Troubleshooting etcd

etcd Database Too Large — Cluster Becomes Read-Only

The Problem: kubectl apply returns errors. The cluster is read-only. etcd has exceeded its storage quota. No new resources can be created. You need to compact and defragment etcd to reclaim space and restore write capability.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Direct etcd access required
1

📋 Check etcd Status + Simulate Storage Issue

📖 APP STORY: kubectl commands start returning "etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded". The cluster is read-only. etcd hit its 2GB quota. No new resources can be created. The easypj team can't deploy a hotfix — the API server rejects all writes. Lesson: Monitor etcd DB size. Default quota is 2GB. Use etcdctl compaction and defrag to reclaim space. Schedule regular maintenance.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S38): 
easypj/
└── (No new files — etcd is a cluster-level component, diagnose on control plane)
BASH — Check etcd health and storage 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S38: etcd Storage Full
# ============================================

# Check etcd endpoint status (storage usage)
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint status --write-out=table

# Check DB size
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint status --write-out=table | grep DB

# If DB size exceeds quota (default 2GB), etcd becomes read-only!
# kubectl apply fails with "etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded"
2

⚠️ Observe — Cluster Read-Only

✗1. kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml → "etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded"
✗2. Can still read (get, describe) but can't write (apply, create, delete)
3

🔍 Debug — Check etcd Storage

1Check etcd status: etcdctl endpoint status — look at DB SIZE
→ DB size near or exceeding quota (e.g., 2.1GB / 2GB)
2Root cause: etcd has a storage quota (default 2GB). When reached, etcd becomes read-only. Fix: compact historical revisions, then defragment to reclaim space.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
kubectl apply fails → Check etcd
②
DB size exceeded → Compact
③
Defrag → Reclaim space
④
alarm disarm → Cluster writable again!

Tenet: etcd stores ALL Kubernetes state. Default quota: 2GB. Exceeding it raises a LATCHED NOSPACE alarm that puts the cluster in a read-only state. Compact removes old revisions, defrag reclaims disk space — but neither alone restores writes: the alarm must be explicitly cleared with etcdctl alarm disarm, or the cluster stays read-only even with plenty of free space. Run compaction/defrag periodically in production. CKA exam: etcd maintenance is a core skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table ENDPOINT ID VERSION DB SIZE IS LEADER https://127.0.0.1 abc123def456 3.5.x 2.1 GB true ← EXCEEDED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table | grep DB DB SIZE: 45 MB ✅ Compacted from 2.1 GB!
$ kubectl create deploy test --image=nginx:alpine deployment.apps/test created ✅ Cluster writable again!
5

🔧 Fix — Compact + Defrag etcd

BASH
ETCDCTL="sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key"

# Get current revision
REV=$($ETCDCTL endpoint status --write-out="json" | grep -o '"revision":[0-9]*' | cut -d: -f2)
echo "Compacting to revision: $REV"

# Compact (removes old revisions)
$ETCDCTL compaction $REV

# Defrag (reclaims disk space)
$ETCDCTL defrag

# Disarm the NOSPACE alarm — compaction + defrag alone do NOT restore writes!
# The alarm LATCHES: even with space reclaimed, etcd stays read-only until disarmed
$ETCDCTL alarm list
$ETCDCTL alarm disarm

# Verify DB size reduced and cluster is writable again
$ETCDCTL endpoint status --write-out=table
6

✅ Verify — Cluster Writable

kubectl apply works again. etcd DB size is below quota. Rule: schedule regular etcd compaction (daily/weekly) and monitor DB size with alerts.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Verify etcd Health

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete the throwaway test deployment created during the Fix step's write-verification
kubectl delete deploy test --ignore-not-found

# Compaction, defrag, and alarm disarm were done during fix
# Verify etcd is healthy
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health

# Verify kubectl works
kubectl get nodes
S39
🧪 SCENARIO S39 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Certificates

kubeadm Certificate Expired — kubectl Returns x509 Error

The Problem: kubectl suddenly returns "x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid". The kubeadm certificates (1 year validity) have expired. The cluster is still running but you can't manage it. Your job: check certificate expiration and renew them.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — kubeadm cluster certificate management
1

📋 Check Certificate Expiration Dates

📖 APP STORY: It's month 13 after cluster setup. kubectl suddenly returns "Unauthorized". All API calls fail. The kubeadm certificates expired at the 1-year mark. The entire cluster is inaccessible — job board DOWN. Lesson: kubeadm certs expire after 1 year. Use kubeadm certs check-expiration to monitor. Renew with kubeadm certs renew all before expiry.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S39): 
easypj/
└── (No new files — certificate renewal is a control-plane operation)
BASH — Check cert expiry + renew if needed 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S39: kubeadm Certificate Expiry — Renew Before Expiry
# ============================================

# Check ALL certificate expiration dates
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration

# Look for certificates expiring soon or already expired
# Output shows each cert name, expiry date, and remaining time

# If kubectl returns x509 errors:
# "Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate has expired"

# Also check kubeconfig certs
kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.users[0].user.client-certificate-data}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates
2

⚠️ Observe — kubectl x509 Error

✗1. kubectl get nodes → "x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid"
✗2. sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration → shows expired certs
3

🔍 Debug — Find Expired Certificates

1Check all certs: sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration
→ Lists expiration dates for all kubeadm-managed certs
2Check admin.conf cert: openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf -noout -dates
→ Client certificate expired!
3Root cause: kubeadm certificates have 1-year validity. After expiry, TLS connections fail. Fix: run kubeadm certs renew all to renew ALL certificates.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
x509 error → Check certs
②
kubeadm certs check-expiration
③
Expired → kubeadm certs renew all
④
kubectl works again!

Tenet: kubeadm certificates expire after 1 year. Check with kubeadm certs check-expiration regularly. Renew with kubeadm certs renew all. After renewal, restart control plane components. Update kubeconfig if using client certificates. On CKA: cert expiry is a common troubleshooting scenario.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration CERTIFICATE EXPIRES RESIDUAL TIME admin.conf Jan 01, 2025 00:00 UTC EXPIRED! apiserver Jan 01, 2025 00:00 UTC EXPIRED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration | head -5 CERTIFICATE EXPIRES RESIDUAL TIME apiserver Jun 05, 2027 10:00 UTC 364d ✅ Renewed!
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION easy Ready control-plane 90d v1.32.13 ✅ kubectl works!
5

🔧 Fix — Renew All kubeadm Certificates

BASH
# Renew ALL kubeadm certificates
sudo kubeadm certs renew all

# Update kubeconfig with new certificates
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

# Restart control plane static pods
sudo crictl pods --name kube-apiserver -q | xargs sudo crictl stopp
sudo crictl pods --name kube-controller-manager -q | xargs sudo crictl stopp
sudo crictl pods --name kube-scheduler -q | xargs sudo crictl stopp
# Kubelet will restart them automatically

# Verify kubectl works
kubectl get nodes
6

✅ Verify — kubectl Working

kubectl get nodes returns successfully. Rule: set a calendar reminder 30 days before cert expiry. Automate renewal with kubeadm or cert-manager.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Verify Certs Renewed

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Certs were renewed during fix
# Verify cluster is operational
kubectl get nodes

# Check new cert expiry dates
kubeadm certs check-expiration
S40
🧪 SCENARIO S40 — Category 2: Troubleshooting Control Plane

API Server Down — Corrupted Static Pod Manifest

The Problem: kubectl returns "connection refused". The API server is DOWN. The kube-apiserver static pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ picked up a bogus CLI flag during an edit — the YAML itself is still syntactically valid, so kubelet parses and starts the container fine, but kube-apiserver's own flag parser rejects the unrecognized flag and exits immediately. Your job: find and fix the bad flag to restore the API server.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Control plane recovery drill
1

📋 Corrupt the API Server Manifest (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A well-meaning admin edits /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml to add a feature gate — but a botched sed edit splits one valid flag into two list items, introducing a bogus flag alongside it. The YAML stays syntactically valid — kubelet parses and starts the container fine — but kube-apiserver's own argument parser rejects the unrecognized flag and exits immediately, so kubelet just keeps restarting a crashing container. kubectl returns "connection refused". The entire cluster is headless. Lesson: kube-apiserver.yaml is a static pod manifest — kubelet only guarantees the YAML parses, not that the arguments inside it are valid flags for the binary. Always backup manifests before editing. Recovery: fix the bad flag, kubelet auto-restarts the pod.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S40): 
easypj/
└── (No new files — API server manifest is at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml)
BASH — Corrupt kube-apiserver.yaml + recovery drill 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S40: API Server Static Pod Crash
# ⚠️  WARNING: This kills your API server. Recovery required!
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Backup the manifest (CRITICAL!)
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup

# STEP 2: Corrupt the manifest (simulate YAML error)
# Introduce an intentional YAML syntax error
sudo sed -i 's/--advertise-address/--advertise-address
    - --broken-flag-that-doesnt-exist/' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Kubelet will detect the change and try to restart API server — IT WILL FAIL
# kubectl will stop working in ~30 seconds
2

⚠️ Observe — kubectl Connection Refused

✗1. kubectl get nodes → "The connection to the server was refused"
✗2. sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver → NOT running!
✗3. Cluster is alive (pods running) but UNMANAGEABLE!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the API Server Down?

1Check static pod manifest: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
→ Syntactically valid YAML — but the command list has a bogus extra entry: "--broken-flag-that-doesnt-exist=..."
2Check the container itself: sudo crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver and sudo crictl logs <container-id>
→ container starts then exits immediately; logs show "Error: unknown flag: --broken-flag-that-doesnt-exist"
3Root cause: The manifest itself is valid YAML — kubelet parses it and starts the container without complaint. The problem is one level deeper: kube-apiserver's own CLI flag parser rejects the unrecognized flag and the process exits immediately, so kubelet just keeps restarting a container that instantly crashes. Fix: restore from backup or remove the bad flag.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
kubectl down → Check API server
②
crictl ps → No apiserver container
③
Check manifest → Corrupted YAML
④
Restore backup → API server UP!

Tenet: Control plane components (apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd) run as STATIC PODS managed by kubelet from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. Kubelet only guarantees the manifest is valid YAML — it has no idea whether the arguments inside command: are valid flags for the actual binary. A bad flag still starts the container (kubelet's job is done); it's the binary's own flag parser that then rejects it and exits. Always backup manifests before editing. Recovery: restore from backup or remove the bad flag. Kubelet auto-restarts static pods once the manifest changes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get nodes The connection to the server localhost:6443 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?
$ sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver (no output — API server container not running!)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver abc123def456 registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.32.13 Running ✅
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION easy Ready control-plane 90d v1.32.13 ✅ Cluster managed!
5

🔧 Fix — Restore API Server Manifest from Backup

BASH
# Step 1: Restore the backup manifest
sudo cp /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Step 2: Kubelet will detect the fixed manifest and start API server (~30s)
sleep 30

# Step 3: Verify API server is running
sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver
kubectl get nodes

# Step 4: Check all control plane components
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "apiserver|controller|scheduler|etcd"
6

✅ Verify — API Server Restored

kubectl get nodes works. Cluster is manageable again. Rule: ALWAYS backup /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ before editing. Kubelet auto-recovers static pods from valid manifests.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Verify All Control Plane Pods

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Manifest was fixed during the exercise — this scenario creates no other
# namespaced resources, so there's nothing else to delete
# Verify all control plane components are healthy
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "apiserver|controller|scheduler|etcd"

# Verify cluster is fully operational
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A

📦 Category 3: Workloads & SchedulingS41-S55

🔄 Deployments, Rollouts, Scheduling & Autoscaling

Master rolling updates, rollbacks, blue-green/canary deployments, scheduling constraints (nodeSelector, affinity, taints/tolerations), ConfigMap/Secret updates, HPA, PDBs, and ResourceQuotas. All scenarios use the easypj/jobpost Django application.

📌 S41–S45: Deployments & Rollout Strategies

S41
🧪 SCENARIO S41 — Category 3: Workloads Rollout Debug

maxSurge=0 + maxUnavailable=0 — API Rejects the "Safest" Rollout Strategy

The Problem: You try to make the easypj-api rollout maximally safe by patching maxSurge: 0 AND maxUnavailable: 0 together — "zero changes during update = zero risk," or so it seems. The patch fails immediately with a validation error: Kubernetes rejects this combination outright at the API level, because it's a mathematical deadlock (no pods can be created, none can be removed) — the API server won't even let you persist it. Your job: understand the rejection, then apply a strategy that's actually valid.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy easypj-api v2, Then Try the "Safest" RollingUpdate Config (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A junior DevOps engineer thinks "0 changes during update = safest deployment" and tries to patch the easypj-api Deployment's rollingUpdate strategy to maxSurge=0 AND maxUnavailable=0. The patch command errors out immediately — Kubernetes' API validation refuses this combination before it's ever persisted, because with both at 0 there's mathematically no way to replace any pod (can't create extras, can't remove existing ones). The Deployment quietly keeps its previous strategy; the engineer is left staring at a validation error they don't understand, unsure if anything actually changed.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S41): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment with BUG: maxSurge=0 + maxUnavailable=0
└── 02-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
BASH — Deploy + trigger the deadlocked rollout 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S41: maxSurge=0 + maxUnavailable=0 Is Rejected at the API Level
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. DEPLOY API v2 WITH A NORMAL, VALID ROLLING UPDATE STRATEGY
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:1.25-alpine
        env:
        - name: APP_VERSION
          value: "v2"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
# Service — ClusterIP for easypj-api
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF

# Wait for pods to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=60s
kubectl get pods -n easypj

# ❌ BUG! Try to patch BOTH to 0, thinking it's the safest possible update —
# this is REJECTED outright by the API server's own validation, not a silent deadlock
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj -p '
{
  "spec": {
    "strategy": {
      "rollingUpdate": {
        "maxSurge": 0,
        "maxUnavailable": 0
      }
    }
  }
}'
2

⚠️ Observe — kubectl patch Fails Immediately

✗1. kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj -p '...maxSurge:0,maxUnavailable:0...' → errors out immediately with "Invalid value"
✗2. kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A3 rollingUpdate → strategy is UNCHANGED — the rejected patch never took effect
✗3. The engineer isn't sure WHY the patch was rejected, or whether it's safe to just retry
3

🔍 Debug — Why Was the Patch Rejected?

1Read the actual error text carefully: kubectl patch deploy ... output
→ "Invalid value: 0: may not be 0 when `maxSurge` is 0" — this is API-level validation, not a runtime problem
2Confirm nothing actually changed: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A5 rollingUpdate
→ Still maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 1 — the object was never mutated
3Root cause: maxSurge=0 means "don't create extra pods." maxUnavailable=0 means "don't remove any pods." With both at 0, there's mathematically no way to replace ANY pod during a rolling update — so the apps/v1 Deployment API itself validates against this combination and rejects it at admission, before it's ever persisted. Fix: at least one of maxSurge/maxUnavailable must be greater than 0.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Patch fails → Read the error text
②
"may not be 0 when maxSurge is 0"
③
API rejects it — nothing changed
④
Use a valid strategy → Rollout proceeds!

Tenet: Rolling update requires at least one of maxSurge or maxUnavailable to be >0 — this is enforced by the apps/v1 Deployment API's own validation, not just a best-practice suggestion. maxSurge = how many EXTRA pods can be created during update. maxUnavailable = how many pods can be UNAVAILABLE during update. Setting both to 0 doesn't silently deadlock a running rollout — it's rejected outright at the API level before it's ever persisted. On CKA: know this constraint so you recognize the error message instantly instead of debugging a "stuck rollout" that was never actually stuck.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"maxSurge":0,"maxUnavailable":0}}}}' Error from server (Invalid): Deployment.apps "easypj-api" is invalid: spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: Invalid value: 0: may not be 0 when `maxSurge` is 0
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A3 rollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 1 maxUnavailable: 1 ← unchanged! the rejected patch never took effect
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj deployment "easypj-api" successfully rolled out ✅
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-8e9f0-new-abc 1/1 Running 0 30s easypj-api-8e9f0-new-def 1/1 Running 0 20s easypj-api-8e9f0-new-ghi 1/1 Running 0 10s ✅ All v3!
5

🔧 Fix — Use a Valid Strategy, Then Update the Image

BASH — Patch the rolling update strategy, then trigger the update 
# Fix: keep the (already-valid) maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=1 strategy —
# the original patch attempt was simply unnecessary AND invalid
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A3 rollingUpdate

# NOW actually trigger the v2 → v3 update
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api -n easypj api=nginx:1.26-alpine
kubectl annotate deploy/easypj-api -n easypj kubernetes.io/change-cause="Upgrade to v3"

# The rollout proceeds normally — one pod replaced at a time
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=120s
kubectl get pods -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — All Pods Running v3

kubectl get pods -n easypj shows 3 pods running the new image. The rollout completed successfully with the original maxSurge=1/maxUnavailable=1 strategy — no strategy change was ever actually needed. Key rule: at least one of maxSurge or maxUnavailable must be >0, and the Deployment API enforces this at admission — an invalid combination is rejected immediately, it never gets a chance to deadlock a live rollout.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S42
🧪 SCENARIO S42 — Category 3: Workloads Rollback

Rollback to Previous Version — kubectl rollout undo

The Problem: You deployed v3 of easypj-api but users report blank pages — a critical regression. You must rollback to v2 IMMEDIATELY. The Deployment keeps revision history, so you can use kubectl rollout undo to revert. Your job: check the rollout history, identify the last good revision, and rollback.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy v2 (Good), Then "Break" with v3 (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: v3 was supposed to add a new UI for the job board. But the image tag was wrong — nginx:9.9.9-BROKEN doesn't exist. New pods show ImagePullBackOff. Users see broken pages. Must rollback to v2 immediately — every second means lost job applications.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S42): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-web-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment with revision history
BASH — Deploy v2, then v3 with broken image, then rollback 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S42: Rollback to Previous Version
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj

# STEP 1: Deploy v2 (GOOD version — working)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/change-cause: "v2 — stable frontend"
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.25-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-web -n easypj --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Deploy v3 (BROKEN — uses nonexistent image)
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web -n easypj web=nginx:9.9.9-BROKEN
kubectl annotate deploy/easypj-web -n easypj kubernetes.io/change-cause="v3 — BROKEN! blank pages" --overwrite
# ❌ BUG! Image doesn't exist — new pods will be ImagePullBackOff!

# STEP 3: Wait and observe the disaster
sleep 10
kubectl get pods -n easypj

⚠️ Observe — New Pods Failing, Site Down

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → new pods show ImagePullBackOff, old pods may be terminated
✗2. Users report blank pages — the frontend is partially broken
✗3. Must revert to v2 FAST — every second = lost revenue!

🔍 Debug — Check History and Prepare Rollback

1Check rollout history: kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web -n easypj
→ REVISION 1: v2 (stable), REVISION 2: v3 (broken)
2Verify revision details: kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web -n easypj --revision=1
→ Uses image nginx:1.25-alpine — this is the good one!
3Root cause: v3 image tag is wrong/missing. Fix: rollback to revision 1 using kubectl rollout undo. Kubernetes keeps up to 10 revisions by default (revisionHistoryLimit).

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
New pods failing → Check history
②
REV 2 broken, REV 1 good
③
rollout undo → Back to v2!

Tenet: kubectl rollout undo reverts to the PREVIOUS revision. Use --to-revision=N to rollback to a specific revision. Kubernetes stores ReplicaSets for each revision (revisionHistoryLimit, default 10). Rollback creates a NEW ReplicaSet from the old template. On CKA: rollback is a core skill — know rollout history, rollout undo, and --to-revision.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web -n easypj REVISION CHANGE-CAUSE 1 v2 — stable frontend 2 v3 — BROKEN! blank pages ← THIS IS THE PROBLEM!
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-web-7d8f9-abcde 1/1 Running 0 easypj-web-9e0f1-new-xyz 0/1 ImagePullBackOff 0 ← BROKEN!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web -n easypj REVISION CHANGE-CAUSE 2 v3 — BROKEN! blank pages 3 v2 — stable frontend ← Rollback created new REVISION 3 from REVISION 1!
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web-7d8f9-new-abc 1/1 Running 0 10s easypj-web-7d8f9-new-def 1/1 Running 0 5s ✅ Back to v2!

🔧 Fix — Rollback to Previous Revision

kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web -n easypj

# Option B: Rollback to specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web -n easypj --to-revision=1

# Verify the rollback
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n easypj
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web -n easypj

Use kubectl rollout history to see revision history. Rollback is instant — Kubernetes already has the old ReplicaSet template cached.

Blue-Green Deployment — Switch Service Between Two Stacks

The Problem: easypj-web v1 (blue) is live serving production traffic. Your team wants zero-downtime deployment. Deploy v2 (green) with all its pods alongside v1. Verify v2 works in isolation, then switch the Service selector from v1 to v2. If anything goes wrong, switch back instantly — no rollback needed.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3/4 (kind-cl1/cl2) — Can run both stacks on one cluster
1

📋 Deploy Blue (v1) + Green (v2) Side by Side

📖 APP STORY: v2 of the web frontend has a complete redesign. The team wants to deploy it without ANY downtime. Blue-green: deploy v2 fully, test it, then switch the Service selector. Instant rollback by switching back to blue — zero risk deployment.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S43): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-web-blue-deployment.yaml    ← v1 (blue) — current production
├── 02-web-green-deployment.yaml   ← v2 (green) — ready to take over
└── 03-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (switchable selector)
BASH — Deploy both stacks, Service points to blue initially 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S43: Blue-Green Deployment
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj

# STEP 1: Deploy BLUE (v1 — current production)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-blue
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-web
    version: blue
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
      version: blue
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
        version: blue
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.25-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

# STEP 2: Create Service pointing to BLUE (v1)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-web
    version: blue    # ← Currently serving blue!
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l version=blue -n easypj --timeout=60s

# STEP 3: Deploy GREEN (v2 — new version, not yet live)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-green
  namespace: easypj
  labels:
    app: easypj-web
    version: green
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
      version: green
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
        version: green
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.26-alpine    # NEW version!
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l version=green -n easypj --timeout=60s

# Verify both stacks are running but only blue receives traffic
kubectl get pods -n easypj --show-labels
kubectl get endpoints -n easypj

⚠️ Observe — Green Deployed but Not Receiving Traffic

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → 4 pods: 2 blue (v1), 2 green (v2)
✗2. kubectl get endpoints easypj-web -n easypj → only blue pod IPs
✗3. Green pods exist but Service routes ALL traffic to blue — need to CUT OVER!

🔍 Debug — Verify Green Works Before Cutover

1Test green directly: kubectl port-forward -n easypj deploy/easypj-web-green 8080:80 then curl localhost:8080
→ Green returns expected page — v2 looks good!
2Check Service selector: kubectl get svc easypj-web -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A2 selector
→ version: blue — must change to version: green
3Plan the cutover: Blue-green deployment requires a Service selector switch. The Service currently selects version=blue pods. Patch the selector to version=green to cut over traffic. If green has issues, switch back to version=blue — instant rollback.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Both stacks deployed → Service on blue
②
Test green via port-forward → OK
③
Patch Service selector → green
④
Instant rollback: switch back to blue!

Tenet: Blue-green = deploy the new version COMPLETELY before switching traffic. No gradual rollout — it's an atomic switch. The Service selector is the "switch." Rollback is instant: change the selector back. This is the simplest zero-downtime pattern but requires double the resources during deployment.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get endpoints easypj-web -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-web 10.0.1.5:80,10.0.1.6:80 5m ← Only blue IPs!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get endpoints easypj-web -n easypj NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-web 10.0.2.5:80,10.0.2.6:80 5m ← Now green IPs! Zero downtime cutover!

🔧 Fix — Switch Service from Blue to Green

BASH — Cut over traffic to green 
# Switch Service selector from blue to green
kubectl patch svc easypj-web -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"easypj-web","version":"green"}}}'

# Verify endpoints now point to green pods
kubectl get endpoints easypj-web -n easypj

# Emergency rollback (if needed): switch back to blue
# kubectl patch svc easypj-web -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"easypj-web","version":"blue"}}}'
6

✅ Verify — Green Serving All Traffic

Service endpoints now show green pod IPs. Traffic flows to v2. Blue pods are still running (can be deleted after confirming v2 is stable). Blue-green is ideal for mission-critical apps where instant rollback is mandatory. Downside: requires 2x resources during deployment.

Canary Release — 10% Traffic to easypj-api v2

The Problem: You want to test v2 of easypj-api with real users before full rollout. Deploy v2 alongside v1 with fewer replicas (1 v2 + 9 v1 = 10% canary). The Service load balances across all pods equally. Monitor v2 for errors. If good, scale v2 up. If bad, delete v2 — instant cleanup.

📋 Deploy v1 (9 replicas) + v2 Canary (1 replica)

📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S44): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-api-v1-deployment.yaml      ← v1 (stable) — 9 replicas, 90% traffic
├── 02-api-v2-deployment.yaml      ← v2 (canary) — 1 replica, ~10% traffic
└── 03-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP (no version filter)
BASH — Deploy v1 (stable) + v2 (canary) with shared Service 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S44: Canary Release (10% v2, 90% v1)
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj

# STEP 1: Deploy v1 — STABLE (9 replicas = 90% of traffic)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api-v1
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 9
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
      version: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:1.25-alpine
        env:
        - name: APP_VERSION
          value: "v1-stable"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

# STEP 2: Deploy v2 — CANARY (1 replica = ~10% of traffic)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api-v2
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1    # ← Canary: only 1 pod!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
      version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:1.26-alpine    # NEW version
        env:
        - name: APP_VERSION
          value: "v2-canary"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

# STEP 3: Create Service that load balances across ALL 10 pods
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api   # ← Matches BOTH v1 and v2 (no version filter!)
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=120s

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → 10 pods: 9 v1 + 1 v2 (canary)
✗2. ~10% of API requests go to v2. Need to monitor for errors!
✗3. If v2 is bad, delete the v2 Deployment. If good, scale to 9.

🔍 Debug — Monitor the Canary

1Check pod distribution: kubectl get pods -n easypj -l app=easypj-api --sort-by=.metadata.labels.version
→ 9 v1 pods + 1 v2 pod = 10% canary
2Test canary directly: kubectl logs -n easypj -l version=v2
→ Check v2 logs for errors, compare with v1
3Decision: Canary is a MONITORING pattern — you observe real traffic behavior before full rollout. If error rate on v2 is acceptable, scale up. If not, delete v2 Deployment. Key: Service selector (app=easypj-api) matches BOTH versions, so load balancing distributes across all pods.

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Deploy v2 with 1 replica → Canary
②
Service balances across all 10 pods
③
Monitor v2 logs/metrics → Decision
④
Scale v2 or delete — instant!

Tenet: Canary release = deploy a small percentage of new version alongside old, monitor, then decide. Unlike blue-green (atomic switch), canary is gradual. The Service selector should match BOTH versions (use a common label like app). Traffic splitting is proportional to pod count: 1 v2 + 9 v1 = 10% canary. Adjust replica count to change traffic percentage.

$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -L version ... 9 v2 pods running — canary is now 100%!

# Wait for v2 pods to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l version=v2 -n easypj --timeout=60s

# Cut over: Delete v1 Deployment
kubectl delete deploy easypj-api-v1 -n easypj

# EMERGENCY ROLLBACK: If v2 had issues, delete v2 instead:
# kubectl delete deploy easypj-api-v2 -n easypj

v2 scaled to 9 replicas, v1 deleted. All traffic now goes to v2. Canary deployment complete. Key: the Service selector (app=easypj-api) never changed — it always matched both versions, so load balancing was automatic throughout the process.

S45
🧪 SCENARIO S45 — Category 3: Workloads Pause Debug

Deployment Paused — Forgotten kubectl rollout pause

The Problem: You edit the easypj-api Deployment — an image update and an env var change silently queue up and never apply. But a kubectl scale you also ran DID work immediately — pausing only freezes changes to the pod template (image, env, resources), NOT the replica count. The Deployment is PAUSED. Someone ran kubectl rollout pause for maintenance and never resumed. Your job: detect the paused state and resume the rollout.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy + Pause — Then Try to Update (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Maintenance window was scheduled last night. The on-call engineer ran kubectl rollout pause to freeze the Deployment. They went home and FORGOT to resume. Now morning changes (image update, scale, env vars) are piling up but nothing is being deployed — the job board is stuck on yesterday's code.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S45): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment (will be paused!)
BASH — Deploy, pause, then try to update (it won't work!) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S45: Forgotten kubectl rollout pause
# ============================================
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:1.25-alpine --replicas=2
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=60s

# BUG: Pause the Deployment (simulate "maintenance mode")
kubectl rollout pause deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Try to update — image/env changes queue silently, but scale is NOT part of the pod
# template, so it applies immediately even while paused!
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api -n easypj api=nginx:1.26-alpine
kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api -n easypj --replicas=5
kubectl set env deploy/easypj-api -n easypj DEBUG=true

# Check — 5 pods now exist, but ALL still running the OLD image, no DEBUG env!
kubectl get pods -n easypj
kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n easypj | grep Paused
2

⚠️ Observe — Changes Not Taking Effect

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → 5 pods now (scale DID apply!) but ALL still on the OLD image, no env var
✗2. kubectl set image and set env returned SUCCESS but never actually changed a running pod
✗3. Only pod-TEMPLATE changes are frozen — replica count is a separate field the pause doesn't touch
3

🔍 Debug — Why Aren't Changes Applied?

1Check Deployment status: kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n easypj | grep -i pause
→ Paused: true — Deployment is FROZEN!
2Check rollout status: kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
→ "Waiting for deployment spec update to be observed..." — STUCK!
3Root cause: kubectl rollout pause freezes only PodTemplateSpec changes (image, env, resources) — the Deployment controller stops rolling those out until resumed. Replica count is NOT part of the pod template, so scale changes are implemented immediately even while paused. Fix: kubectl rollout resume to apply the queued template changes.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Changes not applied → Check paused
②
describe deploy → Paused: true
③
rollout resume → All changes apply!

Tenet: kubectl rollout pause freezes PodTemplateSpec changes only (image, env, resources) — those are queued but not rolled out. Replica count is a separate field and applies immediately even while paused. Use case: make multiple atomic template changes then resume once. Common pitfall: forgetting to resume. On CKA: you may need to detect a paused Deployment and resume it.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n easypj | grep -i paused Paused: true ← DEPLOYMENT IS FROZEN!
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d8f9-abcde 1/1 Running 0 10m easypj-api-7d8f9-fghij 1/1 Running 0 10m easypj-api-7d8f9-klmno 1/1 Running 0 30s easypj-api-7d8f9-pqrst 1/1 Running 0 30s easypj-api-7d8f9-uvwxy 1/1 Running 0 30s ← 5 pods (scale worked!), all still nginx:1.25-alpine
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n easypj | grep -i paused Paused: false ✅
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-8e9f0-new-a 1/1 Running 0 15s easypj-api-8e9f0-new-b 1/1 Running 0 14s easypj-api-8e9f0-new-c 1/1 Running 0 13s easypj-api-8e9f0-new-d 1/1 Running 0 12s easypj-api-8e9f0-new-e 1/1 Running 0 11s ✅ 5 pods, new image, new env!
5

🔧 Fix — Resume the Deployment

BASH — Resume and watch changes apply 
# Resume the paused Deployment — all pending changes apply at once!
kubectl rollout resume deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Watch the rollout
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
kubectl get pods -n easypj -w
6

✅ Verify — Queued Template Changes Applied

After resume, the queued image and env var changes finally roll out across all 5 pods (the replica count was already 5 — scale applied immediately, even while paused). Key: kubectl rollout pause only freezes the pod template, not the replica count. Check with kubectl describe deploy | grep Paused if template changes aren't taking effect.

📌 S46–S50: Scheduling, Affinity & Topology Spread

S46
🧪 SCENARIO S46 — Category 3: Workloads Scheduling

Pod Stuck Pending — Insufficient CPU on All Nodes

The Problem: The easypj-api pod requests 4 CPUs but all nodes have less than 4 allocatable CPUs. The pod stays Pending forever. The scheduler can't find a node with enough capacity. Your job: check node capacity, understand resource requests vs limits, and fix the pod to fit the cluster.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Impossible CPU Request (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A developer copied resource requests from the AWS production config (m5.xlarge = 4 vCPUs) into the local kind cluster. The kind node only has ~2 allocatable CPUs. The scheduler says "nope" — the easypj-api pod stays Pending forever and the job board can't serve any traffic.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S46): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment with CPU request: 4 (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy pod that can never be scheduled 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S46: Insufficient CPU — Pod Pending Forever
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CHECK NODE CAPACITY + DEPLOY POD (BUG: CPU request exceeds any node)
MAX_CPU=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.allocatable.cpu}' | tr ' ' '
' | sort -rn | head -1)
echo "Max node CPU: ${MAX_CPU} — Requesting $((MAX_CPU + 2)) CPUs (IMPOSSIBLE!)"

cat << EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:1.25-alpine
        ports:

🔍 Debug — Why Can't the Pod Schedule?

1Check pod events: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A5 Events

2Check node capacity: kubectl describe node | grep -A5 "Allocatable"

3Root cause: Pod requests 4 CPUs but node has only ~2 allocatable. requests.memory is also checked. The scheduler sums requests across all pods on a node. If total requests > allocatable, new pods can't schedule. Fix: lower CPU request to 100m (0.1 CPU) which is realistic for a web API.

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Pending → Check node capacity
②
allocatable cpu < request → IMPOSSIBLE
③
Lower request → Pod schedules!

Tenet: Resource requests are the MINIMUM a pod needs. The scheduler uses requests (not limits) to decide where to place pods. A pod requesting 4 CPUs on a 2-CPU node will NEVER schedule. Requests should reflect actual average usage, not peak. Use 100m-500m for web APIs, 1-2 for compute-heavy apps.

EOF

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Pending → nodeSelector mismatch
②
No node has disktype=ssd
③

Tenet: nodeSelector is the simplest scheduling constraint — it's a hard requirement. If no node matches, the pod stays Pending forever. Official docs describe nodeSelector as "the simplest recommended form" of node selection, not something being phased out — nodeAffinity offers more expressive matching (operators, soft preferences) but doesn't replace nodeSelector, which remains fully supported for simple hard-requirement cases like this one. Always verify node labels match before applying nodeSelector.

Bob added podAntiAffinity to spread pods for high availability. Neither checked the other's change. Now only 1 of 3 pods can run — the other 2 are stuck Pending forever because the two rules mathematically conflict. The job board is running at 33% capacity.

🧪 SCENARIO S50 — Category 3: Workloads Topology

Topology Spread Deadlock — Strict maxSkew When a Zone Loses Capacity

The Problem: A Deployment has requiredDuringScheduling topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1 (the strictest valid value — maxSkew must be greater than zero) across 2 zones, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule, and 3 replicas. Zone-b's node then gets cordoned (simulating capacity loss). With only zone-a schedulable, the spread constraint blocks any pod that would push the skew beyond 1 — the math no longer works. Result: only 1 pod runs, 2 stay Pending forever. Your job: find the constraint causing the deadlock and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 3 (kind-cl1) — Works on any cluster with 2+ nodes
1

📋 Deploy with maxSkew=1, Then Lose a Zone's Capacity (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The ops team wants API pods balanced across zones for resilience. They set maxSkew=1 (the strictest valid setting) with DoNotSchedule and deployed 3 replicas across 2 zones — that's fine on its own (2 pods in one zone, 1 in the other satisfies maxSkew=1). But then zone-b's node gets cordoned for maintenance. With only zone-a schedulable, the strict skew requirement blocks any pod beyond the first — 2 pods are stuck Pending forever, and the API runs at 33% capacity.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S50): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
└── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment with maxSkew=1 + 3 replicas, then zone-b cordoned (BUG!)
BASH — Deploy with strict spread constraint, then lose a zone 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S50: Topology Spread Deadlock — Zone Loses Capacity Mid-Flight
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. LABEL NODES AS ZONES + DEPLOY (maxSkew=1 is fine here — 2 zones, 3 replicas)
WORKERS=($(kubectl get nodes -l '!node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'))
kubectl label node ${WORKERS[0]} topology.kubernetes.io/zone=zone-a --overwrite
kubectl label node ${WORKERS[1]} topology.kubernetes.io/zone=zone-b --overwrite
echo "Zone A: ${WORKERS[0]}, Zone B: ${WORKERS[1]}"

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1    # Strictest VALID value (maxSkew must be > 0) — fine with 2 zones/3 replicas alone
        topologyKey: "topology.kubernetes.io/zone"
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule   # Hard constraint!
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: easypj-api
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=60s

# 3. BUG: cordon zone-b's node (simulating capacity loss / maintenance)
kubectl cordon ${WORKERS[1]}
# Now only zone-a is schedulable — the strict skew constraint deadlocks further scheduling
kubectl delete pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api --field-selector spec.nodeName=${WORKERS[1]} --ignore-not-found

sleep 10
kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide
# 1 Running + 2 Pending — DEADLOCK!

⚠️ Observe — 1 Running, 2 Pending

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj → 1 Running, 2 Pending
✗2. kubectl describe pod on pending pods → "node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints"
✗3. 3 replicas but only 1 running — API at 33% capacity!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Can't the Other Pods Schedule?

1Check pending pods: kubectl describe pod -n easypj -l app=easypj-api | grep -A3 Events
→ "node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints"
2Check spread constraints: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n easypj -o yaml | grep -A8 topologySpreadConstraints
→ maxSkew: 1, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule — strict, but this alone is satisfiable with 2 zones!
3Check node schedulability: kubectl get nodes
→ zone-b's node shows SchedulingDisabled — it's cordoned! Only zone-a can accept pods now.
4Root cause: With zone-b cordoned, all 3 pods must land in zone-a — but maxSkew=1 only allows zone-a to have at most 1 more pod than zone-b (which has 0 schedulable capacity). So only 1 pod can land in zone-a before the constraint blocks the rest. Fix: uncordon zone-b, OR relax the constraint (higher maxSkew / ScheduleAnyway) if losing a zone temporarily is expected.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
2 pods Pending → Check constraints
②
maxSkew=1 is fine alone → check nodes
③
zone-b cordoned → only 1 zone left!
④
Uncordon zone-b → All 3 run!

Tenet: topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew controls the maximum imbalance between topology domains — it must be a positive integer (maxSkew=0 isn't a valid value at all; the API rejects it). A constraint that's perfectly satisfiable at deploy time can still deadlock later if a topology domain loses capacity (cordoned node, zone outage) after the fact — DoNotSchedule won't relax itself just because a zone became unavailable. ScheduleAnyway is the soft alternative (pods schedule but the cluster may be imbalanced). On CKA: a pod Pending on topology constraints — check both the constraint AND current node/zone availability.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide NAME READY STATUS NODE easypj-api-7d8f9-abcde 1/1 Running wk1 ← zone-a easypj-api-7d8f9-fghij 0/1 Pending <none> ← STUCK! zone-b cordoned, maxSkew=1 blocks a 2nd zone-a pod easypj-api-7d8f9-klmno 0/1 Pending <none> ← STUCK!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide NAME READY STATUS NODE easypj-api-7d8f9-abcde 1/1 Running wk1 ✅ zone-a easypj-api-7d8f9-fghij 1/1 Running wk2 ✅ zone-b (uncordoned!) easypj-api-7d8f9-klmno 1/1 Running wk1 ✅ zone-a (skew=1 satisfied: 2 vs 1)
5

🔧 Fix — Uncordon the Zone (or Relax the Constraint)

BASH — Restore zone-b's capacity so the existing constraint can be satisfied 
# Primary fix: restore the missing zone's capacity
WORKERS=($(kubectl get nodes -l '!node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'))
kubectl uncordon ${WORKERS[1]}
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=60s
kubectl get pods -n easypj -o wide

# Alternative (if the zone is expected to be down for a while): relax whenUnsatisfiable
# kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[
#   {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/topologySpreadConstraints/0/whenUnsatisfiable","value":"ScheduleAnyway"}
# ]'
6

✅ Verify — All 3 Pods Running

After uncordoning zone-b, the 2 pending pods schedule. Key: maxSkew must be a positive integer — it's not the "impossible math" that deadlocks, it's a strict constraint plus a topology domain silently losing capacity. Production recommendation: monitor node/zone health, and consider whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway if a temporarily-imbalanced deployment is preferable to a stuck one.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Uncordon in case the fix step wasn't run, then remove zone labels (Step 1 overwrote them)
WORKERS=($(kubectl get nodes -l '!node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'))
kubectl uncordon ${WORKERS[1]} 2>/dev/null
kubectl label node ${WORKERS[0]} topology.kubernetes.io/zone- 2>/dev/null
kubectl label node ${WORKERS[1]} topology.kubernetes.io/zone- 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete namespace easypj

📌 S51–S55: Config, Autoscaling & Disruption Budgets

S51
🧪 SCENARIO S51 — Category 3: Workloads ConfigMap

ConfigMap Updated — Pods Still Using Old Config

The Problem: You update the easypj-api ConfigMap (change DEBUG from false to true). But the pods keep using the OLD value. Kubernetes does NOT auto-restart pods on ConfigMap changes. Your job: understand this limitation and trigger a rollout restart to pick up the new config.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy API with ConfigMap, Then Update ConfigMap (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: DevOps enabled debug mode to troubleshoot an issue. They updated the ConfigMap (DEBUG=true) but pods didn't pick up the change. Debug logs aren't appearing. Lesson: ConfigMap changes don't trigger pod restarts — you must manually restart.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S51): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-configmap.yaml              ← easypj-config (DEBUG=false → true)
└── 02-api-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment consuming ConfigMap via envFrom
BASH — Deploy with ConfigMap, update it, observe pods don't reload 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S51: ConfigMap Update — Pods Don't Auto-Restart
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE CONFIGMAP WITH DEBUG=false
kubectl create configmap easypj-config -n easypj --from-literal=DEBUG=false --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info
kubectl get cm easypj-config -n easypj -o yaml

# 3. DEPLOY API REFERENCING THE CONFIGMAP
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: easypj-config
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=30s

# STEP 3: Verify current value
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DEBUG
# DEBUG=false

# STEP 4: Update ConfigMap (BUG — pods won't see it!)
kubectl create configmap easypj-config -n easypj --from-literal=DEBUG=true --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Check again — STILL shows OLD value!
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DEBUG
# DEBUG=false   ❌ BUG! Still old value!
2

⚠️ Observe — ConfigMap Updated but Pods Unchanged

✗1. ConfigMap shows DEBUG=true but pods still show DEBUG=false
✗2. kubectl exec shows old env var values — pods need restart!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Are Pods Using Old Config?

1Check ConfigMap: kubectl get cm easypj-config -n easypj -o yaml
→ DEBUG: "true" — ConfigMap IS updated!
2Check pod env: kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- env | grep DEBUG
→ DEBUG=false — Pod has OLD snapshot of ConfigMap!
3Root cause: ConfigMaps mounted as env vars (envFrom) are READ at pod startup only. Kubernetes does NOT auto-update running pods. Fix: kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api to recreate pods with new config.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
ConfigMap updated → Pods unchanged
②
Env vars read at startup only
③
rollout restart → New config applied!

Tenet: ConfigMap changes do NOT auto-restart pods. For envFrom/secretKeyRef, you must restart. For volume mounts, kubelet syncs changes within ~1 min (if not using subPath). Solutions: (1) kubectl rollout restart, (2) stakater/Reloader controller, (3) checksum annotation to auto-rollout on ConfigMap change.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get cm easypj-config -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data.DEBUG}' true ← ConfigMap is updated!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DEBUG DEBUG=false ← Pod still has old value!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DEBUG DEBUG=true ✅ New config picked up!
5

🔧 Fix — Restart Pods to Pick Up New Config

BASH — Restart the Deployment 
# Trigger a rolling restart to reload ConfigMap
kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Verify new config is loaded
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DEBUG
# DEBUG=true ✅
6

✅ Verify — Pods Using New Config

After rollout restart, pods reflect the updated ConfigMap. Key: ConfigMap changes are not auto-applied. Always run kubectl rollout restart deploy/<name> after ConfigMap/Secret updates. For volume mounts, kubelet syncs within ~1 min.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj
S52
🧪 SCENARIO S52 — Category 3: Workloads Secret

Database Password Rotated — Pods Still Using Old Secret

The Problem: Security policy requires rotating DB passwords every 90 days. You update the Secret with the new password. But pods still mount the OLD password — authentication to PostgreSQL fails. Same issue as ConfigMap: Secrets don't auto-restart pods. Your job: rotate the password and restart pods.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy API with Secret, Then Rotate Password (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Security rotated the database password from oldpass123 to newpass456. PostgreSQL now uses the new password, but API pods still mount the OLD password. All database connections fail with "authentication failed" — the job board can't access its data.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S52): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-secret.yaml                 ← db-creds (password rotated)
└── 02-api-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment consuming Secret via secretKeyRef
BASH — Deploy with Secret, rotate password, observe auth failure 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S52: Secret Rotation — Pods Use Old Password After Update
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. CREATE SECRET WITH OLD PASSWORD
kubectl create secret generic db-creds -n easypj \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=oldpass123

# 3. DEPLOY API USING THE SECRET
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-creds
              key: DB_PASSWORD
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=30s

# STEP 3: Rotate password (BUG — pods won't see new value!)
kubectl create secret generic db-creds -n easypj \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=newpass456 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Check — STILL old password!
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DB_PASSWORD
# DB_PASSWORD=oldpass123   ❌ BUG!
2

⚠️ Observe — Auth Failures After Password Rotation

✗1. Secret updated to newpass456 but kubectl exec shows oldpass123
✗2. Apps failing with "authentication failed" — using wrong password!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Are Pods Using the Old Password?

1Check Secret: kubectl get secret db-creds -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d
→ newpass456 — Secret IS updated!
2Check pod env: kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- env | grep DB_PASSWORD
→ DB_PASSWORD=oldpass123 — Pod has OLD snapshot!
3Root cause: Secrets mounted as env vars are read ONCE at pod startup. Updating the Secret object doesn't update running pods. Fix: kubectl rollout restart to reload secrets.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Password rotated → Auth fails
②
Pods use old Secret snapshot
③
rollout restart → New creds work!

Tenet: Same as ConfigMap — Secrets as env vars are static after pod startup. For volume-mounted Secrets, kubelet syncs periodically. For env vars, you MUST restart pods. On CKA: expect a "password rotation" scenario where you need to update a Secret and restart the Deployment.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secret db-creds -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d newpass456 ← Secret updated!
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DB_PASSWORD DB_PASSWORD=oldpass123 ← Pod still uses old!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DB_PASSWORD DB_PASSWORD=newpass456 ✅ New password loaded!
5

🔧 Fix — Restart to Load New Password

BASH — Restart pods to pick up new Secret 
kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj-api -- env | grep DB_PASSWORD
6

✅ Verify — API Using New Password

Pods restarted with new DB_PASSWORD. Auth succeeds. Key: Secret rotation = update Secret object + restart pods. Without the restart, pods keep the old value indefinitely. For volume mounts, kubelet syncs within ~1 min; for env vars, only restart works.

BASH — copy & paste to clean up
