🧪 SCENARIO S53 — Category 3: Workloads HPA

HPA Not Scaling — metrics-server Missing

The Problem: You create an HPA to auto-scale easypj-api based on CPU at 50% target. But the HPA shows <unknown> / 50% for CPU utilization. The metrics-server is not installed — HPA can't read metrics and won't scale. Your job: install metrics-server and verify HPA works.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy API + HPA Without metrics-server (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Traffic spikes from 100 to 10,000 requests/second on the job board. The HPA should auto-scale from 1 to 10 replicas. But nothing happens — metrics-server is not running. Pods are overloaded, response times skyrocket, and users abandon the site.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S53): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment with CPU requests
└── 02-hpa.yaml                    ← HPA targeting 50% CPU (metrics missing!)
BASH — Deploy API + HPA (metrics missing) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S53: HPA — metrics-server Required for Autoscaling
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace easypj

# 2. DEPLOY API WITH CPU REQUESTS (required for HPA to work)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "64Mi"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

# STEP 2: Create HPA targeting 50% CPU
kubectl autoscale deploy easypj-api -n easypj --cpu=50% --min=1 --max=10

# STEP 3: Check HPA status (BUG!)
kubectl get hpa -n easypj
kubectl describe hpa easypj-api -n easypj | grep -A5 Metrics
# ❌ BUG! TARGETS shows <unknown>/50% — metrics-server not installed!
2

⚠️ Observe — HPA Shows Unknown Metrics

✗1. kubectl get hpa -n easypj → TARGETS: <unknown>/50%
✗2. HPA can't read CPU usage — will NEVER scale!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is HPA Not Getting Metrics?

1Check metrics availability: kubectl top pods -n easypj
→ "error: Metrics API not available" — metrics-server missing!
2Check HPA conditions: kubectl describe hpa easypj-api -n easypj
→ "unable to get metrics for resource cpu"
3Root cause: metrics-server is not installed. HPA relies on metrics-server (or custom metrics adapter) to get CPU/memory metrics from pods. Without it, HPA can't calculate utilization and will never scale. Fix: install metrics-server.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
HPA <unknown> → Check metrics
②
kubectl top fails → No metrics-server
③
Install metrics-server → HPA works!

Tenet: HPA requires a metrics source. Default: metrics-server (resource metrics API). For custom metrics: Prometheus adapter. Without metrics-server: kubectl top fails, HPA shows <unknown>, autoscaling is dead. Install: kubectl apply -f components.yaml from metrics-server releases.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get hpa -n easypj NAME REFERENCE TARGETS MIN MAX REPLICAS easypj-api Deployment/easypj-api <unknown>/50% 1 10 0 ← NO METRICS!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get hpa -n easypj NAME REFERENCE TARGETS MIN MAX REPLICAS easypj-api Deployment/easypj-api 5%/50% 1 10 1 ✅ Metrics working!
5

🔧 Fix — Install metrics-server

BASH — Install metrics-server (required for HPA) 
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l k8s-app=metrics-server -n kube-system --timeout=60s
kubectl get hpa -n easypj
kubectl top pods -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — HPA Reading Metrics

HPA now shows actual CPU percentage. Key: metrics-server is essential infrastructure for HPA and kubectl top. For kind clusters, add --kubelet-insecure-tls arg via the components.yaml patch.

🧪 SCENARIO S54 — Category 3: Workloads PDB

PodDisruptionBudget — Protect API During Node Drain

The Problem: You need to drain a node for maintenance. easypj-api has 3 replicas. Without a PDB, kubectl drain could evict ALL 3 pods simultaneously — causing complete API downtime. Your job: create a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 2 to ensure at least 2 pods always run during voluntary disruptions.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy API Without PDB — Risk of Mass Eviction

📖 APP STORY: Node "kind-worker" needs a kernel update. kubectl drain will evict all pods on that node. Without a PDB, all 3 API pods could be evicted at once. The job board would be completely DOWN during maintenance — unacceptable for a production service.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S54): 
easypj/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj
├── 01-api-deployment.yaml         ← 3 replicas (no PDB = UNPROTECTED!)
└── 02-pdb.yaml                    ← PodDisruptionBudget (TO BE CREATED)
BASH — Deploy API + create PDB to protect it 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S54: PodDisruptionBudget — Missing PDB Risks All Pods Evicted
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE + DEPLOY 3 REPLICAS
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n easypj --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj --timeout=60s

# 2. CHECK CURRENT PDBs — NONE EXIST (BUG: drain could evict ALL 3 pods)
kubectl get pdb -n easypj
# ❌ BUG! No PDB = drain could evict ALL 3 pods!
2

⚠️ Observe — No PDB, Risk of Full Downtime

✗1. kubectl get pdb -n easypj → No resources found
✗2. kubectl drain could evict all 3 pods — no minimum availability guarantee
3

🔍 Debug — Understand the Risk

1Check pod count: kubectl get pods -n easypj
→ 3 pods running — all at risk during drain!
2Root cause: No PDB defined. PDBs set minimum availability during VOLUNTARY disruptions (drain, node maintenance). They do NOT protect against involuntary disruptions (node crash, OOM). Fix: create PDB with minAvailable: 2 (always keep at least 2 API pods running).
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
No PDB → Drain risk
②
Create PDB minAvailable: 2
③
Drain respects PDB → API stays up!

Tenet: PDB = "don't evict more than X pods at once." minAvailable: "at least this many must stay." maxUnavailable: "at most this many can be down." PDBs only affect VOLUNTARY disruptions (drain, node update). Involuntary (crash, OOM) are not limited. On CKA: you'll create a PDB to protect an app during maintenance.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pdb -n easypj No resources found in easypj namespace. ← UNPROTECTED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pdb -n easypj NAME MIN AVAILABLE MAX UNAVAILABLE ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS AGE api-pdb 2 N/A 1 10s ✅ Protected!
5

🔧 Fix — Create PodDisruptionBudget

BASH — Create PDB with minAvailable: 2 
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api-pdb
  namespace: easypj
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
EOF
kubectl get pdb -n easypj
6

✅ Verify — PDB Created, API Protected

PDB guarantees at least 2 of 3 pods stay running during voluntary disruptions. Key: use minAvailable for absolute count, maxUnavailable for percentage-based. PDBs are critical for production workloads that need HA during maintenance windows.

7

BASH — copy & paste to clean up

🧪 SCENARIO S55 — Category 3: Workloads Quota

ResourceQuota — Prevent Dev Namespace from Hogging CPU

The Problem: The easypj-dev namespace has no resource limits. Developers deploy 50 pods consuming 80% of cluster CPU. Production easypj pods can't get resources and are starving. Your job: create a ResourceQuota and LimitRange to cap the dev namespace and protect production workloads.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create Dev Namespace Without Limits (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Dev team deployed a microservices test harness — 50 pods now consume 80% of cluster CPU. Production easypj pods are being OOM killed because the dev namespace has no resource limits. Need ResourceQuota to cap the dev namespace immediately and save production.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S55): 
easypj-dev/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-dev (NO quota!)
├── 01-resourcequota.yaml          ← ResourceQuota (TO BE CREATED)
└── 02-limitrange.yaml             ← LimitRange for defaults (TO BE CREATED)
BASH — Create uncontrolled dev namespace, then lock it down 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S55: ResourceQuota — Prevent Runaway Resource Usage
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE DEV NAMESPACE WITHOUT LIMITS (BUG: no quota)
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev

# 2. DEPLOY 9 PODS (simulating runaway resource usage — 9 here + 1 "extra" below
# = 10 total, matching the pod quota the Fix step will apply)
# Note: kubectl run has no --requests/--limits flags — use --overrides with inline JSON
for i in $(seq 1 9); do
  kubectl run dev-pod-$i -n easypj-dev --image=nginx:alpine --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"dev-pod-'"$i"'","image":"nginx:alpine","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m","memory":"64Mi"},"limits":{"cpu":"200m","memory":"128Mi"}}}]}}'
done
kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev

# STEP 3: Try to create more pods — NO LIMIT!
kubectl run dev-pod-extra -n easypj-dev --image=nginx:alpine --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"dev-pod-extra","image":"nginx:alpine","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m","memory":"64Mi"}}}]}}'
# ❌ BUG! pod created successfully — namespace has NO cap!
2

⚠️ Observe — Dev Consuming Unlimited Resources

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev → many pods, no cap!
✗2. kubectl get resourcequota -n easypj-dev → No resources found
3

🔍 Debug — Check Current Resource Usage

1Check namespace resource usage: kubectl describe ns easypj-dev
→ No ResourceQuota set — unlimited consumption!
2Root cause: No ResourceQuota or LimitRange defined for the dev namespace. Without quotas, any namespace can consume all cluster resources. Fix: create ResourceQuota capping total CPU/memory and pod count, plus LimitRange for default requests/limits on new pods.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Dev consuming too much → Check quota
②
No ResourceQuota defined
③
Create quota + LimitRange → Dev capped!

Tenet: ResourceQuota limits TOTAL resources per namespace (CPU, memory, pods, PVCs, etc.). LimitRange sets DEFAULT requests/limits for pods without explicit values. Together they prevent noisy neighbor problems. On CKA: you'll create a ResourceQuota to cap a namespace.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get resourcequota -n easypj-dev No resources found in easypj-dev namespace. ← NO LIMITS!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get resourcequota -n easypj-dev NAME AGE REQUEST dev-quota 10s requests.cpu: 1000m/2, requests.memory: 640Mi/2Gi, pods: 10/10 ✅ Capped — at the pod limit!
$ kubectl run extra-pod -n easypj-dev --image=nginx --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"extra-pod","image":"nginx","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m"}}}]}}' Error from server (Forbidden): pods "extra-pod" is forbidden: exceeded quota: dev-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=10, limited: pods=10 ✅ Quota blocks — already AT the 10-pod cap!
5

🔧 Fix — Create ResourceQuota + LimitRange

BASH — Cap the dev namespace 
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: dev-quota
  namespace: easypj-dev
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: "2Gi"
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: "4Gi"
    pods: "10"
---
# LimitRange — Sets default CPU/memory for pods in easypj-dev
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: dev-limits
  namespace: easypj-dev
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: "128Mi"
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: "64Mi"
    type: Container
EOF
kubectl describe resourcequota dev-quota -n easypj-dev
6

✅ Verify — Dev Namespace Capped

ResourceQuota limits total CPU to 2 cores, memory to 2Gi, and 10 pods. New pods exceeding quota are rejected. LimitRange sets defaults. Key: ResourceQuota + LimitRange = complete namespace resource governance. Essential for multi-tenant clusters.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespaces

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-dev

🏗️ Category 4: Cluster Architecture Lab ScenariosS56-S80

🔴 Build, Bootstrap, Secure & Extend the Cluster Itself

This is the "build and run the cluster" category — 25% of the CKA exam. These scenarios cover kubeadm bootstrapping, etcd management, RBAC security, certificate lifecycle, Helm/Kustomize deployments, CRDs, operators, admission webhooks, and CNI comparisons. Each scenario is a standalone, isolated lab with intentional bugs to resolve.

📌 S56–S60: kubeadm Bootstrap, Upgrade & Reset

S56
🧪 SCENARIO S56 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture kubeadm Bootstrap

kubeadm init — Bootstrap a Cluster with Missing --pod-network-cidr Flag

The Problem: You initialize a fresh Kubernetes cluster with kubeadm init but forget the critical --pod-network-cidr flag. However, the cluster appears to initialize — but CoreDNS pods stay stuck in ContainerCreating forever because the CNI plugin (Calico) has no pod CIDR to allocate IPs from (they've been scheduled, kubelet just can't finish setting up their network sandbox). Your job: identify the missing flag, reset the cluster, and reinitialize correctly.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Run kubeadm init WITHOUT --pod-network-cidr (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: You're building the easypj production cluster from scratch. The control plane node needs to be initialized with kubeadm. In the rush to get the cluster up, you run kubeadm init without the --pod-network-cidr flag. The init completes, but CoreDNS pods never become Ready. The entire cluster has no working DNS — no pods can discover each other. The job board deployment is blocked.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S56): 
cluster-init/
├── 00-kubeadm-init.sh              ← kubeadm init WITH BUG: missing --pod-network-cidr
├── 01-calico.yaml                  ← Calico CNI manifest (applied but CORE DNS STILL PENDING!)
└── 02-kubeadm-reset-fix.sh         ← Reset + re-init with CORRECT flags
BASH — Initialize cluster WITH the intentional bug 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S56: kubeadm init — Missing --pod-network-cidr
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Run kubeadm init WITHOUT pod-network-cidr (THE BUG!)
sudo kubeadm init \
  --control-plane-endpoint="easy:6443" \
  --upload-certs
# ❌ BUG! Missing: --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16
# Without this, CNI plugins don't know what IP range to use!

# STEP 2: Set up kubeconfig
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

# STEP 3: Install Calico CNI
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/calico.yaml

# STEP 4: Check pods — CORE DNS STUCK PENDING!
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -w
# NAME                                       READY   STATUS
# coredns-76f75df574-abcde                   0/1     ContainerCreating   ← BUG!
# coredns-76f75df574-fghij                   0/1     ContainerCreating   ← BUG!

# STEP 5: Describe CoreDNS pod to see the error
kubectl describe pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns | grep -A5 Events

# The APP STORY:
# 9:00 AM MONDAY — "We need the new production cluster for the easypj launch."
# You run kubeadm init, install Calico, but CoreDNS never starts.
# Without DNS, easypj-web can't find easypj-api can't find easypj-db.
# The entire microservice chain is BROKEN. Launch deadline in 2 hours.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — CoreDNS Stuck in ContainerCreating Forever

✗1. kubectl get pods -n kube-system → CoreDNS pods stuck in ContainerCreating (0/1 READY)
✗2. kubectl describe pod -n kube-system coredns-xxx → Events: "FailedCreatePodSandBox... failed to assign an IP address: no IP pools configured"
✗3. kubectl get nodes → Node is Ready but DNS is non-functional
✗4. Any pod created now will have NO DNS resolution — cluster is fundamentally broken!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Can't CoreDNS Get an IP?

1Check Calico pods: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node
→ Calico-node pods may also show issues or CrashLoopBackOff
2Check Calico node logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=calico-node --tail=20
→ "No pod CIDR configured" or "IPAM not initialized" — Calico doesn't know the pod network!
3Check kubeadm init config: kubectl get cm kubeadm-config -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A3 networking
→ podSubnet is EMPTY or missing! No CIDR was specified during init
4Check CNI config: cat /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist | grep -A5 ipam
→ IPAM block may show an empty or undefined pool — no IPs to assign
5Root cause: kubeadm init was run WITHOUT --pod-network-cidr. The CNI plugin has no IP range defined for pod networking. CoreDNS can't get a pod IP because the network plugin doesn't know what subnet to use. Fix: kubeadm reset → kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16 → reinstall CNI.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
CoreDNS stuck ContainerCreating → Check CNI
②
Calico logs → No pod CIDR
③
Check kubeadm-config → No subnet
④
kubeadm reset → re-init with CIDR
⑤
CoreDNS Running → Cluster healthy

Tenet: --pod-network-cidr is NOT optional — it tells the CNI plugin which IP range to allocate pod IPs from. Each CNI expects a specific CIDR: Calico uses 192.168.0.0/16, Flannel uses 10.244.0.0/16, Cilium uses 10.0.0.0/8. Without it, the CNI has no subnet to manage, pods can't get IPs, and cluster DNS (CoreDNS) can't start. This is the #1 kubeadm init mistake. On CKA: you'll initialize a cluster and must include --pod-network-cidr.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE coredns-76f75df574-abcde 0/1 ContainerCreating 0 5m coredns-76f75df574-fghij 0/1 ContainerCreating 0 5m ← DNS BROKEN!
$ kubectl describe pod -n kube-system coredns-76f75df574-abcde | tail -10 Events: Warning FailedCreatePodSandBox Failed to create pod sandbox: plugin type="calico" failed Warning FailedCreatePodSandBox failed to assign an IP address: no IP pools configured
$ kubectl get cm kubeadm-config -n kube-system -o yaml | grep podSubnet (empty — NO podSubnet was configured!)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE calico-node-xxxxx 1/1 Running 0 2m coredns-76f75df574-new1 1/1 Running 0 2m ✅ DNS WORKING! coredns-76f75df574-new2 1/1 Running 0 2m ✅
$ kubectl get cm kubeadm-config -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A2 networking networking: podSubnet: 192.168.0.0/16 ✅ CIDR is set! serviceSubnet: 10.96.0.0/12
5

🔧 Fix — kubeadm reset + re-init with correct --pod-network-cidr

BASH — Full reset and re-initialization with correct flags 
# Step 1: COMPLETELY reset the broken cluster
sudo kubeadm reset -f
sudo rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d/
sudo rm -rf $HOME/.kube

# Step 2: Re-initialize WITH --pod-network-cidr flag
sudo kubeadm init \
  --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16 \
  --control-plane-endpoint="easy:6443" \
  --upload-certs
# ✅ FIXED! pod-network-cidr specified for Calico

# Step 3: Set up kubeconfig
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

# Step 4: Untaint control-plane node (single-node cluster)
kubectl taint nodes --all node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane-

# Step 5: Install Calico CNI
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/calico.yaml

# Step 6: Wait for all system pods
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n kube-system --timeout=180s

# Step 7: Verify CoreDNS is running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
6

✅ Verify — CoreDNS Running, Cluster Fully Operational

All kube-system pods are Running 1/1. CoreDNS is resolving names. The pod network (192.168.0.0/16) is configured and Calico is managing IP allocations. Key takeaway: always specify --pod-network-cidr during kubeadm init. Each CNI expects a specific range — Calico: 192.168.0.0/16, Flannel: 10.244.0.0/16, Cilium: 10.0.0.0/8. Check /etc/cni/net.d/ for active CNI config.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Reset Cluster

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
sudo kubeadm reset -f
sudo rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d /etc/kubernetes /var/lib/etcd /var/lib/kubelet
sudo rm -rf $HOME/.kube
sudo iptables -F && sudo iptables -t nat -F && sudo iptables -t mangle -F
sudo ipvsadm --clear 2>/dev/null
S57
🧪 SCENARIO S57 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture kubeadm Join

Worker Node Can't Join Cluster — kubeadm Token Expired After 24 Hours

The Problem: Yesterday you generated a kubeadm join token for new workers. Today, a new worker node tries to join the easypj production cluster but gets "token not found" or "discovery failed". Bootstrap tokens have a default TTL of 24 hours — the token expired overnight. Your job: create a fresh token, print the join command, and successfully join the worker.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Generate an Expired Token Simulation (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj production cluster needs to scale — 3 new worker nodes must join to handle the upcoming Black Friday traffic spike. You created a token yesterday during preparation. Today at 8 AM, the new workers arrive. You SSH into worker-4 and run the join command from yesterday's terminal history — "token not found — token may have expired." The token expired at midnight. You have 1 hour before traffic spikes begin. The workers MUST join NOW.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S57): 
cluster-join/
├── 01-create-expired-token.sh      ← Create token with BUG: --ttl 1s (simulates expiry)
├── 02-join-attempt.sh              ← Worker attempts join with expired token → FAILS
└── 03-create-new-token-fix.sh      ← Create fresh token + print join command
BASH — Create expired token, attempt join, debug 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S57: kubeadm Token Expired — Worker Can't Join
# ============================================

# STEP 1: ON CONTROL PLANE — Create a token that expires in 1 second
# (Simulates "created yesterday, expired overnight")
kubeadm token create --ttl 1s --print-join-command 2>/dev/null
# Output (note: token will be EXPIRED by the time you use it):
# kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 --token abcdef.0123456789abcdef \
#   --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1a2b3c4d5e...

# Wait 3 seconds for token to expire
sleep 3

# STEP 2: Verify token is expired
kubeadm token list
# ❌ Token NOT in list — has expired and been cleaned up!

# STEP 3: ON WORKER NODE — Attempt to join with expired token
# (This is what a new worker would run — IT WILL FAIL!)
sudo kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 \
  --token abcdef.0123456789abcdef \
  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1a2b3c4d5e...
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# error execution phase preflight: couldn't validate the identity
# of the API Server: token not found
# → The token has expired or was never valid!

# The APP STORY:
# 8:15 AM — "worker-4 can't join the cluster!"
# You check the token — GONE. Expired at midnight.
# Without these workers, the easypj cluster can't handle today's load.
# You need a NEW token NOW.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Token Not Found / Expired

✗1. kubeadm token list → Token is NOT in the list — expired and cleaned up
✗2. Worker join command fails: "token not found" or "couldn't validate identity"
✗3. kubectl get nodes → Worker node NOT visible in the cluster
✗4. Cluster can't scale — easypj workloads can't be scheduled on new workers!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Did the Join Fail?

1Check token list on control plane: kubeadm token list
→ Token list is EMPTY or the specific token is missing — it expired!
2Check existing tokens: kubectl get secrets -n kube-system | grep bootstrap-token
→ No bootstrap-token Secret found — token cleaned up after expiry
3Check token TTL: Default is 24h. Tokens auto-delete after expiry. kubeadm token create --help | grep ttl
→ --ttl duration (default 24h0m0s) — tokens are TEMPORARY by design!
4Root cause: kubeadm bootstrap tokens expire after 24 hours by default. The token was created yesterday and expired overnight. Kubernetes cleans up expired tokens automatically. Fix: create a NEW token with kubeadm token create --print-join-command and use that on the worker.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Join fails → token not found
②
kubeadm token list → empty
③
Token expired (24h default)
④
Create new token → print command
⑤
Worker joins → node Ready!

Tenet: Bootstrap tokens are temporary by design — they authenticate new nodes during the join process. After 24 hours (default), they expire and are cleaned up. The joined node gets a permanent client certificate from the API server, so the token is only needed during the initial join. On CKA: you'll need to create a new token and use the correct --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash. ALWAYS use --print-join-command for the full command.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubeadm token list TOKEN TTL EXPIRES USAGES (empty — no valid tokens!)
$ sudo kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 --token abcdef.0123456789abcdef --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:xxxx error execution phase preflight: couldn't validate the identity of the API Server: there is no JWS signed token in the cluster-info ConfigMap this token id does not exist: abcdef → TOKEN EXPIRED — WORKER REJECTED! (an x509 "signed by unknown authority" error would instead mean a --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash MISMATCH, a different problem from an expired token)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubeadm token create --print-join-command kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 --token xyz789.0123456789abcde --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:xxx ✅ Fresh token — run this on worker!
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION easy Ready control-plane 7d v1.32.13 worker-4 Ready <none> 30s v1.32.13 ✅ JOINED!
5

🔧 Fix — Create New Token + Join Worker

BASH — Create fresh token and join worker node 
# ON CONTROL PLANE:
# Step 1: Create a NEW token and print the full join command
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
# Output example:
# kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 --token xyz789.0123456789abcde \
#   --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1a2b3c4d5e...

# Step 2: Verify the token exists
kubeadm token list
# TOKEN                     TTL         EXPIRES
# xyz789.0123456789abcde   23h         2026-06-06T08:15:00Z

# ON WORKER NODE:
# Step 3: Run the join command (copy-paste from step 1 output)
sudo kubeadm join 192.168.1.10:6443 \
  --token xyz789.0123456789abcde \
  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1a2b3c4d5e...

# Step 4: Verify worker joined (back on control plane)
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node worker-4 | grep -A5 Conditions
6

✅ Verify — Worker Node Joined and Ready

The worker node appears in kubectl get nodes with STATUS: Ready. Key commands: kubeadm token create --print-join-command (one-liner to get the full join command), kubeadm token list (check active tokens), kubeadm token delete <token> (revoke). For production: create tokens with longer TTL during maintenance windows, or set --ttl 0 for permanent tokens (not recommended for security).

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Token + Remove Worker

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete all tokens
kubeadm token delete $(kubeadm token list -o jsonpath='{.token}' 2>/dev/null) 2>/dev/null

# If worker was actually joined, drain + delete
kubectl drain worker-4 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data 2>/dev/null
kubectl delete node worker-4 2>/dev/null

# On worker: reset
sudo kubeadm reset -f 2>/dev/null
S58
🧪 SCENARIO S58 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture kubeadm Upgrade

kubeadm upgrade Blocked — kubelet Upgraded Before Control Plane (Version Skew)

The Problem: A junior admin tries to upgrade the easypj cluster from v1.31 to v1.32. They upgrade kubelet on ALL nodes FIRST, then attempt kubeadm upgrade apply on the control plane. The upgrade is BLOCKED — Kubernetes enforces a version skew policy: kubelet cannot be NEWER than the API server. The wrong upgrade order has broken the cluster upgrade path. Your job: identify the version skew violation, correct the upgrade order, and complete the upgrade properly.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Upgrade kubelet FIRST — Wrong Order (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj cluster is running Kubernetes v1.31. A critical security CVE requires upgrading to v1.32. The junior admin follows a "bottom-up" approach — upgrade kubelet on all nodes first, then the control plane. But kubeadm upgrade apply FAILS because kubelet v1.32 can't talk to an API server that's still v1.31. The version skew policy says kubelet must be ≤ API server. The upgrade is deadlocked. Production is stuck on a vulnerable version.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S58): 
cluster-upgrade/
├── 01-wrong-order.sh               ← Upgrade kubelet first (THE BUG!)
├── 02-check-version-skew.sh        ← Diagnose the version mismatch
└── 03-correct-upgrade-order.sh     ← Control plane first, then workers
BASH — Simulate wrong upgrade order (check actual versions first) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S58: kubeadm upgrade — Wrong Order Causes Version Skew
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Check current versions
kubectl version --short 2>/dev/null || kubectl version
kubectl get nodes -o wide
# NAME   STATUS   VERSION
# easy   Ready    v1.31.x   ← Current version

# STEP 2: UPGRADE KUBELET FIRST ON ALL NODES (THE BUG!)
# This is WRONG — kubelet must NOT be newer than API server!
sudo apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.32.0-* kubectl=1.32.0-*
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# STEP 3: Now try to upgrade control plane — IT WILL FAIL!
sudo apt-mark unhold kubeadm
sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.32.0-*
sudo kubeadm upgrade plan
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# [preflight] FATAL: this version of kubeadm only supports
# upgrading to v1.32.x, but the kubelet version is v1.32.x
# which is higher than the control plane version v1.31.x
# → VERSION SKEW VIOLATION! kubelet (1.32) > API server (1.31)

# The APP STORY:
# 2:00 PM — "The upgrade is stuck! kubeadm won't proceed."
# The version skew policy says: kube-apiserver must be at version X,
# kubelet can be X-1 or X, but NOT X+1.
# By upgrading kubelet to 1.32 while API server is 1.31,
# we violated the policy. Now the upgrade path is broken.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Version Skew Violation

✗1. kubeadm upgrade plan → FATAL error: "kubelet version is higher than control plane"
✗2. kubectl version → Client (kubectl): 1.32, Server (API): 1.31 — MISMATCH!
✗3. kubectl get nodes → Node shows v1.32 but control plane is still v1.31
✗4. Cluster upgrade is BLOCKED — no forward path without intervention!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the Upgrade Blocked?

1Check all component versions: kubectl version and kubectl get nodes -o wide
→ API server: v1.31.x, kubelet on node: v1.32.x — kubelet is AHEAD!
2Check version skew policy: kube-apiserver must be at or above kubelet version
→ Policy: kubelet can be up to 3 minor versions OLDER than kube-apiserver, never newer
3Check kubeadm error: "kubelet version is higher than control plane version"
→ kubeadm refuses to upgrade when it detects version skew
4Root cause: Wrong upgrade order: kubelet was upgraded BEFORE the control plane. The correct order is: (1) upgrade kubeadm binary, (2) kubeadm upgrade apply on control plane, (3) upgrade kubelet + kubectl on control plane, (4) drain worker nodes, (5) upgrade kubeadm on workers, (6) kubeadm upgrade node, (7) upgrade kubelet on workers, (8) uncordon. Control plane ALWAYS goes first.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Upgrade blocked → version check
②
kubelet (1.32) > API (1.31)
③
Version skew policy violated!
④
Fix order: CP first, then workers
⑤
Upgrade completes → all v1.32

Tenet: The Kubernetes version skew policy states: kube-apiserver is at X. kube-controller-manager/kube-scheduler can be X or X-1 (never newer). kubelet AND kube-proxy can be up to X-3 (up to 3 minor versions older) — a much wider allowance than the control-plane components. kubectl is supported from X-1 to X+1 (it's the one component allowed to be NEWER than the API server). Always upgrade the control plane FIRST, then worker nodes one at a time. The correct order: kubeadm → kubeadm upgrade apply → kubelet/kubectl (on CP) → drain worker → kubeadm upgrade node → kubelet (on worker) → uncordon.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get nodes -o wide NAME STATUS VERSION easy Ready v1.32.x ← kubelet already upgraded! (but API server is still v1.31.x — VERSION SKEW!)
$ sudo kubeadm upgrade plan [preflight] FATAL: this version of kubeadm only supports upgrading to v1.32.x, but the kubelet version is v1.32.x which is higher than the control plane version v1.31.x — version skew violation!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION easy Ready control-plane 7d v1.32.0 ✅ All components aligned!
5

🔧 Fix — Correct Upgrade Order (Control Plane FIRST)

BASH — Correct upgrade procedure for CKA exam 
# CORRECT UPGRADE ORDER — Control Plane FIRST

# Step 1: Upgrade kubeadm binary on control plane
sudo apt-mark unhold kubeadm
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.32.0-*

# Step 2: Check the upgrade plan
sudo kubeadm upgrade plan

# Step 3: Apply the upgrade (upgrades API server, controller, scheduler, etcd)
sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.32.0

# Step 4: Drain the control plane node
kubectl drain easy --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# Step 5: NOW upgrade kubelet + kubectl on control plane
sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.32.0-* kubectl=1.32.0-*
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# Step 6: Uncordon the node
kubectl uncordon easy

# Step 7: Verify
kubectl get nodes
# easy   Ready    control-plane   v1.32.0 ✅
6

✅ Verify — All Components at v1.32, Cluster Healthy

kubectl get nodes shows all nodes at v1.32. kubectl version shows Server Version: v1.32. Key rule: Control Plane FIRST, Workers AFTER. The version skew policy allows kubelet to be 1 minor version BEHIND the API server, never AHEAD. For worker nodes: upgrade kubeadm → drain → kubeadm upgrade node → upgrade kubelet → uncordon. Repeat for each worker one at a time.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Note on Version Management

BASH — Hold versions to prevent unintended upgrades 
# Hold kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl versions to prevent auto-upgrade
sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm kubelet kubectl
# Verify hold
apt-mark showhold

# Check current versions across all components
kubectl version --short 2>/dev/null
kubectl get nodes -o wide
S59
🧪 SCENARIO S59 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture Certificate Expiry

kubectl Returns x509 Error — kubeadm Certificates Expired After 1 Year

The Problem: One morning, kubectl get nodes suddenly returns "x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid". The easypj cluster was bootstrapped 13 months ago with kubeadm, and the default certificate validity is 1 year. All TLS certificates have expired — kubectl can't authenticate, kubelet can't connect, the cluster is unmanageable. Your job: check certificate expiration dates, renew all certificates, and restore cluster access.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Simulate Expired Certificate Scenario (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj cluster has been running smoothly for 13 months. Then Monday morning, kubectl get pods returns "x509: certificate has expired." Panic sets in — the cluster is running but NO ONE can manage it. The kubeadm certificates (validity: 1 year) expired over the weekend. The entire DevOps team is locked out. Production is unmanageable. If a pod crashes, nobody can redeploy it.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S59): 
cert-renewal/
├── 01-check-expiration.sh          ← kubeadm certs check-expiration (SHOWS EXPIRED!)
├── 02-renew-all-certs.sh           ← kubeadm certs renew all
└── 03-restart-control-plane.sh     ← Restart static pods to pick up new certs
BASH — Check certificate expiration (simulated expired scenario) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S59: kubeadm Certificate Expired — Renew All
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Check certificate expiration dates
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration
# ❌ BUG! Output shows:
# CERTIFICATE                    EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL
# admin.conf                     Jan 04, 2026 10:00 UTC  -152d     ← EXPIRED!
# apiserver                      Jan 04, 2026 10:00 UTC  -152d     ← EXPIRED!
# apiserver-kubelet-client       Jan 04, 2026 10:00 UTC  -152d     ← EXPIRED!
# apiserver-etcd-client          Jan 04, 2026 10:00 UTC  -152d     ← EXPIRED!
# etcd                           Jan 04, 2026 10:00 UTC  -152d     ← EXPIRED!

# STEP 2: Attempt kubectl — IT WILL FAIL!
kubectl get nodes
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate has expired
# or is not yet valid: current time 2026-06-05T08:00:00Z is after
# 2026-01-04T10:00:00Z

# STEP 3: Check certificate on disk
sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates
# notBefore=Jan  4 2025 10:00:00 GMT
# notAfter=Jan  4 2026 10:00:00 GMT   ← EXPIRED 5 months ago!

# The APP STORY:
# 9:00 AM MONDAY — PagerDuty explodes.
# "kubectl not working!" "Can't deploy hotfix!" "Cert expired!"
# The cluster was set up last year. Nobody checked cert expiry.
# Now the 1-year clock ran out. All TLS certs are dead.
# You need to RENEW EVERYTHING before the cluster implodes.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — x509 Certificate Expired

✗1. kubectl get nodes → "x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid"
✗2. sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration → All certs show EXPIRED or negative RESIDUAL
✗3. sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates → notAfter is in the PAST!
✗4. Cluster is RUNNING but UNMANAGEABLE — no kubectl, no deployments, no fixes!
3

🔍 Debug — Which Certificates Expired?

1Check ALL certificates: sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration
→ ALL component certs expired (1-year validity). CA cert valid 10 years.
2Check which certs exist: sudo ls -la /etc/kubernetes/pki/
→ ca.crt (10yr), apiserver.crt (1yr), apiserver-kubelet-client.crt (1yr), etcd/*.crt
3Check admin.conf cert: grep client-certificate-data ~/.kube/config (or admin.conf)
→ This cert is also expired — kubectl can't authenticate!
4Root cause: kubeadm certificates have a default 1-year validity. After 1 year, ALL component certs expire. The CA cert (10 years) is still valid. Fix: (1) kubeadm certs renew all, (2) update kubeconfig files, (3) restart control plane static pods (kubelet auto-detects manifest changes). For worker nodes: copy renewed kubelet.conf.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubectl x509 error → expired
②
certs check-expiration → all dead
③
certs renew all → new certs
④
Copy admin.conf → restore access
⑤
Restart CP pods → cluster healthy

Tenet: Certificate expiry is the "ticking time bomb" of kubeadm clusters. Component certs expire after 1 year; the CA cert expires after 10 years. After renewal, control plane static pods auto-restart when kubelet detects manifest changes. Always run kubeadm certs check-expiration monthly. kubeadm has automatically renewed all certificates during kubeadm upgrade apply since v1.15 — this isn't a new or version-gated feature — but between upgrades, certs approaching their 1-year expiry still need a manual kubeadm certs renew. On CKA: you MUST know the renewal workflow cold — check, renew, restart, verify.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get nodes Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid → kubectl DEAD!
$ sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration CERTIFICATE EXPIRES RESIDUAL admin.conf Jan 04, 2026 10:00 UTC -152d ← EXPIRED! apiserver Jan 04, 2026 10:00 UTC -152d ← EXPIRED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration CERTIFICATE EXPIRES RESIDUAL admin.conf Jun 05, 2027 10:00 UTC 364d ✅ RENEWED! apiserver Jun 05, 2027 10:00 UTC 364d ✅ RENEWED!
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION easy Ready control-plane 400d v1.32.13 ✅ kubectl working!
5

🔧 Fix — Renew All Certificates + Restore kubectl Access

BASH — Full certificate renewal procedure 
# Step 1: Renew ALL certificates (does NOT require kubectl to work!)
sudo kubeadm certs renew all

# Step 2: Update admin.conf (restore kubectl access)
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

# Step 3: Restart control plane components
# Method A: Move manifests out and back (triggers kubelet restart)
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml /tmp/
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /tmp/
sleep 10
sudo mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
sudo mv /tmp/kube-controller-manager.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
sudo mv /tmp/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# Method B: Simply restart kubelet (simpler)
# sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# Step 4: Wait for API server to be ready
sleep 15
kubectl get nodes

# Step 5: Verify all certs renewed
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration
6

✅ Verify — All Certificates Renewed, Kubectl Working

kubeadm certs check-expiration shows 364d residual for all certs. kubectl get nodes works again. Key commands: kubeadm certs check-expiration (check), kubeadm certs renew all (renew everything), kubeadm certs renew admin.conf (renew specific). Set a calendar reminder at month 11 and renew BEFORE expiry. For worker nodes: copy /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf after renewal.

sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -dates
kubectl get nodes
S60
🧪 SCENARIO S60 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture kubeadm Reset

kubeadm reset Leaves Residual Config — New Cluster Has Broken Networking

The Problem: Worker node "worker-3" is being decommissioned from the easypj cluster. The admin runs kubeadm reset, then later re-provisions the node into a NEW cluster — kubeadm init/join itself succeeds (reset genuinely cleans what init/join need). But the new cluster has flaky, hard-to-diagnose pod networking — because kubeadm reset explicitly does NOT clean CNI config (/etc/cni/net.d) or iptables/IPVS rules left by the OLD cluster's kube-proxy, and that stale state now conflicts with the new cluster. Your job: perform a COMPLETE node reset, cleaning every trace of the old cluster, before it gets reused.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Run kubeadm reset WITHOUT Full Cleanup (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Worker-3 has been acting flaky — random reboots, intermittent packet loss. The decision is made: decommission worker-3, provision a fresh replacement. The admin runs kubeadm reset, wipes the node, and runs kubeadm init on the fresh OS. kubeadm init actually SUCCEEDS — reset genuinely cleans what init needs. But minutes later, pods on the new cluster are flaky: some can't get IPs, some can't reach Services. Leftover CNI config and stale iptables/kube-proxy rules from the OLD cluster are silently conflicting with the new one. The easypj cluster is unstable during peak traffic.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S60): 
node-reset/
├── 01-incomplete-reset.sh          ← kubeadm reset WITHOUT cleanup (THE BUG!)
├── 02-new-cluster-flaky.sh         ← init succeeds, but new cluster networking is broken
└── 03-complete-reset-fix.sh        ← Full cleanup: CNI, iptables, manifests, etcd
BASH — Incomplete reset, re-init succeeds, networking breaks 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S60: kubeadm reset — Incomplete Cleanup
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Run kubeadm reset (MINIMAL — the bug!)
sudo kubeadm reset -f
# kubeadm reset genuinely cleans what's needed for a fresh kubeadm init/join to succeed —
# it stops kubelet and cleans up its own certs/manifests/config. But per the official docs
# it explicitly does NOT clean: CNI config (/etc/cni/net.d), iptables/nftables/IPVS rules,
# or $HOME/.kube — these survive and belong to the OLD cluster.

# STEP 2: Verify what's left behind
ls /etc/cni/net.d/ 2>/dev/null && echo "STILL EXISTS!" || echo "Gone"
sudo iptables -L -n | grep -c KUBE
# ❌ /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist STILL EXISTS — from the OLD cluster's CNI!
# ❌ iptables still has dozens of KUBE-* chains from the OLD cluster's kube-proxy!

# STEP 3: Reinitialize — this part SUCCEEDS (reset cleaned what init actually checks)
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/calico.yaml
# ✅ kubeadm init succeeds, Calico installs — looks fine so far!

# STEP 4: But new pods are flaky — old CNI config + stale iptables interfere
kubectl run test-pod --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl get pod test-pod -o wide
# ❌ Stuck ContainerCreating, or gets an IP from the OLD cluster's stale CNI config!

# The APP STORY:
# "The replacement node's cluster is unstable!"
# kubeadm init reported success, but invisible leftovers are causing chaos.
# The cluster is flaky during peak traffic. Users are complaining.
# You need a COMPLETE reset — not just kubeadm reset -f.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — New Cluster Has Flaky Networking

✗1. sudo kubeadm init → succeeds (no preflight errors — reset cleaned what init needs)
✗2. kubectl run test-pod ... → stuck ContainerCreating or gets inconsistent networking
✗3. ls /etc/cni/net.d/ → old CNI config files STILL PRESENT from the previous cluster
✗4. sudo iptables -L -n | grep KUBE → dozens of stale iptables chains from the old cluster!
3

🔍 Debug — What Did kubeadm reset Leave Behind?

1Confirm init itself worked fine: kubectl get nodes
→ Control-plane node is Ready — kubeadm reset DID clean what init/join actually check
2Check CNI state: sudo ls /etc/cni/net.d/
→ CNI config files from the OLD cluster remain, conflicting with the newly-installed CNI
3Check iptables: sudo iptables-save | grep -i kube
→ Old KUBE-* chains and rules remain — kube-proxy for the NEW cluster now has to coexist with stale rules
4Check $HOME/.kube: cat $HOME/.kube/config | grep server
→ May still point at the OLD cluster's API server if never manually removed
5Root cause: kubeadm reset genuinely cleans what kubeadm init/join need (certs, manifests, kubelet state) — that's why re-init SUCCEEDS. But per the official docs it explicitly does NOT clean: (1) /etc/cni/net.d/ (CNI config), (2) iptables/nftables/IPVS rules from kube-proxy, (3) $HOME/.kube. These survive from the OLD cluster and silently conflict with the new one. Fix: manually clean these three things for a true factory reset.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
init succeeds, but pods flaky
②
Check leftovers: CNI, iptables
③
Old CNI/kube-proxy state → conflict
④
Complete cleanup → fresh start
⑤
New pods network correctly!

Tenet: kubeadm reset is NOT a complete wipe — but it's also not as incomplete as commonly assumed: it genuinely cleans what kubeadm init/join check at preflight (certs, manifests, kubelet state), so re-init will typically SUCCEED. What it explicitly leaves behind, per the official docs, is narrower but just as dangerous: (1) CNI config in /etc/cni/net.d, (2) iptables/nftables/IPVS rules from kube-proxy, (3) $HOME/.kube. These don't block re-init — they silently corrupt the NEW cluster's networking instead, which is much harder to diagnose than a preflight error. On CKA: know exactly what kubeadm reset does and doesn't clean.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16 [preflight] Running pre-flight checks ✅ PASSED (reset cleaned what init checks!) [kubelet-start] Writing kubelet configuration → CLUSTER INITIALIZED — but keep reading...
$ kubectl run test-pod --image=nginx:alpine && kubectl get pod test-pod -o wide test-pod 0/1 ContainerCreating 0 90s <none> ← STUCK! Stale CNI/iptables state conflicts
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl run test-pod --image=nginx:alpine && kubectl get pod test-pod -o wide test-pod 1/1 Running 0 10s 192.168.55.3 ← ✅ Clean CNI state, networking works!
5

🔧 Fix — Complete Node Reset (Factory Fresh)

BASH — Complete node reset — every trace removed 
# Step 1: Run kubeadm reset (stops kubelet, removes basic config)
sudo kubeadm reset -f

# Step 2: Remove ALL Kubernetes directories
sudo rm -rf /etc/kubernetes/
sudo rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d/
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/kubelet/
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/
sudo rm -rf $HOME/.kube/

# Step 3: FLUSH all iptables rules (removes KUBE-* chains)
sudo iptables -F
sudo iptables -t nat -F
sudo iptables -t mangle -F
sudo iptables -X  # Delete user-defined chains

# Step 4: Clear IPVS (if using IPVS mode for kube-proxy)
sudo ipvsadm --clear 2>/dev/null || true

# Step 5: Stop and disable kubelet (ensure it's truly stopped)
sudo systemctl stop kubelet
sudo systemctl disable kubelet

# Step 6: Remove container images (optional — reclaim disk)
sudo crictl rmi --prune 2>/dev/null || true

# Step 7: Verify cleanup
ls /etc/kubernetes 2>/dev/null && echo "STILL EXISTS!" || echo "✅ Clean"
ls /etc/cni/net.d 2>/dev/null && echo "STILL EXISTS!" || echo "✅ Clean"
sudo iptables -L -n | grep KUBE && echo "❌ iptables NOT clean!" || echo "✅ iptables clean"
6

✅ Verify — Node Completely Clean, New Cluster Networks Correctly

CNI config and iptables rules from the old cluster are gone. Test pods now get IPs and network normally. Key: kubeadm reset alone does clean what kubeadm init checks (which is why re-init "succeeds") — but it explicitly leaves CNI config, iptables/IPVS rules, and $HOME/.kube behind, which corrupt the new cluster's networking silently rather than blocking init outright. This is essential for CKA scenarios where you need to rebuild a broken node cleanly.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Reinstall kubelet for Fresh Join

BASH — Enable kubelet for fresh join 
# Re-enable kubelet for joining a cluster
sudo systemctl enable kubelet
sudo systemctl start kubelet

# Run kubeadm join with fresh token from control plane
# (Generate on control plane: kubeadm token create --print-join-command)

📌 S61–S65: etcd Backup, Restore & Health

S61
🧪 SCENARIO S61 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture etcd Backup

etcd Backup — Snapshot Fails Because of a Typo'd --endpoints Port

The Problem: You need to set up automated etcd backups for the easypj production cluster. You run etcdctl snapshot save but a typo in the --endpoints port (23790 instead of 2379) means it's connecting to nothing — the command errors out and leaves behind a 0-byte or truncated snapshot file. The backup is worthless. When disaster strikes, you'll have nothing to restore. Your job: take a VALID etcd snapshot with full TLS authentication, verify its integrity, and set up a cron job for daily backups.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Attempt etcd Snapshot WITH a Typo'd --endpoints Port (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj cluster has been running for 6 months. The CTO demands: "Do we have backups?" You confidently say yes — you've been running etcdctl snapshot save monthly. But today, the CTO asks for a restore drill. You try to restore the backup and it FAILS — the snapshot is corrupted. You've been taking worthless backups for 6 months because a typo in the --endpoints port (23790 instead of 2379) meant every snapshot connected to nothing. 500,000 job listings, 50,000 user accounts — all at risk with no valid backup.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S61): 
etcd-backup/
├── 01-broken-snapshot.sh           ← etcdctl snapshot save with a typo'd --endpoints port (THE BUG!)
├── 02-verify-snapshot.sh           ← etcdctl snapshot status (shows EMPTY/CORRUPT!)
└── 03-correct-snapshot-fix.sh      ← Full snapshot with certs + correct endpoint + cron job
BASH — Take a BROKEN etcd snapshot (wrong endpoint port) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S61: etcd Backup — Typo'd --endpoints Port
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Attempt snapshot with a typo'd port — 23790 instead of 2379 (THE BUG!)
# Nothing is listening on 23790, so this fails to connect — but the destination
# file still gets created (0 bytes), and the error is easy to miss scrolling by
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:23790 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db
# ❌ BUG! Port 23790 — nothing is listening there, etcd listens on 2379

# STEP 2: Check the snapshot file
ls -lh /backup/etcd-snapshot.db
# -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 Jun 05 10:00 etcd-snapshot.db  ← 0 BYTES! EMPTY!
# OR: -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 5.2K ...etcd-snapshot.db    ← VERY SMALL! CORRUPT!

# STEP 3: Verify snapshot integrity
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot.db
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# Error: snapshot file integrity check failed
# OR: snapshot has 0 total keys — EMPTY!

# STEP 4: Check where etcd is actually listening
sudo netstat -tlnp | grep 2379
# tcp  127.0.0.1:2379   LISTEN   etcd
# etcd IS running and healthy — just not on the port the snapshot command used!

# The APP STORY:
# Disaster Recovery Drill Day — "Restore the cluster from backup."
# You navigate to /backup/etcd-snapshot.db — it's 0 bytes.
# 6 months of "backups" — ALL EMPTY. Silent, worthless snapshots.
# The CTO is watching. The cluster has NO valid backup.
# You have 30 minutes to take a REAL snapshot and prove recovery works.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Snapshot Is Empty or Corrupted

✗1. ls -lh /backup/etcd-snapshot.db → File size is 0 bytes or unusually small
✗2. etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot.db → "integrity check failed" or 0 total keys
✗3. The output scrolled by fast and was easy to miss — the "context deadline exceeded" connection error DID print to stderr, it's not truly silent, just easy to overlook in a busy terminal
✗4. 6 months of automated "backups" are ALL corrupted — cluster has NO valid restore point!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Did the Snapshot Fail Silently?

1Check the snapshot file: ls -lh /backup/etcd-snapshot.db && file /backup/etcd-snapshot.db
→ File is 0 bytes or "data" (not a valid etcd snapshot database)
2Diff the working command against the broken one: --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:23790 vs the correct --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379
→ An extra trailing 0 — 23790 instead of 2379!
3Check what etcd is actually listening on: sudo netstat -tlnp | grep etcd
→ etcd is healthy on 127.0.0.1:2379 — nothing is listening on 23790 at all!
4Root cause: A typo in the --endpoints port meant etcdctl tried to connect to a port nothing was listening on. The connection attempt fails with "context deadline exceeded," printed to stderr — not truly silent, just easy to miss scrolling by in a busy terminal, especially since the destination file still gets created (0 bytes) even though the snapshot never actually ran. The safe practice: ALWAYS verify every snapshot with 'etcdctl snapshot status' immediately after taking it — don't just trust exit code 0 or a file merely existing.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Snapshot taken → verify it
②
ls -lh → 0 bytes — FAILED!
③
Typo'd port in --endpoints
④
Fix the port to 2379
⑤
Verify snapshot → VALID!

Tenet: etcd snapshot save requires THREE things to work correctly: (1) --endpoints flag pointing to the correct etcd URL (the standard port is 2379 — double-check it, a typo fails silently-looking but not truly silent), (2) TLS certificates (--cacert, --cert, --key), (3) ETCDCTL_API=3 environment variable. ALWAYS verify the snapshot with etcdctl snapshot status immediately — never assume it succeeded just because a destination file exists. The status command shows hash, revision, total keys, and file size. A valid snapshot has revision >0 and total keys >0. On CKA: etcd backup/restore is a guaranteed exam task — know the full command cold.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ ls -lh /backup/etcd-snapshot.db -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 Jun 05 10:00 /backup/etcd-snapshot.db ← EMPTY FILE!
$ sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot.db Error: snapshot file integrity check failed — file may be corrupted or truncated → BACKUP IS WORTHLESS!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ ls -lh /backup/etcd-snapshot-valid.db -rw------- 1 root root 3.8M Jun 05 10:05 /backup/etcd-snapshot-valid.db ✅
$ sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot-valid.db 3a7b2c1d4e5f, 35892, 15423, 3.8 MB ✅ hash: valid, revision: 35892, keys: 15423
5

🔧 Fix — Correct etcd Snapshot with Endpoints + Verification

BASH — Proper etcd backup with TLS and integrity check 
# Step 1: Create backup directory
sudo mkdir -p /backup/etcd

# Step 2: Take snapshot WITH endpoints + TLS certs
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /backup/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).db

# Step 3: IMMEDIATELY verify the snapshot
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot status /backup/etcd/snapshot-*.db

# Step 4: Set up daily cron job for automated backups
echo "0 2 * * * root ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /backup/etcd/snapshot-\$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).db" | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/etcd-backup
6

✅ Verify — Valid Snapshot with Integrity Confirmed

The snapshot file is several MB in size, etcdctl snapshot status shows a valid hash, revision >0, and total keys >0. The cron job runs daily at 2 AM. Key commands: etcdctl snapshot save (create), etcdctl snapshot status (verify), etcdctl endpoint health (check cluster). ALWAYS verify the snapshot immediately after creation. Store backups off-node (copy to S3/NFS/remote server).

7

🧹 Cleanup — Remove Backups + Cron

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
sudo rm -rf /backup/etcd
sudo rm -f /etc/cron.d/etcd-backup
# Verify cleanup
ls /backup/etcd 2>/dev/null && echo "Still exists" || echo "✅ Clean"

etcd Restore — Restoring Snapshot to Wrong data-dir Path Causes etcd Startup Failure

The Problem: Disaster strikes — the easypj namespace was accidentally deleted, wiping all job listings and user accounts. You have a valid etcd snapshot from 10 minutes ago. You restore it, but etcd fails to start — the restore command used the wrong --data-dir path. The static pod manifest still points to the old directory. Your job: perform a complete etcd disaster recovery, restoring all cluster state with the correct data-dir path and manifest configuration.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Restore Snapshot to WRONG data-dir Path (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: 2:00 PM — A junior admin accidentally runs kubectl delete namespace easypj --force on the PRODUCTION cluster. Everything is GONE — 50,000 job listings, 10,000 users, all applications. Panic mode. But you have a valid etcd snapshot from 10:00 AM. You rush to restore it. You run etcdctl snapshot restore but etcd WON'T START. The restore command specified --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored but the static pod manifest still points to /var/lib/etcd. The cluster is DOWN and every minute costs the company thousands in lost revenue.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S62): 
etcd-restore/
├── 01-take-valid-snapshot.sh       ← First, take a VALID snapshot (reference point)
├── 02-wrong-restore.sh             ← Restore to WRONG --data-dir (THE BUG!)
├── 03-etcd-fails-to-start.sh       ← etcd pod in CrashLoopBackOff
└── 04-correct-restore-fix.sh       ← Restore + update manifest + restart etcd
BASH — Restore etcd snapshot to wrong directory (FAILS) 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S62: etcd Restore — Wrong data-dir Path
# ============================================

# STEP 1: STOP THE API SERVER FIRST (etcd must be restored in isolation)
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
# Wait for API server pod to stop
sleep 10

# STEP 2: Restore snapshot to WRONG directory (THE BUG!) — using etcdutl, the correct offline restore tool
sudo etcdutl snapshot restore /backup/etcd/snapshot-valid.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored \
  --name=easy \
  --initial-cluster=easy=https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380
# ❌ BUG! Restored to /var/lib/etcd-restored
# But the static pod manifest expects data at /var/lib/etcd!

# STEP 3: Check if etcd pod starts — IT WILL FAIL!
sudo crictl ps | grep etcd
# ❌ BUG! etcd container is NOT running — CrashLoopBackOff!

# STEP 4: Check etcd container logs
sudo crictl logs $(sudo crictl ps -a --name etcd -q | head -1) 2>/dev/null | tail -20
# ❌ "error opening data dir /var/lib/etcd: directory is empty!"
# The manifest says /var/lib/etcd but data is at /var/lib/etcd-restored!

# The APP STORY:
# 2:15 PM — "etcd won't start! The cluster is completely DOWN!"
# You have a valid backup. The restore command ran successfully.
# But etcd crashes on startup — data-dir mismatch between manifest and restore.
# Every minute of downtime costs $5,000 in lost job postings.
# The CEO is on Slack asking for ETA.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — etcd Pod CrashLoopBackOff

✗1. sudo crictl ps | grep etcd → etcd container is NOT running
✗2. sudo crictl logs <etcd-container> → "error opening data dir /var/lib/etcd: directory is empty!"
✗3. kubectl get pods -n kube-system → FAILS — API server is down, kubectl unreachable
✗4. The entire cluster is DEAD — no API server, no etcd, no workloads running!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Won't etcd Start After Restore?

1Check etcd manifest data-dir: sudo grep data-dir /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
→ --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd — the manifest expects data HERE!
2Check where data was restored: sudo ls -la /var/lib/etcd-restored/
→ Data EXISTS at /var/lib/etcd-restored/member/ — but manifest looks elsewhere!
3Check old etcd directory: sudo ls -la /var/lib/etcd/
→ /var/lib/etcd/ is EMPTY (or has old/corrupted data) — manifest can't find restored data!
4Root cause: The etcdctl snapshot restore command placed data in --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored, but the static pod manifest (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml) still has --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd. etcd starts, looks for data at /var/lib/etcd, finds it empty, and crashes. Fix: either (A) restore to /var/lib/etcd directly (overwrite old data) OR (B) update the etcd manifest to point to /var/lib/etcd-restored.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
etcd CrashLoop → check logs
②
"data dir empty" → check path
③
Manifest vs restore mismatch!
④
Restore to correct path OR update manifest
⑤
Restart API server → cluster RECOVERED!

Tenet: etcd restore is NOT just running etcdctl snapshot restore — you must also ensure the static pod manifest's --data-dir matches the restore directory. The complete recovery workflow: (1) Stop API server (move manifest out), (2) Stop etcd (or let kubelet stop it), (3) etcdctl snapshot restore to the CORRECT data-dir (matching the manifest), (4) Kubelet auto-restarts etcd with restored data, (5) Restore API server manifest, (6) Verify cluster. On CKA: etcd restore is a guaranteed exam task — know the exact workflow including manifest paths.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo crictl logs $(sudo crictl ps -a --name etcd -q | head -1) 2>/dev/null | tail -5 etcdmain: error opening data dir /var/lib/etcd: directory is empty → etcd can't find valid member data at the expected path!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo crictl ps | grep etcd a1b2c3d4e5f ...etcd... Running etcd 0 30s ✅ etcd is RUNNING!
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep etcd etcd-easy 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ Cluster RESTORED!
5

🔧 Fix — Complete etcd Disaster Recovery Procedure

BASH — Full etcd restore: stop API → restore → verify → restart API 
# Step 1: STOP THE API SERVER (must be done first!)
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
sleep 10  # Wait for kubelet to stop the API server pod

# Step 2: Remove the OLD data-dir first — restore refuses to write into a non-empty directory
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/etcd

# Step 3: Restore snapshot TO THE CORRECT DIRECTORY (matching manifest!) — use etcdutl, the
# offline restore tool, not etcdctl (which is for live-cluster operations)
sudo etcdutl snapshot restore /backup/etcd/snapshot-valid.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd \
  --name=easy \
  --initial-cluster=easy=https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380

# Step 4: Verify restored data exists
sudo ls -la /var/lib/etcd/member/snap/
# Should show snapshot .db files

# Step 4: Kubelet auto-restarts etcd (it watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests)
# Wait for etcd to be healthy
sleep 15

# Step 5: Restore the API server manifest
sudo mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

# Step 6: Wait for API server to be ready
sleep 15
kubectl get nodes
6

✅ Verify — Cluster Fully Recovered from Disaster

etcd is running with restored data. API server is back online. kubectl get nodes works. All previous cluster state (pods, deployments, services, configmaps) is restored to the snapshot point. Key: always restore to the data-dir that the etcd manifest expects (default: /var/lib/etcd). The recovery workflow must be practiced regularly — this is the most critical CKA exam task.

7

sudo rm -rf /var/lib/etcd-restored
# Verify cluster health
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A | head -20

🧪 SCENARIO S63 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture etcd Quota

etcd NOSPACE Alarm — Cluster Becomes Read-Only After Quota Exceeded

The Problem: The easypj cluster suddenly becomes read-only. Every kubectl create or kubectl apply fails with "etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded". The etcd database hit its quota-backend-bytes limit (default 2GB, but misconfigured to a much smaller 32MB during a recent manifest edit). etcd raises a NOSPACE alarm and refuses ALL writes. The cluster is frozen — you can read but not write. Your job: detect the NOSPACE alarm, compact + defrag the database, increase the quota to a reasonable value, and restore the cluster to read-write.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 etcd quota set to 32MB — Cluster HITS LIMIT and becomes Read-Only (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: 3:00 AM — PagerDuty wakes you. "All deployments failing across the cluster!" You stumble to your laptop and run kubectl get pods — it works. But kubectl create deploy hotfix --image=nginx fails with a cryptic mvcc: database space exceeded error. The etcd quota was accidentally set to 32MB during a manifest update yesterday. The database has been slowly filling up, and at 3 AM it finally hit the limit. etcd raised a NOSPACE alarm and the cluster is FROZEN. 500,000 job listings can't be updated. New users can't register. The job board is in read-only mode during peak hours.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S63): 
etcd-quota/
├── 01-check-alarms.sh              ← etcdctl alarm list (shows NOSPACE!)
├── 02-check-db-size.sh             ← etcdctl endpoint status (DB SIZE = 32MB, HIT QUOTA!)
├── 03-compact-and-defrag.sh        ← Compact history + defrag (THE FIX)
└── 04-fix-quota-manifest.sh        ← Increase quota-backend-bytes in etcd.yaml
BASH — Simulate etcd NOSPACE alarm on kind cluster 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S63: etcd Quota Exceeded — NOSPACE Alarm
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Check current etcd database size
# Since etcd runs as a static pod in the control plane container:
docker exec cp etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  alarm list
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# memberID:a1b2c3d4e5f alarm:NOSPACE   ← ALARM TRIGGERED!

# STEP 2: Check DB size vs quota
docker exec cp etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint status --write-out=table
# ENDPOINT              DB SIZE   IS LEADER
# https://127.0.0.1:2379 32.0 MB   true   ← ❌ HIT 32MB QUOTA! DB CAN'T GROW!

# STEP 3: Try to create ANYTHING — FAILS!
kubectl create deploy test-app --image=nginx:alpine
# ❌ Error from server: etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded
kubectl run test-pod --image=busybox --command -- sleep 60
# ❌ Error from server: etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded

# STEP 4: Check what quota is configured
docker exec cp cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep quota-backend
# --quota-backend-bytes=33554432   ← ❌ 32MB! SHOULD BE 2GB+!

# The APP STORY:
# "The entire cluster is READ-ONLY! Nothing deploys!"
# etcd hit the 32MB quota at 3 AM. All write API calls blocked.
# Deployments can't roll out. ConfigMaps can't update.
# The job board can display listings but can't post new ones.
# Revenue is dropping $10,000/hour during this outage.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — NOSPACE Alarm, All Writes Rejected

✗1. etcdctl alarm list → alarm:NOSPACE — etcd is in read-only mode!
✗2. kubectl create deploy --image=nginx → "mvcc: database space exceeded"
✗3. etcdctl endpoint status → DB SIZE = 32MB, quota is FULL!
✗4. kubectl get works (reads), kubectl apply/create Fails (writes) — CLUSTER FROZEN!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the Cluster Read-Only?

1Check etcd alarms: docker exec cp etcdctl ... alarm list
→ alarm:NOSPACE — etcd has run out of allocated disk space!
2Check quota configuration: docker exec cp cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml | grep quota
→ --quota-backend-bytes=33554432 (32MB) — way too small! Default is 2147483648 (2GB)
3Check actual DB usage: docker exec cp etcdctl ... endpoint status
→ DB size has reached 32MB — exactly matching the quota limit
4Root cause: The etcd --quota-backend-bytes was set to 33554432 (32MB) — possibly a typo during a manifest edit. By default kubeadm sets this to 2GB. When etcd DB size reaches this limit, etcd raises NOSPACE alarm and refuses ALL write operations. Fix: (1) compact history to remove old revisions, (2) defrag to reclaim freed space, (3) disarm the NOSPACE alarm, (4) increase quota-backend-bytes to a reasonable value in the manifest.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubectl create fails → check etcd
②
etcdctl alarm list → NOSPACE
③
DB hit 32MB quota → compact+defrag
④
Disarm alarm → writes restored
⑤
Fix quota in manifest → safe!

Tenet: etcd's --quota-backend-bytes controls the maximum database size. When the DB reaches this limit, etcd raises a NOSPACE alarm and blocks ALL writes — the cluster becomes read-only. The workflow to fix: (1) compact old revisions, (2) defrag to reclaim space, (3) disarm the alarm with etcdctl alarm disarm, (4) increase quota in the manifest. On CKA: knowing how to diagnose and fix a NOSPACE alarm is a critical skill — the cluster literally stops working until you fix it.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker exec cp etcdctl alarm list memberID:a1b2c3d4e5f alarm:NOSPACE ← CLUSTER IS READ-ONLY!
$ kubectl create deploy test-app --image=nginx Error from server (InternalError): etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded → ALL WRITES ARE REJECTED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ docker exec cp etcdctl alarm list memberID:a1b2c3d4e5f alarm:NOSPACE ← (still shows until disarmed)
$ docker exec cp etcdctl alarm disarm ✅ ALARM DISARMED! Writes now accepted!
$ kubectl create deploy test-app --image=nginx deployment.apps/test-app created ✅ CLUSTER IS READ-WRITE AGAIN!
5

🔧 Fix — Compact + Defrag + Disarm Alarm + Fix Quota

BASH — Full NOSPACE recovery procedure 
# FOR KIND CLUSTERS — Access etcd inside the control plane container:
# Step 1: Get current revision
REV=$(docker exec cp etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint status --write-out=json | grep -o '"revision":[0-9]*' | grep -o '[0-9]*')

# Step 2: Compact to remove old revisions
docker exec cp etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  compact $REV

# Step 3: Defrag to reclaim disk space
docker exec cp etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  defrag

# Step 4: DISARM the NOSPACE alarm (critical — unblocks writes!)
docker exec cp etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  alarm disarm

# FOR KUBEADM CLUSTERS — same commands without "docker exec cp":
# sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
#   --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
#   --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
#   --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key compact $REV
6

✅ Verify — Cluster Read-Write Again, NOSPACE Alarm Cleared

etcdctl alarm list shows NO alarms. kubectl create deploy succeeds. Key commands: etcdctl alarm list (check alarms), etcdctl compact (remove old revisions), etcdctl defrag (reclaim space), etcdctl alarm disarm (clear NOSPACE). The disarm step is CRITICAL — compact/defrag alone don't re-enable writes. For production: set quota-backend-bytes to at least 2GB, enable auto-compaction.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Verify etcd Health

kubectl delete deploy test-app --ignore-not-found 2>/dev/null
docker exec cp etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key endpoint health

🧪 SCENARIO S64 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture etcd Members

etcd Member Add Fails — Wrong Peer URL Causes New Member Stuck Unstarted

The Problem: The easypj cluster currently has a SINGLE etcd member — a single point of failure. You need HA with 3 etcd members. You run etcdctl member add to add a second member, but the new member never becomes healthy — it stays stuck in "unstarted" state because the peer URL was specified incorrectly. The wrong URL means the member can't communicate with the existing cluster. Your job: correctly add new etcd members with proper peer URLs and verify the cluster reaches healthy 3-member state.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Add etcd Member with WRONG Peer URL (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj cluster has been running on a single etcd member since launch — a ticking time bomb. If that one etcd node fails, the ENTIRE cluster becomes read-only. Management finally approved the HA upgrade. You add a second etcd member but use the wrong peer URL. The new member appears in the member list as "unstarted" — it can't communicate with the leader. The cluster is still running on a SINGLE member. If the leader dies, the cluster is GONE.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S64): 
etcd-members/
├── 01-check-current-members.sh     ← etcdctl member list (shows ONLY 1 member!)
├── 02-add-member-wrong-url.sh      ← etcdctl member add with WRONG peer URL (THE BUG!)
├── 03-check-member-stuck.sh        ← New member stuck "unstarted" — wrong URL!
└── 04-correct-member-add-fix.sh    ← Add members with CORRECT peer URLs
BASH — Check single-member cluster, attempt to add member with wrong URL 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S64: etcd Member Add — Wrong Peer URL
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Check current etcd cluster status
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list
# a1b2c3d4e5f, started, easy, https://127.0.0.1:2380, https://127.0.0.1:2379, false
# ❌ ONLY 1 MEMBER! Single point of failure!

# STEP 2: ADD NEW MEMBER WITH WRONG PEER URL (THE BUG!)
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member add etcd-2 --peer-urls=http://wrong-host:2380
# ❌ BUG! Peer URL points to "wrong-host" — doesn't exist!
# The member is added to the cluster list but can never join!

# STEP 3: Check member list — new member shows "unstarted"
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list
# a1b2c3d4e5f, started, easy, https://127.0.0.1:2380
# x9y8z7w6v5u, unstarted, etcd-2, http://wrong-host:2380  ← STUCK!
# ❌ BUG! "unstarted" — peer URL is unreachable, member can never join!

# STEP 4: Check endpoint health — new member is NOT healthy
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health
# https://127.0.0.1:2379 is healthy: successfully committed proposal
# ❌ Only 1 endpoint! The new member at wrong-host:2380 is unreachable!

# The APP STORY:
# "We need HA! If this single etcd dies, everything is gone."
# You added a new member but it shows "unstarted" forever.
# The peer URL was a typo — the member can't communicate.
# Now you have 2 members in the list but only 1 is working.
# The cluster is actually LESS reliable than before!

⚠️ Observe the Error — New Member Stuck "unstarted"

✗1. etcdctl member list → New member shows "unstarted" instead of "started"
✗2. etcdctl endpoint health → Only 1 healthy endpoint — new member unreachable
✗3. The peer URL http://wrong-host:2380 doesn't resolve — typo in the URL!
✗4. Cluster is now in a WORSE state — 2 members listed, only 1 working, quorum confusion!
