🔍 Debug — Why Is the New Member Stuck?

1Check the member list for peer URLs: etcdctl member list
→ New member has peer URL "http://wrong-host:2380" — HOST DOESN'T EXIST!
2Verify the peer URL is reachable: curl -k https://wrong-host:2380/health
→ "Could not resolve host: wrong-host" — DNS failure! URL is invalid!
3Understand etcd member states: "started" = member is running and connected. "unstarted" = member was added to the cluster configuration but hasn't connected yet. The peer URL is how etcd members communicate with each other for RAFT consensus. If the URL is wrong, the member can never connect and stays "unstarted" forever.
4Root cause: The --peer-urls flag in etcdctl member add specified an unreachable host. Peer URLs MUST be resolvable and reachable from ALL existing etcd members. Use the ACTUAL node IP/hostname, not a placeholder. Fix: remove the stuck member with 'etcdctl member remove <ID>' and re-add with the correct peer URL.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Member list → new = unstarted
②
Check peer URL → unreachable!
③
Remove stuck member
④
Re-add with correct URL
⑤
All 3 members started → HA!

Tenet: etcd member management requires precise peer URLs. The peer URL is how RAFT members communicate — it must be reachable from ALL existing members. Common mistakes: wrong hostname, wrong port (2380 is the default peer port), HTTP vs HTTPS mismatch, firewall blocking the peer port. Always use etcdctl member list to verify all members are "started". Remove stuck members with etcdctl member remove <ID>. On CKA: know how to add/remove etcd members for HA configuration.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list a1b2c3d4e5f, started, easy, https://127.0.0.1:2380, https://127.0.0.1:2379, false x9y8z7w6v5u, unstarted, etcd-2, http://wrong-host:2380 ← STUCK FOREVER!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list a1b2c3d4e5f, started, easy, https://127.0.0.1:2380, https://127.0.0.1:2379, false b2c3d4e5f6a, started, etcd-2, https://cp-2:2380, https://cp-2:2379, false c3d4e5f6a7b, started, etcd-3, https://cp-3:2380, https://cp-3:2379, false ✅ 3 HEALTHY MEMBERS — HA ACHIEVED!
5

🔧 Fix — Remove Stuck Member + Re-add with Correct Peer URL

BASH — Correct etcd member management for HA setup 
# Step 1: REMOVE the stuck member (use the member ID from member list)
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member remove x9y8z7w6v5u

# Step 2: Add new member with CORRECT peer URL — the output gives you the exact
# --initial-cluster value the NEW member's own etcd process needs (copy it for Step 3)
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member add etcd-2 --peer-urls=https://cp-2:2380

# Step 3: THIS is the step the earlier "bug" version skipped — member add alone only
# registers the member in the cluster's member list, it does NOT start an etcd process.
# On the NEW node (cp-2), actually run etcd with ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=existing and
# the --initial-cluster value from Step 2's output — e.g. via a static pod manifest copied
# from an existing member and edited with cp-2's own name/URLs, or directly:
# NOTE: this ssh step assumes cp-2/cp-3 are genuinely separate VMs/bare-metal nodes, as in
# a real production HA control plane — it's reference material, not runnable as-is on this
# lab's single-node cluster (a single kind/kubeadm node has no separate cp-2/cp-3 to SSH into)
ssh cp-2 "sudo etcd --name etcd-2 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls https://cp-2:2380 \
  --listen-peer-urls https://cp-2:2380 \
  --listen-client-urls https://cp-2:2379,https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --advertise-client-urls https://cp-2:2379 \
  --initial-cluster easy=https://127.0.0.1:2380,etcd-2=https://cp-2:2380 \
  --initial-cluster-state existing \
  --cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  --peer-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.crt --peer-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.key &"
# Without this actual etcd process running, the member stays "unstarted" forever — exactly
# like the original bug, just for a different reason (never started, not a bad peer URL)

# Step 4: Add third member for proper HA (odd number = 3) — repeat Steps 2-3 for cp-3
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member add etcd-3 --peer-urls=https://cp-3:2380
# ...then start etcd on cp-3 the same way as Step 3, with its own --initial-cluster value

# Step 5: Verify ALL members are healthy
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health --cluster
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list
6

✅ Verify — 3 Healthy etcd Members, HA Achieved

etcdctl member list shows 3 members all in "started" state. etcdctl endpoint health shows all 3 endpoints healthy. The cluster now tolerates 1 node failure (3 members, quorum = 2). Key: always use ODD numbers of etcd members (3, 5, 7). Peer URLs must use HTTPS in production. Each member needs its own unique --name, --initial-advertise-peer-urls, and --listen-peer-urls.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Remove Added Members (Single-Node Restore)

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# List all members and capture the IDs of everything except the original leader
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list

# Actually remove the added members from the cluster's member list (replace with real IDs)
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member remove <etcd-2-member-id>
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member remove <etcd-3-member-id>

# If Step 3's etcd process was actually started on cp-2/cp-3 (real multi-node setup only),
# stop it there too — otherwise it keeps running as an orphaned single-member "cluster"
ssh cp-2 "sudo pkill -f 'etcd --name etcd-2'" 2>/dev/null || true
ssh cp-3 "sudo pkill -f 'etcd --name etcd-3'" 2>/dev/null || true

# Verify final state — back to a single healthy member
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health

Your job: find the correct certificate paths from the etcd static pod manifest, verify connectivity with proper TLS, and fix the health check script.

📋 etcd health check with WRONG cert paths — falsely reports DOWN (CONTAINS THE BUG)

# SCENARIO S65: etcd Health Check — Wrong Certificate Paths

# ❌ Error: context deadline exceeded

⚠️ Observe the Error — Health Check Fails, But etcd Is Running

✗1. docker exec cp etcdctl ... --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/etcd/ca.crt endpoint health → "context deadline exceeded"
✗2. kubectl get nodes → WORKS FINE! The cluster is healthy — health check is LYING!
✗3. The cert path /etc/kubernetes/etcd/ca.crt — FILE DOES NOT EXIST!
✗4. False alarm triggers PagerDuty every night at 2 AM — on-call team has alert fatigue!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Does the Health Check Say "unhealthy" When etcd Is Fine?

1Check if the cert files exist: docker exec cp ls -la /etc/kubernetes/etcd/ 2>&1
→ "No such file or directory" — the path is WRONG!
2Find the ACTUAL cert paths from the etcd manifest: docker exec cp grep -E "cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
→ --cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt — the REAL path has pki/!
3Understand TLS in etcd: etcd in kubeadm uses mutual TLS (mTLS). The client (etcdctl) must present a valid certificate signed by the etcd CA. If ANY of --cacert, --cert, or --key point to non-existent files, etcdctl can't establish a TLS connection and reports "context deadline exceeded" — which looks like etcd is DOWN, but it's actually a client-side TLS configuration error.
4Root cause: The health check script uses WRONG certificate file paths. The correct paths (in kubeadm/kind clusters) are always under /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ — NOT /etc/kubernetes/etcd/. The "pki" subdirectory is critical. When etcdctl can't load TLS certs, it reports "context deadline exceeded" which looks like a connectivity problem but is actually a local filesystem error. Fix: find the correct paths from the etcd static pod manifest with 'grep -E "cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml'.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Health check fails → but kubectl works!
②
Check cert file → doesn't exist!
③
grep etcd manifest → REAL path!
④
Fix script with correct paths
⑤
Health check passes → alert cleared!

Tenet: "context deadline exceeded" is etcdctl's generic error for "I couldn't talk to etcd." It can mean etcd is DOWN (real problem) OR your TLS certs are wrong (false alarm). ALWAYS verify cert file existence before assuming etcd is down: ls -la <cert-path>. The canonical etcd cert paths in kubeadm are: --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt, --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt, --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key. On CKA: distinguishing between real etcd failure and TLS misconfiguration is a key exam skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker exec cp ls /etc/kubernetes/etcd/ca.crt ls: cannot access '/etc/kubernetes/etcd/ca.crt': No such file or directory ← PATH WRONG!
$ docker exec cp etcdctl --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/etcd/ca.crt endpoint health https://127.0.0.1:2379 is unhealthy: context deadline exceeded ← FALSE ALARM!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ docker exec cp grep "cacert\|cert-file\|key-file" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml - --cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt - --key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key - --trusted-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt ← REAL PATHS!
$ docker exec cp etcdctl --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt endpoint health https://127.0.0.1:2379 is healthy: successfully committed proposal ✅ HEALTHY!

🔧 Fix — Find Correct Cert Paths + Fix Health Check Script

BASH — Discover correct paths from etcd manifest, then test 
# FOR KIND CLUSTERS:
# Step 1: Find the ACTUAL cert paths from the etcd static pod manifest
docker exec cp grep -E "cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# Output shows the REAL paths. Copy them exactly.

# Step 2: Verify each cert file exists
docker exec cp ls -la /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
docker exec cp ls -la /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt
docker exec cp ls -la /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# Step 3: Run health check with CORRECT paths
docker exec cp etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health

# FOR KUBEADM CLUSTERS (ksw → 1):
# Same approach — certs are at /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/
# sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
#   --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
#   --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
#   --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
#   --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
#   endpoint health
6

✅ Verify — Health Check Passes, No More False Alarms

etcdctl endpoint health returns "is healthy: successfully committed proposal". The correct cert paths are confirmed from the etcd manifest. Key: always derive etcdctl flags from the etcd static pod manifest. The manifest is the source of truth for cert paths, endpoints, and all etcd configuration. For kubeadm/kind: certs are at /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. NEVER hardcode paths — extract them dynamically from the manifest with grep.

S66
🧪 SCENARIO S66 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture RBAC Role

Developer Can't kubectl exec — Role Missing "create" on pods/exec

The Problem: A new developer "alice" joins the easypj team and needs read-only access to the easypj-dev namespace. You create a Role with ["get","list","watch"] on pods and pods/log — Alice can kubectl get pods AND kubectl logs -f just fine (the official RBAC reference's own worked example for "read pods and pod logs" uses exactly get+list, no watch needed — but watch doesn't hurt either). What actually fails is kubectl exec — it's Forbidden, because exec is RBAC-gated as a create on the pods/exec subresource, a completely different resource+verb combination than reading pods. Your job: identify the missing rule, update the Role, and verify Alice can now exec into pods for debugging.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Create Role Covering pods/pods-log Only — Missing pods/exec (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Alice joins the easypj team as a junior developer. She needs to view pods and follow logs to debug application issues in the dev namespace. The DevOps lead creates a Role covering get/list/watch on pods and pods/log. Alice runs kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev — works! kubectl logs -f easypj-api-xxx — also works fine! Then she tries kubectl exec -it easypj-api-xxx -- sh to poke around inside the container — "Error from server (Forbidden): pods "easypj-api-xxx" is forbidden: cannot create resource pods/exec." exec is gated as a CREATE on a totally different subresource. Alice can't shell into her own pods — development is blocked.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S66): 
rbac-readonly/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-dev
├── 01-role-missing-exec.yaml      ← Role with BUG: covers pods/pods-log only — NO pods/exec!
├── 02-rolebinding.yaml            ← RoleBinding: alice → pod-reader
├── 03-test-alice-permissions.sh   ← kubectl auth can-i tests
└── 04-role-fixed-exec.yaml        ← Role with an ADDED pods/exec rule (verb: create)
BASH — Create broken Role and test permissions as alice 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S66: RBAC Role Missing pods/exec — create Verb
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and deploy a test pod
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl run test-api -n easypj-dev --image=nginx:alpine --port=80
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/test-api -n easypj-dev --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Create Role covering pods + pods/log ONLY (THE BUG — no pods/exec rule!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: easypj-dev
  name: pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]      # ✅ Covers get/list/watch AND logs -f fine
EOF
# ❌ BUG! No rule at all for the "pods/exec" subresource — exec needs its own separate rule!

# STEP 3: Create RoleBinding for alice
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  namespace: easypj-dev
  name: alice-pod-reader
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF

# STEP 4: Test permissions as alice
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice -n easypj-dev
# yes ✅ (get works)

kubectl logs -f test-api -n easypj-dev --as=alice
# ✅ Works fine! logs -f only needs get/list on pods/log, which Alice already has.

kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=alice -n easypj-dev
# ❌ BUG! no — there's no rule at all covering the pods/exec subresource!

kubectl exec -it test-api -n easypj-dev --as=alice -- sh
# ❌ BUG! Error from server (Forbidden): pods "test-api" is forbidden:
#    User "alice" cannot create resource "pods/exec" in API group "" in the namespace "easypj-dev"

# The APP STORY:
# "I can see the pods and even follow the logs, but I can't shell in!"
# Alice spends her first 2 hours blocked — can't debug her code interactively.
# get/list/watch on pods works fine, but exec is a DIFFERENT resource entirely.
# The missing pods/exec rule is the silent RBAC trap.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — kubectl exec Returns Forbidden

✗1. kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=alice -n easypj-dev → no
✗2. kubectl exec -it test-api -n easypj-dev --as=alice -- sh → "cannot create resource pods/exec"
✗3. kubectl get pods and kubectl logs -f both work but kubectl exec fails — different resource entirely!
✗4. Developer Alice is BLOCKED — can't shell into pods to debug her application!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Does kubectl exec Need a create Verb?

1Check current Role rules: kubectl get role pod-reader -n easypj-dev -o yaml
→ Only one rule, covering resources: [pods, pods/log] — no rule mentions "pods/exec" at all!
2Test each permission individually: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=alice -n easypj-dev
→ get/list/watch on pods and pods/log are listed; pods/exec doesn't appear at all
3Understand why exec needs create: kubectl logs/logs -f both operate on the pods/log subresource with get-family verbs (reading data). kubectl exec is different — it opens an interactive streaming connection INTO the container, which the API models as CREATING a connection on the pods/exec subresource. The official RBAC reference's own "kubectl exec" example uses exactly resources: [pods/exec], verbs: [create].
4Root cause: The Role only has a rule for ["pods","pods/log"] — there's no rule at all for the "pods/exec" subresource. Reading pods (get/list/watch) and executing INTO pods (create on pods/exec) are governed by entirely separate RBAC rules; having full read access doesn't imply exec access. Fix: add a second rule granting create on pods/exec.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubectl exec fails → Forbidden
②
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec → no
③
No rule covers pods/exec at all!
④
Add a pods/exec rule (verb: create)
⑤
kubectl exec works → alice unblocked!

Tenet: Reading pods (get/list/watch on pods and pods/log) and executing into pods (create on pods/exec) are entirely separate RBAC rules — full read access does NOT imply exec access, and vice versa. This is one of the most commonly misunderstood RBAC subresource splits: exec "feels" like a read/debug operation, but the API models it as a POST/create on a connection subresource. When creating debug-access Roles, explicitly add a rule for pods/exec if interactive access is needed. On CKA: know that subresources (pods/log, pods/exec, pods/portforward) each need their OWN rule.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=alice -n easypj-dev no ← EXEC IS BLOCKED!
$ kubectl exec -it test-api -n easypj-dev --as=alice -- sh Error from server (Forbidden): pods "test-api" is forbidden: User "alice" cannot create resource "pods/exec" in API group "" in the namespace "easypj-dev"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=alice -n easypj-dev yes ✅ EXEC GRANTED!
$ kubectl exec -it test-api -n easypj-dev --as=alice -- sh / # ✅ SHELL ACCESS WORKING!
5

🔧 Fix — Add a pods/exec Rule to the Role

BASH — Patch the Role to add a pods/exec rule 
# Step 1: Add a SECOND rule granting create on pods/exec (a separate subresource from pods/log)
kubectl patch role pod-reader -n easypj-dev --type='json' -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/rules/-","value":{"apiGroups":[""],"resources":["pods/exec"],"verbs":["create"]}}]'

# Step 2: Verify the fix
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=alice -n easypj-dev
kubectl exec -it test-api -n easypj-dev --as=alice -- sh

# Step 3: Check full permission list
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=alice -n easypj-dev
6

✅ Verify — Alice Can Now kubectl exec Into Pods

kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=alice -n easypj-dev returns "yes". kubectl exec opens a shell successfully. Key lesson: pod subresources (pods/log, pods/exec, pods/portforward, pods/attach) each need their OWN RBAC rule — granting get/list/watch on the base "pods" resource does not extend to any of them. exec specifically needs create on pods/exec, not get/list/watch.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace + RBAC

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-dev

CI/CD Pod Gets Forbidden — Using Default ServiceAccount Without RBAC Permissions

The Problem: The easypj CI/CD pipeline runs inside a Kubernetes pod and needs to create Deployments after building Docker images. The pod uses the default ServiceAccount which has NO permissions. Every kubectl apply call returns "Forbidden". The CI/CD pipeline is completely blocked. Your job: create a dedicated ServiceAccount with a Role granting create/update on Deployments, and bind it to the CI/CD pod.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Deploy CI/CD Pod with Default ServiceAccount — No Permissions (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team sets up a GitLab CI/CD pipeline that builds Docker images and deploys them to Kubernetes. The CI/CD job runs as a pod in the easypj-cicd namespace. After building the image, it runs kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml — but gets "Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps is forbidden." The pod is using the namespace's default ServiceAccount, which has ZERO permissions. Every deployment is stuck. The team can't ship hotfixes. The production bug from this morning is still live.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S67): 
rbac-cicd/
├── 00-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-cicd
├── 01-cicd-pod-default-sa.yaml    ← CICD pod with BUG: no serviceAccountName (uses default SA)
├── 02-serviceaccount.yaml         ← Dedicated cicd-bot ServiceAccount (TO BE CREATED)
├── 03-role-deploy-editor.yaml     ← Role: create/update/patch deployments
└── 04-rolebinding-cicd.yaml       ← RoleBinding: cicd-bot → deploy-editor
BASH — Deploy CI/CD pod with default SA (FAILS)

# SCENARIO S67: ServiceAccount RBAC for CI/CD Pod
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and deploy test pod
kubectl create namespace easypj-cicd

# STEP 2: Deploy CI/CD pod using DEFAULT ServiceAccount (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cicd-runner
  namespace: easypj-cicd
spec:
  # ❌ BUG! No serviceAccountName specified — uses "default" SA!
  containers:
  - name: runner
    image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd --timeout=60s

# STEP 3: Try to create a deployment from the CI/CD pod — FAILS!
kubectl exec cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd -- kubectl create deploy test-app \
  --image=nginx:alpine -n easypj-cicd
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps is forbidden:
# User "system:serviceaccount:easypj-cicd:default" cannot create
# resource "deployments" in API group "apps" in namespace "easypj-cicd"

# STEP 4: Check which SA the pod is using

# serviceAccount: default   ← ❌ DEFAULT SA — NO PERMISSIONS!

# "The CI/CD pipeline is broken! Deployments won't apply."
# The GitLab runner pod can build images but can't deploy.
# Every commit triggers a build, but nothing reaches production.
# The hotfix for the payment bug is READY but can't be deployed.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Forbidden: Cannot Create Deployments

✗1. kubectl exec cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd -- kubectl create deploy → "Forbidden"
✗2. Pod is using "default" ServiceAccount — has ZERO permissions!
✗3. kubectl auth can-i create deploy --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-cicd:default -n easypj-cicd → no
✗4. CI/CD pipeline STUCK — hotfixes can't be deployed to production!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the CI/CD Pod Forbidden?

1Check SA used by pod: kubectl get pod cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'
→ "default" — the namespace's default SA has no RBAC bindings!
2Check SA token mount: kubectl exec cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | grep sub
→ Token exists and is mounted (authentication works), but authorization (RBAC) fails!
3Understand SA RBAC: A ServiceAccount provides the pod's IDENTITY (authentication). But permissions (authorization) come from RoleBindings/ClusterRoleBindings. The "default" SA has NO RoleBindings by default — it can authenticate but is authorized for NOTHING.
4Root cause: The CI/CD pod uses the "default" ServiceAccount which has no RoleBindings. A ServiceAccount without a Role/ClusterRole binding has ZERO permissions. Fix: (1) create a dedicated ServiceAccount "cicd-bot", (2) create a Role allowing ["create","update","patch","get","list"] on deployments, (3) bind the Role to cicd-bot via a RoleBinding, (4) update the pod spec to use serviceAccountName: cicd-bot.

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod kubectl → Forbidden
②
Check SA → "default" used
③
Default SA has no RBAC!
④
Create SA + Role + RoleBinding
⑤
CI/CD deploys → pipeline fixed!

Tenet: ServiceAccounts provide IDENTITY (who am I?); RoleBindings provide PERMISSIONS (what can I do?). Every namespace has a "default" SA that is auto-mounted to pods unless overridden — but it has ZERO permissions. For pods that need Kubernetes API access: (1) create a dedicated SA, (2) create a Role with needed verbs, (3) RoleBinding to connect SA to Role, (4) set serviceAccountName in pod spec. On CKA: this is a common exam task — create SA, Role, RoleBinding, and update a pod.

📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd -- kubectl create deploy test-app --image=nginx -n easypj-cicd deployment.apps/test-app created ✅ CICD CAN DEPLOY!

🔧 Fix — Create SA + Role + RoleBinding + Update Pod

BASH — Full CI/CD RBAC setup 
# Step 1: Create dedicated ServiceAccount
kubectl create sa cicd-bot -n easypj-cicd

# Step 2: Create Role for deployment management
kubectl create role deploy-editor -n easypj-cicd \
  --verb=create,update,patch,get,list \
  --resource=deployments

# Step 3: Bind Role to ServiceAccount
kubectl create rolebinding cicd-deploy -n easypj-cicd \
  --role=deploy-editor \
  --serviceaccount=easypj-cicd:cicd-bot

# Step 4: Delete old pod and recreate with new SA
kubectl delete pod cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cicd-runner
  namespace: easypj-cicd
spec:
  serviceAccountName: cicd-bot  # ✅ FIXED! Dedicated SA with RBAC!
  containers:
  - name: runner
    image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd --timeout=60s
6

✅ Verify — CI/CD Pod Can Now Create Deployments

kubectl exec cicd-runner -n easypj-cicd -- kubectl create deploy test-app --image=nginx -n easypj-cicd succeeds. The pod uses the dedicated cicd-bot ServiceAccount with explicit RBAC permissions. Key: ServiceAccount = Identity, RoleBinding = Authorization. Never grant permissions to the "default" SA — create dedicated SAs for each workload.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Namespace

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-cicd
S68
🧪 SCENARIO S68 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture ClusterRoleBinding

New Developer Can't List Pods — ClusterRoleBinding Missing for "developers" Group

The Problem: A new developer "bob" joins the easypj team. The DevOps lead creates a ClusterRole "pod-reader" granting get/list/watch on pods. But when Bob runs kubectl get pods --all-namespaces, he gets "Forbidden". The ClusterRole exists but the ClusterRoleBinding that connects Bob's "developers" group to the ClusterRole was never created. The Role is orphaned — no one can use it. Your job: identify the missing binding, create the ClusterRoleBinding, and verify Bob gets access.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Create ClusterRole WITHOUT ClusterRoleBinding (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Bob joins the easypj SRE team. He needs to see all pods across all namespaces for monitoring. The DevOps lead creates a ClusterRole called "pod-reader". Bob tries kubectl get pods -A — "Forbidden." The ClusterRole exists perfectly, but the ClusterRoleBinding to connect Bob's group "developers" to the ClusterRole was FORGOTTEN. Bob has been onboard for 3 days and still can't do his job. The SRE team is understaffed and can't respond to incidents fast enough.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S68): 
rbac-cluster/
├── 01-clusterrole-pod-reader.yaml   ← ClusterRole: get/list/watch pods (EXISTS — correct!)
├── 02-clusterrolebinding.yaml       ← ClusterRoleBinding (MISSING! — THE BUG!)
└── 03-test-bob-permissions.sh       ← kubectl auth can-i tests as bob
BASH — Create ClusterRole but FORGET the ClusterRoleBinding 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S68: Missing ClusterRoleBinding
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create ClusterRole (this is CORRECT — the role itself is fine!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
EOF

# STEP 2: Check the ClusterRole exists
kubectl get clusterrole pod-reader
# NAME         CREATED AT
# pod-reader   2026-06-05T10:00:00Z  ← Role EXISTS!

# STEP 3: BUT — is there a ClusterRoleBinding?
kubectl get clusterrolebinding | grep pod-reader
# ❌ BUG! NO ClusterRoleBinding! The role is ORPHANED!

# STEP 4: Bob tries to list pods — FORBIDDEN!
kubectl get pods --as=bob --as-group=developers --all-namespaces
# ❌ BUG! Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden:
#    User "bob" cannot list resource "pods" in API group ""
#    at the cluster scope

# STEP 5: Check Bob's effective permissions
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=bob --as-group=developers -A
# ❌ no — The ClusterRole exists but NO ONE is bound to it!

# The APP STORY:
# "I still can't see any pods. What's wrong with my permissions?"
# Bob has been asking for 3 days. The ClusterRole was created day 1.
# But the ClusterRoleBinding was NEVER created.
# The role is like a key with no lock — perfectly defined, totally useless.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — ClusterRole Exists But Access Denied

✗1. kubectl get clusterrole pod-reader → EXISTS — role is correctly defined
✗2. kubectl get clusterrolebinding | grep pod-reader → NOTHING — no binding!
✗3. kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=bob -A → no
✗4. The ClusterRole is ORPHANED — perfectly defined but bound to NO ONE!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is Access Denied When the Role Exists?

1Verify Role exists: kubectl describe clusterrole pod-reader
→ Role is correct: verbs=[get,list,watch] on pods — but UNUSED!
2Check all ClusterRoleBindings: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -A5 pod-reader
→ NO MATCH — no binding references "pod-reader"!
3Understand the binding relationship: A ClusterRole alone is just a definition. A ClusterRoleBinding is the CONNECTION between subjects (users/groups/SAs) and the ClusterRole. Without a binding, the role grants permissions to NO ONE. Think: Role = "what can be done", Binding = "who can do it". Both are required.
4Root cause: The ClusterRoleBinding connecting the "developers" group (which includes bob) to the "pod-reader" ClusterRole was never created. The ClusterRole exists but is orphaned. Fix: create a ClusterRoleBinding that maps Group: developers → ClusterRole: pod-reader.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Bob Forbidden → check Role
②
ClusterRole exists → correct!
③
Check CRB → NOTHING FOUND!
④
Create ClusterRoleBinding
⑤
Bob can list pods → unblocked!

Tenet: RBAC has a 3-part model: Subject (who) → RoleBinding (connection) → Role (what). All three must exist for access to work. Role/ClusterRole = defines verbs on resources. RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding = connects subjects to roles. A role without a binding is orphaned — perfectly valid YAML, zero practical effect. Always verify with kubectl auth can-i after creating RBAC resources. On CKA: creating the binding is the most commonly forgotten step.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get clusterrole pod-reader NAME CREATED AT pod-reader 2026-06-05T10:00:00Z ← ROLE EXISTS!
$ kubectl get clusterrolebinding | grep pod-reader (empty — NO BINDING EXISTS!) ← ROLE IS ORPHANED!
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=bob --as-group=developers -A no ← DESPITE ROLE EXISTING, ACCESS DENIED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=bob --as-group=developers -A yes ✅ ACCESS GRANTED!
$ kubectl get pods --as=bob --as-group=developers --all-namespaces NAMESPACE NAME READY STATUS kube-system coredns-xxx 1/1 Running ✅ BOB CAN SEE ALL PODS!
5

🔧 Fix — Create Missing ClusterRoleBinding

BASH — Create ClusterRoleBinding connecting developers group to pod-reader 
# Step 1: Create the ClusterRoleBinding (imperative — CKA fast method)
kubectl create clusterrolebinding developers-pod-reader \
  --clusterrole=pod-reader \
  --group=developers

# Step 2: Verify the binding exists
kubectl get clusterrolebinding developers-pod-reader

# Step 3: Test Bob's access
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=bob --as-group=developers -A
kubectl get pods --as=bob --as-group=developers -A
6

✅ Verify — Bob Can Now List Pods Cluster-Wide

kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=bob --as-group=developers -A returns "yes". The ClusterRoleBinding connects Group:developers → ClusterRole:pod-reader. Key: Role = WHAT, Binding = WHO. Both must exist. Use kubectl auth can-i to test permissions immediately. ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide access; RoleBinding grants namespace-scoped access.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Remove RBAC Resources

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding developers-pod-reader
kubectl delete clusterrole pod-reader
S69
🧪 SCENARIO S69 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture CSR Approval

New Engineer Can't Get kubectl Access — Client Certificate CSR Stuck Pending

The Problem: A new engineer joining the easypj team needs their own client certificate for kubectl access. They generate a CSR and submit it. It stays stuck in Pending — unlike a NODE's bootstrap CSR (which kubeadm auto-approves via a dedicated ClusterRoleBinding), an arbitrary human user's client-auth CSR is never auto-approved by kube-controller-manager's built-in approver — that approver only recognizes the specific kubelet-bootstrap and kubelet-serving-rotation patterns. Your job: find the Pending CSR, approve it, and issue the engineer their certificate.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Node Joins But CSR Stays Pending — Manual Approval Required (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team just hired a new SRE, Dana, who needs her own kubectl client certificate (not a shared kubeconfig). She generates a CSR and submits it via kubectl apply. It sits in Pending forever. Unlike a worker node's bootstrap CSR — which kubeadm's kubeadm:node-autoapprove-bootstrap ClusterRoleBinding auto-approves via kube-controller-manager's built-in csrapproving controller — arbitrary human client-auth CSRs are never auto-approved. Until an admin manually approves it, Dana has no cluster access.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S69): 
csr-approval/
├── 01-create-csr.yaml              ← Dana's client-cert CSR (real openssl-generated CSR)
├── 02-list-pending-csrs.sh         ← kubectl get csr (shows Pending!)
└── 03-approve-csr-fix.sh           ← kubectl certificate approve + issue kubeconfig
BASH — Submit a real client-cert CSR and diagnose the issue 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S69: Client-Cert CSR Stuck Pending — Manual Approval Required (by design)
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Generate a REAL CSR with openssl for Dana's kubectl access
# Generate a private key
openssl genrsa -out /tmp/dana.key 2048
# Generate a CSR — CN becomes the username, O becomes the group (e.g. a "easypj-sre" RBAC group)
openssl req -new -key /tmp/dana.key \
  -subj "/O=easypj-sre/CN=dana" \
  -out /tmp/dana.csr
# Base64 encode and create the CSR object using the GENERIC client signer (correct for a
# human user — this is different from kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet, which
# is reserved specifically for node-bootstrap client certs)
cat << EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  name: dana-access
spec:
  request: $(cat /tmp/dana.csr | base64 -w0)
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client
  usages:
  - client auth
EOF

# STEP 2: Check CSR status — STUCK IN PENDING!
kubectl get csr
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# NAME          AGE   SIGNERNAME                        REQUESTOR   CONDITION
# dana-access   5m    kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client   admin    Pending

# STEP 3: Check CSR details
kubectl describe csr dana-access
# Conditions:
#   Type    Status  Reason
#   Approved  False   Pending   ← ❌ MANUAL APPROVAL REQUIRED — no auto-approver covers this signer for arbitrary users!

# STEP 4: Dana tries to use her cert
kubectl --client-certificate=/tmp/dana.crt --client-key=/tmp/dana.key get pods
# ❌ Fails — the cert was never issued because the CSR was never approved!

# The APP STORY:
# "I submitted my CSR but I still can't run kubectl!"
# Dana's CSR is well-formed and correctly signed.
# But it's PENDING — no one approved the certificate.
# This is expected: kube-controller-manager's auto-approver only recognizes the
# kubelet-bootstrap and kubelet-serving-rotation patterns, not arbitrary user CSRs.
# An admin must manually review and approve.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — CSR Shows Pending, Dana Has No Access

✗1. kubectl get csr → CSR shows CONDITION: Pending — awaiting manual approval
✗2. kubectl describe csr dana-access → Approved: False
✗3. No certificate has been issued — kubectl get csr dana-access -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' is empty
✗4. Dana can't run any kubectl commands — she's completely blocked on day one!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is Dana's CSR Stuck Pending?

1List all CSRs: kubectl get csr
→ Shows CSR in Pending state — expected for a human user's client-auth request
2Check CSR condition: kubectl get csr dana-access -o yaml | grep -A5 conditions
→ Approved: False — needs manual kubectl certificate approve
3Understand what IS auto-approved: kube-controller-manager's built-in csrapproving controller only auto-approves two specific patterns, both scoped to nodes: node-bootstrap client CSRs (signerName kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet, requested by identities in system:bootstrappers, via kubeadm's kubeadm:node-autoapprove-bootstrap binding) and kubelet CLIENT-certificate renewal/rotation from an already-registered node (same signer, self-requested by system:nodes, via kubeadm:node-autoapprove-certificate-rotation). Kubelet SERVING certs are explicitly NOT auto-approved by this controller — that's a separate, well-known gap third-party tools like kubelet-csr-approver exist to fill. Dana's CSR matches none of these — it's a generic human-user request on the kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client signer.
4Root cause: There is no auto-approver for arbitrary client-auth CSRs from human users — this is by design, not a misconfiguration. Someone must manually review and run 'kubectl certificate approve <csr-name>'. Fix: approve the CSR, then Dana can extract her issued certificate and build a kubeconfig.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Dana blocked → check CSR
②
kubectl get csr → Pending
③
Human-user CSR — no auto-approver covers it
④
kubectl certificate approve
⑤
Cert issued → Dana has access!

Tenet: CertificateSigningRequests are the mechanism for both nodes AND users to obtain signed certificates from the cluster CA. kube-controller-manager's built-in csrapproving controller auto-approves exactly two patterns, both scoped to NODES only: node-bootstrap client CSRs (kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet, from system:bootstrappers, via kubeadm:node-autoapprove-bootstrap) and kubelet CLIENT-cert renewal/rotation from an already-registered node (same signer, self-requested by system:nodes, via kubeadm:node-autoapprove-certificate-rotation). Kubelet SERVING-cert CSRs are NOT auto-approved by this controller. Everything else — including any arbitrary human user's client-auth CSR — is ALWAYS manual. The workflow: (1) kubectl get csr — find Pending CSRs, (2) kubectl certificate approve <csr-name> — approve it, (3) The API server issues a signed cert, (4) extract it into a kubeconfig. On CKA: know exactly which CSR patterns are auto-approved vs. always manual.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get csr NAME AGE SIGNERNAME REQUESTOR CONDITION dana-access 5m kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client admin Pending ← NOT APPROVED!
$ kubectl get csr dana-access -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' ← EMPTY! No certificate issued yet.
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get csr NAME AGE SIGNERNAME REQUESTOR CONDITION dana-access 6m kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client admin Approved,Issued ✅
$ kubectl get csr dana-access -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > /tmp/dana.crt ✅ Certificate extracted — ready to build Dana's kubeconfig!
5

🔧 Fix — Approve the Pending CSR

BASH — Approve CSR and verify node becomes Ready 
# Step 1: List all Pending CSRs
kubectl get csr

# Step 2: Review, then approve the specific CSR
kubectl certificate approve dana-access

# Step 3: Verify CSR is now Approved,Issued
kubectl get csr dana-access

# Step 4: Extract the issued certificate and build Dana's kubeconfig
kubectl get csr dana-access -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > /tmp/dana.crt
kubectl config set-credentials dana --client-certificate=/tmp/dana.crt --client-key=/tmp/dana.key --embed-certs=true
kubectl config set-context dana-context --cluster=$(kubectl config current-context) --user=dana

# Step 5: Approve ALL pending CSRs (bulk operation) — use with caution, only after reviewing each one
# kubectl get csr -o name | xargs kubectl certificate approve
6

✅ Verify — CSR Approved, Dana Has Cluster Access

The CSR shows CONDITION: Approved,Issued. Dana's certificate is extracted and wired into a kubeconfig context. Key commands: kubectl get csr (find Pending), kubectl certificate approve <name> (approve), kubectl certificate deny <name> (reject). Remember: auto-approval only ever applies to node-scoped signers — bootstrap AND client-cert renewal, both self-requested by an already-trusted node identity — a real node join via a valid kubeadm token IS auto-approved via kubeadm's own ClusterRoleBinding, but any human user's CSR is always manual by design. On CKA: know exactly which CSR patterns are auto-approved vs. always manual.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Delete Approved CSR

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete the approved CSR (approved CSRs auto-delete eventually) and Dana's kubeconfig context
kubectl delete csr dana-access 2>/dev/null
kubectl config delete-context dana-context 2>/dev/null
kubectl config delete-user dana 2>/dev/null
rm -f /tmp/dana.key /tmp/dana.csr /tmp/dana.crt
S70
🧪 SCENARIO S70 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture kubeconfig

kubectl Commands Go to Wrong Cluster — current-context Points to Production

The Problem: You have 6 Kubernetes clusters managed by ksw. You run kubectl delete namespace easypj thinking you're on the dev cluster — but your current-context is pointing to the PRODUCTION kubeadm cluster. You just deleted the production easypj namespace! Your job: craft a merged kubeconfig file, verify current-context before every destructive command, and create a safe workflow with explicit context switching.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → ALL — Multi-cluster: kubeadm + 4 kind + minikube
1

📋 Wrong Current-Context — Accidentally Targeting Production (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: 11:30 PM — You're working late deploying a test easypj instance to the dev cluster. You type kubectl delete namespace easypj --force to clean up a failed test. 3 seconds later, PagerDuty explodes — the production easypj namespace is GONE. Your current-context was pointing to kubeadm (production), not kind-cka-lab (dev). You deleted 50,000 job listings, 10,000 users, and all applications in ONE command. The company just lost 6 months of data. The restore will take hours.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S70): 
multi-kubeconfig/
├── 01-check-current-context.sh     ← kubectl config current-context (SHOWS WRONG CLUSTER!)
├── 02-list-all-contexts.sh         ← kubectl config get-contexts
├── 03-safe-context-switch.sh       ← kubectl config use-context + verify
└── 04-merged-kubeconfig.yaml       ← Combined kubeconfig with all 6 clusters
BASH — Diagnose wrong current-context and learn safe practices 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S70: Multi-Cluster kubeconfig — Wrong Context
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Check what cluster you're CURRENTLY targeting!
kubectl config current-context
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# kubernetes-admin@kubernetes   ← THIS IS PRODUCTION KUBEADM!
# You THOUGHT you were on kind-cka-lab!

# STEP 2: List all available contexts
kubectl config get-contexts
# CURRENT   NAME                            CLUSTER
# *         kubernetes-admin@kubernetes      kubernetes          ← PRODUCTION!
#           kind-cka-lab                     kind-cka-lab        ← dev
#           kind-cl1                         kind-cl1            ← test
#           kind-cl2                         kind-cl2            ← staging
#           kind-cl3                         kind-cl3            ← multi
#           minikube                         minikube            ← local

# STEP 3: THE DANGEROUS DEMO — Prove you're on the WRONG cluster (SAFE test!)
# NEVER actually delete anything! Use a safe diagnostic instead:
kubectl cluster-info
# ❌ BUG! Output shows:
# Kubernetes control plane is running at https://192.168.1.100:6443
# This is the PRODUCTION kubeadm cluster, NOT kind-cka-lab!

# Confirm by checking node names:
kubectl get nodes
# ❌ BUG! Shows "easy" (kubeadm production) instead of "cp,wk1,wk2" (kind dev)!

# If you had run: kubectl delete namespace easypj --force
# It would have hit PRODUCTION, not dev. This is how outages happen.

# STEP 4: Check which namespace is set
kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace
# namespace: default   ← You didn't even set a namespace context!

# The APP STORY:
# 11:30 PM — Slack: "Production is DOWN!"
# You check kubectl and realize your current-context was production.
# You just deleted the ENTIRE easypj namespace in production.
# The CEO is calling. The outage will cost $50,000+.
# This is why you ALWAYS check current-context before destructive commands.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Current-Context Points to Wrong Cluster

✗1. kubectl config current-context → kubernetes-admin@kubernetes (PRODUCTION, not dev!)
✗2. You THOUGHT you were on kind-cka-lab — context mismatch between intent and reality!
✗3. Destructive commands run on WRONG cluster — production data at risk!
✗4. No context verification before running kubectl commands — operator error!
3

🔍 Debug — How to Safely Manage Multiple Clusters

1Check all contexts: kubectl config get-contexts
→ Shows current context marked with * — always verify before commands!
2View full kubeconfig: kubectl config view
→ Shows clusters:, users:, contexts: — the triple mapping
3Understand kubeconfig structure: A kubeconfig has 3 sections: (a) clusters: — API server URLs + CA certs, (b) users: — credentials (certs/tokens), (c) contexts: — combinations of cluster + user + namespace. current-context selects which context is active. Switch with kubectl config use-context <name>.
4Root cause: No context verification before running destructive commands. The operator assumed they were on the dev cluster but the current-context pointed to production. Fix: (1) ALWAYS run 'kubectl config current-context' before destructive commands, (2) set namespace per context, (3) use different terminal colors/prompts for production, (4) use ksw for explicit cluster switching, (5) consider using separate kubeconfig files per cluster with KUBECONFIG env var.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Check current-context FIRST
②
Wrong cluster → STOP!
③
kubectl config use-context
④
Set namespace per context
⑤
Safe operations → no disasters!

Tenet: The #1 cause of production disasters in multi-cluster environments is wrong current-context. ALWAYS run kubectl config current-context before ANY destructive command (delete, drain, scale-down). Best practices: (1) use ksw for explicit cluster switching, (2) set namespace per context: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev, (3) use separate kubeconfig files per cluster, (4) add a shell prompt indicator showing current cluster. On CKA: you'll work with multiple clusters — context management is essential.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl config current-context kubernetes-admin@kubernetes ← PRODUCTION! Expected: kind-cka-lab!
$ kubectl config get-contexts CURRENT NAME CLUSTER NAMESPACE * kubernetes-admin@kubernetes kubernetes kind-cka-lab kind-cka-lab ← Dev cluster, NOT active!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl config use-context kind-cka-lab Switched to context "kind-cka-lab". ✅ NOW ON DEV CLUSTER!
$ kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev Context "kind-cka-lab" modified. ✅ NAMESPACE SET!
5

🔧 Fix — Safe Context Management Workflow

BASH — Set up safe multi-cluster workflow 
# Step 1: ALWAYS verify current context before commands
kubectl config current-context

# Step 2: Explicitly switch to the correct context
kubectl config use-context kind-cka-lab

# Step 3: Set a namespace for the context (safety net!)
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev

# Step 4: Verify the switch
kubectl config get-contexts | grep "^\*"

# Step 5: Use ksw as the primary switching tool
# ksw → choose 2 (kind-cka-lab) → automatically sets context

# Step 6: BONUS — Add current context to shell prompt (add to ~/.bashrc)
# PS1='[\$(kubectl config current-context 2>/dev/null || echo "none")] \u@\h:\w\$ '
6

✅ Verify — Correct Context, Safe Operations

kubectl config current-context shows kind-cka-lab. Namespace is set to easypj-dev. Key practices: (1) VERIFY context before every destructive command, (2) use ksw for explicit cluster switching, (3) set namespace per context, (4) never run delete/scale-down without checking current-context first. A 2-second check prevents 2-hour outages.

7

🧹 Cleanup — Restore Default Context

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Restore to production context (or use ksw)
kubectl config use-context kubernetes-admin@kubernetes
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=default
kubectl config current-context

📌 S71–S75: Helm, Kustomize & CRDs

S71
🧪 SCENARIO S71 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture Helm Install

Helm Install Fails with ImagePullBackOff — Wrong Image Tag in values.yaml

The Problem: You package the easypj application as a Helm chart and install it. The install completes but pods go straight to ImagePullBackOff. The values.yaml file has the image tag set to "1.99-beta" — a tag that doesn't exist in the registry. Helm rendered the template correctly, but the wrong tag prevents the pod from pulling the image. Your job: debug the Helm release, identify the wrong image tag, fix values.yaml, and upgrade the release.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Create Helm Chart with Wrong Image Tag (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj DevOps team decides to standardize deployments using Helm. They create a chart for the easypj-api deployment. The first install goes through — helm install reports success. But the pods never start — ImagePullBackOff. The values.yaml specifies image tag "1.99-beta" which doesn't exist in the registry. A simple tag typo means the entire API is DOWN.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S71): 
helm-chart/
├── Chart.yaml                      ← name: easypj-api, version: 1.0.0
├── values.yaml                     ← BUG: image tag "1.99-beta" (DOESN'T EXIST!)
└── templates/
    └── deployment.yaml             ← Go template: image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
BASH — Create broken Helm chart and install 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S71: Helm Install — Wrong Image Tag
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create Chart.yaml
mkdir -p ~/easypj-chart/templates
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: easypj-api
description: easypj job board API
version: 1.0.0
appVersion: "2.0"
EOF

# STEP 2: Create values.yaml with WRONG tag (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-chart/values.yaml
image:
  repository: nginx
  tag: 1.99-beta    # ❌ BUG! nginx:1.99-beta does NOT exist!
replicaCount: 1
EOF

# STEP 3: Create deployment template
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF

# STEP 4: Install the chart — helm says SUCCESS but pods fail!
helm install easypj-api ~/easypj-chart
kubectl get pods
# ❌ BUG! ImagePullBackOff — nginx:1.99-beta doesn't exist!
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Pods in ImagePullBackOff After Helm Install

✗1. kubectl get pods → ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull
✗2. helm list → Release shows "deployed" — helm thinks everything is OK!
✗3. helm get values easypj-api → shows tag: 1.99-beta (WRONG!)
✗4. Helm install succeeded but application is DOWN — silent failure!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is the Helm Release Broken?

1Check release values: helm get values easypj-api
→ image.tag: "1.99-beta" — this tag doesn't exist in the registry!
2Check deployed pod: kubectl describe pod -l app=easypj-api
→ "Failed to pull image nginx:1.99-beta: manifest for nginx:1.99-beta not found"
3Helm doesn't validate image existence: Helm only validates YAML syntax and template rendering. It does NOT verify that images exist in registries. The release can deploy "successfully" with non-existent images.
→ Helm deployment success ≠ application is running!
4Root cause: values.yaml has an incorrect image tag that doesn't exist in the container registry. Helm rendered the template correctly but the resulting Deployment references a non-existent image. Fix: update values.yaml with the correct tag (e.g., nginx:alpine) and run 'helm upgrade easypj-api ~/easypj-chart' to apply the new values.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Helm deployed → pods failing
②
describe pod → ImagePullBackOff
③
helm get values → wrong tag!
④
Fix values.yaml → helm upgrade
⑤
Pods running → app healthy!

Tenet: Helm validates templates but NOT container image existence. A successful helm install does not guarantee a running application. Always verify: (1) helm list → check status, (2) kubectl get pods → check actual pod state, (3) helm get values → verify rendered values. For image validation: use helm template to preview manifests before installing. On CKA: Helm chart creation and debugging is a common exam task.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-api-7d8f9-abc 0/1 ImagePullBackOff 0 ← BROKEN!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS easypj-api-9e0f1-xyz 1/1 Running 0 ← FIXED!
5

🔧 Fix — Update values.yaml + helm upgrade

BASH — Fix image tag and upgrade release
# Option 1: Fix values.yaml and upgrade
sed -i 's/tag: 1.99-beta/tag: alpine/' ~/easypj-chart/values.yaml
helm upgrade easypj-api ~/easypj-chart
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api --timeout=60s

# Option 2: Override value directly (CKA fast method)
helm upgrade easypj-api ~/easypj-chart --set image.tag=alpine
6

✅ Verify — Pods Running with Correct Image

helm get values easypj-api shows correct tag. Pods are Running. Key: Helm deploy success ≠ app running. Always verify pod status after install/upgrade.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH
helm uninstall easypj-api
rm -rf ~/easypj-chart

🧪 SCENARIO S72 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture Helm Rollback

Helm Upgrade to v3 Broke the App — Must Rollback to v2 Immediately

The Problem: You upgrade the easypj-api Helm release from revision 1 (v2/working) to revision 2 (v3/broken). The new version has a critical bug — the API returns 500 errors on every request. Users are seeing blank pages. You need to rollback to the previous working revision. Your job: check helm history, identify the broken revision, and rollback to the last working version using helm rollback.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Install v2 (working), then upgrade to v3 (broken) (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team deploys v2 of the API via Helm — everything works. Confident, they upgrade to v3. Within minutes, PagerDuty fires: "API error rate is 100%." v3 introduced a DB connection bug. Every request returns HTTP 500. 5,000 employers can't post jobs. The only fix is an immediate rollback to v2. Every second of downtime costs real money.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S72): 
helm-rollback/
├── 01-install-v2-working.sh        ← helm install revision 1 (nginx:alpine = WORKING)
├── 02-upgrade-v3-broken.sh         ← helm upgrade revision 2 (nginx:9.9.9-broken = BROKEN!)
├── 03-check-history.sh             ← helm history → show both revisions
└── 04-rollback-to-v2-fix.sh        ← helm rollback api-v2 1 → restore working version
BASH — Simulate install v2, upgrade to broken v3, rollback
# STEP 1: Create a local chart for the demo
mkdir -p ~/helm-rollback-chart/templates
cat << 'EOF' > ~/helm-rollback-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: api
version: 1.0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > ~/helm-rollback-chart/values.yaml
image:
  repository: nginx
  tag: alpine
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > ~/helm-rollback-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
EOF

# STEP 2: Install v2 (working — correct image tag)
helm install api-v2 ~/helm-rollback-chart --set image.tag=alpine
kubectl get pods
# ✅ Pod Running — Revision 1 is WORKING

# STEP 3: "Upgrade" to v3 (BROKEN — fake image tag)
helm upgrade api-v2 ~/helm-rollback-chart --set image.tag=9.9.9-broken
# ❌ BUG! Pods enter ImagePullBackOff — v3 is BROKEN!

# STEP 4: Check revision history
helm history api-v2
# REVISION  UPDATED                  STATUS      DESCRIPTION
# 1         Thu Jun 04 10:00 2026    superseded  Install complete (v2 WORKING)
# 2         Thu Jun 04 10:05 2026    deployed    Upgrade complete (v3 BROKEN!)
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — v3 Upgrade Broke the Application

✗1. helm history api-v2 → Revision 2 = BROKEN!
✗2. kubectl get pods → ImagePullBackOff after upgrade
✗3. Application returns errors — users affected!
✗4. Need immediate rollback to Revision 1!
3

🔍 Debug — Identify Broken Revision and Rollback

1Check history: helm history api-v2 -n easypj
→ Revision 2 is deployed (BROKEN), Revision 1 was working
2Check current values: helm get values api-v2 -n easypj
→ Shows the broken tag — confirms what went wrong
3Root cause: helm upgrade deployed a broken image tag. Helm stores each release revision as a Secret in the namespace. Rollback re-deploys the previous revision's manifest. Fix: 'helm rollback api-v2 1 -n easypj' to restore Revision 1 (the working v2 deployment).
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Upgrade broke app → check history
②
Rev 2 broken, Rev 1 working
③
helm rollback api-v2 1
④
Rev 3 created (copy of Rev 1)
⑤
App restored → users back!

Tenet: Helm rollback creates a NEW revision that's a copy of the target revision. Rolling back to rev 1 creates rev 3 (a copy of rev 1). Helm stores each revision as a Secret. helm history shows all revisions. On CKA: helm rollback is a key recovery command.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS api-v2-7d8f9-abc 0/1 ImagePullBackOff 0 ← BROKEN!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS api-v2-9e0f1-xyz 1/1 Running 0 ← ROLLED BACK!
5

🔧 Fix — Rollback to Working Revision

BASH — Helm rollback to last working version
# Step 1: Check revision history
helm history api-v2

# Step 2: Rollback to Revision 1
helm rollback api-v2 1

# Step 3: Verify pods are healthy
kubectl get pods
kubectl rollout status deploy/api-v2 --timeout=60s
6

✅ Verify — Application Restored to v2

Pods are Running 1/1. helm history shows Revision 3 (Rolled back to 1). Helm rollback = instant recovery. Key: helm rollback RELEASE REVISION.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH
helm uninstall api-v2
rm -rf ~/helm-rollback-chart
S73
🧪 SCENARIO S73 — Category 4: Cluster Architecture Kustomize Overlay

Security Leak — Dev Overlay Uses Production Database Password

The Problem: You create Kustomize overlays for dev, staging, and production. But the dev overlay accidentally references the production database password Secret. Developers can now connect to the production database from the dev namespace — a critical security leak. Your job: find the leaked production password in the dev overlay, isolate it, and ensure each environment uses its own credentials.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create Kustomize Overlays — Dev Leaks Prod Password (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team adopts Kustomize for environment management. They create base/ + overlays/dev/ + overlays/staging/ + overlays/prod/. Everything deploys correctly. But a security audit reveals: the dev overlay references the same DB_PASSWORD Secret as production! Any developer can read the prod DB password. Even worse, the dev pods connect to the production PostgreSQL — test data is being written to the prod database. This is a P0 security incident.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S73): 
kustomize-envs/
├── base/
│   ├── deployment.yaml             ← Base: image placeholder, env from secretRef
│   └── kustomization.yaml          ← Resources: deployment.yaml
├── overlays/
│   ├── dev/
│   │   ├── kustomization.yaml      ← BUG: secretGenerator uses PROD password!
│   │   └── env-patch.yaml          ← Wrong DB_HOST=prod-db.easypj-prod.svc
│   ├── staging/
│   │   └── kustomization.yaml      ← Staging: correct staging credentials
│   └── prod/
│       └── kustomization.yaml       ← Production: correct prod credentials
BASH — Create Kustomize base + overlays with the security bug
# STEP 1: Create base deployment
mkdir -p ~/kustomize-demo/{base,overlays/{dev,staging,prod}}
cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/base/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-creds
              key: password
        - name: DB_HOST
          value: PLACEHOLDER
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/base/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- deployment.yaml
EOF

# STEP 2: Dev overlay with PRODUCTION password (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../../base
secretGenerator:
- name: db-creds
  literals:
  - password=prod-super-secret-password-1234   # ❌ BUG! PRODUCTION PASSWORD IN DEV!
patches:
- path: env-patch.yaml
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/env-patch.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        env:
        - name: DB_HOST
          value: prod-db.easypj-prod.svc   # ❌ BUG! DEV POINTS TO PROD DB!
EOF

# STEP 2b: For comparison, staging and prod overlays with their OWN correct credentials
cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../../base
secretGenerator:
- name: db-creds
  literals:
  - password=staging-only-password-5678
EOF

cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../../base
secretGenerator:
- name: db-creds
  literals:
  - password=prod-super-secret-password-1234
EOF

# STEP 3: Build and check what the dev overlay generates
kubectl kustomize ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/ | grep -A2 password
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Dev Uses Production Credentials

✗1. kubectl kustomize overlays/dev/ → Shows prod-super-secret-password-1234!
✗2. Dev overlay DB_HOST = prod-db.easypj-prod.svc — points to PROD!
✗3. Any developer can read the production password from the overlay files!
✗4. Dev pods writing test data to PRODUCTION database — data corruption!
3

🔍 Debug — Find the Leaked Credentials

1Build dev overlay: kubectl kustomize overlays/dev/ | grep password
→ "prod-super-secret-password-1234" — PRODUCTION password visible!
2Check DB_HOST: kubectl kustomize overlays/dev/ | grep DB_HOST
→ "prod-db.easypj-prod.svc" — connecting to PRODUCTION database!
3Root cause: The dev overlay's secretGenerator contains the production database password, and the env-patch points DB_HOST to the production database Service. Fix: (1) create separate credentials for dev, (2) point DB_HOST to the dev database Service, (3) use Kustomize's namePrefix or nameSuffix to create environment-specific resource names.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubectl kustomize → inspect output
②
Prod password visible in dev!
③
DB_HOST points to production
④
Fix dev overlay credentials
⑤
Isolated environments → secure!

Tenet: Kustomize overlays must NEVER share secrets across environments. Each overlay should have its own secretGenerator with environment-specific credentials. Always use kubectl kustomize to preview the rendered output before applying. Check for leaked credentials by grepping the output. On CKA: Kustomize overlay management is a common exam task.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl kustomize ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/ | grep password password: prod-super-secret-password-1234 ← PROD PASSWORD LEAKED IN DEV!
$ kubectl kustomize ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/ | grep DB_HOST - name: DB_HOST value: prod-db.easypj-prod.svc ← DEV POINTS TO PRODUCTION DATABASE!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl kustomize ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/ | grep password password: dev-password-only-for-dev ← DEV-ONLY PASSWORD!
$ kubectl kustomize ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/ | grep DB_HOST value: dev-db.easypj-dev.svc ← DEV DATABASE — ISOLATED!
5

🔧 Fix — Isolate Dev Credentials

BASH — Fix dev overlay with isolated credentials
# Fix secretGenerator to use DEV credentials
cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../../base
namePrefix: dev-
secretGenerator:
- name: db-creds
  literals:
  - password=dev-password-only-for-dev  # ✅ Fixed: DEV-only password
patches:
- path: env-patch.yaml
EOF

# Fix env-patch to use DEV database
cat << 'EOF' > ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/env-patch.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        env:
        - name: DB_HOST
          value: dev-db.easypj-dev.svc   # ✅ Fixed: DEV database
EOF

# Verify the fix
kubectl kustomize ~/kustomize-demo/overlays/dev/ | grep -E "password|DB_HOST"
6

✅ Verify — Dev Isolated from Production

Dev overlay now uses dev-specific credentials and dev DB host. Key: always use kubectl kustomize to preview before applying. Each overlay should have its own secretGenerator.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH
rm -rf ~/kustomize-demo
