🧪 SCENARIO S85 — Category 5: Services & Networking ExternalName

ExternalName Service CNAME Points to Wrong RDS Endpoint — Connection Refused

The Problem: The easypj-api pod needs to connect to an external Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database. You create an ExternalName Service to create a DNS CNAME alias — so pods can use easypj-db-ext instead of the long RDS endpoint. But the CNAME points to wrong-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com — a hostname that doesn't exist (typo in the endpoint). Pods get "connection refused" because DNS resolves to nothing. Your job: find the wrong ExternalName target, fix it to the correct RDS endpoint, and verify connectivity from a pod.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Create ExternalName Service with WRONG CNAME Target (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team migrates their PostgreSQL to AWS RDS. The API pods need to connect to the new database. Instead of hardcoding the long RDS endpoint in every pod, the DevOps lead creates an ExternalName Service as a clean DNS alias. They test with psql -h easypj-db-ext and get "could not translate host name." The ExternalName target has a typo — wrong-rds vs prod-rds. The entire API layer can't reach the database. Job postings, user logins, search — ALL DOWN because of one wrong character in the CNAME.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S85): 
externalname-service/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-ext
├── 02-externalname-broken.yaml    ← ExternalName with BUG: CNAME typo!
├── 03-test-pod.yaml               ← Busybox pod to test DNS resolution
└── 04-externalname-fixed.yaml     ← Correct CNAME target
BASH — Create ExternalName Service with typo in CNAME 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S85: ExternalName Service — Wrong CNAME Target
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace easypj-ext

# STEP 2: Create ExternalName Service with WRONG target (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-db-ext
  namespace: easypj-ext
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: wrong-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com  # ❌ BUG! TYPO! Should be "prod-rds"!
EOF

# STEP 3: Deploy a test pod to verify DNS
kubectl run test-pod -n easypj-ext --image=busybox --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/test-pod -n easypj-ext --timeout=60s

# STEP 4: Test DNS resolution — FAILS!
kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-ext -- nslookup easypj-db-ext
# ❌ BUG! "can't resolve easypj-db-ext" or resolves to a non-existent host!
# The CNAME wrong-rds... doesn't exist — DNS chain is broken!

# STEP 5: Try to "connect" to the database — FAILS!
kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-ext -- wget -O- --timeout=3 http://easypj-db-ext:5432 2>&1
# ❌ "bad address" or "Name or service not known"

# The APP STORY:
# "The API can't connect to the database — all requests failing!"
# The ExternalName Service was created to abstract the RDS endpoint.
# But the CNAME has a typo: "wrong-rds" instead of "prod-rds".
# DNS resolution fails silently — pods can't reach the database.
# 500 Internal Server Error on every API endpoint.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — DNS Resolution Fails for ExternalName Service

✗1. nslookup easypj-db-ext from pod → "can't resolve" or wrong address!
✗2. kubectl get svc easypj-db-ext -n easypj-ext → Shows externalName but it's WRONG!
✗3. The CNAME target "wrong-rds..." doesn't actually exist — typo in the endpoint!
✗4. API pods can't reach RDS — every database operation FAILS with connection errors!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Can't Pods Reach the External Database?

1Check ExternalName target: kubectl get svc easypj-db-ext -n easypj-ext -o yaml | grep externalName
→ externalName: wrong-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com — TYPO in hostname!
2Test DNS chain: kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-ext -- nslookup wrong-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
→ "server can't find wrong-rds..." — the RDS endpoint doesn't exist with this name!
3Understand ExternalName: ExternalName Services don't use selectors or endpoints. They create a CNAME DNS record pointing to the externalName field. CoreDNS returns this CNAME, and the pod's DNS resolver follows it to the final IP. If the externalName is wrong or unresolvable, the DNS chain breaks and the pod gets "NXDOMAIN" or "SERVFAIL."
4Root cause: The ExternalName Service's externalName field has a typo: "wrong-rds" instead of the correct RDS endpoint. CoreDNS faithfully returns this as a CNAME, but since the target hostname doesn't exist, DNS resolution fails entirely. Fix: update the ExternalName Service with the correct RDS endpoint. NOTE: externalName field CAN be patched (unlike clusterIP).
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
DB connection fails → check Service
②
ExternalName → check externalName field
③
CNAME target has TYPO!
④
Patch ExternalName → correct endpoint
⑤
DNS resolves → DB connection works!

Tenet: ExternalName Services create CNAME DNS records without any selectors or endpoints. They're purely DNS aliases. Use cases: (1) abstracting external database endpoints so pods use a friendly name, (2) cross-namespace service access (Service in ns-a can ExternalName to Service in ns-b), (3) federated services across clusters. On CKA: ExternalName is a lesser-known Service type but can appear in exam scenarios.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-ext -- nslookup easypj-db-ext Server: 10.96.0.10 Address: 10.96.0.10:53 ** server can't find easypj-db-ext: NXDOMAIN ← CNAME TARGET DOESN'T EXIST!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-ext -- nslookup easypj-db-ext easypj-db-ext.easypj-ext.svc.cluster.local canonical name = prod-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com Name: prod-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com Address: 10.0.1.50 ← CORRECT RDS IP RESOLVED!
5

🔧 Fix — Patch ExternalName with Correct Target

BASH — Fix the ExternalName CNAME target 
# Option 1: Patch the externalName (CKA fast method)
kubectl patch svc easypj-db-ext -n easypj-ext --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/externalName","value":"prod-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com"}]'

# Option 2: Delete and recreate (if patch fails)
kubectl delete svc easypj-db-ext -n easypj-ext
kubectl create service externalname easypj-db-ext -n easypj-ext \
  --external-name=prod-rds.abcdef.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com

# Verify DNS resolves correctly
kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-ext -- nslookup easypj-db-ext
6

✅ Verify — ExternalName Resolves to Correct RDS Endpoint

nslookup easypj-db-ext returns the correct RDS CNAME. Key: ExternalName creates a pure DNS CNAME — no selectors, no endpoints, no ClusterIP. The externalName field can be patched (unlike clusterIP). Use for external service abstraction and cross-namespace DNS aliases.

S86
🧪 SCENARIO S86 — Category 5: Services & Networking CoreDNS

CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff — Corefile ConfigMap Has YAML Syntax Error

The Problem: After editing the CoreDNS ConfigMap to add a custom stub domain, ALL CoreDNS pods go into CrashLoopBackOff. DNS resolution is DOWN cluster-wide — no Services resolve, no pods can communicate. The edit introduced a syntax error in the Corefile — a missing closing brace } in the stub domain block. CoreDNS fails to parse the config and crashes on startup. Your job: find the syntax error in the Corefile, fix it, and restore DNS for the entire cluster.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — CKA exam practice cluster
1

📋 Edit CoreDNS ConfigMap with Syntax Error in Corefile (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj network team wants to add a stub domain for internal corporate services (*.corp.easypj.com). They edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap to add a forward block for the corporate DNS server at 10.0.0.53. They save the ConfigMap. Within 30 seconds, CoreDNS pods crash. ALL DNS resolution stops. New pods can't start because they can't resolve image-registry hostnames, and every in-cluster service-to-service call by hostname fails — kubectl itself still works fine against the API server (that talks to etcd directly, not CoreDNS), but the applications running IN the cluster are effectively DEAD. One missing closing brace in the Corefile brought down the whole cluster's service discovery.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S86): 
coredns-crash/
├── 01-backup-corefile.sh          ← kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml > backup
├── 02-broken-coredns-cm.yaml      ← ConfigMap with BUG: missing } in stub block!
├── 03-coredns-crashloop.sh        ← kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns
└── 04-fixed-corefile.yaml         ← Correct Corefile with proper brace closure
BASH — Break CoreDNS with syntax error in Corefile 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S86: CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff — Corefile Syntax Error
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Check current CoreDNS status (healthy)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns
# coredns-xxx   1/1     Running   0   7d

# STEP 2: View current Corefile
kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.Corefile}'
# .:53 {
#     errors
#     health
#     kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
#        pods insecure
#        fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
#     }
#     prometheus :9153
#     forward . /etc/resolv.conf
#     cache 30
#     loop
#     reload
#     loadbalance
# }

# STEP 3: Edit the REAL "coredns" ConfigMap with a BROKEN Corefile (THE BUG!)
# Add stub domain but FORGET the closing brace! (this MUST target the actual "coredns"
# ConfigMap that the coredns Deployment mounts — a differently-named ConfigMap would
# never be read by CoreDNS at all, and wouldn't reproduce this bug)
kubectl create cm coredns -n kube-system --from-literal=Corefile='.:53 {
    errors
    health
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
       pods insecure
       fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
    loadbalance
    # ❌ BUG! Missing closing } for stub domain block!
    corp.easypj.com:53 {
        forward . 10.0.0.53
    # ❌ BUG! Missing } here! CoreDNS can't parse this!
' --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -

# STEP 4: Restart CoreDNS to pick up broken config
kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system

# STEP 5: Watch CoreDNS crash!
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -w | grep coredns
# ❌ BUG! CoreDNS pods go from Running → CrashLoopBackOff!

# The APP STORY:
# "EVERYTHING IS DOWN! kubectl commands are hanging!"
# CoreDNS crashed because of a missing } in the Corefile.
# Without DNS: Services don't resolve, pods can't communicate.
# The cluster is effectively dead — all because of one missing brace.
# CoreDNS logs show: "plugin/forward: 'corp.easypj.com' is not closed"
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff, DNS Dead

✗1. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns → CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/coredns → "is not closed" / "unexpected token"
✗3. nslookup kubernetes.default → "server can't find" — DNS is DEAD!
✗4. kubectl itself still works fine (talks to the API server, which reads directly from etcd) — but every in-cluster app that resolves Service names by hostname is effectively OFFLINE!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is CoreDNS Crashing?

1Check CoreDNS logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/coredns --tail=20
→ "plugin/forward: 'corp.easypj.com' is not closed" — SYNTAX ERROR!
2Check ConfigMap: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A20 Corefile
→ The stub domain block is missing its closing brace } — unclosed block!
3Understand Corefile syntax: Corefile uses a curly-brace block structure similar to nginx config. Each plugin block must be closed with }. A missing brace makes the entire file unparseable. CoreDNS validates the config at startup — if invalid, it exits immediately, causing CrashLoopBackOff.
4Root cause: The CoreDNS ConfigMap was edited to add a stub domain block for corp.easypj.com, but the closing } was forgotten. CoreDNS parses the Corefile at startup and exits with a fatal error when the syntax is invalid. Fix: (1) restore the ConfigMap from backup, or (2) edit the Corefile to add the missing closing brace, then restart CoreDNS.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
DNS dead → check CoreDNS pods
②
CrashLoopBackOff → check logs
③
"is not closed" → Corefile syntax
④
Fix closing brace → restart CoreDNS
⑤
DNS restored → cluster healthy!

Tenet: CoreDNS is the DNS brain of Kubernetes. If CoreDNS crashes, ALL service discovery stops. The Corefile is stored in a ConfigMap — editing it incorrectly is one of the fastest ways to take down a cluster. ALWAYS backup the ConfigMap before editing: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml > backup.yaml. On CKA: CoreDNS troubleshooting (check logs, verify ConfigMap, ensure Corefile syntax) is a high-frequency exam topic.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns coredns-7d8f9-abc 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 5 (30s ago) 2m ← CRASHED!
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/coredns --tail=5 plugin/forward: 'corp.easypj.com' on line 12 is not closed CoreDNS-1.11.1 linux/amd64 ← FATAL SYNTAX ERROR!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns coredns-9e0f1-xyz 1/1 Running 0 30s ← RESTORED!
$ nslookup kubernetes.default Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local Address: 10.96.0.1 ← DNS IS WORKING!
5

🔧 Fix — Restore CoreDNS ConfigMap + Restart

BASH — Fix the Corefile and restore CoreDNS 
# Step 1: Edit the ConfigMap to fix the Corefile
# Add the missing closing brace } after the stub domain block
kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system
# OR: restore from a known-good backup
# kubectl apply -f coredns-backup.yaml

# Step 2: Restart CoreDNS to reload the fixed config
kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system

# Step 3: Verify CoreDNS pods are Running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep coredns

# Step 4: Test DNS resolution
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup kubernetes.default
6

✅ Verify — CoreDNS Running, DNS Resolution Restored

CoreDNS pods are Running 1/1. nslookup kubernetes.default resolves correctly. Key: always backup the CoreDNS ConfigMap before editing. A syntax error in the Corefile takes down DNS for the ENTIRE cluster. The Corefile uses curly-brace blocks — every opening { must have a closing }.

S87
🧪 SCENARIO S87 — Category 5: Services & Networking DNS ndots

External DNS Lookups Are Extremely Slow — ndots:5 Generates 5 Queries Per Hostname

The Problem: The easypj-api pod makes HTTP calls to external services like api.github.com and auth.google.com. Every DNS lookup takes 2-3 seconds because ndots:5 in the pod's /etc/resolv.conf causes Kubernetes DNS to try 5 search domain variations before trying the absolute domain. For api.github.com, CoreDNS receives queries for: api.github.com.easypj.svc.cluster.local, api.github.com.svc.cluster.local, api.github.com.cluster.local, api.github.com (4 queries!). Your job: identify the ndots performance issue, understand the DNS search path, and fix the pod's dnsConfig to optimize external DNS resolution.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Default ndots:5 — External DNS Crawls (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj API team starts integrating with GitHub OAuth and Google SSO. They deploy the integration, but response times are terrible — 3 seconds per API call. Profiling reveals the bottleneck: DNS resolution. Every external hostname lookup generates 4-5 DNS queries because ndots:5 (the default) causes the resolver to try every search domain for names with fewer than 5 dots. The API makes 200 external DNS calls per page load. 200 × 5 queries = 1,000 DNS requests per second to CoreDNS. CoreDNS CPU is pegged at 95%. User logins timeout. OAuth fails.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S87): 
dns-ndots/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-dns
├── 02-pod-default-ndots.yaml      ← Pod with BUG: no dnsConfig → ndots:5 (default)
├── 03-test-dns-resolution.sh      ← nslookup to show search domain cascade
└── 04-pod-fixed-ndots.yaml        ← Pod with dnsConfig ndots:1 → single query
BASH — Demonstrate the ndots:5 DNS query explosion 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S87: DNS ndots:5 — Excessive Queries
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace easypj-dns

# STEP 2: Deploy pod with DEFAULT ndots:5 (THE BUG!)
kubectl run api-pod -n easypj-dns --image=busybox --command -- sleep 3600

# STEP 3: Check the pod's /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl exec api-pod -n easypj-dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# ❌ BUG! Output shows:
# search easypj-dns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# options ndots:5    ← DEFAULT! Means: names with <5 dots get search appended!

# STEP 4: Test DNS — watch the query cascade!
kubectl exec api-pod -n easypj-dns -- nslookup api.github.com
# ❌ BUG! CoreDNS receives (check coredns logs):
# 1. api.github.com.easypj-dns.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN
# 2. api.github.com.svc.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN
# 3. api.github.com.cluster.local → NXDOMAIN
# 4. api.github.com → SUCCESS (finally!)
# 4 DNS queries for ONE hostname! 3 of them wasted!

# STEP 5: Compare with absolute (FQDN) lookup
kubectl exec api-pod -n easypj-dns -- nslookup api.github.com.
# Trailing dot = FQDN. Only 1 query needed! Much faster!

# The APP STORY:
# "Why is the GitHub OAuth login taking 5 seconds?"
# Every external API call triggers a DNS lookup cascade.
# ndots:5 + 3 search domains = up to 4 queries per hostname.
# The API makes 50+ external calls per request.
# 50 × 4 = 200 DNS queries per user request to CoreDNS.
# CoreDNS is drowning in NXDOMAIN responses for search domains.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — DNS Query Explosion for External Hostnames

✗1. cat /etc/resolv.conf → options ndots:5 + 3 search domains!
✗2. nslookup api.github.com → 4 DNS queries for 1 hostname (3 are NXDOMAIN!)
✗3. External API calls take 2-3 seconds instead of 200ms — DNS is the bottleneck!
✗4. CoreDNS overloaded — 1,000+ queries/sec, 80% are wasted NXDOMAIN responses!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Is DNS So Slow for External Hostnames?

1Check resolv.conf: kubectl exec api-pod -n easypj-dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
→ options ndots:5 — any name with <5 dots gets search domains appended!
2Count the dots: "api.github.com" has 2 dots. ndots:5 means names with less than 5 dots trigger search domain suffixing. So CoreDNS tries: api.github.com.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local, then api.github.com.svc.cluster.local, then api.github.com.cluster.local, THEN finally the absolute name.
3Root cause: ndots:5 (Kubernetes default) is optimized for internal cluster DNS (e.g., "my-service" with 0 dots gets resolved as my-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local). But for external hostnames with 2-3 dots (api.github.com), it causes 3-4 unnecessary NXDOMAIN queries before reaching the actual hostname. Fix: set ndots:1 or ndots:2 in the pod's dnsConfig to reduce search domain queries for external names, OR use FQDN (trailing dot) for external hostnames.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Slow external DNS → check resolv.conf
②
ndots:5 + search domains → query cascade
③
3 wasted NXDOMAIN per hostname
④
Set ndots:1 or use FQDNs
⑤
DNS resolves in 1 query → fast!

Tenet: ndots controls when the DNS resolver appends search domains. ndots:5 means "if hostname has <5 dots, try search domains first." For external names like api.github.com (2 dots), this triggers wasted queries. Solutions: (1) set ndots:1 via pod dnsConfig, (2) use trailing dot for FQDN (api.github.com.), (3) use dnsPolicy: None with custom resolv.conf. On CKA: ndots and DNS performance is a common troubleshooting scenario.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec api-pod -n easypj-dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf search easypj-dns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local nameserver 10.96.0.10 options ndots:5 ← DEFAULT! 3 wasted queries per external hostname!
$ time kubectl exec api-pod -n easypj-dns -- nslookup api.github.com real 0m2.347s ← 2.3 SECONDS for ONE DNS lookup!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec api-pod-fixed -n easypj-dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf options ndots:1 ← FIXED! Only 1 query for external names!
$ time kubectl exec api-pod-fixed -n easypj-dns -- nslookup api.github.com real 0m0.047s ← 47ms! 50x faster!
5

🔧 Fix — Set ndots:1 via Pod dnsConfig

BASH — Deploy pod with optimized DNS config 
# Create pod with custom ndots:1
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api-pod-fixed
  namespace: easypj-dns
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
  dnsConfig:
    options:
    - name: ndots
      value: "1"   # ← FIXED! Only 1 query for names with 1+ dots!
EOF

# Verify the fix
kubectl exec api-pod-fixed -n easypj-dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl exec api-pod-fixed -n easypj-dns -- nslookup api.github.com
6

✅ Verify — DNS Resolution Fast, Single Query Per Hostname

cat /etc/resolv.conf shows options ndots:1. External hostname lookups complete in <50ms. Key: ndots:5 (default) is optimized for internal cluster DNS. For pods making many external API calls, set ndots:1 or ndots:2. Use FQDNs with trailing dot (api.github.com.) to skip search domains entirely.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-dns

🔍 Debug — Why Can't Pods Resolve .internal Domains?

1Check CoreDNS stub config: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A5 "corp.internal"
→ forward . 10.0.0.53 — old DNS server IP! DNS server is decommissioned!
2Check if old DNS server is alive: kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-internal -- nslookup google.com 10.0.0.53
→ "connection timed out; no servers could be reached" — old server is DEAD!
3Understand stub domains: Stub domains in CoreDNS override the default forwarding for specific domain suffixes. When a pod queries *.corp.internal, CoreDNS matches the "corp.internal" stub zone and forwards the query to the configured DNS servers. If those servers are unreachable, the query fails — CoreDNS does NOT fall back to the default forwarders for stub domains.
4Root cause: The CoreDNS ConfigMap has a stub domain for corp.internal forwarding to 10.0.0.53 — the OLD corporate DNS server that was decommissioned 30 days ago. The new DNS server is at 10.0.0.54. Tenet: CoreDNS stub domains override forwarding for specific domain suffixes. The syntax: {domain}:53 { forward . {dns-server-ip} }. Stub domains do NOT fall back to default forwarders — if the configured DNS server is unreachable, queries fail. Always verify DNS server IPs are current. S89
🧪 SCENARIO S89 — Category 5: Services & Networking CoreDNS Cache

Service IP Changed but DNS Returns OLD IP for a Few Seconds — Cache TTL

The Problem: The easypj-api Service was deleted and recreated with a NEW ClusterIP (10.96.45.99 → 10.96.45.200). But pods that already cached the old answer keep resolving easypj-api to the OLD IP for a few seconds. kubeadm's default Corefile has cache 30, but that's only a CEILING on how long anything can be cached — CoreDNS's kubernetes plugin actually issues Service records with its own default record TTL of 5 seconds, and the effective staleness window is the SHORTER of the two (5s), not the 30s cap. The old Service IP no longer routes to any pod — connections hang and timeout during that window. Your job: identify the stale DNS cache, flush it by restarting CoreDNS, and understand the cache/correctness tradeoff before changing the TTL.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Delete and Recreate Service — DNS Returns Old Cached IP (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-api Service was reconfigured with new port mappings. The DevOps lead deletes the old Service and creates a new one with the same name. kubectl get svc shows the new ClusterIP (10.96.45.200). But pods keep connecting to the OLD IP (10.96.45.99). For a few seconds, some pod-to-API traffic goes to a dead IP. Health checks pass (they use pod IPs directly) but a handful of requests briefly fail. The job board shows a flicker of "API unavailable" for a few unlucky users.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S89): 
coredns-cache/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-cache
├── 02-create-service-v1.yaml      ← Original Service (gets ClusterIP 10.96.x.y)
├── 03-delete-and-recreate.yaml    ← Delete v1, recreate v2 → NEW ClusterIP!
├── 04-check-stale-dns.sh          ← nslookup shows OLD IP for a few seconds!
└── 05-flush-cache-fix.sh          ← Restart CoreDNS to flush cache
BASH — Simulate Service IP change and stale DNS cache 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S89: CoreDNS Cache — Stale DNS After IP Change
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and deploy a test pod
kubectl create namespace easypj-cache
kubectl run test-pod -n easypj-cache --image=busybox --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/test-pod -n easypj-cache --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Create a Service (v1) and check its IP
kubectl expose pod test-pod -n easypj-cache --name=easypj-api --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl get svc easypj-api -n easypj-cache
# NAME         TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)   AGE
# easypj-api   ClusterIP   10.96.45.99     <none>        80/TCP    1m

# STEP 3: Resolve the Service name — returns IP
kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-cache -- nslookup easypj-api
# easypj-api.easypj-cache.svc.cluster.local → 10.96.45.99

# STEP 4: Delete and recreate the Service (simulate migration)
kubectl delete svc easypj-api -n easypj-cache
kubectl expose pod test-pod -n easypj-cache --name=easypj-api --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl get svc easypj-api -n easypj-cache
# easypj-api   ClusterIP   10.96.45.200    <none>        80/TCP    5s   ← NEW IP!

# STEP 5: Resolve AGAIN immediately — STILL RETURNS OLD IP (within the ~5s window)!
kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-cache -- nslookup easypj-api
# ❌ BUG! Returns 10.96.45.99 (OLD IP) — CoreDNS cache NOT expired yet!
# The kubernetes plugin issues records with a 5-second TTL — that's the actual staleness
# window here, NOT the "cache 30" directive (which is only an upper CAP on cache duration)!

# The APP STORY:
# "Why is the API still down? I deployed the fix just now!"
# The new Service has a different ClusterIP, but DNS is briefly stale.
# CoreDNS cached the old A record with its 5-second record TTL.
# Pods keep connecting to 10.96.45.99 (old, dead IP) for a few seconds.
# The fix is deployed but a handful of early requests go NOWHERE.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — DNS Returns Old IP After Service Recreated

✗1. kubectl get svc easypj-api → Shows 10.96.45.200 (NEW IP)
✗2. nslookup easypj-api from pod → Returns 10.96.45.99 (OLD IP!)
✗3. The kubernetes plugin's own record TTL (5s default) governs staleness here — DNS record is stale for a few seconds, not the full 30s "cache" ceiling
✗4. Pod traffic briefly goes to a DEAD IP — service appears flaky for a few seconds despite being healthy!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Does DNS Return the Old Service IP?

1Check CoreDNS cache config: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep cache
→ "cache 30" — this is only a CEILING on how long any answer can be cached, not a guaranteed duration. The kubernetes plugin that actually serves Service records issues them with its own default record TTL of 5 seconds, and the shorter of the two numbers wins — so the real staleness window is ~5s here, not 30s.
2Understand DNS caching: CoreDNS's cache plugin honors the TTL embedded in each answer — it doesn't invent its own fixed duration or extend a short TTL up to its ceiling. When a Service is deleted and recreated with the same name, the previously-cached 5-second-TTL record simply hasn't expired yet, so a query landing within that ~5s window still returns the old IP.
3Root cause: CoreDNS's cache plugin cached the old Service ClusterIP for its record's TTL (5 seconds, from the kubernetes plugin — NOT the 30s "cache" ceiling). When the Service was deleted and recreated with a new IP, the cache kept returning the old record until that short TTL expired. Fix: (1) restart CoreDNS to flush the cache immediately, or (2) just wait out the ~5s window, or (3) use a different Service name after IP changes to avoid any cache overlap at all.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
New IP → DNS returns old → cache!
②
Check CoreDNS TTL → ~5s (not the 30s cap)
③
Cache serves stale A record
④
Restart CoreDNS → flush cache
⑤
New IP resolves → traffic restored!

Tenet: CoreDNS's cache plugin caches DNS responses for performance, but it honors each answer's own TTL — the kubernetes plugin's default record TTL (5 seconds) governs Service record staleness, NOT the Corefile's "cache 30" directive (which is only an upper ceiling on cache duration, not a fixed/extended one). After Service delete+recreate with same name, the cache may hold a stale record for that short window. Solutions: (1) restart CoreDNS (kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system) to flush immediately, (2) just wait out the ~5s window, (3) use cache 30 { servfail 10s } for negative caching. On CKA: understanding that "cache 30" is a ceiling, not a guarantee, is important for troubleshooting "Service works but DNS returns wrong IP" scenarios.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get svc easypj-api -n easypj-cache NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE easypj-api ClusterIP 10.96.45.200 <none> 80/TCP 2m ← NEW IP!
$ kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-cache -- nslookup easypj-api Name: easypj-api.easypj-cache.svc.cluster.local Address: 10.96.45.99 ← OLD IP! CACHE IS STALE!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-cache -- nslookup easypj-api Address: 10.96.45.200 ← NEW IP! CACHE FLUSHED!
5

🔧 Fix — Flush CoreDNS Cache by Restarting

BASH — Restart CoreDNS to flush stale cache 
# Step 1: Restart CoreDNS to flush ALL caches
kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system

# Step 2: Wait for CoreDNS to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/coredns -n kube-system --timeout=60s

# Step 3: Verify DNS now returns the NEW IP
kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-cache -- nslookup easypj-api

# Step 4 (optional): Reduce cache TTL in Corefile for faster propagation
# kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system → change "cache 30" to "cache 5"
6

✅ Verify — DNS Returns New ClusterIP After Cache Flush

nslookup easypj-api returns 10.96.45.200 (new IP). Key: CoreDNS caches Service DNS records for the TTL embedded in each answer. The kubernetes plugin's default record TTL is 5 seconds — that's the real staleness window, not the Corefile's "cache 30" ceiling. After Service delete+recreate, restart CoreDNS to flush stale cache immediately, or just wait out the short window. For critical Service changes, consider using different Service names to avoid cache issues entirely.

7

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-cache
S90
🧪 SCENARIO S90 — Category 5: Services & Networking NetworkPolicy

Default-Deny NetworkPolicy Blocks DNS — Pods Can't Resolve Any Hostnames

The Problem: You secure the easypj namespace with a default-deny-all Ingress NetworkPolicy — that part alone is harmless to DNS, since it doesn't touch egress at all. But you ALSO add a second, egress-restricting NetworkPolicy to allow only web→api traffic out — and that one blocks DNS, because any NetworkPolicy with policyTypes: [Egress] switches the selected pods to default-deny for ALL egress, and you forgot to explicitly allow UDP 53 to CoreDNS. Your job: identify the missing DNS egress rule, add it to the NetworkPolicy, and verify DNS and pod-to-pod communication both work.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Apply Default-Deny NetworkPolicy — DNS Gets Blocked (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj security team implements zero-trust networking. They apply a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy to the production namespace, then selectively add allow rules. After applying, the CISO reviews and approves — security is tight. But then PagerDuty explodes. The API can't reach the database. The web servers can't reach the API. Even internal Service DNS names don't resolve. The security team forgot one critical thing: DNS requires EGRESS to CoreDNS on UDP 53. Without it, pods can't resolve ANY hostname — not even kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local. The entire application is dead in the name of security.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S90): 
netpol-dns/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-secure
├── 02-web+api-pods.yaml           ← Two pods: web (label app=web), api (label app=api)
├── 03-deny-all-netpol.yaml        ← Default-deny all Ingress (BLOCKS DNS!)
├── 04-netpol-with-dns.yaml        ← Fixed: add egress rule for UDP 53 to CoreDNS
└── 05-verify-connectivity.sh      ← wget web→api, nslookup (DNS test)
BASH — Apply default-deny NetworkPolicy that kills DNS 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S90: NetworkPolicy — Default-Deny Blocks DNS
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and deploy test pods
kubectl create namespace easypj-secure
kubectl run web -n easypj-secure --image=nginx:alpine --labels=app=web
kubectl run api -n easypj-secure --image=nginx:alpine --labels=app=api
kubectl expose pod api -n easypj-secure --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web -n easypj-secure --timeout=60s
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/api -n easypj-secure --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Apply default-deny INGRESS policy (harmless to DNS — egress is untouched by this one)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: easypj-secure
spec:
  podSelector: {}     # Applies to ALL pods in namespace
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress            # Only blocks ingress — egress remains default-allow with JUST this policy
EOF

# STEP 2b: Apply an EGRESS-restricting policy for web→api — THIS is what actually breaks DNS (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: web-egress-to-api-only
  namespace: easypj-secure
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Egress              # ❌ BUG! ANY policy with Egress switches selected pods to default-deny for ALL egress!
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: api
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
  # ❌ BUG! No rule allowing UDP 53 to CoreDNS — DNS egress is silently blocked too!
EOF

# STEP 3: Test basic operations — ALL FAIL!
kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://api
# ❌ wget: bad address 'api' — CAN'T RESOLVE DNS!

kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- nslookup kubernetes.default
# ❌ ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached — DNS BLOCKED!

# The APP STORY:
# "We secured the namespace — why is everything down?"
# The default-deny NetworkPolicy blocks all ingress (correct).
# But DNS is an EGRESS operation — pods need to reach CoreDNS on UDP 53.
# Without an egress rule for DNS, pods are completely blind.
# They can't resolve Service names, external hosts, or even kubernetes.default.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — DNS Resolution Completely Blocked

✗1. nslookup kubernetes.default → "connection timed out; no servers"
✗2. wget http://api → "bad address 'api'" — can't resolve Service name!
✗3. NetworkPolicy has Ingress policyType but NO Egress — DNS blocked silently!
✗4. Pods can't resolve ANY hostname — internal or external — application is DEAD!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Are Pods Blind After Applying NetworkPolicy?

1Check the Ingress-only policy first: kubectl describe netpol deny-all-ingress -n easypj-secure
→ PolicyTypes: Ingress only — this one leaves egress completely untouched (still default-allow). It is NOT the cause of the DNS failure.
2Check the second policy: kubectl describe netpol web-egress-to-api-only -n easypj-secure
→ PolicyTypes: Egress — the moment ANY policy with an Egress policyType selects a pod, that pod flips to default-deny for ALL egress, not just the traffic the policy mentions.
3Check its egress rules: kubectl get netpol web-egress-to-api-only -n easypj-secure -o yaml | grep -A10 egress
→ Only one rule: web→api TCP 80. No rule at all for DNS (UDP 53 to CoreDNS) — so DNS egress is silently blocked too.
4Root cause: The web-egress-to-api-only NetworkPolicy has policyTypes: [Egress], which implements default-deny for ALL egress traffic from web pods — not just the traffic it explicitly restricts. The security team added a rule for web→api TCP 80 but FORGOT to add a DNS egress rule to CoreDNS (UDP 53). Without DNS egress, pods can't resolve any hostnames. Fix: add an egress rule allowing UDP port 53 to kube-system (where CoreDNS runs).
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Default-deny applied → DNS dead!
②
Check NetworkPolicy → has Egress rule
③
Egress allows web→api but NO DNS!
④
Add DNS egress → UDP 53 to kube-dns
⑤
DNS resolves → app works + secure!

Tenet: NetworkPolicy with policyTypes: [Egress] implements default-deny for ALL egress. Every required egress (DNS, external APIs, monitoring) must be explicitly allowed. The #1 forgotten egress rule is DNS (UDP 53 to CoreDNS/kube-dns). Without it, pods can't resolve any hostname. On CKA: NetworkPolicy creation with proper egress rules (especially DNS) is a guaranteed exam topic.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- nslookup kubernetes.default ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached ← DNS EGRESS BLOCKED!
$ kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- wget -O- http://api wget: bad address 'api' ← CAN'T RESOLVE SERVICE NAME!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- nslookup kubernetes.default Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local Address: 10.96.0.1 ← DNS WORKS!
$ kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://api <!DOCTYPE html>...Welcome to nginx! ← CONNECTIVITY RESTORED!
5

🔧 Fix — Add DNS Egress Rule to NetworkPolicy

BASH — Add DNS egress + selective ingress rules 
# Delete both broken policies (the Ingress-only one was actually fine, but we're
# consolidating into a single correct policy)
kubectl delete netpol deny-all-ingress web-egress-to-api-only -n easypj-secure

# Create CORRECT NetworkPolicy with DNS egress
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: secure-easypj
  namespace: easypj-secure
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: web
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
  egress:
  # CRITICAL: Allow DNS queries to CoreDNS!
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
  # Allow pod-to-pod traffic within namespace
  - to:
    - podSelector: {}
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
EOF

# Verify DNS works
kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl exec web -n easypj-secure -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://api
6

✅ Verify — DNS Resolves, Pod-to-Pod Traffic Works, Security Enforced

nslookup resolves internal and external hostnames. wget http://api succeeds from web pod. Key: every NetworkPolicy with Egress rules MUST include a DNS egress rule (UDP 53 to kube-system). Without it, pods are blind. The #1 mistake in NetworkPolicy design is forgetting DNS egress.

7

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-secure

S91
🧪 SCENARIO S91 — Category 5: Services & Networking NetworkPolicy Ports

API Partially Reachable — NetworkPolicy Allows TCP 8000 but App Also Needs UDP

The Problem: You create a NetworkPolicy allowing easypj-web → easypj-api on TCP port 8000. HTTP requests work, but a separate UDP-based metrics heartbeat the api sends/receives on port 8081 fails silently, because the NetworkPolicy only permits TCP. Your job: identify that the app needs both TCP and UDP, update the NetworkPolicy to allow the UDP port, and verify both protocols work.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create NetworkPolicy Allowing TCP Only — UDP Heartbeat Silently Blocked (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj security team tightens network policies. They allow web→api on TCP 8000. HTTP traffic flows perfectly — the job board works fine for users. But the monitoring team notices the UDP-based metrics heartbeat (web pinging api on port 8081, checked manually via nc -u) is silently failing. The NetworkPolicy only allows TCP. The UDP heartbeat packets are silently dropped by iptables — no error on either side, the packets just vanish. Metrics dashboards show gaps; nobody notices until someone manually tests the UDP path.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S91): 
netpol-ports/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-ports
├── 02-web+api-pods.yaml           ← web pod + api pod serving both HTTP (TCP 80) and a UDP heartbeat listener
├── 03-netpol-tcp-only.yaml        ← NetworkPolicy: TCP 8000 only (THE BUG! — missing UDP!)
├── 04-netpol-tcp-udp-fixed.yaml   ← Fixed: TCP 8000 + UDP 8081
└── 05-verify-protocols.sh         ← Test TCP (curl) + UDP (nc -u) connectivity
BASH — Create NetworkPolicy allowing only TCP, UDP silently blocked 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S91: NetworkPolicy — TCP OK, UDP Blocked
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and deploy pods. The "api" pod runs TWO containers sharing
# one pod IP: real nginx serving HTTP on 80, plus a socat sidecar serving a UDP
# metrics-heartbeat listener on 8081 — both are reachable via Services on that pod IP.
kubectl create namespace easypj-ports
kubectl run web -n easypj-ports --image=nginx:alpine --labels=app=web
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: easypj-ports
  labels:
    app: api
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
  - name: udp-heartbeat
    image: nikolaik/socat
    command: ["socat", "-v", "UDP-RECVFROM:8081,fork", "SYSTEM:echo alive"]
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8081
      protocol: UDP
EOF
kubectl expose pod api -n easypj-ports --port=8000 --target-port=80 --name=api-svc
kubectl expose pod api -n easypj-ports --port=8081 --target-port=8081 --protocol=UDP --name=api-heartbeat-svc
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web -n easypj-ports --timeout=60s
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/api -n easypj-ports --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Apply NetworkPolicy with TCP ONLY (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: web-to-api
  namespace: easypj-ports
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: web
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP    # ❌ BUG! Only allows TCP!
      port: 8000       # Missing: UDP 8081 for the metrics heartbeat!
EOF

# STEP 3: Test TCP (works!)
kubectl exec web -n easypj-ports -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://api-svc:8000
# ✅ TCP works — real HTTP response returned from nginx

# STEP 4: Test UDP (FAILS!)
kubectl exec web -n easypj-ports -- timeout 3 nc -u api-heartbeat-svc 8081
# ❌ BUG! UDP packet DROPPED by iptables — NetworkPolicy only allows TCP!

# The APP STORY:
# "Why do metrics dashboards show gaps in the api heartbeat?"
# The UDP heartbeat traffic from web to api → silently dropped by NetworkPolicy.
# No error on either side — the packets just vanish.
# TCP traffic works fine (HTTP requests succeed).
# But UDP is invisible until someone manually tests it with nc -u.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — TCP Works, UDP Silently Blocked

✗1. wget http://api-svc:8000 → TCP WORKS! HTTP returns 200
✗2. nc -u api-heartbeat-svc 8081 → UDP DROPPED! No response!
✗3. NetworkPolicy only has protocol: TCP — no UDP rule!
✗4. No errors anywhere — the UDP heartbeat just silently vanishes, invisible unless someone tests it directly!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Does UDP Silently Fail While TCP Works?

1Check NetworkPolicy ports: kubectl describe netpol web-to-api -n easypj-ports
→ Ingress rule: TCP port 8000 only. NO UDP rule!
2Understand protocol filtering: NetworkPolicy rules can filter by protocol: TCP, UDP, or SCTP. If no protocol is specified, it defaults to TCP. Each protocol needs its own port entry. A single rule allowing TCP:8000 does NOT automatically allow UDP:8000 or any other UDP port.
3Root cause: The NetworkPolicy only specifies protocol: TCP for port 8000. The API's UDP metrics heartbeat on port 8081 requires a separate rule with protocol: UDP. Fix: add a second ingress rule allowing UDP on port 8081 from the web pod selector.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
TCP works, UDP fails → check policy
②
Policy only has protocol: TCP
③
UDP heartbeat port not covered
④
Add UDP 8081 ingress rule
⑤
Both TCP and UDP work!

Tenet: NetworkPolicy protocol filtering is explicit. TCP ≠ UDP. Each protocol needs its own port rule. If your app uses multiple protocols (TCP for HTTP, UDP for metrics/DNS), you MUST add separate rules for each. Default protocol is TCP if omitted. UDP is connectionless, so a blocked UDP packet produces NO error on either end — unlike a blocked TCP connection, which at least times out loudly. On CKA: multi-protocol NetworkPolicy creation is a tested skill — know to specify protocol: UDP for DNS rules.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec web -n easypj-ports -- timeout 3 nc -u api-heartbeat-svc 8081 (no response — UDP packet dropped by NetworkPolicy) ← SILENTLY BLOCKED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec web -n easypj-ports -- timeout 3 nc -u api-heartbeat-svc 8081 Connection to api-heartbeat-svc 8081 port [udp] succeeded! ← UDP ALLOWED!
5

🔧 Fix — Add UDP Rule to NetworkPolicy

BASH — Add UDP port rule for the metrics heartbeat 
# Patch the NetworkPolicy to add UDP port 8081
kubectl patch netpol web-to-api -n easypj-ports --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/ingress/0/ports/-","value":{"protocol":"UDP","port":8081}}
]'

# Verify the policy now has both TCP and UDP rules
kubectl describe netpol web-to-api -n easypj-ports

# Test UDP connectivity
kubectl exec web -n easypj-ports -- timeout 3 nc -u api-heartbeat-svc 8081
6

✅ Verify — Both TCP and UDP Traffic Flow

TCP port 8000 and UDP port 8081 both pass. The metrics heartbeat resumes. Key: NetworkPolicy protocols are explicit — TCP, UDP, and SCTP are separate. Each protocol needs its own port rule. For DNS, always add protocol: UDP port 53. For apps with UDP traffic, add explicit UDP rules — and remember a blocked UDP packet fails silently, with no error on either end, unlike TCP.

kubectl delete namespace easypj-ports
S92
🧪 SCENARIO S92 — Category 5: Services & Networking Egress Policy

Pod Can't Pull Images or Call External APIs — Egress NetworkPolicy Too Restrictive

The Problem: You lock down egress from the easypj namespace — allow DNS (UDP 53) and HTTPS to api.github.com only. But after applying, new pods can't start (can't pull images from registry) and OAuth login fails (the app also needs oauth.google.com). The egress policy is missing the container registry and the Google OAuth endpoint. Your job: identify all required egress destinations, add missing rules for the container registry and OAuth provider, and verify both image pulls and API calls work.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Apply Strict Egress Policy — Missing Registry and OAuth (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj security team implements a strict egress policy: pods can only talk to DNS and a whitelist of external APIs. They deploy the policy. Within minutes: new deployments stall in ImagePullBackOff — pods can't reach the container registry to pull images. Existing pods can't authenticate users — Google OAuth is blocked because the egress policy only allows api.github.com. The security lockdown is so tight that the application can't function. Every new deployment is stuck. Every user login fails.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S92): 
netpol-egress/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-egress
├── 02-test-pod.yaml               ← Pod to test egress connectivity
├── 03-strict-egress-broken.yaml   ← Egress: DNS + api.github.com ONLY (THE BUG!)
├── 04-egress-fixed.yaml           ← Fixed: + Docker Hub + oauth.google.com
└── 05-verify-egress.sh            ← Test DNS, GitHub API, Google OAuth, image pull
BASH — Apply strict egress that blocks registry and OAuth 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S92: Egress NetworkPolicy — Too Restrictive
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and test pod
kubectl create namespace easypj-egress
kubectl run test-pod -n easypj-egress --image=busybox --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/test-pod -n easypj-egress --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Apply strict egress — only DNS + api.github.com (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: easypj-egress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  # Allow DNS to CoreDNS
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
  # Allow ONLY api.github.com (too restrictive!)
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 140.82.0.0/16   # GitHub's IP range (approximate)
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  # ❌ BUG! Missing: Docker Hub (registry-1.docker.io) for image pulls!
  # ❌ BUG! Missing: oauth.google.com for Google login!
EOF

🔍 Debug — What Egress Destinations Are Missing?

1Check blocked destinations: kubectl exec test-pod -n easypj-egress -- nslookup registry-1.docker.io
→ DNS resolves (allowed), but TCP 443 to Docker Hub IPs is BLOCKED!
2Identify ALL required egress: Container registries (Docker Hub, GCR, ECR), OAuth providers (Google, GitHub, Microsoft), monitoring (Datadog, Prometheus remote write), logging (Elasticsearch, Loki). Each needs an explicit egress rule with destination IP range + port.

Missing destinations: Docker Hub (for image pulls), oauth.google.com (for Google SSO), and any other external services the app depends on. ①

🔧 Fix — Add Missing Egress Rules

BASH — Add Docker Hub and Google OAuth to egress rules 
# Delete restrictive policy + recreate with all required egress
kubectl delete netpol restrict-egress -n easypj-egress
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: allow-required-egress
  namespace: easypj-egress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
  - to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 140.82.0.0/16}}]    # GitHub API
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 443}]
  - to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 142.250.0.0/15}}]   # Google (OAuth + APIs)
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 443}]
  - to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0}}]        # Container registries (broad — for lab only)
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 443}]
EOF
# For production: use specific registry CIDRs, not 0.0.0.0/0!

🧪 SCENARIO S93 — Category 5: Services & Networking CNI Policy Support

NetworkPolicy Applied but Traffic STILL Flows — CNI Plugin Doesn't Support NetworkPolicy

The Problem: You create a default-deny NetworkPolicy to isolate pods. kubectl get netpol shows the policy exists. But traffic still flows unrestricted — pods can communicate as if the policy doesn't exist. The cluster is running Flannel as the CNI plugin, which does NOT implement NetworkPolicy enforcement. Kubernetes accepts the YAML and stores it in etcd, but no controller enforces the rules. Your job: identify that the CNI plugin lacks NetworkPolicy support, verify by checking which CNI is installed, and understand the CNI requirements for NetworkPolicy.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Apply NetworkPolicy on Cluster Without NetworkPolicy-Supporting CNI (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj security team spends weeks designing perfect NetworkPolicies. They test on the dev cluster (Calico) — everything works. They deploy to staging. A month later, a penetration test reveals: pods in staging have ZERO network restrictions. The NetworkPolicies were applied months ago and kubectl shows them as active, but traffic flows completely unrestricted. The staging cluster runs Flannel, which silently ignores all NetworkPolicies. For 3 months, the staging environment had NO network security. The pen test report is devastating.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S93): 
cni-netpol-check/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-cni
├── 02-web+api-pods.yaml           ← Two test pods for connectivity
├── 03-deny-all-netpol.yaml        ← Default-deny NetworkPolicy (applied but IGNORED!)
├── 04-check-cni-support.sh        ← Identify CNI + check NetworkPolicy support
└── 05-cni-support-matrix.md       ← Calico/Cilium/Weave ✅, Flannel ❌
BASH — Apply NetworkPolicy, prove it's silently ignored 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S93: NetworkPolicy Silently Ignored — CNI Issue
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and test pods
kubectl create namespace easypj-cni
kubectl run web -n easypj-cni --image=nginx:alpine --labels=app=web
kubectl run api -n easypj-cni --image=nginx:alpine --labels=app=api
kubectl expose pod api -n easypj-cni --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web -n easypj-cni --timeout=60s
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/api -n easypj-cni --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Test BEFORE policy (should work)
kubectl exec web -n easypj-cni -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://api
# ✅ Connection succeeds

# STEP 3: Apply default-deny NetworkPolicy
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: easypj-cni
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
EOF

# STEP 4: Verify policy EXISTS
kubectl get netpol -n easypj-cni
# NAME       POD-SELECTOR   AGE
# deny-all   <none>         30s   ← POLICY IS ACTIVE!

# STEP 5: Test AFTER policy — STILL WORKS!
kubectl exec web -n easypj-cni -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://api
# ❌ BUG! Connection STILL succeeds! Policy has NO EFFECT!
# If the CNI supported NetworkPolicy, this would timeout!

# STEP 6: Check which CNI is installed
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|flannel|cilium|weave"
# ❌ Shows "flannel" — Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy!

# The APP STORY:
# "We have NetworkPolicies everywhere — staging is secure!"
# 3 months later, pen test: "Zero network restrictions in staging."
# Flannel accepted all the YAML but enforces NOTHING.
# Kubernetes doesn't warn you — the policies exist but are dead.

⚠️ Observe the Error — NetworkPolicy Exists But Traffic Still Flows

✗1. kubectl get netpol → Policy EXISTS and is ACTIVE!
✗2. wget http://api → Traffic STILL FLOWS after deny-all!
✗3. CNI plugin is Flannel — does NOT implement NetworkPolicy!
✗4. Policy stored in etcd but NO controller enforces it — silent failure!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Doesn't the NetworkPolicy Work?

1Check installed CNI: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|flannel|cilium|weave"
→ Flannel is running — Flannel handles pod networking but NOT policy enforcement!
2Verify policy is stored: kubectl get netpol deny-all -n easypj-cni -o yaml
→ Policy is correctly stored in etcd — Kubernetes API accepts it fine!
3Root cause: NetworkPolicy resources are just YAML definitions. They require a CNI plugin that IMPLEMENTS policy enforcement (iptables/eBPF rules). Flannel only provides pod networking (IP assignment + routes). CNIs that SUPPORT NetworkPolicy: Calico, Cilium, Weave Net, Kube-router, Antrea. Flannel by itself does NOT. Fix: switch to a NetworkPolicy-supporting CNI like Calico or Cilium, or add Calico policy layer on top of Flannel (Canal).

⑤
Policy enforced → network secured!

Tenet: NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes API resource — it's just YAML until a CNI plugin implements it. Always verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy BEFORE relying on it for security. Testing: apply a deny-all and verify with actual traffic. On CKA: this is a common exam trap — "Why doesn't the NetworkPolicy work?" → check the CNI.

🧪 SCENARIO S94 — Category 5: Services & Networking Ingress

Ingress Created But Shows No Address — Missing IngressClass / No Controller

The Problem: You create an Ingress resource to expose easypj-web externally. kubectl get ingress shows the Ingress exists but the ADDRESS column is empty — no IP or hostname assigned. Hours pass and nothing happens. The Ingress resource requires an Ingress Controller (like NGINX Ingress) to be installed in the cluster, AND an IngressClass to link the Ingress to the controller. Without both, the Ingress is just dead YAML. Your job: install NGINX Ingress Controller, create an IngressClass, and verify the Ingress gets an address.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create Ingress Without Ingress Controller — Stays Addressless Forever (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team wants to expose their web application via a proper URL (jobboard.easypj.com) instead of NodePort IPs. The DevOps lead creates an Ingress resource following the Kubernetes docs. They run kubectl get ingress — ADDRESS is empty. They wait. An hour passes. Still empty. The cluster has no Ingress Controller installed. The Ingress resource is like a job posting with no applicants — it exists but nobody is fulfilling it. The CTO wants the public URL live for the investor demo in 20 minutes. Without an Ingress Controller, there's NO external access.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S94): 
ingress-nocontroller/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-ingress
├── 02-web-deployment+svc.yaml     ← Web deployment + ClusterIP Service
├── 03-ingress-no-controller.yaml  ← Ingress resource (BUG: no IngressClass!)
├── 04-install-nginx-ingress.sh    ← Install NGINX Ingress Controller
└── 05-ingress-with-class.yaml     ← Fixed: Ingress with ingressClassName
BASH — Create Ingress, watch ADDRESS stay empty forever 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S94: Ingress — No Controller, No Address
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and web deployment

kubectl create deployment easypj-web -n easypj-ingress --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web -n easypj-ingress --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/easypj-web -n easypj-ingress --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Create Ingress resource (THE BUG! No IngressClass specified!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-ingress
  namespace: easypj-ingress
spec:
  # ❌ BUG! Missing: ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: jobboard.easypj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: easypj-web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# STEP 3: Check the Ingress — NO ADDRESS!
kubectl get ingress -n easypj-ingress
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# NAME                 CLASS    HOSTS                  ADDRESS   PORTS   AGE
# easypj-web-ingress   <none>   jobboard.easypj.com             80      5m
# ADDRESS is EMPTY — no controller handles this Ingress!

# STEP 4: Check if any IngressClass exists
kubectl get ingressclass
# ❌ No resources found — NO IngressClass, NO Ingress Controller!

# The APP STORY:
# "Why doesn't jobboard.easypj.com work? The Ingress was created hours ago!"
# The Ingress resource is valid YAML, stored in etcd, visible in kubectl.
# But without an Ingress Controller, nobody provisions the actual load balancer.
# It's like writing a check with no bank account — the paper exists but it's worthless.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Ingress Exists But ADDRESS Is Empty

✗1. kubectl get ingress -n easypj-ingress → ADDRESS: empty
✗2. kubectl get ingressclass → No resources found
✗3. kubectl describe ingress → No events — nothing is happening!
✗4. No external access to the application — investor demo is DEAD!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Doesn't the Ingress Get an Address?

1Check for IngressClass: kubectl get ingressclass
→ No IngressClass resources — no controller registered!
2Check for Ingress Controller pods: kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress
→ No ingress controller pods running in any namespace!
3Root cause: An Ingress resource is just a declaration. It needs an Ingress Controller (like NGINX Ingress, Traefik, HAProxy, or cloud-specific ALB/GCLB) to actually provision a load balancer, configure routing rules, and assign an external address. Without a controller + IngressClass, the Ingress stays addressless forever. Fix: install NGINX Ingress Controller, which auto-creates an IngressClass, then reference it in the Ingress spec with ingressClassName.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Ingress ADDRESS empty → no controller
②
Check IngressClass → none found!
③
Install NGINX Ingress Controller
④
Add ingressClassName to Ingress
⑤
ADDRESS populated → external access!

Tenet: Ingress = Ingress Controller + IngressClass + Ingress Resource. All three must exist. The Ingress Controller is the actual proxy (NGINX, Traefik, etc.) that runs as pods. The IngressClass links Ingress resources to a specific controller. The Ingress resource defines routing rules. Without a controller, Ingress is dead YAML. On CKA: installing and configuring an Ingress Controller + creating working Ingress is a core exam skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get ingress -n easypj-ingress NAME CLASS HOSTS ADDRESS PORTS AGE easypj-web-ingress <none> jobboard.easypj.com 80 10m ← NO ADDRESS!
$ kubectl get ingressclass No resources found ← NO CONTROLLER INSTALLED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get ingress -n easypj-ingress NAME CLASS HOSTS ADDRESS PORTS AGE easypj-web-ingress nginx jobboard.easypj.com 172.18.0.3 80 12m ← ADDRESS ASSIGNED!
5

🔧 Fix — Install NGINX Ingress Controller + Add IngressClass

BASH — Install NGINX Ingress Controller on kind 
# Step 1: Install NGINX Ingress Controller
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.10.0/deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller -n ingress-nginx --timeout=120s

# Step 2: Verify IngressClass was auto-created
kubectl get ingressclass
# nginx (default) should appear

# Step 3: Patch the Ingress to reference the nginx IngressClass
kubectl patch ingress easypj-web-ingress -n easypj-ingress --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/ingressClassName","value":"nginx"}]'

# Step 4: Check ADDRESS now populated
kubectl get ingress -n easypj-ingress
curl -H "Host: jobboard.easypj.com" http://localhost/  # Test locally

✅ Verify — Ingress Has Address, External Traffic Routed

ADDRESS column shows the load balancer IP. curl -H "Host: jobboard.easypj.com" returns the Nginx welcome page. Key: Ingress = Controller + IngressClass + Resource. All three are required. Without an Ingress Controller, the Ingress resource is just dead YAML stored in etcd.
