S95
🧪 SCENARIO S95 — Category 5: Services & Networking Ingress Paths

Sub-Paths Fall Through to Web — /api Uses pathType: Exact Instead of Prefix

The Problem: You configure Ingress path-based routing: / → easypj-web and /api → easypj-api. Requests to exactly /api work — but /api/jobs falls through to easypj-web. This is NOT a declaration-order issue — Kubernetes Ingress always resolves overlapping paths by LONGEST MATCH regardless of YAML order, so listing / first would be harmless on its own. The real bug: /api uses pathType: Exact, which matches ONLY the literal string /api — not any sub-path. /api/jobs doesn't match Exact /api at all, so it falls through to the Prefix / catch-all. Your job: fix the pathType so all API sub-paths route correctly.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Ingress Path Order — Prefix / Before /api Swallows All Traffic (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj platform has two services: easypj-web (serves the frontend at /) and easypj-api (serves REST API at /api). The DevOps lead creates an Ingress with two path rules. They test jobboard.easypj.com/api — the API responds! They test jobboard.easypj.com/api/jobs — returns the front page HTML instead of JSON! The /api rule uses pathType: Exact, which matches ONLY the literal path /api — sub-paths like /api/jobs don't match it and fall through to the Prefix / catch-all. The mobile app is broken because it expects JSON from /api/jobs but gets HTML from the web server. 10,000 mobile users see garbled data.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S95): 
ingress-paths/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-paths
├── 02-web-deployment+svc.yaml     ← Web: serves HTML (port 80)
├── 03-api-deployment+svc.yaml     ← API: serves JSON (port 80)
├── 04-ingress-exact-pathtype.yaml ← /api uses pathType: Exact (BUG! sub-paths fall through)
└── 05-ingress-fixed-prefix.yaml   ← /api uses pathType: Prefix (matches sub-paths too)
BASH — Ingress with wrong pathType: Exact instead of Prefix on /api 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S95: Ingress pathType Exact — Sub-Paths Fall Through to Catch-All
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and both services
kubectl create namespace easypj-paths
kubectl create deployment web -n easypj-paths --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl create deployment api -n easypj-paths --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment web -n easypj-paths --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl expose deployment api -n easypj-paths --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/web -n easypj-paths --timeout=60s
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/api -n easypj-paths --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Create Ingress where /api uses the WRONG pathType (THE BUG!)
# NOTE: declaration order genuinely does NOT matter here — Kubernetes always resolves
# overlapping Ingress paths by LONGEST MATCH, regardless of which rule is listed first
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: path-routing
  namespace: easypj-paths
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: jobboard.easypj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
      # ❌ BUG! pathType: Exact only matches the LITERAL "/api" — sub-paths like /api/jobs don't match!
      - path: /api
        pathType: Exact
        backend:
          service:
            name: api
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# STEP 3: Test — exactly /api works, but /api/jobs falls through to web (WRONG!)
# kubectl port-forward -n ingress-nginx service/ingress-nginx-controller 8080:80 &
curl -H "Host: jobboard.easypj.com" http://localhost:8080/api/jobs
# ❌ BUG! Returns web HTML, not API JSON! /api/jobs doesn't match Exact "/api", falls through to Prefix /

# The APP STORY:
# "The mobile app is showing HTML instead of job listings!"
# /api/jobs requests go to the web server, which returns the homepage.
# The mobile app parses HTML as JSON and crashes.
# pathType matters: Exact only matches the literal path, Prefix matches sub-paths too.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — /api/jobs Routes to Web Instead of API

✗1. curl -H "Host: ..." /api/jobs → Returns HTML instead of JSON!
✗2. curl -H "Host: ..." /api (exact) → Works fine, returns JSON!
✗3. The /api rule uses pathType: Exact — it does NOT match sub-paths like /api/jobs!
✗4. Mobile app crashes — HTML where JSON expected — every API sub-path is broken!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Does /api/jobs Fall Through to Web?

1Check Ingress rules: kubectl describe ingress path-routing -n easypj-paths
→ /api uses Path Type: Exact — this is the actual bug, NOT the order the rules are listed in
2Understand path matching: Kubernetes always resolves overlapping Ingress paths by LONGEST MATCH — declaration order in the YAML is irrelevant. But pathType still matters: Exact matches ONLY the literal path string with no trailing segments, while Prefix matches the path AND any "/"-delimited sub-paths. /api/jobs simply isn't the same string as /api, so the Exact rule never matches it — it falls through to the Prefix / catch-all, which does match (every path starts with /).
3Root cause: The /api rule uses pathType: Exact instead of Prefix. Exact matching means only literal /api requests hit the api service — every sub-path (/api/jobs, /api/users, etc.) falls through to the Prefix / catch-all instead. Fix: change /api's pathType to Prefix so it matches the whole /api subtree.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
/api/jobs returns HTML → wrong backend
②
Check Ingress → /api uses Exact!
③
Exact doesn't match sub-paths
④
Change /api to pathType: Prefix
⑤
Correct routing → web + API work!

Tenet: Kubernetes always resolves overlapping Ingress paths by LONGEST MATCH — declaration order in the YAML never matters, so a catch-all "/" listed first is harmless on its own. What DOES matter is pathType: Exact matches only the literal path string (no sub-paths), Prefix matches the path plus any "/"-delimited sub-paths, ImplementationSpecific is controller-defined. On CKA: Ingress pathType confusion (Exact vs Prefix) is a classic exam trap — don't assume it's a declaration-order issue.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s -H "Host: jobboard.easypj.com" http://localhost:8080/api/jobs | head -3 <!DOCTYPE html><html>...<h1>Welcome to nginx!</h1> ← WEB HTML, NOT API JSON! (Exact "/api" doesn't match "/api/jobs")
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -H "Host: jobboard.easypj.com" http://localhost:8080/api/jobs | head -3 {"jobs": [...]} ← CORRECT! Prefix "/api" now matches "/api/jobs" too!
5

🔧 Fix — Change /api's pathType from Exact to Prefix

BASH — Patch pathType so sub-paths match too (declaration order is unaffected/irrelevant) 
# Just patch the pathType — no need to delete/recreate or reorder anything
kubectl patch ingress path-routing -n easypj-paths --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/http/paths/1/pathType","value":"Prefix"}
]'

# Verify: both /api and /api/jobs now route to the api service, regardless of which
# path rule appears first in the YAML — Kubernetes resolves by longest match, always
kubectl get ingress path-routing -n easypj-paths -o yaml | grep -A2 pathType

# Verify routing
curl -H "Host: jobboard.easypj.com" http://localhost:8080/api/jobs # → API
curl -H "Host: jobboard.easypj.com" http://localhost:8080/         # → Web
6

✅ Verify — /api and All Sub-Paths Route to API, / Still Routes to Web

Both paths route correctly, including /api/jobs. Key: Ingress paths always resolve by longest match — declaration order in the YAML is never the cause of a routing bug. pathType is what actually matters: Exact for a single literal path, Prefix when sub-paths need to match too. On CKA: pathType confusion is tested — you WILL get a broken Ingress to fix, and it's rarely about ordering.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-paths

📌 S96–S100: Ingress TLS & Gateway API

S96
🧪 SCENARIO S96 — Category 5: Services & Networking Ingress TLS

HTTPS Ingress Returns 502 — TLS Secret Has Wrong Key Names (cert.pem vs tls.crt)

The Problem: You create a TLS Secret for HTTPS on the Ingress and reference it. But curl https://jobboard.easypj.com returns 502 Bad Gateway or a default NGINX certificate. The TLS Secret was created with key names "cert.pem" and "key.pem", but Kubernetes TLS Secrets REQUIRE the keys to be named "tls.crt" and "tls.key" exactly. The Ingress controller can't find the certificate because the key names don't match the expected format. Your job: identify the wrong Secret key names, recreate the Secret with correct keys, and verify HTTPS works.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create TLS Secret with Wrong Key Names — Ingress Can't Use It (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj security team mandates HTTPS for all external endpoints. The DevOps lead generates a self-signed certificate with openssl and creates a Kubernetes Secret. They configure the Ingress with TLS. But HTTPS requests fail — users see certificate warnings or 502 errors. The Secret was created with key names cert.pem and key.pem (the openssl default output names), but Kubernetes TLS Secrets REQUIRE tls.crt and tls.key exactly. The Ingress controller reads the Secret, finds no tls.crt key, and falls back to its default fake certificate. All HTTPS traffic is broken.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S96): 
ingress-tls/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-tls
├── 02-web-deployment+svc.yaml     ← Web deployment + ClusterIP Service
├── 03-generate-certs.sh           ← openssl gen self-signed cert
├── 04-tls-secret-broken.yaml      ← Secret with BUG: cert.pem + key.pem (WRONG!)
├── 05-ingress-with-tls.yaml       ← Ingress referencing the broken TLS Secret
├── 06-tls-secret-fixed.yaml       ← Secret FIX: tls.crt + tls.key (CORRECT!)
└── 07-verify-https.sh             ← curl -k https://... → verify TLS works
BASH — Create TLS Secret with wrong key names, watch HTTPS fail 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S96: Ingress TLS — Wrong Secret Key Names
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and web service
kubectl create namespace easypj-tls
kubectl create deployment easypj-web -n easypj-tls --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web -n easypj-tls --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/easypj-web -n easypj-tls --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Generate self-signed certificate
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout /tmp/cert.key -out /tmp/cert.crt \
  -subj "/CN=jobboard.easypj.com/O=easypj"

# STEP 3: Create Secret with WRONG key names (THE BUG!)
kubectl create secret generic easypj-tls -n easypj-tls \
  --from-file=cert.pem=/tmp/cert.crt \
  --from-file=key.pem=/tmp/cert.key
# ❌ BUG! Key names are "cert.pem" and "key.pem"!
# Kubernetes TLS expects "tls.crt" and "tls.key" EXACTLY!

# STEP 4: Create Ingress with TLS referencing the broken Secret
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-tls
  namespace: easypj-tls
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - jobboard.easypj.com
    secretName: easypj-tls   # References Secret with WRONG key names!
  rules:
  - host: jobboard.easypj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: easypj-web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# STEP 5: Test HTTPS — FAILS!
curl -k -v https://jobboard.easypj.com/ 2>&1 | grep -E "subject:|issuer:|HTTP"
# ❌ BUG! Shows "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate" — NOT our cert!
# The Ingress controller couldn't find tls.crt, used its default fake cert!

# The APP STORY:
# "Why is HTTPS showing a fake certificate? We created the Secret!"
# The Secret exists. kubectl get secret shows the data.
# But the key names are cert.pem + key.pem, NOT tls.crt + tls.key.
# Kubernetes TLS is strict about key names — one character off = broken.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — HTTPS Uses Fake Default Certificate

✗1. curl -k -v https://jobboard.easypj.com/ → Shows "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate"
✗2. kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj-tls → Secret EXISTS and has data!
✗3. kubectl get secret easypj-tls -o yaml | grep -E "cert|key" → cert.pem, key.pem (WRONG!)
✗4. Kubernetes TLS requires tls.crt + tls.key — one character off = completely broken!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Isn't the TLS Certificate Being Used?

1Check Secret data keys: kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj-tls -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq 'keys'
→ ["cert.pem","key.pem"] — Kubernetes expects ["tls.crt","tls.key"]!
2Verify Secret type: kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj-tls -o yaml | grep type
→ type: Opaque — should be type: kubernetes.io/tls!
3Root cause: Kubernetes TLS Secrets have STRICT requirements: type must be "kubernetes.io/tls", data keys must be exactly "tls.crt" and "tls.key". Using "cert.pem"/"key.pem" or any other names means the Secret is just a generic Opaque Secret — the Ingress controller ignores it. Fix: recreate the Secret with the correct key names, OR use 'kubectl create secret tls' which auto-sets the correct format.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
HTTPS shows fake cert → check Secret
②
Secret keys: cert.pem + key.pem!
③
K8s TLS requires tls.crt + tls.key
④
Recreate with correct key names
⑤
HTTPS serves correct certificate!

Tenet: Kubernetes TLS Secrets must use type: kubernetes.io/tls and data keys tls.crt and tls.key exactly. Use kubectl create secret tls to auto-generate the correct format. NEVER use kubectl create secret generic for TLS certs — it creates Opaque type with wrong key expectations. On CKA: TLS Secret creation with correct format is a guaranteed exam task.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj-tls -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq 'keys' ["cert.pem","key.pem"] ← WRONG KEY NAMES! Should be tls.crt, tls.key!
$ curl -k -v https://jobboard.easypj.com/ 2>&1 | grep subject subject: O=Acme Co; CN=Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate ← FAKE CERT!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -k -v https://jobboard.easypj.com/ 2>&1 | grep subject subject: CN=jobboard.easypj.com; O=easypj ← CORRECT CERTIFICATE!
5

🔧 Fix — Recreate TLS Secret with Correct Key Names

BASH — Create proper kubernetes.io/tls Secret 
# Step 1: Delete the broken Secret
kubectl delete secret easypj-tls -n easypj-tls

# Step 2: Create TLS Secret with CORRECT format (CKA fast method)
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n easypj-tls \
  --cert=/tmp/cert.crt \
  --key=/tmp/cert.key
# This auto-creates type: kubernetes.io/tls with keys: tls.crt + tls.key!

# Step 3: Verify the Secret format
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj-tls -o yaml | grep -E "type:|tls"
# type: kubernetes.io/tls
# tls.crt: LS0tLS1...
# tls.key: LS0tLS1...

# Step 4: Test HTTPS
curl -k -v https://jobboard.easypj.com/ 2>&1 | grep subject
6

✅ Verify — HTTPS Serves Correct Certificate

curl -k https://jobboard.easypj.com/ shows the correct certificate with CN=jobboard.easypj.com. Key: Kubernetes TLS Secrets MUST use type: kubernetes.io/tls with data keys tls.crt and tls.key exactly. Use kubectl create secret tls — it handles the correct format automatically. Never use kubectl create secret generic for TLS.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-tls
rm -f /tmp/cert.crt /tmp/cert.key
S97
🧪 SCENARIO S97 — Category 5: Services & Networking cert-manager

Certificate Resource Stuck Pending — ClusterIssuer Not Found

The Problem: You install cert-manager and create a Certificate resource for automatic TLS. But the Certificate stays Pending forever — no certificate is issued. The Cert-Manager logs show "ClusterIssuer not found". You created an Issuer (namespace-scoped) but the Certificate references a ClusterIssuer (cluster-scoped) named "letsencrypt-prod" which doesn't exist. Your job: identify the Issuer vs ClusterIssuer mismatch, either create the ClusterIssuer or fix the Certificate to reference the correct Issuer.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Certificate References ClusterIssuer That Doesn't Exist (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team automates TLS with cert-manager. The DevOps lead creates a self-signed Issuer in the easypj namespace for testing, then creates a Certificate resource. But they copy-pasted from the production config and the Certificate references "letsencrypt-prod" as a ClusterIssuer — which doesn't exist yet. The Certificate stays Pending for hours. cert-manager can't find the ClusterIssuer. The deployment deadline is today and HTTPS is still not working. The security audit flags the site as "no valid TLS" and blocks the production launch.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S97): 
cert-manager-issuer/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-certs
├── 02-install-cert-manager.sh     ← kubectl apply cert-manager manifests
├── 03-selfsigned-issuer.yaml      ← Issuer (namespace-scoped) — EXISTS and works!
├── 04-certificate-broken.yaml     ← Certificate BUG: issuerRef → ClusterIssuer "letsencrypt-prod"!
├── 05-certificate-fixed.yaml      ← Fixed: issuerRef → Issuer "selfsigned-issuer"
└── 06-verify-cert-ready.sh        ← kubectl get certificate → Ready: True
BASH — Create Issuer, then Certificate referencing non-existent ClusterIssuer 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S97: cert-manager — Certificate Stuck Pending
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace easypj-certs

# STEP 1b: Install cert-manager itself FIRST — the Issuer/Certificate/ClusterIssuer
# CRDs don't exist on a fresh cluster until this is applied
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment --all -n cert-manager --timeout=120s

# STEP 2: Create a working self-signed Issuer (namespace-scoped!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Issuer
metadata:
  name: selfsigned-issuer
  namespace: easypj-certs
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
EOF

# STEP 3: Create Certificate referencing NON-EXISTENT ClusterIssuer (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: easypj-tls-cert
  namespace: easypj-certs
spec:
  secretName: easypj-tls-secret
  dnsNames:
  - jobboard.easypj.com
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod   # ❌ BUG! ClusterIssuer "letsencrypt-prod" doesn't exist!
    kind: ClusterIssuer       # ❌ Should be kind: Issuer with name: selfsigned-issuer!
EOF

# STEP 4: Check Certificate status — STUCK PENDING!
kubectl get certificate -n easypj-certs
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# NAME              READY   SECRET             AGE
# easypj-tls-cert   False   easypj-tls-secret  5m   ← NEVER Ready!

kubectl describe certificate easypj-tls-cert -n easypj-certs | tail -10
# ❌ "Issuer letsencrypt-prod not found" — ClusterIssuer doesn't exist!

# STEP 5: Verify the Issuer exists (it does!)
kubectl get issuer -n easypj-certs
# NAME               READY   AGE
# selfsigned-issuer  True    10m   ← WORKING Issuer exists!
# But Certificate references a ClusterIssuer, not this Issuer!

# The APP STORY:
# "Why isn't the TLS certificate being issued? It's been pending for hours!"
# Issuer (namespace) was created. But Certificate references ClusterIssuer.
# The copy-paste from production config kept the production ClusterIssuer name.
# In dev, we need a self-signed Issuer, not Let's Encrypt ClusterIssuer.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Certificate Never Ready, Issuer Not Found

✗1. kubectl get certificate -n easypj-certs → READY: False
✗2. kubectl describe certificate → "Issuer letsencrypt-prod not found"
✗3. kubectl get issuer -n easypj-certs → selfsigned-issuer EXISTS and Ready!
✗4. Certificate references wrong kind (ClusterIssuer vs Issuer) and wrong name!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Won't the Certificate Issue?

1Check Certificate issuerRef: kubectl get certificate easypj-tls-cert -n easypj-certs -o yaml | grep -A3 issuerRef
→ kind: ClusterIssuer, name: letsencrypt-prod — NEITHER exists!
2Compare with available Issuers: kubectl get issuer,clusterissuer -A
→ Only selfsigned-issuer (Issuer in easypj-certs) exists. No ClusterIssuer at all!
3Root cause: The Certificate's issuerRef points to a ClusterIssuer named "letsencrypt-prod" which doesn't exist. The actual Issuer is a namespace-scoped Issuer named "selfsigned-issuer". Fix: change the Certificate's issuerRef to kind: Issuer, name: selfsigned-issuer. ClusterIssuer is cluster-wide (available to all namespaces); Issuer is namespace-scoped.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Certificate Pending → check issuerRef
②
References ClusterIssuer → not found!
③
Actual Issuer exists but different kind
④
Fix issuerRef → kind: Issuer
⑤
Certificate Ready → TLS provisioned!

Tenet: cert-manager has two issuer types: Issuer (namespace-scoped) and ClusterIssuer (cluster-wide). A Certificate's issuerRef must match the kind and name exactly. ClusterIssuer can be used from any namespace; Issuer only within its own namespace. On CKA: cert-manager Certificate + Issuer troubleshooting is a common exam scenario — know the difference between Issuer and ClusterIssuer.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get certificate -n easypj-certs NAME READY SECRET AGE easypj-tls-cert False easypj-tls-secret 10m ← STUCK PENDING!
$ kubectl describe certificate easypj-tls-cert -n easypj-certs | grep -A5 Status Status: Conditions: Message: Issuer letsencrypt-prod not found ← WRONG ISSUER!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get certificate -n easypj-certs NAME READY SECRET AGE easypj-tls-cert True easypj-tls-secret 12m ← CERTIFICATE ISSUED!
5

🔧 Fix — Correct Certificate issuerRef

BASH — Patch Certificate to reference correct Issuer 
# issuerRef is a mutable field — cert-manager reissues automatically when it changes, no delete/recreate needed
kubectl patch certificate easypj-tls-cert -n easypj-certs --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/issuerRef/name","value":"selfsigned-issuer"},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/issuerRef/kind","value":"Issuer"}
]'

# Verify certificate becomes Ready
kubectl get certificate -n easypj-certs -w
6

✅ Verify — Certificate Ready, Secret Provisioned

kubectl get certificate shows READY: True. TLS Secret is auto-created. Key: Certificate issuerRef must match the kind (Issuer vs ClusterIssuer) and name exactly. ClusterIssuer is cluster-wide; Issuer is namespace-scoped. cert-manager is the standard for automatic TLS in Kubernetes.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-certs
# cert-manager was installed cluster-wide in Step 1 — remove it too if not needed elsewhere
kubectl delete -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml --ignore-not-found
S98
🧪 SCENARIO S98 — Category 5: Services & Networking Ingress 502

Ingress Returns 502 Bad Gateway — Backend Pod Readiness Probe Failing

The Problem: Users report 502 Bad Gateway from jobboard.easypj.com. The Ingress exists and has an address. The Service exists. But kubectl get endpoints shows <none> — the backend pod has a failing readiness probe pointing to port 8080, but the app listens on port 80. The pod is Running but Not Ready, so the EndpointSlice controller removes it from the Service. The Ingress has no backend to route to. Your job: trace the 502 chain (Ingress→Service→Endpoints→Pod), identify the failing readiness probe, and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Wrong Readiness Probe Port — Endpoints Empty (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-web deployment gets a config update. The DevOps lead updates the deployment YAML, adding a readiness probe for health checking. They deploy. Suddenly, the website returns 502 Bad Gateway for every request. The pod IS running — kubectl get pods shows Running. But 0/1 Ready. The readiness probe was configured with port 8080, but Nginx listens on port 80. The probe fails every check. The pod is never marked Ready, so Endpoints are empty, so the Service has no backends, so the Ingress returns 502. Four layers of failure from one wrong port number.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S98): 
ingress-502/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-502
├── 02-web-deploy-broken.yaml      ← Deployment with BUG: readiness probe port 8080 (app on 80!)
├── 03-web-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service (port 80)
├── 04-ingress.yaml                ← Ingress routing to the Service
├── 05-web-deploy-fixed.yaml       ← Fixed: readiness probe port 80
└── 06-trace-502-chain.sh          ← Debug: curl→Ingress→Svc→Endpoints→Pod
BASH — Deploy pod with broken readiness probe, trace the 502 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S98: Ingress 502 — Readiness Probe Wrong Port
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace easypj-502

# STEP 2: Deploy pod with WRONG readiness probe port (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj-502
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080   # ❌ BUG! Nginx listens on 80, NOT 8080!
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
EOF

# STEP 3: Expose the deployment + create Ingress
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web -n easypj-502 --port=80 --target-port=80
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj-502
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: jobboard.easypj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: easypj-web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/easypj-web -n easypj-502 --timeout=30s 2>/dev/null || true

# STEP 4: Check pod — RUNNING but NOT READY!
kubectl get pods -n easypj-502
# ❌ BUG! Output:
# NAME                          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# easypj-web-7d8f9-abc         0/1     Running   0          2m   ← 0/1 READY!

# STEP 5: Check endpoints — EMPTY!
kubectl get endpoints -n easypj-502
# ❌ BUG! ENDPOINTS: <none> — no pods are Ready!

# The APP STORY:
# "502 Bad Gateway — the entire website is DOWN!"
# Pod is Running but not Ready → Endpoints empty → Service has no backends.
# Ingress routes to Service → Service has no endpoints → 502.
# All because the readiness probe checks the wrong port by 1 digit.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — Pod Running But 0/1 Ready, Endpoints Empty

✗1. kubectl get pods -n easypj-502 → 0/1 READY (pod is Running but Not Ready!)
✗2. kubectl get endpoints -n easypj-502 → <none> (no endpoints!)
✗3. kubectl describe pod → "Readiness probe failed: ... connect: connection refused" — nothing is even listening on 8080 to return a status code
✗4. Ingress → Service → no endpoints → 502 Bad Gateway for every user!
3

🔍 Debug — Trace the 502 Chain: Ingress → Service → Endpoints → Pod

1Check the 502 chain (top-down): 502 means Ingress got no response from backend. Check: (a) Ingress → valid (has address), (b) Service → exists and has ClusterIP, (c) Endpoints → <none>! This is the break. (d) Pod → Running but 0/1 Ready. The readiness probe is the root cause.
2Check readiness probe details: kubectl describe pod -n easypj-502 | grep -A10 Readiness
→ probe port: 8080 — but the container only exposes port 80!
3Root cause: The readiness probe httpGet specifies port: 8080, but Nginx listens on port 80. The probe fails every check. The pod never becomes Ready, so the EndpointSlice controller never adds it to the Service's endpoints. Without endpoints, the Ingress has no backend and returns 502. Fix: change the readiness probe port to 80.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
502 Bad Gateway → check chain
②
Ingress OK → Service OK → Endpoints <none>!
③
Pod Running but 0/1 Ready → probe failing
④
Probe port 8080 ≠ app port 80
⑤
Fix probe port → Endpoints populated → 200!

Tenet: The Ingress debugging chain: Ingress (check address + rules) → Service (check selector + ports) → Endpoints (check for pod IPs) → Pod (check Ready status) → Readiness Probe (check port + path). A failing readiness probe cascades up: pod Not Ready → no endpoints → Service has no backends → Ingress returns 502/503. On CKA: 502 debugging is a high-frequency exam scenario — know the full chain.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj-502 NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web-7d8f9-abc 0/1 Running 0 5m ← 0/1 READY!
$ kubectl describe pod -n easypj-502 | grep -A5 Readiness Readiness: http-get http://:8080/ delay=5s timeout=1s Warning Unhealthy Readiness probe failed: Get http://10.244.1.5:8080/: dial tcp 10.244.1.5:8080: connect: connection refused
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n easypj-502 NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web-9e0f1-xyz 1/1 Running 0 30s ← 1/1 READY!
5

🔧 Fix — Correct the Readiness Probe Port

BASH — Fix readiness probe port from 8080 to 80 
# Patch the deployment to fix readiness probe port
kubectl patch deployment easypj-web -n easypj-502 --type='json' -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/port","value":80}
]'

# Wait for rollout
kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj-web -n easypj-502 --timeout=60s

# Verify pod is Ready + endpoints populated
kubectl get pods -n easypj-502
kubectl get endpoints -n easypj-502
6

✅ Verify — Pod Ready, Endpoints Populated, No More 502

kubectl get pods shows 1/1 Ready. kubectl get endpoints shows pod IP. Key: readiness probe port must match the actual container port. The 502 debugging chain: Ingress → Service → Endpoints → Pod → Probe. Always check Readiness probe when you see 502 with Running pods.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-502
S99
🧪 SCENARIO S99 — Category 5: Services & Networking Ingress 504

Large Report Downloads Return 504 — Ingress Controller Proxy Timeout Too Short

The Problem: The easypj-api has an endpoint /reports/export that generates large CSV files — it takes 90 seconds to complete. Users get 504 Gateway Timeout after exactly 60 seconds. The NGINX Ingress Controller has a default proxy-read-timeout of 60 seconds. The backend IS working (the report completes at 90s), but the Ingress cuts the connection at 60s. Your job: identify the timeout mismatch, increase the Ingress proxy timeout via annotations, and verify long-running requests complete successfully.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Ingress Default 60s Timeout Cuts Off 90s Report Generation (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj HR team uses a "Export All Applicants" report that queries 500,000 applications and generates a CSV. It takes 90 seconds. After the new Ingress was deployed, every report download fails at exactly 60 seconds with 504 Gateway Timeout. The backend pod completes the report successfully at 90 seconds, but the Ingress already closed the connection. The HR team can't export compliance data for the quarterly audit. The deadline is today. The report endpoint works when accessed directly via pod IP — the issue is the Ingress proxy timeout.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S99): 
ingress-504/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-504
├── 02-slow-api-deployment.yaml    ← API with /slow endpoint (sleeps 90s, simulates report)
├── 03-api-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service
├── 04-ingress-default-timeout.yaml ← Ingress WITHOUT timeout annotation (BUG!)
├── 05-ingress-timeout-fixed.yaml  ← Ingress WITH proxy-read-timeout: 120s
└── 06-verify-long-request.sh      ← curl --max-time 120 → verify 200 OK
BASH — Deploy slow endpoint, Ingress times out at 60s 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S99: Ingress 504 — Proxy Timeout Too Short
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and deploy a "slow" API (sleeps 90 seconds)
kubectl create namespace easypj-504
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: slow-api
  namespace: easypj-504
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: slow-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: slow-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ["python3","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          import http.server, time
          class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
              def do_GET(self):
                  if self.path == '/reports/export':
                      time.sleep(90)    # REAL 90-second delay simulating report generation
                      self.send_response(200)
                      self.end_headers()
                      self.wfile.write(b'"name","email","status"\n"Alice","alice@corp.com","hired"\n')
                  else:
                      self.send_response(200)
                      self.end_headers()
          http.server.HTTPServer(('0.0.0.0', 80), Handler).serve_forever()
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
EOF
kubectl expose deployment slow-api -n easypj-504 --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/slow-api -n easypj-504 --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Create Ingress WITHOUT timeout annotation (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: slow-api-ingress
  namespace: easypj-504
  # ❌ BUG! No timeout annotations — defaults to 60s proxy-read-timeout!
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: reports.easypj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /reports
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: slow-api
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# STEP 3: Test the slow endpoint — 504 after 60s!
time curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 120 \
  -H "Host: reports.easypj.com" http://localhost/reports/export 2>/dev/null
# ❌ BUG! Returns 504 after ~60 seconds!
# The backend needs 90 seconds, but Ingress cuts off at 60s!

# The APP STORY:
# "Every report download fails at exactly 60 seconds!"
# The backend generates the 90-second report perfectly.
# But the Ingress proxy-read-timeout defaults to 60s.
# The connection is severed before the report finishes generating.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — 504 Gateway Timeout at Exactly 60 Seconds

✗1. curl --max-time 120 /reports/export → 504 Gateway Timeout after ~60s!
✗2. Backend pod logs show the request completing at 90s — backend IS working!
✗3. Ingress has NO proxy-read-timeout annotation — defaults to 60 seconds!
✗4. Every report export fails — HR can't submit quarterly compliance data!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Does the Report Always Fail at 60 Seconds?

1Check Ingress annotations: kubectl get ingress slow-api-ingress -n easypj-504 -o yaml | grep annotations -A10
→ No proxy-read-timeout annotation — using default 60s!
2Understand NGINX Ingress timeouts: proxy-read-timeout (default 60s) = maximum time to read the backend response. proxy-send-timeout (default 60s) = maximum time to send request to backend. proxy-connect-timeout (default 5s) = maximum time to establish connection. For long-running requests, increase proxy-read-timeout.
3Root cause: The NGINX Ingress Controller defaults proxy-read-timeout to 60 seconds. The /reports/export endpoint takes 90 seconds to generate. At 60 seconds, NGINX terminates the connection and returns 504. Fix: add annotation 'nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: 120' to the Ingress to allow up to 120 seconds for backend responses.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
504 at exactly 60s → timeout!
②
Backend works direct → Ingress is bottleneck
③
Missing proxy-read-timeout annotation
④
Add annotation: 120 seconds
⑤
Long requests complete → 200 OK!

Tenet: NGINX Ingress timeout defaults: proxy-read-timeout=60s, proxy-send-timeout=60s, proxy-connect-timeout=5s. For slow backends, increase via annotations. 502 = bad gateway (backend down/unreachable). 503 = service unavailable (no healthy backends). 504 = gateway timeout (backend too slow). On CKA: 504 debugging with timeout annotations is a tested skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ time curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -H "Host: reports.easypj.com" http://localhost/reports/export 504 real 1m0.234s ← EXACTLY 60 SECONDS — INGRESS DEFAULT TIMEOUT!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ time curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -H "Host: reports.easypj.com" http://localhost/reports/export 200 real 1m31.456s ← 200 OK after 91 seconds! Ingress waits for backend!
5

🔧 Fix — Add proxy-read-timeout Annotation

BASH — Increase Ingress proxy timeout to 120 seconds 
# Add proxy-read-timeout annotation to the Ingress
kubectl annotate ingress slow-api-ingress -n easypj-504 \
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout="120" --overwrite

# Also consider these for complete timeout control:
# kubectl annotate ingress slow-api-ingress -n easypj-504 \
#   nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout="120" --overwrite
# kubectl annotate ingress slow-api-ingress -n easypj-504 \
#   nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-connect-timeout="10" --overwrite

# Verify annotation applied
kubectl get ingress slow-api-ingress -n easypj-504 -o yaml | grep proxy-read-timeout

# Re-test the long request
time curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" --max-time 120 \
  -H "Host: reports.easypj.com" http://localhost/reports/export
6

✅ Verify — Long Requests Complete Successfully, No More 504

curl --max-time 120 /reports/export returns 200 after ~90 seconds. Key: NGINX Ingress default proxy-read-timeout is 60 seconds. For slow backends, add the annotation nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "120". 502/503/504 have distinct meanings — 504 specifically means the backend response took too long.

7

🧹 Cleanup

BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete namespace easypj-504
S100
🧪 SCENARIO S100 — Category 5: Services & Networking Gateway API

HTTPRoute Traffic Goes Nowhere — Backend Service Name Typo in HTTPRoute

The Problem: You deploy the Gateway API (GA/stable since v1.0 — not experimental) with a GatewayClass, Gateway, and an HTTPRoute to split traffic 90% to v1 and 10% to v2 of easypj-api. But all traffic returns 500 — the HTTPRoute references "easypj-api-v1" but the actual Service is named "api-v1". Without a valid backend, the Gateway controller can't route any traffic. Your job: identify the Service name mismatch in the HTTPRoute backendRef, fix it, and verify traffic flows correctly.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 HTTPRoute References Non-Existent Backend Service (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj platform team adopts Gateway API — the future of Kubernetes ingress. They deploy a Gateway and HTTPRoute for canary deployments: 90% traffic to api-v1, 10% to api-v2. But after deploying, all traffic returns 500 errors. The HTTPRoute was copy-pasted from a different environment where the Service was named "easypj-api-v1". In this environment, the Service is simply "api-v1". The Gateway API can't resolve the backend — a single Service name typo breaks ALL traffic routing. The canary deployment is dead in the water.
📁 FILE STRUCTURE for easypj/jobpost (S100): 
gateway-api/
├── 01-namespace.yaml              ← kubectl create ns easypj-gw
├── 02-api-v1-deployment+svc.yaml  ← Service named "api-v1" (NOT "easypj-api-v1"!)
├── 03-api-v2-deployment+svc.yaml  ← Service named "api-v2"
├── 04-httproute-broken.yaml       ← HTTPRoute BUG: backendRef → "easypj-api-v1" (doesn't exist!)
└── 05-httproute-fixed.yaml        ← Fixed: backendRef → "api-v1" + "api-v2"
BASH — Deploy Gateway API with wrong backend Service name 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S100: Gateway API — HTTPRoute Wrong Backend
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create namespace and deploy two versions of the API
kubectl create namespace easypj-gw
kubectl create deployment api-v1 -n easypj-gw --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl create deployment api-v2 -n easypj-gw --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl expose deployment api-v1 -n easypj-gw --port=80 --target-port=80 --name=api-v1
kubectl expose deployment api-v2 -n easypj-gw --port=80 --target-port=80 --name=api-v2
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/api-v1 -n easypj-gw --timeout=60s
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deployment/api-v2 -n easypj-gw --timeout=60s

# STEP 2: Verify Services exist with CORRECT names
kubectl get svc -n easypj-gw
# NAME     TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      PORT(S)   AGE
# api-v1   ClusterIP   10.96.1.10      80/TCP    2m
# api-v2   ClusterIP   10.96.1.11      80/TCP    2m

# STEP 2b: Install the Gateway API CRDs + a real controller implementation (e.g. NGINX
# Gateway Fabric), then create the GatewayClass + Gateway — an HTTPRoute needs a live,
# Accepted parent Gateway to receive any traffic at all; without one there's no listener
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.1.0/standard-install.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nginxinc/nginx-gateway-fabric/v1.5.0/deploy/crds.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nginxinc/nginx-gateway-fabric/v1.5.0/deploy/default/deploy.yaml
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.nginx.org/nginx-gateway-controller
---
# Gateway — listens on port 80, attached to the nginx GatewayClass
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: easypj-gateway
  namespace: easypj-gw
spec:
  gatewayClassName: nginx
  listeners:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    protocol: HTTP
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Accepted gateway/easypj-gateway -n easypj-gw --timeout=60s

# STEP 3: Create HTTPRoute with WRONG backend ref (THE BUG!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: api-canary
  namespace: easypj-gw
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: easypj-gateway
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api
    backendRefs:
    - name: easypj-api-v1   # ❌ BUG! Service "easypj-api-v1" doesn't exist!
      port: 80
      weight: 90            # 90% of traffic
    - name: easypj-api-v2   # ❌ BUG! Service "easypj-api-v2" doesn't exist!
      port: 80
      weight: 10            # 10% of traffic
EOF

# STEP 4: Check HTTPRoute status — shows error!
kubectl describe httproute api-canary -n easypj-gw
# ❌ BUG! "Service easypj-api-v1 not found" — backendRef name is WRONG!

# The APP STORY:
# "The canary deployment isn't routing any traffic!"
# HTTPRoute references Services that don't exist.
# Copy-paste from another environment kept old Service names.
# Gateway API is the future — but a typo still breaks everything.
2

⚠️ Observe the Error — HTTPRoute Backend Service Not Found

✗1. kubectl describe httproute api-canary -n easypj-gw → "Service easypj-api-v1 not found"
✗2. kubectl get svc -n easypj-gw → Services are "api-v1" and "api-v2" (correct!)
✗3. HTTPRoute backendRef names don't match actual Service names!
✗4. All /api traffic returns 500 — canary deployment is completely broken!
3

🔍 Debug — Why Doesn't the HTTPRoute Route Traffic?

1Check backendRef names: kubectl get httproute api-canary -n easypj-gw -o yaml | grep "name:"
→ backendRefs reference "easypj-api-v1" and "easypj-api-v2" — WRONG!
2Compare with actual Services: kubectl get svc -n easypj-gw -o name
→ service/api-v1, service/api-v2 — names DON'T match!
3Root cause: The HTTPRoute backendRef names ("easypj-api-v1") don't match the actual Service names ("api-v1"). Gateway API validates backendRefs and reports "Service not found" in the HTTPRoute status. Fix: update the HTTPRoute backendRef names to match the actual Service names.
4

🧠 Answer — Diagnostic Tenet & Expected Outputs

🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Traffic not routing → check HTTPRoute
②
"Service not found" → mismatch!
③
Compare backendRef names vs actual Svc
④
Fix backendRef to match Service names
⑤
Traffic splits 90/10 → canary works!

Tenet: Gateway API is the GA/stable successor to Ingress (not experimental) — it provides more expressive routing (traffic splitting, header-based routing, cross-namespace references), but it still needs a real controller implementation installed (NGINX Gateway Fabric, Istio, Envoy Gateway, etc.) plus an Accepted GatewayClass/Gateway before any HTTPRoute can route traffic at all. HTTPRoute backendRef.name must match an actual Service name in the same namespace. Gateway API reports status conditions for invalid configurations — always check HTTPRoute status with kubectl describe httproute.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe httproute api-canary -n easypj-gw | grep -A3 Status Status: Parents: Message: Service "easypj-api-v1" not found ← BACKEND SERVICE DOESN'T EXIST!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get httproute api-canary -n easypj-gw NAME HOSTNAMES AGE api-canary 15m ← HTTPRoute ACCEPTED — traffic flowing 90/10!
5

🔧 Fix — Correct HTTPRoute Backend Service Names

BASH — Patch HTTPRoute with correct backendRef names 
# Delete the broken HTTPRoute and recreate with correct names
kubectl delete httproute api-canary -n easypj-gw

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: api-canary
  namespace: easypj-gw
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: easypj-gateway
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api
    backendRefs:
    - name: api-v1   # ✅ CORRECT! Matches actual Service name!
      port: 80
      weight: 90
    - name: api-v2   # ✅ CORRECT!
      port: 80
      weight: 10
EOF

# Verify HTTPRoute accepted
kubectl describe httproute api-canary -n easypj-gw
6

✅ Verify — HTTPRoute Routes Traffic 90/10 to Correct Services

HTTPRoute status shows Accepted. Traffic flows: 90% to api-v1, 10% to api-v2. Key: Gateway API HTTPRoute backendRef.name must exactly match a Service name — and it also needs an Accepted parent Gateway (backed by a real controller) before any of that matters. Gateway API is GA/stable, offering declarative traffic splitting, header matching, and cross-namespace routing beyond what Ingress supports.
