🌳 Decision Trees — Systematic TroubleshootingDT1–DT15

Decision trees provide a step-by-step flowchart to diagnose common Kubernetes issues. Each node is a question — answer YES or NO to navigate to the next step. Follow the path to find the root cause and fix.

DT1
🌳 DECISION TREE DT1 — Pod Stuck Pending

Pod Stuck in Pending — Systematic Diagnosis Flowchart

The Problem: A pod is stuck in Pending state and won't schedule. This is the #1 most common Kubernetes issue. The scheduler can't place the pod on any node. Your job: follow this decision tree to find WHY and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Any cluster
▶

🚦 START — Pod Is Pending

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-api pod was deployed 20 minutes ago. It's still Pending — users can't access the job board. Is it resources? nodeSelector? Taints? PVC? Follow the tree to find out.
kubectl get pods -n easypj

🌿 NODE 1 — What does kubectl describe show?

Run this command first
kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod-name> | tail -20
Events Section — What Does It Show?
  • "0/N nodes available"
    → Go to NODE 2
  • "pod has unbound PVC"
    → Go to NODE 3
  • "node(s) had taint"
    → Go to NODE 4
  • "insufficient cpu/memory"
    → Go to NODE 5
  • "didn't match selector"
    → Go to NODE 6
  • No events / empty
    → Check scheduler logs
N2

🔴 NODE 2 — "0/N nodes are available"

Check node status
kubectl get nodes
Node Availability — Are ALL Nodes Ready?
  • YES → Check if node is cordoned:
    kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.unschedulable}'
    If true → Node is cordoned! Uncordon it.
  • NO → Some nodes NotReady → Check conditions:
    kubectl describe node <node> | grep Conditions
    MemoryPressure/DiskPressure/PIDPressure?
  • SSH to node — check kubelet:
    systemctl status kubelet
    journalctl -u kubelet -n 50
Restart kubelet on broken node
kubectl uncordon <node-name> sudo systemctl restart kubelet
N3

🔴 NODE 3 — "pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims"

Check PVC status
kubectl get pvc -n easypj
PVC Diagnosis — Why Is It Stuck?
  • "no persistent volumes available"?
    kubectl get pv — check if any PV matches
    StorageClass mismatch? PV capacity < PVC request? accessMode mismatch?
  • "storageclass not found"?
    kubectl get sc — does the SC exist?
    Provisioner broken? Check CSI driver pods
  • VolumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer?
    PVC stays Pending until a Pod uses it — this is NORMAL, deploy the pod first
Fix StorageClass name — storageClassName is IMMUTABLE on an existing PVC, the API server rejects a patch to it. Delete and recreate the PVC instead
kubectl apply -f pv.yaml kubectl delete pvc <name> -n easypj kubectl apply -f pvc-corrected.yaml
N4

🔴 NODE 4 — "node(s) had taint that the pod didn't tolerate"

Check node taints
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.taints}{"\n"}{end}'
Check pod tolerations
kubectl get pod -n easypj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 tolerations
Taint Fix Options
  • Option 1: Add toleration to pod spec
    Patch the Deployment to tolerate the taint
  • Option 2: Remove taint from node (if safe)
    kubectl taint node <node> <key>-
    Only do this if other workloads SHOULD run on this node
Add toleration to pod (patch deployment)
kubectl taint node <node> node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule- kubectl patch deploy <name> -n easypj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/tolerations","value":[{"key":"key","operator":"Equal","value":"val","effect":"NoSchedule"}]} ]'
N5

🔴 NODE 5 — "insufficient cpu/memory"

Check node capacity
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Allocated resources" kubectl top nodes
Resource Fix Options
  • Reduce pod resource requests
    Lower CPU/memory requests to fit available capacity
  • Add more nodes to the cluster
    Scale horizontally if this is a persistent need
  • Remove old pods to free resources
    kubectl delete pod <old-pod>
  • Use Cluster Autoscaler (cloud only)
Lower CPU request
kubectl patch deploy <name> -n easypj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu","value":"100m"} ]'
N6

🔴 NODE 6 — "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector"

Check pod's node selector
kubectl get pod -n easypj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 nodeSelector
Check pod's node affinity
kubectl get pod -n easypj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A20 affinity
Check node labels
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
Selector/Affinity Diagnosis
  • Does any node have the required label?
    kubectl get nodes --show-labels
    If NO → Label a node: kubectl label node <node> key=value
  • Is podAntiAffinity or topologySpreadConstraints blocking?
    podAntiAffinity: other pods with the same label already on that node (a separate mechanism)? OR topologySpreadConstraints: maxSkew too strict for the current pod/zone distribution (note: maxSkew itself must be ≥1, "maxSkew=0" isn't a valid value — the API rejects it)?
    For podAntiAffinity: relax the rule or add more nodes. For topologySpreadConstraints: increase maxSkew or use whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
Remove impossible nodeSelector
kubectl label node <node> disktype=ssd kubectl patch deploy <name> -n easypj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"remove","path":"/spec/template/spec/nodeSelector/disktype"} ]'
✓

✅ Decision Tree Complete — Pod Pending Resolution

Quick reference:
kubectl describe pod → Read Events → Follow the path.
N2 = Nodes not available · N3 = PVC not bound · N4 = Taints · N5 = No resources · N6 = Selector mismatch
Pro tip: 90% of Pending pods are N4 (taints) or N6 (selectors). Start there.

DT2
🌳 DECISION TREE DT2 — CrashLoopBackOff

Pod CrashLoopBackOff — Systematic Diagnosis Flowchart

The Problem: Pod keeps restarting every few seconds. STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff. The container starts, crashes, and Kubernetes restarts it — over and over. Your job: find why it's crashing and fix it.
▶

🚦 START — Pod Is CrashLoopBackOff

📖 APP STORY: easypj-api was deployed 10 minutes ago. RESTARTS=47. The pod keeps crashing. Users get 503 errors. What's killing it?
Check exit code
kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> | grep "Exit Code"
Check logs (previous instance too!)
kubectl logs -n easypj <pod> --previous
Exit Codes & What They Mean
  • Exit Code: 0 — Normal exit
    Did the command finish? Is it a Job/CronJob? If Deployment: check args/command.
  • Exit Code: 1 — Application error
    kubectl logs <pod> --previous
    Missing env vars? Wrong config? Database connection failed?
  • Exit Code: 137 — OOMKilled (SIGKILL)
    Memory limit too low! Increase limits.
    kubectl describe pod | grep OOMKilled
    kubectl top pods
  • Exit Code: 143 — SIGTERM (graceful shutdown)
    App received termination signal. Normal behavior.
  • Exit Code: 255 — Entrypoint error
    Wrong CMD/ENTRYPOINT? Missing binary? Check the image.
    kubectl exec into a running copy to test
🔥

🔴 Action Paths

Application Crash (Exit 1)
kubectl logs -n easypj <pod> --previous | tail -30 → Fix the app code or configuration
OOMKilled (Exit 137)
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"512Mi"}]'
Missing command/entrypoint (Exit 255)
kubectl edit deploy <name> -n easypj → Fix command/args in spec.template.spec.containers
Probe kills pod (Liveness failing)
kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> | grep -A5 Liveness → Adjust initialDelaySeconds or fix probe endpoint
DT3
🌳 DECISION TREE DT3 — ImagePullBackOff

Pod Stuck in ImagePullBackOff — Image Pull Failure Diagnosis

The Problem: Pod shows ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull. Kubernetes can't download the container image. The pod never reaches Running.
▶

🚦 START — Pod Can't Pull Image

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team pushed a new API image to a private registry. The Deployment YAML references it but Kubernetes can't pull it. Pod shows ImagePullBackOff. The new feature can't go live until the image pulls successfully.
Check the exact error
kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> | grep -A5 "Failed"
Image Pull Error Types
  • Image name / tag correct?
    kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep image
    Check for typos, wrong tag, wrong registry
  • Public image — can you pull it manually?
    docker pull <image> from your laptop
  • Private image — imagePullSecrets created?
    kubectl get secrets -n easypj
    "unauthorized: authentication required" → Create docker-registry secret
  • "manifest unknown" / "not found"
    Image or tag doesn't exist in registry
  • "dial tcp: i/o timeout"
    Network issue — can node reach registry? Check proxy/firewall/DNS
Patch deployment to use the secret
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n easypj \ --docker-server=myregistry.com \ --docker-username=user --docker-password=pass kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/imagePullSecrets","value":[{"name":"regcred"}]} ]'
DT4
🌳 DECISION TREE DT4 — Node NotReady

Node NotReady — Systematic Node Diagnosis

The Problem: A node shows NotReady. Pods on that node show Unknown or Terminating. New pods can't schedule there.
▶

🚦 START — Node Is NotReady

📖 APP STORY: 4:00 AM — PagerDuty fires: "Node worker-2 is NotReady". Half the easypj API pods were running on that node. Users see 503 errors. Database connections are failing. Every minute of downtime costs real job postings.
Check node conditions
kubectl describe node <name> | grep -A10 Conditions
Node Condition Diagnosis
  • KubeletReady=False → SSH to node:
    systemctl status kubelet
    journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager
    cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
  • MemoryPressure=True → Node out of RAM
    kubectl top node <name>
    Free memory by evicting pods or add more RAM/nodes
  • DiskPressure=True → Disk full
    ssh: df -h /
    crictl rmi --prune / journalctl --vacuum-size=200M
  • NetworkUnavailable=True → CNI not running
    kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|flannel|cilium'
Restart CNI plugin
sudo systemctl restart kubelet kubectl rollout restart ds <cni-daemonset> -n kube-system
DT5
🌳 DECISION TREE DT5 — Service Not Accessible

Service Not Accessible — End-to-End Connectivity Diagnosis

The Problem: curl to a Service IP or name returns timeout or connection refused. The Service exists but traffic doesn't reach pods.
▶

🚦 START — Service Unreachable

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-web frontend can't reach easypj-api. curl to the Service ClusterIP hangs. The job board loads but shows "API Error" for all job listings. The Service exists, pods are Running — but traffic isn't flowing.

# What type of access is failing?

Service Connectivity Checklist
  • ClusterIP not working:
    kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n easypj (or the current mechanism: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> -n easypj)
    ENDPOINTS: <none> → No pods matched! Check selector vs pod labels
  • Check pods are READY (not just Running):
    kubectl get pods -n easypj — check READY column
    If 0/1 → Readiness probe failing!
  • NodePort not working:
    ss -tlnp | grep <port> on the node
    Firewall blocking? Check iptables: sudo iptables -L -n | grep <port>
Open NodePort firewall
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 30080 -j ACCEPT
DT6
🌳 DECISION TREE DT6 — PVC Stuck Pending

PVC Stuck in Pending — Storage Binding Diagnosis

The Problem: PersistentVolumeClaim shows Pending forever. Pods that reference it can't start. The PVC can't find a matching PV.
▶

🚦 START — PVC Stuck Pending

📖 APP STORY: The easypj database needs persistent storage. DevOps created a PVC for 50Gi but it's been Pending for 2 hours. The PostgreSQL pod can't start. The entire job board is down waiting for storage.
Check PVC status and events
kubectl describe pvc -n easypj <pvc-name> | tail -15
PVC Binding Checklist (ALL must match!)
  • StorageClass exists? kubectl get sc → If not found: Create SC or fix SC name in PVC
  • PV with enough capacity exists? kubectl get pv --sort-by=.spec.capacity.storage → PV capacity must be ≥ PVC request
  • accessModes match? PVC: ReadWriteOnce vs PV: ReadWriteMany → FAIL → Both sides must match exactly
  • storageClassName matches? PVC: fast-ssd vs PV: standard → FAIL → Use "" (empty) for no SC, or match exactly
  • Dynamic provisioning: SC provisioner working? kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep provisioner → Check provisioner pod logs for errors
  • VolumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer? → This is NORMAL — deploy the pod first
Create matching PV
kubectl apply -f - << EOF apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolume metadata: {name: new-pv} spec: {capacity: {storage: 10Gi}, accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce], storageClassName: standard, hostPath: {path: /mnt/data}} EOF
DT7
🌳 DECISION TREE DT7 — Out of Memory (OOM)

OOMKilled / Memory Exhaustion — Diagnosis & Prevention

The Problem: Pods being killed with exit code 137 (OOMKilled). Node shows MemoryPressure. Applications crashing due to insufficient memory.
▶

🚦 START — OOM / Memory Issues

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-api Django pod keeps getting OOMKilled every 15 minutes. Users submit job applications but get 500 errors when the pod restarts. Memory graphs show a sawtooth pattern — the pod hits its limit and gets killed.
Check if pod was OOMKilled
kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> | grep -i oom kubectl get pod -n easypj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 lastState
Memory Recovery Actions
  • If OOMKilled (confirmed above): raise the container's own memory limit
    This is the actual fix for THIS symptom — the container exceeded its own cgroup limit. Node-level actions below don't touch that limit at all.
  • Delete unused pods/namespaces
    Only relevant for a DIFFERENT problem — new pods stuck Pending due to node capacity, not an already-OOMKilled container
  • Reduce resource requests of other pods
    Also a node-capacity/scheduling action, not applicable to fixing an OOMKilled container's own limit
  • Add more nodes (cluster autoscaler)
    Scale out if this is genuinely a capacity issue — not a fix for OOMKilled itself
Increase memory limit
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"1Gi"}, {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/memory","value":"512Mi"} ]'
DT8
🌳 DECISION TREE DT8 — Certificate Issues

Certificate Expiry / TLS Errors — Diagnosis & Renewal

The Problem: kubectl returns "Unauthorized" or "certificate expired". TLS connections fail. API server inaccessible. Certificates are the most overlooked Kubernetes component.
▶

🚦 START — TLS/Certificate Issues

📖 APP STORY: It's been 13 months since the easypj cluster was set up with kubeadm. Suddenly kubectl returns "Unauthorized". The certificates expired at the 1-year mark. No one set a calendar reminder. The entire ops team is locked out.
Check certificate expiration (kubeadm)
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration
Client Certificate Issues
  • Check ~/.kube/config for client-certificate-data
    Is the certificate still valid? Check expiry date
  • Expired? Regenerate:
    sudo kubeadm certs renew all
    Or use cert-manager for automated renewal
Renew kubeadm PKI certificates and restore access
sudo kubeadm certs renew all sudo systemctl restart kubelet sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config
DT9
🌳 DECISION TREE DT9 — DNS Resolution Failure

DNS Not Working — Service Discovery Diagnosis

The Problem: Pods can't resolve Service names. nslookup fails. "Could not resolve host" errors everywhere. DNS is the nervous system of Kubernetes.
▶

🚦 START — DNS Not Working

📖 APP STORY: easypj-web can't resolve easypj-api.svc.cluster.local. nslookup times out. The microservice chain is broken — web can't reach API, API can't reach DB. CoreDNS pods are running but not responding to queries. Every service call fails.
Test DNS from a debug pod
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default
CHECKLIST
  • Are CoreDNS pods running? kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns → Check CoreDNS ConfigMap (Corefile) for errors
  • Is CoreDNS Service up? kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns → ClusterIP should be 10.96.0.10 (default)
  • Is /etc/resolv.conf correct in pods? kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf → search should include <ns>.svc.cluster.local
  • NetworkPolicy blocking DNS? → Default-deny egress blocks DNS by default
  • CoreDNS ConfigMap corrupted? kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml → kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/coredns
  • kube-dns service has endpoints? kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system kube-dns → <none> = CoreDNS pods not matching Service
Allow DNS in NetworkPolicy (add egress rule)
kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system kubectl apply -f - << EOF apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: easypj} spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Egress], egress: [{to: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}}], ports: [{port: 53, protocol: UDP}]}]} EOF
DT10
🌳 DECISION TREE DT10 — API Server Unreachable

API Server Unreachable — kubectl Connection Refused

The Problem: kubectl returns "The connection to the server ... was refused". API server is down or unreachable. The cluster is headless.
▶

🚦 START — kubectl Can't Connect

📖 APP STORY: A junior admin edited the kube-apiserver.yaml manifest to add a feature gate — but made a YAML indent error. The API server static pod crashed. kubectl returns "connection refused". No one can access the cluster. easypj is completely unmanageable.
Test connectivity
kubectl cluster-info curl -k https://127.0.0.1:6443/healthz
CHECKLIST
  • Is API server static pod running? sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver
    sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml → YAML syntax error? Fix and save — kubelet auto-restarts static pods!
  • Is port 6443 listening? sudo ss -tlnp | grep 6443
    sudo journalctl -u kubelet | grep apiserver → Check kubelet logs for API server errors
  • Is kubeconfig correct? kubectl config view → client-certificate — expired?
  • Is keepalived / VIP working? (HA setups) → ping <control-plane-endpoint>
  • etcd is prerequisite — is etcd running? sudo crictl ps | grep etcd → See DT11: etcd Issues
Check kubelet is running (manages static pods)
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.bak \ /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml sudo systemctl status kubelet sudo systemctl restart kubelet
DT11
🌳 DECISION TREE DT11 — etcd Issues

etcd Problems — Database Space Exhaustion & Prevention

The Problem: kubectl returns "etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded" or "etcd cluster is unavailable". etcd is the brain of Kubernetes — when it fails, everything fails.
▶

🚦 START — etcd Issues

📖 APP STORY: kubectl apply returns "etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded". The cluster is READ-ONLY. The easypj team can't deploy a critical hotfix. No resources can be created or modified. etcd hit its 2GB quota — the entire cluster is frozen.
Check etcd health
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \ --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \ --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \ --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \ endpoint health
etcd Prevention
  • Schedule regular snapshots (cronjob)
    Daily automated etcd backups via CronJob
  • Monitor DB size (alert at 70%)
    Set up Prometheus alerts for etcd DB size
  • Compaction + defrag monthly
    etcdctl compact <rev>
    etcdctl defrag
Compact + Defrag + Disarm etcd (all three are required — compact/defrag alone do NOT restore writes if a NOSPACE alarm already fired)
REV=$(sudo etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \ --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \ --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \ --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \ endpoint status --write-out=json | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]['Status']['header']['revision'])") sudo etcdctl compact $REV sudo etcdctl defrag sudo etcdctl alarm list sudo etcdctl alarm disarm
DT12
🌳 DECISION TREE DT12 — Network Policy Blocking

NetworkPolicy Blocking Traffic — Connectivity Diagnosis

The Problem: Pod A can't reach Pod B. curl times out. Nginx ingress returns 502. NetworkPolicy might be silently blocking traffic.
▶

🚦 START — Pod-to-Pod Communication Fails

📖 APP STORY: The security team applied new NetworkPolicies to lock down the easypj namespace. Now the web frontend can't reach the API. curl hangs and times out. The policies are silently dropping packets — no error messages, just dead connections.
Test connectivity from source pod
kubectl exec -n easypj <src-pod> -- curl -s --connect-timeout 3 http://<target-svc>
ISOLATION CHECKLIST
  • Are there ANY NetworkPolicies in the namespace?
    kubectl get networkpolicies -n easypj
    If none, traffic is ALLOWED by default
  • Does a policy select the SOURCE pod?
    kubectl describe networkpolicy -n easypj
    Check podSelector — matches source pod labels?
  • Does the policy allow EGRESS to the target?
    Check egress rules: to.namespaceSelector? to.podSelector? to.ipBlock?
  • Does a policy select the TARGET pod?
    Check ingress rules on target namespace
    from.podSelector matches source pod?
  • Default-deny in place? (empty podSelector {})
    Blocks ALL unless explicitly allowed. Must add allow rules BEFORE applying deny-all.
  • DNS blocked? (UDP 53 to kube-system)
    Common with default-deny egress
    → See DT9: DNS Resolution Failure
  • DEBUG: Temporarily delete policies to isolate:
    kubectl delete networkpolicy --all -n easypj
    If traffic works → policy was blocking it!
Create allow-egress-to-API policy
kubectl apply -f - << EOF apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: {name: allow-web-to-api, namespace: easypj} spec: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-web}} policyTypes: [Egress] egress: - to: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}}] ports: [{port: 80, protocol: TCP}] EOF
DT13
🌳 DECISION TREE DT13 — OOMKilled Deep Dive

OOMKilled — Container Memory Limit Exceeded

The Problem: Pod shows OOMKilled and restart count climbing. Exit code 137. The Linux kernel's OOM killer terminated the container because it exceeded its memory limit.
▶

🚦 START — Pod Was OOMKilled

📖 APP STORY: easypj-api keeps getting killed with exit code 137. RESTARTS=89 and climbing. The Django application processes image uploads — each image consumes 200MB in memory. With a 512Mi limit, processing 3 concurrent uploads triggers OOMKill. Job applications with resume attachments are failing.
Confirm OOMKilled
kubectl describe pod -n easypj <pod> | grep OOMKilled kubectl get pod -n easypj <pod> -o yaml | grep -A10 lastState | grep reason
OOM DIAGNOSIS
  • What is the current memory limit? kubectl get pod -o yaml | grep -A2 'limits:' → If limit ≤ actual usage → OOMKilled
  • What is the actual memory usage? kubectl top pod -n easypj
    (if pod restarted, check historical metrics)
  • For Java apps: -Xmx should be ≤ 75% of container limit
    Use: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
    If -Xmx=1G but limit=512Mi → OOMKilled
  • For Python/Django apps: Check worker processes × memory per worker
    Gunicorn workers: --workers × --max-requests
  • For Node.js apps: Check --max-old-space-size (heap limit)
    Should be ≤ container memory limit
  • Is there a memory leak? Monitor usage over time with kubectl top -w
    If usage grows continuously → memory leak
Increase container memory limit
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n easypj --type=json -p='[ {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"1Gi"}, {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/memory","value":"512Mi"} ]'
DT14
🌳 DECISION TREE DT14 — DiskPressure

DiskPressure — Node Disk Full Diagnosis

The Problem: Node shows DiskPressure=True. Pods being evicted. New pods can't schedule. Container images and logs have filled the disk.
▶

🚦 START — Node Has DiskPressure

📖 APP STORY: Node "easy" shows DiskPressure=True. Pods are being evicted. The easypj database pod was killed mid-transaction. Container images from 6 months of CI/CD builds have accumulated. /var/lib/containerd is at 92%. The disk is choking the cluster.
Verify DiskPressure
kubectl describe node <name> | grep DiskPressure
SSH to Node — Check Disk
ssh <node> 'df -h / /var /var/lib/containerd /var/log'
DISK CLEANUP STRATEGIES
  • Container images (usually BIGGEST culprit)
    sudo crictl rmi --prune
    (Removes all unused images — can free 10GB+)
  • Container logs
    sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M
    sudo find /var/log/pods -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete
  • Docker/buildah build cache
    sudo docker system prune -a -f
  • Old snapshots/backups
    ls -la /tmp/*.db /var/backups/
    Remove old etcd snapshots if safe
  • /var/log is huge
    du -sh /var/log/* | sort -rh | head -10
    Clean up old rotated logs
  • Set up log rotation (PREVENTION)
    The --container-log-max-size/--container-log-max-files CLI flags still work but are deprecated — set containerLogMaxSize: 10Mi / containerLogMaxFiles: 5 in the KubeletConfiguration file instead (typically /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml)
Clean up images and logs to reclaim disk space
sudo crictl rmi --prune sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M sudo find /var/log/pods -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete df -h /
DT15
🌳 DECISION TREE DT15 — kubeadm Join Failed

kubeadm Join Failed — Worker Node Registration Diagnosis

The Problem: kubeadm join returns errors. New worker node can't join the cluster. The token, discovery, or network is broken.
▶

🚦 START — kubeadm join Fails

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team is scaling out — adding 3 new worker nodes for the upcoming job fair traffic spike. But kubeadm join keeps failing on all 3 nodes. The token expired after 24 hours. The fair starts in 2 hours and the cluster needs more capacity NOW.
Typical join command format
sudo kubeadm join <control-plane-ip>:6443 \ --token <token> \ --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>
JOIN FAILURE CHECKLIST
  • "token not found" / "token expired" kubeadm token create --print-join-command → Generate new token on control plane:
  • "could not find the information for the CA cert" openssl x509 -pubkey -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt | \
    openssl rsa -pubin -outform der 2>/dev/null | \
    openssl dgst -sha256 -hex | sed 's/^.* //' → Get correct hash:
  • "connection refused" / "no route to host" → Check --control-plane-endpoint resolves
  • "different Kubernetes version" sudo apt install kubeadm=1.32.x-* → Install matching version:
  • "container runtime not running" → Check /etc/containerd/config.toml exists
  • "preflight check: kubelet not running" → sudo systemctl start kubelet
  • "swap is enabled" → Comment out swap line in /etc/fstab
Check control-plane reachability from worker
kubeadm token create --print-join-command curl -k https://<cp-ip>:6443/version

⌨️ Appendix A: Top 50 CommandsQuick Reference

Essential commands for the CKA exam. Memorize these — they cover ~80% of exam tasks.

Pod & Deployment Management
  • kubectl get pods -A — List all pods
  • kubectl describe pod <name> -n <ns> — Pod details + events
  • kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --previous — Previous crash logs
  • kubectl exec -it <pod> -n <ns> -- /bin/sh — Shell into pod
  • kubectl create deploy <name> --image=<img> --replicas=2 — Quick deploy
  • kubectl rollout restart deploy <name> -n <ns> — Restart pods
  • kubectl rollout undo deploy <name> -n <ns> — Rollback
  • kubectl scale deploy <name> --replicas=5 -n <ns> — Scale
  • kubectl run <name> --image=<img> --rm -it --restart=Never -- <cmd> — One-off pod
  • kubectl edit deploy <name> -n <ns> — Edit live
Node & Cluster
  • kubectl get nodes -o wide — Node list with details
  • kubectl describe node <name> — Node conditions + capacity
  • kubectl top nodes / kubectl top pods -A — Resource usage
  • kubectl cordon <node> / kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets — Node maintenance
  • kubectl taint node <node> key=value:NoSchedule — Add taint
  • kubectl label node <node> key=value — Label node
  • sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration — Cert expiry
  • sudo kubeadm certs renew all — Renew all certs
  • sudo systemctl restart kubelet — Restart kubelet
  • sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager — Kubelet logs
Storage
  • kubectl get pv,pvc -A — List volumes
  • kubectl describe pvc <name> -n <ns> — PVC events
  • kubectl get sc — Storage classes
  • kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-literal=key=val — Create secret
  • kubectl create configmap <name> --from-literal=key=val — Create ConfigMap
Networking
  • kubectl get svc,endpoints -A — Services + endpoints
  • kubectl expose deploy <name> --port=80 --target-port=8080 — Create Service
  • kubectl get networkpolicies -A — Network policies
  • kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.28 --restart=Never -- nslookup <svc> — DNS test
  • kubectl port-forward pod/<name> 8080:80 — Local port forward
YAML Generation & Output
  • kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml > pod.yaml — Export YAML
  • kubectl explain pod.spec.containers — API docs
  • kubectl create deploy <name> --image=<img> --dry-run=client -o yaml — Generate YAML
  • kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' — JSONPath
  • kubectl apply -f <file> / kubectl delete -f <file> — Declarative
  • kubectl patch deploy <name> --type=json -p='[...]' — Patch
  • kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp — Events
  • kubectl api-resources — List all API resources
  • kubectl explain <resource> --recursive — Full resource docs
  • alias k=kubectl — Save keystrokes!
etcd
  • kubeadm etcd enforces mutual TLS — every live etcdctl command below needs the same --endpoints/--cacert/--cert/--key flags, not just backup.
  • sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /tmp/backup.db — Backup
  • sudo etcdutl snapshot restore /tmp/backup.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore — Restore (offline, no TLS flags needed — etcdutl is the current tool for this since etcd v3.5)
  • sudo etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key endpoint health — Health check
  • sudo etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key endpoint status --write-out=table — Cluster status
  • sudo etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key compact <rev> && sudo etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key defrag — Maintenance

📁 Appendix B: easypj/jobpost File StructureLayout

Complete file structure for the easypj/jobpost Django job board application used across all scenarios — both Kubernetes manifests and Django source.

Kubernetes Manifests (easypj/)
  • 00-namespace.yaml — Namespace with labels
  • 01-storageclass.yaml — StorageClass (fast-ssd-sc)
  • 02-persistentvolume.yaml — PV (hostPath or CSI)
  • 03-postgres-pvc.yaml — PVC for PostgreSQL
  • 04-postgres-statefulset.yaml — PostgreSQL StatefulSet + PVC template
  • 05-postgres-service.yaml — DB ClusterIP (port 5432)
  • 06-redis-deployment.yaml — Redis Deployment (session cache)
  • 07-redis-service.yaml — Redis ClusterIP (port 6379)
  • 08-api-deployment.yaml — Django REST API Deployment
  • 09-api-service.yaml — API ClusterIP (port 8000)
  • 10-api-hpa.yaml — HorizontalPodAutoscaler (CPU 70%)
  • 11-web-deployment.yaml — Nginx frontend Deployment
  • 12-web-service.yaml — Web ClusterIP (port 80)
  • 13-ingress.yaml — Ingress with TLS termination
  • 14-tls-secret.yaml — TLS certificate (kubernetes.io/tls)
  • 15-network-policy.yaml — NetworkPolicy (web→api→db)
  • 16-configmap.yaml — Django settings as ConfigMap
  • 17-db-credentials-secret.yaml — DB password, secret key
  • 18-resourcequota.yaml — Namespace ResourceQuota
  • 19-pod-disruption-budget.yaml — PDB for API
Django Application Source (easypj/jobpost/)
  • Dockerfile — Multi-stage Python 3.11 + Gunicorn build
  • Dockerfile.dev — Development with hot-reload
  • docker-compose.yml — Local dev (PostgreSQL + Redis + Django)
  • requirements.txt — Python dependencies (Django, DRF, psycopg2, Celery, redis)
  • manage.py — Django management CLI
  • easypj/settings.py — Django configuration (DB, static, CORS, DRF)

  • jobpost/models.py — Job, Company, Application Django models
  • jobpost/views.py — Web and API views
  • jobpost/serializers.py — Django REST Framework serializers

Complete Kubernetes manifest reference for the easypj/jobpost application — same 20 numbered files used across every Part 2/3 scenario (see Appendix B for the full file tree). Each file with its purpose.

Kubernetes Manifest Files & Purpose
  • 00-namespace.yaml — Namespace with labels for resource organization

🌳 Appendix D: Decision Tree FlowchartsOverview

Quick-reference index of all 15 decision trees with their diagnostic paths.

Decision Tree Index
  • DT1: Pod Stuck Pending — 6-node flowchart: Events → Nodes/PVC/Taints/Resources/Selectors
  • DT2: CrashLoopBackOff — Exit codes 0/1/137/143/255 + 4 action paths
  • DT3: ImagePullBackOff — 4 error types: auth/manifest/timeout/typo
  • DT4: Node NotReady — 4 conditions: Kubelet/Memory/Disk/Network
  • DT5: Service Not Accessible — 3 checks: ClusterIP endpoints/pod readiness/NodePort firewall
  • DT6: PVC Stuck Pending — 6-point binding checklist: SC/capacity/accessMode/className/provisioner/WaitForFirstConsumer
  • DT7: Out of Memory — Pod-level OOM (Exit 137) + Node-level MemoryPressure
  • DT8: Certificate Issues — kubeadm cert expiry + client cert (kubeconfig)
  • DT9: DNS Resolution Failure — 6-point checklist: CoreDNS/Service/resolv.conf/NetworkPolicy/ConfigMap/endpoints
  • DT10: API Server Unreachable — 5 checks: static pod/port/kubeconfig/VIP/etcd
  • DT11: etcd Issues — Space exhaustion (NOSPACE alarm) + prevention
  • DT12: Network Policy Blocking — 7-point isolation checklist
  • DT13: OOMKilled Deep Dive — Memory limits + Java/Python/Node.js specifics
  • DT14: DiskPressure — 5 cleanup strategies + log rotation prevention
  • DT15: kubeadm Join Failed — 7 failure reasons: token/cert/network/version/runtime/kubelet/swap

🏗️ Appendix E: Architecture DiagramsReference

Key Kubernetes architecture — control plane, request flow, pod lifecycle, and application topology.

1. Control Plane + Worker Nodes
  • API Server :6443 (the hub — every other component only talks to this)
    ↕ Scheduler ↕ Controller Manager ↕ etcd :2379
    Scheduler and Controller Manager never talk to each other or to etcd directly — only to the API Server. Control Plane — typically 3 nodes for HA
    Worker 1
    kubelet · containerd · kube-proxy     Worker 2
    kubelet · containerd · kube-proxy     Worker 3
    kubelet · containerd · kube-proxy
2. Request Flow: kubectl → API Server → etcd
  • kubectl apply → AuthN → AuthZ (RBAC) → Admission Controllers → etcd (persist)
3. Pod Lifecycle
  • Pending
    (incl. "ContainerCreating" status)     → Running → Succeeded / Failed
    Only 5 official Pod phases exist: Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown. "ContainerCreating" is a kubectl-displayed STATUS (from a container's Waiting-state reason), not a separate phase — node assign, PVC bind, image pull, and init containers all happen while the phase is still Pending. CrashLoopBackOff = Running → Crash → Restart → Crash → ...
4. Service + Endpoints + kube-proxy
  • Service (ClusterIP 10.96.x.x)
    ├── Endpoints: [10.0.1.5:80, 10.0.2.7:80]
    │ (only READY pods appear here)
    └── kube-proxy → iptables/ipvs DNAT: ClusterIP → PodIP
    curl 10.96.x.x:80 → iptables DNAT → Pod 10.0.1.5:80
5. Ingress → Service → Pod Traffic Path
  • Internet → Ingress Controller (Nginx)
    ├── /api/* → easypj-api Service → Pod api:8000
    ├── / → easypj-web Service → Pod web:80
    └── TLS terminated at Ingress
6. easypj/jobpost Application Topology
  • Ingress → easypj-web
    Nginx :80     → easypj-api
    Django :8000     → easypj-db
    PostgreSQL :5432
    easypj-redis
    Redis :6379 (session/cache)
    Desired=3 replicas → Scheduler → kubelet → containerd → Actual=3 ✓
7. etcd RAFT Consensus (3-node cluster)
  • LEADER
    node1
    writes →
    Follower
    node2
    Follower
    node3
    Quorum = 2/3 = majority required for writes
    etcdctl snapshot save → backup etcdctl snapshot restore → recover

☁️ Appendix F: AWS Integration NotesCloud

How the easypj/jobpost Kubernetes patterns translate to AWS cloud services. Useful for CKAD (which includes cloud-native concepts) and real-world deployments.

AWS Service Mapping
  • EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) vs self-managed kubeadm
    EKS manages the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler). You manage worker nodes and pods. kubeadm gives full control but requires self-management.
  • AWS Load Balancer Controller — ALB/NLB for Services
    kubectl annotate svc easypj-api service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type=external service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type=ip
    Creates real AWS NLB when you create a Service of type LoadBalancer in EKS. Note: a bare aws-load-balancer-type=nlb is a legacy value handled by the in-tree cloud provider, not this controller — use external to actually route through the AWS Load Balancer Controller.
  • EBS CSI Driver for PersistentVolumes
    Replaces hostPath with actual EBS gp3 volumes. StorageClass provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com. Supports ReadWriteOnce by default; io1/io2 volumes with Multi-Attach enabled can support ReadWriteMany for raw block devices across multiple nodes.
  • EFS CSI Driver for ReadWriteMany volumes
    Use when multiple pods across nodes need the same volume (e.g., shared uploads directory). NFS-based, supports RWX.
  • IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
    kubectl annotate sa easypj-api eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=arn:aws:iam::123:role/S3Access
    Pods get AWS IAM permissions without static credentials — no secrets needed for AWS API access
  • RDS (Relational Database Service) as external database
    Run PostgreSQL in RDS instead of StatefulSet for production. Connect via ExternalName Service or direct endpoint in ConfigMap.
  • ElastiCache (Redis) for Celery task queue
    Replace in-cluster Redis with managed ElastiCache for production durability. Connection string in Secret.

🎯 Appendix G: Exam Day Survival GuideStrategy

Everything you need to know about the CKA exam environment, time management, and common pitfalls.

Exam Environment (PSI Bridge)
  • Remote proctored exam — 2 hours, 15-20 performance-based tasks
    You get a clean Ubuntu desktop with terminal, browser, and the exam clusters pre-configured
  • Allowed browser tabs — kubernetes.io/docs, kubernetes.io/blog, helm.sh/docs, gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io
    Bookmark these! One extra tab open to docs can save you on obscure YAML fields. Also always available in-terminal (no policy needed, not a website): kubectl explain, kubectl --help.
  • Multiple clusters (exact count varies by exam version) — use kubectl config use-context to switch
    CHECK YOUR CONTEXT before every task! Run kubectl config get-contexts first — many people fail by running commands on the wrong cluster
Essential Aliases (set these FIRST)
  • alias k=kubectl — Save keystrokes on every command
  • export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml" — Generate YAML fast: k create deploy nginx --image=nginx $do
  • export now="--force --grace-period=0" — Force delete stuck pods
  • alias kn="kubectl config set-context --current --namespace" — Switch namespace quickly
Time Management Strategy
  • 120 minutes ÷ 17 tasks ≈ 7 minutes per task
    Spend 5 min solving, 2 min verifying. Flag hard tasks and come back.
  • First pass (90 min): Complete all easy/medium tasks. Skip hard ones.
    Second pass (30 min): Return to flagged tasks. Partial credit is better than zero.
  • Last 5 minutes: Verify all contexts, namespaces, and that resources are actually created
Common Pitfalls
  • Wrong context/namespace — Always verify: kubectl config current-context
  • YAML indentation — Use spaces, not tabs. 2-space indentation. Validate with --dry-run=client
  • Forgetting to save — In vim: :wq, in nano: Ctrl+O Enter Ctrl+X
  • Not reading the question fully — Look for "in namespace X" or "using the existing ServiceAccount Y"
Pre-Exam Checklist
  • ✅ System test passed (run at least 24h before)
  • ✅ Government-issued photo ID ready
  • ✅ Quiet, private room — no one else can enter
  • ✅ Clear desk — no papers, phone, second monitor
  • ✅ Water in a clear bottle (no labels)
  • ✅ Webcam + microphone working

📋 Appendix H: Cheat SheetReference

One-page quick reference for the CKA exam. YAML templates, imperative commands, resource abbreviations.

Resource Abbreviations
  • po = pods · deploy = deployments · svc = services · pvc = persistentvolumeclaims
  • pv = persistentvolumes · ns = namespaces · cm = configmaps
  • sa = serviceaccounts · no = nodes · netpol = networkpolicies · ing = ingresses
  • sc = storageclasses · hpa = horizontalpodautoscalers · pdb = poddisruptionbudgets
  • ds = daemonsets · sts = statefulsets · cj = cronjobs
  • secret, role, clusterrole — no dedicated kubectl short name registered; kubectl get secret/role/clusterrole works via singular-name matching, not a true abbreviation like the ones above
Imperative Commands (Fast YAML Generation)
  • k create deploy nginx --image=nginx --replicas=2 $do > deploy.yaml — Pod/Deployment
  • k expose deploy nginx --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=ClusterIP $do — Service
  • k create cm my-config --from-literal=KEY=val $do — ConfigMap
  • k create secret generic my-secret --from-literal=KEY=val $do — Secret
  • k create secret tls my-tls --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem $do — TLS Secret
  • k create sa my-sa $do — ServiceAccount
  • k create role my-role --verb=get,list --resource=pods $do — Role
  • k autoscale deploy nginx --min=2 --max=10 --cpu=70% $do — HPA
  • k create ingress my-ing --rule="host/path=svc:port" $do — Ingress
  • k run test --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes — Debug pod
JSONPath & Custom Columns
  • k get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' — All pod names
  • k get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}' — Node IPs
  • k get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,IP:.status.podIP,NODE:.spec.nodeName — Custom table
  • k get pods --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp — Sort by field
  • k get pods -l app=api --field-selector spec.nodeName=worker-1 — Label + field selector
Common Patching Patterns
  • k patch deploy nginx -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}' — Scale via patch
  • k patch deploy nginx --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image","value":"nginx:1.25"}]' — JSON patch
  • k patch pvc my-pvc -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}' — Resize PVC
  • k patch svc my-svc -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}' — Change Service type

🗺️ Appendix I: Learning RoadmapProgression

Structured path from Novice → Professional → Beyond CKA. Follow this roadmap to master Kubernetes.

🟢 Novice Phase (Weeks 1-4)
  • Containers & Kubernetes fundamentals — Sections F.1-F.5 in this guide
  • Storage basics + Workloads & Scheduling — Categories 1 & 3
  • Storage troubleshooting fundamentals — PVC binding, StorageClass mismatches, access modes (S1-S10 lab scenarios)
  • Goal: Understand Pods, Deployments, Services, PVCs. Deploy a working app.
🟡 Intermediate Phase (Weeks 5-8)
  • Services & Networking deep dive — Category 5 (Ingress, NetworkPolicy, CoreDNS)
  • Cluster Architecture + Troubleshooting — Categories 4 & 2
  • 50+ lab scenarios — HPA, RBAC, Ingress, NetworkPolicies, etcd backup
  • Goal: Diagnose and fix ANY common Kubernetes issue. Understand the control plane.
🔴 Advanced/Professional Phase (Weeks 9-12)
  • High Availability patterns — etcd disaster recovery, multi-master, cluster upgrades
  • Operators, CRDs, admission webhooks — Extending Kubernetes
  • Full-length timed practice exams — All 100 lab scenarios under time pressure (exam simulation)
  • Goal: Pass the CKA exam with confidence. Handle production incidents.
🚀 Beyond CKA (Ongoing)
  • CKAD: Application design, multi-container pods, deployment strategies (blue-green, canary)
  • CKS: Security hardening, Pod Security Standards, OPA/Gatekeeper, runtime security (Falco), supply chain
  • Real-world: Helm/Kustomize, GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux), observability (Prometheus/Grafana/Loki), service mesh (Istio)
  • Goal: Senior/Staff platform engineer. Design and operate multi-cluster Kubernetes at scale.

Every scenario, MCQ, and decision tree rated by difficulty. Use this to gauge your readiness and focus your study.

🚀 Appendix K: Beyond CKA — CKAD & CKSNext Steps

After CKA certification, where should you go next? Roadmap for CKAD, CKS, and real-world platform engineering.

CKAD: Certified Kubernetes Application Developer
  • Focus: Application design, build, and deployment on Kubernetes
  • Overlap with CKA: Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingress, HPA
  • New in CKAD: Multi-container pod patterns (sidecar, adapter, ambassador), deployment strategies (blue-green, canary), Jobs/CronJobs. (Helm itself is already in CKA's own curriculum — installing cluster components; CKAD goes deeper into packaging/deploying application charts.)
  • Key difference: CKAD is about USING Kubernetes to deploy apps. CKA is about OPERATING Kubernetes itself.
CKS: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist
  • Focus: Security hardening, supply chain security, runtime security, compliance
  • Prerequisite: Must hold CKA before taking CKS
  • Key topics: Pod Security Standards (PSS), OPA/Gatekeeper, Falco, ImagePolicyWebhook, NetworkPolicy hardening, etcd encryption, TLS everywhere, CIS benchmarks
  • Real-world: Security is the #1 concern for platform teams. CKS validates you can harden a Kubernetes cluster from development through production.
Real-World Platform Engineering Path
  • GitOps: ArgoCD / Flux — Declarative continuous delivery for Kubernetes
  • Observability: Prometheus + Grafana (metrics), Loki (logs), Tempo (traces) — The LGTM stack
  • Service Mesh: Istio / Linkerd / Cilium — mTLS, traffic splitting, zero-trust networking
  • Infrastructure as Code: Terraform / Pulumi for cluster provisioning, Crossplane for internal platforms
  • Policy as Code: Kyverno / OPA Gatekeeper — Automated compliance and security guardrails

⚡ Appendix L: CKA Exam Day — 20 Command Patterns You MUST KnowCRAM SHEET

🏆 Master Summary — How to Use These 20 Patterns

This appendix is your last-30-minutes-before-exam cram sheet. Every pattern here has appeared on real CKA exams. They are organized by domain weight — start with Troubleshooting (30%) and Cluster Architecture (25%) patterns first, as they make up 55% of your score.

📖
Step 1: Read all 20 patterns once (15 min)
✍️
Step 2: Type L.1, L.2, L.6, L.10 from memory (10 min)
✅
Step 3: Verify each command & take the exam (5 min buffer)
🎯 Implementation Strategy — How Each Pattern Maps to Exam Tasks
  • L.1–L.2 (etcd + kubeadm upgrade): These are guaranteed 2 tasks. etcd backup/restore is worth heavy points. kubeadm upgrade sequence must be exact. Type these from memory 5 times before exam.
  • L.3, L.13, L.17 (RBAC + SA + CSR): Security tasks appear in every CKA exam. Know RBAC imperatives cold. ServiceAccount + RoleBinding is a common combo task.
  • L.4, L.5, L.19 (Debug + Logs + Monitoring): Troubleshooting is 30% of your score. The debug pod pattern (kubectl run --rm -it) and log flags (--tail --since --previous) are your primary diagnostic tools.
  • L.6, L.10 (Imperative YAML + Rollouts): Your #1 speed hack. Generate YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml instead of typing 20-line manifests. Saves 30+ minutes across the exam.
  • L.7, L.11 (Node maintenance + Static pods): Cordon → drain → work → uncordon is tested on most exams. Static pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — remember: delete the FILE, not the pod.
  • L.8, L.17 (TLS + Certificates): TLS Ingress with kubernetes.io/tls Secret type. Certificate approval for joining nodes. Know: kubeadm certs check-expiration and kubectl certificate approve.
  • L.12, L.14 (NetworkPolicy + CronJob): NetworkPolicy is a frequent task — create a policy targeting specific pods with correct Ingress/Egress direction. CronJob: 5-field syntax, suspend/resume, manual trigger.
  • L.15, L.16, L.18, L.20 (Safe apply + JSONPath + Context + etcdctl): These are your "finishing touches" patterns. kubectl diff before applying. JSONPath for extracting specific fields. Context switching to avoid managing the wrong cluster. etcdctl deep dive for troubleshooting.

These are the 20 command patterns that appear on EVERY CKA exam. Memorize them cold. Practice typing them from memory — the exam has no autocomplete beyond kubectl built-in completion. Read this appendix in the 30 minutes before your exam.

L.1 — etcd Backup & Restore (Full TLS Flags)
1

Backup:

ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db

Restore (offline operation — since etcd v3.5, use etcdutl not etcdctl for this; no TLS flags needed):

etcdutl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore

⚠️ After restore: Update etcd static pod manifest (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml) to point --data-dir to the new path, then restart kubelet. snapshot restore already regenerates the member/cluster IDs automatically — there is no separate manifest field to edit for this. (--initial-cluster/--initial-cluster-token only matter when restoring a multi-member cluster, and are passed on the restore command itself, not edited afterward.)

L.2 — kubeadm Cluster Upgrade Sequence
2

On Control Plane:

# 1. Unhold and upgrade kubeadm

apt-mark unhold kubeadm && apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubeadm='1.30.x-*'
apt-mark hold kubeadm
# 2. Verify plan
kubeadm upgrade plan
# 3. Apply upgrade
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.x
# 4. Drain the control-plane node before touching kubelet
kubectl drain <cp-node> --ignore-daemonsets
# 5. Upgrade kubelet & kubectl
apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl && apt-get install -y kubelet='1.30.x-*' kubectl='1.30.x-*'
apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
# 6. Uncordon
kubectl uncordon <cp-node>

On Each Worker:

# 1. Drain the worker first (from CP)

kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# 2. SSH to worker, upgrade kubeadm package, run upgrade node — BEFORE touching the kubelet binary
apt-get install -y kubeadm='1.30.x-*'
kubeadm upgrade node
# 3. Now upgrade kubelet & restart
apt-get install -y kubelet='1.30.x-*'
systemctl restart kubelet
# 4. Uncordon
kubectl uncordon worker-1
L.3 — RBAC: auth can-i, Impersonation & Dry-Run
3
# Test if user can do something

kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=alice -n dev
kubectl auth can-i delete secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:api-sa -n dev

# List ALL permissions for a user
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=alice -n dev

# Create RBAC imperatively (FAST — use on exam!)
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n dev
kubectl create rolebinding alice-pod --role=pod-reader --user=alice -n dev
kubectl create clusterrole secret-reader --verb=get,list --resource=secrets
kubectl create clusterrolebinding alice-secret --clusterrole=secret-reader --user=alice

# For ServiceAccounts
kubectl create rolebinding sa-binding --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=dev:api-sa -n dev
L.4 — Debug Pod & Network Testing
4
# Temporary debug pod (auto-deletes on exit)

kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sh

# Test DNS from debug pod
kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -- nslookup -type=SRV _port._tcp.svc.ns

# Test connectivity
kubectl run curl-test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
  curl -v http://svc-name.ns.svc.cluster.local:8080

# Port forward for local debugging
kubectl port-forward svc/easypj-api 8080:80 -n easypj
kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-api-7d8f9 5432:5432 -n easypj

# Copy files to/from pods — kubectl cp only accepts [namespace/]podname:path, NOT a pod/name TYPE/NAME prefix
kubectl cp config.yaml easypj/name:/etc/config.yaml
kubectl cp easypj/name:/var/log/app.log ./app.log
L.5 — Logs: --tail, --since, --timestamps, --previous
5
# Logs from a specific container in a multi-container pod

kubectl logs pod/name -c sidecar -n easypj

# Last N lines
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api --tail=50 -n easypj

# Logs since a relative time
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api --since=10m -n easypj
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api --since=1h -n easypj

# Logs with timestamps
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api --timestamps -n easypj

# Logs from PREVIOUS (crashed) container
kubectl logs pod/name --previous -n easypj

# Follow logs in real-time
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api --follow -n easypj

# Combined: last 100 lines from previous container with timestamps
kubectl logs pod/name --previous --tail=100 --timestamps -n easypj
L.6 — Imperative YAML Generation (Your #1 Exam Speed Hack)
6
# Generate Deployment YAML without creating it

kubectl create deploy nginx --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

# Generate Pod YAML
kubectl run nginx --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml

# Generate Service YAML (expose a deployment)
kubectl expose deploy nginx --port=80 --target-port=8080 --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml

# Generate Service of type NodePort
kubectl expose deploy nginx --port=80 --type=NodePort --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml

# Generate ConfigMap from literal
kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=DEBUG=true --from-literal=DB_HOST=pg \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml

# Generate Secret (TLS) — MUST use kubectl create secret tls
kubectl create secret tls my-tls --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem -n ns \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > tls-secret.yaml

# Generate Secret (generic)
kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=password=s3cret \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > secret.yaml

# ⚠️ ALWAYS use --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate YAML quickly on the exam!
L.7 — Node Maintenance: Cordon → Drain → Work → Uncordon
7
# Mark node unschedulable (no NEW pods)

kubectl cordon worker-1

# Evict all pods safely (respects PDB, grace period)
kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# If drain hangs (PDB blocking):
# Option 1: Temporarily increase replicas
kubectl scale deploy/name --replicas=3
# Option 2: --disable-eviction bypasses the PDB check (use sparingly); --force separately allows draining unmanaged/standalone pods
kubectl drain worker-1 --disable-eviction --force

# After maintenance — allow scheduling again
kubectl uncordon worker-1

# Verify node status
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 Taints
L.8 — TLS Ingress & Certificate Commands
8
# Generate self-signed cert (for testing)

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -subj "/CN=easypj.com/O=easypj"

# Create TLS Secret (TYPE MUST BE kubernetes.io/tls)
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n easypj

# Verify TLS Secret keys (must be tls.crt and tls.key)
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq 'keys'

# Check certificate expiration
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' \
  | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates

# Check kubeadm certificates
kubeadm certs check-expiration
kubeadm certs renew all           # Renew ALL certs
kubeadm certs renew admin.conf    # Renew specific cert

# Approve/Deny CSRs
kubectl get csr
kubectl certificate approve csr-abc12
kubectl certificate deny csr-xyz99
L.9 — ConfigMap & Secret Imperative Creation
9
# ConfigMap from literals

kubectl create configmap app-config -n easypj \
  --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres.easypj.svc \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=false

# ConfigMap from file
kubectl create configmap nginx-config -n easypj --from-file=nginx.conf

# Secret from literals (values auto-base64-encoded by kubectl)
kubectl create secret generic db-creds -n easypj \
  --from-literal=username=admin \
  --from-literal=password=s3cret!

# Secret from file
kubectl create secret generic db-creds -n easypj \
  --from-file=password=./password.txt

# Docker registry secret (for private image pulls)
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n easypj \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=user --docker-password=pass

# ⚠️ Kubernetes AUTO-decodes Secrets when mounting. Don't base64-decode in your app!
L.10 — Scaling, Rollout & Rollback
10
# Scale deployment

kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=5 -n easypj

# Update image (triggers rolling update)
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api api=easypj/api:v2 -n easypj

# Set resource requests/limits
kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-api -n easypj \
  --requests=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi --limits=cpu=500m,memory=512Mi

# Watch rollout
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# View rollout history
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Rollback to previous version
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Rollback to specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api --to-revision=3 -n easypj

# Pause/resume rollout (useful for controlled rollouts)
kubectl rollout pause deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
kubectl rollout resume deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Restart pods (picks up new ConfigMap/Secret)
kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n easypj
L.11 — Static Pods & Manifest Paths
11
# Static pod manifest directory (kubelet watches this)

# Default: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# Configurable via staticPodPath in the kubelet's KubeletConfiguration (/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml)
# The --pod-manifest-path CLI flag still exists but is deprecated in favor of staticPodPath

# Create a static pod — just write a YAML to the directory
cat > /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-nginx.yaml <# Static pod appears as: static-nginx-
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep static-nginx

# Delete static pod: REMOVE the manifest file
rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-nginx.yaml

# ⚠️ Static pods CANNOT be deleted via kubectl delete pod!
# They are managed by kubelet, not the API server controller.
L.12 — NetworkPolicy Quick Patterns
12
# Allow ingress from specific namespace to pod

# Ingress = INTO the selected pod; Egress = OUT OF the selected pod
kubectl create -f - <# ⚠️ Key rules:
# 1. Always allow DNS: port 53/UDP to kube-system namespace
# 2. Always allow API server: your control-plane CIDR, port 6443
# 3. Default-deny-ALL (both directions) needs BOTH podSelector: {} AND explicit policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
#    (podSelector: {} alone denies Ingress by default, but leaves Egress wide open unless policyTypes says otherwise)
# 4. CNI MUST support NetworkPolicy: Calico ✅, Flannel ❌
L.13 — ServiceAccount & automountServiceAccountToken
13
# Create a ServiceAccount

kubectl create serviceaccount api-sa -n easypj

# Use SA in a pod/deployment
spec:
  serviceAccountName: api-sa
  # Prevent auto-mounting the token (security best practice)
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: easypj/api:v2

# ⚠️ automountServiceAccountToken: false in pod spec means:
# The SA token is NOT mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
# Use this when your pod doesn't need to talk to the API server.
# Can also be set at the ServiceAccount level:
kubectl patch sa api-sa -n easypj -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken":false}'

# Bind RBAC to SA
kubectl create rolebinding api-sa-binding --role=pod-reader \
  --serviceaccount=easypj:api-sa -n easypj
L.14 — CronJob & Manual Job Trigger
14
# Create a CronJob (runs every day at 2 AM)

kubectl create cronjob db-backup --image=busybox --schedule="0 2 * * *" -n easypj \
  -- /bin/sh -c 'echo "backup completed"'

# Check CronJob status
kubectl get cronjobs -n easypj
kubectl describe cronjob db-backup -n easypj

# ⚠️ Cron syntax: 5 fields = minute hour day month weekday
# * * * * *  = every minute
# */5 * * * * = every 5 minutes
# 0 2 * * *  = 2:00 AM daily
# 0 0 1 * *  = midnight on the 1st of every month

# Manually trigger a CronJob (creates an ad-hoc Job)
kubectl create job manual-backup --from=cronjob/db-backup -n easypj

# Check the manually created job
kubectl get jobs -n easypj
kubectl logs job/manual-backup -n easypj

# Suspend/resume a CronJob
kubectl patch cronjob db-backup -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'
kubectl patch cronjob db-backup -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"suspend":false}}'
L.15 — kubectl diff & Safe Apply
15
# Preview what will change BEFORE applying

kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml

# Validate YAML without applying
kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f deploy.yaml
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml  # Validates server-side (RBAC, admission)

# Apply with force (replaces resources that can't be patched)
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml --force

# Replace a resource entirely
kubectl replace -f deploy.yaml --force

# Force-delete a stuck pod (skip graceful shutdown)
kubectl delete pod stuck-pod -n easypj --force --grace-period=0

# Delete all pods matching a label
kubectl delete pods -l app=easypj-api -n easypj

# Edit a resource in-place (opens $EDITOR)
kubectl edit deploy/easypj-api -n easypj

# Patch using JSON merge
kubectl patch deploy/easypj-api -n easypj -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'

# Patch using strategic merge (automatic for K8s types)
kubectl patch deploy/easypj-api -n easypj --type=strategic -p \
  '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"api","image":"v3"}]}}}}'
L.16 — JSONPath Extraction (Exam Favorite)
16
# Get node internal IPs (CLASSIC exam task)

kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}'

# Get pod names and their node names
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}{end}'

# Get specific container image
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].image}'

# Get all container images in a deployment
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n easypj -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}'

# Custom columns (simpler alternative to jsonpath)
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,IMAGE:.spec.containers[0].image

# Sort and filter
kubectl get pods -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get pods -A --sort-by=.status.startTime
kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Running -A
kubectl get pods --field-selector=spec.nodeName=worker-1 -A

# Events sorted by time
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Failed -A
L.17 — Certificate Signing Requests (CSR)
17
# List all CSRs

kubectl get csr

# Check CSR details
kubectl describe csr csr-abc12

# Approve a CSR (new node joins)
kubectl certificate approve csr-abc12

# Deny a CSR
kubectl certificate deny csr-xyz99

# Bulk approve all pending CSRs
kubectl get csr | grep Pending | awk '{print $1}' | xargs kubectl certificate approve

# ⚠️ Pending CSRs = new nodes can't fully join. After joining via kubeadm join,
# the kubelet creates a CSR. Approve it to issue the node's client certificate.

L.20 — etcdctl Deep Dive: member list, endpoint health
20
# Set API version (REQUIRED for etcdctl v3)

export ETCDCTL_API=3

# Common TLS flags for kubeadm clusters
ETCD_FLAGS="--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key"

# Check health of all endpoints
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS endpoint health

# Check detailed status (DB size, leader, raft index)
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS endpoint status -w table

# List all members
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS member list

# Remove a failed member
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS member remove <member-id>

# Add a new member (run on healthy member, then start etcd on new node)
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS member add <name> --peer-urls=https://<new-node-ip>:2380

# Check alarm list (e.g., NOSPACE)
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS alarm list

# Compact & defrag (if DB >2GB)
CURRENT_REV=$(etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS endpoint status --write-out=json | jq .[0].Status.header.revision)
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS compact $CURRENT_REV
etcdctl $ETCD_FLAGS defrag

# ⚠️ etcd stores ALL cluster state. Backup BEFORE any destructive operation.
🏆 EXAM DAY SPEED TIPS
  • Alias kubectl: alias k=kubectl; source <(kubectl completion bash); complete -F __start_kubectl k — saves 30+ keystrokes per command
  • Use imperative + dry-run: Generate YAML in 2 seconds instead of writing 20 lines from scratch
  • Verify context FIRST: Every task starts with kubectl config use-context <given-context>
  • Use kubectl explain: Forget a field? kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive
  • Copy-paste carefully: The exam terminal supports copy-paste but verify after pasting
  • Flag order matters: kubectl logs pod-name -n ns --tail=10 NOT kubectl logs --tail=10 pod-name
  • Weighted scoring: Troubleshooting (30%) > Cluster Architecture (25%) = 55% of your score. Prioritize these!
  • Leave no task blank: Partial solutions get partial credit. Even creating the namespace and YAML file earns points.
